0.title: Luke: The Gospel of the Saviour of the World
0.overview:
The message. Luke tells the world that its Saviour has come. The angel’s words to the shepherds sum up the book: “I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord” (2:10–11). What happened in a small province of the empire was not a local religious event but the turning point of history, the fulfilment of God’s promises to Israel and the hope of every nation. And this Saviour comes in ways nobody expected: to the poor, to women, to Samaritans and Gentiles, to tax collectors and sinners, the people respectable religion had written off. “The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (19:10). Luke wrote so that his readers “may have certainty” (1:4) that it is all true.

Background: the writer. The Gospel never names its author, but the early church agreed that it was Luke, “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14), Paul’s fellow worker (Philemon 24) and the friend who stayed when others left: “Luke alone is with me” (2 Timothy 4:11). In Colossians 4:10–14 Paul names his only Jewish fellow workers and lists Luke separately, so Luke was probably a Gentile, and if so the only Gentile author in the New Testament. Yet he understood the Jewish roots of everything he described: his Gospel begins and ends in the temple (1:9; 24:53), and its first two chapters read like the Old Testament come to life.

A careful historian. Luke tells us how he worked (1:1–4). Others had already written accounts, the eyewitnesses had handed the story on, and he had “followed all things closely for some time past” to write “an orderly account”. Most scholars think Mark’s Gospel was among his sources, alongside much found only in Luke. He was in Judea during Paul’s two years in custody at Caesarea (Acts 24:27), when many who had known Jesus were still alive, and his account of the birth may well go back to Mary herself (2:19, 51). He anchors events in world history, under Caesar Augustus and Quirinius (2:1–2), and in “the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea” (3:1). Details once called errors have repeatedly proved accurate, though some questions, such as the census under Quirinius, are still debated.

Theophilus and the first readers. Luke writes to “most excellent Theophilus” (1:3), the form of address Paul uses to the governor Festus (Acts 26:25), so he was probably a man of rank, perhaps a patron who paid for copies to be made. He had already been taught the faith, and Luke writes to make him sure of it. Through him the book speaks to the wider Greek-speaking world, people who knew little of Palestine. So Luke explains Jewish customs and places, traces Jesus’ line not just to Abraham but to “Adam, the son of God” (3:38), and shows that the gospel is for every nation.

The world of the story. Augustus had brought peace to the empire and was hailed as saviour and lord; Luke announces another. Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas, who beheaded John the Baptist (9:9), and Judea by a Roman governor. The Pharisees had the people’s respect, tax collectors, who gathered Rome’s revenue and often cheated, were despised as traitors, and Jews and Samaritans avoided each other. Jesus’ parables are full of fields, debts, servants and shared meals, and the scandal is whom he will eat with: “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (15:2).

The first of two volumes. The Gospel tells “all that Jesus began to do and teach” (Acts 1:1), and Acts what he went on to do by his Spirit through the church. The Gospel ends with the ascension and the promise of the Spirit, where Acts begins. In the Gospel everything moves toward Jerusalem; in Acts the good news moves out from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. Many scholars date the Gospel to the 80s. But Acts ends with Paul still awaiting trial in Rome about AD 62, saying nothing of his death or the fall of Jerusalem, and the Gospel came first, so this commentary takes it as probably written in the late 50s or early 60s.

How the book makes its case. After the preface (1:1–4), the birth narratives (1:5–2:52) are full of angels, songs and old saints waiting for the consolation of Israel. John prepares the way, and Jesus is baptised, traced to Adam and tested in the wilderness (3:1–4:13). At Nazareth he reads Isaiah, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor” (4:18), and says, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (4:21); the rest of the Gospel shows what that means. In Galilee (4:14–9:50) he calls disciples, heals, forgives, preaches the Sermon on the Plain and receives Peter’s confession. Then comes the turning point: “he set his face to go to Jerusalem” (9:51). The long journey (9:51–19:27) holds much that only Luke records: the good Samaritan, Martha and Mary, the lost sheep, coin and son, the rich man and Lazarus, the Pharisee and the tax collector, Zacchaeus. In Jerusalem (19:28–21:38) he enters as king, cleanses the temple, silences his questioners and foretells the city’s fall. Chapters 22–23 tell of the Last Supper, Gethsemane, the trials and the cross, and chapter 24 of the empty tomb, the road to Emmaus and the ascension.

Threads to follow. Jesus prays at every turning point, from his baptism (3:21) and the choosing of the Twelve (6:12) to Gethsemane and the cross. The Holy Spirit is present from the first chapter to the last (1:15; 4:18; 24:49). “Today” sounds through the book (2:11; 4:21; 19:9; 23:43): salvation is not only promised but arriving. And joy runs from the angels’ song to the joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (15:7) and the disciples returning to Jerusalem “with great joy” (24:52).

Where it leads: to Christ. Jesus is the son of David who receives “the throne of his father David” (1:32), the anointed one of Isaiah, and the Son of Man who must suffer. On the road to Emmaus the risen Lord shows that this was the burden of the whole Old Testament: “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (24:27). The cross was no accident: “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (24:26). A dying thief is promised paradise that very day (23:43), and a tax collector who can only plead for mercy goes home “justified” (18:14): salvation is by grace, received by faith, not earned. And the ending looks outward: “repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations” (24:47).

For us. Luke gives a believer certainty: the faith rests on events that happened and were carefully checked. No one is too far gone for Jesus to seek, and no one too respectable to need him, so his church must welcome those he welcomed. It shows a Saviour who prayed, and calls us to pray; promises the Spirit to those who ask (11:13); and warns hard about money while opening our hands to the poor. And it ends where every believer may live, worshipping the risen Lord with great joy.

1.title: The Announcement of the King
1.overview:
Where we are. Luke 1 opens the Gospel. After a historian’s preface (vv. 1–4), the story steps back into the world of the Old Testament, where the long story of promise is reaching its fulfilment before Jesus has said a word in public.

The message. God has remembered his promises and is keeping them, beyond anything his people dared to ask. After centuries without a prophet he speaks again, and what he announces is the coming of the Lord himself: first a forerunner in the spirit of Elijah, then the Son of the Most High, conceived by the Holy Spirit in a virgin, heir of David’s throne for ever, the Saviour who brings forgiveness of sins.

Why it was said. Theophilus had been taught the faith and needed to be sure of it (v. 4). Luke shows him a faith that is no new superstition but history, set in a named reign and a known country, fulfilling promises made to Abraham and David long before Rome (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Luke builds in pairs. Two announcements: Gabriel comes to an old priest in the temple, who asks for proof and is silenced (vv. 5–25), and to a girl in Nazareth, who believes (vv. 26–38). Two mothers meet, and the unborn John leaps for joy at his Lord (vv. 39–45). Two songs answer: Mary’s praises the God who lifts the humble and keeps his word to Abraham (vv. 46–56), and after John’s birth and naming (vv. 57–66) Zechariah’s praises the God who has visited his people to forgive their sins (vv. 67–80). Even the names carry the theme: Zechariah, “the LORD remembers”; Elizabeth, “my God is an oath”; John, “the LORD has been gracious”; Jesus, “the LORD saves”.

Where it leads. Every line points past John to the child Mary carries. He is the Lord before whom the greatest of the prophets goes, God come to dwell with his people, the King whose kingdom has no end, the sunrise from on high. And he comes by the low door, through a girl nobody had heard of. The God who swore an oath to Abraham will keep it at the cost of his own Son.

For us. This chapter asks what we do with God’s word when it seems impossible: answer with Zechariah’s “how shall I know?” or with Mary’s “let it be”. It assures the waiting, the childless and the overlooked that God sees, remembers and keeps his promises in his own time. And it teaches us to end where Mary and Zechariah ended, praising the God who has come to save.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Luke tells us how he wrote, so that we may be sure of what we believe. He stands in a line of careful accounts that rest on people who saw the events and spent their lives serving the word (vv. 1–2). He has traced everything from the source and set it in an order that can be followed (v. 3). And he writes to one man by name, most excellent Theophilus, already taught the faith, so that he may have certainty (asphaleia), the firm ground of knowing that what he believes is true (v. 4). A book researched like this is still God’s word (see the note on vv. 1–2).
verseByVerse.theology:
Luke does not begin with timeless spiritual principles. He begins with what happened. The things accomplished among us are events: the birth, the miracles, the death and the resurrection took place in a named reign, in a known country, in front of people who could be questioned about them.

And Luke’s goal is pastoral: to confirm the faith of someone already taught (see the note on v. 4). That is what preaching rooted in history does in every generation: it settles believers in a faith that rests on what God has done.
verseByVerse.examples:
The prologue shows how to handle the gospel: go back to the sources, investigate carefully, set out the findings in order, and do it for the hearer’s sake. A Christian wrestling with doubt is rarely helped by being told just to trust. He is helped by being shown why trust is reasonable, which is what the rest of this Gospel does.

The certainty Luke offers is the settled confidence of someone who has looked at the evidence and found it solid (see “Afraid to look” in the note on v. 4).

verseByVerse.quote: Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been accomplished among us, just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word have delivered them to us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel Luke tells rests on events that really happened, handed on by the people who saw them. His one long, balanced opening sentence (vv. 1–4), in polished literary Greek like the prefaces of the Greek historians, announces researched, reliable history.

He opens with paperwork. Luke does not open with a vision or a genealogy. He is about to tell a story with an angel in it, and he begins by saying where he got it.

Many have undertaken. Others had already written accounts of Jesus, narratives that carry a reader through the events: most likely Mark, probably the earliest Gospel, and other written and oral accounts from the eyewitnesses. Luke does not attack them. A man forging a religion would be tempted to suppress the rival accounts; a man reporting an event can welcome them, because more witnesses make a case stronger, not weaker. He was not an eyewitness himself, but he went to those who were (v. 2).

Accomplished among us. Accomplished means fulfilled, brought to completion (peplērophorēmenōn). Luke is not describing incidents that merely happened but promises God had made and has now kept. This is a key theme of the whole book, and the risen Christ will say it in the last chapter: everything written about him in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled (24:44).

Eyewitnesses. The apostles and others who had been with Jesus from the start (Acts 1:21–22). The word is autoptai, those who saw it with their own eyes. The Gospel rests on eyewitness testimony, not legend.

Ministers of the word. Servants, attendants (hypēretai), the word Luke uses of the synagogue attendant who took the scroll from Jesus (4:20). They did not invent the message; they served it, and spent their lives handing it on.

Delivered. Handed down (paredosan), the technical word for passing on a tradition carefully, the word Paul uses when he says he delivered as of first importance what he also received (1 Corinthians 15:3). Luke places himself in the second generation. The chain between Jesus and your Bible is short and can be named: the men and women who saw him, then a careful writer who questioned them, then the book in your hands.

Who was Luke? The early church named Luke, the beloved physician and Paul’s companion (Colossians 4:14), as the author of this Gospel and of Acts, its second volume (Acts 1:1), where he slips into “we” when he was present (Acts 16:10–17; 20:5–28:16). On the author, see the introduction.

The word they served had a face. Luke names one group with two roles, eyewitnesses and servants of the word, because what they handed on was what they had seen. Luke does not call Jesus the Word, as John does, but his witnesses could have said what John says: that “which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life” (1 John 1:1). The gospel is not an idea about God illustrated by a life. It is a life: a birth, a ministry, a death and an empty tomb.

In everyday life. When someone at work says the Gospels are legends written long afterwards, you do not need to panic or to bluff. You can say, honestly, that the author tells us he checked his material against the people who were there, and invite them to read him and judge.

If Luke did research, how is this God’s word? It is both Luke’s careful work and God’s word, and the one does not crowd out the other. The same Spirit who fills Elizabeth and Zechariah later in this chapter was at work in the physician who went looking for people who had been there, guiding the questions he asked, the witnesses he found, the material he kept and the order he set it in (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21). God did not bypass Luke’s mind; he used it. Here the research is not a rival to inspiration but the way God inspired this book. So you can read Luke with both a historian’s confidence and a worshipper’s reverence.
verseByVerse.note: Luke did not claim to be an eyewitness himself; he gathered the testimony of those who were.

verseByVerse.quote: it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke has traced the story to its source and set it in an order that can be followed, for one man by name.

Followed all things closely. To follow alongside, to trace a matter back along its course: one word in Greek (parēkolouthēkoti). And “for some time past” is stronger than it sounds: anōthen, from the top, from the source. During Paul’s two years in custody at Caesarea (Acts 24:27) he could have met Mary, James the brother of Jesus (Acts 21:18), and others. The birth narratives may come from Mary herself, who treasured these things and pondered them in her heart (2:19, 51). And he goes back to the very start: not, as Mark does, to a grown man at the Jordan, but to an old couple in the hill country and a girl in Nazareth.

An orderly account. In sequence (kathexēs), each thing in its proper place. Luke is not promising a diary timed to the day but an account with a shape that can be followed, as when he sets the rejection at Nazareth at the head of the ministry because it is the doorway into everything after it (4:16–30).

Most excellent Theophilus. The name means “friend of God” or “loved by God”. “Most excellent” (kratiste) was a title for Roman officials and people of rank; Luke uses it of the governors Felix and Festus in his second volume (Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25). Theophilus was probably a real person of high standing, perhaps Luke’s patron, who paid for the book to be copied and circulated, and he was already instructed in the faith (v. 4). Luke addressed the longest book in the New Testament to one man who needed it, by name.

An order that leads to a cross. Luke’s order has a shape, and the shape is Christ’s. The Gospel opens in the temple with a priest who cannot bless the waiting people (1:22), and it closes in the temple with disciples praising God after Jesus has lifted his hands and blessed them (24:50–53). Its long middle is one journey: “when the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem” (9:51). An orderly account of this life cannot help but lead where he himself was going, to a city, a cross and an empty tomb.

In everyday life. Read a Gospel straight through in a sitting, as Theophilus would have heard it. And remember that God’s largest works often come with one person’s name at the top: the letter, the book, the conversation you give to one particular person may be the thing God uses.

Does it matter that the Gospels differ in order? No. Ancient writers, like good modern biographers, often arranged material by theme as well as by date, and no one thought that dishonest. Where the Gospels differ in order or detail, they are like four honest witnesses describing one event: their differences show they did not copy each other mechanically, and their agreement on everything that matters is all the stronger for it. When you meet a difference, ask what each writer is emphasising.

But was Luke not biased, writing as a believer? Every historian writes from somewhere, and caring about a subject does not make a writer unreliable. The question is whether he tells you his sources and lets you check him. Luke does: he names rulers, places and dates that could be tested (3:1–2), and archaeology has repeatedly confirmed the titles and details of his second volume. And see what he does not hide: the doubt of a priest (v. 20), the slowness of the disciples, the denial of Peter (22:54–62). A man inventing heroes would have tidied them away. Not every question about his dates is settled (the census of 2:2 is the best known), but a writer who gives you the means to check him is not hiding from you.
verseByVerse.note: Theophilus means “friend of God.” “Most excellent” was a title used for Roman officials, which suggests a man of rank.

verseByVerse.quote: that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke wrote so that a believer may know that what he has been taught is true, and stand on it.

That you may have certainty. Certainty is firmness, security (asphaleia), the word Luke uses of a prison locked securely (Acts 5:23). It is built from a (not) and sphallō (to trip, to make to stumble): literally, un-trippability. It comes last in the Greek sentence, for emphasis. Luke wrote not so that Theophilus would feel warmer about Jesus, but so that when he put his weight down, the floor would hold. God gave us not a mood but a record, written by a man who checked his sources, about a Saviour who really lived, really died and really rose.

The things you have been taught. Taught means instructed by word of mouth, and the word (katēchēthēs) gives us catechism. Theophilus had been instructed in the faith, and Luke thinks he needs a book anyway. Evidence is not only for enquirers: a whole Gospel was written to make a Christian sure.

Know for certain who he is. Luke uses the matching adverb, asphalōs, at the climax of the first Christian sermon: “let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 2:36). That is the certainty Luke’s two volumes exist to give, and it is first the risen Lord’s own gift. When the disciples met him, frightened and doubting, he did not tell them to believe harder. He said: “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see” (24:39). Christ himself handed over the evidence, and Luke is only carrying it on. Our certainty rests on him, and he does not trip.

Not advice but news. Many assume that every religion is a technique for finding inner peace, true for you if it works for you, and beyond the reach of evidence. Luke flatly disagrees. Timothy Keller often pointed out that the gospel is not first advice about what you must do but news about what has been done, and news is either true or false. That is why Luke checks his sources. And this is the difference that frees the heart. Advice, however wise, leaves the weight on you: try harder, go deeper, find your centre. News puts the weight somewhere else: a Saviour has been born, has died and has risen. If it happened, you are not asked to save yourself, only to believe the report and come home.

In everyday life. Do not be afraid to look: certainty in this book is not a confident personality but the settled mind of a man who went and looked (John 20:31; 1 Peter 3:15). Take one thing you believe about Christ and ask how you know it. If the honest answer is that you have always been told so, that is where Theophilus was, and God thought it worth a whole Gospel to move him past it. Spend this week looking into one such question, perhaps how you know Jesus rose.

Is certainty the same as assurance of salvation? Related, but not the same. Luke’s certainty is first about the facts: that these things really happened and mean what the apostles said they mean. Assurance of salvation is a believer’s confidence that he himself is in Christ. The first feeds the second; the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession both say that assurance rests on the truth of God’s promises, on the inward evidence of grace, and on the witness of the Spirit (Westminster 18.2; 1689 18.2). The promises come first, and they are only as solid as the history behind them. So when your assurance wavers, do not begin by examining your feelings. Begin where Luke begins: with what God has done in Christ.

What if I still have doubts after reading? Doubt is not the same as unbelief, and a doubting believer is still a believer. Bring the doubt into the open: name it, ask a pastor or a mature friend, read what thoughtful Christians have written on the question. Keep reading the Gospels themselves, because Christ is his own best evidence, and keep using the means of grace, the word, prayer and the Lord’s Supper, while the question is being answered. A doubt honestly faced often leaves faith firmer than before.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–25 — Birth of John the Baptist Foretold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God breaks four centuries of silence to keep his promise, and he begins in the most ordinary place: an old priest at his duty and a childless wife at home. Zechariah and Elizabeth are faithful, old and barren, in the line of Sarah and Hannah (vv. 5–7). In the middle of a routine service, chosen by lot to burn the incense while the people pray outside, Zechariah meets Gabriel, last seen in Daniel, who promises a son filled with the Spirit from the womb, going before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah (vv. 8–17; Malachi 4:5–6). Zechariah asks for proof and is given silence until the promise comes true (vv. 18–23; on why, see vv. 18–20). Elizabeth conceives, and her first recorded words are about God: he has looked on her and taken away her reproach (vv. 24–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
Again and again in Scripture a barren woman is given a child, and each time it shows the same thing: we cannot, and God can (on the line that runs from Sarah’s son to the virgin’s, see the note on v. 7).

Gabriel’s description of John’s work picks up the last words of the Old Testament prophets, the promise of Elijah (Malachi 4:5–6). And the long silence ends not with a king or an army but with an old priest’s vision at the incense altar.
verseByVerse.examples:
Zechariah’s theology was correct, and his trust in the moment was smaller than his knowledge. He knew the God who opens barren wombs, and when the answer stood in front of him he asked for evidence. That gap between what we confess and what we trust is one of the most honest things the Bible shows about faith (on how God met it, see vv. 18–20).

Elizabeth’s five months of seclusion show another wisdom (see the note on vv. 24–25).

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. And he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s new work begins with an old, faithful couple, in the days of a cruel king.

The style changes. The polished Greek of the prologue stops, and the next sentence could have come out of the book of Judges. From here to the end of chapter 2 Luke writes a Greek full of Hebrew idiom, because the story of Jesus continues the story of Israel. Romans dismissed new superstitions but respected what was ancient, and Luke shows Theophilus a faith far older than Rome. Our English Old Testament ends with Malachi’s promise of Elijah coming (Malachi 4:5–6); this Gospel begins with the birth of the one who comes in Elijah’s spirit (v. 17).

In the days of Herod. Herod the Great ruled the Jewish land as Rome’s client king from 37 to 4 BC: an Idumean (Edomite), not a son of David, a builder of vast ambition (the temple included), and a paranoid tyrant who murdered his wife and three of his sons. Luke names that throne in his first narrative sentence so that nobody mistakes what kind of night it was when the light came. Since Herod died in 4 BC, Jesus was born probably around 6–5 BC (our calendar, calculated in the sixth century, is a few years out).

Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. Zechariah means “the LORD remembers”, which is what this chapter is about (vv. 54, 72). There were several thousand priests in Jesus’ day, organised since David’s time into twenty-four divisions; Abijah’s was the eighth (1 Chronicles 24:1–19). Each served in the temple for a week twice a year, and all at the great feasts.

The daughters of Aaron. Elizabeth was also of priestly descent, priestly on both sides, which was considered a special blessing. Her name (Elisheba) means “my God is an oath”, or “my God is fullness”; Aaron’s wife had the same name (Exodus 6:23). Together the two names are the chapter in miniature: “the LORD remembers”, and “my God has sworn an oath”, as Zechariah will sing, “the oath that he swore to our father Abraham” (v. 73).

Righteous before God, walking blamelessly. Not just in the eyes of men. Luke knew the same Scriptures that say none is righteous, no, not one (Psalm 14:3; Romans 3:10–12), and he is not contradicting them. This is how the Old Testament speaks of people who walk faithfully with God, as it is said of Noah (Genesis 6:9) and of Job (Job 1:1). It does not mean sinless; Zechariah will doubt (v. 20). It means that when they sinned they brought the sacrifice God had appointed, and no neighbour could point to an open wrong in their lives. While Herod built his palaces in blood, God was watching an old couple in the hill country and wrote their names in his book as righteous. No tyrant’s throne can hide his faithful ones from his eyes.

Two kings in one chapter. Luke’s first sentence names a king, and before the chapter is out an angel names another. Herod held the throne of Judea by Rome’s favour, without a drop of David’s blood. To Mary, Gabriel will say that the Lord God will give her son the throne of his father David, and of his kingdom there will be no end (vv. 32–33). Herod built a temple to make his name great; the true King will be carried into it as a baby (2:22–38). Herod’s kingdom was divided among his sons as soon as he died. The kingdom of David’s son has no end.

Were they saved by their blamelessness? No. Their righteousness before God was the righteousness of faith, the same by which Abraham believed the LORD and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6). They looked forward to the promised redemption, offered the sacrifices that pointed to it, and lived out their trust in obedience. Their blameless walk was the fruit of grace, not the price of it. So the word is a comfort, not a threat: God counts you righteous in Christ, and then works in you a life that can, by his grace, be honestly called blameless.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome until 4 BC. The priests were organised in twenty-four divisions, each serving in the temple for a week at a time; Abijah’s was the eighth.

verseByVerse.quote: But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one thing missing from this faithful home is a child, and the lack sets the stage for a gift only God can give.

Because Elizabeth was barren. The Bible’s great births often begin with barrenness: Sarah (Genesis 18), Rebekah, Rachel, Samson’s mother (Judges 13) and Hannah (1 Samuel 1). Each time God opened the womb for a child with a key part in his purposes, so that nobody could mistake where he came from. And “both were advanced in years”, like Abraham and Sarah (Genesis 18:11): humanly, it was impossible.

Stage it properly. Children were seen as God’s blessing (Psalm 127:3–5). There is a room in that house that was going to be for a child. There were the early years of quiet confidence, then the years of remedies and of very specific prayers, then the year, and every couple who has walked this road can name it, when they stopped saying “when” and started saying “if”, and then stopped saying anything at all. Elizabeth has held other people’s babies for decades and handed them back. And in first-century Judea childlessness was a public verdict as well as a private grief: a barren woman walked through the market under a rumour that God had looked at her and turned away. Elizabeth’s own word for it, when it is lifted, is oneidos: disgrace, the thing people say about you (v. 25).

The circumstance is not the verdict. The silence of God is not the absence of God. Luke has just called these two righteous before God, so the barrenness was no punishment; the village had got the sentence exactly backwards. And the reason for their waiting was not in them at all: the forerunner of the Messiah could not be born until the Messiah was six months away. For all those years the reason lay in the future, where they could not see it.

From a barren womb to a virgin’s. The line of closed wombs is not a string of separate miracles but a road, and this verse stands near its end. Six months later the same angel will go to a girl in Nazareth with a greater impossibility, and he will point her to this very house (v. 36). Every barren womb God opened prepared the way for the day when a child would come who had no human father at all, because he was not merely a gift to the line of Adam but God’s own Son entering it. Sarah’s son carried the promise. Mary’s Son is the promise. Elizabeth stands at the hinge between them, the last of the barren mothers and the sign given to the virgin.

So what may a childless couple take from this? Not a pattern with your name in it: Elizabeth conceived, and so did Hannah and Sarah, but thousands of women just as righteous, who prayed just as long, did not. God has not promised that you will conceive, and anyone who makes the promise for him is unkind. Take this instead: your childlessness is not God’s verdict on you, and it is not a punishment. He sees the grief, the empty room, the conversations that change direction when you come in. Your life is not second-class in his kingdom; some of the most fruitful servants in Scripture had no children, and our Lord himself had none. You may pray honestly for a child, use wise medical help, consider adoption, and weep. And you may know that the God who held Elizabeth’s sorrow for all those years is holding yours, with purposes that may be stored far ahead of you.

And for those around them? Do not ask young couples when they are going to have children. Do not offer formulas or stories of friends who conceived after they relaxed. Remember the childless on Mother’s Day and Father’s Day, and at the dedication of babies. And never, by look or word, become the village that passed a sentence on Elizabeth.
verseByVerse.note: Barrenness was a deep sorrow and often a social shame. Scripture’s great births often begin with a barren woman.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while he was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty, according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God met Zechariah in the middle of his appointed duty, on a day God himself had chosen. The once-in-a-lifetime honour fell to an old priest at the end of a faithful, unremarkable career.

He was chosen by lot. There were thousands of priests and exactly one incense altar, and the duties of each day were assigned by lot. The highest honour was to burn incense alone at the golden altar in the Holy Place. Later Jewish tradition records that a man once chosen was taken out of the draw: once in a lifetime, and many never did. This was Zechariah’s once. The lot is not chance: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). God chose this day, this man.

To burn incense. The temple here is the sanctuary building itself (naos), which only priests could enter. Incense was offered every morning and evening on the golden altar (Exodus 30:7–8), its smoke rising before the curtain that hid the Most Holy Place. It was a picture of prayer rising to God: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you” (Psalm 141:2; Revelation 5:8; 8:3–4).

At the hour of incense. Probably the evening sacrifice, around 3 p.m.: a crowd in a courtyard praying, and one old man alone in the smoke, on the settled understanding that God does not answer out loud any more. He went to work that morning knowing it was the biggest day of his career, with no idea it was the biggest day in four centuries.

The curtain he stood before. Zechariah stood alone at the golden altar with one curtain between him and the Most Holy Place, a curtain he would never pass and only the high priest could, once a year, with blood (Hebrews 9:7). When Jesus hung on the cross, there was darkness from the sixth hour to the ninth, and the curtain of the temple was torn in two (23:44–45); the ninth hour was the afternoon hour of prayer (Acts 3:1). Generations of priests had burned incense before that veil, waiting without knowing it for the death that would tear it. Zechariah stood once in a lifetime before the curtain; our great High Priest has passed through it for ever, and lives always to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25; 10:19–22). There is no draw to win and no once in a lifetime. The way into the holy place is open.

In everyday life. God chose to interrupt not a revival meeting but an appointed duty, taken in its turn by a man whose name had come out of a container. Routine and meeting God are not opposites. Go to the shift, the school run, the weekly meeting, the Sunday service, expecting nothing dramatic and everything from God. And pray with God’s people: the crowd in the courtyard was part of the answer.

Does God still direct things through chance? Yes, in the sense that nothing is chance to him. The Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession say that God orders all things, including what seem to us accidents, by his providence (Westminster 5.2; 1689 5.2). That does not mean deciding by lots or by opening the Bible at random; after Pentecost the apostles never again cast lots, because the Spirit and the Scriptures guide the church. It does mean that the shuffle of your week, the job allocation, the seat on the train, the person next to you at the hospital, is not random. You may walk into it expecting God to be there.
verseByVerse.note: With so many priests, the honour of offering incense in the holy place came to few, perhaps once in a lifetime. It was offered morning and evening while the people prayed outside.

parallels.desc: let my prayer be counted as incense

verseByVerse.quote: And there appeared to him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense. And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After centuries without a prophet, God sends his messenger, and a godly man is terrified in the presence of holiness.

An angel of the Lord. The silence is broken. Jews of the time spoke of a long age, stretching back to Malachi, in which prophets had ceased to appear among them (1 Maccabees 9:27). In the middle of a fixed liturgy, in a room he had never stood in before, Zechariah raised his eyes and somebody was there.

On the right side of the altar. The right side was the side of favour, and the detail says the visitor was not passing through. Zechariah had been chosen by lot that morning; the messenger was waiting at that altar by appointment.

Fear fell upon him. Fear before divine visitation is a recurring note in Luke (1:29–30, 65; 2:9; 5:8–10; 8:37), and again and again an angel has to begin by saying “do not be afraid”. Daniel fell on his face in terror when Gabriel, the very angel who now stands before Zechariah, came near him (Daniel 8:17). In the presence of someone who has never sinned, a sinner sees his own sin with nothing to hide behind. Such fear is not a failure of faith but seeing the truth about yourself all at once.

The thing the equipment was for. Zechariah has spent his life inside the machinery of holiness: the divisions, the lots, the incense, the curtain, all designed to manage the distance between a holy God and a people who could not survive him without a go-between and a sacrifice. Now a messenger from God’s presence stands in the room to say that what the machinery was for is on its way. The forerunner is coming, and behind him the Lord himself, in a body of flesh (vv. 17, 35). The fear that fell on Zechariah is answered in Luke by Christ. When Peter fell at his knees and said, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord”, Jesus said to him: “Do not be afraid” (5:8–10). The holy one came near so that sinners could stand in his presence and live.

Do angels still appear today? Scripture does not slam the door: they are sent out to serve those who will inherit salvation, and “some have entertained angels unawares” (Hebrews 1:14; 13:2). But in every appearance in the Bible nobody summons one and nobody has a method. They arrive on God’s errand, say what they were sent to say, and go: they come not to be looked at but to carry a message. Since the message of the gospel is now complete and written down, we should not expect angels to bring new revelation, and we should test anyone who claims one has (Galatians 1:8). Angels serve us still, mostly unseen. From the moment Gabriel opens his mouth, he is no longer the interesting thing in the room.
verseByVerse.note: The altar of incense stood just before the curtain of the Most Holy Place.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to him, 'Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has heard, and his answer is a son whose very name means “the LORD has been gracious”.

Do not be afraid. The first words of God’s messengers to frightened people throughout Luke (1:30; 2:10; 5:10; 8:50; 12:7, 32). God does not appear in order to destroy.

Your prayer has been heard. Which prayer? The text never says, and whatever the old man had once prayed about a son, he had very likely stopped praying it years ago. Two answers are both true. The first is that the prayers of twenty and thirty and forty years ago were heard when they were prayed, and the answer was timed to fit another birth (see v. 7). The second is probably nearer the mark. The priest at the incense altar prayed for Israel: for the redemption of Jerusalem, for the coming of the Lord to his temple, for the end of the silence. And the answer he is handed is a son, because the son is how the nation gets its answer. Both readings say the same thing about God: he does not lose requests, and when he answers, he often answers on a scale that makes the request look like a rough draft.

Call his name John. God names him, not the father. John (Yôḥānān) means “the LORD has been gracious”, or “the LORD has shown favour”. The name is the message.

The answer behind the answer. John is not the end of the answer but its first word. The prayer at the incense altar was for the Lord to come to his people, and Gabriel’s reply is a herald whose whole life will say: “he is coming, and he is right behind me.” Before the year is out the old priest will sing that God has visited and redeemed his people and raised up a horn of salvation in the house of David (vv. 68–69). He asked for the redemption of Israel. God answered with his own Son.

Heard is not the same as granted. Paul asked three times and was told no, and the no was itself the answer (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). What this verse forbids is the conclusion the silence keeps pressing: that the request fell into a room with nobody in it. God has never once not been listening. He has often not yet been speaking.

A reason for the delay. Born when Elizabeth was thirty, the child would have comforted his parents; born in her old age, he was a sign to a nation. That explains nobody else’s waiting, but it shows that God can have a good reason for a long delay, even when we are never told it.

Should I keep praying for something I have prayed about for years? Yes, unless God has plainly closed the door, as he did for Paul, or the thing itself has become impossible or wrong. Jesus told a parable precisely so that his people would always pray and not lose heart (18:1). Keep praying, but let the prayer grow to hold the grief, the questions and your submission to his will, as Jesus did in Gethsemane. Many long prayers end not with the thing asked for but with a heart reshaped to want God more than the thing. Either way, the prayer was heard.
verseByVerse.note: John means “the LORD has been gracious.”

parallels.desc: Sarah will bear you a son

verseByVerse.quote: And you will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great before the Lord. And he must not drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John’s birth will bring joy to many, because God has set him apart from the womb for a great work, filled not with wine but with the Spirit.

Joy and gladness. Joy is a theme of Luke’s Gospel from beginning (2:10) to end, when the disciples return to Jerusalem “with great joy” (24:52). Gladness here is exultation, a joy that cannot keep still, and “many will rejoice” looks well past the neighbours of v. 58: this birth is a public event.

Great before the Lord. Not great in the world’s eyes: John will be beheaded in Herod’s prison (9:9; Mark 6:21–28). Yet Jesus said no one born of women is greater than John (7:28). Of Jesus, the angel will say simply “he will be great” (v. 32), with no qualification. John is great before the Lord; Jesus is the Lord before whom John is great.

No wine or strong drink. Like the rule for a Nazirite, a person set apart to God by a vow (Numbers 6:1–4), though Gabriel says nothing of the uncut hair. Samson and Samuel were Nazirites from birth (Judges 13:4–5; 1 Samuel 1:11). But a Nazirite took the vow himself, or a parent dedicated a child, as Hannah did; here God imposes it before the boy exists. The consecration is not the family’s offering to God but God’s claim staked on a child not yet conceived.

Filled with the Holy Spirit. Instead of being filled with wine, he will be filled with the Spirit (compare Ephesians 5:18), from before birth, as Jeremiah was known and consecrated before he was formed (Jeremiah 1:5), and as the Servant was called from the womb (Isaiah 49:1). Luke means that God equipped John for his task from the start; he is not teaching that infants are converted in the womb. The filling becomes visible when John leaps in the womb as Mary arrives with the unborn Jesus (v. 41). The boldness the crowds would later meet at the Jordan was not a strong temperament but God’s gift (compare v. 80).

In everyday life. Pray for the unborn children you know. And measure greatness the way Gabriel did: a faithful, unseen life is measured in heaven, not on social media.

Does this make total abstinence the higher path? No, and Luke himself blocks that road. Jesus says that John came eating no bread and drinking no wine and they said he had a demon, and the Son of Man came eating and drinking and they called him a glutton and a drunkard (7:33–34). The same Bible gives Christ at a wedding in Cana where the wine ran out (John 2:1–11). John’s abstinence is a uniform, not a law, marking the wilderness prophet who stands outside the system and calls it to repent. A believer who abstains is free to, and many do for good reasons: their own weakness, a family history, a brother who struggles. A believer who drinks in moderation is not a lesser Christian, though drunkenness is always sin. And anyone using this verse to grade another man’s holiness should remember that John’s own Master drank wine.

What does this say about the unborn? The child in the womb is a person, known and called by God. John was filled with the Spirit before he was born, and in v. 41 he leaps in Elizabeth’s womb at the coming of the Lord. Scripture speaks of the unborn as persons whom God knows and forms (Psalm 139:13–16; Jeremiah 1:5). These verses are not a full argument on their own, but they fit the whole biblical witness that life in the womb is human life, made in God’s image, to be protected. And see the direction of grace: before John could believe, refuse or want anything at all, God had already begun.

And for parents who have lost a child before birth? God knew that child, formed that child and loved that child, and the child’s life was real and is not lost to him. Grieve it as the death of a person, because it was. Scripture gives good hope for those who die in infancy: David said of his dead baby, “I shall go to him” (2 Samuel 12:23), and the Reformed confessions, the 1689 London Baptist Confession and the Westminster Confession, teach that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (1689 10.3; Westminster 10.3). Believing parents may rest that child in the hands of a merciful God. The word “elect” is not there to cast a shadow over your child: many Reformed pastors have held that all who die in infancy are among the elect, and the God to whom your child has gone is kinder than our fears.
verseByVerse.note: No wine or strong drink was the rule for a Nazirite, someone set apart to God.

parallels.desc: before you were born I consecrated you

verseByVerse.quote: And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and he will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
John’s life work will be to turn Israel back to God and make a people ready for the Lord himself, who is coming after him.

He will go before him. Grammatically, before “the Lord their God” of the previous line: John goes before the Lord God himself, and the one who comes after John is Jesus. Malachi had promised a messenger to prepare the way, and then: “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple” (Malachi 3:1). Isaiah’s voice in the wilderness prepares the way of the LORD, a highway for our God (Isaiah 40:3), and Luke will apply it to John and Jesus (3:4–6). When John finally stood aside, it was not for a greater prophet. It was for God come in the flesh.

In the spirit and power of Elijah. Elijah confronted a wicked king and queen (1 Kings 18–21); John will confront Herod and Herodias (3:19–20).

The hearts of the fathers. Gabriel is quoting the closing words of Malachi, the last page of our English Old Testament (Malachi 4:5–6): “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes. And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers.” God announces the greatest turning point in the history of the world, and among the first effects named is that fathers will turn towards their children. Where a nation goes cold towards God, the cold shows first at the kitchen table, and where God returns, so does the thaw. Revival that leaves a family as it was is not what Malachi promised.

The disobedient to the wisdom of the just. John will turn many (3:3), not to a programme, a party or a temple, but to God himself, and rebels to the understanding and way of life of the righteous. Repentance is not only feeling sorry; it is a change of mind that becomes a change of path.

A people prepared. Everything about John exists to get a people ready for somebody else. He is the road, not the city.

The deepest turning of a father’s heart. The God who closed the prophets with a promise reopened history by keeping it, word for word. And the deepest turning of a father’s heart was never ours but God’s own. Jesus would tell of a father who saw his son a long way off, felt compassion, and ran (15:20). That is the Father the forerunner went before: a God whose heart is turned toward rebellious children, who sent his Son to bring them home.

In everyday life. The Father has turned his heart toward you in Christ. If there is a relationship your repentance needs to mend, do one concrete thing this week: a phone call, a letter, an apology without excuses, a meal.

Was John Elijah or not? Gabriel’s exact wording solves a puzzle. When the priests asked John point-blank, “Are you Elijah?”, he answered, “I am not” (John 1:21). Yet Jesus said of him, “he is Elijah who is to come” (Matthew 11:14). They are answering two different questions. John denies what his questioners meant: that he was Elijah himself, returned in person from heaven. Jesus affirms what Malachi meant: that the promised forerunner had come at last, in the spirit and power of Elijah, exactly as Gabriel says here. The prophecy was never that a man would come back but that a ministry would: the same blunt voice and rough clothing, the same summons to turn round before the LORD arrives. And it gives no support to reincarnation, which Scripture rules out (Hebrews 9:27).

What if the relationship cannot be mended? Sometimes the other person refuses, or is dead, or is dangerous. Repentance asks you to do what lies with you (Romans 12:18): drop the grudge before God, confess your own part, make the approach if it is safe and wise, and keep the door open. It does not ask you to put yourself or your children back under abuse, and reconciliation with an abuser needs genuine repentance on his side, proven over time, with wise help. Where the other person will not come, you can still forgive in your heart and leave the matter with God. The turning of hearts begins with yours.

parallels.desc: Elijah will turn the hearts of fathers to their children
he is Elijah who is to come

verseByVerse.quote: And Zechariah said to the angel, 'How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zechariah answers God’s promise by weighing it against his age, and asks for proof.

How shall I know this? Why is Zechariah struck dumb for asking, when Mary asks what looks like the same question sixteen verses later and is answered kindly? Gideon laid out a fleece twice (Judges 6:36–40); Abraham asked how he could know, in almost these words, and was given a covenant ceremony instead of a rebuke (Genesis 15:8). But Zechariah had an angel of God standing in front of him, in the temple, with the incense still rising, telling him what God would do, and still asked for proof.

For I am an old man. He looks at the circumstances, not at God. He knows about Abraham and Sarah, but cannot believe it for himself; he is not asking Gabriel to explain but explaining to Gabriel. Mary’s question (v. 34) is “how”, not “whether”, and Gabriel’s diagnosis says precisely this: “because you did not believe my words.”

The sign God was already giving. Zechariah wanted a sign to prove the promise, and he could not see that the promise was the beginning of the sign. In Luke, God’s answer to “how shall I know” keeps turning out to be his Son. The shepherds will be told: “this will be a sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger” (2:12). And when a later crowd demands proof, Jesus will refuse them every sign but one, the sign of Jonah (11:29–30), his own rising from the dead. Zechariah asked for something he could hold. Within the year God would put the answer in human arms.

In everyday life. Listen for your own little “for”: “I cannot be forgiven for that, for I have done it too often”; “God cannot use me, for I am too old.” Each one weighs his word against your record. Turn the sentence round, and put his faithfulness after the “for”.

Does God strike down those who doubt? No. The psalmists shout at God for whole psalms, and the shouting is in the Scriptures. Job argues for thirty chapters and is vindicated over his tidier friends. A father cries “I believe; help my unbelief!”, and gets his son back the same hour (Mark 9:24). Thomas demands the wound and is offered it (John 20:27). God has never once been rattled by an honest question. What happened to Zechariah is not the punishment of doubt but the granting of a request. He asked for a sign, and the sign was himself: he wanted evidence he could hold, and God gave him nine months of it, attached to his own face. It is one of the oldest mercies in Scripture that God so often gives us exactly what we asked for, in the form we would never have chosen. Gabriel does name the cause, “because you did not believe” (v. 20), so it was discipline too; but it was a father’s discipline, with an end date, given to a man God had already called righteous.

So what is the difference between honest doubt and unbelief? Honest doubt brings its struggle to God and wants to believe; it says “help my unbelief”. Unbelief has already weighed God’s word against something else and decided the something else is more reliable. The first is weak faith asking for help; the second is a verdict against God. You can tell which by what you do with the question: take it to God and his word, or use it as a reason to stay away. If you fear your doubts mean you have no faith, the very fear often shows that you want to trust him.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel answered him, 'I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day that these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word does not wait for our faith to come true: it will be fulfilled in its time, and Zechariah’s silence will be both his sign and his discipline.

I am Gabriel. He does not argue biology; he gives his name and his post. Gabriel (“God is my strength”, or “man of God”) appears in the Old Testament only in Daniel (8:16; 9:21), where he came to a man in exile with a message about how long the waiting would be: the seventy weeks decreed for Daniel’s people, and at the end of them an Anointed One (Daniel 9:24–27). Gabriel is the angel of the countdown, and a priest who knew Daniel is being told by him that the clock has run out, and asks him for a sign. “I stand in the presence of God” is a courtier’s phrase: these words have just come out of the throne room, and to weigh them against a doctor’s estimate is to treat God’s word as one more human opinion.

This good news. To bring good news is the verb from which “gospel” and “evangelise” come (euangelisasthai). The gospel begins here, in an old man’s ear, beside an altar. The next time an angel uses the word, it is to say: “I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord” (2:10–11). Daniel’s countdown ended in an Anointed One, and here the messenger of the countdown brings the first news of him. The good news is never only that God has done something. It is that God has sent someone.

You will be silent and unable to speak. The sign he asked for, and a discipline. He could not believe the word, so he will not be able to speak a word; verse 62 suggests he could not hear either. A priest whose work runs on words loses the one faculty his office depends on. It was also a mercy: nine months is exactly the time it takes to watch a promise you refused to believe come true in your own house.

Until the day. A limit is written into the sentence, and the end date is the fulfilment. God does not leave him in the dark, but puts him there until the light he refused to believe in comes into the room.

Fulfilled in their time. Gabriel is untroubled: the word will be fulfilled because God said it, not because Zechariah came round. Unbelief only robs the doubter of joy. The promises of God do not draw their strength from the faith of the person who hears them, which is why people whose faith is thin can lean on them.

Does God discipline his children today? Yes, and Hebrews says it is a mark of sonship, not rejection: “the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6). But read your circumstances carefully: not every hardship is discipline for a particular sin; Elizabeth’s barrenness was not. Where God does discipline, it is a Father training a child, never a judge punishing a criminal, because the punishment for our sin fell on Christ. Discipline always has a purpose and a limit, as Zechariah’s did. If you suspect a trouble is his correction, do not despair or dig for hidden reasons. Confess what you know is wrong, and trust the Father to bring you through to the day of fulfilment.
verseByVerse.note: Gabriel appears in the Old Testament only in Daniel.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they were wondering at his delay in the temple. And when he came out, he was unable to speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he kept making signs to them and remained mute. And when his time of service was ended, he went to his home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priest who should have blessed the waiting people comes out unable to speak, a sign that God has done something and that the true blessing is on its way.

The people were waiting. The incense offering was short, and the priest normally came out quickly to pronounce the priestly blessing over the people from the temple steps. A long delay was worrying: a priest who offended God could die in the Holy Place (Leviticus 16:2, 13).

He was unable to speak to them. The priest could not give the blessing, some of the oldest words in Israel’s worship: “The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:24–26). The blessing the waiting crowd expected never came.

He had seen a vision. They could not know what, but they knew God had done something in that room. And Zechariah did not leave early. He served out the rest of his days in silence, doing everything that did not require a voice, with the greatest news of his life locked inside him. Obedience is largely what a person keeps doing after the moment of glory has passed and he is back on the roster with nothing to show for it.

The blessing on its way. On the day God finally spoke, the man appointed to bless Israel was struck dumb, because the LORD was about to make his face shine upon them in a way no formula could carry. The blessing was not cancelled but on its way in person. At the very end of his Gospel, Luke shows Jesus lifting up his hands and blessing his disciples (24:50–51), the blessing the priest could not give: a priest who cannot bless at the beginning, and a Priest who blesses as he ascends at the end. He was carried into heaven still blessing them, and he has never lowered his hands. Every believer now lives under the raised hands of the risen Priest.
verseByVerse.note: The people waited for the priest to come out and pronounce the blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and for five months she kept herself hidden, saying, 'Thus the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my reproach among people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elizabeth receives her child as God’s personal kindness: he has looked on her and lifted the shame she carried for years.

Kept herself hidden. We are not told why. In a village where everyone has known for decades that she cannot have children, she waits until the pregnancy is beyond doubt and God is the only possible explanation, and only then lets herself be seen. The sixth month will be when Gabriel comes to Mary (v. 26), and her pregnancy will be Mary’s sign (v. 36).

Thus the Lord has done for me. Her first words are praise, and she takes no credit. The Lord did it; the Lord looked.

He looked on me. With favour, with grace. It is the look of Exodus, when God saw the affliction of his people in Egypt and came down to do something about it (Exodus 3:7–8): not casual noticing but the look that ends in action. He saw Hagar in the desert, Israel in Egypt and Elizabeth in the hill country, and he has looked on us in Christ, who bore our reproach outside the gate so that we might never be put to shame.

My reproach. Rachel said the same: “God has taken away my reproach” (Genesis 30:23). And see what was taken away: not the barrenness but the reproach, oneidos, the thing people said. God took away not only a medical condition but a sentence a whole village had passed on her, and which she had heard them pass. Yet the only verdict Scripture records about her is the one in verse 6, and it had read “righteous before God” the whole time.

Not every mercy needs announcing. The instinct to publish everything at once is not faith; sometimes it is a hunger to be seen to be blessed. Elizabeth had lived for decades under the village’s verdict, and she did not rush to win it back. God’s look was enough for her.

In everyday life. Watch your words about others: never be the voice whose verdict someone has to live under for years.

What about shame that God has not yet removed? Some shame echoes other people’s cruelty, like Elizabeth’s; some is the right sting of our own sin. Christ deals with both. For our sin, he bore the shame of the cross, despising it (Hebrews 12:2), so that the guilt is gone and the shame no longer defines us. For the shame others put on us, he gives a verdict that outweighs theirs. You may still feel it, and the feeling may take years to fade. But the feeling is not the verdict. In Christ, God has looked on you with favour, and “Those who look to him are radiant, and their faces shall never be ashamed” (Psalm 34:5).

parallels.desc: Rachel: God has taken away my reproach

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s Son is coming into the world through a humble virgin, by the power of the Holy Spirit, to reign for ever on David’s throne. Gabriel goes now not to a priest in the temple but to a betrothed girl in Nazareth (vv. 26–27; on the contrast, see there), and greets her as one on whom God’s grace has freely fallen (vv. 28–29; on what the greeting does and does not mean, see the box “Where Christians differ: full of grace” in that note). He makes four claims about her son, each higher than the last: he will be great, called the Son of the Most High, given the throne of his father David, and his kingdom will have no end (vv. 30–33; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Daniel 7:14). Mary asks “how”, not “whether”, and is told that the Holy Spirit will come upon her, as the cloud of God’s presence covered the tabernacle (vv. 34–37; Exodus 40:35). Her answer, “let it be to me according to your word”, is surrender that is also worship (v. 38).
verseByVerse.theology:
Gabriel joins two lines of promise in one child, David’s and Daniel’s (see vv. 32–33).

The conception by the Holy Spirit shows that the incarnation is God’s act, not a human achievement; the child is fully human and at the same time the eternal Son of God (see the note on v. 35). Gabriel does not explain the mystery. He announces it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary says yes without knowing how it will happen or what it will cost (on what that faith is, see the note on v. 38).

And the greatest conversation in this chapter took place in the house of an ordinary girl in a town nobody thought much of (see vv. 26–27).

verseByVerse.quote: In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David. And the virgin's name was Mary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends his greatest news not to the temple but to an unknown girl in an obscure village, pledged to marry a son of David.

The contrast. Luke means the reader to feel the drop. The first annunciation was in the temple, to a priest in the middle of the liturgy, about a child born to a barren woman. The second is in a village in despised Galilee, to a girl with no title or office, about a child born to a virgin. The first is wonderful; the second is greater. And the date is the sixth month of Elizabeth’s pregnancy: Luke dates the coming of the Son of God by the swelling of an old woman’s body in the hill country.

Nazareth. A small, obscure village in the hills of lower Galilee, never mentioned in the Old Testament, in Josephus or in the Mishnah and Talmud. Archaeology suggests a few hundred people off the main road. Hence Nathanael’s question, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” (John 1:46).

To a virgin. A young unmarried woman who has not had sexual relations (parthenos). Luke makes this unmistakable: he says “virgin” twice in this verse, and Mary herself says she has not known a man (v. 34). This echoes Isaiah 7:14 (Matthew 1:23).

Betrothed. Jewish marriage had two stages. Betrothal was a binding agreement, often made when the girl was in her early teens: the couple were legally husband and wife, and breaking it required a divorce (Matthew 1:19). But they did not yet live together; about a year later came the wedding. So Mary is legally bound to Joseph and still living at home, exactly the condition in which a pregnancy is a catastrophe.

Of the house of David. Joseph was a descendant of King David, and as Jesus’ legal father he gave him the legal right to David’s throne (3:23–31; Matthew 1:1–16). In Israel a legal son, named and received by his father, was a true heir.

The Son comes round the back. Luke’s whole Gospel is in this contrast: shepherds before scholars, a Samaritan before a priest, a tax collector before a Pharisee, a dying thief before the men who arranged the cross. And it begins with the Son of God himself. The heir of David’s throne does not come in at the palace gate but round the back, through a girl nobody had heard of. Isaiah had said he would grow up like a young plant, like a root out of dry ground, with no form or majesty that we should look at him (Isaiah 53:2). The King chose the low door, so that no one would ever be too low to reach him. That is the best news the overlooked have ever heard. If you live somewhere nobody has heard of, in a church of thirty people, you are standing on exactly the kind of ground God likes to choose. Enthroned above every name, he still answers to Jesus of Nazareth (Acts 22:8).
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth was a small village in the hills of Galilee. Betrothal was a binding agreement, stronger than modern engagement; the couple did not yet live together.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to her and said, 'Greetings, O favored one, the Lord is with you!' But she was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has freely shown Mary his favour and is with her, and she, humble and thoughtful, wonders what such a greeting can mean.

Greetings. The ordinary Greek greeting (chaire), literally “rejoice”. There may be an echo of the prophets’ calls to the daughter of Zion to sing and rejoice, because the King of Israel, the LORD, is in her midst (Zephaniah 3:14–17; Zechariah 9:9).

O favored one. Kecharitōmenē, from charis, grace. Its form is a perfect passive participle: something was done to her, and the result stands. The plainest English is: “you who have been graced.” God is the one acting, not Mary. The same verb is used of all believers in Ephesians 1:6: “his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us” (literally “graced us”) “in the Beloved”.

The Lord is with you. The promise given to the great servants of God when he called them: Moses, Joshua, Gideon (Judges 6:12), Jeremiah.

Greatly troubled. Not by the angel, as Zechariah was, but by his words. Gabriel has not yet mentioned a child, and in her humility she cannot see why God’s favour should rest on her.

Tried to discern. She thought it through (dielogizeto). Mary is thoughtful (2:19, 51): the first thing Luke tells us about her mind is that it went to work.

Nearer than she knew. Every servant who heard “the Lord is with you” before heard it as a promise of help: God would go with Moses to Pharaoh and with Gideon against Midian. To Mary the words are about to become literal. Within weeks the Lord will be with her in her own body, and Elizabeth will greet the unborn child as “my Lord” (v. 43). The God who had promised to dwell among his people chose first to dwell beneath one girl’s heart. That is the favour: not that Mary was raised up to God, but that God came down to her. All the favour any of us will ever receive flows from the Son Mary carried, and none of it flows through anyone but him. He is the fountain, and we are all, Mary first among us, cups held out to be filled.

In everyday life. If you are in Christ, you too have been graced (Ephesians 1:6), and “the Lord is with you” is said to every believer (Matthew 28:20). When the day goes badly, do not read it as a change in his face towards you. Say it over to yourself: “I have been graced, and the Lord is with me.”

If God favours me, why is my life so hard? Because his favour is not a promise of ease but of himself, a far better thing to be given and a far heavier thing to carry. God’s favour brought the most favoured woman in history poverty, exile, a pregnancy nobody would believe, a fiancé who nearly divorced her (Matthew 1:19), a birth among animals, and an old man in the temple telling her that a sword would pierce through her own soul. Hardship is not evidence that God has withdrawn his favour; often it is the very road his favour takes. Look at what the favour was for: Christ came to her and through her. In your hard place, the question is not whether God has stopped favouring you, but what he is bringing to you, and through you, in it.

Where Christians differ: full of grace. The Latin Vulgate translated the word gratia plena, full of grace, giving the familiar Hail Mary, full of grace. Roman Catholic teaching has understood Mary as filled with grace from her conception, and so preserved from original sin (the Immaculate Conception, defined in 1854), as remaining sinless all her life, and as one who can dispense grace to others and may be prayed to. Mary is the most highly favoured woman who ever lived; the Reformers said so without embarrassment. This commentary’s view: the Greek word means one who has been shown favour, not one who is a source of grace. Grace by definition is neither owed nor earned; the greeting tells you that Mary received something, which is exactly what a woman needing nothing could not do. Mary was a sinner saved by grace, who calls God my Saviour (v. 47). Only the drowning have any use for a lifeboat. She is to be honoured as the most blessed of women, the mother of our Lord, and a model of faith and obedience (v. 45). But she is not to be prayed to, and she does not dispense grace. Grace comes from God alone, through Christ alone.

Textual note: blessed are you among women. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV and NKJV, add “blessed are you among women” to Gabriel’s greeting here; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit it. The words are certainly Luke’s, but they belong to Elizabeth (v. 42).

parallels.desc: “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valour”

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to her, 'Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary has not earned God’s favour but been given it, and she will bear a son whose name says what he will do: “the LORD saves”.

Found favor. The phrase used of Noah in a world God had already decided to flood: “But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD” (Genesis 6:8). To find favour is to be given it, not to earn it.

Conceive and bear a son. The words echo Isaiah 7:14: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel”, as Matthew makes explicit (Matthew 1:22–23). And the eternal Son enters the world through nine months of nausea and backache: not a dignified entrance, but a real one.

The hinge of the Bible. From the promise in Eden that a woman’s offspring would crush the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15), through the covenant sworn to Abraham, through the throne promised to David, through the prophet who said “the virgin shall conceive” and “to us a child is born”, the entire weight of it comes down on one sentence spoken to a girl in Galilee.

Call his name Jesus. The Greek form of Joshua (Yeshua), meaning “the LORD saves”, or “the LORD is salvation”. Matthew gives the meaning: “for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Joshua led Israel into the promised land; Jesus brings his people into God’s eternal rest (Hebrews 4:8–10). The child is not called “the LORD reigns” or “the LORD judges”, which would have been true, but “the LORD saves”. And he is named before he is conceived: the rescue was decided before the rescuer had a body. Joshua bore the name as a hope; this child bears it as a fact. Luke will let us hear the name thrown back at him on the cross: “He saved others; let him save himself” (23:35). He would not, and that is the glory of the name. He kept it by refusing to save himself, so that he could save a dying thief beside him that same afternoon, and every sinner since who has called on him. When you sin today, do not hide from him; go to him by name.

Saves from what? First and most deeply, from our sins: from their guilt, which he carried in our place on the cross, bearing the punishment we deserved; from their power, which his Spirit breaks in us; and finally from their presence, when he returns. He also saves from everything sin has brought: death, the fear of death, and the judgment to come. He cares about loneliness, debt and anxiety, but the name points to the root. If he saves you from your sins, everything else is on its way to being put right.

Did Isaiah really say virgin? The Hebrew word in Isaiah 7:14 (ʿalmah) means a young woman of marriageable age, who would be expected to be a virgin; the Greek translation of the Old Testament, made long before Jesus, rendered it “virgin” (parthenos), and Matthew quotes it in that form (Matthew 1:23). Matthew and Luke both say plainly that Mary conceived without a man (v. 34), so the question of the word does not touch the fact. And the sign Isaiah promised was meant to be a wonder, a child who would be called God with us.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua, meaning “the LORD saves.”

verseByVerse.quote: He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary’s son will be God’s own Son and David’s promised heir, and his kingdom will never end. Each of Gabriel’s four claims climbs higher than the last.

He will be great. John was to be great before the Lord (v. 15): his greatness is measured by someone greater than himself. Jesus is simply great, because there is no one greater to measure him against. This is the language used of God himself: “Great is the LORD” (Psalm 48:1).

Son of the Most High. The Most High (Hypsistos) is a name for God (Genesis 14:18–20; Psalm 91:1). “Called” in Hebrew idiom means “will be, and be recognised as”. Israel’s kings were spoken of as God’s sons by adoption at their coronation (Psalm 2:7; 2 Samuel 7:14). This one is the Son before anybody crowns him.

The throne of his father David. The fulfilment of God’s covenant with David, made a thousand years earlier: “I will raise up your offspring after you … and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son” (2 Samuel 7:12–16; also Psalm 89; Isaiah 9:6–7). The last Davidic king had been dragged off to Babylon six centuries before. The promise was not dead; it was waiting for the right heir.

The house of Jacob. Jacob was renamed Israel; the house of Jacob is God’s people. And it now includes all who belong to Christ by faith, Jew and Gentile: “if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (Galatians 3:29; 6:16).

No end. Here the language stops being merely royal. Daniel had watched one like a son of man come to the Ancient of Days and receive an everlasting dominion that would not pass away (Daniel 2:44; 7:13–14); Isaiah had promised a child of the increase of whose government there will be no end (Isaiah 9:6–7). No merely human king ever gets that sentence, for the plain reason that human kings die. Thrones have risen and fallen, Herod’s and Caesar’s among them, and his has not moved.

If Jesus reigns now, why is the world such a mess?
