How do I know my sins are forgiven? Not by a feeling, though feelings of peace often come, but by God’s promise to everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Christ. If you have come to him confessing your sin and relying on his death for you, he has forgiven you, completely, because he is faithful to his word and just to the blood of his Son (1 John 1:9). Forgiveness is not a probation; it is a verdict. Your sins are not filed away to be brought out later; they are removed as far as the east is from the west (Psalm 103:12). When you sin again, as you will, come again. The fountain does not run dry.

parallels.desc: a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins

verseByVerse.quote: because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this springs from God’s tender mercy: light is about to dawn from heaven on people sitting helpless in the dark, to lead them into peace.

Tender mercy. Literally “the bowels of mercy” (splanchna eleous): the inner organs, the seat of the deepest emotions, compassion felt physically. Its verb is used of Jesus when he sees the widow of Nain walking behind her son’s body out of the town gate (7:13). The reason given here for the whole plan of redemption is not God’s justice or his glory, though both are true, but that something in God moved. That does not mean his holiness has softened or his justice been set aside. It means the holy God, “who will by no means clear the guilty” (Exodus 34:7), was moved to find a way to be both “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). The mercy is tender because it is costly.

The sunrise from on high. Sunrise (anatolē) carries two meanings at once, both of which this priest knew. It is the ordinary word for the dawn. It is also the word the Greek Old Testament uses to translate “Branch”, a title for the Messiah, the promised shoot from David’s stump: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch” (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8; 6:12). Zechariah picks the one word that says dawn and David’s heir in the same breath. “But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings” (Malachi 4:2).

In darkness and in the shadow of death. “The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone” (Isaiah 9:2). Isaiah wrote this of “Galilee of the nations” (Isaiah 9:1), where Jesus would minister, and he speaks of the servant as a light for the nations (Isaiah 42:6–7; 49:6): the light is for Gentiles too (2:32).

Those who sit. Not those who walk in darkness, or search in it, but “those who sit”: the posture of somebody who has stopped moving, because there is nowhere to go and no way of seeing the way there. Anyone who has sat with someone six weeks after the funeral, or lain awake at four in the morning with a diagnosis, knows that position. The Bible’s picture of humanity apart from God is not a traveller who has taken a wrong turning. It is somebody who has sat down in the dark.

Nobody helps the sun come up. Nothing whatever is contributed by the people sitting in the valley. The light arrives from above, on its own schedule, whether or not anyone below is ready, and when it comes, the same people who could not find the path can suddenly see the whole country. That is what grace is. Not a lamp handed to a man so that he can go looking. A sunrise.

The way of peace. Peace (eirēnē, Hebrew shalom) is the fullness of well-being that comes from being right with God: “peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1), and the wholeness that flows from it. The angels will sing of it at Jesus’ birth (2:14).

The Dayspring himself. Centuries of night, and a world sitting in the shadow of death since a garden gate closed behind it. And then over the eastern rim, without one hand raised anywhere to help it: the Dayspring himself, the Branch of David, to set our feet in the way of peace. He rose then. He has not set since.

In everyday life. Someone you know is sitting in the dark this week, grieving, depressed, far from God. You cannot make the sun rise for them, but you can sit with them, pray for them and tell them that the light is coming from above.

What if I am a Christian and still sitting in darkness? It happens, and Scripture does not hide it: Isaiah speaks of one who fears the LORD and walks in darkness and has no light, and tells him to trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God (Isaiah 50:10). Darkness in a believer’s feelings is not the same as being outside the light; the sun has risen whether or not clouds cover it today. Keep to the means of grace, tell a pastor or trusted friend, and if the darkness is depression, seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up; that is not a lack of faith. And wait for him, as those who watch for the morning (Psalm 130:6). He has never failed to bring it.

Textual note: shall visit or has visited? Some manuscripts read “has visited us”, matching v. 68; others, including some of the earliest, read “shall visit”, which the ESV follows. Either way the sunrise is God’s doing.

parallels.desc: the sun of righteousness shall rise
light on those in the land of deep darkness

verseByVerse.quote: And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John grows up strong in spirit, hidden in the wilderness until God’s time to show him to Israel. Luke has spent the chapter on little more than a year; now he covers three decades in a sentence and moves on.

Grew and became strong in spirit. Similar words are used of Samuel (1 Samuel 2:21, 26) and of Jesus (2:40, 52): growth in body and in spirit, by the Spirit with whom he was filled.

In the wilderness. The wilderness of Judea, between the hill country and the Dead Sea: limestone ridges and dry gorges, almost waterless. It was where Israel had been formed, where Elijah had fled, and where the prophets had said God would make a way (Isaiah 40:3). The son of a priest had a hereditary right to serve in the temple, in the rota his own father had drawn the lot in. He never took it up.

Until the day. About thirty years later (3:1–2). The greatest man born of women, by Christ’s own reckoning, spent thirty of his thirty-odd years doing, so far as the record goes, nothing whatever.

In the flow. Luke has built this chapter in pairs: two announcements, two mothers, two songs. This verse parks John in the wilderness so that the stage is clear for the birth of Jesus, and a sentence almost the same will close Jesus’ childhood (2:40).

Formed for one sentence. Everything the desert made of John, it made for the sake of someone else. Thirty years of formation produced a voice, and the voice had one message: “he who is mightier than I is coming” (3:16). The wilderness that shaped him is the same wilderness into which Jesus will be led by the Spirit for forty days (4:1–2), not to be made ready to point to another, but to face temptation where Israel had failed, and win. John’s hidden years made a herald; Jesus’ hidden years (2:52) made ready the Lamb. When John finally appeared to Israel, the first thing he did with all that the desert had given him was step aside for Christ.

The waiting room. This is a hard verse for anybody whose life feels like a waiting room: the years that count for nothing on any visible ledger, the training never used, the gifts nobody has asked for. Luke’s summary says thirty such years were not lost. Plain speech that could not be bought, the nerve to tell a king the truth about his marriage: that is what the desert made.

What if my wilderness never ends in public ministry? Then it was still not wasted. Most of God’s servants never have a public appearance to Israel; their whole life is the hidden part, and God counts it. The point of John’s desert was not that it led to fame but that God was with him in it, forming him for whatever he had appointed. Your hidden years may be preparing you for a single conversation, a child raised in the faith, a quiet faithfulness that holds a church together, or simply for heaven. Nothing done for God in obscurity is lost (Matthew 6:4; 1 Corinthians 15:58).

Was John connected with Qumran? Some have suggested that John was raised by the Essene community at Qumran, near the Dead Sea, where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found. They took in boys, lived in the wilderness and quoted Isaiah 40:3, so it is possible but unproved. Luke says nothing of it, and John’s message, a call to all Israel to repent and a baptism given once, was quite unlike the separatist community’s repeated washings. He was in the wilderness because God was preparing him there.

parallels.desc: the word of God came to John in the wilderness

1.text: <sup>1</sup> Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been accomplished among us, <sup>2</sup> just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word have delivered them to us, <sup>3</sup> it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, <sup>4</sup> that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught. <sup>5</sup> In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. And he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. <sup>6</sup> And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord. <sup>7</sup> But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years. <sup>8</sup> Now while he was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty, <sup>9</sup> according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. <sup>10</sup> And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense. <sup>11</sup> And there appeared to him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense. <sup>12</sup> And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him. <sup>13</sup> But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. <sup>14</sup> And you will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, <sup>15</sup> for he will be great before the Lord. And he must not drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb. <sup>16</sup> And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, <sup>17</sup> and he will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.” <sup>18</sup> And Zechariah said to the angel, “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.” <sup>19</sup> And the angel answered him, “I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. <sup>20</sup> And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day that these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.” <sup>21</sup> And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they were wondering at his delay in the temple. <sup>22</sup> And when he came out, he was unable to speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he kept making signs to them and remained mute. <sup>23</sup> And when his time of service was ended, he went to his home. <sup>24</sup> After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and for five months she kept herself hidden, saying, <sup>25</sup> “Thus the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my reproach among people.” <sup>26</sup> In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, <sup>27</sup> to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David. And the virgin's name was Mary. <sup>28</sup> And he came to her and said, “Greetings, O favored one, the Lord is with you!” <sup>29</sup> But she was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be. <sup>30</sup> And the angel said to her, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. <sup>31</sup> And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. <sup>32</sup> He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, <sup>33</sup> and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.” <sup>34</sup> And Mary said to the angel, “How will this be, since I am a virgin?” <sup>35</sup> And the angel answered her, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God. <sup>36</sup> And behold, your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son, and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren. <sup>37</sup> For nothing will be impossible with God.” <sup>38</sup> And Mary said, “Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.” And the angel departed from her. <sup>39</sup> In those days Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a town in Judah, <sup>40</sup> and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. <sup>41</sup> And when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary, the baby leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit, <sup>42</sup> and she exclaimed with a loud cry, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! <sup>43</sup> And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me? <sup>44</sup> For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. <sup>45</sup> And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.” <sup>46</sup> And Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord, <sup>47</sup> and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior, <sup>48</sup> for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed; <sup>49</sup> for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name. <sup>50</sup> And his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation. <sup>51</sup> He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; <sup>52</sup> he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; <sup>53</sup> he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty. <sup>54</sup> He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, <sup>55</sup> as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever.” <sup>56</sup> And Mary remained with her about three months and returned to her home. <sup>57</sup> Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. <sup>58</sup> And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her. <sup>59</sup> And on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child. And they would have called him Zechariah after his father, <sup>60</sup> but his mother answered, “No; he shall be called John.” <sup>61</sup> And they said to her, “None of your relatives is called by this name.” <sup>62</sup> And they made signs to his father, inquiring what he wanted him to be called. <sup>63</sup> And he asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” And they all wondered. <sup>64</sup> And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God. <sup>65</sup> And fear came on all their neighbors. And all these things were talked about through all the hill country of Judea, <sup>66</sup> and all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying, “What then will this child be?” For the hand of the Lord was with him. <sup>67</sup> And his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying, <sup>68</sup> “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people <sup>69</sup> and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, <sup>70</sup> as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old, <sup>71</sup> that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us; <sup>72</sup> to show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, <sup>73</sup> the oath that he swore to our father Abraham, to grant us <sup>74</sup> that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, <sup>75</sup> in holiness and righteousness before him all our days. <sup>76</sup> And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, <sup>77</sup> to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins, <sup>78</sup> because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high <sup>79</sup> to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.” <sup>80</sup> And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.

keyVerse.quote: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people
keyVerse.note: Zechariah’s first words after his silence gather up the whole chapter: after centuries of quiet, God has not merely sent a message but come himself to rescue his people. The announcements, the meeting of the two mothers and both songs are this one visit arriving, and the visitor is the child in Mary’s womb (vv. 32–35, 76). Zechariah speaks of the redemption as already done, because what God has promised is as good as done.

1.reflection:
Zechariah and Mary both ask the angel a question (vv. 18, 34), yet one is silenced and the other blessed (v. 45). What was the difference between them? Where are you tempted to weigh God’s word against your circumstances?

Elizabeth lived for years under her village’s verdict (vv. 7, 25), and Mary went home to face suspicion (v. 56). How does the God who “looked on” the lowly (vv. 25, 48) speak to people who feel overlooked or misjudged, and how can our church reflect his way of seeing them?

Mary sings that God scatters the proud, brings down the mighty and fills the hungry (vv. 51–53). Who are the proud, the rich and the hungry in her song, and which of them are you most like?

Everything in this chapter points to the child Mary carries: the Son of the Most High, David’s heir whose kingdom has no end, the horn of salvation, the sunrise from on high. Which of these pictures of Jesus most moves you to worship, and why?

2.title: The Birth of the King
2.overview:
Where we are. After the two promised births of chapter 1, chapter 2 tells of Jesus’ birth and boyhood and closes Luke’s account of his beginnings; we next meet him at about thirty, at the Jordan (3:21–23).

The message. God’s Saviour has been born, and he has come low. The child in the feeding trough is Saviour, Christ and Lord (v. 11), God’s salvation, a light for the nations, and the Son who calls God “my Father” (v. 49). Yet he comes to a poor family, under the law, recognised only by people who were waiting for him. Luke holds the glory and the lowliness together on every page, because the lowliness is how the glory saves.

Why it was said. Luke’s readers lived under an empire that hailed Augustus as saviour and lord and called his birthday good news (see the introduction). They needed to be sure that the real Saviour was the Galilean a Roman governor had crucified: truly David’s son, born in David’s town, raised in a law-keeping home rather than a rebel’s, and announced in God’s own temple as light for Gentiles like them.

How the chapter makes its case. Caesar’s decree carries Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem, where the promised king is laid in a manger (vv. 1–7). Heaven’s armies announce him to shepherds on the night shift, who find everything as they were told (vv. 8–20). Presented in the temple under the law, the child is recognised by two old saints, Simeon and Anna, as God’s salvation; but Simeon also speaks the first shadow, a sword (vv. 21–40). At twelve Jesus speaks for himself for the first time, of his Father, then goes home and obeys his parents for eighteen hidden years (vv. 41–52).

Where it leads. The chapter already leans toward the cross. The baby wrapped and laid in a manger will be wrapped and laid in a tomb (23:53). The boy lost for three days at the Passover in Jerusalem will be lost there again at the Passover, and found alive on the third day. The “must” of his Father’s plan (v. 49) runs all the way to Calvary and the empty tomb, and all of it was for us.

For us. Look for Christ where God has put him, not where the impressive look. Receive the news as the shepherds did, at once; keep it as Mary did, turning it over; and wait on God’s promises as Simeon and Anna did, until you too can say, “my eyes have seen your salvation”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Birth of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The true Saviour and Lord is born, not in Caesar’s palace but in a feeding trough, and Caesar’s own decree brings him there. Augustus, hailed as saviour and bringer of peace, orders a registration of the empire (vv. 1–2), and Luke never raises his voice to point out the contrast. God uses that order to bring a Galilean couple of David’s line to Bethlehem, where Micah said Israel’s ruler would be born (vv. 3–5; Micah 5:2). He works through the harsh machinery of politics without removing its cost, and in a crowded house with no room to spare the Son of God is laid in a manger (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Augustus commanded armies and moved millions with a decree. The child in the manger would command no army, spend his public life in a minor province and die as a criminal. Yet it is the child whose kingdom has no end. From the first chapter Luke asks his reader to see that the power which actually runs the universe does not look like the power that runs an empire.
verseByVerse.examples: Mary and Joseph did not choose to travel to Bethlehem at the end of a pregnancy (on a life moved about by other people’s decisions, see the note on vv. 3–5). And the manger has comforted every believer who has felt overlooked or without a place: the Son of God did not insist on suitable accommodation, and no circumstance is too humble for God to be present in it.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered. This was the first registration when Quirinius was governor of Syria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God brings his Son into the world by way of a pagan emperor’s decree, at a moment fixed in real history.

Caesar Augustus. Augustus was Octavian, adopted son of Julius Caesar, who ended a century of civil wars and ruled as the first Roman emperor from 27 BC to AD 14. The Senate named him Augustus, revered one; he was styled divi filius, son of the deified one, and hailed in inscriptions as saviour and lord, and a famous decree in Asia Minor called his birthday the beginning of the good news (euangelia) for the world. Every one of those words is about to be given to somebody else, by an angel over a field of sheep: good news, a Saviour, a Lord, and peace (vv. 10–14). One man’s decree moved the world; the other could not yet hold up his own head.

That all the world should be registered. “All the world” (oikoumenē) means the Roman Empire; a census served taxation and military service. Luke’s first readers would also notice that Jesus’ family did exactly what Caesar required. A movement whose founder Rome had executed was easily suspected of sedition, and Luke shows again and again that Jesus’ followers were not rebels against Rome (23:4, 14–15; Acts 18:14–15; 26:31–32).

When Quirinius was governor of Syria. A real historical puzzle. Publius Sulpicius Quirinius is known to have governed Syria from AD 6, when he took a census in Judea after it came under direct Roman rule; Luke mentions the revolt of Judas the Galilean that it provoked (Acts 5:37). But Jesus was born before Herod died, usually dated 4 BC, so on the face of it Luke is a decade out. Either Quirinius held an earlier office in the region during which an earlier census began, or the verse distinguishes this registration from the famous later one (see the box below).

How providence works. Augustus wants a tax register; God wants a Galilean couple in Bethlehem, where Micah said Israel’s ruler would be born. The most powerful man on earth signs an order and, without knowing it, serves a prophecy he has never read. God governs history through people convinced they are governing it themselves: he turned Caesar’s census into a road for a pregnant girl, so that a seven-hundred-year-old promise would land in the right town on the right night.

A line in Caesar’s ledger. Augustus wanted every name in his empire on a list, and never knew that the Name above every name was about to be written on it. The Lord of heaven and earth let himself be counted as one more subject of Rome. Caesar’s titles have crumbled into museum stones. The child on his list is Saviour and Lord for ever, and he writes his people’s names in heaven, where no empire can strike them out (10:20).

Did Luke make a mistake? Luke plainly knew of the AD 6 census, since he reports its consequences, so he is hardly the man to have muddled it with another. Where this careful historian (1:3) can be checked he has generally proved accurate, getting a mass of shifting local titles right. Such a man has earned the benefit of the doubt where our own records happen to be thin. The puzzle is not settled, but it is no proof of error, and honesty serves better here than invented certainty.

Uncertain wording. The Greek word usually translated “first” can also mean “before”, and the ESV footnote allows: “This was the registration before Quirinius was governor of Syria”. That is a less common use of the word, but a possible one; if Luke meant it, he is deliberately distinguishing this census from the well-known one of AD 6. It is the simplest answer to the puzzle, though not a certain one.
verseByVerse.note: Augustus ruled the Roman Empire from 27 BC to AD 14. The ESV notes that verse 2 can also be read “This was the registration before Quirinius was governor of Syria”. The dating of this census is debated.

parallels.desc: the revolt “in the days of the census”

verseByVerse.quote: And all went to be registered, each to his own town. And Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the town of Nazareth, to Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David, to be registered with Mary, his betrothed, who was with child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph obeys Caesar’s order and takes Mary to Bethlehem, and so David’s son is carried to David’s town to be born.

Each to his own town. The town of his family’s origin, or where he held property; an Egyptian census edict of AD 104 likewise sent people back to their home districts.

The city of David. Bethlehem, about five miles (8 km) south of Jerusalem, was David’s home town (1 Samuel 16:1; 17:12). Its name means house of bread, and the Bread of Life is born there (John 6:35). Micah had prophesied: “But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days” (Micah 5:2).

Of the house and lineage of David. Jesus’ legal descent from David came through Joseph (1:27). A shepherd boy was anointed in that town a thousand years before (1 Samuel 16:1–13); six centuries before, the line was carried to Babylon; now David’s family walks back to be counted as taxpayers of a foreign empire. The dynasty had come to this.

His betrothed. Still betrothed: Joseph had taken her as his wife but had no union with her until the child was born (Matthew 1:24–25). Luke’s wording is exact, as a witness’s would be: this is how they looked to everyone on that road, where everybody counted the months. Mary’s yes to the angel (1:38) went on costing all the way to Bethlehem, and the cost was not glorious: tiredness, dust, and about ninety miles (145 km) of road.

The road was not shortened. Four or five days on foot for people who are not pregnant, and Mary is near the end of a first pregnancy, every mile ordered by a man in Rome who wanted his revenue figures. We tell the story as though God arranged a gentle providence for the holy family. He arranged a tax census, a long walk and an overcrowded town, and did not remove one inch of the road to spare the mother of his Son. Nor did he spare his Son the greater road ahead.

The shoot from the stump comes home. David’s house looked like the stump of a felled tree. Yet God had sworn that a son of David would sit on a throne for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16; 1:32–33), and Isaiah had said a shoot would come up from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1). Here it is, carried home inside his mother to be born where David was anointed. Joseph brings him the legal right; God brings him the throne.

What about my life being pushed around by other people’s decisions? Many lives are moved about by decisions taken in rooms they never enter: a restructure, a landlord, a letter from an office. Being inside God’s will has never meant being outside other people’s decisions. Joseph and Mary were at the centre of God’s plan and also two more names on a Roman list. You may appeal, object or plan around the decision where that is right, but you need not believe the people in the room are in control. Your Father is, and he can turn their decree into your road.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth to Bethlehem is a journey of roughly 80–90 miles.

verseByVerse.quote: And while they were there, the time came for her to give birth. And she gave birth to her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of God is born as a real, ordinary baby and laid in a feeding trough, because there was no room for the family.

She gave birth to her firstborn son. The most important birth in history, told in a handful of words with no adjectives. “While they were there”: we do not know how long they had been in Bethlehem, and the tradition that she gave birth the night they arrived is not in the text. “Firstborn” carries legal rights and the sense of being set apart to God (v. 23; Exodus 13:2). Christ is also “the firstborn of all creation” and “the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1:15, 18), meaning not the first thing God made but first in rank, for “all things were created through him and for him” (Colossians 1:16).

And wrapped him in swaddling cloths. Strips of cloth wrapped snugly round a newborn to keep the limbs straight and warm. Not a sign of poverty: every mother did it, and Luke says Mary did it herself; he mentions no midwife. The child was not neglected (Ezekiel 16:4). This is a real infant, with real limbs that need binding.

And laid him in a manger. A feeding trough, perhaps of stone or wood. Luke says it three times in ten verses, his way of underlining. The one who would say “I am the bread of life” was laid, on his first night, in the box the animals ate from, in the town called house of bread. The tradition of a stable or cave comes from the manger; many houses kept animals at night at their lower end.

No place in the inn. “Inn” (katalyma) is not the word for a commercial inn, which is pandocheion (10:34); it means a lodging place or guest room, the word for the upper room of the Last Supper (22:11). The likeliest picture is a crowded family house, its one guest room taken, perhaps by relatives in town for the census, and the couple put in the lower part where the animals came in at night. Nobody turned them away; there simply was no room. It was the first sign of the welcome the world would give him: “his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11). “Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

The Word lying in straw. The Word by whom all things were made lies in straw in a back room, and nobody in the world knows it but two tired parents and, soon, a few shepherds. He who upholds the universe by the word of his power is held up by his mother, because he cannot hold up his own head. There is no distance in the universe like the distance he came, and he came all of it.

Does it matter whether it was an inn or a guest room? Not to the gospel, but it helps us read honestly. The cruel innkeeper is not in the text, and preaching against him misses Luke’s emphasis, which is not anyone’s unkindness but God’s chosen lowliness. It also brings the story closer to home: he came into the kind of overcrowded, makeshift family arrangement many people know.

Where Christians differ: did Mary have other children? Luke could have written her son. That he writes her firstborn son is, on the plainest reading, the ordinary way of speaking of a first child, and naturally implies others came after, though it does not require it. Read it with Matthew’s note that Joseph knew her not until she had given birth (Matthew 1:25), and the four brothers and the sisters named later (Matthew 13:55–56; Mark 6:3). Rome and the Orthodox East, and some of the Reformers too, hold that Mary remained a virgin all her life and that the brothers were cousins or Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage. The word alone does not settle it: firstborn was also a legal term for the son who opened the womb and carried the firstborn’s rights, the very status that sends this family to the temple fifteen verses later. This commentary’s view: the natural reading is the right one, and nothing in Scripture requires straining past it: Mary and Joseph went on to have a family in the ordinary way. Nothing precious is lost by taking it plainly. Mary’s honour never rested on what happened after Bethlehem, but on the virgin conception, on the child she bore, and on the faith with which she received him.
verseByVerse.note: Swaddling cloths were strips of cloth wrapped snugly around a newborn. A manger is a feeding trough. The word for “inn” can mean a guest room, the same word used for the upper room in 22:11.

parallels.desc: though he was rich, he became poor

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–20 — The Shepherds and the Angels
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The birth of God’s Saviour is good news for the lowly, and it is announced to them first. Heaven’s glory, unseen in Israel since Ezekiel watched it leave the temple, shines on shepherds at work by night (vv. 8–9). The angel names the child Saviour, Christ and Lord, and gives the strangest of signs, a baby in a feeding trough (vv. 10–12), and an army of angels praises God for glory in heaven and peace on earth (vv. 13–14). The shepherds go at once, find everything as they were told, and tell what they heard (vv. 15–18). The neighbours wonder, Mary ponders (vv. 18–19), and the shepherds go back to their sheep praising God (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology:
The choice of shepherds is the first instance of the great reversal that runs through Luke: the humble are lifted up, and those the world dismisses are the ones God honours.

Luke is also careful about how the news is received. The neighbours “wondered”, a word he never confuses with faith. Mary, in the same room, treasured and pondered what she heard (v. 19), and the contrast is the point.
verseByVerse.examples: The shepherds go at once, and then become the first to announce the Saviour’s birth, with nothing to commend them except that they had seen what they had seen. That is still the pattern of Christian witness: not credentials or eloquence, but people who have met Christ and tell what God has said about him.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the same region there were shepherds out in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. And an angel of the Lord appeared to them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were filled with great fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God announces his Son’s birth first to shepherds on the night shift, and his long-absent glory shines on them. The news goes first to men with no standing, because it is news of grace.

Shepherds out in the field. Shepherds were humble working men, not the gentle figures of the Christmas card, near the bottom of Jewish society; their work made it practically impossible to keep the law’s rules of ceremonial cleanness. Some later rabbinic writings even listed herdsmen with tax collectors as men whose testimony was not accepted in court. Not the emperor, nor the high priest a few miles away, but men with no standing, purity or legal credibility hear first. And David, the shepherd king, was from Bethlehem; Jesus is the good shepherd (John 10:11).

Keeping watch by night. Taking turns through the watches of the night against thieves and wild animals: not a spiritual retreat but work, at an hour when everybody with a choice is in bed.

The glory of the Lord. The shining brightness of God’s presence, which filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter and the temple so that the priests could not stand (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:11). Scripture records no return of that glory to Israel since Ezekiel watched it leave the temple for the mountain east of the city before the exile (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23). Six centuries later it comes back in a field, to men who could not have entered the temple courts without a wash. God brought the weight of his presence down to the bottom of the social ladder, in the dark. That is the gospel before a word of it is spoken: the holy God has come to the unclean, and come to save.

Why the glory came back tonight. Because the Lord of the glory has just been born a few fields away. The light around the shepherds is the reflection; its source lies in a feeding trough. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14); God has given “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). What Israel once met in a cloud over a tent it would now meet in a face. The glory had come not to visit but to live in a man.

In everyday life. If you work nights, care for animals, clean offices or drive the early bus, you are in exactly the company God chose for the first announcement of his Son.

What does this do to the date of Christmas? Flocks were kept in the open from spring to autumn, and sometimes all year in the milder Judean climate, so Luke’s detail does not fix the season. The church chose 25 December centuries later; we do not know the time of year, and no doctrine hangs on it. Christians may gladly celebrate Christ’s birth then, as long as they do not mistake a tradition for a command. What Luke does tell us is the hour, night, and he means it: the whole chapter is about a light arriving in the dark.
verseByVerse.note: Shepherds were humble working men, often looked down on.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to them, 'Fear not, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel announces the gospel itself: today, in David’s town, the Saviour has been born for you, and he is the Christ and the Lord.

Fear not. Again the first word is comfort. God knows exactly what his presence does to people, and he never leaves them standing in it.

I bring you good news. One verb in Greek (euangelizomai), whose noun is the word we translate gospel. This is the gospel. The empire used it for official news of a victory or an heir’s birth; heaven puts it in an angel’s mouth over a sheep field.

Great joy for all the people. “The people” (laos) usually means Israel in Luke, but the joy will spread beyond (v. 32), and Luke spends twenty-two more chapters showing what “all” means: a Samaritan, a centurion, a sinful woman, a tax collector, a thief on a cross.

This day. “Today” (sēmeron) is a key word in Luke: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled” (4:21); “Today salvation has come to this house” (19:9); “today you will be with me in paradise” (23:43). The gospel is never a rumour about the distant past or a hope for a vague future. It is today.

A Saviour. The title the empire gave Augustus. This is the true Saviour, who saves from sin (Matthew 1:21; Acts 5:31), and the only place in Matthew, Mark and Luke where Jesus is given the title (John has it once, 4:42).

Who is Christ the Lord. Three titles in one breath, two of them claimed for Caesar that year. “Christ”: the Anointed One, the promised king of David’s line. “Lord” (Kyrios): the title the Greek Old Testament used for God’s own name. Caesar took it too; only one of the two was entitled to it. The exact phrase “Christ the Lord” appears only here in the New Testament. A newborn baby is the Saviour, the Messiah and the Lord God. The empire’s saviour and lord died in his bed at Nola like any other man. Ours was laid in a feeding trough, nailed to a cross, raised from the tomb, and he reigns.

Joy for a hard December. For some, Christmas is mainly an empty chair. The angel does not command anyone to feel joyful; he reports an event: “unto you is born this day”. A joy that depends on your heart goes down with your heart. A joy resting on a birth that has already happened cannot be taken away by grief, only hidden by it for a while.

Saved from what? A modern reader may say he needs no Saviour, only a little help and a better year. The angel’s word assumes what the whole Bible says plainly: our deepest trouble is not our circumstances but our guilt before a holy God, which no improvement in circumstances touches (Romans 3:23). Augustus could end a war; he could not forgive one sin or open one grave. So heaven announces a Saviour, not an adviser. The person who feels no need of one is not the exception to this verse; he is the reason for it.

So what do I do if I cannot feel the joy this year? Do not fake it, and do not conclude you have lost your faith. Let the joy rest where the angel put it. Go to church anyway, and let others sing the words you cannot. Tell a friend or pastor how hard it is. Weep if you need to; Jesus wept at a grave. Read the angel’s words slowly and say them back to God: “This is true, even tonight.” The feeling may come later, or not this year. The fact does not depend on it, and he will carry you until it returns.
verseByVerse.note: “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah; “Lord” was the title the Greek Old Testament used for God’s name.

parallels.desc: he will save his people from their sins
to us a child is born
the feet of him who brings good news

verseByVerse.quote: And this will be a sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sign by which the shepherds will know the Saviour is his lowliness: an ordinary baby in a most unusual bed.

A sign for you. God’s signs in Scripture are usually remarkable: a burning bush, a fleece, a shadow going backwards on a sundial. Here the sign is a baby in a feeding trough. The cloths were normal; every baby in Bethlehem was wrapped that way, and they say he is completely human, with no halo and nothing about him out of the ordinary. The manger was not normal. The shepherds were given no street and no name, but in a village the size of Bethlehem there would almost certainly be only one newborn lying in a manger.

The opposite of what you would expect. Kings are found in palaces; this King is found where the animals eat. Part of every heart still measures worth by impressiveness, and would have walked past a feeding trough on the way to the palace. God put his Son where the impressive would not look, so that he would be found by those who had stopped trusting their own standing. And the shepherds could come: they would not have been let into a palace, but they could go into a place with animals.

Wrapped and laid, twice. At the end of his Gospel Luke uses almost the same words: the body of Jesus is wrapped in a linen shroud and laid in a tomb where no one had yet been laid (23:53). Wrapped and laid at his coming, wrapped and laid at his dying, and both times the lowliness was the sign. Blessed are the eyes that see the glory of God lying there.

A sign, not a scene. Asking for a sign is often really asking for a scene, something loud enough to end the possibility of doubt. God’s sign could be walked past by anybody not told what to look for, and the pattern has not changed. What God offers his people is usually not a blaze in the sky but appointed ordinary things: bread, wine, water, a book, a gathering of unimpressive people. The world sees a feeding trough. Faith sees exactly what it was told it would find.

Should I ask God for a sign? Not as a condition of believing what he has already said. The shepherds were given a sign; they did not demand one, and Jesus refused signs to those who wanted proof on their own terms (11:29). We have something better: the full record of his life, death and resurrection. In decisions, ask God for wisdom (James 1:5), study his word, seek counsel and pray; do not lay out fleeces as a test. And look for him where he has promised to be found: in his word, his people and his ordinances.

parallels.desc: the LORD himself will give you a sign

verseByVerse.quote: And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying, 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heaven’s army breaks into praise: this birth brings God the highest glory and brings his peace to the people on whom his favour rests.

A multitude of the heavenly host. “Host” (stratia) means an army: the massed host of heaven (1 Kings 22:19), drawn up over a field outside a village, come not to fight but to announce peace. Luke does not say they sang; they were “praising God and saying”.

Glory to God in the highest. In Latin Gloria in excelsis Deo, sung in Christian worship for centuries. Heaven’s first response is not relief, or wonder at how it was done, but glory given to God: this birth is not chiefly about us. It is about him.

And on earth peace. Peace with God: the end of hostility between the holy God and rebellious humanity (Ephesians 2:14–17), and the wholeness and well-being (shalom) that flow from it. Not the Pax Romana, which lasted as long as the legions; nor the absence of conflict, which he did not come to bring (12:51). It is the end of the war between heaven and earth, the peace Christ makes by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20): “Since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). The God glorified in the highest heaven has made peace at the lowest point of the world.

Among those with whom he is pleased. Literally among men of his good pleasure (en anthrōpois eudokias), that is, God’s: those on whom his favour rests, whom he has chosen in grace; Ephesians 1:5 and 9 use the same word for God’s choosing will. The peace is not for those good enough to please God, but for those God has chosen to favour. Scripture calls this election: before the world began, God freely chose a people and set his love on them, for reasons found in his mercy and not in them (Ephesians 1:4–5). That makes the news warmer, not colder. The older reading familiar from carols (see the textual note below) announces goodwill to everybody in general, which guarantees it to nobody in particular. The angels announce peace with an owner’s name on it, resting not on how its recipients turn out but on God’s good pleasure, the one foundation that does not move.

How do I know if God’s good pleasure rests on me? Not by peering into God’s hidden counsels, but by looking at the Son he has given. The gospel is offered freely to everyone: whoever comes to him, he will never cast out (John 6:37). If you have come to Christ, trusting him and turning from your sin, that is the evidence that God’s favour rests on you, because no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). Election is not a locked door to worry about; it is the reason the door was opened to you. If you are not sure you have come, come now. The peace is for all who believe.

Textual note. The King James Version, following later manuscripts, reads: “on earth peace, good will toward men”. The difference is one letter in Greek: eudokia, good will, standing on its own as a third item, or eudokias, of good pleasure, attached to the men. The earliest and best manuscripts have eudokias, giving the ESV’s reading. The old reading is familiar from carols, but the better text points to God’s good pleasure.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV’s “among those with whom he is pleased” follows the better manuscripts; older translations read “good will toward men.”

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: When the angels went away from them into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, 'Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.' And they went with haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in a manger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shepherds take the angel’s message as the Lord’s own word and go at once, and they find everything just as they were told.

Let us go over to Bethlehem. The sky closes, and the shepherds say the only sensible thing. “Thing” is literally word (rhēma), both the event and the message. They do not doubt like Zechariah, but obey like Mary.

Which the Lord has made known to us. No debate, no waiting for daylight; and they get the theology right in passing: not the angel told us, but the Lord did. A messenger is a mouth, not a source.

And they went with haste. Leaving their flocks. Luke has used the phrase once before, of Mary going to the hill country (1:39), and keeps it for people whose response to God’s word is to start moving. They walked into a crowded house in the middle of the night with a story that must have sounded insane, and there in the animals’ quarters was exactly what they had been told. That is the reward of obedience here: not a further revelation, but confirmation of the one they had.

They found the message lying in a manger. The angels had given them a message: a Saviour, Christ the Lord. When they arrived, the message was a baby. That is the peculiar glory of the gospel: its content is not finally an idea to weigh but a person to find, and all God’s promises “find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20). The Lord still makes him known, through the word read and preached, so that people who were never in Bethlehem may come to him today. He has never yet sent anyone to look for Christ and let them come back empty.

The interval where faith dies. A great deal of faith quietly dies in the gap between hearing God and acting on it, rarely by a decision to disobey, usually by delay: a thing is weighed, put off until the season is better, and then no longer feels urgent. What is remarkable about these men is not their piety but that the interval was about ten seconds long.

But is it not wise to wait and think before acting? About many decisions, yes; Scripture commends counsel and care (Proverbs 15:22). But where God has spoken plainly, waiting is usually a polite form of not obeying. You need not pray about whether to forgive, to tell the truth, to come to Christ, or to be baptised as a believer; he has already said. Think hard about how; do not linger over whether. And with the call of the gospel itself, delay is the most dangerous thing of all: “now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw it, they made known the saying that had been told them concerning this child. And all who heard it wondered at what the shepherds told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having seen the child, the shepherds tell everyone what they were told about him, and their hearers are amazed; but amazement is not yet faith.

They made known the saying. Nobody commissioned them, but having looked, they told everyone, and became the first evangelists. Men whose testimony counted for little were God’s first witnesses to the birth of Christ, as women would be to the resurrection.

Concerning this child. They did not tell their experience, the light or the fear, but what had been said about him: Saviour, Christ, Lord. The child was the news, and he still is, and the message these despised men carried has outlived the empire that despised them.

And all who heard it wondered. “Wondered” (ethaumasan): were amazed. Crowds marvel at Jesus all through this Gospel, and marvelling saves nobody. It is possible to be moved by this story every December for fifty years and remain where those neighbours were: amazed, and nothing more. Wonder is a good doorway, and Luke never sneers at it; but a doorway is for walking through, and Mary did something different with the same news (v. 19).

What should I say when I tell someone about Jesus? Start with him, not yourself. Your story matters as a witness to what he has done, but the heart of it is who Jesus is, that he died for sinners and rose again, and that he calls everyone to turn and trust him. Say it simply, as the shepherds did. You need not answer every objection; you can say, “I do not know, but I know this.” And do not be discouraged if people only wonder. Your task is to tell; it is the Spirit’s work to turn wonder into faith.

verseByVerse.quote: But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary does not merely wonder: she keeps everything that has happened and goes on thinking it through.

But Mary treasured up all these things. The “but” does real work: everybody else wondered; Mary went deeper. “Treasured up” (synetērei): kept carefully, as one stores something valuable. This is probably one of Luke’s hints at his source: who else could have told him these things but Mary herself (1:2–3)?

Pondering them in her heart. “Pondering” (symballousa): literally throwing together, comparing, seeking the meaning; not daydreaming. She has an angel’s announcement, a relative’s prophecy, a birth among animals, and shepherds at midnight with a story of an army in the sky, and she lays the pieces side by side and keeps turning them. She did not understand everything (v. 50), but like the hill-country neighbours (1:66) she neither forces a meaning onto what she cannot explain nor lets it go.

The child at the centre of the pieces. Every piece concerned one person. The angel had called him the Son of the Most High, whose kingdom would have no end (1:32–33); the shepherds had heard him called Saviour and Lord; and she had just laid him where the animals ate. Mary was among the first to hold together in one heart what the church would spend centuries learning to confess: the baby she nursed was her Lord, truly man and truly God, one person. She could not yet see how. She did not let go of either half.

The whole picture, which is himself. Luke says the same of her twelve years later (v. 51). God did not leave her holding the pieces for ever: after the cross and the empty tomb she is in the upper room, praying with those who now knew who her son was (Acts 1:14). The child she pondered in the straw was the risen Lord she worshipped. He is patient with his ponderers, and in his time he gives them the whole picture, which is himself.

What does Christian meditation look like? Not emptying the mind, as in Eastern practices, but filling it with God’s word and turning it over. Take a short passage, read it slowly several times, and ask: what does this say about God? About Christ? About me? What does it command, promise or warn? Connect it with other Scripture, as Mary connected the angel’s words with the shepherds’ story. Then turn it into prayer and praise. Ten unhurried minutes on a few verses often do more than an hour of skimming. Psalm 1 calls the man blessed who meditates on God’s law day and night.

parallels.desc: his father kept the saying in mind

verseByVerse.quote: And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shepherds go back to the same work, changed, praising God because everything they heard and saw matched what they had been told. The night did not lift them out of ordinary life; it went with them into it.

And the shepherds returned. To their flocks and ordinary work. Their circumstances were the same; they were not. Luke records no one leaving his trade. They went home in the dark, singing, to a job nobody respected: very nearly a definition of the Christian life.

Glorifying and praising God. They join the angels’ song (v. 14). After a high moment with God it is tempting to think the real thing was back there. The shepherds show the opposite: the glory came to them in the middle of a shift, and sent them back to the same sheep praising.

As it had been told them. Heard from the angel and seen in the child, everything matched. A decree signed in Rome, a prophecy kept in Bethlehem, an announcement in a field: every part fitted.

The angels left, and the child stayed. What they had seen was not a vision that faded with the light. The angels went back into heaven (v. 15); the child stayed. The glory had not visited a hillside and withdrawn, as it once withdrew from the temple in Ezekiel’s day. It had taken flesh, and would die for the sins of men like them. That is still the Christian’s footing on a Monday: not the memory of a high moment, but a living Lord present in the ordinary because he once entered it.

What it means to glorify God. “Glorify” can sound like a church word for singing louder, as though God needed topping up. The Hebrew word for glory carries the sense of weight, and to glorify God is to give him his true weight: to see how great and good he is, and say so. Timothy Keller often pointed out that to glorify someone is to praise, enjoy and delight in them, not for what they can get you but for who they are. Everyone leans their weight on something, mostly on things too light to hold it: a career, a reputation. The shepherds had seen where God’s weight really lies, in a baby laid in a feeding trough to save men like them. The night before he died, that child, grown, would say to his Father, “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4). We glorify God when we lean our whole weight on that finished work and are glad in him for it. This week, when you want the credit for something, give it away: tell someone plainly what God has done for you. See Glory in the Theological Dictionary.

Should a new believer leave his job to serve God? Usually not. Paul told the Corinthians to remain in the condition in which they were called, and serve God there (1 Corinthians 7:17–24). God calls some to leave their nets and preach, and the church should test such a call. But most believers glorify God by going back to the sheep: doing ordinary work honestly, well and joyfully, “for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). The question is not whether your job is spiritual enough, but whether you do it with praise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–40 — Jesus Presented at the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The child brought to the temple under the law is God’s salvation for Israel and the nations, and he will divide every heart. Jesus is circumcised and named (v. 21), and presented with the offering of the poor (vv. 22–24). Simeon, promised by the Spirit that he would see the Lord’s Christ, takes him in his arms and sings that he has seen God’s salvation, a light for the Gentiles (vv. 25–33). Then the shadow falls: the child is appointed for the fall and rising of many, and a sword will pierce Mary’s soul (vv. 34–35). Anna, the second witness, speaks of him to all who are waiting (vv. 36–38), and one sentence covers his growing up in Nazareth (vv. 39–40).
verseByVerse.theology:
Simeon’s light for the Gentiles fulfils Isaiah’s songs about the Servant of the LORD and looks ahead to the mission to the nations in Acts (see the note on vv. 29–32).

Simeon also says that the child will reveal the thoughts of many hearts: no one can be neutral toward him (see the note on vv. 34–35).
verseByVerse.examples: Simeon shows a death well prepared for (see the note on vv. 29–32). Anna shows long faithfulness (see the note on vv. 36–38).

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the eighth day Jesus is circumcised under the law and given the name Jesus, “the LORD saves”. The Son of God steps under the law he gave, and receives the name that says why.

When he was circumcised. On the eighth day, as the law required (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3), like John (1:59). Circumcision marked a boy as belonging to the covenant people, under its promises and its obligations. John’s naming set the hill country talking (1:59–66); Jesus’ passes in half a verse, because the greater child came more quietly. The verse starts a thread that runs through the chapter: everything is done as the law required (vv. 22–24, 27, 39).

He was called Jesus. The LORD saves (1:31). A common enough name, and that is part of the point: the name over the cross would be an ordinary name from an unremarkable town. It was settled by the angel before there was anything to name, and Mary and Joseph obeyed exactly.

Under the law, all the way down. Eight days old, and the first blood he shed was shed in obedience to the law he himself had given: “born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Galatians 4:4–5). There was no way to redeem people who were under something except by getting under it with them.

The knife and the name. On the day the child is cut into the covenant, he is given the name that says how the covenant will finally be kept. Knife and name will arrive together again at the cross: his blood shed and his people saved in one event. And Jesus does nothing in this verse; he is carried, held, named and cut. The first thing the Saviour did about our salvation he did by being handed over to others’ hands, and the last thing too. The Lord of the law became its subject, so that its subjects might become sons.

Why did Jesus need to keep the law for us? Because we have not kept it, and God’s law still stands. Christ bore the penalty for our disobedience on the cross, and he lived the perfect obedience we owed, from the eighth day to the last. Both are counted to everyone who trusts him: our sins to him, his righteousness to us (2 Corinthians 5:21). So a believer stands before God not merely pardoned but accepted as righteous. Paul’s word for it is justification: God’s verdict that a sinner stands righteous in his sight, not for anything the sinner has done but because Christ’s obedience and death are reckoned to his account (Romans 4:5). Your record before God is not your week; it is his life.

parallels.desc: the name given by the angel

verseByVerse.quote: And when the time came for their purification according to the Law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord (as it is written in the Law of the Lord, 'Every male who first opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord') and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the Law of the Lord, 'a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary and Joseph keep the law for a mother after childbirth and for a firstborn son, and their offering shows that they were poor.

The time came for their purification. Luke combines two requirements of the law in one visit. After bearing a son, a mother was ceremonially unclean for forty days, then brought a lamb for a burnt offering and a pigeon or dove for a sin offering (Leviticus 12:1–8). “Unclean” did not mean that childbirth was sinful, or that she was dirty or guilty, but that for that time she could not touch anything holy or enter the sanctuary (Leviticus 12:4). The law prescribes purification for the mother alone, so a reader with Leviticus open will trip over “their”. Luke is probably describing the family’s observance as a whole: the household went up together, and “their” covers the visit rather than the rite.

To present him to the Lord. Every firstborn son belonged to God, who had spared Israel’s firstborn at the Passover when Egypt’s died (Exodus 13:2, 12–15). He was redeemed, bought back, for five shekels paid to a priest (Numbers 18:15–16). Luke does not mention the payment, but speaks of presenting him, as Hannah presented Samuel (1 Samuel 1:22–28): the firstborn handed over to the Lord, who will himself pay a much larger price.

A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. The offering of the poor (Leviticus 12:8): they could not afford a lamb. Anyone who has stood at a counter and taken the smaller thing because the larger was out of reach has stood where Mary stood that morning, and it was by God’s choice that her child grew up in that house.

The Lamb in a poor girl’s arms. Of everyone in the temple courts that day, this child alone has nothing whatever to be purified from, and he is brought in anyway, counted in with every other son of Israel. His mother could not afford a lamb, and she was carrying the Lamb of God (John 1:29). The God who asked a lamb of every mother in Israel provided the one Lamb for every sinner, and laid him first in the arms of a poor girl holding two birds. The birds were offered and forgotten. The Lamb grew up, walked back into the same courts, and offered himself once for all, so that no mother and no sinner need ever bring another.

Was Mary a sinner? The law required a mother to bring a sin offering after childbirth (Leviticus 12:6–8), and Mary brought it like every mother. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Mary was preserved from all sin. But Mary herself calls God my Saviour (1:47), and Scripture says “all have sinned” (Romans 3:23), with the single exception of her Son. She too was a sinner who needed her sins paid for, and the one who would pay for them was in her arms.

Does Jesus understand money worries? From the inside. He grew up in a house that counted coins, worked with his hands, later had nowhere to lay his head, and depended on others’ gifts (8:3; 9:58). Bring your bills, your fears about the rent and your shame about being poor to him in prayer; he knows the counter where you take the cheaper thing. And if you are not poor, remember that the Lord was raised by people who chose the two birds, and look out for those in your church choosing them now.

Textual note. Some later copies smoothed “their purification” to “her”, which is why the King James Version reads “her purification”; but “their” is the harder wording and the one found in the best manuscripts, and a copyist is far likelier to have tidied a difficulty than to have created one.
verseByVerse.note: Forty days after the birth of a son the mother brought a purification offering. Firstborn sons belonged to the LORD and were redeemed. Two birds instead of a lamb was the offering of the poor.

parallels.desc: every firstborn is holy to the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon is one of the faithful few still waiting for the comfort God had promised Israel, and the Spirit has told him he will see the Christ before he dies.

A man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon. Simeon is not said to be a priest, but an ordinary godly man, old by his own words (v. 29): righteous, like Zechariah and Elizabeth (1:6), and devout (eulabēs), careful and reverent toward God.

Waiting for the consolation of Israel. “Consolation” (paraklēsin): comfort. The phrase comes from the great turn in Isaiah, “Comfort, comfort my people, says your God” (Isaiah 40:1), the announcement that the exile is over and God is coming back to his people. Simeon is waiting for God to keep a specific promise, one of the faithful remnant (Romans 11:5) with Anna (v. 38) and Joseph of Arimathea (23:51).

And the Holy Spirit was upon him. Three times in three verses Luke ties Simeon to the Spirit (vv. 25, 26, 27): upon him, revealing to him, moving him into the temple. Israel had been without a prophet for some four hundred years; now the Spirit is everywhere in the story.

The Lord’s Christ. God’s own anointed one (Psalm 2:2). We are not told when the promise was given. He may have carried it for decades, unable to prove it, with no date attached and a body running out of time.

The comfort was coming as a child. Isaiah’s comfort was never going to be a better political season. Its heart was that God himself would come: “Behold your God!” (Isaiah 40:9), the chapter Luke quotes when John the Baptist appears (3:4–6). So the consolation Simeon waited for was not an event but a person, the Lord’s own Christ, and when he came he was small enough to hold. Every promise of comfort in the prophets had been travelling toward this child, and every comfort the church has known since has flowed from him.

The promise not yet kept. Many older believers know Simeon’s position: the thing God once made you sure of, which has still not happened, and which you long ago stopped mentioning. Simeon’s promise was kept at the far end of a long life, in a place he had walked through a thousand times, on a morning like every other. He did not miss the Christ when he came through the gate in the arms of a poor couple carrying two pigeons, because he had spent his life learning what to look for.

Should I expect personal promises from God like Simeon’s? Simeon lived at a unique moment, when the Spirit was announcing the Messiah’s arrival. Today God speaks through his completed word, and its promises are ours in Christ, more sure than any private impression (2 Peter 1:19). Be careful about treating a strong feeling as a promise from God; many have been badly hurt by doing so. But the shape of Simeon’s life is ours: we too wait, for Christ’s return, on the strength of God’s word, and that promise will be kept as surely as his was.
verseByVerse.note: “The consolation of Israel” means the comfort God had promised his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came in the Spirit into the temple, and when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the Law, he took him up in his arms and blessed God and said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Led by the Spirit at exactly the right moment, Simeon takes the child in his arms and turns at once to praise God.

In the Spirit. Simeon did not merely decide to go to the temple that morning; he was led there at the right moment. The temple complex covered something like thirty-five acres, and the courts were full of families doing the same small, ordinary thing. So far as Luke tells us, Simeon had a promise, not a description, and out of all that crowd he walks straight to the right child. Most of God’s appointments look like that from the inside: no sense of a scene being staged, only God quietly bringing about a meeting he had been arranging for longer than anyone present had been alive.

He took him up in his arms. Simeon stands here for the old covenant, God’s arrangement with Israel under Moses, with its temple and sacrifices. In this old man it takes into its arms the one who brings the new. The whole system is holding the one it was built to announce, who will make it unnecessary.

And blessed God. Not a speech to the crowd. The first response of a man who has received what he waited a lifetime for is to turn from the gift and speak to the Giver. When God gives you a good gift, speak about it to him first.

How can I know the Spirit is leading me? The Spirit leads above all through the Scriptures he inspired, never contrary to them. He also guides through godly counsel, through providence, and through desires he shapes in a heart soaked in his word, as Simeon’s was. Most of his leading is not felt at the time but seen afterwards, when you notice you were in the right place. So do not wait for a sensation before you act. Obey what is written, pray for guidance, and trust that he is ordering your steps even when you cannot feel it.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon can die in peace, because he has held God’s salvation in person: a light for the nations and the glory of Israel.

The Nunc Dimittis. Simeon’s song is named from its first words in Latin (now you dismiss), and has been sung at evening services for something like fifteen hundred years.

Letting your servant depart. “Lord” here is Master, a slave’s word for his owner (despotēs, not the usual kyrios), and “servant” is the slave (doulos). “Depart” (apolyeis): release, discharge, as a watchman is relieved at the end of his shift. Simeon is not saying he wants to die, but that his watch for the Messiah is over and he may go off duty. A man who has seen Christ is ready to die.

My eyes have seen your salvation. Simeon does not say he has seen the one who will bring salvation, but salvation itself, in his arms. Salvation is not a thing or a system; it is a person. “All the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God” (Isaiah 52:10).

A light for the Gentiles. Here the song opens out to the Gentiles. Simeon echoes Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6, where it is too small a thing for the LORD’s Servant merely to restore Israel: “I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.” In Israel’s temple, before Jesus has spoken a word, a devout old Jew announces this Jewish baby as salvation for the Gentiles. This is the theme of Luke and Acts: the gospel goes from Jerusalem to the nations (24:47; Acts 1:8; 13:47, where Paul quotes the same verse). Every Gentile who has come to Christ came in through a door Simeon saw standing open.

And for glory to your people Israel. The Messiah is Israel’s greatest glory, in whom all her history and hope are fulfilled: “from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all” (Romans 9:5).

A death well prepared for. Simeon’s readiness does not rest on achievement; we are told nothing of what he accomplished. He can go because “my eyes have seen your salvation”. There is a whole doctrine of contentment in an old man who holds the Christ and says, “That will do.” No one now will hold the infant Christ in the temple, but the salvation Simeon saw is offered to faith, and whoever has taken hold of it has exactly what Simeon had, and may leave this life in the same peace.

The subject we no longer mention. In 1955 the English anthropologist Geoffrey Gorer published an essay called “The Pornography of Death”, arguing that death had taken the place sex held for the Victorians: the thing decent people did not talk about. We have only got better at looking away: people die in wards, we speak of “passing”, and our days are too full for the question to get a quiet minute. But a fear we will not name leaks into everything else. If this life is all there is, every year has to deliver and growing old feels like being robbed. The older answers were not much better: the Stoic steeled himself, and the religious man hoped his record would hold. Simeon does neither. He is not being brave, and he is not counting his merits. He is holding someone. The only peace about death that is not denial belongs to a person who has been given what death cannot take, and the child in Simeon’s arms would one day go down into death himself, and come out the other side.

In everyday life. If you have seen Christ by faith, you can face death in peace. Pray Simeon’s prayer at the end of the day; every night’s sleep is a small rehearsal of the last one.

What happens to a believer at death? “Depart in peace” is exactly right. The believer’s soul goes at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). There is no purgatory, because Christ has already made full purification for sins (Hebrews 1:3), and no sleep of the soul: the dying thief was promised, “today you will be with me in paradise” (23:43). The body rests in the grave until Christ returns and raises it in glory (the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). So a Christian may face death as Simeon did, not with bravado but with peace, because his watch is over and his Master is calling him home.
verseByVerse.note: Simeon’s song is known as the Nunc Dimittis, from its first words in Latin.

parallels.desc: my salvation to the end of the earth
all the ends of the earth shall see

verseByVerse.quote: And his father and his mother marveled at what was said about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph and Mary are still astonished at what is said about their son. Even after angels and shepherds there was more in the child than they had grasped, perhaps especially in the words about the Gentiles.

His father. Luke calls Joseph Jesus’ father, as Mary does (v. 48). Luke has spent a chapter and a half establishing that Joseph is not this child’s father (3:23: “as was supposed”), yet Joseph is his father in every way that shows in daily life: he named him, presented him, taught him a trade, and raised him.

Never exhausted. If the mother of Jesus, with Gabriel’s words still ringing, could be astonished by what a stranger said about her own son, then finding Christ greater than you had understood is not immaturity. It is a sign that you are seeing him truly. Those who knew him best were still being astonished, and the saints in glory will be astonished for ever. There is no bottom to his riches and no edge to his glory.

A word for stepfathers and adoptive fathers. Any man raising a child not his by blood may take heart. The Son of God was brought up by one, and Scripture calls that man his father without a footnote. Naming, providing, teaching and protecting are real fatherhood in God’s eyes. And it pictures the gospel: God adopts sons who were not his by nature, and is not ashamed to be called their Father.
