verseByVerse.quote: And Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother, 'Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is opposed (and a sword will pierce through your own soul also), so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon warns that this child will divide Israel and lay bare every heart, and that his suffering will pierce his mother too.

And Simeon blessed them. Simeon has blessed God; now he blesses the parents, not the child, who is the source of blessing. Then he turns to Mary alone, perhaps because Joseph would not live to see what follows.

Appointed for the fall and rising. “Appointed”: placed there on purpose, and fall comes first. Some will stumble over him; others will rise through faith in him. He is the stone that some trip over and others build on (Isaiah 8:14–15; 28:16; 1 Peter 2:6–8), laid in the middle of Israel’s road, so that no one can walk past without either tripping over him or standing on him. No one can be neutral toward him.

And for a sign that is opposed. A sign spoken against: this child points to God, and people will speak against him for it. Being opposed is part of what he was appointed for. Whoever hopes that a sufficiently attractive presentation of Christ will stop people objecting hopes for something Simeon ruled out before Jesus could speak.

And a sword will pierce through your own soul also. The great broad sword (rhomphaia), the Greek Old Testament’s word for Goliath’s weapon. Mary’s son will be rejected and misunderstood, even by his own family (Mark 3:21; John 7:5), and she will stand by the cross and watch him die (John 19:25), with nothing whatever she can do.

So that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed. The purpose that explains the rest. How people respond to Jesus exposes what they really are (5:22; 6:8; John 3:19–21): he does not merely divide people; he shows what was already there.

In the flow. Until now every voice in Luke 1 and 2 has spoken of joy; this is the first shadow. From here both halves of Simeon’s word come true: tax collectors and sinners rise, while his own town tries to throw him off a cliff (4:28–29) and the leaders plot his death. At the cross the halves meet in the two men crucified beside him, one mocking and one asking to be remembered (23:39–43).

The sword and the spear. The child in Simeon’s arms was appointed for a cross, and the sword that pierced his mother’s soul was the shadow of the spear that, as John records, pierced his side. God did not spare his Son, nor the mother who loved him, because he was determined to spare us. The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone, and all who rest their weight on him will never be put to shame.

When a child suffers. This is a word to a mother about her son, and should be handled as one. Some parents reading this have watched a child suffer and could do nothing: an illness, an addiction, a court, a coffin. Two things stand in this verse for such a reader. Mary was told some thirty years in advance, and it did not make it easier; God does not seem to think forewarning is the same as sparing. And, heavier and better: the sword went through her because the nails went through him, by God’s appointment, and what looked from the foot of the cross like the end of everything was the hour the world had waited for since Eden. The grief was real. It was not the last word about the grief.

Why do people react so strongly to Jesus? Because he allows no neutrality. He claims to be Lord and Saviour, and that claim draws a person or offends him. Jesus puts his finger on the heart: our pride, our self-righteousness, our love of sin. So do not be surprised when friends are hostile, and do not water down the gospel to avoid offence. Pray for them, love them, and remember that some who stumble over him today may rise through him tomorrow. Paul himself first opposed the sign.

parallels.desc: a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a prophetess, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years, having lived with her husband seven years from when she was a virgin, and then as a widow until she was eighty-four. She did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day. And coming up at that very hour she began to give thanks to God and to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anna, an aged widow who had prayed in the temple for decades, recognises the child and tells everyone waiting for God’s redemption that it has come. God gives his second witness, and her long years turn out to be the making of that hour.

Anna, the daughter of Phanuel. Luke gives Anna a genealogy, unusual for a woman in an ancient text. Anna is the Greek form of Hannah, grace, the name of Samuel’s mother, whose prayer Mary echoed (1:46–55). Phanuel is Peniel, face of God, where Jacob wrestled with God (Genesis 32:30).

Of the tribe of Asher. One of the northern tribes, carried off by Assyria in 722 BC and popularly written off as lost. Yet a daughter of Asher stands at the presentation of the Messiah. Whatever else the exile did, it did not lose anybody God intended to keep.

A prophetess. Like Miriam, Deborah and Huldah (Exodus 15:20; Judges 4:4; 2 Kings 22:14), and the daughters of Philip (Acts 21:9): God gave prophecy to men and women at the dawn of the gospel, as Joel had promised (Acts 2:17). The law required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and God provides them, an old man and now an old woman; Luke often pairs a man and a woman.

Seven years, then a widow. Probably married young and widowed young (on her age, see the box below); either way, a very long widowhood. Widows were among the most vulnerable people in Israel. Anna did not remarry but devoted herself to God, like the widow who “has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day” (1 Timothy 5:5).

Night and day. Decades of fasting and prayer in a temple grown corrupt, with no congregation, no title and, so far as anyone could tell, no answers. She kept praying anyway.

At that very hour. Not that day; that hour. After perhaps sixty years of showing up she walks into the right court at the right moment and begins to give thanks, literally to confess, acknowledge, praise.

To all who were waiting. “Redemption” (1:68) is the setting free God had promised: “the LORD has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem” (Isaiah 52:9). Anna told the whole waiting circle that he had come. Her long years there meant she knew who those people were.

The redemption of Jerusalem was a child. Luke lets the phrase echo to the end. On the Emmaus road two disciples say, with the light gone out of them, “we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel” (24:21). Anna was right, and so were they; they had not yet understood how it would be done. Jerusalem would be redeemed not by a sword but by this child’s blood, shed outside its walls, and sealed by his rising on the third day, as the risen Lord himself showed them from the Scriptures (24:26–27).

For the one whose life looks like the long years. Some believers have prayed for a marriage, a child or a church for decades and watched nothing move. Anna’s years were not the waiting room for her ministry but the making of it: they produced a woman who could recognise God in a poor family’s arms when the priests around her saw a queue. The single hour was the harvest; the decades were the field.

In everyday life. If you are older, alone or widowed, your prayers are not the leftovers of a life; they may be its centre. If you are younger, find the Annas of your church and ask them to pray for you.

Should Christians fast today? Yes, as a voluntary help to prayer that earns nothing: Jesus assumed his disciples would fast after he was taken from them (5:35).

Does Anna show that women should prophesy or preach today? Anna’s gift belongs to the time when God was making his new work known, before the Scriptures were complete; it is no pattern for new revelation today, since the canon is closed and the foundational gifts have ceased. And she spoke to those who came to the temple courts; she did not lead Israel’s worship, which belonged to the priests. The New Testament reserves the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), while honouring women’s gifts in countless ways.

What Anna does show. A godly woman’s prayer and witness are precious to God, and she may and should speak of Christ to everyone who will listen. Many faithful Christians, Pentecostal and charismatic believers among them, hold that prophecy continues today, and some read Paul on women in the church differently. We hold our view because the apostles and prophets were the church’s once-laid foundation (Ephesians 2:20), and because Paul grounds his instruction in creation rather than custom (1 Timothy 2:13); and we gladly own those who differ as brothers and sisters in Christ.

Uncertain wording. The Greek of v. 37 can mean that Anna was a widow until she was eighty-four, as the ESV reads, or, as its footnote has it, that she had been a widow for eighty-four years, which with seven years of marriage from girlhood would make her over a hundred. The words allow both; the ESV’s reading is perhaps the more natural.
verseByVerse.note: Asher was one of the northern tribes. The ESV notes that verse 37 can also mean she had been a widow for eighty-four years.

parallels.desc: the widow who continues in prayers night and day

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. And the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom. And the favor of God was upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having done everything the law required, the family goes home to Nazareth, where Jesus grows up as a real child with the Father’s favour resting on him.

Everything according to the Law. Luke closes the infancy with obedience to the law (vv. 22, 23, 24, 27, 39): the Saviour came from an obedient, devout Jewish home.

The child grew. His humanity was real: he learned to walk, talk and read, and in his human mind he was not born knowing everything but was filled with wisdom as he grew (v. 52). Luke uses nearly the same words of John (1:80).

And the favour of God was upon him. “Favor” (charis): grace, not a reward earned but the settled delight of a Father in his Son. The Son of God spent most of his earthly life doing nothing anybody thought worth writing down, and the Father’s favour rested on every day of it. He made ordinary life holy by living it.

In everyday life. If your days are made of school runs, spreadsheets and meals, you are walking a road the Son of God walked for longer than any other.

Did Jesus do miracles as a child? No. The Gospels say nothing of it, and John tells us the wine at Cana was the first of his signs (John 2:11); the stories of a wonder-working boy are later legends. That silence teaches: the eternal Son lived for thirty years as an ordinary village boy and working man, without display, pleasing his Father in hidden obedience. Those years were not a delay before the real work; they were part of the perfect life he lived for us.

Do Luke and Matthew contradict each other? Better faced than stepped over. Matthew has the magi, the flight into Egypt, Herod’s killing of Bethlehem’s boys, and only after Herod’s death the settling in Nazareth; Luke moves from the temple to Nazareth in a sentence. But his sentence claims only that they “had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord”: he is closing the temple business, not publishing the next morning’s itinerary.

The room Matthew leaves. Matthew leaves exactly the room Luke needs. The magi come to a house (Matthew 2:11), not a stable, and Herod kills the boys two years old or under, reckoning by what the magi had told him (Matthew 2:16), which places their visit months, possibly more than a year, after the manger. So one sequence holds both accounts without strain: birth, circumcision on the eighth day, presentation on the fortieth, a settled stay in Bethlehem, the magi, Egypt, Herod’s death, the return north. And Matthew supplies the reason for the move Luke reports unexplained: they went to Nazareth rather than Bethlehem because Archelaus was reigning in Judea and Joseph was afraid to go there (Matthew 2:22). Not every step of the timing can be fixed, but neither account rules out the other.

Two witnesses, not competitors. Matthew writes from Joseph’s side, with Judea’s danger in view; Luke from Mary’s, with the temple’s faithfulness in view. Luke is not concealing Egypt. He told us he had sifted and arranged his material (1:3), and no witness who selects is thereby lying about what he leaves out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–52 — The Boy Jesus in the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even as a boy Jesus knows God as his Father and his Father’s claim on him as first, and he honours it by going home to obey his parents. This is the only story of his childhood in the four Gospels, and there is no miracle in it. At twelve, at the Passover, he stays behind in the temple (vv. 41–45). After three days his parents find him among the teachers, listening and asking questions (vv. 46–47). His first recorded words tell his mother he must be in his Father’s house, and they do not understand (vv. 48–50). Then he goes home, submits to them, and grows in every way (vv. 51–52).
verseByVerse.theology: Here Jesus uses the word must (dei) for the first time (on its place in Luke and Acts, see the note on vv. 48–49). Yet his going home in obedience (v. 51) answers anyone who reads his words in the temple as a claim to be above ordinary duty. And he truly grows in wisdom and stature (v. 52): the Son of God did not put on humanity like a costume; he lived a real human life from the inside.
verseByVerse.examples: For the second time in the chapter Mary holds on to what she does not understand (vv. 19, 51). And the hidden years in Nazareth show how God usually forms his people: slowly, in ordinary work and family life, long before any public work begins.

verseByVerse.quote: Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. And when he was twelve years old, they went up according to custom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus grows up in a devout family that keeps the Passover in Jerusalem every year, and at twelve he goes up with them.

The only story of Jesus’ boyhood. The Gospels tell us nothing of Jesus between infancy and about thirty except this episode, and in it he does nothing miraculous (on the later legends, see the note on vv. 39–40): he asks questions in the temple, goes home and does as he is told. Until now others have spoken about Jesus; here he speaks for himself for the first time, and his first words are about his Father (v. 49). When we next meet him, at the Jordan, the Father’s voice calls him “my beloved Son” (3:22). Here the Son says “my Father”; there the Father says “my Son”.

Every year at the Passover. The law required every Jewish man to go to the sanctuary for three pilgrim feasts a year: Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles (Deuteronomy 16:16). Mary went though women were not required to: a devout family, and a poor one, for whom the journey cost the better part of two weeks’ work every spring.

Twelve years old. In Jewish practice, as later written down in the Mishnah, a boy of thirteen became a son of the commandment, responsible to keep the law himself; the bar mitzvah ceremony came later still, and how fixed the age was in Jesus’ day we cannot be sure. This is the threshold of his responsible life, the moment Luke shows him once before drawing the curtain for eighteen more years.

They went up according to custom. Families travelled together in large caravans for safety and company.

The Lamb at the Passover. The Passover is the feast of the lamb whose blood on the doorposts meant the destroyer passed over the house, and the Lamb of God, twelve years old, has come up to keep it. The last time he keeps it, he will take the bread and say what no one had ever said of it: “This is my body, which is given for you” (22:19). He lived inside the story of redemption before he finished it.

How can a family make worship a habit today? Begin with the Lord’s Day: be in church with your children every week, not when it suits, so that gathering with God’s people is simply what your family does. Add something simple at home: a short Bible reading and prayer at a meal, a psalm or hymn, praying for one another by name. Let children see you read Scripture and pray, and talk about the sermon on the way home. Jesus learned the rhythm of worship in a household where it was fixed and costly. Children notice what their parents treat as non-negotiable.
verseByVerse.note: Every Jewish man was to go up to Jerusalem for the great feasts; families travelled together in large groups.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the feast was ended, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. His parents did not know it, but supposing him to be in the group they went a day's journey, but then they began to search for him among their relatives and acquaintances, and when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, searching for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem on purpose, and his parents, assuming he is in the caravan, travel a day before they miss him and go back to search.

When the feast was ended. Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread lasted eight days. Some pilgrims left after two; Jesus’ parents stayed for the whole feast.

The boy Jesus stayed behind. Deliberately, as his answer shows (v. 49), but not in disobedience: his parents had not told him to stay with them, and a twelve-year-old in that culture had considerable independence. Nor was it neglect: in a caravan of extended family he could plausibly have been with any party, and each parent may have thought he was with the other.

They went a day’s journey. About 20 miles (30 km). Then the evening camp, the same question asked of one face after another, and a day’s walk back to a city full of Passover crowds.

When God seems lost. There are seasons when someone who has known God for years cannot find him: prayer goes flat, and nothing is there. Mary and Joseph did not press on to Nazareth hoping he would turn up. They went back to the last place they had him, and kept looking until they found him. And he was not lost at all, nor hiding, nor withdrawn in displeasure. He was in his Father’s house, where he had always been; it was they who had walked a day in the wrong direction. The searching is a going back, not a going further on: back to the word, back to the last thing he actually said. He is never as far as our fear supposes. He is where he said he would be, and he waits there to be found.

Can a Christian lose Christ? Not in the sense of losing salvation. No one will snatch those the Father has given him out of his hand (John 10:28–29), and true believers can neither totally nor finally fall from grace (the Westminster Confession 17.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 17.1). But a believer can lose the sense of his presence, through sin, neglect or a trial God sends, sometimes for a long time (Westminster 18.4; 1689 18.4). The remedy is the one in this passage: do not assume, go back. Return to his word, confess what you know is wrong, come to the Lord’s Table, keep company with his people, and keep seeking. He has not moved.

verseByVerse.quote: After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. And all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After three days his parents find Jesus among the teachers in the temple, listening and asking questions, and everyone is amazed at his understanding.

After three days. Probably one day out, one back, and a day searching. It is fair to hear an echo of Easter. The next time Mary’s son is lost to her, it will be in the same city at the same feast, and the grief will be immeasurably worse; on the third day he will be found again, alive, and still about his Father’s business.

Sitting among the teachers. Probably in the colonnades of the temple courts, where the teachers of the law sat with their pupils, especially around the feasts. Not a boy lecturing the professors: he sits among them as a student, listening and asking questions, which was how Jewish teaching worked.

Amazed at his understanding. “Understanding” (synesei): insight. At twelve he holds his own with Israel’s teachers in the temple. Some twenty years later teachers in this same temple would be astonished, and then furious, at his answers (20:26, 40).

Remarkable, and learning. His understanding is beyond what the teachers can account for, and yet he is learning: the eternal Son is a boy with a real human mind that has to be taught, by ordinary teachers, out of the Scriptures. He took no shortcut that is closed to us, but came to know the Scriptures by sitting where they are taught, listening and asking, and he did it perfectly.

He asked questions about his own word. He who gave the law to Moses listened to men explain it, and asked them questions about his own word. There is no humility like his. And in him “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3), opened to everyone who comes to learn from him.

Is it all right to ask questions in church? Yes, and Jesus did. Ask your pastor about the sermon, join a Bible study where questions are welcome, ask older believers about a hard passage. Good questions come from humility and a desire to understand and obey, not from a wish to catch someone out or show off. When you are asked, do not be afraid to say, “I do not know; let us look it up together.” A church where nobody asks questions is usually a church where nobody is listening.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers of the law sat with their pupils in the temple courts, teaching by question and answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his parents saw him, they were astonished. And his mother said to him, 'Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.' And he said to them, 'Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary’s anguished reproach meets Jesus’ first recorded words: he belongs first to his Father, and they should have known where to find him.

Son, why have you treated us so? The natural reproach of a frightened, relieved mother at the end of three days, and Luke does not clean it up. She is asking what every frightened parent asks the moment fear turns to relief: “How could you do this to us?” The mother of the Lord speaks sharply to the Son of God, and the Bible does not correct her tone, which gives real permission to people taught that they must make their words polite before they can be honest with God.

In great distress. “Distress” (odynōmenoi): anguish, pain, a foretaste of the sword Simeon said would pierce her soul (v. 35).

Why were you looking for me? The first words of Jesus anybody wrote down are a question answering a question. Not rudeness, but surprise: you should have known where I would be.

Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house? Mary said “your father”, meaning Joseph; Jesus says “my Father”, meaning God. At twelve he knows his unique relationship to God as his Father. “Must” (dei): it has to happen, because God has planned it. Luke uses the word again and again: the Son of Man must suffer (9:22) and rise on the third day (24:7), and the Scripture must be fulfilled in him (22:37; 24:26). It appears here for the first time, on a twelve-year-old’s lips, and everything that follows in Luke and Acts works it out. He was not pushed along against his will: the Father’s plan made his road certain, and the Son gladly made it his own; “I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18).

A prior claim. He is not disowning Joseph, whom he will go home and obey for years. He is telling his mother, once, and then not again for a long time, that a claim on him comes before theirs, and that she of all people had the means to know it. The boy who said “my Father” now brings many sons to glory, and is not ashamed to call them his brothers.

Did Jesus sin by worrying his parents? A careful reader is entitled to ask. He was under the fifth commandment, and he had just caused his parents three days of anguish. If he broke it, the whole gospel comes apart, because a Saviour who needs saving cannot save anybody. He did not, and his reply shows why. He had not run away and had not been forbidden to stay; he had assumed, and expected them to assume, that everyone would know where the son of this family would be. His “did you not know” is not insolence but genuine surprise that after twelve years they had to be told. Causing distress is not always a sin; the sin would have been disobedience or disregard, and there was neither.

Uncertain wording. Literally Jesus says “in the things of my Father”. That can mean his Father’s house, the temple, as the ESV takes it, or his Father’s affairs, “about my Father’s business”, as the King James has it. The Greek carries either sense, so if your Bible reads the second, nothing is wrong. They are not rivals, since the house is where the business is done, though “house” fits slightly better, since he is answering where they should have looked.
verseByVerse.note: These are Jesus’ first recorded words.

verseByVerse.quote: And they did not understand the saying that he spoke to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even Mary and Joseph, with all they had been told, did not understand what he meant. Understanding Jesus comes slowly, and only he can give it.

They did not understand. A writer building a legend would have had the parents nod wisely; Luke records that the two people closest to Jesus heard him explain himself and did not follow. Mary is not portrayed as all-knowing; she too had to learn. Yet they had Gabriel, the shepherds, Simeon and Anna; if anyone had the material to understand, they did. Who Jesus was, and what his relationship to his Father meant, was too great to take in at once.

Understanding comes in instalments. In Scripture understanding is not the entry fee for faith but one of the things faith is given, in instalments, over a long time, and usually later than we would like.

Not understood until he opened it. Luke uses almost the same words of the Twelve: when Jesus tells them he must be delivered up and suffer, “they did not understand this saying” (9:45; compare 18:34). His sayings about his Father and his road were too large for those who loved him best, until the evening of the resurrection, when the risen Lord “opened their minds to understand the Scriptures” and showed them that the Christ should suffer and rise on the third day (24:45–46). Jesus himself opens his sayings, in the light of the cross and the empty tomb.

Two ways with what we do not understand. One quietly disposes of it, filed under things that will make sense one day and never returned to. The other is Mary’s (v. 51): put it somewhere safe and go on carrying it. She was still carrying this one twenty years later, when she stood at the foot of a cross and it began, at last, to make sense.

What should I do with a passage I cannot understand? Do not throw it away and do not force it. Read it in context, compare it with clearer passages, since Scripture interprets Scripture (the Westminster Confession 1.9; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.9), and ask a good commentary or a pastor. If it still will not open, shelve it with a note and keep reading. The things necessary for salvation are plain in Scripture (Westminster 1.7; 1689 1.7); harder things can wait. Many believers find a passage that baffled them for years suddenly opens in a hard season, because they kept it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them. And his mother treasured up all these things in her heart. And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes home and lives under his parents’ authority, and grows as a real human being in mind, body, and favour with God and people.

Submissive to them. The boy who has just spoken of a Father greater than Joseph walks home and puts himself under the authority of a village builder and a poor woman for some eighteen years more. “Submissive” (hypotassomenos) is not one act of compliance but a settled condition, sustained into manhood as he worked as a carpenter (Mark 6:3). Knowing his heavenly Father did not lead him to despise his earthly parents.

Higher calling, nearer duty. Verse 49 and verse 51 do not contradict; the pairing is the point. Being about his Father’s business, for a twelve-year-old in Nazareth, meant obeying his mother. Anyone who uses a sense of higher calling to neglect a plain nearer duty has read this passage exactly backwards.

His mother treasured up all these things. The second time, with the same verb as v. 19. She still does not understand, and she still will not let it go.

Increased in wisdom. In his human nature Jesus really learned and developed: “although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8). How can the eternal Son, through whom all things were made and “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3), increase in wisdom? Did he not already know everything?

Two natures, one person. The church has confessed from the beginning that in the one person of the Son there are two whole natures, divine and human, not blurred into a third thing (the Westminster Confession 8.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 8.2). According to his divine nature he knew all things and never learned anything. According to his human nature he really was a boy in Nazareth who had to learn his letters, memorise the Scriptures, listen to the teachers, and grow, mind and body together, as every child grows. He did not merely appear to be a developing child; he was one. It is the same reality met from the other side when he says he does not know the day of his return (Mark 13:32): all-knowing as God, genuinely limited as man, one undivided person.

In stature, and in favor. Stature may also mean years, or maturity. The same was said of the boy Samuel (1 Samuel 2:26). This is growth of the whole person, in mind, body, with God and with people, silently covering the hidden years of work, family, synagogue and prayer.

Eighteen unrecorded years. He did not play at being human. He became it, and lived it out through eighteen unrecorded years in a hill town, so that a fully human life could be offered to the Father with nothing missing. Every year of it was obedience, and every year was for us. He was once twelve, and once seven; he knows growing up from the inside, and what it is to learn slowly. Bring your child’s struggles, and your own memories of growing up, to one who has been there.

The fear of being ordinary. Many people carry a quiet dread that their lives will not add up to much. Earlier generations wanted to be good or respectable; we want to matter, and in a world of screens that means being seen, so a life nobody records can feel like one that did not quite happen. Set beside that the plain arithmetic of the Gospels: of the Son of God’s thirty-odd years on earth, all but about three were spent in a hill town, at a workbench, among neighbours who later could not believe he was anyone special (4:22). If significance depended on being noticed, those were wasted years. They were not. The Father’s voice at the Jordan, “with you I am well pleased” (3:22), came before a single sermon or miracle, spoken over those workshop years. That frees us from both our usual strategies, straining to make a name and despairing of ever having one. A believer is already known by name to the only one whose notice lasts, and an unseen life of faithfulness is not a failure to arrive. It is the shape his own life took, for us.

In everyday life. If you are a child or a teenager, Jesus obeyed his parents perfectly for you, and his Spirit in you will help you honour yours. At any age, ask which of his four kinds of growth is being neglected in your life this year, and take one step in it.

What if my parents are not godly or ask me to do wrong? Honour them still: speak respectfully, help them, care for them in age. But obedience to parents is always “in the Lord” (Ephesians 6:1), and God’s command comes first. If a parent tells you to sin, you must “obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29), and say so as gently as you can. If a parent is abusive, you are not required to submit to harm; tell a trusted adult, a pastor or the authorities, and get safe. Jesus obeyed Mary and Joseph because they were godly and asked nothing against his Father’s will. Your obedience, like his, is first to the Father.

How does a Christian grow? Not by climbing up into God’s favour. Jesus grew in favour as the sinless Son, and a believer already stands in that favour because of him, the grace “with which he has blessed us in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6). We grow from acceptance, not towards it, along the same four lines. In wisdom: stay under the word, a passage on most days and the preaching every Lord’s Day, as the boy sat listening to the teachers. In body: receive it as a gift, and sleep, work, eat and rest as someone who belongs to God. With God: pray, and come to the Lord’s Table; these ordinary means are how the Spirit feeds faith. With people: be someone others are glad to live and work beside, honouring those set over you as he honoured Mary and Joseph. Expect it to be slow and mostly unseen, like eighteen years in a hill town, and do not carry it as a weight. We are told to “grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (2 Peter 3:18), and the growing is his work before it is ours: “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

parallels.desc: the boy Samuel grew in favour with the LORD and with man

keyVerse.quote: For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.
keyVerse.note: The angel’s sentence names everything the chapter shows: a real birth, on a real day, in David’s town, of one who is Saviour, Messiah and Lord God at once. Every title in it was being claimed for Caesar that year, and heaven gives them to a baby in a feeding trough. “Unto you” makes it news for the hearer, not just a fact about the past.

2.reflection:
God announced the birth of his Son not to the emperor or the high priest but to shepherds on the night shift, and gave them a baby in a feeding trough as the sign (vv. 8–12). What does this tell us about God, and where are we tempted to look for him only in the impressive?

The neighbours wondered, but Mary treasured up these things and pondered them (vv. 18–19). What is the difference between being moved by the Christmas story and believing it? What helps you keep and turn over what God says, rather than letting it pass?

Simeon could face death in peace because he had seen God’s salvation (vv. 29–32), and Anna had prayed for decades before the hour came (vv. 36–38). What would it mean for you to wait for God’s promises like them, and to face your own death as Simeon did?

At twelve Jesus said he must be in his Father’s house, and then went home and was submissive to his parents for eighteen unrecorded years (vv. 49–52). How does this shape the way you think about ordinary duties, hidden years and the fear of a life that does not seem to count?

3.title: The Voice and the Son
3.overview:
Where we are. Luke’s account of Jesus’ birth and boyhood is over, and eighteen silent years have passed in a single verse (2:52). Chapter 3 opens the public story with the forerunner’s ministry, the baptism of Jesus and his family line, which together prepare for his testing in the wilderness (4:1–13) and his first sermon at Nazareth (4:16–30).

The message. God is coming to his people, so get ready: turn round, and look to the one who is coming. The word of God, silent for centuries, speaks again, with a warning and a promise. No pedigree will shelter anyone from the judgment at the door, and repentance must show in ordinary life. But one mightier than John is coming, and when he steps into the water, heaven opens to say who he is: the Father’s beloved Son, anointed with the Spirit, and a son of Adam for the sake of all Adam’s children.

Why it was said. Luke’s readers needed to be sure the gospel rested on real events (see the introduction), so he dates this one by emperor, governor, tetrarchs and high priests. They needed to know where John stood: he was a famous prophet, and some still knew only his baptism (Acts 18:25; 19:1–7), so Luke shows him as the herald who pointed away from himself. And Gentile readers needed to see that this Jewish Messiah was theirs too: Isaiah’s “all flesh” (v. 6), and a line that runs back to Adam.

How the chapter makes its case. In vv. 1–6 the word comes to John, the voice of Isaiah 40. In vv. 7–14 he strips away false security and shows what repentance looks like for crowds, tax collectors and soldiers, none of whom is told to leave his work. In vv. 15–18 he points to the one who will baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire, and Luke calls even the warnings good news. In vv. 19–20 Herod silences him. In vv. 21–22 Jesus is baptised among sinners, and while he prays the Spirit descends and the Father speaks. In vv. 23–38 the genealogy traces him back through forgotten and disgraced ancestors to Adam, the son of God.

Where it leads. The chapter opens with the rulers who will condemn Jesus and closes with the Father who delights in him. The holy one takes his place with sinners in the river, the first step on a road that ends at the cross, and the Father’s words name him both King and suffering Servant. Adam, the first son of God, failed his test; the last Adam now goes into the wilderness to be tested in our place, and to win.

For us. Ask whether you are leaning on anything other than Christ, a family, a church, a past experience, and turn from it to him. Let repentance reach your wallet and your work. And hear, in Christ, the Father’s verdict over everyone joined to him: beloved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — John the Baptist Prepares the Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word comes again, and it calls even God’s own people to turn round, because the Lord is coming and no privilege will shelter anyone who refuses. Luke names the powers of the day, and the word passes them all to reach John in the wilderness (vv. 1–2). John is Isaiah’s voice, preparing the Lord’s way so that all flesh may see his salvation (vv. 3–6). He knocks away the claim that descent from Abraham is enough (vv. 7–9), and gives the crowds, the tax collectors and the soldiers each a concrete answer; none is told to leave his work (vv. 10–14). Then he points to the mightier one who will baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire, and Luke calls it all good news (vv. 15–18). Herod shuts him in prison: the herald is silenced just as the King steps forward (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
John’s saying that God can raise children for Abraham from stones does not abolish the covenant with Abraham; it shows what that covenant always meant (see the note on vv. 8–9). The people of God are marked by repentance and faith, not by descent.

The baptism with the Spirit and fire holds together two sides of one coming (see the note on vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.examples:
John’s three answers show that repentance is not only a feeling but a change of direction that can be seen. For the crowd it meant sharing a spare tunic and food; for the tax collector, honest accounts; for the soldier, no threats and no false charges. For two of the three it meant staying in a compromised trade and doing it straight (see the note on vv. 12–13).

John also took his message to the palace, where it was dangerous, and finished in a cell (see the note on vv. 19–20).

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At a moment that can be dated in world history, God breaks centuries of prophetic silence, and his word passes every ruler of the day to reach John in the wilderness.

Luke the historian. Ancient historians dated great events by listing rulers, and Luke gives seven names in strict order of rank: one emperor, one governor, three tetrarchs, two high priests. Then the sentence turns, and the word of God passes every one of them to land on a man in a desert whom nobody had put on any list.

The fifteenth year of Tiberius. Tiberius succeeded Augustus in AD 14, so his fifteenth year was about AD 28–29, depending on how the years were counted; Jesus’ ministry began shortly after. Pilate was prefect of Judea from AD 26 to 36.

Herod tetrarch of Galilee. Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39; a tetrarch was a minor ruler under Rome. He would imprison and behead John (v. 20; 9:9). His brother Philip ruled the lands north-east of Galilee, and rebuilt Caesarea Philippi.

And Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene. Abilene lay north-west of Damascus. This name was long used to convict Luke of carelessness, since the only Lysanias known was a king executed in 36 BC, sixty years too early. Then an inscription found near Damascus, from the reign of Tiberius, named a Lysanias as tetrarch: a later man, holding exactly the office Luke gives him, in exactly his period. Luke was right.

Luke can be checked. Not every question is closed (the census of chapter 2 is still debated), but detail after detail once called a blunder has proved precise, as with the politarchs of Thessalonica (Acts 17:6) and the chief man of Malta (Acts 28:7); see the introduction. He reports something that happened, at a time that could have been marked on a Roman calendar.

Annas and Caiaphas. Officially there was one high priest. Annas held the office from AD 6 until the Romans deposed him in AD 15, but he remained the power behind it: five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas (AD 18–36) held it after him. Since the office was meant to be for life, many Jews may still have counted Annas the true high priest.

The word of God came to John. The standard formula for the call of a prophet: the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:2), to Hosea, to Joel, to Jonah. For centuries no prophet had been called in those words. Now the word comes again, not in Rome or Jerusalem, palace or temple, but in the wilderness, to John, the son of a country priest, as it once came to Moses at the back of the desert and Elijah at a brook. Not one of the men on Luke’s list could command a single word from heaven. God is the King of history, and his word waits on no one’s permission.

The court that would try the King. Many of these names will meet Jesus at the end. Pilate will sentence him (23:24); Herod will mock him and send him back in a splendid robe (23:11); the high priest’s house will hold him on the night of his arrest (22:54; John 18:13). Luke names, at the opening of the ministry, the very men before whom it will close. The word that passed them by was preparing the way of the one they would crucify, and whom God would raise and seat above every ruler on that list.

Does God still speak like this today? Not by calling new prophets with new words to add to Scripture. John was the last prophet of the old order, and God’s word came to its fullness in Christ, his final word (Hebrews 1:1–2), now written, complete and sufficient (the Westminster Confession 1.6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 1.6). But God still speaks it through the Scriptures, and still bypasses the powerful to do it: the word that came to John comes to you, with the same authority, when you open your Bible. Many faithful Christians believe prophecy continues in the church today, though nearly all agree that nothing may be added to Scripture; this commentary holds that such revelatory gifts belonged to the laying of the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20), and gladly owns those who differ as brothers and sisters.
verseByVerse.note: Luke dates John’s ministry like a historian: Tiberius’s fifteenth year was about AD 28–29. Philip ruled lands north-east of the lake; Abilene lay north-west of Damascus. Annas had been deposed as high priest but still held great influence; his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet, 'The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John calls Israel to turn back to God and be washed as a sign of forgiveness, and so he is Isaiah’s herald, clearing the road for the Lord himself.

Into all the region around the Jordan. The Jordan valley, north of the Dead Sea, was a place of crossing: Israel had entered the promised land across the Jordan under Joshua, out of forty years in the wilderness (Joshua 3). John stands at that river calling the nation to come out and start again, as if its whole history had to be wound back to the crossing.

Proclaiming a baptism of repentance. A baptism that expressed repentance (metanoia): a change of mind leading to a change of life, turning from sin to God. It is not first an emotion. A man can weep over his sin all night and repent of nothing, or turn round with a dry face and have repented completely. The test is not how sorry you felt but which way you are now facing.

Whom he baptised. Jews knew ritual washings, and Gentile converts to Judaism were probably baptised as they entered the covenant people. The startling thing was whom John baptised: Jews, God’s own people, washed like Gentiles, as if being born into the covenant people was not enough and Israel itself needed converting.

For the forgiveness of sins. John promised forgiveness to the truly repentant. The water did not forgive; it was the sign of a repentance God would honour, and it pointed forward to the one who would win forgiveness by his death.

Prepare the way of the Lord. Isaiah 40:3–5 opens Isaiah’s great prophecies of comfort and return from exile (“Comfort, comfort my people”, Isaiah 40:1), and John is its voice in the wilderness, the herald of the King. The picture is a road gang sent ahead of a visiting king to fill the holes, cut through the ridges and straighten the route. In Isaiah it is the LORD God himself who is coming, to lead his people home. John prepares for Jesus, so Jesus is the LORD who is coming. John is the road crew, and what he is levelling is the hearts of a nation.

A way in. The King sends his herald ahead not to keep sinners away but to make a way in. He does not wait for us to level our own hearts; he sends his word to do it, and then comes himself along the road. Zechariah sang that his son would give God’s people knowledge of salvation in the forgiveness of their sins (1:76–77), and Luke will end his Gospel with the same two words, repentance and forgiveness of sins, proclaimed to all nations (24:47). John’s message is the first form of the gospel.

How do I know if I have really repented? Look at the direction, not the feelings. Do you see your sin as an offence against God, not merely a mistake? Have you turned to him for mercy in Christ, rather than trying to make up for it yourself? Are you, by his grace, setting yourself against it, even if you still stumble? Repentance is not perfection but a changed direction that keeps turning back to God each time you fall. If you still love the sin and have no wish to leave it, ask God to grant you repentance (2 Timothy 2:25): he gives what he commands. And if you both love the sin and hate it, that tug of war is not proof that you have never repented; it is the fight the Spirit himself starts in every believer (Galatians 5:17).

Did John’s baptism itself forgive sins? No. Forgiveness came from God to those who repented; the washing was the sign of their turning, and those who had received it were later baptised in the name of Jesus (Acts 19:4–5). Christian baptism, too, does not forgive by the water; it signs a forgiveness received by faith, which is why it belongs to those who have repented and believed (Acts 2:38, 41). The water is precious as a sign, and nothing in it saves.

Where Christians differ: who should be baptised? Many faithful Christians baptise the infants of believers, seeing baptism as the sign of God’s covenant promise to families, as circumcision was. This commentary’s view: the New Testament pattern is repentance and faith first, then baptism; those who differ are honoured as brothers and sisters who trust the same Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Lord comes, everything in his way is levelled, the proud brought low and the crushed lifted up, and his salvation is shown to the whole human race.

Every valley filled. A landscape made passable: valleys come up, mountains come down, and everybody walks at the same height, the reversal Mary sang of (1:52). Nobody arrives on the level he was standing on. The person crushed flat by failure or shame is lifted; the person standing tall on his own ability and on being right is brought down. Both are necessary, and the ones who find it hardest are not usually the ones in the valley.

The crooked made straight. Crooked lives made straight, like the tax collectors and soldiers who come to John. Every honest person knows something in himself that answers to it: the habit of self-protection, the small dishonesty so old it feels like part of us. Isaiah says the road crew has been sent for that too.

All flesh. Here is why Luke kept quoting. Matthew and Mark quote only the first verse of Isaiah’s passage; Luke, writing with the whole world in view, goes on to reach this line, his great theme. “All flesh” means all humanity, Gentiles as well as Jews, as Simeon sang (2:30–32), and Acts ends with this salvation sent to the Gentiles (Acts 28:28). Isaiah’s highway runs through every landscape there is, and the salvation of God has been set where all flesh will see it: lifted up on a cross outside Jerusalem, and proclaimed to the ends of the earth.

What it does not mean. Not that all flesh shall be saved, but that all flesh shall see: a promise about the reach of the announcement, not the response to it. John goes straight on to show that seeing and receiving are not the same.

What about people who have never heard? They are not saved by their ignorance, nor condemned for rejecting a Christ they never heard of; they are condemned for their sin against the light they had (Romans 1:18–20; 2:12). That is exactly why this verse matters: God has determined that all flesh shall see his salvation, and has given his church the task of showing it to them (Romans 10:13–15). The right response is not speculation but prayer, giving and going; and we may trust that the Judge of all the earth will do right.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke continues the quotation to “all flesh shall see the salvation of God.”

parallels.desc: my eyes have seen your salvation

verseByVerse.quote: He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptized by him, 'You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
verseByVerse.commentary:
John warns the crowds that running from God’s judgment without any change of heart is not repentance.

He said therefore to the crowds. Not enemies, but people who had walked into the desert to be baptised, and this is how he greets them. Matthew says he addressed it to the Pharisees and Sadducees (Matthew 3:7); Luke applies it to the crowds, many of whom had perhaps come because it was the thing to do.

You brood of vipers. When fire swept through the dry scrub, snakes came racing out ahead of the flames. John looks at a crowd streaming down to the river and says: you look like the wildlife leaving a fire, running from judgment without any change of nature. “Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?” is sarcastic: did you think a dip in the river would be enough to escape God’s judgment?

Why so hard on people doing the right thing? Because he can see what they have come for. Religion can be pure damage limitation: get the ritual done, get the insurance in place, and change nothing whatever. A man may sincerely want to escape the consequences of his sin and have no interest at all in leaving it. John will not baptise that, and his terms follow at once: fruit that matches repentance.

What is the wrath of God? It is regularly caricatured, so it needs saying plainly. It is not divine temper, God losing control or taking offence. It is the settled, holy, entirely just opposition of God to everything that ruins what he has made. A God who looked at cruelty, abuse and betrayal and felt nothing would not be kinder but morally empty; we do not call a man good because he can watch a child harmed and remain unmoved. The wrath of God is the shadow cast by his love: it exists because he cares, infinitely, about what is being done to his world and the people in it.

Should a Christian fear God’s wrath? Not as one still under it. If you are in Christ, the wrath your sins deserved fell on him; he propitiated it, turning it away by bearing it himself (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2). Jesus delivers us from the wrath to come (1 Thessalonians 1:10), and there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1). So a believer fears God with reverence and awe, not with the terror of a condemned man. If you are not in Christ, the fear is a mercy: God’s warning while there is still time to flee to the only shelter.

verseByVerse.quote: Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Real repentance shows in a changed life, and no family tree or religious privilege can take its place, because God’s judgment is already at hand.

Fruits in keeping with repentance. Not a general improvement, but a visible change that fits the particular sin repented of, as a healthy tree is known by its fruit (6:43–45); John gives three worked examples (vv. 10–14). Paul preached the same: “that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance” (Acts 26:20).

Fruit is evidence, not payment. Here an anxious believer can be badly hurt. Fruit is evidence of repentance, not its cause, and it earns nothing: a tree does not become an apple tree by producing apples, but the apples are how you can tell. And no one’s fruit is without blemish: it is Christ’s perfect obedience, counted as ours, that makes our imperfect fruit acceptable to God for his sake (Philippians 3:9).

We have Abraham as our father. The answer everybody had ready: descent from Abraham, circumcision, membership of the covenant people. Some later rabbis taught that Abraham sat at the gate of hell to turn back any Israelite. John says: your ancestry will not save you.

From these stones. He is probably pointing; the Jordan valley is full of stones, and there may be a pun in Aramaic between children (banayya) and stones (abnayya). The God who made Isaac out of a dead womb can make a son of Abraham out of a rock. And he will: Gentiles, as dead to God as stones, will become Abraham’s children by sharing his faith (Romans 4:11–12; Galatians 3:7).

The axe is laid to the root. Not the branches: the root. This is not pruning. “Even now” means the blade is already resting against the wood, the axeman standing there; the fire is God’s judgment. Jesus would later tell of a fruitless fig tree given one last year to bear (13:6–9).

The green wood took the blow. The promises were made to Abraham and his offspring, and that offspring is Christ (Galatians 3:16, 29), the one tree in all Israel that bore every fruit God looked for; people become Abraham’s children by being joined to him. On the way to the cross Jesus called himself the green wood (23:31): the one living tree that deserved no fire took the blow, so that dead wood might be joined to him and live. God does not need any of us, and he chooses us anyway. He who can raise children for Abraham from the stones of the Jordan raised us, dead as stones, and made us his children.

The modern credentials. Christian parents; baptism, as an infant or as a believer; membership of a good church; thirty years in the same pew. Every one is a genuine mercy, and not one is repentance: a man may be inside all of it and never once have turned round to God.

Then is a Christian upbringing worthless? Far from it. It is one of the greatest privileges there is: hearing the gospel from childhood, seeing faith lived, being prayed for daily (2 Timothy 3:15). But privilege is not possession. Every child of believing parents must personally repent and trust Christ, and every one may. If you grew up in the church, thank God for it, and make sure you have done more than inherit the vocabulary. If you are a parent, do not assume your children are saved because they are yours; pray for them, teach them, and call them to Christ.

What if I look at my life and see so little fruit? Some self-examination is faithful and some corrosive, and the difference is where it looks for the answer. The corrosive kind stands under the tree counting, dislikes the number, and concludes it is not really a Christian. The faithful kind notices the shortage and goes back to the root; a man frightened by his own lack of fruit is in the exact condition John was preaching for. So do not despair: go back to Christ, abide in him, and ask for his Spirit; fruit grows from the vine, not from anxiety (John 15:5). And ask a trusted believer what they see; others often see fruit that we cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds asked him, 'What then shall we do?' And he answered them, 'Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repentance shows first in plain generosity: whoever has more than he needs shares with the one who has nothing.

What then shall we do? The right question, the one the preaching was for (Acts 2:37; 16:30). Nobody objects to being called snakes; told that the axe is at the root, they ask the only sensible thing. Three groups ask it (vv. 10, 12, 14), and only Luke records this exchange.

The most surprising answer. The last of the prophets, with the whole Old Testament behind him, is asked point-blank what repentance requires. He does not say: come to the temple; fast, pray, keep the feasts, tithe, study. He says: share.

Two tunics. The tunic was the basic garment worn next to the skin. Many poor people probably had only one; a second was a luxury. So the instruction is not to sell everything, nor to give until you are destitute. It is startlingly modest and startlingly concrete: if you have two and somebody near you has none, that is what the second one is for (1 John 3:17–18).

The one who was stripped of everything. John asks for the second tunic; the one whose way he prepares would give far more. Paul grounds all Christian giving here: “you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). At the cross the soldiers cast lots for his garments (23:34): the Lord of all was stripped of the last thing he had. People who have seen what Christ gave do not need to be argued into handing over a coat.

Whose is the second coat? The honest sums are uncomfortable: few of us own two tunics; we own thirty, several unworn in two years. John’s test is not what percentage we give away but whether the surplus is understood to be ours or to be for somebody. The person who thinks of the second coat as his property, to give from now and then, will give a little and feel good about it. The person who thinks of it as already belonging to whoever has none will simply hand it over, and not think of it as generosity at all.

What it does not mean. Not that salvation is earned by giving things away; not a political programme of enforced equality; not that it is wrong to own more than one of anything, or to save for the future (Proverbs 6:6–8; 1 Timothy 5:8). But a heart that has truly turned to God will turn toward the needy.

So how much should I give? Scripture sets no fixed percentage for the new covenant, but it gives principles. Give first to the Lord’s work through your local church, regularly and in proportion to what you have been given (1 Corinthians 16:2), generously and cheerfully (2 Corinthians 9:6–7). Many believers find the Old Testament tithe a helpful starting point, not a ceiling. And keep your eyes open, as John says, for the person near you who has none: the brother out of work, the neighbour with an empty fridge. Generosity starts with what is in front of you.
verseByVerse.note: The tunic was the inner garment; a second one was a spare.

verseByVerse.quote: Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him, 'Teacher, what shall we do?' And he said to them, 'Collect no more than you are authorized to do.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the despised tax collectors may repent, and for them repentance means doing the same job honestly, whatever it costs.

Tax collectors also came to be baptized. Tax collectors were Jews working the Roman revenue system. The right to collect tolls and customs was commonly sold to the highest bidder, who kept whatever he could collect above it: a system that invited extortion, and made him, to his neighbours, a traitor and a thief with legal protection. Yet they came to John, as they would to Jesus (5:27–32; 15:1; 19:1–10), and they call John “Teacher”, a courtesy the crowds did not bother with.

No more than you are authorized. John does not tell them to quit a profession soaked in injustice and tied to a pagan empire, but to do the job honestly. The state has the right to taxes (20:25; Romans 13:6–7). Repentance does not usually mean leaving your calling, but living differently in it.

What it cost. John is telling these men to accept a permanent drop in income for a clear conscience, while colleagues who go on overcharging do better. That is far harder than resigning: resigning is over in a day; this is every day.

Friend of tax collectors. John sends these men back to the tax table honest. The one he was preparing for would sit down at their tables and be called “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (7:34). Zacchaeus is not told to repay anyone; he is found and welcomed, and the repayment pours out of him unasked (19:8). John could describe the fruit; Jesus makes the tree new, for “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (19:10). No profession is so despised that his grace cannot walk into it and make a man new.

Should I leave a job in a compromised industry? Sometimes leaving is right: if your job requires you to lie, cheat or take part in what God forbids, you must “obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). But John’s answer to men in a corrupt trade was to send them back into it clean. Ask whether you can do this work without sinning. If you can, stay and be the honest one, at whatever cost. If you cannot, seek counsel, pray, and plan your way out.
verseByVerse.note: Tax collectors typically profited from whatever they could collect above the amount owed.

verseByVerse.quote: Soldiers also asked him, 'And we, what shall we do?' And he said to them, 'Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soldiers too may repent and keep their post, but they must stop using their power to take what is not theirs, and learn to be content.

Soldiers also asked him. “And we?” Is there anything for men like them? These were probably Jewish soldiers in Herod’s service, or police who protected the tax collectors: men with power, weapons and poor pay, and the temptations that go with them.

Threats and false accusation. “Extort by threats” is literally shake down; “false accusation” (sykophantēsēte) is blackmail. A soldier could report a man, the report would be believed, and the man would pay to make it go away.

Content with your wages. The root of their sins was discontent and greed, and contentment is the cure (Philippians 4:11–12; 1 Timothy 6:6–10; Hebrews 13:5). Deal with extortion by prohibition alone and you have a man permanently resentful, obeying with clenched teeth; deal with it by contentment and the temptation has nothing left to take hold of. Contentment is not a temperament but something acquired, slowly, by people who have found something they cannot lose and measure everything else against it.

Three answers, all at the wallet. Asked what repentance looks like, the last prophet of the old covenant answered three times, to the crowd, the tax men and the soldiers, at the wallet. Not because money is the worst of sins, but because what a man does with his money shows, in figures, what he really believes, whatever he says.

A centurion at the cross. Luke keeps soldiers in view to the end; they mock Jesus on the cross (23:36–37). The one man who had all power refused to use it for himself, and when he died, the centurion in charge praised God and said, “Certainly this man was innocent!” (23:47). John told soldiers to stop taking by force. Jesus showed a soldier what power is for: laid down, to save others.

In everyday life. List the small powers you hold, over a child, an employee, a customer, a spouse, and ask whether any of them is being used to get what you want at someone else’s cost.

May a Christian serve as a soldier or police officer? Yes. John does not tell the soldiers to leave the army, but to be honest and content in it, and held to justice: no abuse of power, no cruelty.

How do I learn contentment? Paul learned its secret, in prison (Philippians 4:12), so it can be learned. Give thanks, specifically and daily, for what you have; gratitude starves discontent. Notice the comparisons that feed it, the adverts, the feeds, the friend’s new house, and starve them. Remember what you cannot lose: Christ has said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you”, the reason Hebrews gives for being content (Hebrews 13:5). And give some away; generosity loosens money’s grip. Contentment does not mean you may never seek a better wage, but that your peace does not depend on getting it.
verseByVerse.note: These were probably Jewish soldiers serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John, whether he might be the Christ, John answered them all, saying, 'I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the people wonder whether John is the Messiah, he points away from himself to one far greater, who will do what water cannot: baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire.

In expectation. Hope for the Messiah was intense, and here was a prophet like Elijah. Malachi had promised that Elijah would come before the great day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5), and John even dressed like him (2 Kings 1:8; Mark 1:6). Many under Roman rule hoped for an anointed son of David who would drive out the foreigners and purify Jerusalem, a hope voiced in the Psalms of Solomon a century before. A prophet’s voice, heard again after some four hundred years, set every heart asking whether the hour had come.

Whether he might be the Christ. After the three questions of vv. 10–14, the question underneath surfaces: is John the answer? He could have had the title merely by not correcting them. He did not let the question hang for a sentence.

I baptize you with water. Only water, an outward sign, which can wash a man’s skin and leave his heart untouched. What people need is someone who can change them from the inside, and John cannot. So he points away from himself, as he always did: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

Not worthy to untie. Untying a master’s sandals was the job of the lowest slave; later rabbis said a disciple should do anything for his teacher except that. The greatest of the prophets (7:28) counts himself unworthy to be the Messiah’s slave: not a poor self-image but the true measure of the distance between them, and knowing it set John free. A man who needs the crowd’s admiration will always keep a little of it for himself; John could give all of it away, because his joy was in the voice of the bridegroom (John 3:29). And this Lord, whose sandals the greatest man born of women was not worthy to untie, would kneel and wash his disciples’ feet.

The Holy Spirit and fire. John’s baptism was outward; the Messiah’s will be inward, a drenching in God himself, as Ezekiel and Joel promised (Ezekiel 36:25–27; Joel 2:28–29), fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:1–4). John can put a man under the water; only God can put the Spirit inside him. To be baptised with the Spirit is to have God himself come to live in you, so that the change reaches the place water cannot: a new heart that begins to love God, trust Christ and turn from sin (Romans 5:5; 8:9).

I have been told I lack the baptism of the Spirit. What now? If you trust in Christ, you have the Spirit; you could not call Jesus Lord without him (1 Corinthians 12:3). You are not a second-class Christian waiting for a missing experience, and the years of anxiety some believers spend over this are not from God. Thank him that you are already joined to Christ by his Spirit. Then ask, as Jesus told us to (11:13), for more of the Spirit’s work: more love, holiness, boldness and joy, sought through the means he has given, the word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and fellowship, rather than through a particular sensation.

Where Christians differ: the baptism of the Spirit. Pentecostal teaching holds that baptism in the Spirit is a second experience after conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues, pointing to the Samaritans and the Ephesian disciples, who received the Spirit after believing (Acts 8:14–17; 19:1–7), and to the disciples themselves at Pentecost. Many who hold that view love Christ better than most of us. This commentary’s view: all believers are baptised by the Spirit into Christ at conversion: in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body, and anyone without the Spirit does not belong to Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13; Romans 8:9). Those moments in Acts were special occasions when the gospel crossed new frontiers, and Pentecost was the once-for-all outpouring at the start of the new age. Peter applies John’s words to Cornelius’s household the moment they believed: God gave them the same gift as he gave to us when we believed (Acts 11:16–17). Believers are commanded to be continually filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), not to seek a second baptism; and that is the ground for asking for more of his work, out of security rather than fear.

Uncertain wording. What John meant by “and fire” is not certain. Some take it as the tongues of fire at Pentecost (Acts 2:3), others as a refining of believers (Malachi 3:2–3), others as the fire of judgment on the unrepentant (v. 17); fire in Scripture can purify or destroy. The likeliest reading, as the winnowing fork goes on to show, is one baptism with two outcomes: the Spirit for those who repent, and the fire of judgment for the chaff. John announces a Messiah who will both save and judge.
verseByVerse.note: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job.

verseByVerse.quote: His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The coming one will finally separate his true people from the rest: the wheat gathered safely into his barn, the chaff burned in a fire that never goes out.

His winnowing fork is in his hand. After threshing, grain was tossed into the air with a winnowing fork, a broad wooden shovel, on a threshing floor open to the wind. The heavy grain fell back; the light chaff blew away, to be swept up and burned. The tool does not create the difference between wheat and chaff; it reveals it. And the fork is already in his hand: not fetched when needed, held.

The wheat into his barn. The true people of God, the repentant, are named first, because the whole operation exists for the barn.

The chaff he will burn. There is no honest way to soften that. The unrepentant will be judged with fire that cannot be put out (Mark 9:43, 48), and no one in Scripture says so more often or more plainly than Jesus himself. The Messiah is not only Saviour but Judge (John 5:22; Acts 17:31).

Nobody has to be chaff. The winnower is announced beforehand, while there is still time, by a man standing in a river. Nobody has to be chaff; that is why he is shouting. The Judge with the fork in his hand is the Saviour who went into the fire for his wheat, and he will not lose one grain of it.

How can this be good news? Yet Luke calls it good news (v. 18). A universe with no final sorting is one where nothing is ever put right: the fire is terrible, but a harvest with no fire in it would be a harvest with no justice in it (see the note on v. 7).

How can a loving God send anyone to hell? Because he is holy and just, and sin against an infinitely holy God is infinitely serious. Hell is God giving people, justly, what their sin deserves and what they have chosen: a life without him, for ever. And the same God sent his Son to bear that very judgment in the place of all who trust him. No one goes to hell who wanted Christ and was refused. If the doctrine troubles you, let it drive you to Christ, and to pray and speak for those who do not know him. It troubled the apostles too, and it made them preachers.

Where Christians differ: is hell conscious and eternal? Some evangelicals hold, as John Stott tentatively did, that the wicked will finally be destroyed and cease to exist, pointing to the picture of chaff burned up and to words like destroy (Matthew 10:28). This commentary’s view: the mainstream of the church has not read it so, and Christ’s words are hard to bend that way. The fire here is unquenchable; Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence (Matthew 25:46); the smoke of their torment goes up for ever and ever (Revelation 14:11). The punishment is conscious and unending (the Westminster Confession 33.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 32.2). The reality and finality of the judgment are not in dispute among any who take the text seriously, and those who hold the other view are brothers and sisters wrestling honestly with the same texts.
verseByVerse.note: A winnowing fork tossed threshed grain into the wind; the heavy grain fell back and the chaff blew away.

verseByVerse.quote: So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke calls all of John’s preaching good news, warnings included, because it announced the Saviour who was coming. With many other exhortations: we have the shape of months of preaching, not the transcript.

He preached good news to the people. “Preached good news” (euēngelizeto): evangelised. John called the congregation a nest of snakes, knocked away their one credential and finished with a fire that cannot be put out, and Luke calls it good news. The warnings are not something to be got through before the good news starts; Luke sees one thing, not two, and calls all of it gospel, because the bad news makes the good news necessary and precious. A gospel without warning of judgment is not the gospel. If the axe really is at the root, the man who tells you so is not being harsh; he is being kind at some personal cost, and the man who assures you the tree is fine is not being kind at all. Nobody thanks a watchman who saw the sword coming and kept quiet (Ezekiel 33:6).

Good news because of who was coming. What made John’s warnings good news was the one they announced. The axe was at the root, but the mightier one was at the door, coming to baptise with the Spirit, to gather his wheat, and to save. John brought good news by pointing to another; Jesus would bring it by coming himself (4:18; 16:16). The gospel John preached to the ordinary people of Judea was, in the end, a person.

How do I warn someone without driving them away? Let them see that you warn them because you love them, not because you enjoy it or want to win. Speak of sin and judgment as one under the same need, never from above, plainly but gently and patiently (2 Timothy 2:24–26). Never stop at the warning: point to Christ, the way of escape, in the same breath. Choose your moment and listen first. And remember that it is the Spirit who convicts; your part is to be faithful and kind.

verseByVerse.quote: But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John told Herod the truth about his sin, and Herod, instead of repenting, locked him up.

Reproved for Herodias. Herodias, Herod’s niece, had been married to his half-brother (called Philip in Mark 6:17; not the tetrarch of v. 1). To marry her, Herod divorced the daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, an insult that later cost him a war. The marriage broke God’s law: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife” (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). John told Herod to his face that it was unlawful (Mark 6:18): a prophet confronting a king, as Nathan confronted David.

He did not have to. Nobody required a preacher at the Jordan to address the tetrarch’s marriage; John could have preached repentance for years without mentioning the palace, and died an old man. He went to the one man in the country who could have him killed, and told him the truth about his private life.

All the evil things. Not one sermon about one marriage: John kept at it, across the whole range of the man’s conduct, and Mark adds that Herod was greatly perplexed by him and yet heard him gladly (Mark 6:20). It is possible to enjoy sermons for years and still hold on to the one sin they keep naming. Herod could bear to hear about his sin; he could not bear to give up Herodias. A man who will not let go of his idol will in the end silence whoever names it.

Added this to them all. Instead of repenting, he silenced the preacher.
