The Jewish historian Josephus says John was held in the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea, and Herod later had him beheaded (9:9; Mark 6:17–29). Luke tells of the imprisonment here, before Jesus’ baptism (v. 21), though it happened later, to round off John’s story and clear the stage: John decreases; Jesus increases. The voice is silenced just as the Word begins to speak. Herod could shut the door on John; he could do nothing whatever about the man standing in the water at verse 21.

The forerunner goes first into the dark. John goes before Jesus even here. Herod will hear of Jesus and say, “John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?” (9:9), and when at last they meet, Jesus will give him no answer at all (23:9). The prison at Machaerus is the first shadow of the cross. The one whose sandals John was not worthy to untie would follow his herald into the hands of wicked men, not because he could not escape them, but because he had come to die for sinners, those like Herod and those like John.

Faithfulness is not always repaid here. John did exactly what he was sent to do, without flinching and without ambition, and he finished in a cell, executed at a birthday feast because a girl danced well and her mother held a grudge. His reward was not in this life, and Jesus would say of him that “among those born of women none is greater” (7:28).

In everyday life. Who last told you a hard truth about yourself? Did you thank them, or shut the door? Silencing the one who names your sin only adds to it, while the Christ they point you to stands ready to forgive.

Should Christians speak out about the sins of public figures? Sometimes, yes, as John, Nathan and Elijah did. Church leaders must declare God’s law plainly, to the powerful too, and Christians may rightly say that what a ruler does is wrong. But notice John’s manner: he spoke to Herod, not merely about him; he was moved by the law of God, not by party politics; and he paid for it himself. Speak truth about public sin without gossip, without glee, and without forgetting the sins nearer home. And pray for rulers, including the ones you must oppose (1 Timothy 2:1–2).
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas. Herodias had been married to his half-brother. Luke tells of John’s imprisonment here, ahead of the story, to close his account of John.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At his baptism Jesus takes his place with sinners, and heaven declares who he is. Luke tells the baptism itself almost as an aside: Jesus goes into the water of repentance with the people he came to save, though he had nothing to repent of (v. 21). What Luke dwells on is what happened while he was praying: the heavens opened, the Spirit came down like a dove, and the Father spoke (v. 22). The Father’s words join Psalm 2:7 with Isaiah 42:1: Jesus is both the King who will reign and the Servant who will suffer.
verseByVerse.theology: The Father declares his delight in the Son before Jesus has preached a sermon or done a miracle, and those who are in Christ share that standing (see the note on v. 22).
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus prays at his baptism, and Luke shows him praying at every great turning point after it (see the note on v. 21). And at the Jordan the three persons of the Trinity are present together and distinct: the doctrine is not a puzzle invented by later councils, but the church’s attempt to describe what happened here.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heavens were opened,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, who had nothing to repent of, is baptised among the crowd of sinners, and as he prays, heaven opens.

When all the people were baptized. Luke does not describe the baptism itself, only where Jesus stood: among the crowd, one of the people, in the same river, receiving the same sign.

Jesus also. What is the one man with nothing to repent of doing in the water of repentance? Matthew records John’s objection, and Jesus’ answer: let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness (Matthew 3:14–15). He is not there because he needs what the water means. On the first day of his public life he took his place among the sinners he came to save, and he never stepped out of that place until he had carried their sins to the cross.

And was praying. Only Luke notes this, the first of many times. Prayer marks every turning point of Jesus’ life in Luke: here, before choosing the Twelve (6:12), before Peter’s confession (9:18), at the transfiguration (9:28–29), in Gethsemane and on the cross. It is not a technique that opens the heavens, but the posture of a Son who depends on his Father for everything.

The heavens were opened. As Isaiah prayed: “Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down” (Isaiah 64:1). The barrier between heaven and earth is opened, and God is about to speak.

The opening move of the great exchange. What begins in the Jordan is finished on a hill where he dies the sinners’ death, numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12; Luke 22:37). He takes the place of sinners, with their guilt and punishment, and they are given his place: his righteousness, which means his perfect record of doing right, and his welcome with the Father. God “made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Does Jesus’ baptism mean I should be baptised? Yes, though for a different reason. He was baptised to identify with sinners; we are baptised as sinners who have been joined to him, to show that we have died and risen with Christ (Romans 6:3–4). He commanded his disciples to baptise those who become disciples (Matthew 28:19), and the New Testament pattern is that those who believe are baptised (Acts 2:41; 8:12, 36–38). If you trust Christ and have never been baptised as a believer, speak to your pastor. It does not save you, but it is the obedience of the saved, and the Lord who stepped into the Jordan for you asks it of you. (On Christians who baptise infants, dear brothers and sisters, see the note on vv. 3–4.)
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke notes that Jesus was praying.

verseByVerse.quote: and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, 'You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father declares from heaven that Jesus is his beloved Son, and the Spirit comes upon him: in one sentence he is named both the promised King and the Servant who will suffer.

The Trinity. The Father speaks from heaven, the Son is baptised, the Spirit descends: one of the clearest revelations in Scripture of one God in three persons, each distinct and each active.

And the Holy Spirit descended on him. Anointing him for his ministry. He has been the Christ, the Anointed One, from his birth (2:11); now he is publicly anointed with the Spirit (4:18; Acts 10:38). To anoint is to set apart and equip for a task: he did not become divine at the Jordan, but as a man was publicly commissioned and filled with power for his work as Prophet, Priest and King, as Isaiah foretold: “the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him” (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1).

In bodily form, like a dove. Only Luke says “in bodily form”: a visible appearance, not a private impression. Why a dove? A dove came back to Noah over a drowned world, and the judgment was over (Genesis 8:8–12); and at the beginning the Spirit hovered over the face of the waters (Genesis 1:2). The Spirit is over the water again: a new creation begins.

You are my beloved Son. The voice weaves two Scriptures together. “You are my Son” is Psalm 2:7, the psalm for the crowning of David’s royal sons. “Beloved” may also echo Genesis 22:2, Isaac, Abraham’s beloved only son, who was to be sacrificed.

With you I am well pleased. Isaiah 42:1: “Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him.” This opens the first of Isaiah’s songs of the Servant of the LORD, whom the later songs show crushed for the sins of many (Isaiah 53). In one sentence the Father declares Jesus both Son-King and suffering Servant: the throne and the cross, laid on him together. And the delight is not a wage paid for work completed; it is the settled love of the Father for the Son, older than the world (John 17:24).

In the flow. “Son” ties the next chapter and a half together: Adam, the son of God (v. 38), the devil’s “If you are the Son of God” (4:3, 9), and Nazareth’s “Is not this Joseph’s son?” (4:22). Whatever Satan suggests and the neighbours assume, heaven has already said who he is.

For believers. The one the world was made for, come to mend its ruin, stands in a river one morning, and heaven is entirely delighted with him. The Father, pleased with his Son before the first sermon or healing, is pleased with us in him (Ephesians 1:6): not earned, not on trial, not reviewed annually. You do not work in order to be loved. You are loved, and then you work.

How can God be pleased with me when I keep failing? Because his pleasure in you rests on Christ, not on your record: he sees a believer clothed in his Son’s righteousness, and delights in him as in his Son. Your failures grieve him, as a father is grieved, and he will discipline you for your good, but they do not change his verdict, because it was never based on you. So when you fail, do not hide; run to him, confess, and hear again over your head what he said over his Son’s: “beloved”. That is not licence to sin; it is the only soil in which real obedience grows.

Did Jesus become the Son of God at his baptism? No. He was the Son from eternity, and Luke has already said that the child to be born would be called the Son of God (1:35). The baptism was the public anointing of the Son for his work, not his becoming Son.

Textual note. Some ancient manuscripts here read “today I have begotten you” (the words of Psalm 2:7), which some took to mean he was adopted as Son at the Jordan; the better-attested text reads “with you I am well pleased”.

parallels.desc: the servant in whom God delights

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–38 — The Genealogy of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is a true son of Adam, come for the whole human race, and the Son of God declared at the Jordan. Luke’s genealogy differs from Matthew’s: it runs backwards, from Jesus to Adam; it comes after the baptism rather than before the birth; and it goes past Abraham to Adam, and past Adam to God. Matthew presents Jesus as the fulfilment of Israel’s story; Luke, writing with the world in view, as the answer to the human story. The two lists differ in many names between David and Joseph, though both trace Jesus to David (vv. 23–31). The line runs through foreigners, deception and disgrace which God did not clean up first (vv. 32–34), and ends with the son of Adam, the son of God (vv. 35–38).
verseByVerse.theology: By tracing Jesus to Adam, Luke shows that his humanity is one with that of every person who has ever lived, and lays the foundation for Paul’s contrast between Adam and Christ (see the note on vv. 35–38).
verseByVerse.examples: Readers often skip genealogies, but this one is the gospel in miniature. Salvation came not through power or privilege but through the long, winding and sometimes scandalous history of real families, most of whom had no idea what they were part of. A Jesus who was only divine could not represent us; a Jesus who was only human would have no righteousness to give. The son of Adam who is the Son of God is the Saviour we need.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus begins his public work at about thirty, legally Joseph’s son though not by blood, and Luke now traces his human family line.

Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age. “About thirty” is what a careful historian writes when he lacks the precise date. Thirty was the age for public service: Levites at the sanctuary (Numbers 4:3), David on the throne (2 Samuel 5:4). Eighteen years of that life had gone by since the last thing Luke recorded, and not one line of them survives.

As was supposed. Luke guards the virgin birth. After two chapters establishing that Joseph is not this child’s father, he will not quietly contradict himself. Jesus was Joseph’s son by law, by household, by trade and by every register in Galilee; not by blood. He who is the eternal Son allowed himself to be supposed something less, content to be thought the carpenter’s son.

Why the genealogy is here. Matthew opens his Gospel with the genealogy, tracing Jesus forward from Abraham to show him the son of Abraham and of David, the Jewish Messiah (Matthew 1:1–17). Luke places his after the baptism, just before the temptation, and traces it backward to Adam, the son of God (on why, see the note on vv. 35–38).

The son of Heli. Set Luke’s list beside Matthew’s, and from David onwards they do not match: Matthew says Joseph’s father was Jacob (Matthew 1:16), and comes down through Solomon and the kings; Luke comes through Nathan (see the note on vv. 25–31).

Why do the two genealogies differ? Christians have given three main answers. One: Luke gives Mary’s line, and Heli was Mary’s father, Joseph being reckoned son of Heli as his son-in-law. That fits Luke’s careful “as was supposed” and his close interest in Mary through chapters 1 and 2, though Luke writes “son of Heli”, not “father of Mary”. Two: Matthew gives the royal, legal line of succession through Solomon, and Luke the physical descent of Joseph through Nathan. Three: levirate marriage, by which a man who died childless had offspring raised up to his name by his brother (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), so that one man could have a legal and a biological father under two names; Julius Africanus (about AD 220) gave this explanation, saying it came from Jesus’ own relatives.

Which is most likely? Each answer carries a difficulty, and genealogies in that world were kept to make a point, not to satisfy a modern registrar. The more likely answer is that Matthew traces Joseph’s legal, royal line through Solomon, while Luke traces the physical line through Nathan, probably Mary’s, with Heli as Joseph’s father-in-law. But any of these is possible, and we cannot now be sure which is right; believers may hold both lists true while leaving that question open. Either way both Gospels trace Jesus to David, and the difference does real work rather than real damage: the crown comes down one branch of David’s family, and the blood, most likely, down another, and they meet in him.

Uncertain wording. In Greek, every name in the list carries the small word rendered “the son of” except Joseph’s. Some therefore read the bracket as covering Joseph alone, being the son (as was supposed, of Joseph) of Heli, that is, truly descended from Heli through his mother, which would support the view that Luke traces Mary’s line. The grammar allows that reading but does not require it, so it cannot settle the question.
verseByVerse.note: Thirty was the age of maturity for public service. Luke’s genealogy runs backward and differs from Matthew’s after David; many think Luke traces Mary’s line or Joseph’s legal line.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai, the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda, the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri, the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er, the son of Joshua, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim, the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David,
verseByVerse.commentary:
From Joseph back to David the line runs through forgotten names and through Nathan rather than Solomon, and God kept every link of it until David’s promised Son was born.

Names we do not know. Most of these men appear nowhere else in Scripture: Maath, Naggai, Esli, Josech. No stories, no deeds; ordinary people, faithful or unfaithful, in whose line God was working toward the birth of his Son.

The son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel. Apart from Nathan and David, the only two names here found elsewhere in Scripture. Zerubbabel led a return of the Jews from exile in Babylon, and laid the foundation of the second temple (Ezra 3; Haggai 1–2). Both genealogies include him and his father Shealtiel, perhaps because the two lines crossed there.

The son of Nathan, the son of David. Luke’s line runs through Nathan, a son of David by Bathsheba (2 Samuel 5:14). Matthew’s runs through Solomon, the line with the legal right to the throne, and also the line of King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), of whom the LORD said that none of his offspring would succeed in sitting on the throne of David (Jeremiah 22:30). A curse lies across the royal succession.

The crown and the blood. Luke’s line runs through a son who never reigned and so never came under that curse. On one common reading, Jesus, descended by blood through Nathan, escapes the curse while inheriting the legal right to the throne through Joseph. However the details are explained, God kept every promise he made to David, through curses and exile and centuries of obscurity, until the Son of David came.

God kept their names. History has kept nothing about these men except that they existed, married and had a son; God kept their names. Not one lived to see the point of his place in the list, and every one was necessary, because the Son of God came through their houses.

Does an ordinary, unremembered life matter to God? Yes, more than we can see. Most believers leave no name on a plaque, but God records what the world forgets. He numbers the hairs of your head (12:7), writes the names of his people in the book of life (Philippians 4:3), and remembers a cup of cold water given in his name (Matthew 10:42). A faithful marriage, children raised in the faith, honest work, prayers for a grandchild: these are the links through which he has always carried his purposes. You may never see what your place in the line was for. He does.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s line runs through Nathan, David’s son, not Solomon.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon, the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The line of the promise runs through foreigners, scandal and failure, and God did not clean the family up before sending his Son through it.

Jesse, Obed, Boaz. Now the names become recognisable: this is the last page of the book of Ruth (Ruth 4:18–22). Boaz married Ruth, a Moabite widow, from a people the law had barred from the assembly of the LORD to the tenth generation (Deuteronomy 23:3). Luke does not name her, but the line of the Messiah runs through a woman who by birth had no right to be anywhere near it: God’s plan included Gentiles from the beginning.

The son of Perez, the son of Judah. Here the list goes where most family trees would rather not. Perez was born to Judah by Tamar, his widowed daughter-in-law, whom Judah failed to provide for and then took for a prostitute at a roadside without recognising her (Genesis 38). It is one of the ugliest chapters in Genesis, and that is where the line runs. Yet Jacob had prophesied that the sceptre, the king’s rod of rule, would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10): the King would come from this family.

Jacob, Isaac, Abraham. The patriarchs of the promise (Genesis 12:1–3): Jacob the deceiver; Isaac, born to parents long past hope; Abraham, who twice passed his wife off as his sister to save his own skin, and was given the promise anyway. Matthew begins here; Luke goes further back, to Terah and Nahor, Abraham’s father and grandfather, who lived beyond the Euphrates and served other gods (Joshua 24:2). God called Abraham out of a pagan family.

He did not clean it up first. Without a word of comment, this stretch says that God brought his Son into the world through a family history of deception, prostitution, foreignness, cowardice, idolatry and long stretches of nothing at all, and has had it read aloud in public for two thousand years. The family did not have to be made clean first, because the child at the end of it would make it clean. The Son of God took a family tree full of sin so that he could carry the sin itself: God made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). The one born of Judah and Tamar’s line is the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5), and the Lamb who was slain to ransom people from every tribe.

What about my family history? A family history is one of the things people are least able to change and most often ashamed of: the divorce, the addiction, the prison sentence, the abuse, the generations who never knew God. Luke quietly reports that the Saviour of the world has one too, and that God did not require it to be respectable before he would work through it. Your family’s past does not decide your future in Christ. Patterns can be broken by grace (Ezekiel 18:14–17). Grieve what was wrong, forgive what you can, seek help where you need it, and begin a new line of faithfulness. God has done it before.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke traces Jesus past Abraham to Adam, and past Adam to God: he belongs to the whole human race, and he has come as its new head.

Beyond Abraham. Matthew stops at Abraham; Luke runs back past the flood to the first man, and one step further, and the difference is the whole shape of his Gospel. Jesus is not only the Jewish Messiah but the Saviour of the human race, Luke’s great theme: “all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (v. 6).

The son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad. For the reader with Genesis open: this Cainan (v. 36) is not in the Hebrew text of Genesis 11:12, which runs Arphaxad, then Shelah, but appears in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), which Luke and his readers used. Whether the Greek preserves a dropped name or a copyist’s eye slipped cannot be settled. Ancient genealogies could skip generations, since “son of” can mean “descendant of”; Matthew does so openly.

Noah, Enoch, Seth. Noah, in whom the human race came through the flood, narrowed to one boat. Enoch, who “walked with God, and he was not, for God took him” (Genesis 5:24). Seth, born after Abel’s murder; in his days “people began to call upon the name of the LORD” (Genesis 4:26).

The son of Adam, the son of God. The climax. Adam had no human father; created directly by God, he is called God’s son. Jesus too had no human father; he is the eternal Son of God made man. Now the reason for placing the genealogy after the baptism is plain: at verse 22 a voice from heaven said, “You are my beloved Son”, and at verse 38 the list arrives at the same title from the other end. The Son declared at the Jordan is traced back, through seventy generations of ordinary and disgraceful and forgotten people, to Adam, and past Adam to God.

One of us. That is the point of every name in the list. He was no visitor wearing the costume of our race; he entered the human story in one particular family, with real ancestors all the way back to the beginning. He is inside the race Adam ruined, as one of us, related by blood to every person who has ever lived.

The last Adam. Adam, the first son of God, failed his test in a garden and plunged humanity into sin and death. Jesus, the true Son, is about to be tested in the wilderness (4:1–13), and will not fail. He is the last Adam, the head of a new humanity (Romans 5:12–21; 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45–49). As head, what he does counts for all who belong to him: Adam’s one disobedience brought condemnation on everyone in him; Christ’s obedience, shown first in the wilderness and finished on the cross, brings a right standing with God and life to everyone joined to him by faith (Romans 5:18–19).

At the end of the list. Between the two men at the head of the human race runs a chain of dust returning to dust, from a garden to a river in Judea. At its end, the Spirit resting on him and his Father’s voice still in the air, stands the one who came to break it: the last Adam, who would go down into the dust himself and come up on the third day with a new humanity in him.

Does it matter whether Adam was a real man? Yes. Luke lists Adam as a real ancestor alongside David and Abraham, and Paul’s argument in Romans 5 depends on one man’s sin bringing death and one man’s obedience bringing life: without a first Adam, the parallel with the last Adam loses its footing. Christians discuss many questions about Genesis and science, and should do so humbly; but the Bible’s teaching that all humanity descends from one man created by God, who fell, and that Christ came as the second head of a redeemed humanity, is part of the gospel itself.
verseByVerse.note: Luke traces the line back to Adam: Jesus belongs to all humanity. The Cainan of verse 36 appears in the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 11, not the Hebrew.

3.text: <sup>1</sup> In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, <sup>2</sup> during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness. <sup>3</sup> And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. <sup>4</sup> As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. <sup>5</sup> Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways, <sup>6</sup> and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.’” <sup>7</sup> He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptized by him, “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? <sup>8</sup> Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. <sup>9</sup> Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.” <sup>10</sup> And the crowds asked him, “What then shall we do?” <sup>11</sup> And he answered them, “Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.” <sup>12</sup> Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him, “Teacher, what shall we do?” <sup>13</sup> And he said to them, “Collect no more than you are authorized to do.” <sup>14</sup> Soldiers also asked him, “And we, what shall we do?” And he said to them, “Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.” <sup>15</sup> As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John, whether he might be the Christ, <sup>16</sup> John answered them all, saying, “I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. <sup>17</sup> His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.” <sup>18</sup> So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people. <sup>19</sup> But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, <sup>20</sup> added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison. <sup>21</sup> Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heavens were opened, <sup>22</sup> and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.” <sup>23</sup> Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, <sup>24</sup> the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph, <sup>25</sup> the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai, <sup>26</sup> the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda, <sup>27</sup> the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri, <sup>28</sup> the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er, <sup>29</sup> the son of Joshua, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, <sup>30</sup> the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim, <sup>31</sup> the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David, <sup>32</sup> the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon, <sup>33</sup> the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, <sup>34</sup> the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor, <sup>35</sup> the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, <sup>36</sup> the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, <sup>37</sup> the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, <sup>38</sup> the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.

keyVerse.quote: and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.”
keyVerse.note: Here heaven answers the question the whole chapter raises: who is the mightier one John announced? The Father names Jesus his beloved Son, the Spirit anoints him, and the words join the King of Psalm 2 to the suffering Servant of Isaiah 42. The genealogy traces the same title back to Adam, and the devil will test it at once (4:3).

3.reflection:
John’s hearers trusted their descent from Abraham (v. 8). What do people lean on in the same way today, and what are you most tempted to trust instead of turning to Christ?

Asked what repentance looks like, John spoke about spare clothes, honest tax collecting and soldiers’ wages (vv. 10–14). Why do you think he went straight to money and work? What would fruit in keeping with repentance look like in your job and your spending?

Luke calls John’s preaching of the axe, the winnowing fork and the fire good news (vv. 17–18). How can warning of judgment be part of the good news, and how can we speak of it to others with love?

Jesus, who had no sin, was baptised among sinners and heard the Father call him beloved (vv. 21–22). What difference does it make that, in Christ, the Father’s pleasure rests on you too, especially when you fail?

4.title: The Testing and the Anointing
4.overview:
Where we are. Jesus has just been baptised, named the Father’s beloved Son, and traced back to Adam (3:21–38). Chapter 4 opens his public work: the testing, the sermon that announces it, and a first day that shows it.

The message. The Spirit-anointed Son has come, and his word has authority over everything that holds people captive. He will not be turned from his Father’s way by hunger, power or a religious short cut; he announces that God’s promised release begins today; and that release reaches past those who think they own it to outsiders.

Why it was said. Luke’s largely Gentile readers needed to be sure of what they had been taught (1:4; see the introduction). Here they learn what kind of Messiah Jesus is: not a wonder-worker for hire nor a king who rules by the world’s methods, but the obedient Son who brings God’s favour to the poor and the foreigner.

How the chapter makes its case. In the wilderness (vv. 1–13) he answers the devil’s offers of bread, power and protection, each a way round the cross, with Scripture, and stands where Adam and Israel fell. At Nazareth (vv. 14–30) he reads Isaiah 61 and says it is fulfilled today; the town admires him, dismisses him as Joseph’s son, and, when he recalls Elijah’s Sidonian widow and Elisha’s Syrian general, tries to throw him off a cliff. In Capernaum (vv. 31–44) the programme is carried out: his word teaches with authority, drives out a demon and rebukes a fever, his hands rest on every sick person, and at dawn he leaves for other towns, because he must.

Where it leads. The devil departs “until an opportune time” (v. 13), and that time is the cross. The man who would not throw himself from the temple, and whom Nazareth could not throw from a cliff, will let himself be lifted up on a cross. He stopped reading before “the day of vengeance of our God” because he came first to bear that vengeance himself, so that the year of the Lord’s favour could stay open.

For us. We fight temptation behind a champion who has beaten the tempter. The “today” of Nazareth is still addressed to us: the release is for the poor and captive now. And the chapter warns against two ways of keeping Jesus at a distance: filing him under what we already know, as Nazareth did, and keeping him for what he does for us, as Capernaum tried to.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Son of God wins, as a man and in our place, the battle Adam and Israel lost, by trusting and obeying his Father’s word. The Father has just said “You are my beloved Son” (3:22), and the devil’s challenge begins, “If you are the Son of God”. Will he use his power for his own relief (vv. 3–4), take the world’s kingdoms by the world’s methods (vv. 5–8), or force the Father to prove his care (vv. 9–12)? Each assault echoes a wilderness failure of Israel: the grumbling for bread (Exodus 16), the golden calf (Exodus 32), the testing at Massah (Exodus 17:1–7). Jesus stands with the means every Israelite had, the word of God believed and obeyed, and the devil departs “until an opportune time” (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology:
The temptation shows Jesus as the second Adam as well as the true Israel (see the note on vv. 1–2). What the first Adam lost, the second wins back (Romans 5), not by raw divine force but by trusting the word of God.

The devil’s departure “until an opportune time” (v. 13) points to the passion, where the temptations return almost word for word (see the note on v. 13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus’ weapon against every temptation is Scripture, remembered and spoken with precision (see the note on vv. 3–4).

The devil quotes Psalm 91 accurately, but with a clause removed (on how Scripture is misused, see the note on vv. 9–11).

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil. And he ate nothing during those days. And when they were ended, he was hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Led by the Spirit, Jesus goes out to meet the devil in the wilderness, and stands where Adam and Israel fell. The Son whom the Father has just named at the Jordan is tested for forty days, and the testing is real.

Full of the Holy Spirit … led by the Spirit. The Spirit who came down at the Jordan (3:22) leads him into the desert, deeper into the Father’s purpose: the temptation was part of God’s plan, not an accident. Being full of the Spirit does not mean being spared temptation but being equipped for it. The place was probably the wilderness of Judea, scene of Israel’s failure and of the scapegoat sent away carrying sin (Leviticus 16:10).

For forty days. The number is not decorative. Israel was forty years in the wilderness and failed there (Deuteronomy 8:2); Moses was forty days on the mountain without bread (Exodus 34:28). Jesus goes where Israel went, on Israel’s terms, and does what Israel could not do.

Being tempted by the devil. The Greek suggests he was tempted all through the forty days, and the three temptations Luke records came at the end. The devil (diabolos, the slanderer) is a real, personal being, the enemy of God and of man.

He was hungry. Forty days without food takes a body to the edge of survival, and the attack comes at the point of greatest weakness, where such attacks generally come.

The second Adam and the true Israel. The genealogy has just ended with Adam, the son of God (3:38), and now the new Son of God faces the test the first Adam failed. Adam was tested in a garden, with every tree but one to eat from, and fell; Jesus is tested in a wilderness, starving, and stands. God also called Israel his firstborn son (Exodus 4:22), and Israel failed its forty years of testing. Here the story of the human race and of Israel is lived again by one man, this time without failing: the second Adam walking alone into the wasteland the first Adam made.

In everyday life. Expect temptation especially when you are weak: tired, hungry, lonely, ill, or just after a high point. Prepare for that hour beforehand, with Scripture already in your memory and someone you can be honest with. And do not read the hard season as a sign that God has left you. The Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness, and he will be there.

If God tempts no one, why does the Spirit lead Jesus into temptation? James says plainly that God tempts no one (James 1:13). But one Greek word (peirasmos) covers two things English keeps apart. It can mean a test, a trial meant to prove and strengthen, as God tested Abraham (Genesis 22:1) and tested Israel to know what was in their heart (Deuteronomy 8:2); or a temptation, an enticement meant to make a person fall. The same moment can be both. From the Father’s side this is a test, proving and displaying an obedience the world would need to see; from the devil’s side it is a temptation, every word designed to make Jesus fall. God ordains the testing; Satan supplies the enticing; and God never does the second.

Then what am I asking when I pray, lead us not into temptation? Not that God might otherwise tempt us. When he leads you into hard testing he is proving a faith he intends to carry through, and he has bound himself to provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13). It is the prayer of people who know their weakness, asking the Father to keep the test from becoming a fall. The sinless Son did not need to pray it for himself. We do, every day.

Is being tempted a sin? No, and this settles a question that torments sensitive believers. If the pull itself were the fall, the Lord who was “tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15) could not be our Saviour. Sin is welcoming the thought, entertaining it, turning it over with pleasure, and acting on it (James 1:14–15). So when an ugly thought arrives uninvited, do not conclude that you are a hypocrite; turn at once to the one who faced the same and stood. Feeling the pull is the battlefield, not the defeat.

Where Christians differ: could Jesus have sinned? This commentary’s view: being God, he could not sin, yet the temptation was real and fully felt: a strong bridge cannot fall, but the weight on it is real.

verseByVerse.quote: The devil said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.' And Jesus answered him, 'It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus refuses to use his power as Son to feed himself apart from his Father, and answers the devil with the lesson Israel failed to learn in the same desert. Life comes from trusting God’s word, not from seizing what we need.

If you are the Son of God. The Greek does not express doubt; it means something like “since you are”. A Son with a Father like that, the devil suggests, ought not to be this hungry, and if the Father will not do something about it, the Son should. The temptation is to use his sonship for himself, independently of his Father.

Command this stone to become bread. There is nothing wrong with bread; he will make it for five thousand (9:10–17). The temptation is to a good thing, taken by the wrong hand at the wrong moment: to step out of dependence on the Father who had led him into the wilderness to hunger. He would not use his divine power to escape the human weakness he came to share (Philippians 2:7).

The shape of temptation. Temptation rarely suggests that God does not exist. It suggests that he is not looking after you, and you had better see to yourself, as the serpent did in the garden: he is keeping something good from you. The lie is always about the Father’s heart.

It is written. Three times Jesus answers from the written word, the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17), and stops; he does not argue. His weapon was available to every Israelite and is available now. If Jesus needed Scripture to resist temptation, how much more do we; and the Spirit who filled him now lives in us to wield it.

Man shall not live by bread alone. Deuteronomy 8:3, and the context is the whole point. God let Israel hunger in the wilderness and fed them with manna, to teach them that life comes from “every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD”. Israel was hungry, grumbled and demanded. Jesus is hungrier, and quotes the lesson Israel refused to learn, in the same desert. His food was to do the will of the one who sent him (John 4:34).

He would not feed himself. The Son of God went hungry so that hungry people could be fed with the bread that does not perish. He would not turn one stone into bread for himself, and on the last night he broke bread and said, “This is my body, which is given for you” (22:19). Everything he would not take for himself, he gives to us.

In everyday life. A real need will meet a wrong way of meeting it: money by a small dishonesty on an expense claim; comfort from a bottle or a screen at the end of a hard day; affection from someone else’s spouse who seems to understand you. The need is genuine; the offer feeds you without going through the Father’s hand (he usually feeds us through ordinary means, which we should not neglect). The question underneath is always: is he going to look after me, or had I better see to it myself?

How do I fight temptation with Scripture? Not by opening the Bible at random under pressure; Jesus had the words ready because he had lived in them. Know your battleground. Most of us are tempted in the same two or three places; name yours. Find the lie about the Father underneath: he will not provide, he is not looking, this will satisfy where he will not. Store the answer. Learn by heart one or two verses that answer that lie: “I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11). Say it, and move. When the pull comes, say the verse, pray it, and get up and do something else; Scripture is a sword to be used, not a charm to be carried. Stand on his victory. When you fail, the same word tells you that he was “tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15), in your place, and that “if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us” (1 John 1:9). You do not fight to win his favour but from it, behind the one who has already beaten the tempter.

Does this mean physical needs do not matter? No. Jesus fed the hungry and taught us to pray for daily bread (11:3), and the verse says we do not live by bread alone. Bread keeps the body alive for a time; God keeps the whole person alive for ever, and gives the bread too. The point is dependence: a real need is not to be met by stepping outside the will of the Father who gives both the command and the food. If obeying God and getting what you need ever collide, the need is safer in his hands than in yours.

parallels.desc: man does not live by bread alone

verseByVerse.quote: And the devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, and said to him, 'To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devil offers Jesus the kingdoms of the world, the very inheritance the Father has promised him, if he will take them without the cross by bowing to the usurper. It is the right goal by the wrong road.

In a moment of time. No mountain is mentioned, and the phrase suggests a vision rather than an ordinary view: every empire, every capital, every throne, laid out in an instant.

It has been delivered to me. Is he lying? If the claim were simply false the temptation would have no force, and Jesus refuses the price without denying that Satan has power; he himself calls him “the ruler of this world” (John 12:31), and “the whole world lies in the power of the evil one” (1 John 5:19). But the word is “handed over”: held on licence from someone who can revoke it. The devil is a usurper administering territory that was never his, on a lease he cannot extend. All authority finally belongs to God, who gives the kingdom of men to whom he will (Daniel 4:17), and Satan is “a liar and the father of lies” (John 8:44). His claim is partly true, and far smaller than it sounds.

It will all be yours. The subtlest of the three, because the kingdoms of the world are exactly what the Father has promised him: “Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage” (Psalm 2:8). The devil offers him his own inheritance by a short cut: the nations without Gethsemane, the crown without the cross, at a price that looks small. Peter would later put the same temptation to him, and receive the same answer (Mark 8:32–33).

The order. Matthew has the temple second and the kingdoms last (Matthew 4:1–11). Luke simply joins his scenes with “and”, making no claim about their order, and ends with Jerusalem and the temple because Jerusalem is the goal of his whole Gospel, which began in the temple and will end there (9:51; 24:53). His order shows where the story is heading, not which temptation came first.

He went the long way round. He was offered the world for one bow, and he would not bow. So the world came to him another way: through nails, a borrowed tomb and an empty one. He refused the throne from the usurper’s hand and received it from his Father’s, and it will never be revoked. He went the long way round, by the cross, because we were on that road, and he would not reach the kingdom without us.

In everyday life. This temptation is the right thing by a wrong route: church growth built on a softened gospel; the promotion gained by the quiet betrayal of a colleague; the peace in a family bought by pretending an offence never happened. To want a church to grow is not bowing to Satan. The question is what you are willing to bow to in order to get it.

Does Satan really control the world, so that Christians should withdraw from it? No. His power is real but borrowed, limited and already broken, and the earth is the LORD’s (Psalm 24:1). We must not be naive about one who blinds minds and holds people captive (2 Corinthians 4:4; 2 Timothy 2:26). But Jesus came to bind the strong man and plunder his house (11:21–22), and all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (Matthew 28:18). So Christians go into the world not as enemy territory but as the King’s ambassadors, working, raising families and serving their neighbours under a better Lord.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s order of the temptations differs from Matthew’s; Luke ends at Jerusalem, the goal of his whole Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, 'It is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus will worship God alone, whatever is offered, and that one answer settles the whole bargain. He does not argue about who owns the kingdoms or on what terms; he goes straight to the word that decides it: worship.

It is written. Deuteronomy 6:13, just after the Shema, where Moses warns Israel about growing comfortable in the land, with cities they did not build, wells they did not dig and vineyards they did not plant (Deuteronomy 6:10–12). The danger is prosperity, not persecution. Israel repeatedly bowed to idols for the sake of prosperity and security; Jesus will not.

Only. The word is not in the Hebrew of Deuteronomy 6:13, but it is in some copies of the Greek Old Testament, and the whole passage implies it, going straight on: “you shall not go after other gods” (Deuteronomy 6:14). A man who worships two things has one master he admits to and one he obeys. “No servant can serve two masters” (16:13).

Jesus, who is God, worships God. Not that there are two gods, or that the Son is less divine than the Father. The eternal Son took a true human nature, and in it lived the life of worship every human being owes to God and none of us has given. He will receive all the kingdoms, but from the Father’s hand, through obedience and the cross (Philippians 2:8–11).

The hinge of all three. Bread, kingdoms or proof, underneath every temptation is the same question: who is God here? Behind the extra glass or the figure adjusted on the form is a quiet transfer of allegiance, something other than God trusted to give what only God can give. So the test is usually decided beforehand, by what a person has come to worship on ordinary days. Jesus came into the wilderness with the answer already fixed, and the devil found nothing in him to negotiate with (John 14:30).

His worship was single and burning. He would not bow, so that we might be set free from bowing to everything else. He is the only man who ever gave God the whole of his worship, and he did it as our representative: our worship is divided and cold; his was single and burning, and in him the Father counts it ours.

How do I know what I actually worship? Ask what loss would make life feel unliveable, and what you daydream about, spend on without thinking, or get angry about when it is threatened. Whatever answers is being worshipped, whatever it is called. It may be a good thing: a child, a marriage, health, a career. Good things become idols by being loved in God’s place. The cure is not to love them less but God more, bringing them with open hands to the one who would not bow for a world and who holds them, and you, more safely than you can.

parallels.desc: worship and serve the LORD alone

verseByVerse.quote: And he took him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’ and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devil’s last offer is the most religious: take God’s promise of protection and make him keep it on demand, in public. It is the only temptation that comes with chapter and verse.

He took him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple. The third assault moves to the holy city, whether in a vision or physically Luke does not say, and to a high place (see the box below): not a private test but a proposal for a public one.

Throw yourself down. Prove your sonship; force God to act. A rescue in front of the temple crowds would be a sign from heaven, the very thing his enemies would demand (11:16). The temptation is not to doubt the promise but to use it: to manufacture a crisis that obliges God to act, and to call that faith.

For it is written. Now the devil quotes Scripture too, accurately: Psalm 91:11–12, a genuine promise. But the psalm promises angels “to guard you in all your ways”, and he hides that point (Matthew 4:6 drops the clause altogether). God guards his people in the paths of obedience, and jumping off a building to see whether he will catch you is not one of them. And the devil stopped one verse before the line that foretells his own defeat: “You will tread on the lion and the adder” (Psalm 91:13).

The angels held back at Calvary. He would not jump from the temple; some years later, outside the same city, he let them lift him up on a cross. He refused to make his Father prove his love, and instead gave himself up to prove his Father’s love to us. The angels who would have caught him at the temple were held back at Calvary. There was no rescue for him, so that there would be rescue for us.

How Scripture is nearly always misused. Not by inventing a verse, which anyone can check, but by quoting a true one with the qualifying clause removed or the occasion changed. The man who knows a hundred verses can be beaten by a hundred and one. The man who knows what God is doing in Scripture as a whole can hear a true verse being used against its own purpose, and say so.

How do I read a promise in context? Ask who is speaking, and to whom; what the paragraph and chapter say; whether the promise is for one person and occasion or for all God’s people; and whether your reading agrees with the rest of Scripture and with the way Jesus and the apostles used it. Psalm 91 promises real protection, and Christians may lean on it in danger. It does not promise that a believer will never suffer (Hebrews 11:36–38), but that nothing will touch him outside his Father’s will, and that in the end no harm will undo him.

Uncertain wording. “Pinnacle” translates a word meaning “little wing” (pterygion), and no one knows for certain which part of the temple it named. It was a high point of the temple complex, perhaps a corner of the outer wall above the valley, where the Jewish historian Josephus said looking down made you dizzy; others suggest a balcony or the top of a gateway. The sense is clear either way: a high, public place where a fall would be fatal and a rescue would be seen.
verseByVerse.note: The pinnacle was a high point of the temple complex, perhaps a corner of its outer wall.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, 'It is said, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus refuses to make his Father prove himself: trust obeys God and leaves the outcome with him, and does not set him tests. The devil had a text; Jesus answers Scripture with Scripture, because he has the whole Bible.

It is said. Deuteronomy 6:16, and Moses finishes the sentence with the place name that explains it: “as you tested him at Massah”. At Massah (Exodus 17) Israel is thirsty, and instead of asking, they quarrel and demand. Their question is recorded because it lies underneath all such demands: “Is the LORD among us or not?” (Exodus 17:7).

What testing God is. Not asking him for something, which Scripture is full of people doing, but making his response the condition of believing him. Trust says: he is good; I will do what he has told me and leave the outcome with him. Testing says: I will force his hand, and read the result as a verdict on whether he loves me. Jesus could have jumped, and the angels would have come. He would not make his Father prove himself, because he had heard the voice at the Jordan.

Faith perfected. On the cross he stayed, and trusted his Father in the dark: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (23:46). Here is faith perfected, in a man who never once put God to the test, and who was tested in our place to the uttermost.

The Rock at Massah. When Israel tested the LORD at Massah, God did not strike the people. He told Moses to strike the rock, saying that he himself would stand before him on it, and water came out for the people to drink (Exodus 17:6). Paul says that “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4, 9). The Son in this desert is the Lord whom Israel tested, and he will be the struck Rock: at the cross the blow falls on him, not on the people who quarrelled, and out of him flows the living water (John 7:37–39).

How it happens without our noticing. The silent bargain at two in the morning: if this scan comes back clear, I will know he is with me. The resignation handed in without a plan and called stepping out in faith. And the terrible weight when the scan is not clear, because you had made it a verdict on his love, which God never agreed to. He does not owe us a demonstration.

In everyday life. Trust God in the path of obedience, without taking reckless risks and expecting him to bail you out, such as refusing a treatment your doctor urges because God must heal you without it, or spending money you do not have. But a missionary going somewhere dangerous, or a believer losing her job for refusing to lie, acts in faith, not presumption. The difference is not the size of the risk but whether God asked you to do it.

But God says through Malachi, put me to the test, and Gideon asked for signs. Yes (Malachi 3:10; Judges 6:36–40). The forbidden testing demands that God prove himself on our terms, as at Massah. Malachi’s call is God inviting his people to trust a promise he has made. Gideon’s fleece was a weak man’s request that God graciously answered, not a pattern for guidance now that God has spoken in his word.

Then how do I seek guidance without laying a fleece? Begin with what God has said: is the choice commanded, forbidden, or left free by Scripture? If it is free, pray for wisdom, which God promises (James 1:5); think it through, ask the counsel of mature Christians who know you, weigh your gifts, responsibilities and open doors, and then decide, trusting that God rules even your mistakes. A Christian who has done that and chooses between two good paths is not out of God’s will whichever he takes.

Is it wrong to ask God for evidence? No. God does not ask for blind faith: Luke wrote to give certainty (1:4), and the risen Christ gave many proofs that he was alive (Acts 1:3). What Jesus refuses is setting the terms on which God must perform before we trust him. The sceptic who says, “If God is real let him do this for me now”, and the believer who says, “If he loves me he will do this by Friday”, make the same demand. God has given evidence enough in Christ, above all in his resurrection.

parallels.desc: do not put the LORD to the test

verseByVerse.quote: And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devil is beaten and withdraws, but only to wait for a better moment, and that moment will be the cross.

When the devil had ended every temptation. The arsenal was emptied: appetite, power, and presuming on God’s protection. Many have heard in them John’s list, “the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life” (1 John 2:16), and the three pulls Eve felt at the tree, good for food, a delight to the eyes, and desired to make one wise (Genesis 3:6). Where Eve took the fruit, the last Adam met all three at their strongest and gave the enemy nothing, and the devil, resisted, fled (James 4:7).

Until an opportune time. The enemy withdraws to wait, and Luke means it as a signal. Satan next moves openly against Jesus as the Passover draws near: “Then Satan entered into Judas” (22:3); “this is your hour, and the power of darkness” (22:53). At Gethsemane and the cross the temptations came back in almost their original shapes: save yourself; if you are the Christ; if you are the King of the Jews (23:35–39).

Twice he met the enemy, and twice he won. At the cross too Satan found nothing in Jesus to work on, and his defeat was total, because the death he arranged was the death that undid him. Our champion has met the enemy twice and won twice, once by refusing every temptation and once by bearing every sin. We fight a beaten foe, under a Captain who has never lost.

The victory is real, and it is not yet final. That is true of the Christian life as well. A sin fought and prayed through may stand in the doorway again eighteen months later. A returning temptation does not prove that your earlier resistance was a sham. It shows that the war is longer than the battle.

The opportune time is the hour of exhaustion. The devil chose the end of forty days without food, and later the last night, in the dark, when the friends were asleep. That is a good reason to be more careful, not less, when you are tired, and no reason at all to conclude, when temptation comes, that you have gone backwards.

If Jesus defeated Satan here, why does the devil still trouble me? Because his defeat comes in stages: beaten in single combat in the wilderness, disarmed and put to open shame at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and at Christ’s return thrown into the lake of fire for ever (Revelation 20:10). We live between the second and the third, facing an enemy defeated and doomed but still active, like an army that has lost the decisive battle and fights on in the hills. He can tempt, accuse and harass you, but he cannot condemn you or take you out of Christ’s hand (John 10:28).

parallels.desc: your hour, and the power of darkness

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus announces that the release God promised has arrived in him, and his own town rejects him because the grace he brings is free to outsiders. He reads Isaiah 61, with its echo of the Jubilee, Israel’s year of release, and stops before “the day of vengeance of our God”: the favour has come, and the judgment waits for his return (vv. 16–21). The congregation admires him and dismisses him in one breath (v. 22). When he recalls from their own Scriptures how the blessing passed by Israel to a foreign widow and an enemy general (vv. 23–27), they try to throw him from the hill; he walks through them, because the hour and place of his death are not theirs to choose (vv. 28–30).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Jubilee was Israel’s built-in rehearsal of release (see the note on vv. 18–19). Jesus announces the real one: the debt of sin cancelled, captivity to Satan ended, the blind given sight.

The rage at the Elijah and Elisha stories is the rage of people who thought God’s blessing was theirs by right. Nazareth wanted a Messiah who would bless Israel and defeat its enemies, not one who would take the blessing to the enemies. Every generation of the church is tempted to resent grace when it reaches people who had been written off.
verseByVerse.examples:
In Luke the gospel is always a present-tense announcement: salvation arrives today (see the note on vv. 20–21).

Jesus walking through the crowd that means to kill him (v. 30) is the first of several moments in Luke where he moves through danger untouched, because his hour has not come (see vv. 28–30). And the scene warns about familiarity (see the note on v. 22).

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus comes back from the wilderness in the Spirit’s power and begins teaching across Galilee, welcomed by everyone, for now. The testing did not drain his anointing; it proved it.

In the power of the Spirit. He went into the wilderness full of the Spirit; he comes out in power. Luke stresses throughout that Jesus’ ministry is empowered by the Spirit (v. 18; Acts 10:38).

To Galilee. The northern region, where most of his ministry will take place (4:14–9:50). Luke passes over a period of ministry that John’s Gospel probably fills in, with the wedding at Cana and a first visit to Jerusalem (John 1–4), and simply notes that word was spreading; Jesus will soon refer to things done at Capernaum that Luke has not yet described (see the note on vv. 23–24).

And he taught in their synagogues. Synagogues were local meeting places for prayer and for the reading and teaching of Scripture, in every Jewish town, and probably began during the exile. Visiting teachers could be invited to speak, and Jesus, and later Paul, used them for preaching (Acts 13:15). The gospel began its journey in the ordinary weekly gatherings of ordinary people.

Being glorified by all. At first, universal acclaim; fifteen verses later his own village tries to throw him off a cliff (v. 29). The early approval is real, and worth almost nothing, because it has not yet been tested by anything he came to say, as in Jerusalem the cheering turned within days into the cry to crucify him. Here is a Saviour who cannot be flattered into silence or frightened into retreat, who knew exactly what the cheering was worth, and loved them anyway.

Is it wrong to want to be liked? No. Scripture commends a good name (Proverbs 22:1); Jesus grew in favour with God and man (2:52), and elders must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7). The danger is needing it: letting approval decide what you say, or measuring faithfulness by popularity. Be glad of it, and do not lean on it; in the beloved Son you already have the Father’s approval. The approval that lasts is the one you will hear at the end: “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21).

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written,
verseByVerse.commentary:
On an ordinary Sabbath in his home town Jesus does what he has always done, worship with God’s people, and then stands to read the Scripture that is about himself. Luke places the scene at the start of the Galilean ministry as a manifesto of what Jesus came to do (on its place in time, and the similar rejection in Matthew and Mark, see the note on vv. 23–24).

Nazareth. His home town, a small village in the hills of lower Galilee, where everyone knew him as the carpenter (Mark 6:3).

As was his custom. Week after week, for most of his life, the Son of God sat through the service in a small building in an unremarkable village: a handful of families, the same faces, and teaching that was probably very ordinary. It was not instruction he needed. He went anyway, every week, including this Sabbath, to a congregation that would try to kill him that same day.

And he stood up to read. A service included the Shema, prayers, readings from the Law and the Prophets, and a sermon. Readers stood to read, out of respect, and sat to teach.

He unrolled the scroll and found the place. The book of Isaiah was a long scroll, wound by hand to the passage. Whether or not it was the appointed reading, he was handed the book he had inspired, and he found the sentence about himself, because the whole book is about him.

The Lord of the Sabbath kept the Sabbath. The one to whom every synagogue prayer was addressed stood among the villagers and prayed it with them, born under the law he had given, and himself the rest every Sabbath awaited (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). If the sinless Son worshipped with God’s people every week, how much more we, who draw near by his blood (Hebrews 10:19–25).

What if my church is weak, or the preaching is thin? Jesus had better grounds than anyone for staying away, and did not use them. Go as a giver as well as a receiver: to pray with others, to sing, to encourage the person next to you, to hear God’s word read even if the sermon is poor. A church that has abandoned the gospel itself is a different matter, and you may need one that preaches Christ. But dullness, weakness and ordinary faces are no reason to stay at home. They are the setting in which Jesus worshipped for thirty years.
verseByVerse.note: A synagogue service included readings from the Law and the Prophets; a visiting teacher could be invited to read and speak.

parallels.desc: Paul invited to speak after the readings

verseByVerse.quote: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus reads Isaiah’s promise of the Spirit-anointed one who brings good news and release, and takes it as the description of his own work. Every clause names something the following chapters will show him doing.

The passage. Isaiah 61:1–2, woven together with a phrase from Isaiah 58:6, largely in the words of the Greek Old Testament, sharpening the note of release. In Isaiah the Lord’s anointed announces return from exile; Jesus claims it as his own job description.

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. The man on whom the Spirit came at the Jordan (3:22) reads out the passage about the man on whom the Spirit rests. Father, Son and Spirit are all in the first line: the Spirit of the Lord, upon me.

Because he has anointed me. “Anointed” (echrisen) is the verb behind “Christ”, and its Hebrew equivalent is behind “Messiah”. He is anointed not with oil but with the Spirit (Acts 10:38), and he is reading his own title aloud.

To proclaim good news to the poor. The poor (ptōchois) are the destitute and needy, and in the Old Testament especially the humble poor who depend on God (Psalm 34:6; Isaiah 66:2). Both material and spiritual poverty are in view. The gospel comes first to those who know they have nothing (6:20; 7:22), and Luke’s Gospel will be full of them, from shepherds to a widow with two small coins.

To proclaim liberty to the captives. “Liberty” (aphesis) is the same word Luke uses for forgiveness (1:77; 3:3; 24:47). Forgiveness is a release: God cancels the debt, and the guilty go free as a prisoner walks out of an open cell (Colossians 2:13–14). Jesus sets free those bound by sin, by Satan and by disease (13:16).

And recovering of sight to the blind. From the Greek Old Testament of Isaiah 61:1, where the Hebrew has “the opening of the prison to those who are bound”. Jesus will heal the physically blind (7:21; 18:35–43), and open the eyes of the spiritually blind (Acts 26:18).

To set at liberty those who are oppressed. From Isaiah 58:6: the crushed and broken, bruised under a weight they cannot lift.

To proclaim the year of the Lord’s favour. The phrase echoes the Jubilee of Leviticus 25:8–55: the fiftieth year, when the trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement, debts were cancelled, slaves walked free, and land sold off in hard times went back to the family that had lost it. He stands up in a village synagogue and says the real one has arrived.

Where he stopped. Isaiah went on: “and the day of vengeance of our God” (Isaiah 61:2). Jesus breaks off in the middle of the line, and the silence speaks. His first coming is for salvation; the day of vengeance comes at his return (21:22; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). Every year since that morning, this one included, falls in the pause before that unread half sentence: the year of favour is still open (2 Corinthians 6:2).

He came to bear the vengeance. The one who stopped reading in the middle of the verse is holding the year of favour open. The day of vengeance is coming; but first he came to bear the vengeance himself, so that for everyone who comes to him the day of favour will never end.

In everyday life. Find yourself in the list first: you were the poor, the captive, the blind and the crushed, and he came for you. Then look at those still there, the colleague trapped in a habit, the lonely neighbour, the family at church who cannot pay a bill, and bring them the news and help. The Jubilee has begun in Christ, and will be complete when he comes again.

Are these promises literal or spiritual? Both. Actual blind men receive sight in this Gospel, and actual poor people are fed; and the same Gospel says the deepest poverty is not being rich towards God (12:21), and the worst blindness is in people whose eyes work perfectly. A Christianity that spiritualises every clause has stopped doing what Jesus did; one that keeps them all material has stopped saying what he said.

So is the church meant to fight poverty or preach the gospel? Both, in their order. The church’s distinctive task, which no one else will do, is to proclaim Christ and the forgiveness of sins (24:47). But those who hear it are given new hearts, which love their neighbours with food, money, time and justice (1 John 3:17; James 2:15–16). Mercy is neither a substitute for the gospel nor an optional extra; it is what the gospel produces. A congregation that preaches release and ignores the widow down the road has misheard the sermon at Nazareth.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add “to heal the brokenhearted”; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit it.
verseByVerse.note: “The year of the Lord’s favour” recalls the Year of Jubilee, when debts were cancelled and slaves set free. Jesus stops before Isaiah’s next words, “the day of vengeance of our God.”

parallels.desc: to let the oppressed go free

verseByVerse.quote: And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. And he began to say to them, 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sits down to teach and says, in one sentence, that Isaiah’s promise is coming true in front of them, today. He did not come to explain the prophecy; he came to be it.

He gave it back to the attendant and sat down. The attendant was the synagogue official who looked after the scrolls. Luke slows the film: three ordinary actions, one at a time, and then a silence. Sitting was the posture for teaching, and the room knows a sermon is coming.

A sermon of one sentence. There may have been more (he “began to say”), but this is the whole of it. Prophets said, “Thus says the LORD.” This man reads a seven-hundred-year-old prophecy and says: that is about me, and it is happening now, in this room. He is deluded, or lying, or the year of the Lord’s favour has just begun in a small village. Being impressed is not an option, though admiring the delivery is exactly what the congregation is about to attempt.

Today. Today (sēmeron) is one of Luke’s favourite words. “Unto you is born this day” (2:11); “Today salvation has come to this house” (19:9); “today you will be with me in paradise” (23:43). Salvation is not filed under history or postponed to the future; it keeps arriving in the present tense, at a particular address. And it is fulfilled in a room about to reject him, because the “today” depends not on the response but on who has just sat down.

It is addressed to you. Seven hundred years of longing had come down to a carpenter sitting in a synagogue, saying, “Today.” Whatever burden you are carrying, the release he announced is not for some future day when you are better; it is offered now, in your hearing.

How is the whole Old Testament about Jesus? Not every verse is a hidden prediction, but the whole story heads towards him. Its promises are fulfilled in him (2 Corinthians 1:20); its sacrifices, priests and temple picture what he would do; its kings and prophets point to the King and Prophet to come; its failures show why he was needed. The risen Lord showed his disciples himself in Moses and all the Prophets (24:27, 44). So read the Old Testament asking not only what it meant then but what it shows of the Christ who was coming.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach.

parallels.desc: everything written about me must be fulfilled

verseByVerse.quote: And all spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said, 'Is not this Joseph's son?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The congregation admires his words and in the same breath dismisses him: he is only Joseph’s son. They think they already know all there is to know about him.

And all spoke well of him. Or bore witness to him (see the box below). At first, admiration, like the wonder after the shepherds came (2:18). But wonder is not faith; it is what a person feels when something has been interesting and nothing has yet been decided.

Gracious words. Literally words of grace, God’s favour freely given to the undeserving. “Grace is poured upon your lips”, sang the psalmist of the King (Psalm 45:2). He has just announced that the Jubilee has arrived in their village, and the congregation is appraising the performance.

Is not this Joseph’s son? The turning point: the compliment and the problem arrive in one breath, and the second cancels the first. The question is not yet hostile, only a small town astonished at one of its own. They knew him at nine, knew the family and the trade, had watched him buy timber. That is the difficulty: he is filed under people we know, and nothing greater can be true of him. Matthew and Mark record that they took offence at him (Matthew 13:57; Mark 6:3).

Whose son is he? Luke has given the reader the answer the synagogue lacked. Jesus was the son, as was supposed, of Joseph (3:23), and so legally the heir of David’s throne (1:32). But by nature he is the Son of the Most High (1:35), the one the Father had just called beloved over the Jordan (3:22). That is why the words were gracious: they came from the Word made flesh, “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

He did not glow. He grew up among them so quietly that they could not believe he was more than the carpenter, and that is the glory of the incarnation: the eternal Son was so truly man, working with wood and sawdust for years, that his neighbours mistook him for an ordinary one. And the words of grace that came from his mouth that morning are still coming, to people who think they know him already. He is always larger, kinder and holier than our file on him.

The particular danger of growing up near the things of God. Familiarity usually produces not hostility but a mild, unthreatened appreciation: an account of Jesus in place since childhood, not wrong so much as too small, and never requiring anything. Nazareth had thirty years of information about him, and there, Mark tells us, he could do few mighty works (Mark 6:5). Those who received him were often people with no prior file: a Roman officer, a woman with a bad name, a tax collector up a tree, a dying criminal. And God still often speaks through people we think we have already filed.

I grew up in church. How do I stop Jesus becoming familiar? Knowing the gospel from childhood is a great privilege; the danger is assuming you know what a passage says before you have read it. Read the Gospels slowly, perhaps in another translation, and ask what surprises you; notice how people react who meet him for the first time. Above all, pray: “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). Only the Spirit makes the old story new, and he loves to do it.
