Uncertain wording. The verb means “bore witness to him”, and which way the witness went is not quite certain. Most take it, as the ESV does, as approval. A few scholars read it as hostile, “they bore witness against him”, making the whole verse a protest. The marvelling that follows and his welcome elsewhere in Galilee (v. 15) favour approval, with the turn coming at “Is not this Joseph’s son?”.

parallels.desc: “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph?”

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself.’ What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.' And he said, 'Truly, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus names the demand behind their admiration, prove yourself here, for us, and answers that no prophet is welcome in his home town. They want signs on their own terms, not faith.

Physician, heal yourself. Jesus answers the question they have not asked aloud. The proverb here means: prove yourself; do for your own people what you did elsewhere. On the cross they will throw the same taunt: “He saved others; let him save himself” (23:35).

What we have heard you did at Capernaum. Luke tells of Capernaum only eight verses later (vv. 31–41). He has set the Nazareth visit at the head of the ministry, ahead of events that had already happened, because it explains everything that follows: why Jesus is based at Capernaum and not at home, why the message goes to outsiders, and how it will end.

The demand underneath. They want a miracle by right of local loyalty: we knew you first, so we have first call. He has just come from forty days of refusing exactly this, and the wilderness is still on his clothes.

No prophet is acceptable in his hometown. “Acceptable” (dektos) is the word translated favour in the year of the Lord’s favour (v. 19): he proclaims the acceptable year, and is not acceptable to his own. He stands in the line of prophets rejected and killed by the people who had the Scriptures (Jeremiah 11:21; Acts 7:52). He would be “despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3), so that we, who rejected him, might be accepted in the Beloved.

In everyday life. If those closest to you are least willing to hear the gospel from you, you are in good company: the brother who still sees you as a teenager, the parents who smile at your faith as a phase. Jesus went on loving the town that refused him; let your life speak over years. But ask honestly whether the offence is the gospel or you: sometimes people are rightly put off by our pride, preachiness or inconsistency.

Why would God not do a miracle for people who asked for one? Because they were setting terms, not asking in faith. Jesus never refused anyone who came in need and trust; he refused the demand for proof as a condition of believing, the very thing he had refused the devil, and later called the mark of an evil generation (11:29). A sign given to people who have already decided what they will accept does not produce faith; it produces spectators. When God seems silent to your prayers, it is not because he withholds favours from those who have not earned them; sometimes he is drawing you from wanting a display to wanting him.

Is this the same visit as Matthew 13 and Mark 6? Matthew and Mark record a rejection at Nazareth much later (Matthew 13:54–58; Mark 6:1–6). Whether that is this visit in its chronological place, or a second visit to a town that had not changed its mind, cannot be settled; the details allow either. Luke knew what he was doing when he put it first, and none of the Gospels claims to be a diary.

verseByVerse.quote: But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months, and a great famine came over all the land, and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
From their own Scriptures Jesus shows that God’s mercy has never been Israel’s by right: Elijah was sent to a Gentile widow, and Elisha cleansed an enemy general. He chose the two stories that would turn admiration into a lynch mob.

Many widows. During the famine God sent in Ahab’s time (1 Kings 17–18), Israelite widows were starving in every village. Jesus gives three years and six months, as James 5:17 does; 1 Kings 18:1 probably counts from a different point.

Only to Zarephath. 1 Kings 17:8–24. Zarephath was a Gentile town on the coast near Sidon, Jezebel’s home country. God sent his prophet Elijah past all the widows of Israel to a foreign widow, fed her through the famine with a jar of flour that did not run out, and raised her son from death.

Only Naaman the Syrian. 2 Kings 5. Syria (Aram) was the enemy, and Naaman commanded the army that raided Israel’s borders. He was healed when he humbled himself and washed seven times in the Jordan, as Elisha told him, and Israel’s lepers were not.

The point. Both stories are in their own Bible, and together they say: the blessing being near you does not mean it is for you, and God has a settled habit of taking it past his own people to somebody they despise. This is the story of Luke and Acts in miniature (Acts 13:46; 28:28).

Grace is grace. To them this is worse than an insult. He is not saying they are unworthy and Gentiles worthy, but that grace is owed to no one and may land wherever God pleases; no one puts him in his debt by birth or religious upbringing (Romans 11:35). Theirs is the rage of the elder brother (15:28–30) and of the workers hired at dawn (Matthew 20:11–12): religious people discovering that what they thought they had earned is a gift. God sent his prophet to the wrong address on purpose, so that the whole world would know that his mercy is not a family inheritance. Then he sent his Son farther still, past every claim and merit, all the way down to us. We were the foreigners, the enemies, the lepers outside the camp, and grace came looking for us.

A greater prophet than Elijah. At Nain Jesus raises a widow’s only son and gives him to his mother, in the very words used of Elijah at Zarephath (7:15; 1 Kings 17:23), and the one cleansed leper who gives thanks is a foreigner like Naaman (17:15–18). Israel remembered Elijah’s and Elisha’s outsiders as startling exceptions. In Jesus that mercy becomes the plan: “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (2:32).

In everyday life. There is probably some category of person you have quietly written off: a nationality, a lifestyle, a political tribe, an individual with a name. Would you find it hard to be glad if God saved them tomorrow? Whoever came to mind is your Naaman, and Naaman is the one the story is about. Pray for that person this week, and thank God that his grace reached outsiders, including you.

Is it unfair of God to bless some and pass by others? Fairness would give everyone what they deserve, and all of us deserve condemnation (Romans 3:23; 6:23); no widow had a claim on Elijah, and no leper a right to be healed. That God shows mercy to any is grace; where he shows it is his right as God (Romans 9:15–16). The astonishing question is why he came to anyone at all. And if a Sidonian widow and an enemy general were welcomed, no one who comes to Christ will be turned away (John 6:37).
verseByVerse.note: Both of these beneficiaries were Gentiles. Zarephath lay on the coast near Sidon.

parallels.desc: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. But passing through their midst, he went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The suggestion that grace is free turns the congregation into a mob, but Jesus walks through them, because his death will come at his Father’s hour, not theirs.

All in the synagogue were filled with wrath. Six verses ago the same room was speaking well of him, and nothing has happened in between except two Bible stories. What turned a congregation into a mob was the suggestion that God’s grace is free (see the note on vv. 25–27). The same reaction met Paul when he mentioned the Gentiles (Acts 22:21–22).

They drove him out. These are worshippers fresh from the Sabbath reading of Scripture, men who have known him since he was a boy, and with no trial they mean to kill.

The brow of the hill. Nazareth sits on a hillside with steep drops nearby, and the plan was to throw him down the cliff. The devil had just suggested he throw himself down from a height. He refused to do it for the devil, and he will not let them do it to him.

Passing through their midst. Perhaps by sheer authority, perhaps by a miracle; Luke does not say. He does not vanish or call for angels; he simply walks through them and leaves. Whatever happened, the reason is the one the Gospels give again and again: “his hour had not yet come” (John 7:30; 8:59). He cannot be killed early, or in the wrong place: he would die in Jerusalem, not Nazareth (13:33; John 10:18).

Never the victim of the crowd. Three years later he walked out of Jerusalem to a cross, and that time he did not pass through their midst, because the hour had come. The one who could not be thrown from a cliff in Galilee chose to be lifted on a cross in Judea, for the very people shouting at him. He was never the victim of the crowd. He was always its Saviour.

The pattern of the whole Gospel. Grace offered, rejected by his own, and going on to others: the first congregation Jesus preached to tried to murder him, and he walked away and kept preaching. It is a fair warning to anyone who imagines that faithful preaching is chiefly a matter of being well received.

How can religious people become so violent? Religion without grace makes people possessive of God. When your standing rests on heritage, correctness or record, God welcoming outsiders on the same terms feels like theft, and the more you have invested in your own goodness, the angrier you become; so it was the devout who most wanted Jesus dead. The cure is not less seriousness about God but a deeper knowledge of our own need: someone who knows he was saved by grace alone cannot be furious when grace saves somebody else. When it irritates you that someone with a worse past is welcomed and blessed, recognise the voice of Nazareth in your heart, and go back to the grace that welcomed you.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth is built on a hillside with steep drops nearby.

parallels.desc: Jesus hid himself and went out

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What Nazareth refused, Capernaum sees: the kingdom of God arriving through the authoritative word of Jesus. In what seems a single Sabbath he teaches with authority (vv. 31–32), silences and casts out a demon with one sentence (vv. 33–37), rebukes a fever in Simon’s house (vv. 38–39), and at sunset lays his hands on every sick person brought to the door (vv. 40–41). The first to name him aloud is a demon, and its knowledge saves it nothing. At dawn he refuses to be kept: he was sent to preach the kingdom, and he goes on to the other towns (vv. 42–44).
verseByVerse.theology:
The title “the Holy One of God” appears elsewhere in the New Testament, outside this scene and its parallel (Mark 1:24), only on Peter’s lips (John 6:69). The demon confesses what the disciples will grasp only gradually, and it does it no good (see the note on vv. 33–34).

Jesus says he must preach (v. 43), and here is Luke’s first mention of the kingdom of God (on both, see the note on vv. 42–43).
verseByVerse.examples:
The demon’s terror is the correct reading of what the kingdom means for the powers of darkness. Every healing, exorcism and act of forgiveness in the Gospels is territory changing hands, and a church that prays for the sick, names fear, guilt and lies for what they are, and proclaims forgiveness in Jesus’ name is doing in its own place what he did in Capernaum.

The crowds “would have kept him from leaving them” (v. 42). The wish to keep Jesus local, the property of one congregation or tradition, is always well meant, and he always refuses it (see the note on vv. 42–43).

verseByVerse.quote: And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. And he was teaching them on the Sabbath, and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Capernaum Jesus teaches, and his hearers recognise in his word an authority no other teacher had. The word Nazareth drove out is the word that will set another town free.

He went down to Capernaum. “Down” from the hills of Nazareth to the lakeside, about 700 feet (200 m) below sea level: a fishing town on the trade road, larger and more mixed than Nazareth, with a customs post (5:27) and a centurion (7:2). It became his base (Matthew 4:13). The town that received him got him; the town that had him from childhood lost him.

One long day. From here Luke follows Mark closely (Mark 1:21–39), with his own touches: a sermon, an exorcism, a healing in a house, a whole town at the door at sunset, and a departure at dawn.

His word possessed authority. Authority (exousia), the right to act backed by the power to do it, is the key to the rest of the chapter. A scribe taught by citation: Rabbi Hillel said this, Rabbi Shammai that. Jesus quotes Scripture constantly but never props himself on a rabbi, and soon says “I say to you” as no scribe would have dared (6:27). The scribes passed on what others had said about God’s word; Jesus spoke as the one whose word it is.

The same authority in the sermon and the exorcism. Four verses later the crowd uses the word again: “with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits” (v. 36). Luke will not let us separate sermon and exorcism: the word that breaks a demonic hold and the word read on a Sunday morning are one word, and the reason preaching is worth anything at all is that it carries it.

Not a report about God but God speaking. The Creator who said, “Let there be light”, stood in a fishing town and taught, and the people heard in his voice something they had never heard from any rabbi.

Does a sermon today carry that authority? Only as far as it faithfully says what Scripture says; a preacher’s opinions, illustrations and jokes carry none. But when he explains truly what God has said, the hearer is dealing with Christ, not merely with a man (1 Thessalonians 2:13). So test every sermon by the Bible (Acts 17:11), and when it passes the test, receive it not as advice to consider but as the Lord’s word to obey, from the voice that sets captives free and gives what it asks.
verseByVerse.note: Capernaum was a fishing town on the north-west shore of the lake, and became Jesus’ base in Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, 'Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the synagogue a demon cries out in terror, because it knows exactly who Jesus is and what his coming means for it. Yet knowing who he is does it no good at all.

A rescue in church. The first miracle of the public ministry in Luke is a rescue, in the synagogue, on the Sabbath. A man has sat there, perhaps for years, with an unclean spirit, perhaps unnoticed, until the presence of Jesus made it impossible to stay hidden. Being in a religious place is no proof of a clean heart, and the arrival of Christ does not create trouble so much as reveal it.

The spirit of an unclean demon. Luke, writing for Gentiles, for whom “demon” could mean a neutral spirit, adds “unclean”: an evil spirit.

What have you to do with us? A Hebrew idiom: what do we have in common? (1 Kings 17:18). “Us”: the demon speaks for all the demons, because the kingdom of God has invaded their territory.

Have you come to destroy us? Yes: they know their end is coming (Matthew 8:29; 1 John 3:8).

The Holy One of God. The first in the crowds to name him aloud is a demon: “the Holy One of God”, set apart by God, sinless, belonging to God (1:35). It shrieks because absolute purity has walked into the room, and may be trying to gain power over him by naming him, as ancient magic believed. But knowing saves nothing: “Even the demons believe, and shudder!” (James 2:19). Knowing who Jesus is and being willing to have him are two entirely different things.

The holiness that is their doom. The demons know his name and tremble, and we know his name and sing. The one before whom unclean spirits shriek is the one who calls us his friends, and the holiness that is their doom is the holiness he shares with us.

What is a demon, and does this still happen? Scripture gives less than curiosity would like, and enough to go on. Demons are personal, created, spiritual beings in rebellion against God, angels who fell (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6): creatures, not God’s equals, and Luke will show one obeying a single command. They are not the explanation of ordinary sin, illness or sorrow; Luke the physician distinguishes the demonised from the sick (vv. 40–41). But they are real, not a first-century name for epilepsy. Scripture never suggests the enemy has gone out of business, and missionaries report encounters they cannot otherwise explain, though in the modern West a person is far likelier to be destroyed by respectable idolatry than by anything dramatic. To see a demon behind every difficulty is an error; to stop believing in the enemy at all is the commoner one, and it suits him better.

Could a Christian be held like the man in the synagogue? No. Sitting in a synagogue is not belonging to Christ. A believer is indwelt by the Holy Spirit, and “he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4). The New Testament never describes a believer possessed, nor tells believers to cast demons out of one another. Christians can be tempted, deceived and attacked, and must resist the devil with the armour God gives (James 4:7; Ephesians 6:10–18). Some speak of believers being oppressed or harassed by evil spirits, a real distinction; what Scripture rules out is a demon owning one who belongs to Christ.

Then what is the difference between my faith and the demon’s knowledge? The demon knows who Jesus is and hates him. Saving faith knows who he is and trusts him: it agrees that what God says about Christ is true, and rests on him personally for forgiveness and life (the Westminster Confession 14.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 14.2). The demon says, “Have you come to destroy us?” Faith says, “You have come to save me.” The test is whether you want him and lean on him. A frightened believer who clings to Christ has what this demon, for all its accurate theology, can never have.

Uncertain wording. The demon’s first word, “Ha!” (ea), is probably a cry of dismay or anger, but it could also come from the verb “let alone”, giving “Leave us alone!”, as the ESV footnote allows. Either way it is the sound of a creature that wants nothing to do with Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: “The Holy One of God” is a title for the one set apart by God. The demon names who Jesus is.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus rebuked him, saying, 'Be silent and come out of him!' And when the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. And they were all amazed and said to one another, 'What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!' And reports about him went out into every place in the surrounding region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With one sentence Jesus silences the demon and sends it out, and the people see that the authority of his teaching and his power over evil are one. No ritual and no struggle: he speaks, and it is done.

Be silent. Literally, be muzzled. The demon has said nothing false, yet he shuts it up, as he will again (v. 41). He will not accept testimony from unclean spirits: the messenger discredits the message, and if he were announced as Messiah too early, the crowds would try to make him the wrong kind of king. Above all, truth spoken by an enemy in terror is not witness. Witness comes from people who have been rescued and love him, and by the end of Luke’s second volume there will be thousands of them.

And come out of him! That is the whole exorcism. Jewish exorcists of the period used elaborate techniques; Jesus uses one sentence, with no ritual, no formula and no appeal to other authorities.

Having done him no harm. A detail only Luke, the physician, records. The demon threw the man down on its way out, and Luke, as if checking him over, reports that he was unhurt: the note of someone who cared what happened to the person and not only to the story.

What is this word? Or, what is this message? It covers both his teaching and his command. The crowd asks not about technique or training but about the word, and has grasped Luke’s connection: the authority in the teaching and the authority over the spirits are one thing.

With authority and power. Authority (exousia) is the right to command; power (dynamis) is the ability to enforce it, and Luke often pairs them (9:1). Men may have authority without power, like a king in exile, or power without authority, like a thief with a gun. Jesus has the right and the might, perfectly joined.

They come out! The kingdom of God has come, and Satan’s power is being broken (11:20). The strong man’s house is entered by someone stronger, and there is no struggle in the doorway (11:21–22).

There has never been a rival. Everything that holds a human being, the powers of darkness and death itself, takes orders from the voice that made it. He speaks once, and what has held a man for years lets go. There has never been a rival; only a King, and a rebellion that had not yet been told it was over.

Should Christians today try to cast out demons? The New Testament gives no technique of exorcism, and Jesus’ authority here was his own; the apostles cast out demons in his name as signs of the kingdom. What is laid on every Christian is to resist the devil, firm in faith (James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:9), put on the armour of God, and pray. Where someone seems genuinely oppressed by evil, the answer is not drama but the gospel: patient prayer, the word of God, the elders of the church, and wise care, including medical care where illness may be part of the picture. The power is in Christ’s name and word, not in a ritual.

verseByVerse.quote: And he arose and left the synagogue and entered Simon's house. Now Simon's mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. And he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same word of authority that freed a man in the synagogue heals a sick woman at home, and she at once uses her restored strength to serve.

Simon’s house. Simon has not yet been called in Luke (5:1–11), another sign that Luke arranges by theme rather than strict order; he must already have known Jesus. And he had a mother-in-law: the leader of the apostles was a married man (1 Corinthians 9:5).

Ill with a high fever. Luke, the doctor, grades the fever. Only he says “high”; Greek physicians distinguished great and small fevers.

They appealed to him on her behalf. A household asked for a woman too ill to ask for herself: intercession, and a comfort to anyone who has ever sat by a bed with nothing to offer but a request.

He rebuked the fever. The same verb as for the demon (v. 35) and the storm (8:24). Not that the fever was demonic: it is the same sovereign word applied to a different enemy. Jesus confronts illness as an enemy, part of the disorder sin has brought into the world, and he has authority over every power that harms.

Immediately she rose and began to serve them. Complete healing, with none of the weakness that usually follows a high fever, and her first act with a restored body is to feed the people in her house. “Serve” (diēkonei) is the word for ministry. That is the shape of the thing all through Luke: what is received is not kept.

No kitchen too small. The authority that silenced a demon in public walks into somebody’s kitchen: the Lord of glory stands by the bed of a woman with a fever. He did not think a kitchen too small for his authority or a mother-in-law too unimportant for his care.

Why does God heal some people and not others? Someone will read this chapter who prayed for years and buried the person anyway. Luke never says he is describing the normal experience of God’s people: Paul left a co-worker ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20), and his own thorn was not removed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). These days in Capernaum show not a policy but a person: what he is like and what he will finally do. Every fever he rebuked came back eventually, and everyone he healed later died; these are signs of the morning, not the noon. If your prayer was not answered with healing, it was not because you lacked faith or God lacked love. The full healing is still coming, at the resurrection (Revelation 21:4).

Does Christ still heal like this today? God still hears and answers prayer for the sick, sometimes with healing, often through ordinary means. The church prays for the sick (James 5:14–15) and leaves the outcome to God. But the healing miracles of Jesus and the apostles were signs that confirmed who he was and what they preached (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12).

Where Christians differ: does the gift of healing continue? Many Christians believe it does, and that God still gives healing as a gift to particular people. This commentary’s view: such sign gifts more likely belonged to the foundational period. Hebrews speaks of these signs as confirming the message to the first hearers, in the past tense, Paul calls them the signs of an apostle, and the instant, complete healings of the Gospels and Acts do not appear as a regular gift in later church life. Those who believe the gift continues are faithful Christians who love the same Lord, and we agree that God still heals in answer to prayer.
verseByVerse.note: Luke, a doctor, notes that it was a high fever. Simon (Peter) was married.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. And demons also came out of many, crying, 'You are the Son of God!' But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At sunset the whole town brings its sick, and Jesus heals them one by one, with his own hands, while silencing the demons who name him.

Now when the sun was setting. Luke gives the hour because it explains the crowd. The Sabbath ended at sundown, and carrying a sick relative on a mat counted as work under the rules about carrying burdens (Jeremiah 17:21). So the moment the sun is down the doors open all along the street.

He laid his hands on every one of them. Only Luke says he laid his hands on each one. A word over the crowd would have taken four seconds; he touched them one at a time, after a long day, into the night.

He would not allow them to speak. Luke links “Son of God” and “the Christ”. As in the synagogue, he will not be announced by demons (11:15; see the note on vv. 35–37); he would reveal himself in his own way, culminating in the cross.

The untouched. Some of those he touched had not been touched by anybody for years; some conditions made a person ceremonially unclean, and left them alone. Touching each one is not efficiency. It is what he is like, and there is no one so far gone, so long untouched, or so far down the line that he stops before he gets there.

In everyday life. Bring the people you love to him in prayer, one face at a time. And in a busy week, choose one person who is easy to overlook, the housebound neighbour, the elderly member who no longer comes, the colleague nobody eats with, and give them your full attention, unhurried, for an hour.

Does Jesus still notice individuals, when millions pray to him? Yes. He laid his hands on every one of them, and he has not changed (Hebrews 13:8). The risen Lord knows his sheep by name (John 10:3), and because he is God his attention is not divided: he is no less present to you for being present to someone else. When you pray, you are not a number in a queue but one person, known completely, with his full attention.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown; only then could people carry the sick without breaking the Sabbath rules.

verseByVerse.quote: And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. And the people sought him and came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them, but he said to them, 'I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus will not be kept by one town: he was sent to preach the kingdom of God to others too, and he must go on. The healings are real, but the preaching is the mission.

A desolate place. After a night like that, he leaves; Mark says he went to pray (Mark 1:35), as Luke showed him praying at the Jordan (3:21). It comes the morning after his most successful day so far, with the town at his feet. Success has its own temptation: to live from the crowd’s need of us rather than the Father’s love for us. Jesus went to his Father before the crowd could set the agenda.

They would have kept him. This is Capernaum at its best, not hostility. Nazareth drove him out; Capernaum tried to hold him in. Both wanted him on their own terms, and he goes anyway.

I must. There is the “must” again, dei, the divine necessity that first appeared on the lips of a twelve-year-old in the temple (2:49) and will drive him all the way to Jerusalem. And it is attached not to healing but to preaching. The healings are the announcement made visible, not the mission. Bodies healed die again. The word of the kingdom gives eternal life.

The kingdom of God. Its first mention in Luke: not a place or a programme, but God’s reign, his rule breaking into a world in rebellion, in the person of the King, to save and to judge. That is why its arrival looks like this: demons evicted, bodies mended, the poor given news, debts cancelled. Wherever he goes, the territory changes hands.

Sent for this purpose. “I was sent” picks up the Nazareth reading (v. 18), and the programme cannot be held in one place: the word keeps moving outward, town after town, until it is preached openly in Rome (Acts 28:31). He was sent not to be kept but to be followed. That “must” is why the gospel reached you: he would not stay where he was wanted, because he was sent for those who did not yet know him, and he has been coming to the next town ever since.

A Saviour on our terms. We are consumers by training, and bring the habit to Jesus. Capernaum wanted him because he healed; Nazareth wanted nothing more to do with him once he said something unwelcome. They look like opposites and are the same posture: customers deciding what he is for. The modern version is a faith kept because it helps with stress, the children or a sense of meaning, and quietly dropped when it asks for something we did not plan to give. But a Jesus kept on our terms can only be as large as our needs, and our needs are smaller than we are. He says “I must”, and he goes. And that is the good news hidden in his refusal: a Lord who could be kept by one town could never have come looking for you in yours.

In everyday life. Do not let good things crowd out the main thing: the Christian worker so busy meeting needs that the gospel is never spoken; the parent so busy with activities that the children never hear about Christ at home. And when a week goes well, take time alone with God before the next demand arrives, as he did.

Is it wrong to want our church to keep what God is doing? Not to be thankful for it, but to turn blessing inward, as though God’s work existed for us. A church blessed with gifted people, money and growth should ask not only how to keep them but where to send them: planting another congregation, supporting missionaries, releasing its best people to go. The church in Antioch, at the height of its blessing, sent away two of its leading teachers (Acts 13:1–3). Healthy churches give away what they have been given.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke sums up a long period in one sentence: Jesus kept on preaching in the synagogues throughout the land of the Jews. The chapter began with one man alone in a desert and ends with a preaching circuit across a nation, synagogue by synagogue, exactly as he said (v. 43).

He was preaching. The tense means he kept on preaching: a summary of an extended period of ministry.

In the synagogues. The same institution whose Nazareth branch had just tried to kill him. He did not abandon the synagogue because a synagogue rejected him; he went to the next one. If a door has closed on you somewhere, as Nazareth closed on him, do not conclude that God has finished with you.

He took it to the next town. The trumpet of the Jubilee was shouted down in one village, so he took it to the rest, and has never stopped. In the wilderness and the synagogue, at the cliff edge and in the kitchen, at sunset and at dawn, he was the same: the Son who would not bow, the King whose word cannot be resisted, the Saviour whose hands reached every one.

Does a difference between manuscripts mean we cannot trust the Bible? No. Differences are real, and honest translations footnote them, but most are tiny matters of spelling or word order, and no doctrine rests on a doubtful reading alone. Here (see the box below) the meaning is the same either way. We have far more early copies of the New Testament than of any other ancient book, and by comparing them scholars can recover what was written with remarkable confidence. God has kept his word.

Textual note: Judea or Galilee? Older translations may have Galilee here. The manuscripts divide: some, followed by the KJV and NKJV, read Galilee, but the best read Judea, which is also the harder reading, and the harder reading is usually the original, since copyists smooth difficulties rather than create them. Everything in this chapter happens in Galilee, and Mark 1:39 has Galilee, so Judea looks like a slip that invited correction. But Luke uses Judea elsewhere for the whole land of the Jews, Galilee included (1:5; 6:17; 7:17; 23:5; Acts 10:37), so he is saying that the preaching spread throughout the Jewish land.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Galilee. Luke sometimes uses “Judea” for the whole land of the Jews.

4.text: <sup>1</sup> And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness <sup>2</sup> for forty days, being tempted by the devil. And he ate nothing during those days. And when they were ended, he was hungry. <sup>3</sup> The devil said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.” <sup>4</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone.’” <sup>5</sup> And the devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, <sup>6</sup> and said to him, “To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. <sup>7</sup> If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.” <sup>8</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.’” <sup>9</sup> And he took him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, <sup>10</sup> for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’ <sup>11</sup> and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’” <sup>12</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is said, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’” <sup>13</sup> And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time. <sup>14</sup> And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. <sup>15</sup> And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all. <sup>16</sup> And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. <sup>17</sup> And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written, <sup>18</sup> “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, <sup>19</sup> to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.” <sup>20</sup> And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. <sup>21</sup> And he began to say to them, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” <sup>22</sup> And all spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said, “Is not this Joseph's son?” <sup>23</sup> And he said to them, “Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself.’ What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.” <sup>24</sup> And he said, “Truly, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown. <sup>25</sup> But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months, and a great famine came over all the land, <sup>26</sup> and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. <sup>27</sup> And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.” <sup>28</sup> When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. <sup>29</sup> And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. <sup>30</sup> But passing through their midst, he went away. <sup>31</sup> And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. And he was teaching them on the Sabbath, <sup>32</sup> and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority. <sup>33</sup> And in the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, <sup>34</sup> “Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.” <sup>35</sup> But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent and come out of him!” And when the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. <sup>36</sup> And they were all amazed and said to one another, “What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!” <sup>37</sup> And reports about him went out into every place in the surrounding region. <sup>38</sup> And he arose and left the synagogue and entered Simon's house. Now Simon's mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. <sup>39</sup> And he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them. <sup>40</sup> Now when the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. <sup>41</sup> And demons also came out of many, crying, “You are the Son of God!” But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ. <sup>42</sup> And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. And the people sought him and came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them, <sup>43</sup> but he said to them, “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.” <sup>44</sup> And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.

keyVerse.quote: Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.
keyVerse.note: This one-sentence sermon tells us who Jesus is and what the whole chapter is about: Isaiah’s Spirit-anointed liberator has come, and the release he promised begins now. Everything else in the chapter tests or displays that claim, from the obedient Son in the wilderness to the captives set free in Capernaum. And “today” still stands: the year of the Lord’s favour is open to the one who hears it.

4.reflection:
Jesus met each temptation with a word of Scripture he already knew and trusted (vv. 4, 8, 12). Where are you most often tempted, what lie about God lies underneath it, and which part of God’s word answers that lie?

Nazareth admired Jesus’ words and dismissed him in the same breath: “Is not this Joseph’s son?” (v. 22). In what ways can growing up with the gospel make us think we already know all there is to know about him? What helps you hear him afresh?

The congregation was furious when Jesus reminded them that God sent Elijah to a Sidonian widow and healed a Syrian general (vv. 25–29). Who are the people we find it hard to imagine God welcoming, and what does our reaction show about how we think of our own salvation?

Capernaum wanted to keep Jesus, but he said, “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well” (v. 43). How might we try to keep Jesus on our own terms, as individuals or as a church, and what would it look like to share what we have been given?

5.title: Calling, Cleansing, and the New Wine
5.overview:
Where we are. At Nazareth Jesus announced that God’s promised release had begun (4:18–21), and he has left Capernaum to preach in other towns (4:43). Here that preaching gathers its first followers and meets its first organised opposition, which hardens through 6:11.

The message. Jesus has God’s own authority, and spends it calling sinners to himself. His holiness exposes and his grace keeps: the fisherman who cries “Depart from me” is sent out, the unclean man is touched, the paralysed man is forgiven, the tax collector is called from his booth. And what he brings is too new for the old forms to hold, because the bridegroom himself has come.

Why it was said. Luke’s mostly Gentile readers needed certainty (1:4; see the introduction), and to know whether people like them could belong. Here they see whom Jesus calls and who objects: the line runs not between the respectable and the disreputable but between those who know they are sick and those who think they are well.

How the chapter makes its case. A catch that nearly sinks two boats shows Simon who is in his boat; exposed and drawn at the same moment, he confesses his sin and is answered with a calling (vv. 1–11). A leper is touched, made clean and sent back to his people (vv. 12–16). A paralysed man let down through a roof is forgiven before he is healed, and the visible healing proves the invisible authority (vv. 17–26). A tax collector is called and throws a feast for sinners, and the Pharisees’ grumbling draws out the doctor’s logic of the gospel (vv. 27–32). A dispute about fasting explains it all: the bridegroom is present, and forms built for a world still waiting for him cannot contain him (vv. 33–39).

Where it leads. The first shadow of the cross falls at a wedding: “the bridegroom is taken away” (v. 35). The holy one who touched the leper would be numbered with the transgressors; the Son of Man who forgave sins on earth would be counted a blasphemer and bear those sins himself, so that his pardon, free to us, is never cheap.

For us. No one is too unclean, too helpless or too compromised for Jesus to call. The danger is to think we are well, or to be too settled in a good religion to want what he brings. Come as you are, expect not to stay as you are, and carry others to him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Jesus Calls the First Disciples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus’ holiness exposes Simon as a sinner, and his grace makes the sinner a fisher of men. On the shore of Gennesaret Jesus borrows Simon’s boat as a pulpit (vv. 1–3), then tells him, after a night of catching nothing, to let down the nets again; Simon obeys “at your word” (vv. 4–5), and the catch nearly sinks two boats (vv. 6–7). The fish show Simon who is in his boat, and he falls at Jesus’ knees with words like Isaiah’s (vv. 8–9; Isaiah 6:5). Jesus does not deny that he is a sinner or send him away; he gives him a task, because the calling never rested on Simon’s worthiness. They leave everything, the catch of their lives included (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
The catch proves who is calling: the one who commands the fish is the one who made them (see the note on vv. 6–7).

Catching men describes a rescue (see the note on vv. 10–11). And the shape of the morning is the shape of every conversion: Christ comes first, a sinner is left with nothing to stand on, confesses it, and is called anyway.
verseByVerse.examples:
Simon’s obedience is not blind: he states the futility plainly, and obeys because the one who commands can be trusted.

Not every disciple is told to leave a trade, but everyone who follows has something to leave on the beach (see the note on vv. 10–11).

verseByVerse.quote: On one occasion, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret, and he saw two boats by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And he sat down and taught the people from the boat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Jesus calls Simon, he borrows his boat and makes him listen to the word of God. The call that will change these fishermen’s lives begins with a sermon and a small favour asked of tired men.

To hear the word of God. Luke introduces the first disciples through a sermon, not a miracle. “The word of God” is Luke’s phrase for Jesus’ preaching, and the crowd is hungry for it. Here that preaching (4:43) begins to gather the company who will one day be his witnesses (24:48).

The lake of Gennesaret. Luke’s precise name for the Sea of Galilee, from the fertile plain of Gennesaret on its north-western shore. Luke, who knew the Mediterranean, does not call a lake 13 miles long a sea.

Washing their nets. The last job of a night’s fishing: working boat owners at the end of a wasted night (v. 5), wanting to go home, and a teacher climbs into the boat and asks a favour.

The setting. Only Luke tells of the great catch. Matthew and Mark give the call in a few brisk lines (Matthew 4:18–22; Mark 1:16–20). Luke gives a whole morning, and plainly not their first meeting (4:38–39; John 1:35–42). The call came in stages: they met him at the Jordan, came to know him in Capernaum, and on this morning left everything.

Simon’s boat. Jesus borrows what belongs to Simon, as a first step in claiming Simon himself. The Lord of the sea climbs in among wet nets and makes it a pulpit: water carries sound, and a boat pushed out a few yards turns a beach into an auditorium. Before Simon is called, he is made to listen. Jesus enters their exhaustion and disappointment before he asks anything of them, and asks for something small before he asks for everything. He borrows our small things to give us great ones.

How does God usually call people? Most people are called as Simon was: step by step, until a day when it becomes decisive. Some can name the hour they first believed; many came over months or years, through a Christian home, a friend, a church, a slow dawning. Both are real conversions. What matters is not whether you can date it but whether you are now following him. If your story is gradual, do not doubt it for that reason: God was at work in every stage, as he was with Simon at the Jordan, in his house and in his boat.
verseByVerse.note: The lake of Gennesaret is the Sea of Galilee. Nets were washed and mended after a night’s fishing.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, 'Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.' And Simon answered, 'Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon obeys a command that makes no sense to a fisherman, for one reason only: Jesus said it. This is faith in its first form, an honest objection followed by obedience to a word.

Put out into the deep. Simon has fished this lake all his working life. Net fishing was done at night, and he has just worked the whole of it for nothing. It is now morning, the worst time, and a carpenter from an inland village is telling a fisherman how to fish. “Your nets” is plural: the whole crew is to do it.

Master. Simon states the professional reality plainly, and he is right. “Master” (epistatēs), a word Luke alone uses, means someone in charge. It is a real title, but not yet “Lord” (v. 8). He knows enough to obey, not yet whom he is obeying, and that is where most obedience begins.

At your word. Simon claims no expectation of fish and no inner assurance, only “at your word”. This is faith: not blind, but trust in the word of a person he had begun to trust. The objection is stated honestly, and then he obeys anyway, because of who is speaking. And the cost is real: hours more work with clean nets, in front of a crowd who know it will not work. He is not risking his life, only looking a fool, which for most people is harder.

Whose word it was. Simon did not yet know it, but the word he leaned on was the word that had made the lake. “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made”, and “he spoke, and it came to be” (Psalm 33:6, 9). Simon’s faith was small and his reasons thin; the one he trusted was neither. Faith saves not because it is large but because of the one it trusts, and a fisherman’s grudging “at your word”, spoken to the Creator, was enough to fill two boats.

In everyday life. Where does Christ’s word tell you to do what experience calls pointless: forgive the relative who never changes, keep praying for the child who shows no interest? Say with Simon: at your word, I will. Your obedience will be halting, as his was, yet the Father accepts it for the sake of the Son whose obedience never faltered and is counted yours.

Does this mean I should obey any impression that comes to me? No. Simon obeyed a word spoken audibly by Jesus himself. For us, Christ’s word is Scripture, and there we look for his commands (2 Timothy 3:16–17). A strong feeling or inner voice should be tested by the Bible and wise counsel, not obeyed as his voice. But where Scripture speaks, to forgive, to give, to be honest, to keep a vow, Simon is our pattern: obey, even when experience says it will not work.
verseByVerse.note: Fishing on the lake was done at night; daytime in deep water was the wrong time and place.

parallels.desc: a night of nothing, then a great catch

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. They signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. And they came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The catch is so large that the nets break and two boats begin to sink: the fish of the sea are obeying Jesus. The excess is the message, for no fisherman’s luck could explain it.

They enclosed a large number of fish. Luke describes not the fish arriving but the equipment failing: the nets “were breaking”, beginning to break, the miracle reported by men trying to cope with it. Psalm 8 says God put all things under the feet of the son of man, even the fish of the sea, and Hebrews sees that psalm fulfilled in Jesus (Psalm 8:6–8; Hebrews 2:8–9). In this boat the fish of the sea are doing as he says.

Their partners. James and John (v. 10): a small fishing business. Even both crews together barely coped, and the catches God gives are still usually too big for one boat.

So that they began to sink. A moderate catch could have been put down to luck; this could not. Jesus shows his authority not in a synagogue but in their own trade, where their competence was greatest and had just failed. The catch is also a picture of the harvest of people the gospel would bring (v. 10; Acts 2:41).

Grace that breaks every container. The God of the overflowing net does not deal in moderate measures. He fills boats until they sink, wine jars to the brim, baskets of leftovers after the crowds are fed, and cups until they run over. After the resurrection, on the same lake, a voice from the shore says, “Cast the net on the right side”, and the net comes up full and unbroken (John 21:6, 11). Simon’s story begins and ends with a catch he did not earn, from a word he did not expect, in water he had worked all night for nothing.

Will obeying Christ always bring visible success? No. Scripture is full of faithful people whose obedience brought prison, loss or apparent failure: Jeremiah preached for some forty years and was largely ignored; Paul was beaten and imprisoned. The promise is not that obedience always brings results we can measure, but that it is never wasted (1 Corinthians 15:58). God sometimes gives the overflowing net to show what he can do; more often he asks us to keep letting down the nets and trust him with what comes up.

parallels.desc: the net full of large fish

verseByVerse.quote: But when Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.' For he and all who were with him were astonished at the catch of fish that they had taken,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The catch shows Simon who is sitting in his boat, and the nearness of holiness makes him confess that he is a sinful man. It was a blessing, not a rebuke, that broke him open.

He fell down at Jesus’ knees. Luke calls him Simon Peter, the only time before 6:14, as if to mark the moment. He does not count the fish or ask how it was done; he goes down on his knees in a sinking boat.

Depart from me. A surprising response to a miracle of blessing. Nothing has been said about sin, only a boatload of fish. But the fish have shown him who is in his boat, and his conscience cannot bear to stand next to him. God’s kindness leads to repentance (Romans 2:4).

O Lord. “Master” has become “Lord”. The word could mean no more than sir, but on his knees in a sinking boat it carries the weight of the title Israel’s Scriptures give to God himself: he has understood that the gap between himself and this man is not the ordinary gap between two men.

The oldest pattern in Scripture. Isaiah sees the LORD high and lifted up and cries: “Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips … for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!” (Isaiah 6:5). Job meets God and repents in dust and ashes (Job 42:5–6). It is what happens when a creature with a conscience comes close to holiness, and holiness is not first a rule but what God is: utterly pure, wholly unlike anything he has made, a blazing goodness no sinner can see and live (Exodus 33:20). Conviction of sin is the beginning of true discipleship.

The Holy One stayed. Simon asked the Holy One to leave his boat, and the Holy One stayed. His holiness is not the kind that keeps its distance from the unclean; it came all the way down to stand among them, and would go further still, to bear Simon’s sins in his own body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). The nearness Simon dreaded was the very nearness that saved him.

What happened to the fear of God? When the sociologist Christian Smith and his colleagues surveyed thousands of American teenagers in the early 2000s, the God most of them believed in wanted people to be nice and feel good about themselves, and otherwise stayed out of the way unless needed. They called it “moralistic therapeutic deism”, and it is hardly confined to teenagers. The moralist thinks God can be managed by good behaviour; the secular person pictures him as a celestial counsellor. Both have shrunk him to something safe, and no one has ever fallen on his knees before that God. A God too small to fear is too small to save you, and his love is worth about as much as a pleasant mood. Only a God this great could make his kindness this astonishing.

The shame that wants to be left alone. Some shame does not want to be forgiven so much as to be left alone; it would rather be far off than be seen. Simon is right about himself and wrong about what to do with it. “A sinful man” is the accurate diagnosis, and the reason Jesus got into the boat.

I feel more sinful now than before I was a Christian. Is something wrong? Usually, something is right. The clearer the light, the more dust you see in the room; Paul near the end of his life called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). A deepening sense of sin is not going backwards, provided it drives you to Christ and not away from him. The danger is concluding, as Simon did for a moment, that you must keep your distance. The right response is the one Simon made next: to stay at Jesus’ knees and hear him say, “Do not be afraid.”

parallels.desc: woe is me, for I am lost

verseByVerse.quote: and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, 'Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.' And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers Simon’s fear not by leaving but by calling him: from now on he will catch people alive. Grace does not deny the sin; it is greater than the sin, and the fishermen leave everything to follow.

James and John. James and John, with Simon, became the inner three, present at the raising of Jairus’ daughter and on the mountain of transfiguration (8:51; 9:28).

Do not be afraid. Gabriel said it to Zechariah and Mary, the angel to the shepherds (1:13, 30; 2:10): holiness always produces the fear, and the answer is always the same word. Jesus does not argue with Simon’s verdict on himself; a sinful man is exactly the kind of man he calls. The Lord who could have sent Simon away instead sent him out.

Catching men. “From now on” is a phrase Luke reserves for turning points. The word for catching is zōgreō, to take alive, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for sparing captives in battle rather than killing them (Numbers 31:18). Fishing is not good news for the fish; the net means death. This net means the opposite: Simon will pull people out alive, out of the water that was drowning them.

The same trade, reversed. Nothing of who Simon is gets thrown away; the fisherman’s patience and nerve are put to a new use. The first great haul comes on a morning in Jerusalem when about three thousand are taken alive in a day (Acts 2:41). And the net Simon would cast at Pentecost had been woven first around Simon himself, by the Lord who catches men alive.

They left everything. Only Luke says “everything”, and everything includes the fish: the catch of a lifetime, enough money to change a family’s year, left with the boats and the nets. Jesus was worth more. This is what following him means (14:33; 18:28).

Must every Christian leave his job to follow Jesus? No. Luke’s own Gospel is full of people sent home (8:39). Most Christians serve Christ as fishermen, nurses, accountants and parents (1 Corinthians 7:17, 20). What every follower must leave is the claim of anything else to be first, and what is left on the beach is often the thing that had just started going well: a job, an ambition, a relationship, a habit, or the right to run your own life.

Is every Christian meant to be catching people? Yes, though not all in the same way. The Twelve had a unique apostolic office, and some are called to preach. But every believer belongs to a church sent into the world with the gospel (Matthew 28:19–20), and is to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in him (1 Peter 3:15). For most that means praying for people by name, living a visible faith, inviting friends to hear the gospel, and speaking of Christ when the door opens. You catch people alive by bringing them to the one who saves; you do not have to do the saving.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is as willing as he is able to make the unclean clean. A man “full of leprosy”, shut out from worship and from touch though he had done nothing to earn it (Leviticus 13:45–46), is sure of Jesus’ power and unsure only of his will (v. 12). Jesus touches him and says, “I will” (v. 13). Then he sends him to the priest (Leviticus 14), whose verdict was his way back to his family and town (v. 14). The instruction to tell no one fails at once, and as the crowds grow, Jesus keeps withdrawing to desolate places to pray (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology:
The touch is the incarnation in a single gesture. The Son of God did not keep his distance from our condition; he entered it and gave his own wholeness to the sufferer, a picture of the exchange in 2 Corinthians 5:21: “he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”

The leper’s “if you will” is the question of everyone who suspects that God may not want them, or that their case is too far gone, and Jesus answers it (see the note on v. 13).
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus’ withdrawal to pray as his popularity grew (v. 16) was a habit, not an episode (see the note on vv. 15–16): the demands fruitfulness creates can be carried only in communion with the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was in one of the cities, there came a man full of leprosy. And when he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, 'Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man cut off by his disease throws himself before Jesus, certain of his power and unsure only whether he is willing.

A man full of leprosy. Only Luke, the physician, says “full”: an advanced case. Leprosy in the Bible (Hebrew tsara‘at) covers a range of chronic, disfiguring skin diseases, not only what we now call leprosy (Hansen’s disease). The sufferer was ceremonially unclean, had to wear torn clothes and cry out, “Unclean, unclean”, to warn people away: “He shall live alone; his dwelling shall be outside the camp” (Leviticus 13:45–46). No one could touch him without becoming unclean.

A living death. No home, no synagogue, no temple, no work. Very likely nobody has touched him in years, and he was not necessarily being punished for anything; the condition simply put him outside. Yet here he is in a city, breaking every convention to reach Jesus.

If you will, you can. “You can” is not a request but a statement: he has no doubt about the power. “If you will” is where the uncertainty is, less doubt than knowing he has no right to demand anything. He does not bargain; he puts the whole thing in the other man’s hands, as real petition does, expecting everything, commanding nothing. Underneath is a fear many carry: not, is God able? but, is God willing, for someone like me? And “clean” means not just healed but restored: to God’s people, to worship, to his own family.

Am I God, to make alive? The leper’s “you can” is a larger confession than he may have known. When Naaman arrived in Samaria asking to be cured, the king of Israel tore his clothes and said, “Am I God, to kill and to make alive?” (2 Kings 5:7). Later rabbis likened a leper’s cure to raising the dead, and Israel had no remedy, only a law to diagnose it and a camp to keep it outside. So a man who kneels and says, “Lord … you can”, is ascribing to Jesus what the Old Testament reserves for God, and he is right. The Lord who kills and makes alive has come in person to the place where the law could only say “unclean”, and he would go outside the camp himself, bearing reproach (Hebrews 13:12–13), so that those outside could be brought in.

Should I add if it is your will to every prayer? It depends on what you are asking. Where God has plainly promised something, such as forgiveness to those who confess (1 John 1:9), wisdom to those who ask (James 1:5), or the Spirit to his children (11:13), you need not pray “if you will”; he has told you he wills it. Where he has not promised, healing, a job, a spouse, a particular outcome, ask boldly and add, as Jesus did in Gethsemane, “not my will, but yours, be done” (22:42). That is not weak faith but trust in a Father who knows better than we do.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprosy” in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases. A leper had to live apart and was ritually unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, 'I will; be clean.' And immediately the leprosy left him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus touches the untouchable man and makes him clean: his will is as ready as his power. The cleanness travels from Jesus to the leper, not the uncleanness from the leper to Jesus.

He touched him. The miracle inside the miracle. A word would have been enough (7:7). Instead the hand lands on the one body in Galilee that nobody had been permitted to touch for years.

I will; be clean. Two words in Greek, answering exactly what the man was unsure of: not “I can”, but “I will”. His will and his power are one. He does not have to be persuaded, and he has never once recoiled from anybody who came to him. The hand goes out first.

Immediately. Skin diseased for years made whole in a moment: a sign that the Messiah had come, for the “lepers are cleansed” (7:22).

Holiness is contagious in him. Under the law, touching a leper made a person unclean. Here it runs the other way: the holiness is the stronger thing, and it moves outward. In that one gesture is the reason the Son of God became man, and the exchange Paul describes: “for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). He takes what is ours; we receive what is his.

The hand that had made it. Sin, like leprosy, defiles, isolates, spreads and kills, beyond any human cure. Years of exclusion had taught this man to expect a no; the first hand to rest on his skin again was the hand that had made it, with not a hair’s breadth of hesitation, only, “I will.” The will that went out to the leper is the will that held him to the cross, where the clean one was numbered with the transgressors so that the unclean could be clean for ever.

Does I will mean that God always wills to heal every sick person who asks in faith? No. This healing was a sign that the kingdom had come in Jesus. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed, and was told, “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Every prayer for healing is rightly prayed as the leper prayed, “if you will”. And if healing does not come, his will towards you is no less kind; the Lord who touched the leper has promised a body that will never fall ill again.

What does it mean for me that Jesus touched the leper? That there is nothing about you that makes him recoil. People who carry deep shame, from abuse suffered, sin committed, or a body or mind that does not work as it should, often feel untouchable, as if God would keep his distance if he really knew. He comes nearest to what we hide. Bring him the thing you are most ashamed of, by name, in prayer; and if you can, tell a mature Christian, so that you hear his welcome spoken aloud. Then become his hand to others: notice who in your church or street is untouched, and go near.

verseByVerse.quote: And he charged him to tell no one, but 'go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a proof to them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sends the healed man to the priest, not to spread his fame but to be declared clean and restored to his people. “Tell no one” and “show yourself to the priest” do not cancel each other: the second is a legal procedure, not a publicity campaign.

He charged him to tell no one. A restraint Jesus imposes repeatedly in Galilee. A reputation as a healer would bury the preaching under a crowd of the desperate, which is exactly what happens anyway (v. 15).

Go and show yourself to the priest. Leviticus 14 lays down the week-long ritual by which a healed leper is examined, declared clean and restored; without it he cannot re-enter the town or his family’s house. Jesus heals the disease in a second, then sends the man through the process that heals what the disease had done to the rest of his life. Grace does not despise slow, ordinary steps. The Lord who cleanses the heart in an instant patiently walks us back into every relationship that sin had broken.

For a proof to them. The phrase carries an edge. Leprosy was rarely if ever cured, and now a priest had to declare clean a man who had been full of it. The establishment that would shortly decide Jesus was a blasphemer had been handed, by its own procedure, a public proof of what he could do.

The shadow and the substance. The law could examine a leper and pronounce him clean; it could never make him clean. Its ritual was a shadow cast ahead of time by the reality that had now come (Hebrews 10:1). The priest who certified the leper clean had no idea that the true High Priest had already done it, with a touch.

In everyday life. The man was cleansed first and sent to the priest after: obedience follows the gift, and still has to be carried through, step by step. A person converted from fraud still needs to pay back what he took; a believer restored after a fall still needs the patient rebuilding of trust. The cleansing is his gift, complete; the process restores the life around it.

Why did Jesus tell people to keep quiet, when we are told to tell everyone? Because before the cross a reputation as a wonder worker would have drawn crowds wanting a political Messiah; after the resurrection the command is the opposite (Matthew 28:19).

verseByVerse.quote: But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The more the crowds came, the more Jesus withdrew to pray. In a growing ministry prayer seems a luxury; Jesus treated fruitfulness as a reason to pray more, not less.

The report went abroad. The instruction to keep quiet has failed; Mark tells us the man spread the news everywhere (Mark 1:45).

To hear and to be healed. “To hear” comes first, and Luke does not sneer at them. They want the word and they want their bodies mended, a perfectly reasonable pair of things to want.

But he would withdraw. The tense means it was his habit: the busier it got, the more he went away. The pressure of an admiring crowd, to be what they want and believe their estimate of you, is not resisted by good intentions; he met it by leaving. He took his sense of who he was from his Father’s voice, “You are my beloved Son” (3:22), not from theirs, and that is the only place where anyone is safe from the crowd.

Never too busy for his own. The one through whom all things were made went out alone to speak with his Father, and he still prays now: he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). He has never once grown too busy to pray for his own.

Why did the Son of God need to pray? Because he was truly man, living in dependence on his Father, and prayer is the communion of the Son with the Father, not a sign of lack. Hebrews says he “offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7). As a true man he lived each day by trusting his Father, and showed us what a human life lived wholly towards God looks like.

I am too busy to pray much. What do I do? Be honest that busyness is the reason to pray more, not the excuse to pray less. Then be practical. Choose a fixed time, even fifteen minutes, before the day’s demands begin, and guard it like a meeting with your employer. Find a place, as he did: a room, a parked car, a walk. Let a psalm or the Lord’s Prayer guide you, so you are not left staring at a blank wall. And pray in the gaps, briefly and often (1 Thessalonians 5:17). Small, regular prayer will do more than occasional heroic efforts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, and he proves it by a healing everyone can see. The religious authorities appear in Luke for the first time, seated as if for an inspection, while the power of the Lord is with Jesus to heal (vv. 17–18). Friends, blocked by the crowd, take a roof apart to lower a paralysed man before him, and Luke calls it their faith (v. 19). Jesus forgives the man first; the scribes are right that only God can forgive sins, and wrong about the man in front of them (vv. 20–21). So he does what can be checked as evidence for what cannot (vv. 22–24), and the man walks home glorifying God (vv. 25–26).
verseByVerse.theology:
Forgiveness before healing shows the priority of Luke’s Gospel: the deepest human need is not physical. Jesus removes the paralysis too, and he does not suggest it was caused by the man’s sin (see the note on vv. 20–21). But he deals first with what would still have been wrong after the legs worked.

He never disputes the scribes’ starting point, that only God can forgive sins (see the note on vv. 20–21). He forgives anyway, and calls himself the Son of Man (see the note on vv. 22–24).
verseByVerse.examples:
The four friends show what serious intercession looks like: not eloquence or technique, but the refusal to accept that the door is the only way, and a willingness to look foolish for somebody else.

And the faith Jesus saw was theirs: the carrying counts (see the note on v. 19).

verseByVerse.quote: On one of those days, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the religious experts sit in judgment, the power of God is with Jesus to heal, and friends are carrying a helpless man towards him. Luke sets the two responses to Jesus side by side before a word is spoken.

Pharisees and teachers of the law. The religious authorities appear in Luke’s narrative for the first time, and they are sitting down. Teachers of the law were the same as the scribes (v. 21), experts in the law of Moses. They have come from every village and from Jerusalem: the gathering has the shape of an inspection. A new teacher drawing crowds was exactly what the guardians of the law felt bound to examine, as Jerusalem had sent priests and Levites to question John (John 1:19) and would send scribes again (Mark 3:22).

The power of the Lord. Luke states it before anything happens, like a stage direction. “The Lord” here means God: the power of God by the Spirit (4:14, 18), resting on the man the experts have come to examine, and not on them.

Carried. Outside, while the inspection proceeds, men are carrying a friend on a mat; Mark says four (Mark 2:3). Somebody had to decide it was worth a day, and carry a paralysed body through the streets, slowly and in public, to a house so full there was no way in, and then not go home. The man on the mat will not say a word in the whole passage. Everything that happens to him happens because other people would not give up on getting him in front of Jesus.

Who were the Pharisees? A movement of devout laymen, over six thousand in Herod’s day according to Josephus, zealous to keep the law of Moses in every detail of daily life and guarding it with a large body of oral tradition (see Pharisees). They tithed even their herbs and fasted twice a week, and ordinary people respected them as the most serious believers in Israel. Their fault was not that they cared about God’s law, which was good, but that they trusted in their own keeping of it and looked down on others (18:9). Paul had been one (Philippians 3:5), and some came to faith (Acts 15:5).

In the flow. Here begins a run of five scenes (5:17–6:11) in which Jesus’ authority meets the religious leaders: over sin, the company he keeps, fasting, and twice over the Sabbath. Each time the question underneath is, “Who is this?”, and each time the opposition hardens (6:11).

How do I carry someone to Jesus today? In prayer, naming them before God regularly and specifically, for years if need be. In friendship: time, practical help, meals, honest conversation. Bring them where Jesus is spoken of, and when the moment comes, tell them plainly about him yourself. Carry them together with others, as these men did; it is too heavy a load for one person. And remember that your task is to bring them, not to heal them. That is his part.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers of the law were the same as the scribes, experts in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: but finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down with his bed through the tiles into the midst before Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blocked by the crowd, the friends take a roof apart to bring the man to Jesus, and Luke will call it faith. Faith is not particular about the route; it is certain about the destination.

No way in. The crowd was an obstacle, as crowds often are to those who need Jesus most (18:39; 19:3).

They went up on the roof. Houses had flat roofs, reached by an outside stair. Familiarity has made this scene charming, and it was not. Dust and debris must have come down on the heads of the seated Pharisees, and somebody’s roof is being taken apart with no sign that anybody asked the owner. It is rude, destructive and entirely out of order. The friends did not have better theology than the men in the room; they had a friend they refused to leave outside.

Into the midst before Jesus. Every effort in the scene ends at one spot: in front of Jesus, not the teachers from Jerusalem, who had the seats and the learning and no power to heal. Luke keeps moving the helpless to that same place (7:38; 17:16; 23:42), because there is no one else to bring a paralysed man to. Peter will say it in Jerusalem: “there is salvation in no one else” (Acts 4:12).

Tiles or clay? Some say this detail shows Luke did not know Palestine. Mark says the men dug through the roof (Mark 2:4), which fits an ordinary Galilean house of beams, branches and packed clay; Luke says “through the tiles”. But tiled roofs, normal in Greek and Roman building, had appeared in the region’s towns, and Luke, writing for readers across the empire, puts the scene in terms they could picture. Two writers describing the same hole for different readers is not a contradiction.

He broke open heaven. Four men broke open a roof to bring their friend down to Jesus; he had broken open heaven to come down to us.
