He came by a lower road than any outside stair, to lie where the helpless lie: in a manger, at last in a borrowed tomb. We were the man on the mat, unable to move one muscle towards him, and he is the friend who would not leave us outside. Every rescue that ever ended at his feet began with his own descent.

The man who could do nothing. His entire contribution was to lie there; Jesus saw “their” faith. People do get carried. There are seasons when a believer cannot pray or come, through grief, depression, exhaustion or shame, and will not get himself into the room. Somebody else has to do the carrying, and the carrying counts.

In everyday life. Be persistent and creative in love: when the friend says no to church a third time, try a meal at home; when a sick member cannot come, take the service to them. But creative love is no licence to trick people or pressure them until they give in. The men broke a roof, not a person’s will. Bring people to Jesus; do not drag them.

I am the one who cannot pray right now. Am I failing? No. Scripture does not condemn the Christian who, in illness, grief or darkness, can hardly pray. “The Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26), Christ intercedes for us at the Father’s right hand (Romans 8:34), and God gives brothers and sisters to carry us. Let them. Tell one or two trusted friends that you are struggling and ask them to pray for you. Keep coming to church if you can, even if you only sit there. You are not less a Christian because you are on the mat for now.
verseByVerse.note: Luke speaks of tiles, the roofing his Greek readers knew; Mark describes digging through a roof of packed earth.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he saw their faith, he said, 'Man, your sins are forgiven you.' And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying, 'Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus meets the man’s deepest need first by forgiving his sins, and the scribes rightly see that he is claiming what belongs to God alone. They reason correctly from a true premise, and still reach the wrong verdict.

And when he saw their faith. A hole in the roof is faith made visible. Our faith and prayers can matter for others.

Man, your sins are forgiven you. Nobody in that room expected that sentence. The Greek verb form means: your sins have been forgiven, and stand forgiven. He did not ask for sacrifices; he was about to become the sacrifice. No one else has the right to say it, and he says it gladly.

The deeper need. A man healed and unforgiven has a working body for a few more decades, and his debt to God still stands. To be forgiven by God is to have that debt cancelled, not hidden. He does not bring it up again, now or at the judgment: “as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12).

Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Blasphemy is speaking against God, or claiming what belongs to him alone, and the penalty was death by stoning (Leviticus 24:16). Notice where the charge is made: inwardly. They “began to question”, Luke says; they had not yet spoken it aloud (v. 22).

Who can forgive sins but God alone? Their theology is entirely correct. All sin is ultimately against God (Psalm 51:4), and the Old Testament says plainly that only he forgives it: “I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake” (Isaiah 43:25). They have the principle right, and the observation right: this man has just forgiven sins. Instead of following the argument where it leads, they reach for blasphemy. If Jesus is not God, he is a blasphemer; and he does not leave them to take his word for it, but offers evidence the whole room can check (v. 24). All through Luke, the people who reject Jesus are rarely those who understand him least; they are usually those who have grasped exactly what he is claiming.

Who has the right to forgive? Our age is rightly angry when an institution announces that it has forgiven a man who harmed someone in its care: only the one wronged has the right to release the debt. C. S. Lewis used this instinct, in Mere Christianity, to show how strange Jesus’ words are. A man forgiving what is done to him we understand; a man who, untouched himself, forgave you for what you had done to others would be absurd, unless he really was the God whose laws are broken in every sin. Jesus speaks as though every wrong this man ever did was done to him. And the one most wronged is about to pay himself, which is why his word of pardon is not cheap.

Was the man’s paralysis caused by his sin? Not necessarily, and the passage can be heard cruelly. Jesus does not say the paralysis does not matter; he removes it. Nor does he say the man’s sin caused it. Some Jews believed sickness always came from sin. Sometimes it does (John 5:14), but Jesus denies that reasoning about the man born blind (John 9:2–3). He is treating the deeper condition first, in a man who had not come about it. If you are ill, do not assume God is punishing you. All sickness belongs to a fallen world; your illness may have no link to any particular sin at all.

Can someone else’s faith save a person? No. Luke does not say the paralysed man lacked faith, and the friends’ faith brought him to Jesus, which is what faith on behalf of others can do. We may carry others to Christ in prayer and witness, but each person must come to him in his own faith.
verseByVerse.note: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him alone.

parallels.desc: I am he who blots out your transgressions

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them, 'Why do you question in your hearts? Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins'—he said to the man who was paralyzed—'I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus proves his unseen authority to forgive sins by a healing everyone can see. The checkable miracle is the evidence for the claim no one can check.

When Jesus perceived their thoughts. Jesus answers the argument going on inside their heads, and it is the LORD who sees and searches the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10): another sign pointing to who he is.

Which is easier, to say, Your sins are forgiven you, or to say, Rise and walk? The question is sharper than it looks. Which is easier to say? Plainly the first. Anyone can announce forgiveness, because nothing visible follows. “Rise and walk” to a paralysed man is the dangerous sentence: in three seconds the room will know whether it worked. In another sense, forgiveness is far harder, because it is a divine act, and would cost Jesus his life.

That you may know. So Jesus does the checkable one, as proof of the one nobody can see: the logic of miracle throughout the Gospels. A Jesus who heals bodies and cannot deal with guilt would be a remarkable physician and no use at all at the end.

The Son of Man. Jesus’ most frequent name for himself, used here for the first time in Luke. It can sound modest; it was not. He is drawing on Daniel 7:13–14, where “one like a son of man” is given an everlasting dominion. In a room full of men who knew Daniel, choosing that title while forgiving sins was not a retreat from the claim. It was the claim, doubled.

On earth. Everyone in that room believed sins were forgiven in heaven, through the appointed sacrifices. Jesus says the authority is here, at ground level, in a crowded house in Capernaum. What the whole temple system existed to deal with has walked into a room and dealt with it, in one sentence, freely, for a man who did not ask.

Rise. Three commands, impossible for a paralysed man. The word of Jesus gives the power to obey, as his Spirit now does in us (Ezekiel 36:27). As Augustine prayed, “Give what you command, and command what you will.”

How can I know my sins are really forgiven, when I cannot see it? By the logic Jesus used here. You cannot see forgiveness, but he has given evidence enough: his miracles, his death, and above all his resurrection, by which God declared his sacrifice accepted (Romans 4:25). Your forgiveness rests not on your feelings, which rise and fall, but on his word: “everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name” (Acts 10:43). If you have come to him trusting him, you are forgiven, as surely as that man walked. Feelings of guilt may linger; take them to his promise, not his promise to your feelings.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately he rose up before them and picked up what he had been lying on and went home, glorifying God. And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying, 'We have seen extraordinary things today.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The healed man walks home glorifying God, and the whole room is seized with awe, though awe is not yet faith.

He rose up before them. Luke lingers on the bed. The bed that had carried him, he now carried, out through the doorway they could not get him in by, past the seated dignitaries.

Glorifying God. Only Luke records his praise. Somewhere in Capernaum a family had probably been carrying this man for years, and that evening he walked in on his own feet, carrying the mat, to tell them what God had done.

Extraordinary things. Now all of them glorify God with awe, the delegation from Jerusalem included. “Extraordinary” is paradoxa, things contrary to expectation, and the thing most contrary to expectation was not finally the walking man. It was that God’s own prerogative had been exercised, out loud, by a man on earth.

The paradox would deepen. The holy God forgives the guilty and remains just, because the Son of Man would carry our sins as that man carried his mat, all the way out of the room. Counted a blasphemer, he would be crucified and raised, so that forgiveness of sins would be proclaimed in his name to all nations (24:46–47). The crowd saw the first page of it. And that street in Capernaum, loud with praise, is a foretaste of the morning when the lame will leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:6), every mat will be rolled up for the last time, and the whole forgiven company will glorify God.

Amazed and unchanged. Luke does not say they believed; he says they were amazed and afraid, and by chapter 6 the scribes and Pharisees among them will be watching him to accuse him (6:7). Amazement is not faith. The man who went home with the mat had been forgiven; the men who went home with an anecdote had only been impressed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus came for sinners as a doctor comes for the sick, and he calls them to repentance. He calls Levi from his tax booth with two words; to every devout passer-by Levi was beyond hope, and unlike the fishermen he could never go back (vv. 27–28). His first act as a disciple is a great feast for the only people he knows, with Jesus in the middle, and the Pharisees and their scribes complain, a serious objection, since to share a table was to declare acceptance (vv. 29–30). Jesus answers with a doctor’s logic: the sick need a physician (vv. 31–32).
verseByVerse.theology:
Levi is Matthew (Matthew 9:9): the kingdom comes to the most unexpected people.

Jesus’ saying about calling not the righteous but sinners does not divide humanity into those who need him and those who do not, for “none is righteous, no, not one” (Romans 3:10). It describes two ways people see themselves (see the note on vv. 31–32).
verseByVerse.examples:
Levi’s banquet is the instinctive evangelism of someone who has just received grace: no method, just a house, his friends, and Jesus in the same room.

The wish to keep the table clean rests on a real principle, that holiness is kept by separation (see the note on vv. 29–30). Jesus’ table is where the sick come for medicine, not where the well congratulate each other on their health.

verseByVerse.quote: After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. And he said to him, 'Follow me.' And leaving everything, he rose and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls a despised tax collector with two words, and Levi leaves everything to follow him. Nothing in Levi’s life made the call reasonable; the call made Levi.

A tax collector named Levi. Matthew’s Gospel calls him Matthew (Matthew 9:9); he had both names, as Simon was also Peter and Saul was also Paul. Levi probably collected tolls for Herod Antipas on goods passing along the trade route through Capernaum.

Sitting at the tax booth. At work, in the place of his sin. To everyone walking past, Levi is a collaborator, a thief with legal protection (see 3:12; tax collectors), and, in many eyes, ritually unclean from contact with Gentiles. And he was very probably rich.

Follow me. He stops at the most despised table in town. No preliminaries, no probation. It is the voice that had just said “rise” to a paralysed man (v. 24), and it works the same way: the command carries the power to obey it. The Son of Man who has authority on earth to forgive sins spends it on him, in public, at the booth.

Leaving everything. The same phrase as at verse 11, and for Levi it costs differently. The fishermen could go back to their boats (John 21:3); there is no going back to a tax booth once you have walked away from one. Money had been Levi’s security and his compensation for everyone’s contempt, and when Christ called it lost its grip at once. That is how idols usually fall: not by being argued down, but by being outshone.

The man who wrote it down. The man rising from that booth is the man the church has long believed wrote the Gospel that opens the New Testament, and only its apostle list calls him “Matthew the tax collector” (Matthew 10:3), as though he never got over the wonder of it.

In everyday life. No one is beyond Christ’s call. Picture the person you consider least likely to become a Christian. Levi was that man in Capernaum. Pray for them as for a future disciple.

What did Levi do about the money he had taken? Luke does not tell us, but Zacchaeus, another tax collector, gave half his goods to the poor and repaid fourfold anyone he had defrauded (19:8). Grace forgives the sin before God freely and completely; it also makes us want to put right what we can. If you have cheated someone, the gospel does not ask you to earn forgiveness by repaying, but it will lead you, gladly, to repay.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew’s Gospel calls Levi “Matthew.” Tax collectors were despised as collaborators and cheats.

verseByVerse.quote: And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying, 'Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Levi celebrates his new Master with a feast for his fellow outcasts, and the Pharisees object that Jesus shares their table. Their question is serious, because it is about who belongs to the people of God.

A great feast. Levi’s first act as a disciple is to throw a party. He has no theology yet; he has a house and a contact list.

A large company. Luke’s polite way of describing the social world of a man in that trade. Levi fills the room with the only people he knows and puts Jesus in the middle: not a strategy, just a man who has been given something and wants his friends to meet the giver.

Reclining at table with them. To recline at a man’s table was to declare peace with him, to accept him, to be publicly associated with him: closer to a signed statement than to a meal.

They grumbled. The word used of Israel grumbling in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7–8). And they complain, not to Jesus, but round him to his disciples: an old form of religious criticism, raised where it will do most damage and cost least.

Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners? The objection deserves understanding. The Pharisees kept separate from “sinners”, those who did not keep the law as they interpreted it and the openly immoral, since eating with them made you unclean. Their premise was that you keep clean by keeping away. It is not a stupid premise; it is much of Leviticus, and it had kept Israel identifiable through centuries of pressure. What they had not reckoned with was a holiness that works the other way round, which Luke has just shown: a hand stretched out to a leper, and the cleanness travelling from the toucher to the touched (5:13). For the Pharisees holiness meant separation from sinners; for Jesus, going to them. The charge will come again (7:34; 15:2; 19:7).

At home among them. The holy Son of God was not slumming or making a point; he was at home among the people he came to save. One day, in the kingdom, he will sit down to the great feast with people from east and west and north and south (13:29), and the guest list will be full of Levis.

In everyday life. Levi’s method is open to anyone: a meal, a house, and the people you already know. Invite a neighbour and a Christian friend to dinner together; open your home at Christmas to someone who would be alone. He “receives sinners and eats with them” (15:2), and every one of us is at his table only because he does.

But does the Bible not tell us to avoid bad company? Yes: “Bad company ruins good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33), and we are not to walk in the counsel of the wicked (Psalm 1:1). The difference is the direction of influence. Jesus ate with sinners as their physician; he was never drawn into their sin, and they were drawn to him. Paul forbids close company with a professing brother living in open sin, not with the immoral of this world, or you would need to go out of the world (1 Corinthians 5:9–11). So be a friend to unbelievers, with open doors and real love; but if a friendship is pulling you into sin rather than you drawing them to Christ, step back.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, 'Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus eats with sinners as a doctor visits the sick, for he came to call sinners to repentance.

A physician. A proverb nobody can disagree with. A doctor found among the sick is not compromising his profession; he is doing it. He does not catch their disease; he heals it. So the question, why do you eat with sinners?, answers itself the moment you know what he came for.

I have not come to call the righteous. The word is ironic. Jesus is not conceding that the Pharisees are righteous: “none is righteous, no, not one” (Romans 3:10, quoting the Psalms). He is using their own self-description back at them.

Everyone in the house is sick. The two groups at Levi’s dinner differ not in their condition but in what they know about themselves. A man who does not believe he is ill will not send for a doctor however available the doctor makes himself. The Pharisees were disciplined and orthodox, and misjudged themselves in the one way that makes a person refuse treatment: they thought they were well. It takes God himself to open such eyes, as he later opened the eyes of a Pharisee named Saul, who came to count all his religious gain as loss for Christ (Acts 9:18; Philippians 3:4–9).

But sinners to repentance. Only Luke adds “to repentance”. Repentance is a turning round: coming to agree with God about your sin, and leaving it to come to him (Acts 26:20). The table at Levi’s house is a doctor’s visit, and doctors do not visit in order to agree with the disease. Grace receives sinners and changes them.

Never yet lost a patient. The Great Physician makes house calls, and he goes to the worst cases first, because he loved the diseased. His remedy is costly as no earthly doctor’s ever was: “with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). He has never yet lost a patient who put himself in his hands.

Does that mean Jesus accepts me as I am? Yes, and he will not leave you as you are. He receives anyone who comes, however sinful, without first requiring a clean-up: the leper came full of leprosy, and Levi straight from the booth. But the same Jesus calls you to repentance, and his acceptance is the beginning of a new life, not a seal of approval on the old one. You come as you are; you do not stay as you are. Both halves are love.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With Jesus something has come that the old forms cannot hold: the bridegroom himself. Asked why his disciples do not fast like John’s and the Pharisees’, Jesus answers that wedding guests do not fast while the bridegroom is with them, though the days will come when he is taken away (vv. 33–35). The garment and the wineskins press the point: what he brings is not a patch on the old system but its fulfilment, which the old forms, though God gave them, were never designed to contain (vv. 36–38). The last saying explains the resistance: people used to the old say it is good enough (v. 39).
verseByVerse.theology:
The bridegroom language places Jesus where the prophets place the LORD, and Revelation carries the image to the end: the marriage supper of the Lamb and the new Jerusalem prepared as a bride (Revelation 19:7–9; 21:2).

Verse 39 describes people content with something genuinely good, the law and the tradition God gave, in the presence of something better (see the note on v. 39).
verseByVerse.examples:
The bridegroom’s presence is the reason for Christian joy, and the resurrection confirmed it. Christian fasting is the fast of people who live between his going and his return, and want him back (see the note on vv. 33–35).

The wineskins test every tradition honestly, by asking whether the form is still carrying the life (see the note on vv. 37–38).

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to him, 'The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.' And Jesus said to them, 'Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fasting does not fit while the bridegroom is present, but it will when he is taken away. In answering a question about religious practice, Jesus puts himself in the place the Old Testament gives to God.

They fast often. The third complaint of the section, and the observation is accurate. The law commanded only one yearly fast (Leviticus 16:29), but Pharisees fasted twice a week (18:12), and the followers of John were austere, and their teacher was in prison.

Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? He answers with a wedding. A Jewish wedding feast could last up to a week, and later Jewish writings say wedding guests were excused from certain religious duties, including fasting. Fasting expressed mourning and longing, so fasting at a wedding is not deeper devotion, just the wrong time. While Jesus is here, the time of longing is over.

The bridegroom. The image does much more than settle a dispute about diet. In the Old Testament there is one bridegroom, and he is God. “Your Maker is your husband” (Isaiah 54:5); “as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5); “I will betroth you to me” for ever (Hosea 2:19–20). So when Jesus says the bridegroom is present, he is placing himself where the Old Testament places God (compare John 3:29). The wedding feast God promised for the days of the Messiah has begun.

Taken away. Then the shadow. A bridegroom does not leave his own wedding feast; the word suggests a removal by force (Isaiah 53:8). This is the first hint of the cross in Jesus’ own teaching in Luke, and nobody at that table could have understood it.

Snatched away for his bride. The bridegroom of Israel came in person and sat down at a feast, knowing he would be snatched away to a cross for his bride, to present her to himself without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). Our fasting now is the longing of a bride whose bridegroom has gone ahead, and our feasting the foretaste of the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9).

Should Christians fast, and how? Jesus plainly assumes it: “they will fast in those days”, and those days are these (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). But it is not the fast of the men asking the question, nor mourning without hope. It is the fast of people who have known the bridegroom and want him back: not a technique for getting God’s attention, but a body saying what the heart already knows. In practice it means going without food, or some meals, for a set time given to prayer: before a big decision, in repentance, in grief, or in longing for God’s work. Do it quietly (Matthew 6:16–18). Begin modestly, with one meal; take medical advice if you have a health condition; never treat it as earning anything from God. And do not make your pattern a rule for others or look down on those who fast differently: that is exactly the error of the men who asked the question.
verseByVerse.note: The law commanded one yearly fast, on the Day of Atonement. A wedding lasted days and was no time for fasting.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told them a parable: 'No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Jesus brings is not a patch to mend the old religion but something wholly new, and sewing it onto the old would ruin both. Three short parables (vv. 36–39) explain why his disciples do not follow the old patterns.

A new garment. Luke’s version is sharper than the others. Matthew and Mark speak of unshrunk cloth on an old garment (Mark 2:21); Luke has a man cutting up a new garment to patch an old one. The loss is doubled: the new garment is torn, and the patch does not match the old one.

The point. He brings the kingdom of God and the new covenant sealed in his own blood (22:20), which cannot be stitched onto the old ways of fasting and rule-keeping. The gospel is not a supplement to religion; it is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).

The old garment was not bad. God gave it, and Jesus honours it: he sends the leper to the priest and goes to the synagogue weekly. It is not being criticised. It is being finished with, because what it was for has come.

Not one thread of it is theirs. He came with a whole new garment, cut from his own life: the righteousness he wove in years of perfect obedience, given entire to people who had nothing to wear but rags, the robe of righteousness Isaiah sang of in the chapter Jesus read at Nazareth (Isaiah 61:10). Now he wraps sinners from head to foot in what he alone has made, and not one thread of it is theirs.

In everyday life. Do not treat Jesus as a patch on your old life: church added to the week but the business kept dishonest, prayer added to the marriage but the temper unchecked. Becoming new does not mean discarding your family, culture or honest gifts; Christ takes them up and makes them his.

How the saying is abused. In both directions. Some use it to junk the creeds and twenty centuries of the church’s thinking. But the newness in this parable is not new ideas. It is the gospel of the crucified and risen Christ, which is the oldest thing there is. Others treat every inherited practice as a doctrine, which is the Pharisees’ error exactly. What is genuinely new is a person, a covenant sealed in his blood, and a Spirit poured out on ordinary people.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
New wine needs fresh wineskins: the life Jesus brings cannot be forced into forms that have set hard. The saying is not that the old is expendable, but that forcing new life into hardened forms wastes the life and wrecks the form.

Wineskins. The same point, with a better image. New wine is still fermenting and expanding. A new goatskin stretched with it; an old one was set hard (see wineskins).

Fresh wineskins. “Must” (blēteon): it is necessary. Living things expand, and whatever contains them has to give. So it was, literally, in the first Christian generation: within thirty years the gospel had gone to Gentiles with no food laws, no temple and no priesthood, told that the whole system of temple and sacrifice had been a shadow of what had now come (Colossians 2:17). Not because the shadow was false, but because the substance had arrived.

He is the wine. The new wine of the kingdom is Christ’s own life, poured out in the Spirit, and it burst the old skins of temple and ritual and ran out into the whole world, to Gentiles and slaves and children, in every language under heaven. He is the wine, and he is the one who pours it, and he has never run dry.

How do I tell a wineskin from the wine in my own church? Ask whether a thing is commanded in Scripture or chosen by people. The gospel, the preaching of the word, prayer, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, the ordering of the church and the moral law are given by God; they are the wine and must not move. The time of the service, the style of music, the building, the translation used, are wineskins: they may be good and well loved, and may be changed when they no longer carry the life. Age is no argument either way. Ask: is this form still carrying the life, or has it set hard around a shape the life has outgrown? What must never move is the wine. Everything else is leather.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add “and both are preserved”; the earliest do not.
verseByVerse.note: Wineskins were goatskins. New wine is still fermenting; an old skin has lost its stretch and splits.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
People who have grown used to the old wine do not even want to taste the new: “The old is good.” Only Luke adds this wry saying, and it explains why so many good and religious people refused Jesus.

Old wine. Old wine is smooth; new wine is raw. Jesus is not commending old wine but describing a taste that has become fixed.

The old is good. Good enough: why change? Having settled into something, we always find a reason to stay, and the old is good, which is what makes it so hard to leave. The Pharisees’ problem was never that they had chosen something bad. They had something genuinely good, a law given by God, real discipline, real Scripture, and they were comfortable in it, and it had made the arrival of something better feel like a disturbance rather than a fulfilment.

In the flow. A fisherman, a leper, a paralysed man and a tax collector have tasted the new wine while the experts objected, and the Sabbath scenes that follow (6:1–11) show the same palate at work. The dividing line runs not between the religious and the irreligious but between those who know they need what Jesus brings and those who are content without him.

The new wine was standing in front of them. What they refused to taste was not a recipe but a person. The bridegroom was at the table (v. 34), and the one of whom Moses and all the prophets had written was reclining at Levi’s feast (24:27). Their old wine was good because it had come from him, laid down for this very day; to prefer it to him was to prefer the promise to the one who kept it. The old covenant was never meant to be held against Christ; it was meant to make Israel thirsty for him.

A dangerous spiritual position. To be in it, you need something good to settle into. Levi was reached in two words; the men outside had spent a lifetime acquiring a taste that made the new wine unpalatable. If you fear this describes you, take heart: the truly comfortable rarely worry about being comfortable, and the Lord who reached Levi in two words is well able to reach a settled heart. Honest questions about Jesus are another matter, and Luke wrote his Gospel to answer them (1:1–4).

Does this mean tradition is bad and new is always better? No. Many novelties in the church’s history have been errors. The new wine is not a new idea but Jesus himself, the fulfilment of everything the old covenant promised, and Scripture tells us to hold fast to the traditions of the apostles (2 Thessalonians 2:15). The warning is against a heart so settled in its religion that it no longer needs Christ, or cannot hear him when he does not taste like what it is used to.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “better”, but the best read “good”: the old is good enough.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke adds this saying, a wry comment on those content with the old ways.

5.text: <sup>1</sup> On one occasion, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret, <sup>2</sup> and he saw two boats by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. <sup>3</sup> Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And he sat down and taught the people from the boat. <sup>4</sup> And when he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.” <sup>5</sup> And Simon answered, “Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.” <sup>6</sup> And when they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. <sup>7</sup> They signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. And they came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink. <sup>8</sup> But when Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.” <sup>9</sup> For he and all who were with him were astonished at the catch of fish that they had taken, <sup>10</sup> and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.” <sup>11</sup> And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him. <sup>12</sup> While he was in one of the cities, there came a man full of leprosy. And when he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” <sup>13</sup> And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I will; be clean.” And immediately the leprosy left him. <sup>14</sup> And he charged him to tell no one, but “go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a proof to them.” <sup>15</sup> But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. <sup>16</sup> But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray. <sup>17</sup> On one of those days, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. <sup>18</sup> And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus, <sup>19</sup> but finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down with his bed through the tiles into the midst before Jesus. <sup>20</sup> And when he saw their faith, he said, “Man, your sins are forgiven you.” <sup>21</sup> And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying, “Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” <sup>22</sup> When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them, “Why do you question in your hearts? <sup>23</sup> Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? <sup>24</sup> But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the man who was paralyzed—“I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.” <sup>25</sup> And immediately he rose up before them and picked up what he had been lying on and went home, glorifying God. <sup>26</sup> And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying, “We have seen extraordinary things today.” <sup>27</sup> After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. And he said to him, “Follow me.” <sup>28</sup> And leaving everything, he rose and followed him. <sup>29</sup> And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. <sup>30</sup> And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying, “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>31</sup> And Jesus answered them, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. <sup>32</sup> I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.” <sup>33</sup> And they said to him, “The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.” <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said to them, “Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? <sup>35</sup> The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.” <sup>36</sup> He also told them a parable: “No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old. <sup>37</sup> And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. <sup>38</sup> But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins. <sup>39</sup> And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’”

keyVerse.quote: I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.
keyVerse.note: This sentence explains every meeting in the chapter: a fisherman who confesses he is a sinful man, a leper, a paralysed man forgiven before he is healed, a tax collector called from his booth. It also explains the objections, because those who think themselves well never send for the doctor. Jesus receives sinners as they are and calls them to turn, and both halves are his love.

5.reflection:
Simon’s first response to the kindness of Jesus was “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” (v. 8), and Jesus answered, “Do not be afraid.” When has a sense of your own sin made you want to keep your distance from God? What does this scene tell you to do with it instead?

The leper was sure Jesus could heal him but unsure whether he would (v. 12). Why is it often easier to believe in God’s power than in his willingness towards us? What do Jesus’ touch and his “I will” say to that fear?

The paralysed man reached Jesus because his friends would not give up, and Jesus “saw their faith” (vv. 18–20). Who might you carry to Jesus, in prayer and in practical love, and who could share the load with you?

The Pharisees complained that Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners (v. 30), and Jesus said that those used to the old wine say, “The old is good” (v. 39). How can a comfortable religion keep us from seeing our need of him, and how could our homes and church become places where people like Levi’s friends meet him?

6.title: The Sermon on the Plain
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 6 completes the opening phase of Jesus’ work in Galilee. The conflicts of chapter 5 over forgiveness, table company and fasting come to a head over the Sabbath and bring the first plot against him; he answers by praying all night, choosing the Twelve, and preaching the Sermon on the Plain, Luke’s counterpart to Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount.

The message. Jesus is Lord: Lord of the Sabbath, Lord who founds a renewed Israel around himself, and the Lord whose words a life must be built on. And the people he gathers are to bear the family likeness of a merciful Father. God’s blessing runs to the poor, the hungry, the weeping and the hated, and his warning to the comfortable; his children love their enemies, refuse to condemn, give without expecting return, and do what their Lord says. The kingdom is given before anything is asked; then everything is asked.

Why it was said. Luke’s readers, Jews and Gentiles in mixed churches, some poor and some well off (see the introduction), were already disputing over the Jewish calendar and already being hated, excluded and hauled before magistrates. They needed to know whose authority stood over the old rules, what kind of people Jesus was gathering, and how to treat those who hated them.

How the chapter makes its case. The grainfield (vv. 1–5) and the withered hand (vv. 6–11) establish his authority: he is lord of the Sabbath, and he uses the day to do good, while the rage it provokes casts the first shadow of the cross. After a night of prayer he chooses twelve, the founders of a renewed Israel (vv. 12–16). Then, before a crowd from Judea to Tyre and Sidon already healed by his power (vv. 17–19), he blesses the poor and laments over the rich (vv. 20–26). The heart of the sermon is love for enemies, grounded in the Father who is kind to the ungrateful and the evil (vv. 27–36); then mercy instead of condemnation, the log before the speck, and the tree known by its fruit (vv. 37–45). Two houses close it: only the life that hears and does his words will stand (vv. 46–49).

Where it leads. Jesus lived every line of this sermon before he died. Struck, he did not strike back; stripped, he let his clothes go; nailed up, he prayed for those who did it. He became poor, hungry and rejected so that the beatitudes could be true for us, bore the woe so that the comfortable could come home, and went down into the flood of God’s judgment and was not moved. He is the rock.

For us. This sermon is not a ladder up to God but a portrait of his children. Ask where you still love only those who love you, judge, cling, or call him Lord without doing what he says; then come back to the Father whose mercy came first, and build on his Son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Jesus Is Lord of the Sabbath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus has the authority of the God who gave the Sabbath, and he uses it to feed his hungry followers, not to load them with rules. When the Pharisees charge the disciples with reaping on the holy day (vv. 1–2), Jesus answers for them from Scripture: David, God’s anointed king, rejected and on the run, ate the holy bread with his men (vv. 3–4). Then comes the claim that turns a quarrel about grain into a question about who he is: “The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath” (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: To call himself lord of the Sabbath is to claim authority over God’s own covenant sign, one of the clearest claims to deity in the first three Gospels, and his lordship is for giving rest, not abolishing it (see the note on v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples: The grain-field complaint shows what happens when a law loses touch with what it was for (see the note on vv. 1–2). Jesus does not abolish the day; he frees it from what had buried it.

verseByVerse.quote: On a Sabbath, while he was going through the grainfields, his disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. But some of the Pharisees said, 'Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ hungry disciples eat grain as they walk on the Sabbath, and the Pharisees charge them with breaking the holy day. The most ordinary moment in the chapter starts a fight that ends at a cross.

On a Sabbath. Two conflicts over the Sabbath (vv. 1–11) follow the conflicts over forgiveness, table company and fasting in chapter 5. The seventh day of rest (Exodus 20:8–11) was one of the great marks of Jewish identity, with circumcision and the food laws.

Rubbing them in their hands. Only Luke mentions the rubbing, to remove the husks. Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field while walking through was explicitly allowed: “you may pluck the ears with your hand” (Deuteronomy 23:25). The law was full of provision for the hungry traveller, because the God who gave it feeds; and now the Lord of the harvest walks through a grainfield with his hungry friends, and lets them eat.

Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath? The objection was not theft but the day. By the Pharisees’ rules, plucking was reaping, and rubbing was threshing and winnowing. It sounds absurd, but if we make them cartoon villains we learn nothing. The fourth commandment forbids work without defining it, so the rabbis, trying to obey, drew up definitions, reaping and threshing among them, and built around them what they called a fence: further restrictions, so that a man would stop well short of the line and never break the commandment by accident. The Mishnah’s tractate on the Sabbath runs to twenty-four chapters. It began not in wickedness but in a serious desire not to sin, among people whose nation had gone into exile for ignoring precisely this commandment (Jeremiah 17:27).

A gift turned into an audit. But a day of rest and delight (Isaiah 58:13), given to relieve working people, had gathered so many rulings that only people with time to study could master them. The drift needs no bad motives: a good practice, a rule to protect it, a rule to protect the rule, and three generations on, people who know exactly what is forbidden and have forgotten what the day was for. Underneath grows a quieter danger. A man who keeps every rule can begin to feel he has satisfied God; then the rules stop guarding a gift and become a scoreboard, with his own name near the top.

He answers for his men. The charge is laid against the disciples but aimed at the one they follow: in Mark the Pharisees put it to Jesus himself (Mark 2:24), and in Luke it is Jesus who answers (v. 3). He steps between his hungry friends and their accusers and takes the question onto himself. That is the shape of his whole work. When the accuser speaks against his people, Christ answers: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect?” It is Christ Jesus who died, who was raised, who intercedes for us (Romans 8:33–34).

Is it wrong to have church rules and customs that the Bible does not command? No. Every church needs ordered customs, such as a time for the service and an order of worship, and wise guidelines can protect good things, as when a family keeps Sunday free of sport so that they can worship together. The error comes when a human rule is treated as God’s law, binding other people’s consciences (Mark 7:8), or is kept at the expense of the people it was meant to serve. Ask of any rule: does Scripture command this, or did we choose it? If we chose it, hold it gladly and lightly, and never let it stand between a hungry person and bread.

Textual note. The KJV’s “on the second sabbath after the first” (v. 1) follows later manuscripts; the earliest simply say “on a Sabbath”, so most modern Bibles omit the phrase.
verseByVerse.note: Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field was allowed; the objection was that plucking and rubbing counted as harvesting and threshing, work forbidden on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, 'Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those with him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers from Scripture: David, God’s anointed king, ate the holy bread with his men in their need, and the Son of David may do far more. God’s law has an order of priorities, and its ceremonies were never meant to be turned against the hungry.

Have you not read. A pointed question to men whose life’s work was reading the Scriptures. In 1 Samuel 21:1–6 David, fleeing from Saul with a handful of men and no food, came to the priest Ahimelech at Nob, where the tabernacle then probably stood, and asked for bread. The only bread was the holy bread.

The bread of the Presence. Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, set out on a golden table in the Holy Place before the Lord each Sabbath, and then eaten by the priests in a holy place (Leviticus 24:5–9).

The argument. Scripture records without a word of censure that David and his men ate the holy bread in their need. Jesus is not saying that rules do not matter or that hunger dissolves the law, but that God’s law has an order of priorities inside it, and its ceremonial provision was never meant to override the life it was given to serve. He does not set Scripture aside; he appeals to it against their reading of it: God desires mercy, not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6; Matthew 12:7).

Why David? Of all possible precedents, Jesus chooses God’s anointed king, not yet on his throne, rejected and on the run with his own small band, doing what the authorities would call unlawful. Here is another anointed king, gathering another company, being told by the officials of the day that what he does is not lawful. So the argument is not chiefly about corn at all, but about who this is, and Jesus is about to say so out loud.

The Son of David asks no one. David had to ask a priest for the holy bread, handed out through a door he could not enter. The Son of David asks no one. He is himself the Presence before whom those twelve loaves were laid. And at the last he is the bread: on the night he was betrayed he took bread, broke it, and gave his own body to his apostles. What only priests could eat at Nob, he gives to every hungry sinner who comes to him.

Does this mean I may break God’s commands when I am in need? No. The holy bread was a ceremonial law about sacred objects, always meant to serve life. God’s moral law (do not steal, do not lie, do not commit adultery) is never set aside for convenience or need; David did wrong when he lied to the priest in this same chapter (1 Samuel 21:2). Hunger does not excuse sin.
verseByVerse.note: The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set before the LORD each Sabbath and eaten by the priests.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus claims authority over the Sabbath itself, which only the God who gave it could claim. A quarrel over a handful of grain has arrived at the question the whole Gospel is about: who is this?

Lord of the Sabbath. Among the largest claims Jesus ever made. God instituted the Sabbath at creation (Genesis 2:2–3), spoke it from the mountain (Exodus 20:8–11), and named it the sign of his covenant with Israel for ever (Exodus 31:17); no institution in Judaism was more directly his. And a Galilean carpenter says he is its lord, with authority to determine its meaning and use. A man may say the Sabbath has been misunderstood; only its author can say he is its lord. Mark adds: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27).

The Son of Man. The title sounds humble in English, but it names the figure of Daniel 7:13–14, given everlasting rule over all peoples. The Pharisees are right to be alarmed: a man who says this is either speaking blasphemy or telling the truth, and Luke sets that choice squarely before his reader.

The setting. For Luke’s first readers the question was not academic. Churches of Jewish and Gentile believers were divided over whether the Jewish calendar still bound them (Romans 14:5–6; Galatians 4:10; Colossians 2:16–17), and these scenes showed them that the answer lay with the Lord of the day himself, not with the scribes’ rules about it.

Lord in order to give rest. He is lord of the Sabbath not to abolish rest but to give it back: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28). The day pictured God’s rest after his finished work, and Israel’s rest from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). He rested in the tomb on the seventh day and rose on the first, and whoever trusts him stops working to earn God’s favour, because Christ has finished the work (Hebrews 4:10). We do not work towards our rest; we begin from it.

So how should I spend Sunday? Begin with gathering: the Lord’s Day is first of all the day his people meet to hear his word, pray, sing and share the Lord’s Supper, and that is the fixed point around which the day is arranged. Then rest: make room for what refreshes body and soul, family, a walk, a meal with others, visiting the lonely, reading. Whether you keep the whole day strictly or use more freedom, do not judge the brother who differs (Romans 14:5–6), and do not let the day become either a burden or just another day.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists hold that Christians must keep Saturday. Many Reformed and Puritan Christians (following the Westminster Confession 21.7–8 and the 1689 London Baptist Confession 22.7–8) hold that the Sabbath command continues, transferred to Sunday, the “Christian Sabbath”, to be kept by resting from work and recreation and devoting the day to worship. Others hold that the Sabbath was a sign of the old covenant fulfilled in Christ. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, who gives the true rest it pointed to (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). The Lord’s Day, the first day of the week, the day of resurrection, is the church’s day of gathering for worship (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10), and it is his gift: Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom, not as a binding law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). The Westminster and 1689 view, that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath under the fourth commandment, is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — A Man with a Withered Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Sabbath was given for doing good, and the Lord of the Sabbath will not withhold mercy to keep himself safe. His critics watch to see whether he will heal a man whose working hand is withered, so that they can accuse him (vv. 6–8). His question, whether it is lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, leaves them no neutral ground, and with a word the hand is restored (vv. 9–10). The answer to the mercy is fury, and the first plotting against him in Luke (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The fury of verse 11 begins the road that ends at the cross. It is about who Jesus is as much as about what he did: he has claimed authority over the Sabbath, healed in defiance of their reading of it, and refused to be intimidated. Either he is a blasphemer or he is what he claims to be. They have decided (see the note on v. 11).
verseByVerse.examples:
The man is told to stand up in the middle, in front of everyone, with his disability on display, and he does. A need kept hidden at the edge of the church is often a need left unmet.

And the Christian life often follows the order of this healing (see the note on vv. 9–10).

verseByVerse.quote: On another Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. And the scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a reason to accuse him. But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand, 'Come and stand here.' And he rose and stood there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On another Sabbath Jesus’ critics watch to trap him over a man with a withered hand, and he walks into the trap with his eyes open, for the man’s sake.

In the flow. The run of conflicts that began at 5:17 reaches its height here, and ends with the first plotting against him (v. 11).

Right hand. Only Luke, the doctor, notes that it was the right hand, the working hand. Where nearly all work was done by hand, that meant the end of a man’s ability to earn. “Withered” means shrunken, paralysed.

Watched him. The word means spied on. The scribes and Pharisees are in a house of God, on the day of God, hoping a disabled man will be healed so that they can bring a charge; his hand interests them only as evidence. Religion that has stopped serving God and started defending itself can sit in a service, look at a suffering man, and see an opportunity. By the rabbis’ rule, healing counted as work, allowed on the Sabbath only if life was in danger. A withered hand could wait until tomorrow.

He knew their thoughts. As at 5:22; only God searches the heart (Jeremiah 17:10). He could protect himself by doing nothing until sundown, but he will not buy his own safety with this man’s withered hand. Here, in one small room, is the pattern of his whole ministry: he sees exactly what mercy will cost him, and he chooses mercy, all the way to the cross.

Come and stand here. He could have healed the man quietly afterwards. Instead he puts him in the centre of the room. The man has probably spent years managing a disability from the edge of the room; now he stands in the middle of it, his hand exposed and a row of officials staring. Some help cannot be received privately.

Should I deliberately provoke people who oppose me? No. Jesus did not seek conflict for its own sake; he sought the man’s good and the truth, and refused to let fear of critics hide either. Christians are to live peaceably with all, as far as it depends on them (Romans 12:18), and to answer opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:24–25). What this scene forbids is the opposite fault: doing good only when no critic is watching, or abandoning what is right because someone is waiting to accuse you.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke, the doctor, notes that it was the right hand. By the rabbis’ rule, healing a condition that was not life-threatening should wait until the Sabbath was over.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, 'I ask you, is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?' And after looking around at them all he said to him, 'Stretch out your hand.' And he did so, and his hand was restored.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus shows that the Sabbath is for doing good, and that refusing to do good when you can is itself doing harm; then he heals with a word.

To do good or to do harm. They came ready for a different argument: healing is work, this condition is not life-threatening, and a hand withered for years can wait until sundown. Jesus refuses the terms. Not, is healing work? but, what is the Sabbath for? By pairing doing good with its opposite he removes the middle ground they stood on. To fail to do good when you can is to do harm.

To save life or to destroy it? “Life” (psychē) can also mean soul. And the irony: Jesus is doing good on the Sabbath, while his critics are plotting on the Sabbath to destroy him (v. 11). Their rule asked how little a man must do; his asks what good can be done, and a day designed by a God who never stops sustaining his creation cannot be a day for withholding mercy.

Looking around at them all. A long, searching look; Mark says “with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart” (Mark 3:5). In that silence they have already answered.

Stretch out your hand. No touch, no medicine, no work that could be charged: only a word. And the word asks the one thing this man cannot do, for a withered hand is exactly a hand that cannot be stretched out. That is very often the order: the command comes before the strength, and the strength comes as we obey. Forgive, he says, to a heart that cannot; love your enemy, to a will that refuses; and the one who commands is the one who gives (Philippians 2:12–13).

He spoke, and it was so. He spoke as he spoke on the first day of the world, because the one standing in that synagogue is the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3). He saved life on the Sabbath while they sat counting how to destroy his, and in the end he let them destroy it, so that withered sinners might live.

But I cannot obey. What do I do with a command I have no strength to keep? Do what the man did: try, in dependence on Christ. Do not wait until you feel able; you may never feel able. Ask his help, then take the first small step he commands: the first sentence of the apology, the first prayer for your enemy, the first refusal of the old habit. God “works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13), and his strength is often felt only in the moving. If you fail, confess it, receive his forgiveness, and stretch out your hand again tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders answer a healed man with senseless rage, and begin to plan against Jesus. From here on, the threat of death never leaves him.

Filled with fury. The word means senselessness, folly (anoias): a rage that has stopped thinking. A disabled man in their own congregation can work again, and the religious leadership answers not with joy but with a plot.

What they might do to Jesus. Mark says they began to plot with the Herodians how to destroy him (Mark 3:6). Luke’s wording is milder at this stage, but the direction is clear.

Why such rage? Not because they were unusually wicked men, but because he had shown in public that their position could not be defended, and they would not change it. To change it was to admit that a Galilean understood God’s law better than its guardians, and that would have cost them everything they were. So the mind turns from the argument to the man who made it. It happens in churches and families too, wherever someone says something true that cannot be answered and the response is to discredit the speaker instead of weighing the words. The fury feels like conviction from the inside. It is nearly always a sign that we have run out of answers.

Hated for doing good. The cause of the plot is not any wrong he did but the good. He is the one man who has lived without sin, and the nearer his goodness comes to sinners, the more it is resented, because light exposes (John 3:19–20). Yet he does not withdraw his goodness to save himself. He goes on healing people who will cry for his death, and he dies for enemies (Romans 5:10). The fury in this room is the first shadow of the cross, and he walks towards it of his own will. Their plot, when it ripened, became the means of our salvation, and the hands they would nail to a cross still restore the withered and the broken.

How do I know whether my anger is righteous? Righteous anger is anger at what grieves God, for the sake of others; it stays under control and seeks good. Jesus was angry in this very scene (Mark 3:5), and he healed the man. Sinful anger is usually about me, my position, my pride, my being shown up, and it seeks to hurt. Ask: what exactly am I angry about? Would God be angry at it? Does my anger make me want to help someone, or to win? “Be angry and do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26); and if you find yourself furious with someone who has told you the truth, stop and listen before you speak.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Facing the first plot against him, Jesus prays all night and then founds a renewed Israel around himself. From the wider band of disciples he chooses twelve, the number of Israel’s tribes, and names them apostles, sent ones (vv. 12–13). The list (vv. 14–16) is a study in unlikely company: Peter, who had begged Jesus to leave him; Matthew the tax collector; Simon the Zealot; men of whom we know nothing but their names. Jesus names them for what his grace will make them, and the list ends with Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.
verseByVerse.theology:
The apostles are sent ones, commissioned witnesses, and their testimony to the life, death and resurrection of Jesus is the foundation of the church’s preaching: the church is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:20).

Judas, chosen with the others after that night, is a warning the reader must not hurry past. Being chosen for an office is not the same as being saved (see the note on vv. 14–16).
verseByVerse.examples:
Not every decision needs a night of prayer, but the decisions that shape God’s people belong first to the Father, and leaders, elders and appointment committees may fairly ask whether they have prayed as seriously as the decision deserves.

And the Twelve rebuke churches divided along political lines (see the note on vv. 14–16).

verseByVerse.quote: In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God. And when day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve, whom he named apostles:
verseByVerse.commentary:
After a whole night in prayer, Jesus chooses twelve men to be the foundation of a renewed Israel, and names them his sent ones.

All night in prayer. Luke has just recorded the first plot against him. The next thing he records, and only he records it, is a night alone on a hillside, from dark to first light: the longest of Luke’s prayers (3:21; 5:16), before the largest decision of his ministry so far. Luke gives us the proportion: a whole night, for twelve men, and Judas among them.

Chose from them twelve. Two stages. He called the disciples, a larger group (Luke will later mention seventy-two, 10:1, where some manuscripts read seventy), and from them chose an inner circle. Twelve is not chosen for convenience: Israel had twelve tribes, and no Jew could miss the meaning. Jesus is not assembling a staff but forming the people of God afresh around himself, and only one with God’s own authority has the right to found Israel anew. At the end of the Bible the wall of the city has twelve foundations, bearing the names of these men (Revelation 21:14).

Apostles. “Apostle” (apostolos) means one who is sent, an authorised representative. They would be sent with his authority to preach (9:1–2) and, after his resurrection, to be his witnesses to the world (24:48; Acts 1:8). As eyewitnesses of the risen Christ (Acts 1:21–22), commissioned directly by him, they laid the church’s foundation through their teaching, which we have in the New Testament (Ephesians 2:20). The word is also used loosely of messengers (2 Corinthians 8:23), but no one now can be an eyewitness of the risen Lord, so the foundation is not laid again.

Two decisions. His enemies made their decision in fury, after a service. His was made alone, on a mountain, after a night of asking his Father, and it is the one still standing.

If Jesus prayed all night and still chose Judas, did his prayer fail? No. Jesus chose Judas knowingly: “Did I not choose you, the Twelve? And yet one of you is a devil” (John 6:70). Prayer is not a guarantee that everything will go smoothly; it is submitting our choices to the Father’s will, and the Father’s will included the betrayal, through which the Scriptures would be fulfilled and the world redeemed (Acts 2:23). So when you pray before a decision and it later brings pain, do not conclude that you missed God’s guidance. He may have led you exactly where he meant to, for purposes you cannot yet see.
verseByVerse.note: “Apostle” means one who is sent. Twelve matches the twelve tribes of Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot, and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Twelve are ordinary, mismatched men whom Jesus names for what his grace will make of them, and one of them became a traitor.

Four lists. The Twelve are listed four times (Matthew 10:2–4; Mark 3:16–19; Luke 6:14–16; Acts 1:13). The order varies, but Peter is always first, and in the three Gospel lists Judas Iscariot is always last (Acts, written after his death, names only eleven). They fall into three groups of four, each headed by the same name (Peter, Philip, James son of Alphaeus).

Peter. Peter (Petros, Aramaic Kēphas) means rock (Matthew 16:18; John 1:42): the fisherman who once begged Jesus to depart from him because he was a sinful man (5:8).

The one who gives new names. In Scripture it is God who renames: Abram became Abraham, Jacob became Israel, each name a promise of what God would make of the man. Jesus does the same, with the same authority. He calls Simon a rock before there is anything rock-like about him, and Luke’s two books show him keeping his word: the man who denies him three times by a fire in a courtyard stands up at Pentecost and preaches Christ to the city that crucified him. The list of the Twelve is a list of what Christ does with people. He takes them as they are, and names them for what his grace will make them.

Andrew, James and John. Andrew first brought his brother to Jesus (John 1:40–42). James and John were Zebedee’s sons, fishermen (5:10); James was the first apostle martyred (Acts 12:2), and John, by early church tradition, wrote the Gospel, letters and Revelation.

Philip, and Bartholomew. Philip was from Bethsaida (John 1:44). Bartholomew (son of Tolmai) is probably the Nathanael of John 1:45–51, since he is paired with Philip.

Matthew. The tax collector Luke calls Levi (5:27); Matthew’s own Gospel names the man at the booth Matthew (Matthew 9:9). He had taken money from his own people on behalf of the ruling power.

Thomas. The twin (John 11:16), remembered for his doubt and for his great confession: “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28).

James the son of Alphaeus. Possibly James the younger (Mark 15:40). Of him the Gospels record nothing but a name, as of several of the Twelve. They gave their lives to this, and history kept only that they were chosen.

Enemies at one table. Simon was called the Zealot, a man of fierce conviction (see below). If the word means what it may, Jesus put a former tax collector for Rome and a man who believed such collectors were traitors in one company of twelve. In ordinary life they would not have shared a road, let alone a purse. Whatever holds a church together, it is not political agreement, and the New Testament never suggests it should be. If Matthew and Simon could eat from the same bag, the divisions that keep Christians from sitting in the same room deserve a harder look than they usually get.

Judas the son of James. Probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark, the same man with two names; also the “Judas (not Iscariot)” of John 14:22.

Who became a traitor. Luke’s terrible aside. Judas was not chosen as a traitor, but became one. He heard and saw everything the others did, was sent out with power like the rest, and held the money bag (John 12:6). Outward closeness to Jesus, however long, is no guarantee of a true heart.

Could I become a Judas? A true believer cannot finally be lost; those to whom Christ gives eternal life will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28–29). Judas was never a true believer, though he looked like one: Jesus called him a devil while he walked with the Twelve (John 6:70), knew from the beginning who would betray him (John 6:64), and said he was lost so that Scripture might be fulfilled (John 17:12). So the warning is meant not to terrify true believers but to wake up false ones. If you fear you are a Judas, that fear is itself a good sign: Judas felt remorse, but never turned to Christ for mercy (Matthew 27:3–5). Examine yourself (2 Corinthians 13:5), and run to Christ; no one who comes to him is cast out (John 6:37).

Uncertain wording. Two phrases are uncertain. “The Zealot” (zēlōtēs) may mean zealous for the law, or a member of the nationalist movement that wanted to overthrow Rome by force; it is not certain what stage that movement had reached by this date. And “Judas the son of James” is literally “Judas of James”. The Greek leaves the relationship unstated; it usually means son, as most modern Bibles take it, though the King James Version reads brother.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s “Judas the son of James” is probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom belongs to those who have nothing to trust but God, and the comfortable are in grave danger. Jesus comes down to a crowd from Judea to the coast of Tyre and Sidon and heals them all, so that grace comes before the sermon’s first word (vv. 17–19). Then he speaks straight to his disciples: blessed are you who are poor, hungry, weeping, and hated for his sake, and when that happens, leap for joy (vv. 20–23). Luke alone adds four matching woes, the prophets’ cry of grief over the rich, the full, the laughing and the universally admired (vv. 24–26).
verseByVerse.theology:
The beatitudes and woes express the great reversal Mary sang of: the mighty brought down, the humble exalted, the hungry filled, the rich sent away empty (1:51–53).

And the reversal is anchored in Christ, who entered the conditions he calls blessed. He became poor though he was rich (2 Corinthians 8:9), hungered in the wilderness (4:2), wept, and was hated, excluded and reviled for us. We are not blessed for managing to be poor or hungry, but by being joined to the one who was made poor so that we might be made rich. The woes are mercy raising its voice, a warning to the comfortable before the day the tables turn.
verseByVerse.examples: The beatitudes comfort those who suffer, and they also search everyone else: in which column do you stand? The woes need honest application (see the note on vv. 24–25). Jesus commands leaping joy under persecution, the joy of people who know how the story ends: “the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us” (Romans 8:18).

verseByVerse.quote: And he came down with them and stood on a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. And those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured. And all the crowd sought to touch him, for power came out from him and healed them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus comes down to a great crowd of Jews and Gentiles and heals them all, so that grace comes before the sermon’s first word.

The Sermon on the Plain. What follows (vv. 20–49) is Luke’s version of Jesus’ great sermon, shorter than Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), with less about the Jewish law and four woes Matthew does not have. It ends with two houses (vv. 46–49), so that no one can treat it as a fine speech and nothing more.

He came down with them and stood on a level place. Some readers hear an echo of Moses coming down from the mountain with the law. Here it is the law of the kingdom.

One sermon or two? Luke says Jesus came down and stood on a level place; Matthew says he went up on the mountain and sat down (Matthew 5:1). The two overlap closely (beatitudes, love of enemies, judge not, the tree and its fruit, the two builders), yet Matthew runs to three chapters where Luke runs to thirty verses, with long stretches on the law, prayer and fasting that Luke places elsewhere. Some take them as one occasion from different angles, since Luke’s phrase can mean a plateau or shelf on the hillside as easily as flat ground below it. Others take them as two occasions: Jesus spent perhaps three years saying these things village by village, and no teacher says a thing once. Either way the words are his, the differences are the ordinary shape of a real ministry, and the same voice is asking for the same life.

Tyre and Sidon. Jews from the religious heartland, and people from the pagan cities of the Phoenician coast, the country Elijah was sent to (4:26). Luke’s map is already the map of Acts: a foretaste of the gospel to all nations.

Power came out from him. The power of God (5:17) flows from him (8:46); healing is not a technique he applies. Many in earshot have just seen the demonised freed and the sick made well; when he says, “Blessed are you who are poor”, he says it to people who have seen his power and his kindness. That is the order of the kingdom: grace first, then the call. The one who would ask them to love their enemies had just poured out his power on people who would one day shout for his death.

Is the Sermon on the Plain a way to be saved, or a way to live? A way to live, for those who are being saved. It is addressed to disciples (v. 20), and it begins not with commands but with blessings: the kingdom is given before anything is asked. Its demands are real and searching, and no one keeps them perfectly; they show us how far we fall short and drive us to Christ, who kept them for us. But they are also the actual shape of the new life he gives. We do not obey this sermon in order to be accepted; we obey it because we have been, and because the one who preached it lives in us by his Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities to the north. Luke’s sermon is given on a “level place”; Matthew’s similar sermon on a mountain.

verseByVerse.quote: And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: 'Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom of God belongs, now, to the poor who have nothing to trust but God. Jesus says it to his disciples’ faces: God’s favour rests on those the world counts as having nothing.

The Beatitudes. Luke gives four blessings (vv. 20–23) and four matching woes (vv. 24–26); Matthew gives eight or nine blessings, depending on how they are counted, and no woes (Matthew 5:3–12). Luke’s say “you”: Jesus looks at his disciples as he speaks, though the crowd hears, and everyone could see how poor they were. Matthew’s say “those who”.

Blessed. Blessed (makarioi) is not happy in a shallow sense, but fortunate, in a good position before God, approved by him. It is God’s verdict, not a feeling (Psalm 1:1).

Poor. Luke’s word means destitute (ptōchoi): a beggar, who depends entirely on what others give. Many of Jesus’ disciples were literally poor, having left everything (5:11, 28). But in the Old Testament the poor were also the humble, who had no one to depend on but God (Psalm 34:6; Isaiah 61:1; 66:2).

Luke and Matthew together. Matthew’s “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3) and Luke’s flat “Blessed are you who are poor” hold two ends of one truth. Take Luke without Matthew and you get the error that poverty itself saves, as though an empty purse were a ticket. Take Matthew without Luke and you get the more respectable error: “poor in spirit” turned into a humble feeling that comfortable people can have while their lives stay exactly as they were. Matthew names the poverty God blesses, that of a man who knows he has nothing to bring; Luke names where such people are usually found. It is far easier to know you have nothing when you actually have nothing, because money is extraordinarily good at hiding from us the emptiness we all have before God.

Yours is the kingdom. It is yours now (12:32). The kingdom of God is God’s saving rule through his King. To have it is to live under that rule now, forgiven, cared for and belonging to him, and to inherit his new world when it comes in full (22:29–30).
