Good news to the poor. At Nazareth Jesus had read Isaiah and claimed it: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor” (4:18). Now he does it. This beatitude is not a wise man’s observation about poverty but the Messiah’s announcement, which is why he can say “yours is”, not “yours will be”: the King is present. The poor are blessed not because their poverty is a virtue but because the King has come to them first, and given himself.

I am not poor. Is this beatitude for me? Yes, if you come the way the poor come. Before God every one of us is destitute, with nothing to offer him that is not already his, and no righteousness of our own (Isaiah 64:6). The comfortable Christian must learn by grace what the poor man often knows by experience, that he lives entirely on what God gives. So hold your possessions as a steward, not an owner; receive salvation as a beggar, not a customer; and let your money flow towards the poor, so that it does not wall you off from them or from God. The kingdom is given to empty hands, whatever is in the bank.

Where it applies: An elderly widow in your church lives on very little, and trusts Christ. Do not pity her as one who has missed out. She is rich in the kingdom, and you may learn more from her than she from you.

Where it would be wrong: Someone thinks poverty in itself makes a person right with God, or that the poor need no help since they are blessed already. The same Lord commands us to open our hands to them (1 John 3:17).

parallels.desc: has not God chosen those who are poor?

verseByVerse.quote: 'Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. 'Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hungry and the weeping are blessed, because God will fill them and turn their tears to laughter.

Hungry now. Only Luke has the “now”. He means real hunger, people who did not eat enough yesterday, though Matthew shows the hunger for righteousness too (Matthew 5:6). Mary sang: “he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty” (1:53). Hunger is not a virtue, but the hunger the world takes as a sign that God has forgotten you is, in his eyes, the state of people about to be filled.

You shall be satisfied. At the messianic banquet (13:29; 14:15; Isaiah 25:6), and in a measure even now. The word means filled right up, and the filling is not a metaphor. There is a table at the end of this book, and the guest list was drawn up from the streets and lanes (14:21).

You who weep now. Those who grieve over suffering, over their own sin, and over the world’s rebellion against God (Matthew 5:4). He does not tell them to stop, or suggest that the tears are a failure of faith. He lets them weep, and promises that the weeping will end.

You shall laugh. God will wipe away every tear (Isaiah 25:8; Revelation 21:4). And the promised end is not relief or resignation but laughter, a startling word for the far side of grief: “Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy!” (Psalm 126:5).

Who is speaking. This is not a technique for feeling better but a claim about how the story ends, made by the only person entitled to make it. The one who promises to fill the hungry had gone forty days without food in a desert (4:2). The one who promises laughter to the weeping wept at a friend’s grave (John 11:35) and over Jerusalem (19:41). He is not calling out advice from the dry ground. He has been in the water.

Disbelieved for joy. On the evening of the first Easter the frightened disciples saw their Lord alive, and they “disbelieved for joy” (24:41). Then he asked for something to eat, and ate broiled fish in front of them. That room is this beatitude coming true in miniature: weeping turned to a joy too large to believe, and a table where the risen Christ himself sits down to eat. The “now” is real, but it is not long.

Is it wrong for a Christian to grieve? No. Paul does not tell the grieving Thessalonians to stop, only not to grieve as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief is love continuing after loss, and the psalms are full of honest lament. You do not have to pretend to be fine, or hurry out of sorrow to prove your faith. Bring your tears to God; he keeps count of them (Psalm 56:8). The promise is not that you will stop feeling the loss tomorrow, but that the one who is with you in the weeping will one day turn it into laughter.

Where it applies: A friend has lost her husband, and three months on she is still crying in church. Do not tell her it is time to move on, or that a strong Christian would be rejoicing by now. Sit with her, let her weep, and remind her gently that Jesus calls her blessed, and that the morning is coming.

Where it would be wrong: A neighbour has no food in the house, and you tell him he is blessed and will be satisfied in the kingdom, and leave it there (James 2:15–16). Bring the promise and the groceries.

parallels.desc: those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy

verseByVerse.quote: 'Blessed are you when people hate you and when they exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man! Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers did to the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Disciples hated and shut out for Christ’s sake are blessed, and are told not merely to endure it but to leap for joy. Their reward is great, and they stand where the prophets stood.

Hate, exclude, revile. The only beatitude about what will happen to the disciples because they follow him, and its four verbs escalate. Hatred: what people feel towards you. Exclusion: being cut off from synagogue, family and community (John 9:22; 16:2). Reviling: insult to the face. Spurning your name as evil: your name, or the name Christian, treated as a curse (1 Peter 4:14–16). A complete social death.

On account of the Son of Man! Not for being obnoxious, but for Christ’s sake. The clause is narrow on purpose: there is no promise for the Christian excluded for being rude, or hated for opinions that have nothing to do with Christ. Suffering for wrongdoing has no blessing (1 Peter 4:15).

Leap for joy. Not endure; not bear it patiently. Leap, like a lamb in spring, or like John in the womb (1:41, the same word), on the very day they lose their standing, livelihood and families. The apostles did exactly this, leaving the council “rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name” (Acts 5:41).

Your reward is great. Not that we earn heaven by suffering, but that God honours faithfulness, and keeps the reward in heaven, where no persecutor can reach it.

So their fathers did to the prophets. To be shut out is to be in good company: the prophets were treated like this, and are now honoured, their tombs built, by the descendants of the men who threw them out (11:47–51; 13:34).

The setting. For Luke’s first readers this was no distant possibility. Believers had been dragged off to prison, driven out of cities, stoned and hauled before magistrates, as his second volume records (Acts 8:1–3; 13:50; 14:19; 17:5–9), and they needed to know that their Lord had seen it coming and called it blessed.

The landing is certain. What makes this command sane rather than cruel is the phrase “on account of the Son of Man”. It binds the sufferer to Christ so closely that what is done to the one is done to the other. When Saul of Tarsus was hunting Christians from house to house, the risen Lord stopped him on the road: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). He is held by the one whose name it is, the Son of Man who has received everlasting dominion, and the reward is with him. He went first down the road he describes: hated without a cause, excluded from his own town, reviled on the cross. Now the name men spurned is the name above every name.

How can I rejoice when it hurts? Rejoicing does not mean pretending it does not hurt. It means looking past the hurt to what it means: you belong to Christ, you stand with the prophets, and a reward is kept for you that no one can take. Paul could be “sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Corinthians 6:10). Begin by thanking God, honestly, even through tears, that you were counted worthy to share a little of his Son’s rejection. Then pray for those who wronged you (v. 28). Joy usually follows the thanks rather than coming before it.

Where it applies: You are left out of a family group chat because you became a Christian. Do not answer with bitterness. Rejoice: you are in the company of the prophets.

parallels.desc: they will put you out of the synagogues

verseByVerse.quote: 'But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. 'Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. 'Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus grieves over the rich, the full and the laughing, who have settled for this world’s comfort and will find it gone. The woes are a lament and a warning, not a curse.

Woe. Only Luke records these woes. “Woe” (ouai) is the prophets’ cry of grief and warning (Isaiah 5:8–23; Amos 6:1): not a wish for harm, but how terrible for you. It is the sound a man makes watching people walk towards a cliff.

You who are rich. Wealth is not sinful in itself, but it tends to make people self-sufficient, satisfied with this world, and blind to their need of God (12:16–21; 16:19–31; 18:24–25).

You have received. “Received” (apechete) is a business word, used on receipts: paid in full. The rich are not shut out; they have already had all the comfort they chose. Abraham said the same to the rich man: “you in your lifetime received your good things” (16:25).

Your consolation. The word Luke used of old Simeon, who was waiting for the consolation of Israel (2:25) and found it when he took the infant Jesus in his arms. Israel’s consolation was a person, and that gives the woe its edge. The rich are condemned not for having comfort but for settling for a comfort that is not him, drawn in advance, in things, with no need felt of the one who stands before them as God’s comfort in flesh. Simeon was content to die once he had held Christ. The rich man in this verse can hold everything except Christ, and calls it enough.

Full now, laughing now. Each woe mirrors a blessing, and each turns on the same “now”. The full are those satisfied with this world’s goods, who feel no spiritual hunger. The laughter is not innocent laughter but the careless laughter of those who do not take God or sin or suffering seriously (James 4:9).

He took the woe on himself. The woes are spoken with grief, by the Lord who would weep over Jerusalem (19:41). And he took the woe on himself. He who was rich became hungry, mourned, and on the cross looked for comforters and found none (Psalm 69:20), so that people who had settled for this world’s comforts might be given a comfort that never runs dry. He tells us where the cliff is because he would rather we came home.

Most of us are rich. By any measure the world has ever used, most readers of this commentary are among the rich. The danger is not enjoying good things but being consoled by them, until the kingdom sounds like an optional extra for people whose lives are not working. A man who has been paid already does not come to collect.

How rich is too rich? Scripture sets no figure, and the question usually hides a hope of being just under the line. Better questions: Am I trusting my money for security instead of God (1 Timothy 6:17)? Could I give a large part of it away without feeling that my life was gone? Is my giving generous, regular and costly, or the leftovers? Do I know any poor people by name? Is my spending shaped by love for others or by keeping up with those around me? If the answers trouble you, the remedy is not guilt but generosity: begin giving more, and more joyfully, and let money become a servant again.

Where it would be wrong: You look down on wealthy Christians, or feel guilty over every good meal. Abraham, Joseph of Arimathea and Lydia were wealthy and faithful (Genesis 13:2; Matthew 27:57; Acts 16:14–15); the rich are told not to hope in riches but to be rich in good works (1 Timothy 6:17–18).
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records these woes, the mirror image of the blessings.

parallels.desc: woe to those at ease in Zion

verseByVerse.quote: 'Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Universal approval is a danger sign for anyone who speaks for God, because it was the reward of the false prophets.

When all people speak well of you. If everyone speaks well of you, either you have said nothing worth opposing, or you have said what people wanted to hear.

The false prophets. One thing marked them out even to an outsider: how they were received. The true prophets were nearly always unwelcome: Micaiah was hated because he never prophesied good concerning the king (1 Kings 22:8). The false prophets had access, standing and a hearing at court, because they told people what they wanted: “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace (Jeremiah 6:14).

When all spoke well of him. Jesus has already lived this verse. At Nazareth all spoke well of him and marvelled at his gracious words (4:22); then he said what they did not want to hear, that Elijah was sent to a widow of Sidon and Elisha cleansed a Syrian, and the congregation that had praised him drove him to the edge of a cliff (4:24–29). He lost the praise of his home town in one sermon and of his nation in one week, and he never bought it back with a softer word, nor ever spoke an unkind one. What he sought was the voice that had spoken over the Jordan: “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased” (3:22). Men may speak ill of us; God has spoken well of us in his Son, and that verdict is never revised.

The temptation to shave the corners off. What the verse forbids is the pursuit of universal approval by someone meant to be carrying a message: finding the version of the truth that will cost nothing with this person, in this room. It works, and it is precisely what the false prophets did.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should try to be unpopular, or that being well thought of is always wrong (Acts 2:47; 1 Timothy 3:7). A man who has made himself unpleasant may console himself that he is being persecuted when he is only being avoided; this woe has the same limit as verse 22, “on account of the Son of Man”. And Luke will shortly commend a centurion whom the Jewish elders of his town warmly praised (7:4–5).

How do I speak the truth without being needlessly offensive? Separate the offence of the message from the offence of the messenger. The cross will offend some whatever you do (1 Corinthians 1:23); your tone, timing and manner should offend no one. Speak when asked, or when love requires it, rather than at every opportunity. Listen first, and understand the person. Say the hard thing kindly, briefly and without contempt, and be honest about your own need of grace. “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt” (Colossians 4:6). If people still object, let it be to Christ, not to you.

parallels.desc: the prophets prophesy falsely, and my people love to have it so

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love your enemies, because that is what your Father is like. The command comes in four rising forms: love, do good, bless, pray (vv. 27–28). The cheek, the cloak, the beggar and the goods taken show a disciple who will not retaliate for personal insult or cling to his rights; they have never been a command to stay within reach of violence (vv. 29–30). The Golden Rule drives it all (v. 31). Even sinners return love for love (vv. 32–34), but God’s children love those who give nothing back, because he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil (v. 35). Hence the summary: “Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful” (v. 36).
verseByVerse.theology:
The command to love enemies is what God has already done for his own: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). The cross is the supreme act of love towards enemies.

Matthew’s “be perfect” (Matthew 5:48) becomes in Luke “be merciful”, and the order of grace and command cannot be reversed (see the notes on vv. 35 and 36).
verseByVerse.examples:
This command lies behind the church’s martyrs (Stephen died praying for his killers, Acts 7:60), its peacemakers, and its reconciliations. It is also easily shrunk into being pleasant to people who are slightly difficult, when the real test is the person who still wishes us harm.

The Golden Rule (v. 31) is stated positively, and that is what makes it so demanding (see the note on v. 31).

verseByVerse.quote: 'But I say to you who hear, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus commands his people to love their real enemies: to seek their good in deed, word and prayer, whatever they deserve.

But I say to you who hear. Before the hardest thing in the sermon, Jesus marks off the people who are actually listening.

Love your enemies. The heart of the sermon. This love (agapē) is not a feeling of liking but a commitment to seek someone’s good, whatever they deserve. And the enemy is real. Hating, cursing, abusing (epēreazontōn, mistreat, harass): Jesus is not talking about a colleague who irritates you, but somebody who wishes you harm and is acting on it.

The commands escalate in cost. Love is shown in four rising steps: love (attitude), do good (deeds), bless (words), pray (prayer). None is a verb of feeling: he commands treatment, and the command does not wait for the emotion. “Do good” can be done at a distance and without much of yourself. “Bless” requires words, and words about a person come from the heart. “Pray for” is the hardest, because it cannot be done insincerely for long: it is very difficult to keep asking God to be good to somebody and go on hating them. Nobody arrives at loving an enemy by working on their feelings. It generally goes the other way round: an act, then a word, then a prayer, and somewhere in the third the heart begins to move.

Four commands, and one who kept them. Jesus kept all four towards his own enemies within a single night and day. He met the betrayer’s kiss with a question meant to wake him (22:48); he did good to one of them, healing the ear a disciple had cut off (22:51); “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23); and from the cross he prayed: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (23:34); some early manuscripts lack this prayer, though most modern Bibles keep it. The sermon on the level place is his own life, described in advance.

We were the enemies. We were not neutral strangers to him but enemies, hostile in mind and doing evil deeds (Colossians 1:21), and he did not wait for us to soften. He loved first, and his love turned enemies into children; now by his Spirit he is making that likeness in us. There is no enemy of yours so hard to love as you were to him.

Is it not weak, or even unjust, to love people who are doing evil? No. Loving an enemy is not approving what he does, or pretending it is fine. It is refusing to answer him in kind and so become like him, and it takes far more strength to bless someone who curses you than to curse him back. Nor does it give up on justice; it leaves justice with God, who says, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay” (Romans 12:19). The Christian can afford to love his enemy because he trusts the Judge.

What it does not mean. Not pretending nothing happened; forgiveness in Scripture never requires the pretence that the wrong was not a wrong. Nor remaining within reach of harm (see vv. 29–30). What is forbidden is the natural, satisfying, entirely human urge to pay back what we were given.

Does this forbid self-defence, military service or the state’s use of force? Jesus is speaking of personal retaliation. The state’s sword is a different matter, given by God to restrain evil (Romans 13:4), and a Christian may serve in it (3:14). Protecting the weak from harm is not hating an enemy.

Where it would be wrong: A former friend’s lie online accuses you of a crime, or will lose you your job. Loving an enemy does not mean letting a damaging falsehood stand. Correct it calmly and truthfully, and if need be ask the platform or the law to deal with it, as Paul defended himself against false charges (Acts 24:10–21).

verseByVerse.quote: To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also, and from one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. Give to everyone who begs from you, and from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Disciples do not hit back at personal insult or cling to their possessions; they absorb the wrong and give freely. These verses concern insult and loss, never a command to stay within reach of violence.

The other cheek. Four illustrations, each the opposite of what we do by instinct. A slap on the cheek was more insult than injury, a contemptuous blow; Jewish law treated it under fines for damaged honour rather than damaged bodies. To offer the other cheek is not to invite a beating but to refuse the insulter’s game: the slap was meant to start a quarrel, and the disciple will not join in. (1 Peter 3:9).

Cloak and tunic. The cloak was the outer garment, the tunic the inner one. Put people before possessions, give readily, and hold goods loosely, not living to get back what you are owed.

He gave his back to those who strike. Isaiah’s Servant said it centuries before: “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard” (Isaiah 50:6). The men guarding Jesus blindfolded him, struck him and mocked him (22:63–64), and at the cross they divided his garments by casting lots (23:34). He did not hit back, and he did not demand them back. Yet this was not weakness. He was holding still for a purpose, bearing an insult owed to us, with his face set towards finishing it. The disciple who turns the other cheek walks a short way down a road his Lord walked to the end.

The Lord who clothes. They stripped him of everything, and he let it go. To beggars who came with nothing he gave not a coin but himself; to sinners standing naked in their guilt he gave his own robe: “he has clothed me with the garments of salvation” (Isaiah 61:10). The Lord who was stripped is the Lord who clothes.

What this verse does not say to the abused. This must be said plainly, because few verses have been so cruelly misused. Turn the other cheek has been quoted to battered wives, abused children, the bullied and the trafficked, to tell them Christ requires them to stay and keep absorbing the blows. He requires no such thing, and it is a wickedness to say he does. Look again at what he describes: an insult to a man’s honour, and a coat taken by force; personal affront and personal loss, the wound to pride and pocket that makes us itch to hit back and stand on our rights. What is forbidden is the reflex of retaliation and the worship of our own dignity. He is not handing a violent man a licence, nor telling his victim to hold still. Jesus himself walked away from a crowd that meant to kill him (4:29–30). Paul invoked his Roman citizenship against an unlawful flogging (Acts 16:37; 22:25) and was lowered over a wall in a basket rather than be murdered (Acts 9:25). And the love that will not retaliate for itself is fiercely bound to protect the weak, sometimes from the very person harming them.

If you are being harmed, hear this clearly. Getting to safety is not a failure of this verse. Removing yourself or a child from a violent home, calling for help, telling your pastor or elders, insisting that the law do its work: none of that is retaliation, and none of it is forbidden here. A church that tells an abused person to go back and submit to the abuse has disobeyed Christ, not obeyed him. What dies in these verses is the right to hit back for your own honour, not the duty to keep the defenceless, including yourself, out of the reach of evil.

Must I give to every beggar, even if the money will be misused? Jesus commands an open hand, a readiness to give rather than an instinct to refuse; he does not forbid discernment. Paul says that “if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10), and the church cared carefully for genuine need (1 Timothy 5:3–16). Sometimes the most loving gift is food rather than cash, or time rather than money. What this verse rules out is the closed hand.

Wrong to let it go: Your house is burgled, or your employer stops paying your wages. Jesus forbids personal revenge and a grasping heart, not justice through proper means. Report the burglary; pursue your wages, for withholding a worker’s pay is a sin God hears (James 5:4).

Where Christians differ: non-resistance. Some (Anabaptists, Quakers, Tolstoy) take these words literally and absolutely: Christians may never use force, serve in the army or police, go to court, or defend themselves, and their costly witness to peace deserves respect. This commentary’s view: these commands govern personal relationships and the disciple’s heart: no personal revenge, no retaliation for insult, generosity rather than grasping. They do not abolish the God-given role of the state to punish evil and protect the innocent (Romans 13:1–4), nor the duty to protect others, nor all legal redress (Paul appealed to Caesar, Acts 25:11). Jesus himself, when struck, did not offer the other cheek literally but protested the injustice (John 18:22–23). The principle is: never repay evil for evil; overcome evil with good (Romans 12:17–21). Giving to everyone who asks is to be exercised with wisdom, for their real good (2 Thessalonians 3:10).
verseByVerse.note: The cloak was the outer garment, the tunic the inner one.

verseByVerse.quote: And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Treat others as you would want to be treated: not only by holding back from harm, but by actively doing them good. This one rule drives every command around it.

The Golden Rule. Others had stated it negatively: Rabbi Hillel, a generation earlier, is reported in the Talmud to have said: “What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour.” Confucius and others said similar things. Jesus states it positively, which is far more demanding. The negative form can be kept by a man who does nothing at all. The positive form requires imagining what you would want in the other person’s place, and doing it, at your own cost. The negative rule permits you to leave the enemy who struck you alone, which is very nearly what you wanted anyway; the positive rule asks what you would want if you were him, and sends you towards him.

As you wish. Jesus tells you to use the one piece of moral knowledge nobody lacks, how you would like to be treated, and to apply it in the other direction. Not as a bargain, treating others well so that they will treat you well: the motive is love, not return (v. 35).

He did not imagine our place; he took it. The rule asks us to picture ourselves where the other person stands. The Son of God did not need to imagine. He came and stood there, “made like his brothers in every respect” (Hebrews 2:17), hungry, tired, misunderstood and tempted, so that he sympathises with our weakness from the inside (Hebrews 4:15). In Matthew this rule is “the Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 7:12), which he came to fulfil, and here is the fulfilment: one life in which this sentence was never once broken, towards friend or enemy. We break it daily; his unbroken obedience is counted as ours who trust him (Romans 5:19), and he exchanged places with us, treated as his enemies deserved so that they might be treated as he deserves.

What if what I would want is not good for me? The rule assumes a sensible, honest wish, not every passing desire. A man who wishes others would let him drink himself to death has not found a licence to supply someone else’s addiction. It is about the treatment any reasonable person wants: honesty, fairness, patience, help in need, the benefit of the doubt, forgiveness, respect. Under all our particular wishes is the deeper wish to be truly loved, and true love sometimes says no. Ask not only what you would like but what you would be grateful for in ten years’ time.

Where it applies: You would want your manager to tell you plainly, but kindly, where your work falls short. Do that in your next review of someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: 'If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love that only returns what it receives is no more than fair exchange, and even sinners manage it. Jesus asks whether anything in your life is more than self-interest could have produced.

What benefit is that to you? “Benefit” (charis) is the word for grace, credit, thanks: what grace is there in that? None, because grace by definition is unearned, and love returned for love is only a fair exchange.

Even sinners. Love, favours, credit: the three main forms of human exchange, and even the openly disreputable manage them. Returning good for good needs no faith, no Spirit, no change of heart, and it is very good at looking like generosity. None of it is wrong, and all of it would happen anyway.

Ten healed, and one came back. Jesus never asked this of his disciples without living it first. Luke will tell of ten lepers all made clean, and of only one, a Samaritan, who turned back to give thanks (17:15–18). Jesus knew that would happen, and healed the ten anyway, because his kindness was never an investment waiting for a return. Every Christian lives on kindness he was never asked to pay back.

Is it wrong to enjoy friendships where love is returned? Not at all. Mutual love is one of God’s best gifts, and Jesus had close friends himself (John 11:5; 15:15). Marriage, family and Christian fellowship are meant to be full of love given and received. The point is to refuse to stop there: enjoy your friends with thanks, then look beyond them to the person who will never return your kindness, and love them as well.

Where it applies: A single mother in your church cannot cover this month’s bills. Lend her what she needs, without setting a date, and be ready never to see it again.

Where it would be wrong: A relative wants you to co-sign a loan you could not repay, or keeps borrowing to cover gambling. Lending that feeds a destructive habit, or puts your own family at risk, is not love (1 Timothy 5:8). Help in ways that actually help.

verseByVerse.quote: But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return, and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love, do good and give to enemies without expecting a return, because that is what God is like, and his children bear his likeness.

Expecting nothing in return. The three commands again (love, do good, lend), with all thought of return taken away. To lend without expecting repayment is really to give, and in a society without banks lending to the poor was a major act of charity.

Your reward will be great. God will repay (14:14). The disciple stops expecting it from the debtor and starts expecting it from God: the money is transferred to a different account.

Sons of the Most High. In Hebrew idiom, to be called the son of something is to bear its character (sons of thunder, son of encouragement). To be a son of the Most High is to be recognisably like him.

Kind to the ungrateful and the evil. What theologians call common grace: the goodness God shows to all people, in life, rain, food, family and beauty. It does not save, but it is real kindness from a God who owes rebels nothing, to people who never acknowledge where it came from (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17). And beyond all common grace, he gave his Son for enemies (Romans 5:8).

The Son of the Most High. Luke has used this title once before, of one person: the angel told Mary that her child would be called the Son of the Most High (1:32). Now Jesus promises his disciples a share in the name. That is the gospel in a phrase. There is one Son of the Most High by nature, and he brings many sons to glory by grace (Hebrews 2:10), so that God is our Father because he is first his. And the family likeness is his likeness: we are being conformed to the image of the Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29).

The family resemblance. So loving enemies is not a height set for spiritual athletes; it is the family likeness. God has done it since the world began, and did the ultimate version of it at a cost nobody had guessed: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). The order cannot be reversed. Nobody becomes a child of God by loving their enemies. It is because he loved his enemies that there is anybody in the family at all.

Does this forbid charging interest or expecting repayment? The law forbade charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 15:7–11), and Jesus goes further: when lending to someone in need, be ready to lose it. That is different from ordinary business lending and investment, which the Bible does not condemn. The heart of the command is generosity to the needy, even the ungrateful.

Is it wrong to want a reward from God? No. Jesus offers it here as a motive, and whoever would draw near to God must believe that he rewards those who seek him (Hebrews 11:6). What is wrong is wanting the wrong reward, or wanting it from the wrong person: doing good to be admired, or to put others in our debt. The reward Jesus promises is God himself, his approval, and the joy of being like him, rewards only a child would want: a son who longs to please his father, not a hired hand bargaining for wages.

Uncertain wording. The verb behind “expecting nothing in return” (apelpizontes) appears only here in the New Testament, and elsewhere normally means to despair; a few older translations render the phrase “never despairing”. But verse 34 has just spoken of lending to those “from whom you expect to receive”, so the context makes the ESV’s meaning by far the likeliest: lend without hoping to get anything back.

verseByVerse.quote: Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole call to love enemies comes down to one command: show others the mercy your Father has shown you.

Be merciful. The summary of verses 27–35. “Merciful” (oiktirmones) means compassionate, full of pity, feeling for others in their need and acting to help. Matthew has: “You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48). Luke shows that God’s perfection is seen above all in his mercy.

What mercy is. Not being nice, not tolerance, not the belief that the offence was minor. Here, in a section about enemies, it is what happens when someone deserves one thing and is given another: it assumes a real debt, and then chooses not to collect it. You cannot forgive someone who has not injured you; you can only be pleasant to them. So the injury must be named as an injury, and then not paid back. Any account of forgiveness that begins by minimising what happened has skipped the only step that makes mercy possible.

As your Father is merciful. God is “the Father of mercies” (2 Corinthians 1:3), “merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love” (Exodus 34:6). The standard is not other people, nor as much mercy as you can manage, nor only as much as the offence seems to deserve, but God himself. That is why no one can ever say he has finished obeying this command.

The tender mercy of our God. Zechariah sang that the Messiah came “because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high” (1:78). The Father’s mercy has a face. It touched a leper, ate with tax collectors, and called a man with a withered hand into the middle of the room. To be merciful as your Father is merciful is, in practice, to watch the Son, because whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9).

Why it is not crushing. The sentence begins with “your Father”. It is addressed to people already in the family, who have received exactly the treatment they are told to give. The mercy comes first, from him, at the cross, unearned and unasked: he did not shrink our debt but laid the whole of it on his Son. The command comes second: not, be merciful in order to become his, but, you have seen how your Father behaves; do it like that. Nothing in this section is possible for someone who has not been on the receiving end of it. Everything in it becomes possible, slowly, for someone who has.

Does being merciful mean there should be no consequences? No. Mercy gives up personal revenge and the desire to see someone suffer; it does not abolish justice or wise protection. A parent can forgive a child and still apply a consequence; a church can forgive a man who stole from it and still not give him the accounts; a victim can forgive an abuser and still give evidence in court. God himself is merciful and just. What mercy refuses is the grudge, the gloating, the long memory kept like a weapon, and it always leaves room for the person to be restored.

Where it applies: Your teenage son crashes the car after you told him to be careful. He is shaken and ashamed. Before you list the cost, put your arm round him; then, together, work out how he will help put it right.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–45 — Judging Others and the Tree and Its Fruit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mercy forbids condemning others, and it begins with honest sight of yourself. “Judge not” does not ban moral assessment; it forbids pronouncing a final verdict on a person, which belongs to the one Judge, and it promises a lavish return to those who forgive and give (vv. 37–38). Blind guides lead their followers into a pit, and every disciple becomes like his teacher (vv. 39–40). The log and the speck correct the order, not the duty: first your own sin, then your brother’s (vv. 41–42). And the tree and its fruit show where conduct comes from: the overflow of the heart (vv. 43–45).
verseByVerse.theology:
The measure-for-measure principle of verse 38 runs through both testaments (Matthew 7:2; Romans 2:1; James 2:13). It is not karma but a reflection of God’s character, who shows himself merciful to the merciful (Psalm 18:25; see the note on vv. 37–38).

The hypocrite of verse 42 is not a conscious fraud (see the note on vv. 41–42), any more than the blind guide of verse 39 (see vv. 39–40). That is why we need Christ to show us ourselves.
verseByVerse.examples:
The log and the speck apply to every relationship with authority in it: parents and children, elders and members, employers and staff. Position does not give the right to speak into another life; honest self-examination does.

Verse 40 matters for anyone choosing whom to learn from (see the note on vv. 39–40). Verse 45 is a searching test of speech, but speech cannot be fixed by monitoring alone (see the note on vv. 43–45).

verseByVerse.quote: 'Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not condemn others, but forgive and give, and God’s generosity will come back to you heaped and overflowing. “Judge not” forbids taking God’s seat, not all moral assessment.

Judge not. “Judge not” is perhaps the most quoted saying of Jesus in the modern world, usually to mean that no one may ever assess anyone’s conduct. But Jesus tells us to recognise trees by their fruit (vv. 43–44), to rebuke a brother who sins (17:3), and to see clearly to take out a brother’s speck (v. 42). What he forbids is a censorious, self-righteous spirit that judges others harshly while excusing itself, assumes the worst, and takes God’s place as judge (Romans 2:1; James 4:11–12).

The judge’s seat. There is a difference between “That was a lie” and “He is a liar”: between assessing what a person did and passing sentence on what they are. The first is often required of us. The second requires knowledge no human being has: motives, history, what a person was given to work with, what they have resisted. A final verdict on a person is the work of a court, and there is only one.

Forgive and give. “Forgive” (apolyete) means release, let go: the mark of those God has forgiven (11:4).

Good measure. From the grain market: grain poured into the lap, a fold of the robe held out as a bag. A generous seller filled the measure, pressed it down, shook it to settle the grain, and heaped it until it overflowed. God gives like that. He gave his Son, and with him graciously gives us all things (Romans 8:32).

The measure you use. Harsh judgment brings harsh judgment; generous mercy brings generous mercy (James 2:13). That is not karma, nor do we earn salvation by forgiving or giving. It describes one kind of person: the one who shows mercy is the one who has truly received God’s mercy, and he will receive it in full at the last.

The Judge who says judge not. The man who says these words will sit in that court. The Father “has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), and God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31). He forbids us the judge’s seat as its rightful occupant, telling us to get down from his chair. And the measure he brings into the world is not the level scoop that gives exactly what is deserved, but the heaped and overflowing measure of a Saviour who came not to condemn the world but to save it (John 3:17). The one Judge with every right to condemn took the condemnation himself, so that for those in Christ there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1).

Why does a culture that says “don’t judge” judge so fiercely? An old post or a clumsy word can bring down a storm of public condemnation in an afternoon, and few societies have been quicker to sort people into the decent and the unforgivable. Judging is not really about the person judged; it is how we justify ourselves. If I can place myself above someone, I feel I am on the right side. The religious do it with a list of sins and the secular with a list of opinions, and it never has enough. Telling people to stop judging does not cure it, because the need underneath has not been met. Only one thing can meet it: to have been judged already, and acquitted. A person who has heard the Judge’s verdict in Christ no longer needs anyone else to be the worse one, and so is free to see a neighbour’s fault clearly and to be merciful about it.

How do I forgive? Forgiveness is not a feeling you wait for; it is a debt you cancel. Name the debt. Tell God honestly what was done and what it cost you; forgiving never requires you to pretend it was nothing. Look at your own cancelled debt. Stand for a while at the cross, where a far larger account against you was settled by someone else, and forgive “as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). Release it before God. Tell him you give up the right to make this person pay, and leave justice in his hands. Stop collecting. Do not bring it up as a weapon, retell it to win sympathy, or replay it at night to keep the wound fresh. Do one good thing. Pray for them by name, and where it is safe and wise, show them a kindness. When the anger comes back next week, as it will, forgive again: the debt is not reopened because the feeling returned. And remember who is speaking. The one who says “forgive” prayed for the men who nailed him to the cross, and the forgiveness he asks you to pass on is his own, given first to you.

Is this a promise that giving money will bring financial return? No. The context is mercy, and the measure returned is God’s generosity in kind. Paul says that “whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully” (2 Corinthians 9:6), but the harvest he means is righteousness and thanksgiving, not wealth (2 Corinthians 9:10–11).

If I struggle to forgive, does that mean God will not forgive me? No, not if you are struggling. The verse describes the settled heart of a forgiven person, not a test that one hard battle can fail. Forgiving a deep wound is often a long road, chosen again and again, and God is patient with those who walk it. Jesus warns against the heart that refuses to forgive at all, that holds the grudge and wants it held, because such a heart has never understood its own forgiveness (Matthew 18:32–35). If you want to forgive but cannot yet feel it, ask God for help, decide not to take revenge, pray for the person, and keep going.
verseByVerse.note: Grain was measured into a fold of the robe used like an apron; a generous seller pressed and shook it down so it held more.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told them a parable: 'Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A guide who cannot see leads his followers into ruin, and every disciple ends up like his teacher, so choose your teacher with care.

Can a blind man lead a blind man? Two short sayings, placed straight after the warning against judging, because they explain it. It is a joke with a knife in it: the audience would have laughed, then stopped laughing, because they knew whom it was aimed at. A judgmental person is blind to his own faults (vv. 41–42), and cannot guide others. Jesus applied this especially to the Pharisees (Matthew 15:14), who claimed to be guides to the blind (Romans 2:19); the men who had watched him in the synagogue, hoping to build a charge out of a withered hand, were the recognised guides of Israel.

Will they not both fall into a pit? Teacher and follower alike come to ruin. And the blind guide is sincere: he genuinely believes he knows the way, which is exactly why the pit is certain. A guide who knew he was blind would stop.

Fully trained. The word is used of mending nets (katērtismenos, Mark 1:19). Training works: a disciple ends up resembling the one who trained him, and will not rise higher than the person he follows, whether or not he intends it.

The one teacher worth becoming like. The sermon’s answer is a person rather than a syllabus. Follow Jesus, and you will become like him: merciful, not condemning, loving even enemies, for God has predestined his people to be “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29). Here is the one Teacher who sees perfectly, who never led anyone into a pit, and whose every disciple, fully trained, will be like him: “when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). He mends us as a fisherman mends a torn net, patiently, knot by knot, until we are whole.

Whose voice is forming you? Not whose books are on the shelf, but whose sentences come out of your mouth when you are tired: the preacher you always listen to, the writer whose tone you have absorbed, the friend whose judgment you repeat, the voices on your phone every evening. You will end up like them, so choose them deliberately. And if you teach, make sure you can see: parents, Sunday school teachers, pastors and mentors reproduce themselves, including the parts they would rather not pass on, and teach most by what they are.

How do I tell whether a teacher can see? Test what he teaches by Scripture (Acts 17:11): does he say what the Bible says, all of it, including the unwelcome parts? Does he exalt Christ as Lord and Saviour, or use him for something else? Look at his life, his humility, his honesty about money and power, his treatment of people who cannot help him (1 Timothy 3:1–7). And look at his followers: do they become more like Christ, more loving, holy and humble, or more like the teacher, proud and quarrelsome? A teacher who can see points away from himself.

Where it would be wrong: You decide no human teacher can be trusted and read the Bible only on your own terms. Christ gave pastors and teachers to his church for our good (Ephesians 4:11–13). The answer to blind guides is not no guides but faithful ones, tested by Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye,’ when you yourself do not see the log that is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother's eye.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deal honestly with your own sin first; then you will see clearly enough to help your brother with his. Humility does not silence correction; it makes it gentle.

The speck and the log. A comic exaggeration from the carpenter’s workshop: a speck of sawdust against a beam of timber, and the log is often the sin of judging itself. We notice the slightest fault in another and walk about with great faults that everybody else can see.

You hypocrite. The Greek word means an actor, one pretending to a righteousness he does not have. But in ordinary English a hypocrite is a conscious fraud, and Jesus pictures somebody who genuinely does not see the log, whose failure of self-knowledge is so complete that he is entirely sincere: more frightening, not less. The comfort is that what we cannot see alone, Christ is willing to show us, and he shows it to heal, not to shame.

First the log. Self-examination comes before correction of others. But the speck is still to come out: what is corrected is the order. Once you have dealt with your own sin, you are able, and responsible, to help your brother, gently (Galatians 6:1). Jesus assumes Christians are meant to help each other see.

The look that removed the speck. Only one man has ever stood with no log in his eye, and Luke shows how he deals with a brother’s fault. In the high priest’s courtyard, as Peter denied him the third time and the rooster crowed, “the Lord turned and looked at Peter” (22:61). No speech, no list. Peter went out and wept bitterly; it broke him, and it began his mending, and on the third day the word went round: “The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!” (24:34). He sees the whole of our fault, and looks at us in a way that heals.

The qualification is honest sight, not moral superiority. Before speaking, ask what this conversation would cost you, and whether you are looking forward to it. If you are, the log is still there.

How do I find the log, if I cannot see it? Ask for help from outside, because the log is by definition in the eye you are using. Ask God: “Search me, O God, and know my heart … and see if there be any grievous way in me” (Psalm 139:23–24). Read Scripture slowly and let it read you. Ask a spouse or close friend, and mean it: what do you see in me that I do not? Notice what irritates you most in others; it often mirrors your own fault. And when you find the log, do not merely regret it; confess it, and ask the person you have wronged to forgive you.

Where it applies: Before you speak to your teenager about time on the phone, look honestly at your own.

verseByVerse.quote: 'For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, for each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What a person does and says flows from what he is, so a changed life needs a changed heart. The fruit does not make the tree; it shows what the tree is.

No good tree bears bad fruit. The sermon turns from what we do to where it comes from. This is not a demand to try harder, for a tree does not decide what fruit to bear. The question it raises is not, what should I be producing? but, what am I?

Known by its own fruit. Figs do not grow on thornbushes. You can tell a person, and a teacher, by the fruit of their life (Matthew 7:15–20); this is right judgment, the discernment Jesus approves.

The abundance of the heart. The heart is a treasury: whatever has been put in over the years is what comes out. Speech is what spills over when the container is full and no longer being watched (James 3:10–12): what comes out when I am tired, when the phone call has gone badly, and what I say about people who are not in the room.

The implication. To change the fruit, the tree must be changed; outward reform cannot produce good fruit from a bad heart. A person needs a new heart, which only God can give (Ezekiel 36:26): not a new personality but new desires at the root, a heart that loves him and wants what he wants in place of one that loves sin and resents him (Ezekiel 36:27). What has to change is the treasury, and only one person restocks it.

What overflowed on the cross. One heart held nothing but good, and Luke lets us hear what came out of it under the worst pressure. Nailed up and mocked, his mouth spoke: “Father, forgive them” (23:34, a prayer some early manuscripts lack). To a dying thief: “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (23:43). And at the last: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (23:46). That was the overflow: mercy, promise and trust. Only one tree has ever borne nothing but good fruit, and it was cut down for us; every good word that comes out of a Christian’s mouth is overflow from him.

One bad word does not prove a bad heart. A tree’s fruit is a pattern over seasons, not one morning’s crop, in yourself or in a friend who once lost his temper badly. Every Christian says things they hate having said.

Then how is the treasury restocked? By God, through ordinary means. The Spirit gives the new heart in the new birth, then fills it over a lifetime as we take in his word: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly” (Colossians 3:16). So fill your mind with Scripture, read and memorised; with prayer; with the worship and teaching of the church; with good books and good friends; and starve what feeds the old heart: the gossip, the bitterness, the screen that leaves you worse. Dwell on whatever is true, honourable, just, pure, lovely (Philippians 4:8). Slowly, the overflow changes.

Where it applies: Whenever a certain colleague’s name comes up, you make a cutting remark. That is fruit, telling you something about the root. Confess the resentment to God, pray for her blessing, and say one good thing about her this week.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 46–49 — Build Your House on the Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hearing Jesus is not enough; only a life that does what he says, resting its weight on him, will stand. The sermon closes with a question that makes the parable necessary: why call him Lord and not do what he says (v. 46)? Then two builders: both come to him, both hear, both build, and the difference is underground. The same flood strikes both houses; one stands, and the other falls at once (vv. 47–49). The rock is not a set of principles but the one whose words these are.
verseByVerse.theology: The fallen house sets the sermon in the light of final judgment. Its commands describe the life that will stand on the day every life is tested, possible only through the new heart the kingdom gives. The question of verse 46 is not an attack on assurance (see the note on v. 46).
verseByVerse.examples:
The two builders mark the difference between a faith that is only heard and a faith that is lived. Every generation of the church has members who have heard much and built little.

Digging deep is unglamorous: prayer and Scripture, honest fellowship, obedience in small things, until the foundation is no longer mood or approval but Christ. Do not start with a general resolve. Take one command from this chapter, with an actual name attached, and ask what it means this week.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
To call Jesus Lord and not do what he says is a contradiction, however warmly it is said.

Lord, Lord. He does not suggest they are insincere. The doubling is the language of warmth, even fervour. The problem is not coldness.

And not do what I tell you? A lord is someone you obey. Kyrios means owner, master, the one whose word settles the matter. To call a man Lord and then decide for yourself what to do with his instructions contradicts the word itself, like calling someone your employer and never coming in. Words of worship without obedience are empty (Matthew 7:21–23; James 1:22). The test of whether Jesus is your Lord is whether you do what he says, including everything in this sermon: love your enemies, do not judge, give.

What I tell you. The prophets said, “Thus says the LORD”, and pointed away from themselves. Jesus points to himself: “my words” (v. 47), “But I say to you” (v. 27). He claims for his own commands the place of God’s commands, and makes a man’s eternal safety hang on whether he does them. Kyrios could mean simply sir, but in the Greek Old Testament it stood for the divine name. Some say the church later put such claims in his mouth, but they run through every strand of the Gospels, and Luke says he wrote from what eyewitnesses handed down (1:1–4). If he said them, either he is mistaken about himself on a scale no prophet ever was, or he is the LORD speaking.

He asks why. Every honest Christian knows roughly the answer: saying it is warm and costs nothing, and doing it costs everything; and one can love the person of Jesus in a general way while quietly arranging one’s life so that nothing he said in this chapter applies.

Why it comes exactly here. Every command in this sermon can be checked, and admiring it is not doing it. Nor has any disciple ever done them perfectly. One man kept this sermon whole, “becoming obedient to the point of death” (Philippians 2:8), and for those who are his, his obedience is counted as theirs (Romans 5:19), so their faltering obedience is accepted for his sake, and the Spirit he gives makes it real in them. One day every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, and every knee will bow, and none of it will be empty.

Does this mean I am not saved if I fail to obey? No. The verse is neither an attack on assurance nor a demand for perfection. Every Christian fails to do all that Jesus says, every day, and the same Lord taught us to pray, “forgive us our sins” (11:4). The question is the direction of a life: whether you call him Lord and are trying, however falteringly, to do what he says, grieving when you fail and getting up again; or whether you call him Lord with no intention of letting it change anything. The first is a weak disciple. The second is not a disciple at all. If you are troubled by your failures, that trouble is itself a sign that he is your Lord.

Where it applies: You sing with real feeling on Sunday that Jesus is Lord of all, and on Monday you are still refusing to speak to your brother over an inheritance. This week, ring him, and begin the conversation Jesus told you to have.

Where it would be wrong: You are so afraid of being a “Lord, Lord” hypocrite that you stop singing, praying aloud or calling him Lord until your obedience is better. Jesus does not tell you to stop confessing him; he tells you to obey the one you confess. Keep calling him Lord, and let him make the words true.

parallels.desc: if I am a master, where is my fear?

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only the life that hears Jesus’ words and does them, resting its whole weight on him, will stand when the storm comes. From the road, on a fine day, the two houses look the same.

Two builders. Both builders come to him, both hear his words, both build houses.

Dug deep. Only Luke says “dug deep”: hard work, through the soil to the bedrock. Nobody admires a foundation. It takes the longest, produces nothing visible, and the man who skips it gets his house up first.

The rock in the rest of Scripture. The text defines the rock as Jesus’ words heard and done (v. 47), and the rest of Scripture shows why that is not a gospel of self-effort. God was the rock of his people (Psalm 18:2), and Isaiah promised a tested stone laid in Zion, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation (Isaiah 28:16), which the apostles identify as Christ (1 Peter 2:4–6; 1 Corinthians 3:11). So the rock is not our obedience considered on its own, but Christ himself, the Lord whose words these are. To dig deep is to come to him, hear him and do what he says; obedience is how a life rests its whole weight on him, and it is that resting, not the effort, that holds the house up.

When a flood arose. Wadis (dry stream beds) flood suddenly in the rainy season. The same stream broke against both houses: the obedient are not protected from trouble. The flood can be almost anything: bereavement, a diagnosis, a betrayal, persecution, the slow wearing away of a faith that never carried any weight, death, and finally the judgment of God. Jesus does not specify, and the vagueness is the point. Something always comes.

Without a foundation. He heard the same sermon; the difference is not in hearing but in doing. His way is easier and quicker, and in fair weather looks just the same.

Immediately it fell. Luke’s “immediately” is grim: no slow sinking, no chance to prop it up. The first serious pressure, and it is over, and the ruin is great, because a life built on nothing does not fail by inches. Luke follows the sermon at once with a Gentile centurion who builds everything on Jesus’ word, trusting him to heal without even coming to the house (7:1–10): a living picture of a house on the rock.

The rock the deluge could not move. Both men heard the sermon. Only one built on the man who preached it. And that man went down into the flood himself. The waters of God’s judgment broke over him at the cross, and he did not give way; the grave closed over him, and on the third day he rose. He is the rock the deluge could not move, and when the last storm breaks over the whole world, not one house that stands on him will fall, because he cannot.

What it does not mean. Not salvation by works. Jesus’ words begin with blessing for the poor and with the Father’s mercy (vv. 20, 36), so doing them starts with receiving mercy, not earning it. But true faith in Christ shows itself in obedience; faith that does not obey is not saving faith (James 2:17).

How do I know whether I have dug deep? Look not at the outside of the house but at what you lean on when the water rises. When trouble comes, do you go to Christ, pray, open his word, and keep doing what he says, even through tears? Or does faith evaporate, and you reach for something else to hold you up? Look too at the ordinary weeks: is there a pattern, however imperfect, of hearing his words and doing them, in forgiveness, honesty, generosity, love for enemies? If you find you have built on sand, it is not too late while the sun is shining. Come to him now, hear him, and begin to dig.

Textual note. Where the ESV has “because it had been well built”, the KJV reads “for it was founded upon a rock”, following later manuscripts; the earliest have “well built”, and the point is much the same.
verseByVerse.note: Wadis (dry stream beds) flood suddenly in the rainy season.

6.text: <sup>1</sup> On a Sabbath, while he was going through the grainfields, his disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. <sup>2</sup> But some of the Pharisees said, “Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?” <sup>3</sup> And Jesus answered them, “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: <sup>4</sup> how he entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those with him?” <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” <sup>6</sup> On another Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. <sup>7</sup> And the scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a reason to accuse him. <sup>8</sup> But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand, “Come and stand here.” And he rose and stood there. <sup>9</sup> And Jesus said to them, “I ask you, is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?” <sup>10</sup> And after looking around at them all he said to him, “Stretch out your hand.” And he did so, and his hand was restored. <sup>11</sup> But they were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus. <sup>12</sup> In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God. <sup>13</sup> And when day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve, whom he named apostles: <sup>14</sup> Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew, <sup>15</sup> and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot, <sup>16</sup> and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor. <sup>17</sup> And he came down with them and stood on a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, <sup>18</sup> who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. And those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured. <sup>19</sup> And all the crowd sought to touch him, for power came out from him and healed them all. <sup>20</sup> And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. <sup>21</sup> “Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh. <sup>22</sup> “Blessed are you when people hate you and when they exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man! <sup>23</sup> Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers did to the prophets. <sup>24</sup> “But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. <sup>25</sup> “Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep. <sup>26</sup> “Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets. <sup>27</sup> “But I say to you who hear, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, <sup>28</sup> bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you. <sup>29</sup> To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also, and from one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. <sup>30</sup> Give to everyone who begs from you, and from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back. <sup>31</sup> And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them. <sup>32</sup> “If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. <sup>33</sup> And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. <sup>34</sup> And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount. <sup>35</sup> But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return, and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. <sup>36</sup> Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful. <sup>37</sup> “Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven; <sup>38</sup> give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you.” <sup>39</sup> He also told them a parable: “Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? <sup>40</sup> A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher. <sup>41</sup> Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? <sup>42</sup> How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye,’ when you yourself do not see the log that is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother's eye. <sup>43</sup> “For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, <sup>44</sup> for each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. <sup>45</sup> The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks. <sup>46</sup> “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you? <sup>47</sup> Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: <sup>48</sup> he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. <sup>49</sup> But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.”

keyVerse.quote: Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.
keyVerse.note: This one sentence sums up the heart of the sermon: everything Jesus asks, from loving enemies to refusing to condemn, is the family likeness of a merciful Father. It is addressed to people who already call God Father, so the mercy comes first and the command second. And the Father’s mercy has a face: the Son who healed on the Sabbath, chose the unlikely and prayed for those who crucified him.

6.reflection:
The Pharisees’ Sabbath rules began in a real desire not to sin, yet they ended up standing between hungry men and bread, and between a disabled man and healing (vv. 1–11). Where might our own customs, at church or at home, have drifted from serving people to protecting ourselves?

Jesus calls the poor, the hungry, the weeping and the hated blessed, and grieves over the rich, the full, the laughing and the admired (vv. 20–26). Which woe describes the pull of your own life most closely, and what would it mean to find your consolation in Christ instead?

Jesus grounds love for enemies in what the Father is like: “kind to the ungrateful and the evil” (v. 35). Think of someone who has wronged you or is hard to love. What would doing good, blessing and praying for them look like this week, and how does remembering that we were once God’s enemies change the way you see them?

Both builders heard Jesus’ words, but only one did them (vv. 46–49). Which part of this sermon do you most admire and least practise, and how can we help one another to dig deep?

7.title: Faith, Doubt, and the Extravagance of Grace
7.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 7 follows straight on from the Sermon on the Plain. Jesus has just said that a life must be built on his words (6:46–49); now Luke shows what those words can do, and brings the question that has followed Jesus through Galilee, who is this?, to a sharp point.

The message. Jesus is the Lord whose word heals at a distance, who raises the dead and who forgives sins, and he gives himself to the people respectable religion had written off: a Gentile officer, a destitute widow, a prophet doubting in prison, a woman known as a sinner. He asks for no one’s worthiness, only for faith in him; and where faith receives his forgiveness, love follows.

Why it was said. Luke’s readers belonged to churches of Jews and Gentiles together (see the introduction). They needed to know that a Gentile is welcomed on faith alone, that suffering and unanswered questions do not mean Jesus has failed, and that a church which befriends sinners stands exactly where its Lord stood.

How the chapter makes its case. Four scenes, and in each the expected is reversed. At Capernaum (vv. 1–10) the elders call the centurion worthy; he calls himself unworthy and asks only for a word, and Jesus finds no such faith in Israel. At Nain (vv. 11–17), unasked, the Lord sees a widow, touches the bier and gives her son back, and the crowd cries that God has visited his people. In the central scene (vv. 18–35) John the Baptist asks whether Jesus is the one who is to come; Jesus answers with the works Isaiah promised, honours John, and exposes a generation that refused both John’s dirge and his own wedding music. At Simon’s table (vv. 36–50) a sinful woman pours out her love, Simon decides Jesus cannot be a prophet, and the parable of the two debtors shows the order of the gospel: forgiveness first, and love following (see the note on v. 47).

Where it leads. The question of who he is runs through every scene: a great prophet? (v. 16); the one who is to come? (v. 19); a prophet at all? (v. 39); and finally, “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” (v. 49). Luke leads his reader from prophet to Lord. In the first scene Jesus’ word reaches a dying body; in the last it reaches a guilty heart, and that is the greater gift. His enemies called him the friend of sinners as an insult, and it is the truest thing anyone said of him: he is the creditor at the table, and he will pay the debt he cancels.

For us. Come as the centurion came, unworthy and asking. Take your questions to Jesus as John did, and not away from him. And ask the question the parable leaves on Simon’s table: how large do you think your debt was? A cool heart towards Christ is not warmed by trying harder, but by seeing more clearly how much he has forgiven.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Jesus Heals a Centurion's Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus’ word is enough, and the faith he praises most is the faith that knows it. The first Gentile whose faith Luke records Jesus commending is a centurion of the occupying power who cares for a dying slave and has built the town’s synagogue (vv. 1–5). The elders plead his merit: “He is worthy.” He sends word that he is not, and asks only for a word, reasoning from his own life as a soldier that sickness must obey Jesus as his men obey him (vv. 6–8). Jesus marvels, and the servant is found well (vv. 9–10). This is the faith the church has lived on ever since.
verseByVerse.theology: The authority Jesus exercises over creation is the authority of its Maker. Jesus marvels at him, and how the Son of God can marvel is treated at vv. 9–10.
verseByVerse.examples: By every outward measure the centurion is among the most impressive people in the story, and he is the one who says he is not worthy. That is not false modesty but an accurate sense of whom he is asking. Ordinary work had taught him true things about God (v. 8). And he never came in person, yet received all he asked (see the note on vv. 6–7).

verseByVerse.quote: After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. Now a centurion had a servant who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Gentile officer of the occupying power loves a dying slave, and the Lord who has just finished preaching is about to show what his word can do.

A house built on his word. The sermon closed with a man who built his house on the words of Jesus (6:47–48), and the very next thing Luke shows us is a Gentile who rests his whole household on one sentence from the Lord’s mouth: “say the word” (v. 7). Words that heal at a distance and raise the dead can bear the weight of a life.

A centurion. A centurion commanded about a hundred men: a career soldier, the rank that kept the empire running day to day. This Gentile probably served Herod Antipas, whose forces were organised on the Roman model: the local face of foreign power. Nearly every centurion in the New Testament is presented favourably (23:47; Acts 10:1–2), and Luke delights to show that the soldiers of the empire were not beyond the reach of grace.

A servant, highly valued. He is a slave (doulos; in v. 7 a boy, pais, perhaps the household’s affectionate word for him), and “highly valued” means dear to him. A Roman writer on farming could call a slave a tool that speaks; few would have expected an officer to go looking for a Jewish miracle-worker on a slave’s behalf. The first evidence of his character is not his religion but how he treats someone with no power over him, and that is one of the first places the reality of faith shows.

The Lord who became a slave. The Lord of glory will set out for a house no rabbi would enter, for a man the law of Rome called property. He took the form of a doulos himself (Philippians 2:7), so that slaves and their masters alike could be brought into the household of God as sons.

Why does Jesus not condemn slavery? Slavery in the Roman world was not race-based chattel slavery, but it was still a system of ownership, and the Bible never praises it. Scripture regulates it and undermines it from within: masters are told they too have a Master in heaven (Ephesians 6:9), Paul urges Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16), and enslavers are listed among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). The teaching that every person is made in God’s image, and that slave and free are one in Christ (Galatians 3:28), did much in the long run to bring slavery down. Christians were not always faithful to it, and some defended slavery from the Bible; but the leading abolitionists argued from these same truths. Jesus heals this slave without first lecturing his owner, because the man in front of him is dying; but the very fact that he goes treats the slave as a person worth the journey.

Was the centurion a believer already? Not in the full sense, for the gospel of the cross and resurrection had not yet been preached.
