But he had plainly turned from the gods of Rome towards the God of Israel (v. 5), and he is about to show a faith that Jesus calls extraordinary. Luke presents him as he presents Cornelius in Acts 10: a Gentile whom God was already drawing, who responds to the light he has and is given more. Nobody comes to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6:44), and the drawing often begins long before the person can name what is happening.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. This one was a Gentile, probably serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. And when they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, 'He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jewish elders plead the centurion’s case on his merits, “He is worthy”, and that is the very case he is about to refuse.

Elders of the Jews. He probably sends them out of consideration, not timidity. A Gentile officer of the occupying army approaching a Jewish teacher directly would embarrass him before his own people, so he uses the one channel that costs Jesus nothing.

He is worthy. Their word is “worthy” (axios), and their evidence a track record: he loves us, he built us something. It is a case built on merit, the way we all naturally think about who deserves help.

He loves our nation. He was probably one of the God-fearers, Gentiles drawn to the God of Israel and synagogue worship without becoming full converts (Acts 10:2; 13:16).

Built us our synagogue. An extraordinary act of respect towards a conquered people’s God. At Capernaum today the remains of a white limestone synagogue from about the fourth century stand on the black basalt foundations of an earlier one, and the stones the centurion paid for may well still be there.

Only one is worthy. The elders say he is worthy; he will say he is not (v. 6). The difference is between two whole religions: coming to God on the strength of your own record, or on the strength of God’s goodness alone. There is one person of whom heaven says, “Worthy are you” (Revelation 5:9), the Lamb who was slain, and every sinner God welcomes is welcomed on his worthiness, not his own. Christians do not bring God their synagogues, but a righteousness not their own, which comes through faith in Christ (Philippians 3:9). The centurion, without yet knowing the cross, stood in exactly the right place: unworthy, and asking.

One man or messengers? Matthew tells the same story and has the centurion come and speak to Jesus directly, with no elders and no friends in sight (Matthew 8:5–13). Both are how people have always reported such things. We say a king built a palace when he had it built, or that a firm wrote to us when a clerk typed the letter; what a man does through those he authorises to speak for him is credited to him. Matthew, writing tightly, gives the centurion’s own words and leaves out how they were carried. Luke, who had carefully followed the eyewitnesses (1:2–3), keeps the messengers, and the detail sharpens Matthew’s point: the man is so persuaded he has no standing before Jesus that he will not even present himself.

So do good works count for nothing? They count for a great deal before people, and nothing as a claim on God. The centurion’s generosity was real and good, and showed what his faith was already doing in him. But it did not put Jesus in his debt, and he knew it. Good works are the fruit of love, and they adorn the gospel (Titus 2:10), but they can never be a bargaining chip. The moment we bring them to God as a reason he should help us, we have joined the elders and left the centurion.
verseByVerse.note: Luke tells us he sent elders; Matthew compresses the story as if he came himself. Some Gentiles admired Judaism and supported synagogues.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him, 'Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion knows he has no claim on Jesus, and believes that one word from him, spoken at a distance, is enough.

Jesus went with them. No enquiry into the man’s religion: a Jewish teacher sets off towards a Gentile officer’s house because a servant is dying.

Not worthy. The elders said he is worthy; he says, through his friends, that he is not (hikanos, sufficient, fit). A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile house (Acts 10:28), and the centurion spares Jesus the difficulty. But it is more than tact: unlike the men who built his case, he knows that nothing he has done puts Jesus under any obligation.

Say the word. He asks for nothing but a sentence: no touch, no ritual, no visit, no sight of the patient. He believes it firmly enough to stop the healer on the road and tell him not to trouble himself to come.

The faith the church lives on. What we have today is exactly what he asked for and received: the word, spoken at a distance, by someone whose authority is not limited by where his feet are. Every prayer for a child at university or a friend in hospital in another city, every sermon trusted to do its work in a heart, rests on what this soldier worked out in Capernaum.

Not only under our roof. His words have been said before the Lord’s Supper for centuries: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should come under my roof; but only say the word.” We are not worthy, and he has come anyway, not only under our roof but into our flesh, and he has spoken over us the word that no illness and no death can disobey.

Is it wrong to want Jesus to come close? No. The centurion is not teaching that we should keep Jesus at arm’s length, but that we do not need to see or feel him for his word to work. Jesus does come close to his people: he promises to make his home with those who love him (John 14:23) and to be with them always (Matthew 28:20). On the days you feel nothing, his word is exactly as powerful as on the days you feel everything.
verseByVerse.note: A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile house.

parallels.desc: he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion reasons from his own command: as soldiers obey his word, sickness must obey the word of Jesus.

Set under authority. He does not say, “I am a man with authority”, but “set under authority”, and only then mentions the men beneath him. His orders are obeyed not because he is impressive but because when he speaks, Rome speaks. His authority is given from above, and it works entirely through words, at any distance.

The reasoning. If my word, backed by Caesar, is obeyed by soldiers and slaves, then your word, backed by God, is obeyed by sickness. Disease and demons, wind and wave, death itself: all are under his orders. The centurion grasped what even the disciples were slow to understand, that Jesus’ word is the word of God, which does what it says and does not return empty (Isaiah 55:11).

A soldier taught by his job. As far as Luke tells us, he worked it out from his life in the army, and he was right: creation obeys its Maker more reliably than a legionary obeys Rome. Anyone who thinks ordinary work spiritually irrelevant should notice: one of the clearest theologians in Galilee that morning was a soldier, and his job had helped to teach him.

In everyday life. Take the thing you are most afraid of this week, the diagnosis, the redundancy, the conversation, and say to yourself plainly: this too is under orders. That does not mean he will always order it away; it means nothing reaches you that he has not permitted, and nothing stays one hour longer than he allows. He “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3), and he uses that authority to heal.

Does “under authority” mean Jesus is less than God? No. The centurion was right as far as he went: Jesus speaks with the Father’s authority, because the Son came to do the Father’s will (John 5:19, 30). But the eternal Son, equal with the Father, came to do that will in the work of salvation, not as a lesser being. The rest of the New Testament shows that Jesus’ word carries God’s authority because he is God the Son, through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). The soldier’s analogy was true, and the truth was greater still.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said, 'I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.' And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus marvels that a Gentile trusts his word more than Israel does, and the word does its work unseen.

He marveled at him. Only twice in the Gospels is Jesus said to marvel (here, with Matthew’s account in Matthew 8:10, and at Nazareth), and the two are exact opposites. Here he marvels at a Gentile’s faith; at Nazareth he marvelled at the unbelief of the people who had watched him grow up (Mark 6:6). Both times faith turned up where nobody expected it, and was missing where everybody expected it.

Not even in Israel. He says it to the crowd: a deliberate lesson to a Jewish audience who, with the law, the prophets and the promises, should have had the greatest faith. It is the point that emptied the synagogue at Nazareth (4:25–27), and a foretaste of the Gentile mission in Acts (Acts 10–11; 28:28); Matthew adds the saying about many coming from east and west to sit at table with Abraham (Matthew 8:11).

They found the servant well. Jesus never saw him, and nobody saw the healing happen: the messengers came back and found him well. The other clear healing at a distance in the first three Gospels is also of a Gentile (Mark 7:24–30). That is often how it looks from inside a Christian life: the word goes out, nothing visible happens where you stand, and you come home to find that something has.

The first of a great multitude. The Lord who marvelled at a soldier’s faith gave that faith in the first place, and the Gentile at Capernaum was the first of a great multitude who would trust a Christ they had never seen (John 20:29) and sit down at his table.

What faith did Jesus commend? Not his generosity or his humility, real as they were, but his confidence that the word of Christ is sufficient: no presence, no procedure, no leverage required. Faith in the Bible is not a feeling of certainty or a force we generate, but trust in a person, resting on what he has said. The centurion’s was great because he saw clearly how great Jesus is.

How can the Son of God be surprised? Luke has already answered it at 2:52, where Jesus grew in wisdom. In the one person of the Son there are two whole natures. According to his divine nature he knows everything and learns nothing; according to his human nature he genuinely met this man’s words on that road and was genuinely moved by them. The wonder was real; he was not acting.

If I have great faith, will God always heal? No. The centurion’s faith was great, but the healing came from Jesus’ will and word, not from the size of the faith, and faith is not a lever that forces God’s hand. Paul, whose faith no one doubts, prayed three times for his thorn to be removed and was told no (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), and he left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). We are to pray boldly for healing, and God often gives it. But when he does not, it is not proof that we believed too little. He has a better purpose, and his grace will be sufficient.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–17 — Jesus Raises a Widow's Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Lord of life meets death at a town gate and turns it back, unasked, out of compassion for a widow. Two crowds meet at Nain, one following Jesus, the other following the body of a widow’s only son, her last protection (vv. 11–12). Nobody asks for anything. The Lord sees her and has compassion (v. 13), touches the bier, though contact with the dead made a man unclean, and with one sentence gives the son back to his mother, in almost the words used of Elijah at Zarephath (vv. 14–15). The crowd calls him a great prophet and says that God has visited his people; both are true, and the second is truer than they know (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The raising at Nain is a sign that points forward, to Christ’s own resurrection and the last day (see the note on vv. 14–15).

The echo of Elijah (4:26) shows Jesus as the fulfilment of the prophets, not one more of them (see vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus’ compassion for the widow came before she asked anything. Compassion begins with seeing, and a Christian may pray to notice the people Christ notices.

His “Do not weep” was no rebuke of grief (see the note on v. 13).

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the town was with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ road crosses a funeral at the gate of Nain, where a widow is burying her only son and, with him, her last protection.

A town called Nain. A village about 6 miles (10 km) south-east of Nazareth, on the slope of the hill of Moreh. Only Luke records this miracle. Nain is near Shunem, where Elisha raised a woman’s son (2 Kings 4:8–37); and at Zarephath, far to the north-west, Elijah had raised a widow’s only son (1 Kings 17:17–24). The crowd will draw the connection (v. 16).

At the gate. Two processions meet at a gate: one crowd following the Lord of life into the town, the other following a corpse out of it, and one of them is going to have to give way. Burial usually took place on the day of death, outside the town; the body was wrapped and carried on an open bier, with mourners, probably flute players and wailing women.

Three closing doors. Three facts, each shutting off more hope: he had died, past every remedy; he was the only son of his mother; and she was a widow. A woman’s security then ran through a man: father, husband, son. She has buried the husband and is burying the son. She is a mother in the worst grief there is, and from that morning faces destitution, with no one to protect her in court, walking behind the body of the last person who stood between her and begging.

Nobody asks. No centurion sending elders, no friends taking a roof apart (5:19). Nobody in that funeral is looking for him; his road simply crosses hers in the hour of her grief. The God who is “Father of the fatherless and protector of widows” (Psalm 68:5) was walking into Nain in human flesh.

Did Jesus plan to meet her? Luke does not say he went to Nain because of the funeral. But whether or not Jesus knew in advance, his Father, who governs every hour, did, and the timing that brought him to that gate was no accident. In your own life too, the meetings that change everything often look like coincidence from the inside.
verseByVerse.note: Nain was a village south-east of Nazareth, near Shunem, where Elisha raised a woman’s son. A widow who lost her only son lost her means of support.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, 'Do not weep.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before anyone asks, the Lord sees the widow, is moved to the depths, and tells her not to weep.

When the Lord saw her. Here, for the first time, Luke himself as narrator calls Jesus “the Lord”: at the gate of Nain, in front of a bier, as he is about to show his power over death. Two crowds, a body and a great deal of noise, and what he saw was the woman. You do not have to be the loudest voice in the room for him to notice you.

He had compassion. The word (esplanchnisthē, from the word for the inward organs) describes something deep, involuntary and physical; it is used of the father seeing the prodigal (15:20) and the Samaritan seeing the man in the ditch (10:33). It is pure grace, and it is what Zechariah had sung of God himself, “the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high” (1:78). The eternal Son, through whom the worlds were made, felt his heart turn over at the sight of a widow nobody else was looking at.

Do not weep. From anyone else, at the funeral of a woman’s only child, those words would be an outrage. He is not telling her that grief is wrong; he wept himself at a friend’s tomb (John 11:35). He tells her to stop because he is about to remove the reason. Only he may say it, and one day he will say it to all his people, when he wipes away every tear from their eyes (Revelation 21:4).

He sees every widow still. He looked at a mother following her only son to the grave, and he knew what lay ahead of him. Simeon had told his own mother that a sword would pierce her soul (2:35). And the Father in heaven would give up his only Son, not to be handed back at a gate, but to be given for us. The compassion that turned over inside him at Nain is the compassion of the God who “did not spare his own Son” (Romans 8:32). He sees every widow still.

So should Christians not grieve? Christians grieve, and should. Jesus wept, Paul speaks of “sorrow upon sorrow” (Philippians 2:27), and the Psalms are full of lament. What Scripture forbids is not grief but grief without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Do not say “Do not weep” to a grieving friend; only Christ has the right to say it. What you can say is what he has promised: that death is not the end for those who are his, and that the day is coming when there will be no more mourning. “Weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15), and hold the hope for them until they can hold it themselves.
verseByVerse.note: This is the first time Luke calls Jesus “the Lord” in his narrative.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. And he said, 'Young man, I say to you, arise.' And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With a touch and one sentence spoken on his own authority, Jesus raises the dead man and gives him back to his mother.

He touched the bier. Under the law, contact with a corpse made a man unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11–16), and a passing teacher had no need to touch it. He put his hand on it, and, exactly as with the leper two chapters earlier (5:13), the traffic runs the other way. Jesus is not defiled by death; death is undone by him.

I say to you, arise. He speaks to a dead man, on his own authority, and there is no prayer. Elijah stretched himself on the widow’s son three times and cried out to the LORD (1 Kings 17:21); Elisha prayed and lay on the Shunammite’s son (2 Kings 4:33–35). The prophets prayed, and God raised. Jesus gives an instruction, because he is the resurrection and the life (John 11:25).

Sat up and began to speak. Luke, the physician, records it in two plain stages, and does not tell us what the young man said. Later legends of raisings often supplied a report from the other side; Luke supplies nothing.

Jesus gave him to his mother. The point of the whole scene: the miracle was for her, and for her future with her son. The words are almost exactly those of 1 Kings 17:23, where Elijah “delivered him to his mother”, and Luke surely meant the echo. But Elijah prayed and waited; here the Lord of the prophets says a single sentence, hands a son back to his mother, and walks on into the town.

What it shows. It was a sign of the final resurrection, when “all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out” (John 5:28–29). He who laid his hand on a bier let himself be laid in a tomb, and came out on the third day holding the keys of death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). Since that morning, every funeral of his people is walking towards a resurrection.

Could he only have been unconscious? Luke’s account gives the idea little room. He calls him a man who had died; his mother and a whole town were mourning him; and people who lived with death at close quarters were seized with fear at what they saw. A man in a faint does not sit up and speak at a stranger’s command at the very moment the command is given. In the end the question is not whether a physician could explain the scene, but who spoke. Luke’s answer is the empty tomb: the Lord who raised this young man was himself raised, and his resurrection is the warrant for all the rest (24:6–7).

Why did Jesus raise some and not others? He did not empty every graveyard he passed. The raisings in the Gospels (this young man, Jairus’s daughter, Lazarus) were signs, pointing to who he is and what he will do on the last day. They were not the final answer to death: the young man of Nain died again, but Jesus rose never to die, the firstfruits of all who belong to him (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). If you have buried someone you loved who trusted Christ, he has not passed them by. Their raising has been kept for the morning when it will be permanent.
verseByVerse.note: The dead were carried on an open bier and buried the same day. Touching it made a person unclean.

parallels.desc: he gave him to his mother

verseByVerse.quote: Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, 'A great prophet has arisen among us!' and 'God has visited his people!' And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd recognises a great prophet and a visit from God, and both are true, though the second is far truer than they know.

Fear seized them all. Holy awe, Luke’s consistent report of what the presence of God does to sinful creatures (2:9; 5:8, 26), and then praise, in two acclamations.

A great prophet has arisen among us! Anybody who knew 1 Kings 17 would reach for Elijah, and perhaps for the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15). It is correct, and not enough: Jesus is more than a prophet (see the note on vv. 14–15).

God has visited his people! This one is larger than the crowd knows. The verb is the one Zechariah used in his song: “he has visited and redeemed his people” (1:68; also 1:78). They mean that God has taken notice of them again; in truth he has arrived in person and is walking through their gate. The Lord who came down to Egypt when he heard his people groaning came down to Nain, and then to Golgotha, and he will come again.

Through the whole of Judea. Judea here probably means the whole Jewish land, not only the southern province (4:44). The news travelled far enough to reach John the Baptist in Herod’s prison.

In the flow. “A great prophet” sets the question for the rest of the chapter (vv. 19, 39, 49): scene by scene, Luke leads his reader from prophet to Lord.

Is calling Jesus a prophet enough? It is true but incomplete. Luke does not despise the crowd’s partial recognition: they knew they had seen God do something, not yet who had done it, and you do not need a complete theology to say, I have seen God do something. Jesus is a prophet, the greatest of them, the one Moses foretold (Acts 3:22). But many today are happy to call him a great prophet or teacher precisely to avoid calling him Lord and God. The crowd at Nain said more than they knew; we are meant to say all of it. If Jesus is only a prophet, he cannot forgive sins (v. 49), and he cannot raise you on the last day. He is God come to visit his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–35 — Messengers from John the Baptist
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is the one who was to come, though not in the way many expected, and those who refused both John and him were refusing God. John, imprisoned by Herod, sends to ask whether Jesus is the one (vv. 18–20). Jesus heals in front of the messengers and sends them back with Isaiah’s promises, stopping short of the vengeance, and with a blessing for whoever does not stumble over him (vv. 21–23). Then he honours John to the crowd: no reed and no courtier, but Malachi’s messenger and more than a prophet, though the least in the kingdom is greater (vv. 24–28). The people had said yes to God in John’s baptism and the Pharisees no (vv. 29–30), and the children in the marketplace show that refusal for what it is: John was called demon-possessed and Jesus a glutton, yet wisdom is proved right by her children (vv. 31–35).
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus treats John’s doubt with complete respect: he answers it with evidence (v. 21), and then honours John in public (vv. 24–26).

The saying about the least in the kingdom is about when a person lives in God’s plan of salvation, not about personal holiness. The least believer now lives after the cross, with a finished redemption and the indwelling Spirit.
verseByVerse.examples:
John’s question is the question of a believer whose expectations have not been met. Jesus’ answer points him to what has actually happened, and that is still the help for faith under pressure (see the note on v. 21).

The children in the marketplace warn against a habit of always having a new objection, so that nothing God sends ever moves us to respond.

verseByVerse.quote: The disciples of John reported all these things to him. And John, calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying, 'Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?' And when the men had come to him, they said, 'John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
John the Baptist, in prison, sends to ask whether Jesus really is the promised one, because what Jesus is doing does not look like what John had announced.

All these things. A centurion’s servant healed at a word, a dead man sitting up at a town gate. And John is in prison for confronting Herod Antipas (3:19–20), in the fortress of Machaerus beyond the Dead Sea, according to Josephus. He has probably been there for months, and he will not come out.

The one who is to come. A way of speaking of the Messiah (ho erchomenos), drawn from texts like Psalm 118:26 and Malachi 3:1. John himself had used it when he said that one mightier than he was coming (3:16).

Or shall we look for another? Take in who is asking. This is the man who leapt in his mother’s womb at the sound of Mary’s voice (1:41), who was filled with the Spirit before he was born, who baptised Jesus and saw the Spirit come down like a dove, who had pointed at this very man as the Lamb of God (John 1:29). That man is now asking whether he got it wrong.

Why did John doubt? We cannot be certain, and several things may be going on. He may be asking for his disciples’ sake rather than his own. More likely he is struggling because Jesus’ ministry does not look like the one he announced. He had preached a Messiah who would come with the axe at the root, the winnowing fork in his hand and the fire of judgment (3:9, 17); what he hears of is healings and dinner parties with sinners, and no fire at all. And John was in prison, while the Messiah was to “proclaim liberty to the captives” (4:18). Or he may simply be in the darkness that a cell and a death sentence can bring on anybody.

The Lamb John had named. The answer to John’s question lay in his own earlier words: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). A lamb does not come swinging an axe; it comes to be offered. The fire and the winnowing fork John preached were real, and the day of judgment will come, but the Messiah would first stand under that judgment himself. The Coming One was doing something greater first: walking towards the cross where the fire would fall on him, so that it need never fall on those who trust him.

He answers in the night. The Lord did not leave his forerunner alone in the dark. He is the Servant Isaiah promised, who does not snap the bent reed or snuff out the wick that has burned low (Isaiah 42:3). He does not scold his sheep for crying out in the night; he answers.

What it does not mean. Not that John lost his faith. If the greatest born of women could come to the edge of this question, doubt is not proof that a faith was never real; it is very often the mark of a real faith under a real weight.

Was John sinning when he doubted? Doubt is not unbelief. Unbelief refuses to trust God; doubt is a believer struggling to hold on while something does not make sense. Scripture is full of believers who asked God hard questions: the psalmists (Psalm 13; 73), Habakkuk, Job, and here John. What they did not do was walk away from God; they took their questions to him. Doubt becomes dangerous when it is nursed in private, fed by resentment and never brought to Christ and his word. Brought to him, it is very often the road to a stronger faith. And John sent his question to the right place: to Jesus himself.
verseByVerse.note: John was in prison, held by Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before he says a word, Jesus answers John’s question with deeds, healing many while the messengers watch.

In that hour. Only Luke records it: John’s messengers are given first not an argument but evidence.

Diseases and plagues and evil spirits. Luke, the physician, distinguishes them: diseases; plagues (mastigōn, scourges), severe afflictions; and evil spirits, which he keeps distinct from the illnesses.

Sight to the blind. Luke gives this a clause of its own, because sight to the blind is what Isaiah returns to again and again, and no first-century physician could do it. “Bestowed” (echarisato) means gave as a gift, from charis, grace.

How Christ answers doubt. It is the same method Jesus will use after the empty tomb, when he shows his hands and feet (24:39). A man in a cell has asked whether his life’s work was pointed at the right person, and the reply is not “Trust me” but what his own messengers saw that afternoon: checkable, specific, and matching texts John had known since boyhood. That is how Christ handles honest doubt: he points at what has actually happened.

Where is the evidence for me? You were not standing there that afternoon. But you have the same evidence John received, written down from what eyewitnesses handed on, so that you may have certainty (1:2–4). You have the empty tomb and the witnesses to the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:3–8), the fulfilled prophecies, and two thousand years of changed lives, very likely some in your own church. And if you are a believer, you have the work of Christ in you: a love for him you once did not have. Faith is not a leap in the dark; it is trust resting on what God has done in history.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, 'Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers John with the works Isaiah promised for God’s coming to save, and blesses whoever does not stumble over the kind of Messiah he is.

What you have seen and heard. Not “Tell John I am the Messiah”, but a list of observable facts, and the list is a quotation, in the language of Isaiah’s promises about the coming of God to save: Isaiah 35:5–6 (“the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer”); Isaiah 29:18 (“the deaf shall hear”); Isaiah 26:19 (“your dead shall live”); Isaiah 61:1 (“good news to the poor”), which Jesus read at Nazareth (4:18). John had built his ministry on Isaiah 40:3. Jesus is saying: you know what the prophets said would happen when he came. Yes, I am the one.

Lepers and the dead. Isaiah’s lists of signs never mention lepers, and the dead living appear in only one of them (26:19); Jesus sets both among the signs from his own works (5:12–13; 7:11–15), and they are greater still. The lepers are an argument in themselves: Scripture records no leper cleansed between Naaman in Elisha’s day (4:27) and Jesus.

Good news to the poor. The climax of the list, placed after raising the dead, perhaps as the greatest sign. A dead body raised will die again; a soul raised by the gospel lives for ever.

Where he stopped. As at Nazareth, Jesus leaves out the vengeance. Isaiah 35:4 says “your God will come with vengeance”; Isaiah 61:2 goes on to “the day of vengeance of our God”. The judgment John expected will come, but not yet. This is the time of grace, the day of vengeance held back so that sinners can be gathered in. Everything John was promised is coming; not everything is coming yet.

Not offended by me. The beatitude is unmistakably meant for the man in the cell. “Offended” (skandalisthē) means caused to stumble, tripped up by something in the road. It is a gentle word and an honest one, naming John’s actual difficulty without embarrassing him: do not stumble because I am not the kind of Messiah you expected.

Where believers stumble. This is where a great many believers stumble: not that Christ has failed to do what he said, but that he has not done it in the order or on the timetable we assumed: the healing that did not come, the prodigal who has not come home. He offers John not an explanation but the evidence, and a blessing for the one who holds on when the answer does not explain everything he asked. And John, so far as the record goes, held on, died in that cell, and was right all along.

Why did Jesus not get John out of prison? We are not told, and the silence is part of the lesson. Jesus could have opened the doors of Machaerus with a word, as he would later send an angel to open a prison for Peter (Acts 12). He did not, and John was beheaded (Mark 6:27). Faithfulness to Christ does not guarantee rescue in this life. What Jesus gave John was not freedom but the assurance that he had not been wrong, and a blessing on his faith. Some believers are delivered from the lions; others die by the sword, and Scripture honours them both (Hebrews 11:33–38).
verseByVerse.note: Jesus answers with the language of Isaiah’s promises.

verseByVerse.quote: When John's messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: 'What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' courts. What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once the messengers have gone, Jesus defends John to the crowd: no wavering reed or pampered courtier, but a prophet, and more than a prophet.

When John’s messengers had gone. A quiet kindness: Jesus waits until the men are out of earshot, and then defends John to a crowd that might have thought less of him for his question.

A reed shaken by the wind? Reeds along the Jordan bent whichever way the air moved, but John was no man to go with whatever was blowing: he rebuked a king and went to prison for it.

A man dressed in soft clothing? John wore camel’s hair (Mark 1:6). The men in splendid clothing are in kings’ courts, which is where John is now: in a cell beneath one.

A prophet? “Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.” The first two questions expected the answer no; this one expects yes, and then gets more than it asked for. John stood in the line of the great prophets, the first in centuries to call the whole nation to repentance. And what is more than a prophet? Every other prophet spoke of one still far off; John was the only one who could point with a finger and say, that man. And he was himself foretold, as the messenger sent ahead of the Lord (Malachi 3:1).

An advocate John never heard. He knows our frame and remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14). John never heard what Jesus said about him that day, but it stands in Scripture for ever, and so it is with all his people: “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1), who speaks for us when we cannot hear it.

In everyday life. When someone is absent and the conversation turns to their weakness, speak of their faithfulness, not their worst moment, as Jesus did of John.

Did Jesus think less of John for doubting? No. He answered John’s question privately, praised him publicly, and never mentioned the doubt to the crowd at all. That is how the Lord treats his struggling servants: he deals gently with the weakness and honours the faithfulness. If you have been through a season of doubt, Christ has not written you off. He judges a life by its direction, not by its worst night in prison.

verseByVerse.quote: This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
John is the messenger Malachi foretold and the greatest of all who came before, yet the least in the kingdom has a greater privilege still.

It is written. Malachi 3:1, combined with Exodus 23:20. In Malachi, God is speaking about himself: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me.” The messenger goes ahead of the LORD, who is coming to his temple.

Before your face. Jesus quotes it with the pronouns changed: “before your face”, “your way before you”. Now God speaks to the Messiah about the forerunner who prepares his way. In Malachi the one whose way is prepared is the God of Israel, and Jesus applies the text to himself without comment. John prepares the way for the Lord, and the Lord is Jesus.

None is greater than John. Not greater than the prophets: greater than anybody. Not Abraham, Moses or Elijah had a higher place in God’s purposes than the man in Herod’s cell wondering whether he had been wrong. The prophets saw Christ from afar; John saw him and pointed.

The least in the kingdom. This does not lower John. The least is greater not in character but in privilege: John belonged to the time of promise, at its very end, and announced the Lamb without living to see the Lamb slain, or raised, or the Spirit poured out. The least believer after the cross and resurrection has what John did not yet have: a finished sacrifice, the forgiveness of sins actually paid for, and the Holy Spirit living in him, as God promised for the new covenant. Not because he is more faithful, but because he lives on the other side of the event John pointed to.

The Spirit of the risen Son. John was filled with the Spirit from the womb; but the least believer now receives the Spirit as the Spirit of the crucified and risen Christ, poured out because Jesus has been glorified (John 7:39), living in him for good and teaching him to call God Abba, Father, through a Son whose work is finished (Romans 8:15–16). John saw the dawn; the least Christian lives in the full day. Do not treat as ordinary what John died longing to see (1 Peter 1:10–12).

Is John in heaven, then? Yes. Being least in the kingdom or greater than John is not about who is saved. John was a man of faith, and he is among those who will sit at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of God (13:28). Old Testament believers were saved by faith in the promised Christ, just as we are saved by faith in the Christ who has come (Romans 4; Hebrews 11). The difference Jesus speaks of is one of privilege and clarity, not of salvation: we know the name, the cross and the empty tomb that John died before seeing.

verseByVerse.quote: (When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptized with the baptism of John, but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ordinary people and tax collectors who had been baptised by John agreed with God about themselves, while the Pharisees and lawyers refused God’s call to them.

And the tax collectors too. One group had said yes to God by being baptised, and the other had said no, and that prepares us for the two people at Simon’s dinner (vv. 36–50). Luke singles out the tax collectors: men notorious for extortion heard John, agreed with God about themselves, and went into the water.

They declared God just. Literally, they justified God: they acknowledged that he is in the right about them, and that when he says you need washing he is not exaggerating. The same word is used the other way round when God justifies a sinner, and that is the heart of the gospel. He pronounces a verdict as a judge: the sinner is not made sinless overnight, but pardoned and accepted, because our sin was counted to Christ and his righteousness is counted to us (2 Corinthians 5:21). The tax collectors who declared God just found him to be the God who declared them clean.

Rejected the purpose of God. Lawyers (nomikoi) were experts in the law of Moses, close to the scribes, and “the purpose of God” (boulē) here is the call to repent. They rejected it “for themselves”: they held correct beliefs about God’s purposes in general, but would not accept that the call to repent was meant for them, for they thought they were righteous and had no need (5:32). Baptism was the public sign of agreeing with God about your sin, and they would not be seen to need it.

The water Jesus entered. When all the people were being baptised by John, Jesus too was baptised (3:21). The sinless Son of God went down into the same river as the tax collectors, standing with sinners in a water of repentance he did not need, because he had come to be numbered with them. John’s baptism always pointed past itself to Jesus (Acts 19:4), so the purpose the lawyers refused was in the end Christ himself, and the water they would not be seen in was water the Lord had already entered for them.

How do I justify God? By agreeing with him about yourself. When his word says you have sinned, you do not argue, minimise or compare yourself with others; you say, “Lord, you are right.” That is what confession is: saying the same thing as God (1 John 1:9). David did it after his adultery, owning that God is justified in his words and blameless in his judgment (Psalm 51:4). And those who justify God are justified by him, freely, through faith in Christ. Those who justify themselves, like the lawyer in 10:29, find that their own verdict is the one God will not accept.

Can God’s purpose be rejected? Does this verse make God’s plan subject to a committee vote in Jerusalem? It does not. Luke will record that Herod and Pilate and the Gentiles gathered to do whatever God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:28). God’s eternal purpose went forward exactly as decreed, and these men were not consulted. What they rejected was the purpose of God for themselves: the gracious call held out to them in John’s preaching, to repent and be washed. That call can be refused, and their refusal was entirely their own; yet God’s plan was not delayed by a single day. That is where Scripture puts the mystery, and leaves it: God is sovereign, people are responsible, and both are true.

Uncertain wording. The ESV prints these verses in brackets as Luke’s own comment, and most agree, though a few read them as Jesus’ words; the meaning is the same either way. The compressed “for themselves” may mean they rejected God’s purpose as it concerned them, or to their own loss; both are true of them.

verseByVerse.quote: 'To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like? They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus compares his generation to sulky children in the square who will join no game, whatever tune is played.

This generation. “The people of this generation” means especially the religious leaders who rejected both John and Jesus.

Children in the marketplace. Children in the square played at weddings and funerals. Whichever game is proposed, one group sits there, sulky and contrary: the person who cannot be pleased, and is never wrong, because the objection simply changes.

Two tunes. John came with the dirge: fasting, camel’s hair, judgment, repentance. Jesus came with the flute: feasts, tax collectors, wine, a wedding. The response to both was the same (see the note on vv. 33–35).

The bridegroom’s music. The flute was wedding music, and Jesus had already said whose wedding it was. Asked why his disciples did not fast, he answered: “Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (5:34). The joy around him was the celebration of the Bridegroom’s arrival (Hosea 2:19), and to refuse to dance at that wedding is to refuse him. And he would sing the dirge too. As he came near Jerusalem he wept over the city, because it did not know the time of its visitation (19:41–44). He played both tunes himself, and wept when neither was answered.

Not confined to Pharisees. This is a very common condition: a person always, quite sincerely, weighing some objection. The preaching is too demanding, or too soft; the church is too formal, or too casual; that Christian is a hypocrite, and that one a fanatic. What gives the game away is that the person never gets up from his seat. The God who kept playing for that generation is patient still (2 Peter 3:9), and gives grace to get up.

But is it wrong to criticise a church or a preacher? Not in itself. Scripture tells us to test everything (1 Thessalonians 5:21), and the Bereans were commended for checking Paul against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11); a church can be unfaithful and a sermon wrong. The question the parable puts is not whether you ever disagree, but what your criticisms are doing. Do they lead you to a better obedience, a more faithful church, a deeper engagement with God’s word? Or do they keep you safely seated, so that nothing ever reaches you? Discernment moves a person towards God; this kind of objection keeps him at a distance.

Uncertain wording. It is not clear which group of children stands for this generation: the ones calling out their complaints that the others will not play, or the ones who will not join in. Readers differ, and the saying works either way, because the sting is the same: whatever tune is played, the same people stay sitting down.
verseByVerse.note: Children played at weddings and funerals; some refused whichever game was offered.

verseByVerse.quote: For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
John and Jesus were rejected for opposite reasons, which shows that the reasons were never the real reason; yet God’s wisdom is proved right by those who respond.

Eating no bread and drinking no wine. John lived a life of strict self-denial, fasting, living on locusts and wild honey (Mark 1:6), as was commanded before he was born (1:15). It was the funeral song of the parable: a call to mourn for sin.

He has a demon. Too strict. The verdict on John was not that he was mistaken but that he was possessed: a fanatic, not right in the head. Nobody argues with a man like that; they just call him mad.

Eating and drinking. At feasts, with sinners (5:29): the wedding music, the joy of the kingdom. He went to Levi’s house full of tax collectors, and he is about to go to a Pharisee’s.

A glutton and a drunkard. Too loose. The charge echoes Deuteronomy 21:20, where a rebellious son who was a glutton and a drunkard was to be stoned. It was not a joke; it was an accusation with a death sentence attached.

The point. Both ministries came from God, and both were refused. People who do not want God’s message will always find an excuse to reject the messenger.

Wisdom is justified by all her children. The language of v. 29 again. Wisdom, in the Old Testament, is God’s own wisdom pictured as a woman, calling in the streets and being ignored (Proverbs 1:20–33). Here she is shown to be right, and the proof is her children: the people who actually responded, the tax collectors who went into the water and the sinners who left his table forgiven. You cannot argue a generation out of an objection that was never about the evidence. You can only point to the changed lives.

A friend of tax collectors and sinners! Meant as an insult, it is one of the truest things anyone said of him in his lifetime, and it is the gospel. They said it to shame him, and it is the hope of everyone who has come to him ashamed. The insult of his enemies has become the song of his church. In the end he was “numbered with the transgressors” (22:37) and laid down his life for his friends (John 15:13).

In everyday life. Who are the tax collectors and sinners in your world, the people your church crowd might be embarrassed to be seen with? Invite one of them for a meal this month, and remember that you were once at that table too.

Did Jesus approve of sin by eating with sinners? No. He ate with sinners as a physician goes among the sick (5:31–32), not to share the disease but to heal it. He was the friend of sinners, not the friend of sin, and his company changed people: Levi left his tax booth, Zacchaeus gave back fourfold, the woman in the next scene left forgiven. Following him means going where sinners are, welcoming them warmly and eating with them, while never pretending that sin does not matter. The church that keeps sinners at a distance has forgotten its Lord; the church that tells them sin is harmless has forgotten why he came.

Uncertain wording. The saying is compressed. Most take “her children” to be those who receive God’s wisdom as it came in John and Jesus, as Matthew’s “wisdom is justified by her deeds” (Matthew 11:19) suggests; some take them to be John and Jesus themselves, wisdom’s messengers. Either way, God’s way is shown to be right by what it produces.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who know how much they have been forgiven love much, and the one who forgives is Jesus. At a Pharisee’s dinner a woman known in the town as a sinner weeps on Jesus’ feet, wipes them with her hair, kisses them and anoints them (vv. 36–38). Simon concludes that Jesus cannot be a prophet (vv. 39–40). Jesus answers with the parable of two debtors (vv. 41–43), sets Simon’s missing courtesies beside her love (vv. 44–46), and declares her many sins forgiven, her love being the evidence of it, not the price (v. 47). The guests ask who this is who even forgives sins, and Jesus tells her that her faith has saved her (vv. 48–50).
verseByVerse.theology: The parable of the two debtors is the key to the scene: forgiveness is the cause and love the effect. “For she loved much” is often misread, and why it cannot mean that her love earned her forgiveness is set out in the note on v. 47.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman gives everything she has left, because what she has received is worth more than all of it.

Simon is not a bad man. He is careful and serious, and he has never seen the size of his own debt, so he cannot understand a woman weeping on the floor. A church helps people most when it helps them see both how much they owed and how freely Christ has forgiven it.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at table. And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The friend of sinners sits at a Pharisee’s table, and a woman known in the town as a sinner comes in because she has heard he is there. Jesus has just said that wisdom is justified by her children; Luke now shows one of them.

A Pharisee’s invitation. Jesus ate with Pharisees as well as with tax collectors (11:37; 14:1). This Pharisee, Simon (v. 40), was curious, perhaps wanting to weigh up the new prophet.

Reclined at table. At a formal dinner, guests lay on low couches around a low table, propped on the left elbow, with their feet stretched out behind them, away from the food. So a woman could stand behind him at his feet without reaching the table. Such dinners were semi-public, and uninvited townspeople could stand round the walls to watch: that is how she gets in.

A woman of the city, who was a sinner. Luke tells us almost nothing: no name, no history. Applied to a woman and stated as her public identity, “sinner” most likely means she was known for sexual immorality, perhaps as a prostitute, though Luke does not say. It was very likely the only thing about her anybody in the room could have told you.

She came because he was there. She came on purpose, at great risk of humiliation, into the last house in town where a woman like her would be welcome, and Luke gives one reason: she learned that he was there. Whatever she had heard him say or seen him do had persuaded her that this man would not drive her out, even in a Pharisee’s house. That is the pull of Christ on the guilty. The Pharisees’ holiness made sinners keep their distance; his holiness drew them in (15:1), and made the coldest room in town the one place she had to be. And she brought an alabaster flask of perfume: she had already worked out what she would do before she got there.

Should a church welcome people like her? Yes, and gladly. If a woman known for sexual sin walked into your church on Sunday, the question is whether she would meet Simon or Jesus. Welcoming her does not mean pretending her past does not matter or that sin is harmless; Jesus is about to speak of her sins as many. It means receiving her as he did: with dignity, without flinching, and with the good news that her sins can be forgiven. Most people who have lived as she lived already know they are sinners. What they do not yet know is that there is a friend of sinners.

Was this woman Mary Magdalene? No. Luke gives no name, and Mary Magdalene is introduced only in the next chapter, as one from whom seven demons had gone out (8:2), with nothing to link her to this story. The identification came much later, chiefly through a sermon of Gregory the Great in the sixth century, and it has no ground in Scripture. Mary Magdalene deserves to be remembered as what the Gospels say she was: a woman set free by Jesus, who supported his ministry, stood by the cross, and was the first to see him risen.

Is this the same anointing as the one at Bethany? Probably not (Matthew 26:6–13; Mark 14:3–9; John 12:1–8). This one happens in Galilee, earlier in the ministry, in a Pharisee’s house, by a woman known as a sinner, and the point is forgiveness. The other is at Bethany days before the cross, by Mary of Bethany, and the point is his burial. That the host in both is called Simon is no difficulty: it was one of the commonest names in the land.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined on couches with their feet stretched out behind them, so a woman could stand at his feet. Doors were often open at such meals and onlookers could come in.

verseByVerse.quote: and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Weeping at his feet, the woman pours out on Jesus every sign of humble, grateful love she can find, and he lets her.

At his feet, weeping. A run of actions in one sentence, and every one a scandal. Standing behind him at his feet: the lowest place in the room. Weeping: since nothing has yet been said to her, whatever moves her began before she arrived. These are tears of repentance and of gratitude, which suggests she had already met Jesus, or heard him preach, and received forgiveness (v. 47); and there were enough of them to wash the dust off a man’s feet.

The hair of her head. A respectable Jewish woman did not unbind her hair in public; later rabbinic discussion treats it as grounds for divorce. She takes down her hair in a Pharisee’s dining room, in front of his guests, and uses it as a towel.

Kissed his feet. And kept on kissing them: Jesus will say she “has not ceased” (v. 45). The feet were the dirtiest part of a man in a sandalled country, the part a slave washed. And the perfume goes on the feet, not on the head, where a guest of honour was anointed: she does not think herself worthy of his head.

He did not stop her. Kissing the feet was homage, given to a benefactor or a king, and Jesus lets it go on and on. When Cornelius fell at Peter’s feet, Peter lifted him up at once: “Stand up; I too am a man” (Acts 10:26). When John fell at an angel’s feet, the angel forbade it and said, “Worship God” (Revelation 19:10). Jesus says neither. He receives it, and then defends it to the host. He is the Lord, and the forgiveness she is weeping over came from him, so the gratitude belongs at his feet.

What she is not doing. She is not performing; there is no sign she is aware of the audience at all, and she asks for nothing. Nor is she trying to earn something (see the note on v. 47). She spends what is left of her dignity, in public, on a man’s feet, because she has been forgiven and can think of nothing else to do with it.

The feet she washed with tears. Those feet would carry him to the cross for her, and after his rising he would show them to his friends: “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself” (24:39). She poured out perfume; he “poured out his soul to death” (Isaiah 53:12).

In everyday life. What is your alabaster flask, the thing of value you have been keeping back? It may be money, time, reputation, or a plan for your life. Love that knows it has been forgiven is extravagant, and does not calculate who will notice.

Do I have to be emotional to love Jesus? No. Tears are not the measure of love, and some of the deepest Christians are quiet people who rarely cry. What this woman shows is not a temperament but a direction: everything she had, poured out on Christ, with no thought for what it cost or who was watching. A reserved believer can love like that in his own way: in costly giving, in obedience nobody sees, in standing with Christ when it is embarrassing. The question is not whether you weep, but whether anything you have is held back from him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, 'If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.' And Jesus answering said to him, 'Simon, I have something to say to you.' And he answered, 'Say it, Teacher.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon silently decides that Jesus cannot be a prophet, and Jesus answers the thought he never spoke.

He said to himself. Simon is far too well brought up for a scene at his own table; he keeps his objection to himself. The people had said Jesus was a great prophet (v. 16); Simon now concludes he is not.

Who and what sort of woman. Simon is no fool, and his reasoning runs like this. A prophet has supernatural knowledge; a prophet who knew what she was would not let her touch him, because touching a sinner would make him unclean; this man is letting her touch him; so either he does not know, or he does not care, and either way he is not a prophet. Simon thinks holiness means separation from sinners. What he cannot conceive is a third possibility: that Jesus knows exactly what she is, better than Simon does, and lets her touch him anyway. “Who and what sort”: in his mind she is a type before she is a person. Underneath the logic is something every religious person can feel. If my standing with God rests on my being better than her, then a welcome for her threatens me. That is why grace offends the respectable before it offends anyone else: it takes away the distance they have worked so hard to keep, and puts them on the same floor as the sinner.

Jesus answering. Jesus replies to an unspoken thought (5:22; 6:8). Simon wanted to know whether this man had prophetic knowledge, and has just had a demonstration without noticing. It is Simon who does not know what sort of woman she is, or what sort of man he himself is. “All are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account” (Hebrews 4:13), and those eyes are the eyes of the one who loved us and gave himself for us. To be fully known by such a Lord is the safest place there is.

I have something to say to you. He uses the man’s name and asks leave to speak: no humiliation in front of the guests, a courtesy Simon had not extended to him. “Teacher” is respectful, and a good deal less than “Lord”, which is what the centurion called him in v. 6 without ever having met him.

Is it wrong to be wary of people with a bad reputation? Not always. Scripture warns against bad company (1 Corinthians 15:33), and wisdom takes care, especially where there is danger to others. Simon’s error was not caution but contempt. He assumed she could not change, and that his own holiness depended on keeping her at a distance. Jesus’ holiness is the kind that touches the unclean and makes it clean. Be careful with sin, especially your own, but never write a person off as a type.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “the prophet”.
verseByVerse.note: Simon was a common name; this Pharisee is not Simon the leper of Bethany.

verseByVerse.quote: 'A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more?' Simon answered, 'The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.' And he said to him, 'You have judged rightly.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a parable of four sentences Jesus makes Simon judge himself: two debtors, both unable to pay, both freely forgiven, and the one forgiven more loves more.

Two debtors. The parable overturns the room’s whole view of who stands where, as Nathan’s made David judge himself (2 Samuel 12:1–7).

Five hundred denarii, and fifty. A denarius was a day’s wage, so the two debts are more than a year and a half’s wages, and about two months’. And sin is a debt to God (11:4; Matthew 6:12): we owed God love with all our heart, and trust and thanks every day of our lives, and every day we have kept back part of it. Nothing we do tomorrow can pay for yesterday, because tomorrow’s obedience is owed already (17:10).

They could not pay. Both were bankrupt, and this is the point Simon misses: he is a debtor too. The difference in size made no difference whatever to the outcome, because fifty denarii a man does not have is as unpayable as five hundred.

He cancelled the debt of both. Entirely the lender’s act; nobody negotiated. “Cancelled” (echarisato) means forgave freely, as a gift, the same verb Luke used of sight given to the blind (v. 21). He graced them both. There is no debtor so deep in debt that the riches of his grace cannot clear the account.

Now which of them will love him more? Love is the response to forgiveness, in proportion to the sense of how much has been forgiven. Simon answers, “The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.” The cautious “I suppose” gives him away: he can see the answer is going somewhere he will not enjoy. “You have judged rightly,” says Jesus, and Simon has condemned himself.

Which way round. Everything turns on this order, cancelling first and loving after, and it is often got backwards (see the note on v. 47). So the question left on Simon’s table is not who is the better person, but how big he thinks his debt was. He is not being told that he is unforgiven, but that his estimate of what he owed is the reason his welcome was so cool.

Who paid the debt? The lender in the parable simply cancels. But a cancelled debt is never free; someone absorbs the loss, and the rest of the New Testament tells us who. God did not wave our debt away as though justice did not matter. He nailed the record of debt that stood against us to the cross (Colossians 2:14), where Christ paid it in full. That is why forgiveness can be completely free to us and completely just in God: it was free because it cost him everything (Romans 3:24–26).

We make mistakes; we do not run up debts. Simon at least believed in moral debts. Many people today speak instead of mistakes and regrets, and the idea that we owe God anything sounds foreign, because a debt needs a creditor and our moral world has nobody at the top of it. That feels like freedom, and it has a hidden cost. If there is no one I owe, there is no one who can release me either, and the old guilt has nowhere to go: we manage it, explain it or carry it, and many carry it alone into the small hours. And there is the cost this parable names: someone who believes he owes nothing will never know what it is to be forgiven much, and so will never love much. The woman at Jesus’ feet had the truer vocabulary. She knew whom she owed, and so whose pardon could set her free, and she wept, not with shame, but with love.

Am I the fifty-denarii debtor? If you have lived a fairly respectable life, the woman’s debt may look larger than yours, and in what people could see, perhaps it was. But both debtors needed the same free cancellation. And anyone who looks honestly at his own heart before a holy God, at the pride, the coldness, the years of ingratitude, soon stops feeling like the small debtor. The Christians who love Christ most are usually not those with the most lurid past, but those who see most clearly what they were saved from.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer; five hundred denarii was more than a year’s wages.

verseByVerse.quote: Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, 'Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sets Simon’s cool welcome beside the woman’s lavish love, and makes the host look at the person he had dismissed.

Do you see this woman? Jesus turns to face her for the first time, since she has been behind him throughout, but he speaks to Simon, so she hears every word with his eyes on her. Simon saw only a sinner (see the note on vv. 39–40). Jesus asks him to look again, and tells him what is actually there: a forgiven woman pouring out love.

Three contrasts. Water for the feet, a kiss of greeting and oil for the head were ordinary courtesies to an honoured guest. None was legally required, and scholars debate how strictly they were expected; but water for a guest’s feet goes back to Abraham’s tent (Genesis 18:4), and a host who meant to honour his guest would offer them. Simon omitted every one. Three courtesies are hardly all forgotten by accident: he wanted Jesus at his table and was not prepared to honour him at it, and everyone would have noticed the slight. Against each omission Jesus sets what she did, and each of hers is far larger: tears for water, kisses on the feet for a kiss of welcome, costly ointment for ordinary olive oil. The one who thought he had little to be forgiven gave little.

He came to his own. What makes the omissions so sad is who the guest was. Simon thought he was hosting a teacher of doubtful credentials, not the Lord who had healed at a distance and raised the dead. The one who made the water was given none for his feet. John says it of his whole coming: “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11). And the woman at his feet is the other half of it: “to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). The same Lord, cold-shouldered at Simon’s table, would later wash his own disciples’ feet (John 13:5), and then give himself for them. He gives the costly maximum to people who give him the minimum.

What does it look like to give Jesus the minimum today? It looks like a Christian life run on courtesies: attending, but not worshipping; reading a chapter, but not listening; giving what will not be missed; mentioning Christ only where it is safe. None of it is scandalous, and that is the point: Simon broke no law. Jesus’ remedy is not that we try harder, but that we look again at how much we owe him. Coolness towards Christ is cured not by guilt, but by grace seen more clearly.
verseByVerse.note: Water for the feet, a kiss of greeting and oil for the head were ordinary courtesies to a guest.

parallels.desc: let a little water be brought, and wash your feet
you anoint my head with oil

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her great love does not earn her forgiveness; it shows that her many sins have already been forgiven.

Which are many. Jesus does not deny that her sins are many. He declares them forgiven. “Are forgiven” (apheōntai) is a perfect tense: an action completed in the past whose result stands in the present. Her sins have been forgiven and remain forgiven. That happened before she entered the house; it is why she came in.

For she loved much. Read quickly, it sounds as though her love bought the forgiveness, and that reading has a long history. It cannot be right, for three reasons drawn from the passage itself. First, it reverses the parable Jesus has just told and Simon has just agreed with: the debt is cancelled, and then the loving follows. Second, the tense: her sins have already been forgiven. Third, three verses later he tells her plainly what saved her, and it is not her love: “Your faith has saved you.”

The for of evidence. So what does “for” mean? It is the “for” of evidence, not of cause: her sins have been forgiven, as you can see from her great love. We use it constantly: it rained last night, for the ground is wet. Nobody thinks the wet ground made it rain; the wet ground is how you know.

He who is forgiven little. Aimed at Simon: not that Simon’s sins were few, but that he thought they were. Feeling little need of forgiveness, he felt little love. Cause and effect run the same way: Simon’s cold hospitality was evidence of his small sense of debt, exactly as her tears were evidence of her large one. Self-righteousness kills love.

The lender at the table. In the story the debtors love the lender; in the room the woman pours out her love on Jesus. So the man reclining at Simon’s table is the creditor. Her sins were debts owed to God, and the one she owes her love to is sitting in front of her. That is why he can say on his own authority, “I tell you, her sins … are forgiven”, and why nobody in the room misses the claim (v. 49). He is not a prophet passing on news of God’s pardon. The pardon is his, and before long he will pay the debt himself.

Why it matters. If love earns forgiveness, every anxious believer must ask whether they have loved enough, and the honest answer is always no. If love is the evidence, the way to love more is not to squeeze harder but to look longer at what you have been forgiven: a finished pardon that still stands over your life, which no later failure can reach back and undo.

My love for Jesus feels small, so am I really forgiven? Your forgiveness rests on Christ’s work and God’s promise, not on the size of your love. If you have come to Christ in faith, your sins are forgiven, however weak your love feels today. But a small love is a call to look again, not to despair. Love for Christ grows as we see more of our sin and more of his grace, and both are the Spirit’s work. Pray for eyes to see. Read the accounts of the cross slowly. Come to the Lord’s Table remembering what the bread and wine mean. Love is not manufactured; it is kindled.

Where Christians differ: love and forgiveness. Some Roman Catholic interpreters, following the Latin, have taken this verse to mean that her love (as an act of contrition and charity) merited or brought about her forgiveness; many Catholic scholars today read the order as the parable gives it. This commentary’s view: the parable (vv. 41–43) makes the order plain: forgiveness first, love second. Jesus will tell her that her faith, not her love, has saved her (v. 50). We are forgiven by grace through faith, and love is the fruit.
verseByVerse.note: Her love is the evidence of forgiveness, not its price, as the parable shows.

parallels.desc: we love because he first loved us

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, 'Your sins are forgiven.' Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, 'Who is this, who even forgives sins?' And he said to the woman, 'Your faith has saved you; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells the woman aloud that her sins are forgiven and that her faith has saved her, while the guests ask who he is to forgive sins.

Your sins are forgiven. He has been speaking about her to Simon; now, for the first time, anyone in the scene speaks to her. She already knew: the thing was settled before she came through the door (v. 47). So why say it? Because she needed to hear it said, in that room, in front of those people. The whole room was watching to see what he would do with the town’s example of a sinner, and he tells her, where everyone can hear, that her sins are gone. Condemned by the town, she is declared forgiven by the Lord.

Assurance spoken. Assurance is not only a private matter between a person and God. People need to be told, in words, on the authority of Christ, that their sins are forgiven, and that is a good part of what preaching, the gospel spoken over a struggling friend, and the Lord’s Table are for.

Who is this, who even forgives sins? The same question as at the paralytic’s healing (5:21), and the right question. Only God can forgive sins committed against God, and everyone at that table knew it. They have understood the claim perfectly and, once again, drawn no conclusion from it. Jesus does not stop to defend himself. He has one more thing to say, and it is not to them.

Your faith has saved you. Not her love, not her tears, not her perfume: her faith, the empty hand that receives forgiveness. The same words are used when Jesus heals (8:48), but nobody in this room is ill: it is her whole standing before God that has been put right. The love was the fruit; the faith was the root, the trust that got her through a door she had no business entering, to the feet of a man she believed would not throw her out. And she was right about him. That is all her faith consisted of, and it was enough.

Go in peace. Literally, go into peace: into a new life of peace with God and wholeness, the Hebrew blessing shalom. She came in weeping; she leaves in peace.

In the flow. The chapter ends where it began, with faith: the centurion trusted Jesus’ word for a dying body (v. 9), this woman for her sins (v. 50), and the second is the greater gift.

He did not flinch. She came in with no name, no standing and no words, into a room full of men who despised her, and put everything she had left at the feet of Christ. He did not flinch. He received it, defended her, told her aloud that she was forgiven, and sent her out through the same door in peace. He forgives sins because he is God, and because he would pay the debt himself on the cross. There has never been a sinner too far gone for that welcome. “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” He is the Lord, and he is the friend of sinners, and he is ours.

What if I have done something worse than she did? There is no sin that Christ cannot forgive for anyone who comes to him in repentance and faith. Paul called himself the foremost of sinners, a blasphemer and persecutor, and said he was shown mercy precisely as an example to everyone who would believe (1 Timothy 1:15–16). Whatever is in your past, the question is not its size but where you take it. Bring it to the feet of Christ, as she did. He has never once turned away anyone who came to him (John 6:37).

Can a pastor say your sins are forgiven? Only Christ forgives sins in his own right. But a minister of the gospel, or any Christian, may and should declare God’s forgiveness to those who repent and believe, because God has promised it. When Jesus gave the apostles authority to declare sins forgiven (John 20:23), it was the authority to proclaim his forgiveness, not to dispense it on their own account. When a Christian friend reminds you from God’s word that if you confess your sins he is “faithful and just to forgive” (1 John 1:9), that is the voice of Christ reaching you through his people. There is no priest standing between you and God, and no purgatory to pay off what remains: Christ’s forgiveness is complete. Roman Catholic Christians understand absolution and purgatory differently, and many of them love Christ sincerely; the reason for this answer is that by a single offering Christ “has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14).

parallels.desc: who can forgive sins but God alone?

7.text: <sup>1</sup> After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. <sup>2</sup> Now a centurion had a servant who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him. <sup>3</sup> When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. <sup>4</sup> And when they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, “He is worthy to have you do this for him, <sup>5</sup> for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.” <sup>6</sup> And Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him, “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. <sup>7</sup> Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed. <sup>8</sup> For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” <sup>9</sup> When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.” <sup>10</sup> And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well. <sup>11</sup> Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. <sup>12</sup> As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the town was with her. <sup>13</sup> And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, “Do not weep.” <sup>14</sup> Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still.
