And he said, “Young man, I say to you, arise.” <sup>15</sup> And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother. <sup>16</sup> Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and “God has visited his people!” <sup>17</sup> And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country. <sup>18</sup> The disciples of John reported all these things to him. And John, <sup>19</sup> calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” <sup>20</sup> And when the men had come to him, they said, “John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?’” <sup>21</sup> In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight. <sup>22</sup> And he answered them, “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. <sup>23</sup> And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.” <sup>24</sup> When John's messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? <sup>25</sup> What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' courts. <sup>26</sup> What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. <sup>27</sup> This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ <sup>28</sup> I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.” <sup>29</sup> (When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptized with the baptism of John, <sup>30</sup> but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.) <sup>31</sup> “To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like? <sup>32</sup> They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’ <sup>33</sup> For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ <sup>34</sup> The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ <sup>35</sup> Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.” <sup>36</sup> One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at table. <sup>37</sup> And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment, <sup>38</sup> and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment. <sup>39</sup> Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, “If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.” <sup>40</sup> And Jesus answering said to him, “Simon, I have something to say to you.” And he answered, “Say it, Teacher.” <sup>41</sup> “A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. <sup>42</sup> When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more?” <sup>43</sup> Simon answered, “The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.” And he said to him, “You have judged rightly.” <sup>44</sup> Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. <sup>45</sup> You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. <sup>46</sup> You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. <sup>47</sup> Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.” <sup>48</sup> And he said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.” <sup>49</sup> Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” <sup>50</sup> And he said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

keyVerse.quote: And he said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”
keyVerse.note: The chapter that began with a centurion’s faith in Jesus’ word for a dying body ends with a sinful woman’s faith in him for her sins, and this is the greater gift. Not her love, her tears or her perfume, but faith, the empty hand, receives what Jesus alone can give: forgiveness that he speaks in his own name. The guests are still asking who he is; she goes out knowing, into peace with God.

7.reflection:
The elders said of the centurion, “He is worthy”; he said of himself, “I am not worthy” (vv. 4–6). In what ways are we tempted to bring God our track record as a reason he should help us, and what would it look like to come to him as the centurion did?

John the Baptist, the greatest of the prophets, asked whether Jesus really was the one (vv. 18–23). What has made you or people you know struggle because Jesus did not act in the way or on the timetable expected? How does Jesus’ answer to John help?

John was called demon-possessed and Jesus a glutton and a drunkard (vv. 33–34). What objections do people around us use to keep the gospel at a distance, and do we ever find ourselves sitting in the marketplace with them?

Simon gave Jesus the minimum; the woman gave him everything (vv. 44–47). Jesus says love grows from knowing how much we have been forgiven. What helps you to see the size of your own debt and the greatness of his forgiveness, and how might that change the way we welcome people with a bad reputation?

8.title: The Word, the Storm, and the Power of the Kingdom
8.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 8 continues Jesus’ ministry in Galilee (4:14–9:50). Chapter 7 ended with two very different hearers at one dinner; now Luke gathers Jesus’ teaching on how the word is heard, then four miracles that lead toward Peter’s confession that he is the Christ of God (9:20).

The message. The word Jesus speaks is God’s own word, and the one who speaks it is Lord of everything. So take care how you hear him: hold his word fast with an honest heart, and trust him when everything says it is over. Wind, demons, long sickness and death itself obey his word; only human hearts refuse it, and his true family are those who hear the word of God and do it.

Why it was said. Luke wrote so that readers already taught the faith might be certain of it (1:4; see the introduction). They had watched the same gospel meet very different hearts: some never let it in, some fell away under pressure, some let worries and wealth choke it. This chapter explains why, assures them the word is not failing, and shows that the one they trust commands what they fear most.

How the chapter makes its case. Those Jesus has rescued walk with him and fund the work (vv. 1–3). The parable of the sower is the key (vv. 4–15): the seed is the word, the soils are the hearers, and much will be lost, but good soil yields a harvest that more than covers the loss. The lamp and the warning to take care how you hear apply it (vv. 16–18), and Jesus names his true family (vv. 19–21). Then his word is shown at work: he speaks to the storm (vv. 22–25), to a legion of demons on a Gentile shore (vv. 26–39), to a woman bleeding for twelve years, whom he calls “Daughter” (vv. 43–48), and to a dead girl: “Child, arise” (vv. 49–56). Each obeys him.

Where it leads. “Who then is this?” (v. 25). The one whose word the sea obeys was himself the perfect hearer of his Father’s word, and he would go further than any storm: into judgment and death on the cross, and out again. So his word to Jairus, “Do not fear; only believe”, is his word at every believer’s grave.

For us. Ask honestly which soil your life is like, and what is trampling, scorching or choking the word. Then do what the disciples did: come back to him and ask. Bring him your storm, your bondage, your shame and your grief; nothing in them is beyond his command.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom Jesus proclaims sets captives free, and the freed become his companions and partners. He goes from town to town with the good news, and with him go the Twelve and a group of women he had healed (vv. 1–2), each described by what he had done for her. Luke names Mary Magdalene, Joanna from Herod’s court and Susanna, and adds that they and many others kept the mission going out of their own money (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus’ practice fits his whole ministry, which welcomed those the religious leaders shut out, and it looks ahead to the honoured place of women in the church (Acts 2:17–18; Galatians 3:28).

Luke sets these women just before the parable of the soils. Here is a company in whom the word took root and bore fruit, and their fruit was that they gave what they had to keep the sowing going. They are also at the cross when the Twelve have scattered (23:49) and at the tomb on the third morning (24:1–11): when the testimony mattered most, they were the witnesses.
verseByVerse.examples:
These women are the New Testament’s first clear picture of money put to work for the gospel. They did not only believe; they paid for the mission, and kept paying. Paul’s teaching on giving (2 Corinthians 8–9; Philippians 4:14–19) grows from the same root: those who share in the blessings of the gospel share their resources with those who carry it.

They did not preach in the synagogues, and there is no sign they tried. What they had was money and the freedom to travel, and they put both under the mission for years without asking anyone to notice.

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus carries the good news of God’s reign from town to town, and the people he has rescued walk with him. The kingdom sets captives free and makes them his companions.

Through cities and villages. Town after town, on foot, saying the same thing: this was his main work, as he had said: “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose” (4:43).

Proclaiming the good news. Two verbs. “Proclaiming” (kēryssōn) is the word for a herald making a public announcement in the king’s name; “bringing the good news” (euangelizomenos) is the verb behind our word gospel. The kingdom of God is not a territory on a map but a reign: God himself stepping in as King to put right what sin and Satan have ruined. That is why, wherever Jesus goes, demons leave and the sick get up (11:20).

And the twelve were with him. The Twelve learned by being with him (Mark 3:14): watching him, walking with him, and hearing the same message in a hundred villages until it was in their bones.

And also some women. Only Luke tells us this in the middle of the Galilean ministry (Mark mentions it only at the cross, Mark 15:41), and it was remarkable in its culture. Rabbis had disciples, and disciples were men; one rabbi, in a saying preserved in later rabbinic writings, said it was better to burn the words of the law than to teach them to a woman. A company that included women invited exactly the accusation his enemies already made, that he was a friend of tax collectors and sinners (7:34). He did it anyway, and Luke records it without a word of defence.

Who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities. Each is described by what was done for her, not by what she brought; like the woman of 7:36–50, they follow because of what he did for them. He does not recruit the impressive; he frees the bound, and then lets them walk with him.

Mary, called Magdalene. A name that needs rescuing from centuries of misreading. Magdala was a fishing town on the western shore of the lake, and the surname simply says where she was from. Mary Magdalene watched at the cross (Mark 15:40; compare 23:49), saw the burial (23:55), was at the tomb on the third morning (24:10), and was the first to see the risen Lord (John 20:11–18).

From whom seven demons had gone out. A severe case of possession, perhaps over a long time. Seven speaks of complete bondage, and of complete deliverance. It is affliction, not scandal, and the only thing Scripture ever says about her past.

The herald who is the news. A herald announces another man’s king and steps aside. This herald cannot, because the kingdom he proclaims has arrived in his own person: the reign of God is seen walking a Galilean road. The Twelve are the beginning of a renewed Israel (22:30); the women are the first people he has won back from Satan, the strong man of 11:21–22. Luke draws the procession like a king’s train after a victory, except that every captive in it has been set free and walks beside the one who freed them.

Not one of them could keep her. Seven demons once held Mary of Magdala, and not one of them could keep her when he spoke. Before long death could not keep him either, and the first person he showed himself to on the morning of his victory was this woman, once owned by darkness, sent to announce the light to the apostles. What has he freed you from? Name it, and let it lead to devotion, as it did for Mary. Glory to the Lord who wins his battles for the bound, and then lets the freed carry the news.

What it does not mean. Nothing in Scripture says Mary Magdalene was a prostitute. She is not the unnamed woman who wept at Jesus’ feet a few verses earlier; the two stories simply stand side by side, which first invited people to merge them. A sermon of Pope Gregory the Great in the sixth century then identified Mary with the sinful woman of 7:37 and with Mary of Bethany, and fixed the idea in the Western imagination for a thousand years. Luke introduces her as a new character, freed from demons, not from immorality.

Why does it matter who Mary Magdalene was? Because the truth honours both Christ and her. The legend made her a symbol of sexual sin repented and obscured what the Gospels say: she was set free from a terrible bondage, gave her money and her life to Jesus, stayed at the cross, and was the first the risen Lord appeared to and sent to the apostles. That is a greater story than the legend, and a warning: tradition, however old and beautiful, must be tested by Scripture.
verseByVerse.note: Mary Magdalene came from Magdala on the western shore of the lake. Nothing in Scripture says she was the sinful woman of chapter 7.

parallels.desc: from whom he had cast out seven demons

verseByVerse.quote: and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Women of every rank, even from Herod’s court, kept Jesus’ mission going out of their own money, and he gladly received it. Giving to the work of the gospel is real ministry.

Joanna, wife of Chuza. Herod is Herod Antipas, and Chuza was his steward (epitropos), a high official over the royal household or estates: he managed the finances of the man who had John the Baptist in a cell and would have his head brought in on a platter. Joanna, a court wife with status, money and a husband employed by the enemy, is walking round Galilee with an itinerant preacher from Nazareth.

The gospel in Herod’s house. Manaen, brought up with Herod, was later among the teachers of the church at Antioch (Acts 13:1), and Paul sends greetings from the saints of Caesar’s household (Philippians 4:22). Joanna is named again at the empty tomb (24:10): whatever it cost her, she was still there at the end. Perhaps she was one of Luke’s sources for the inside story of Herod (9:7–9; 23:8–12).

And Susanna, and many others. A name with no story at all, then a crowd of women nobody named. But she was known to Jesus, and her name is in Scripture for ever.

Who provided for them out of their means. “Provided” (diēkonoun) means served, the root behind our word deacon, and the tense is continuous: they kept on providing, out of their own money. Thirteen men walked from village to village for months with no visible income, and Luke tells us in half a verse where much of the money came from: the Galilean ministry of Jesus Christ was funded largely by women, as Lydia and others would fund Paul’s (Acts 16:14–15).

Fed by those he feeds. The verb Luke uses for these women is the one Jesus will use of himself at the Last Supper: “I am among you as the one who serves” (22:27). Here the Servant of the Lord lets himself be served. He who will soon break five loaves for five thousand eats bread that Joanna paid for; the Lord who owns the cattle on a thousand hills needed a meal and a bed, took them gratefully from people he had healed, and so turned their giving into fellowship with himself.

Is giving money really ministry, or just a lesser support role? It is ministry in the full sense. Paul calls the Philippians’ gift “a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God” (Philippians 4:18). Putting your money under the gospel is one of the plainest ways to serve: the preacher and the giver are partners in the same work (Philippians 1:5).

How much should I give to Christ’s work? Luke records no amount, only the habit and the love behind it. The New Testament sets no fixed percentage, but gives clear principles. Set something aside regularly, as God has prospered you (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give generously, for whoever sows sparingly will reap sparingly (2 Corinthians 9:6), and cheerfully, for “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Give first to the gospel work of your own church, which supports those who teach you (Galatians 6:6), and then beyond it. Many find the Old Testament tithe a helpful starting point, not a ceiling. The real question is not the least I can give, but what this gift says about where my treasure is (12:34).
verseByVerse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas; Joanna came from his court.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–15 — The Parable of the Sower and Its Explanation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The same word of God meets very different hearts, and only a heart that holds it fast bears fruit. Jesus tells the crowd of a sower whose seed falls on four kinds of ground (vv. 4–8). When the disciples come back and ask, he explains that understanding is God’s gift, while for those who refuse him the parables become a judgment, in the words of Isaiah 6 (vv. 9–10). Then he interprets the soils (vv. 11–15): a word snatched away, a joy with no root, a growth slowly choked, and a harvest held fast with patience. The parable is not a rigid classification of people but a mirror for every hearer.
verseByVerse.theology:
In Mark, Jesus asks how the disciples will understand any of the parables if they do not understand this one (Mark 4:13). It sets the pattern for all his teaching: the response to the word decides everything.

The seed does not change, and neither does the generous hand that scatters it. What varies is the heart. The good soil is an honest and good heart, and the last word of the explanation is patience (see the note on v. 15).
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable puts one question to every hearer: not whether you have heard the gospel, but what has happened to the word in you.

The rock soil has troubled sincere believers, and should be handled with care (see the note on v. 13).

The thorns are the soil to watch most closely in a comfortable life, because nothing seems wrong (see the note on v. 14).

verseByVerse.quote: And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable, 'A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word is scattered generously on every kind of heart, but where a heart has been trodden hard it never gets in at all. Jesus begins to explain why the same message meets such different responses.

A great crowd. Luke has just shown two hearers at one dinner: a Pharisee who heard nothing and a forgiven woman who loved much (7:36–50). Now, with people coming from town after town, Jesus tells a story in which three of the four soils yield nothing. It opens a section on hearing (8:4–21). He is preparing his disciples for the years ahead and every century since.

A sower went out. Every listener had watched it done. In that farming, it seems, sowing often came before ploughing: a man walked the field flinging seed in wide arcs, and the ground was turned over afterwards. So the seed really did fall everywhere: on the path, on thin soil over limestone, into corners where last year’s thorns were still rooted.

Along the path. Footpaths through the fields were packed hard by generations of feet. Only Luke adds that the seed was “trampled underfoot”: before the birds arrive, the ordinary traffic of life has walked over it, and lying on the surface it is easy picking. Nothing is wrong with the seed; the surface would not let it in.

The sower is not named. Jesus identifies the seed (v. 11) and all four soils, and says nothing about the man with the bag. That silence is a mercy to everyone who has tried to sow anything: what differs is the ground, not the preacher’s skill, and the sower cannot make good soil.

The sower telling the story. Yet the scene names him. The first sower is standing before this crowd, telling them what his own preaching will meet. He knows most of them will drift away, and he sows anyway, because the seed is his Father’s word and the harvest is his Father’s business. The Son of God did not ration the word to the promising; somewhere among the paths and rocks were hearts his Father had prepared.

So does it not matter how we share the gospel? It matters, but not as we fear. We should speak clearly, kindly and wisely (Colossians 4:5–6), and remove needless obstacles (1 Corinthians 9:19–23). But the parable lifts the burden of thinking the harvest depends on our skill: Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6). Scatter the seed faithfully and widely; the soil is in God’s hands. That frees you to share Christ without manipulation, and without despair when most do not respond.
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.' As he said these things, he called out, 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seed that springs up fast on shallow ground, or grows among thorns, comes to nothing, but in good soil it yields a harvest that more than makes up for all the loss. So everyone must ask how he is hearing.

And some fell on the rock. Not bare stone but limestone bedrock under a thin layer of soil, common in Galilee. The shallow soil warms quickly, so the seed comes up first; then the sun comes, and the roots find rock instead of water. Only Luke mentions moisture. The fastest growth in the field is the first to die.

And some fell among thorns. Here nothing seems wrong: the plant grows, and so does everything else. The thorns were not planted; their roots were already there, unseen. They do not attack the wheat; they grow alongside it, for the same water and light, faster and stronger. Choked: slow death by competition, while the crop is still standing.

A hundredfold. A hundred grains for one is far beyond what a farmer there would normally expect (compare Genesis 26:12, where Isaac reaped a hundredfold because the LORD blessed him). The figure is deliberately extravagant: the fourth soil more than covers everything lost on the other three.

Ears to hear. He “called out”, raising his voice over the crowd. In the Bible hearing means listening, understanding and obeying. A man who hears the parable of the soils and never asks which soil he is has not yet heard it.

Ears for his voice. In the Old Testament the summons to hear belongs to God: “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4); “Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live” (Isaiah 55:3). The prophets said, “Thus says the LORD”, and pointed away from themselves. Jesus points the summons at his own words, as though hearing him and hearing God were the same thing. The Father settles it from the cloud: “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him” (9:35).

Can a person change from one soil to another? Yes, by the grace of God. The parable describes how people respond to the word at a given time, not a fixed caste. God promises to take away the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26), and many Christians look back on years when the word bounced off them before God made the soil good. So we keep sowing, and keep praying for those who have heard and not yet believed.
verseByVerse.note: Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil. A hundredfold would be an extraordinary harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant, he said, 'To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Understanding the kingdom is God’s gift to those who come to Jesus and ask, while for those who refuse him the parables become a judgment.

His disciples asked. They do not assume they have understood; they come back and ask, which is what good soil does. The crowd heard a story about farming and went home. What separates the disciples is not superior insight (Mark records that they had not understood either, Mark 4:13), but that they came back.

To you it has been given. Understanding the kingdom is not achieved by intelligence but given by God (10:21; Matthew 16:17). We did not find the secret; he told it to us.

The secrets of the kingdom. “Secrets” (mystēria) are truths once hidden and now revealed by God: above all, that the kingdom has come in Jesus, in an unexpected form, like a seed and not yet like a harvest (Ephesians 3:3–6).

The secret is a person. Not a key for decoding stories but a person, sitting with them and explaining his own parables: no one knows “who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (10:22). The Twelve are not sharper than the crowd, only closer to him. John tells us that Isaiah, whose words Jesus quotes here, said them because he saw Jesus’ glory (John 12:41): the Lord high and lifted up of Isaiah 6, whose holiness made the prophet cry out that he was lost, is the teacher answering fishermen’s questions.

So that seeing they may not see. One of the hardest sentences in the Gospels, and it should not be softened. Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9–10, God’s commission to Isaiah after the vision of the throne, telling him in advance that his preaching would harden a rebellious people. Luke, unlike Mark, leaves out the end of the quotation (lest they turn and be forgiven), perhaps holding it back for the end of Acts (Acts 28:26–27).

Does God then deliberately blind people? Three things must be held together. First, this is a judgment on people who have already refused what they were given: Isaiah’s commission came after generations of ignored prophets, and Luke has shown us a Nazareth that tried to kill Jesus. To those who reject the light, more light is withheld (v. 18). Second, a parable is not merely a veil but a door held ajar. It hides the thing from the casual and rewards the one who comes back and asks, as the disciples just did. Third, this is mercy as well as judgment. To be told plainly and reject it plainly is far more terrible; a parable leaves the door open longer than a sermon does.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was trying to keep people from salvation; for the hard-hearted, parables confirm a blindness already chosen, as the same sun melts wax and hardens clay. Nor can it excuse one’s own dullness. The remedy is in verse 9: they asked.

If understanding is given, why do some get it and others not? Scripture holds two truths. Understanding is God’s gift, given freely to whom he wills, so that no one may boast (Matthew 11:25–27; 1 Corinthians 4:7). And those who do not understand are not innocent victims; they love the darkness and will not come to the light (John 3:19). God never blinds a willing seeker. If you want to understand, that wanting is itself the beginning of the gift: “ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find” (11:9).

Uncertain wording. The small Greek word behind “so that” (hina) usually expresses purpose, and most take it so here: the parables are given in order that those who have refused the light should not see. Some read it more loosely, as stating the result, or as shorthand for saying that Isaiah’s words are being fulfilled. The grammar allows each, and on every reading the blindness is God’s judgment on people who have already refused him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seed is God’s own word, and from the hardened heart the devil snatches it away before it can lead to faith and salvation.

The seed is the word of God. That settles a great deal. The seed is the gospel, not the preacher or his technique, and it is the same seed in all four soils. Its power is in the seed (Isaiah 55:10–11; 1 Peter 1:23): the word that called light out of darkness and Lazarus out of the tomb. The sower is first Jesus, and then everyone who spreads his word.

The devil comes. The birds are the devil. Something intelligent and hostile is at work between hearing and believing. It does not need to refute the word, only to remove it before it goes in: by distraction, doubt, forgetfulness, the next thing that comes along. The god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4).

What a footpath is. Not naturally hard ground, but ordinary soil walked over so often that nothing can get in, by perfectly innocent traffic. That is the danger of a life with no quiet in it. The word arrives on Sunday, and by the time the car is out of the car park there has been a conversation, a screen, a plan for the afternoon, and it is gone, and nobody did anything wrong.

Believe and be saved. Only Luke adds this: that is what is at stake in a distracted hour. Faith comes from hearing (Romans 10:17), and Satan’s strategy is to stop the hearing from taking root.

The one the devil could not rob. Luke’s readers have watched the devil try this before. In the wilderness he came to Jesus with the same aim, to pry the word of God loose from a hungry man (4:1–13). Three times Jesus answered, “It is written”, and the word stayed where it was. What every heart on the path loses, the Son of Man held, and not for himself only: at the cross he would disarm the powers of darkness, so that the enemy who snatches seed from the path has met one he cannot rob, and those who belong to Christ are kept by the stronger hand.

Can the devil take the word from a Christian? He can steal a particular sermon from a believer’s attention, and often does. But he cannot snatch a true believer out of Christ’s hand (John 10:28), for the Spirit keeps what he has begun. The path describes those in whom the word never went in at all. For the Christian the warning is practical: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7).

In everyday life. You are kept by the one the devil could not rob, so guard the moment after hearing. Next Sunday, before you speak to anyone after the sermon, take two minutes to name to God the one thing he said to you, and on the drive home talk about it instead of the weather.

verseByVerse.quote: And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some receive the word with real joy but no root, and when testing comes they fall away. A quick and happy response is not yet proof of lasting faith.

Receive it with joy. This soil has hurt sensitive consciences, so it must be handled carefully. The joy is real as far as it goes, but joy alone is not proof of genuine faith.

But these have no root. The word has not gone down into heart and will. Root is the part nobody sees until a drought. Only Luke says they “believe for a while”: a real but temporary belief of mind and feelings, not a heart transformed by God.

And in time of testing fall away. “Testing” (peirasmos), as at 4:13, covers both trial and temptation, which English keeps apart and Greek does not; Matthew says, “when tribulation or persecution arises” (Matthew 13:21). “Fall away” (aphistantai) means depart, abandon the faith.

I have prayed for you. “Testing” is Luke’s word again for the hour that came on the Twelve. On the night of his arrest Jesus told them to pray that they might not enter into temptation (22:40), and told Peter that Satan had demanded to sift them like wheat, “but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (22:31–32). Peter fell hard that night, yet did not fall away, because the root of his faith was not his own resolve but the prayer of his Lord. The Father always hears the Son (John 11:42); that is the deepest difference between the rock and the good soil: the Son of God prays for his own, and always lives to intercede for them (Hebrews 7:25).

Is this me? Have I lost my salvation? Three things need saying. First, the passage does not describe someone struggling but someone who fell away and is no longer there. A person worried about this verse is still asking the question, which the rock soil does not do. Second, what God begins he finishes (Philippians 1:6); no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). John says of those who left, not that they lost something, but that they went out from us because they were not of us (1 John 2:19). The rock soil is not a Christian who was lost; it is a plant that never had root.

The remedy. Third, the remedy is never endless introspection: staring at your own root system is exactly what a plant cannot do. What can be done is to go deeper, putting the word where it can reach water, in the unspectacular disciplines nobody sees, before the drought arrives, as it will. And a dry season is not falling away. Doubt, grief and even depression have brought many of God’s dearest children to cry, why are you cast down, O my soul? (Psalm 42:5), and they were still his, still reaching for water.

How do I put down roots? Roots grow in hidden places and over time. Read the Bible daily to meet God, not only for information. Pray, especially when you do not feel like it. Sit under faithful preaching week by week, and come to the Lord’s Table. Join a church where people know you well enough to notice if you wither. Learn the great truths of the faith. And obey what you already know, for obedience is how the word goes down from the head into the will. None of it is dramatic; all of it is how God keeps his people.

In everyday life. If you are a new Christian full of joy, thank God for it and give your attention to the roots. If you lead others, do not measure a conversion by its excitement; walk with new believers through their first drought.

Where Christians differ: can a believer fall away? Arminians (Christians who follow the Dutch theologian Jacobus Arminius, and Wesleyan Methodists after him) take this as a believer who loses salvation, and many hold the view out of deep reverence for the Bible’s warnings. This commentary’s view: the parable describes a faith that was never rooted, never the saving faith of the good soil; its fruit never came. Those whom God truly saves he keeps to the end (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), and those who fall away permanently show they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). This is the perseverance of the saints. But the warning is real: God keeps his people through warnings like this one, not in spite of them. Examine yourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word can be slowly strangled in a heart that keeps it alongside worries, wealth and the ordinary pleasures of life, so that it never ripens into fruit. This is the hardest soil to recognise, because nothing in it looks wrong.

Choked as they go. The plant is still in the field, still green. There is no decision and no turning point; it happens over a decade, in the course of getting on with life, and the verb means strangled, slowly.

Cares, riches and pleasures. Not one of the three thorns is in itself a sin. Cares: anxieties about daily life, money, health, a difficult child, an ageing parent, a job that may not last (12:22–31; 21:34). Riches: having things and keeping them, and the love of money that so easily grows from it (12:15–21; 1 Timothy 6:9–10). Pleasures of life, which only Luke adds: not vice, but the innocent pleasures of an ordinary life, good things that crowd out God.

The thorns are legitimate things. In a comfortable country the word is choked almost entirely by legitimate things. A man strangled by an obvious sin usually knows it; a man strangled by his mortgage, his hobbies and his family’s diary has nothing to repent of that he can name. Underneath, each thorn is a rival saviour. Worry assumes that everything depends on me; riches promise a security God never promised through them; pleasures offer a happiness only he can give.

Their fruit does not mature. There is growth, perhaps the beginning of fruit, but it never ripens. “No servant can serve two masters” (16:13).

The one thing necessary. Luke shows the remedy in a home in Bethany. Martha, “anxious and troubled about many things” (the same word as the cares of this verse), is busy with good work for Jesus; Mary sits at his feet listening to his word, and Jesus says that “one thing is necessary”, and that “Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her” (10:38–42; see Mary and Martha). The thorns are not beaten by more effort but outgrown by a greater love. When Christ himself is the treasure, cares lose their grip, riches become tools, and pleasures become thanksgivings.

He wore the thorns himself. In his presence there is fullness of joy, and at his right hand are pleasures for evermore (Psalm 16:11); the pleasures that choke are thin and brief beside that. The cares that strangle us he bids us cast on him, because he cares for us (1 Peter 5:7), and he knows their weight: the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head and carried a world’s sin, and his heart was never once divided. He wore the thorns as a crown, so that the curse of the ground could be lifted. Every fruit of his obedience came to full ripeness, and that undivided obedience is counted to people whose hearts are divided still. Blessed be the Lord who was never choked, and who is untangling us.

Are the thorn-soil hearers saved? In the parable only the good soil bears a crop, and the more likely reading is that they never truly believed: a faith that bears no fruit at all is not saving faith (compare John 15:2, 6). Some Christians read them as believers who are saved but fruitless. Either way, the warning is not to let worries and riches choke the word.

Is it wrong to enjoy the good things of life? No. God “richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17): food, friendship, marriage, work and rest are his gifts. A pleasure becomes a thorn when it takes the time, attention and love that belong to God, when it becomes the thing you cannot give up. The test is whether you could enjoy it less for Christ’s sake, and whether it leads you to thank him or forget him.

In everyday life. Ask not what sins you are fighting but what has quietly become non-negotiable in your week. Thorns are not planted; they are simply left. Pull one out this week: cancel the thing that always crowds out prayer, give away what has begun to own you, or hand a named worry to God.

verseByVerse.quote: As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good hearer holds God’s word fast with an honest heart and bears fruit by enduring, not by quick enthusiasm. Every mark of the good soil is unspectacular.

Hold it fast. The verb (katechousin) means keep it, grip it, refuse to let it go. It is active, because things get taken. Mary treasured the word (2:19); the good hearer hangs on to it.

In an honest and good heart. Only Luke has this phrase (kalē kai agathē), which in Greek described a person of fine and noble character, and Jesus gives it a new meaning. The heart he commends is the honest one: open to God, not trying to look better than it is, letting the word say what it says without bargaining. Anyone can test himself here: when the word says something I do not like, do I let it stand?

And bear fruit with patience. “Patience” (hypomonē) is endurance, steadfastness under pressure, the opposite of the rocky ground (v. 13). The rock soil was the fastest in the field; the good soil is never praised for speed at all.

The ear that was never closed. One hearer’s heart was wholly honest and good. Isaiah heard the Servant of the Lord say that morning by morning God wakened his ear to hear as one who is taught, and that he was not rebellious and did not turn back (Isaiah 50:4–5). Jesus held his Father’s word fast through his whole life, in Gethsemane and on the cross, and bore fruit with endurance to the end. And the good soil in his people comes from him: the heart that receives the word is the new heart promised in the new covenant (Ezekiel 36:26), sealed by his blood (22:20), and its patience is the endurance of the one who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2).

Where does a good heart come from? It is God’s gift; he prepares the soil. The Lord opened Lydia’s heart to pay attention to what Paul said (Acts 16:14). No one is good soil by nature (Jeremiah 17:9); God breaks the ground and makes it new (Ezekiel 36:26). If your heart has held the word fast, give God the glory; if you long for a better heart, ask him for it. That longing is already his work.

What is the fruit? A changed life: the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), obedience and good works (Colossians 1:10), and, in God’s time, others brought to faith. It is not measured by size or fame: the fruit of the word in you is Christlikeness. Do not compare your harvest with someone else’s; Jesus speaks elsewhere of a hundredfold, sixty and thirty, and all of it is good soil (Matthew 13:23).

In everyday life. The patience is the Spirit’s fruit in you, not a grit you must manufacture. Choose one verse from Sunday’s sermon and carry it with you all week: write it down, repeat it, pray it. That is what holding fast looks like in an ordinary week.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — A Lamp Under a Jar and True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What the disciples have heard is meant to be shown and obeyed, not kept or merely listened to. A lamp is lit to give light, and everything now hidden will come to light (vv. 16–17), so take care how you hear: truth used grows, and truth neglected is lost (v. 18). Then Jesus’ mother and brothers arrive, and he says that his family are those who hear the word of God and do it (vv. 19–21), an open door, not a rejection of Mary.
verseByVerse.theology:
The lamp saying applies the parable to the disciples’ own calling (see the note on vv. 16–17).

The family saying should be read alongside what Luke has already shown of Mary. She is not demoted; she is the first member of this family, the woman who said, “let it be to me according to your word” (1:38). On the brothers, see the note on vv. 19–21.
verseByVerse.examples:
A family made by hearing and doing the word is the root of the church’s fellowship across every natural division. The first churches drew Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, men and women into one household, and every congregation is meant to be that kind of family still.

Take care then how you hear becomes a practical question: not what was preached, but what was done with it between Sunday and Tuesday. And the warning about what a man thinks he has is aimed at the person who is sure he is fine.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The light Jesus has given his disciples is meant to be seen, and in the end everything hidden, the truth of the gospel and the secrets of every heart, will come to light.

Lighting a lamp. Placed here on purpose: a disciple let into the secrets of the kingdom might conclude that they are his to keep. A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick, holding perhaps an hour or two of light, and you light it to give light, not to hide it.

Or puts it under a bed. A jar would smother it, and a bed would catch fire: both destroy the light while pretending to keep it.

On a stand. Not so that the lamp may be admired, but so that those who enter from outside can see (11:33; Matthew 5:14–16). The secrets given to the disciples (v. 10) are to be put where strangers can see by them.

Nothing is hidden. This cuts two ways. First, a promise: the truth now partly hidden in parables will be fully revealed, and the gospel entrusted to twelve men in Galilee will not stay in the house, as Acts records.

Nor is anything secret. The second edge: everything hidden in human hearts will be exposed at the judgment (12:2–3; 1 Corinthians 4:5). There is no permanently private life. For anyone hiding something, that is terrifying; for anyone who has been slandered or quietly written off, it is a deep comfort.

A light for the Gentiles. The lamp has a name in Luke. When old Simeon took the baby in his arms in the temple, he called him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (2:32). The light hidden for now in parables is Christ himself, and the stand it was always meant for is the world: repentance and forgiveness of sins are to be proclaimed in his name to all nations (24:47). The disciples are not the light; they are the household that must not cover it.

What if I have something hidden? Bring it into the light now, before God, and where needed before those you have wronged. The light that will expose everything is the light in which there is forgiveness: if we walk in the light, “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7). What is confessed to God is covered by Christ and will not be held against you on that day. The secrets that destroy are the ones we keep; everything shameful in a Christian’s life has already been dealt with at the cross.

In everyday life. The light is Christ, already lit; your part is not to cover him. Find the one place in your week where no one knows you are a Christian, at work, at the gym, among a set of friends, and ask what it would look like this week to take the jar off.
verseByVerse.note: A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
How you hear matters, because truth received and obeyed grows, while truth neglected is lost, even the truth you think you have.

Take care then how you hear. Not what you hear but how: with an honest heart, holding it fast, obeying it. Hearing is a moral act, with consequences.

To the one who has. It sounds like the rich getting richer, but Jesus is describing how understanding works: it grows by being used. A man who obeys what he has understood finds the next thing opened to him.

From the one who has not. A man who receives and does nothing loses even the ability to receive, not by an arbitrary penalty but as an unused muscle wastes away. Neglected truth is lost.

Even what he thinks that he has. Luke alone has this sharp phrase; Mark says simply “what he has”. Luke’s version is more disturbing: the man never really had what he supposed. He has been carrying a receipt for something that is not in the vault. The rock and thorn soils find that out in the drought and at the harvest. There is mercy in being told now, while he can still come and ask.

More will be given. In Luke the “more” is Christ himself, opened ever more fully. The disciples who listen so slowly keep listening, and at the end the risen Lord walks with two of them and, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, interprets to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (24:27). And the one from whom even what he thinks he has is taken is the man who has the Scriptures without him: the scribes knew every line and refused to come to the one they were about (John 5:39–40).

Information is not the same as hearing. No generation has heard more than ours: sermons and podcasts follow us into the car and the gym, often at double speed. The media critic Neil Postman argued that modern communication had driven down what he called the information-action ratio: we take in a flood of information that asks nothing of us and changes nothing in us. It is easy to treat God’s word as one more stream of content, filed away and never obeyed. Jesus says that kind of hearing is not neutral; it drains away even what we thought we had. The cure is not a better technique of listening but a person worth listening to, who speaks not to inform us but to bring us home. Faith comes by hearing him (Romans 10:17), and he has never yet spoken to anyone merely to add to their knowledge.

What does good listening look like on a Sunday? Come prepared, praying that God would speak, and rested enough to listen. Listen expecting God, not merely a speaker, to address you (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Have your Bible open and test what you hear by it (Acts 17:11). Listen for yourself before you listen for others: what is this saying to me? Afterwards, talk about it, and decide on one thing to do. And keep listening when the preacher is not gifted; the seed is the word, not the sower.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. And he was told, 'Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.' But he answered them, 'My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ true family are those who hear God’s word and do it, and this widens his family rather than rejecting his mother.

His mother and his brothers. Mark names four of the brothers, James, Joses (Joseph), Judas and Simon, and mentions sisters (Mark 6:3). At this stage, “not even his brothers believed in him” (John 7:5). They came to faith only after the resurrection (Acts 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:7), and James became a leader of the church in Jerusalem.

Why had they come? Luke is discreet; Mark is not, and records that his family set out to seize him, because people were saying he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21, 31–35). Whatever exactly is happening at the edge of this crowd, it is not a social visit.

My mother and my brothers. Not a put-down of his mother: he does not disown his family, and from the cross he provided for her (John 19:26–27). He redefines the family, in public, at the very moment the claim of blood was pressed on him: a new family bound not by blood but by obedience to God’s word. It is the good soil of verse 15 given a family name, and it echoes the wise builder at the end of the sermon, who hears Jesus’ words and does them (6:47–49).

Not a rejection of Mary. It is an inclusion of everybody else on the terms Mary met first. The woman who said, “let it be to me according to your word” (1:38), is the founding member of the family, and even her blessedness lies chiefly in hearing and keeping God’s word (11:27–28).

The family he makes. Only someone who can make a family by his word has the right to say who his mother is. Jesus is founding a household around himself. The brothers who thought him mad are later found among the praying disciples in Jerusalem (Acts 1:14), in the family by hearing, like everyone else. Their blood tie gave them no head start. The eternal Son of God is not ashamed to call his people brothers (Hebrews 2:11); he adopts people with no claim of blood through his own blood. So doing the word is not the entrance fee into the family; it is the family likeness. A child does not obey in order to become a child, but a child who truly hears his father begins to look like him (James 1:22–25).

Does following Jesus mean neglecting my family? No. Scripture commands us to honour father and mother (Ephesians 6:2) and says that anyone who does not provide for his own household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). The passage teaches priority, not neglect: when family claims and Christ’s claims collide, Christ comes first (14:26). For many, especially converts from other faiths, that collision is painful, and the promise is precious: they gain, in the church, mothers and brothers and sisters a hundredfold (Mark 10:29–30).

In everyday life. Grace has made you Jesus’ family, and hearing and doing God’s word is its likeness. Your elder Brother did his Father’s will perfectly in your place, and his obedience is counted as yours. Who in your church has no family nearby, or a family that has rejected them for Christ? Invite them to your table this month. And if your own relatives do not yet believe, keep loving them as Jesus loved his brothers: patiently, until the day they too may come in.

Who were these brothers? The natural reading is that they were Mary’s later children, Jesus’ half-brothers (compare 2:7, where Jesus is her firstborn son; Mark 6:3). Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians, holding that Mary remained a virgin, read them as cousins, since the Hebrew and Aramaic word for brother can be broad, or as Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage; some early Protestants, Luther and Zwingli among them, also thought Mary remained a virgin, out of reverence for her. But Scripture never suggests either reading, and the plain one is the more likely.

parallels.desc: blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The one whose word the disciples are learning to hear is Lord of creation. At his own command they set out across the lake, and a storm brings experienced fishermen to the edge of drowning while he sleeps (vv. 22–23). He rebukes the wind and waves as only God does, and the sea goes flat (v. 24). Then he asks where their faith is, and they ask the question the chapter is built around: “Who then is this?” (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology:
In the Old Testament only the LORD commands the wind and the sea: he stills the storm and hushes the waves (Psalm 107:29; compare Psalm 89:9; Job 38:8–11). The disciples’ question has one answer (see the note on v. 25).

The sleep matters as much as the stilling (see the note on vv. 22–23): the one who will tell his disciples not to be anxious (12:22) is at rest in a sinking boat.
verseByVerse.examples:
The disciples have Jesus in the boat and are still terrified. That is an honest picture of discipleship: knowing who he is in general is not the same as trusting him in a particular crisis. In a crisis, faith is more often mislaid than lost.

The story is less about their failure than about the one in the boat with them. He did not scold them for waking him; he stilled the storm, and then asked where their faith had gone, to help them grow.

verseByVerse.quote: One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, 'Let us go across to the other side of the lake.' So they set out, and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Obeying Jesus took the disciples straight into a deadly storm, while he, worn out, slept in perfect peace. With this crossing Luke begins four miracles over nature, demons, disease and death (8:22–56) that show who it is the disciples have been hearing.

Let us go across. The trip was Jesus’ idea, not a detour: they are in that boat, in that weather, because he told them to go, and he intended them to reach the other side. Obedience put them in the storm.

As they sailed he fell asleep. The only time the Gospels tell us that Jesus slept, after a day of preaching to crowds. The Son of Man who will soon say he has nowhere to lay his head (9:58) finds a place in the stern of a fishing boat; Mark adds that it was on the cushion (Mark 4:38). And he sleeps in peace, trusting his Father: “In peace I will both lie down and sleep” (Psalm 4:8).

A windstorm came down. The Sea of Galilee lies about 700 feet (210 m) below sea level in a basin ringed by hills, with ravines funnelling down to the water from the heights to the east. Cold air drops into the warm basin without warning, and the shallow lake goes from flat to dangerous in minutes.

In danger. The men making this verdict include four commercial fishermen who had worked this water all their lives. They have concluded they are going to drown. Sometimes fear is simply an accurate reading of the danger.

Asleep, and still holding the sea. He slept in the storm because he was truly man, sharing our weakness; he stilled it because he was truly God. And the one who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4): even asleep in the stern, the Son of God had never stopped holding the sea.

If I am obeying God, why am I in a storm? Because obedience does not exempt us from storms; sometimes it leads us into them. Paul was shipwrecked on a voyage God had appointed (Acts 27). A storm is not proof that you have taken a wrong turn; it may be the very path on which Christ means to show you who he is. The question is not whether storms will come, but who is in the boat with you.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden violent storms are common.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went and woke him, saying, 'Master, Master, we are perishing!' And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the disciples’ cry Jesus orders the wind and waves to stop, and they obey him at once, as they obey only God.

Master, Master, we are perishing! The doubled address is the sound of men shaking somebody awake, and the verdict is present tense: it is happening. Luke’s version is gentler than Mark’s: “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” (Mark 4:38).

They wake him. Underneath the panic, they do one right thing: they go to the back of the boat, not only to the oars. It is not much of a faith, but it is pointed in exactly the right direction, which is very often what faith looks like at three in the morning.

He rebuked the wind. Luke has used the verb of the demon in the synagogue (4:35) and of a fever (4:39). Jesus speaks to the storm as a master to a disobedient servant; there is no prayer, as a prophet would have prayed, but an order.

A calm. When a wind drops, the swell normally runs on for hours. Here wind and water stop in the same instant, and the boat sits still on a mirror with twelve soaked men in it. What they asked for was rescue; what they received was a sight of who he is.

Jesus does what God does. In the Scriptures these men learned as boys, exactly one person speaks to the sea like that. The LORD “rebuked the Red Sea, and it became dry” (Psalm 106:9); at his rebuke the waters fled (Psalm 104:7); he shut in the sea with doors and said, “Thus far shall you come, and no farther” (Job 38:8–11). The same rebuke has silenced a demon, a fever and now the sea: he is Lord over every disorder, in a soul, a body and the world itself. And they had just woken him up.

Will Jesus always calm my storm? Not always in the way we ask. Sometimes he stills the storm; sometimes he stills his child in it and carries him through; sometimes he brings him home through it. Paul’s thorn was not removed, and many martyrs were not rescued. But this story shows what is always true: nothing in your storm is beyond his command, and you are never in the boat alone. Cry out to him: he hears, and he will bring you to the other side he promised.

parallels.desc: he made the storm be still

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, 'Where is your faith?' And they were afraid, and they marveled, saying to one another, 'Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks where their trust has gone, and his command over the sea leaves the disciples asking who he can be. They have met the Lord of creation in their own boat.

Where is your faith? Gentler than it looks in English. He does not say, “Why have you no faith?” He asks where it has gone, which assumes they have some, mislaid rather than absent. That is the ordinary condition of most believers in most crises, named here without contempt: not an accusation but a search.

What he is not rebuking. Not their fear of the storm, nor their waking him. What has gone missing is the conclusion they should have drawn from what they had already seen. His word, “Let us go across to the other side”, should have been enough. They had watched him command a demon and a fever, and a dead man sit up at a town gate. The storm found them not ignorant, but not applying what they knew.

Afraid, and they marveled. They were more frightened after the storm stopped than during it: the wind had threatened their lives, but this upset all their ideas of who he was. So it is whenever sinful people come close to the holy. Isaiah saw the Lord and cried that he was lost (Isaiah 6:5); Peter, in a boat on this same lake, fell at Jesus’ knees and begged him to depart, because he was a sinful man (5:8). The fear in the boat is not a failure of faith but the right response of creatures when God comes near.

Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him? The question this whole Gospel exists to answer, asked aloud by the men closest to him in a wet boat on a flat sea. Luke leaves it hanging until Peter answers it (9:20). The sea does not negotiate; it has drowned better sailors than these. And it heard a tired man speak from the back of a small boat, and it lay down. Only one has ever been obeyed like that, and he had been asleep a few feet away the whole time. These men had very likely known Psalm 107 since childhood: “then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress; he made the storm be still” (Psalm 107:28–29). They are with the Lord himself.

How do I find my faith again in the storm? Faith is not a feeling you whip up but a grip on what is true. Go back to his word. He had said, “Let us go across to the other side” (v. 22). Find what he has promised you, such as “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5), and say it aloud. Remember what he has done. Recall by name the times he has carried you, and above all the cross, where he has already done the hardest thing. Cry to him. Tell him plainly that you are afraid, as the disciples did. Do the next thing. Bail the water, make the call, keep rowing: faith and oars are not rivals. And see why he can be trusted. Timothy Keller, in King’s Cross, pointed out that this scene echoes Jonah, who slept in a boat in a storm and was thrown into the sea so that the sailors might live. Jesus is the greater Jonah, who on the cross went down into the ultimate storm, the judgment of God against sin, so that his people would never have to face it. If he did not abandon you there, he will not abandon you here.

Is fear always wrong for a Christian? No. The disciples’ first fear (of drowning) was realism; their second (of him) was the beginning of wisdom. What Jesus questions is faith gone missing, forgetting who is in the boat, and the answer to sinful fear is to fear God more. “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you” (Psalm 56:3): the psalmist is afraid and trusting in the same breath.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–39 — Jesus Heals a Man with a Demon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No bondage is beyond Jesus’ power, and no one is too far gone for his mercy. On a Gentile shore he meets a man stripped of clothes, home and self (vv. 26–27). The legion of demons who hold him know exactly who Jesus is and can only beg (vv. 28–31); their destruction of the herd of pigs shows what they had been doing to the man (vv. 32–33). The townspeople find him clothed, sane and at Jesus’ feet, and in fear they ask Jesus to leave (vv. 34–37). The freed man is sent home to tell what God has done for him (vv. 38–39).
verseByVerse.theology:
This deliverance happens in Gentile territory, to a Gentile man: the kingdom of God does not stop at Israel’s borders. He is the Gentile counterpart of the man in the Capernaum synagogue (4:33), freed by the same word.

The restored man sits at Jesus’ feet, where a disciple sits (see the note on vv. 34–37).
verseByVerse.examples:
The townspeople are a warning about valuing what we can count over what we cannot control (see the note on vv. 34–37).

The man’s request to follow, and Jesus’ refusal, is a call many believers know: go back to the people who knew you before (see the note on vv. 38–39).

verseByVerse.quote: Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus crosses into Gentile country and goes straight to a man the devil had stripped of clothing, home and every human tie. No one is too far gone for him.

The country of the Gerasenes. Gentile territory: the region of the Decapolis, east of the lake, Greek-speaking, with pigs on the hillsides, so not Jewish farming country. Luke explains “opposite Galilee” for readers who did not know the geography.

No clothes. Only Luke mentions the nakedness: the loss of the most basic mark of human dignity, and for a long time it was his settled condition.

Among the tombs. No house: no address, no household, no place at anybody’s table. Tombs were caves cut into the hillside, to a Jew the most unclean of places, and to anyone a sign that he lives among the dead because the living will not have him. Here is Satan’s work: degradation, isolation, uncleanness, death.

Liberty to the captives. At Nazareth Jesus read that he was anointed “to proclaim liberty to the captives” (4:18) and reminded his hometown that Elijah was sent to a widow of Sidon and Elisha cleansed Naaman the Syrian (4:25–27), and they tried to throw him off a cliff. Here he acts out that sermon: he crosses a storm to a Gentile shore and goes straight to the most bound man on it, a small preview of Acts, where the gospel goes out to the Gentiles.

One man or two? Luke describes one man, and so does Mark; Matthew says there were two (Matthew 8:28). Neither denies the other: Matthew adds a second man; he does not subtract one. Mark and Luke keep the camera on the one who spoke, who was called Legion and was sent home with a story to tell. The same happens at Jericho, where Matthew has two blind men and Mark names only Bartimaeus.

Was this man demon-possessed, or mentally ill? Luke, a physician, distinguishes healings from exorcisms (4:40–41), and here the demons speak and are cast out. Possession is real, and the New Testament does not say it has ceased. But most mental illness has ordinary causes and needs ordinary care. Christians should neither see demons behind every illness nor deny that the devil works. The modern assumption that nothing personal and evil stands behind the world’s darkness is itself a belief, not a finding; Luke the doctor knew a fever from a demon and records both.

Could a believer end up like the man from the tombs? No. Once Christ claims a person, the ownership has changed hands for good. The Holy Spirit dwells in every believer (1 Corinthians 6:19), who is sealed by him (Ephesians 1:13) and has been rescued from the domain of darkness (Colossians 1:13). A Christian can be tempted, attacked and deceived, and must resist the devil (1 Peter 5:8–9), but need never fear being taken over by him. The one who lives in you is greater than the one who is in the world (1 John 4:4).

In everyday life. Every town has someone everyone has given up on: the addict, the man who sleeps rough, the relative no one mentions. Jesus crossed a stormy lake for a man like that. Pray for that person, and ask what step of love you could take. Use the help God gives through the church and a biblical counsellor, who will also ask for a medical check-up, and bring the bondages no programme has broken to the one before whom every bondage gives way.

Textual note: Gerasenes, Gadarenes or Gergesenes? Manuscripts vary, and the likeliest answer is that the spot was Gergesa (perhaps modern Kursi), where the hills drop sharply to the shore, while Gerasa and Gadara were the well-known cities whose districts reached that coast.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Gadarenes, some Gergesenes. The region lay on the east side of the lake, Gentile country. Tombs were unclean places.

verseByVerse.quote: When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, 'What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.' For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The demons recognise Jesus as the Son of God and their Judge, and all they can do is beg.

He fell down before him. The demon recognises its master and submits: the posture of worship, forced out of an enemy.

What have you to do with me? A stock formula of confrontation, literally “what to me and to you?”, the ancient equivalent of “what do you want with me?” The same words came out of the demon in the Capernaum synagogue (4:34).

Jesus, Son of the Most High God. “Son of the Most High” is the title Gabriel used to Mary (1:32). “Most High God” is a title often used by or to Gentiles for the God of Israel (Genesis 14:18–20; Daniel 3:26; Acts 16:17). The demons know exactly who Jesus is.

I beg you, do not torment me. The first of four beggings in this scene, three of them by the demons. They know a day of judgment is fixed for them; Matthew records them saying, “Have you come here to torment us before the time?” (Matthew 8:29).

Chains and shackles. Luke adds a case history, as a doctor would: “for many a time it had seized him”. The town had tried chains and guards again and again.

Driven into the desert. The demon drove him, as a herdsman drives cattle, and each failed restraint sent him further out. Chains can stop a man harming anybody; they cannot give him back his mind.

The Judge has come as Deliverer. The demons speak of torment because they know who will judge them. The Father “has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), and the demons recognise the Judge before the court has sat; this carpenter is the one appointed to judge the living and the dead (Acts 10:42). But the Judge has come first as Deliverer. He will bear judgment himself at the cross, for sinners, not for demons, and on this beach he spends his authority not on sentencing the man’s captors but on freeing their captive. Heaven named him Son of the Most High before he was born, and now hell names him the same on a Gentile beach. Heaven and hell agree on who he is; only men argue. What the demons confess in terror the redeemed will confess in joy (Philippians 2:10–11), and the one before whom darkness trembles is the one under whose wings his people shelter.

Should Christians fear demons? No. This passage is written to cure that fear. The demons are the ones who are terrified; they fall down, beg, and know their doom. Christ has disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them at the cross (Colossians 2:15). Take the devil seriously and resist him, firm in the faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), but never be fascinated by him or afraid of him; trust the one before whom he trembles.
verseByVerse.note: “Most High God” is a title often used by or to Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then asked him, 'What is your name?' And he said, 'Legion,' for many demons had entered him. And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus speaks to the man as a person, and the answer reveals an army of demons occupying him, who now beg not to be sent to their prison.

Jesus then asked him, What is your name? The only question Jesus asks in the encounter, and not for information: a name is what a person has, and this man has not been addressed as a person in years. The town called him a danger; the tombs were his address. Jesus asks him who he is.

Legion. The answer is horrifying on two counts. A Roman legion numbered about 5,000 to 6,000 soldiers. Literal or not, a legion is not a crowd but an occupying force: organised, under orders, in possession of ground.

For many demons had entered him. The second horror is who answers: the question was put to the man, and the occupation speaks. He has been so comprehensively taken over that when asked for his own name he gives theirs. There is no “I” left to reply.

Not into the abyss. Only Luke mentions the abyss (abyssos), the deep: in the Greek Old Testament it renders the waters of Genesis 1, and in later Jewish writing and in Revelation it is the bottomless pit, the prison of rebel spirits before their final judgment (Romans 10:7; Revelation 9:1–2; 20:1–3). They know he can send them there: the army that had occupied a soul for years begs for terms the moment he sets foot on the beach.

The real occupation. Israel longed for a Messiah who would drive the legions out of the land. Jesus meets a legion on this beach, and it is not Roman. Here is the occupation that really held the human race, and here is the King who really breaks it, not with a sword but with a word. Zechariah had sung of salvation from our enemies (1:71), and on a Gentile shore Luke shows how deep those enemies went and how complete the rescue would be.

Why did Jesus not send them to the abyss at once? Because the time of their final judgment had not yet come (Matthew 8:29). Christ defeated Satan decisively at the cross, but the final sentence will be carried out at his return, when the devil and his angels are thrown into the lake of fire (Matthew 25:41; Revelation 20:10). Until then evil is real but limited, able to do only what God permits (Job 1:12), so we must still resist the devil, and can do so with confidence.

In everyday life. The Lord who will shut Satan in the abyss gave a ruined man back his own name. You too have a name, given by him. Whatever has defined you, the addiction, the diagnosis, the failure, the label others have put on you, it is not who you are in Christ. He “calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3).
verseByVerse.note: A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers. The abyss is the place where evil spirits are confined.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus lets the demons go into the pigs, and their destruction of the herd shows what they had been doing to the man and how completely he is free.

A herd of pigs. Pigs were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:7); Mark says about two thousand (Mark 5:13). Even demons need Jesus’ permission.

Who does the drowning. Jesus grants a request; it is the demons who stampede the herd to its death, doing to a herd in a moment what they had been doing to one man for years. The destruction is theirs, and it unmasks them.

Into the lake. It showed that the demons had left the man, how many there were, and what they had wanted to do to him: the town had called it madness, and now has a hillside of evidence. And unclean spirits went with unclean animals into the deep.

The arithmetic. Sceptics say the drowned herd shows Jesus cared nothing for livelihoods or animals. The loss was real. But one human being, made in the image of God, somebody’s son, is pulled out of a living death; a herd of pigs is lost. He will say in this Gospel that a man is worth more than many sparrows (12:7), and the scale holds here. This is not carelessness of animals (Proverbs 12:10), but a judgment that one man was worth the loss, and it forced the district to decide which mattered more, the man or the pigs.

What a man is worth to him. The town weighed the man against the herd and found the herd heavier. Jesus weighed them the other way, and the cross shows how far his scale tips. One man’s freedom cost the owners a herd of pigs; the freedom of all his people cost the Son of God his own life. “You were ransomed”, Peter writes, “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Nobody values a human being as highly as the one who paid for him. Ask where your own spending of time and money shows that you value things more than people.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the law.

verseByVerse.quote: When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. And those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
