The freed man sits clothed and sane at Jesus’ feet, yet the townspeople, frightened by such power, ask Jesus to leave, and he goes.

What had happened. Every term answers something in verse 27. He had worn no clothes: he is clothed. He had lived among the tombs, driven into the desert: he is sitting. He had been out of his mind: he is in his right mind.

Sitting at the feet of Jesus. The posture of a disciple: where Mary of Bethany will sit (10:39), and where Paul says he sat under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). He has not simply been emptied of demons but given a new place, which matters, because an unclean spirit returns to a house left swept and empty (11:24–26).

Clothed, and in his right mind. No longer naked (v. 27); someone had given him clothes, perhaps from among the disciples. “In his right mind” is sōphronounta: sober, self-possessed, sane, at peace.

Healed. “Healed” (esōthē) is literally saved: the whole man, body, mind and soul. The word runs through the rest of the chapter.

They asked him to depart. The man they had chained and left in the graveyard is sitting in his right mind, and they want the one who did it to leave. Luke names one reason and implies another. The stated one is fear: something has come that they cannot manage, and a madman can at least be chained. The unstated one is the hillside, and the herd in the lake that somebody has to account for. They preferred their pigs, their peace and their way of life to the presence of Jesus, and many still ask him to leave for the same reasons.

He returned. Jesus does not argue or press. He crossed a dangerous lake for one man, and when the district asked him to go, he went. He will not force himself on a community that has counted the cost and decided against him.

A patience that outlasts our refusals. Look at the man at his feet: clothed, quiet, in his right mind. Christ does not tidy the surface; he gives a man back himself and a place at his feet. The same Lord would one day be led out of Jerusalem to a cross, and answer by praying for those who put him there (23:34). There is a patience in Christ that outlasts our refusals, and the man at his feet is what that patience makes of anyone it will not give up.

Can someone ask Jesus to leave for good? Jesus is patient, and he came back to the Decapolis later (Mark 7:31–37). But the Gerasenes had one visit and sent him away, and Scripture warns against hardening your heart today (Hebrews 3:15). If you sense Christ calling and are inclined to send him off because he is costly, do not wait. But if you fear you have already sent him away for good, take heart from the fear itself: the Gerasenes were glad to see him go, and you are not. He has never yet turned away anyone who comes to him (John 6:37).
verseByVerse.note: Sitting at someone’s feet was the posture of a disciple.

parallels.desc: Mary sat at the Lord’s feet

verseByVerse.quote: The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, 'Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.' And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The freed man longs to go with Jesus, but Jesus sends him home to tell what God has done for him, and he tells everyone what Jesus has done.

He begged to be with him. The fourth begging in the passage, and the first from a human being. Now the man begs to go with him, as the redeemed long to be with their Redeemer. It is the only request in the scene that is refused.

A reasonable request. His neighbours had just told Jesus to leave, and everyone there knew what he had been. The boat was leaving with twelve men who had left everything to follow, and he wanted a place among them.

Return to your home. Jesus sent him back: to relatives who had watched him deteriorate, to a town that had chained him and then given up. That is a harder road than the boat.

Declare how much God has done. With perhaps an hour’s instruction, he is sent not to argue but to tell what happened to him, and he becomes, in effect, the first missionary to the Gentiles of the Decapolis. In Jewish territory Jesus often told people to keep quiet; here he sends the man to tell (on why, see the note on vv. 54–56). He had no training and no theology, only a before and an after that a whole district had witnessed.

How much Jesus had done. He was told to speak about God; he spoke about Jesus. Luke sets the two side by side without comment, because what Jesus did, God did: he is the one the demons called “Son of the Most High God” (v. 28). Mark adds that everyone marvelled (Mark 5:20), and when Jesus later returned to the Decapolis, people brought the sick to him (Mark 7:31–37), perhaps in part the fruit of this man’s testimony.

How do I know whether to stay or go? Most Christians are called, like this man, to serve Christ where they already are: in their family, their street, their workplace. Some are called to leave for the gospel, and the church should test and send them gladly (Acts 13:1–3). Being with Jesus is not only a matter of geography; he goes with those he sends. If you are unsure, ask what doors God has opened, seek the counsel of your church, and remember that home is often the hardest and most fruitful mission field there is.

What should I say when I tell people about Jesus? Start where this man started, with what the Lord has done for you. Tell honestly what you were, what Christ did, and what he is to you now (1 Peter 3:15). Then point beyond yourself to him: who he is, that he died for sinners and rose again, and that he receives all who come to him. Your story opens the door; his story is the message.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–56 — Jesus Heals a Woman and Raises Jairus's Daughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus’ word brings wholeness and life where every human hope has run out. Luke folds one story inside another. Jairus, a synagogue ruler, pleads for his dying only daughter (vv. 40–42). On the way a woman unclean for twelve years touches Jesus’ cloak and is healed, and he stops to find her, so that her restoration is public and she is called “Daughter” (vv. 43–48). Then word comes that the girl has died: Jesus tells Jairus not to fear but to believe (vv. 49–50), calls her death a sleep (vv. 51–53), and raises her with a word and his hand (vv. 54–56).
verseByVerse.theology:
Each story interprets the other: the delay has not exhausted Jesus’ power or his compassion, and the messenger’s “too late” is not too late for the Lord of life.

When Jesus says she is not dead but sleeping, he is changing what death means for those who belong to him (see the note on vv. 51–53).

The fringe she touched was probably the tassel of Numbers 15:38–40 (see the note on vv. 43–44). Some have linked it with Malachi 4:2, where the sun of righteousness rises with healing in its wings, since the Hebrew word for wings can mean the corners of a garment.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman came when every other resource was gone, and Jesus commended her faith aloud (see the note on vv. 47–48).

Jairus did everything right, and then came the delay and the news that it was over. On what Only believe asks of such a man, see the note on vv. 49–50.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus' feet, he implored him to come to his house, for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A respected synagogue ruler throws himself down at Jesus’ feet in public, pleading for his only daughter, who is dying.

The crowd welcomed him. One shore had just asked him to leave; the other has been waiting for the boat to come back.

Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue. A ruler of the synagogue was a lay official who organised the services, invited readers and preachers, and carried much of the community’s respect. In a Galilean town he was somebody, close to the circles watching Jesus with growing hostility (5:17; compare 13:14).

Falling at Jesus’ feet. He goes down in the road, in front of people who know exactly who he is. Suffering does that, and it is not always a cruelty: it strips away the pride and caution that keep us from him. He came not because his theology changed but because his daughter was dying and there was nowhere else.

An only daughter. Only Luke says “only”, as with the widow’s son at Nain (7:12) and the boy of 9:38: he notices the depth of grief when an only child is lost. About twelve, in that culture, is the edge of womanhood, when a girl might soon be betrothed. And twelve links her with the woman who had been ill for twelve years (v. 43): the girl had lived as long as the woman had suffered.

The people pressed around him. “Pressed” (synepnigon) means crushed, nearly suffocated: the same word as the thorns that choked the seed (v. 14).

At his feet, three times. Luke keeps putting people in the same place. The freed man sat at the feet of Jesus (v. 35); Jairus falls at his feet (v. 41); the healed woman will fall down before him (v. 47). A Gentile madman, a synagogue ruler and an unclean woman all end up on the same ground. These are the feet of the Lord, and the kneeling begins among the desperate, long before the proud get there.

What if I only come to Jesus because I am desperate? Then you are in good company. Jairus came because his daughter was dying, the woman because every doctor had failed, the prodigal because he was starving. Jesus never asked anyone whether their motives were pure enough before he helped them. Need is not a bad reason to come to Christ; it is the usual one. What matters is that you came to him, and that you stay. Many who came to him for a healing found the Healer.
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services and cared for its building.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman shut out of ordinary life by twelve years of bleeding reaches secretly for the edge of Jesus’ cloak, and is healed at once.

Twelve years. It was probably continuous menstrual bleeding, and it was far more than a medical condition. Under the law, a woman with a chronic discharge was in continuing ritual uncleanness, and anything she lay or sat on, and anyone who touched those things, became unclean (Leviticus 15:25–27). Twelve years unable to worship at the temple, cut off from normal contact, every human touch carrying a consequence for the other person. If she was married when it began, she may well not be now. And it is not her fault.

All her living on physicians. Luke, a doctor, records the failure of his own profession without flinching, but he is gentler than Mark, who adds that she had suffered much under many physicians and had only grown worse (Mark 5:26). Luke says simply that she “could not be healed by anyone”.

She came up behind him. Secretly, and it had to be. Unclean in a dense crowd, she believes her touch will defile a rabbi.

The fringe of his garment. The fringe (kraspedon) is the tassel the law told Israelite men to wear at the corners of their cloaks, to remind them of God’s commandments (Numbers 15:38–40): the furthest edge of him that a person crouching in a crowd could reach. Some believed the tassels of a holy man had power (Matthew 14:36). Her faith was mixed with superstition, but it was faith in Jesus.

Immediately. Luke’s verb means literally that it stood still, perhaps a doctor’s word for a flow stopping.

In Christ, the clean cleanses the unclean. Under the law, the unclean defiled the clean; here the traffic runs the other way: instead of her uncleanness passing to Jesus, his healing passed to her. He took our uncleanness upon himself at the cross, bearing our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24), so that power and wholeness could flow out from him to all who reach for him.

Does Jesus accept a faith that is mixed with superstition? Yes, if it is reaching for him. She thought the power was in the tassel, but Jesus healed her first and corrected her theology afterwards, in front of the crowd: not the cloth, but your faith in me. So he still deals with weak believers. A trembling, half-informed faith in Christ saves; a well-informed faith in anything else does not. And he will not leave a weak faith where he found it.

In everyday life. If you have exhausted every other remedy, and spent all you had, come to him now, even if all you can manage is the edge of the garment. And remember the person in your church who has been sick or isolated for years.

Textual note. Some manuscripts omit the words about her spending all her living on physicians.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the words about the physicians. Her condition made her ritually unclean. The fringe was the tassel the law required on a garment.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said, 'Who was it that touched me?' When all denied it, Peter said, 'Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!' But Jesus said, 'Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stops to find the one person whose touch was faith, because he gives himself to people, not only cures.

Who was it that touched me? On his way to a dying child, he stops the whole procession to ask a question he already knows the answer to, because he wants her to come forward, for her own sake.

The crowds are pressing. Everyone denied it, presumably even the woman at first, and Peter’s exasperation was reasonable: everyone is touching you.

Power has gone out. Many pressed on him; one touched him in faith, and the distinction is the point. “Power” (dynamis) is the power of God, and Luke has used it before of the healing that flowed from him (5:17; 6:19). Something went out of him, and he felt it go. The Lord who is surrounded by the worship of heaven and the noise of the whole earth notices the faintest reaching out of a frightened believer.

Why stop? She has what she came for, and the child is dying up the road. He stops because a healing is not the same as a person, and he has not come merely to hand out cures. She had tried to take the gift and remain invisible, which is entirely understandable, and it would have left her as she was in every way but the physical: unnoticed, as far as her town knew still unclean, nobody’s daughter. He will not let her have it that way. He will bring her to say it aloud and then say something to her she can carry for the rest of her life, and he holds up a dying child’s father in the road to do it.

Does power going out of him mean Jesus has limited power? No. Jesus is fully God, and his divine power is infinite. The phrase tells us that the healing was a real act of his, consciously given, not a magic that leaked from his clothes without his knowledge; he perceived it because he is its source. He did not dispense blessings like a machine: every mercy we receive from Christ is given by him, knowingly, to us.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. And he said to her, 'Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus brings the healed woman to speak in public so that she is restored to her people, then calls her daughter and sends her away whole.

She came trembling. Hiding has failed, and she is shaking, not because she doubts the healing but because of what she has done: an unclean woman has touched a rabbi in public and taken something without asking, in front of a crowd and a synagogue ruler.

In the presence of all. Only Luke has this phrase. Twelve years of it, out loud, to a street full of strangers.

Why did Jesus make her do this? So that everyone would know she was clean. Her healing had been secret; her restoration had to be public. The crowd has heard from her own mouth that she is well, so she can go back to worship, to her family’s kitchen and to ordinary human contact, and nobody can say otherwise. And she would know that she had been healed not by magic but by Jesus, through faith. He did not merely stop the bleeding; he put her back among her people.

Daughter. Luke shows Jesus bringing the excluded back into Abraham’s family with a single word. He will call a woman bent double for eighteen years “a daughter of Abraham” (13:16), and a despised tax collector “a son of Abraham” (19:9). Here, for a woman nobody could touch for twelve years, the word is simply “daughter”, spoken as his own claim on her.

Your faith has made you well. “Made you well” (sesōken) means has saved you, body and soul. Her faith did not manufacture the power; that came out of him. It was simply the hand that reached. She understood little and came in secret and afraid, and he calls it faith and commends it in public.

Go in peace. As to the sinful woman (7:50). Behind the Greek word for peace stands the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, everything put back in its right place. She came for one thing and he gave her the lot: her body, her standing, her place among people, and a name to be called by.

Do I have to tell people what Jesus has done for me? Not necessarily in a crowded street, but Christ calls his people to confess him openly (Romans 10:10): in baptism, the public declaration that you belong to Christ, and then in a life of speaking of him. It is not a test you must pass to be saved, but what Christ draws out of those he has saved. Like this woman, you may tremble. He will meet you there with peace.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, 'Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.' But Jesus on hearing this answered him, 'Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When news comes that the girl has died, Jesus tells her father not to fear but to keep trusting him, and promises that she will be well.

While he was still speaking. The timing is unbearable, and Luke means it to be. Jairus had come while there was still time; then Jesus stopped for the woman, and while she was telling her story his daughter died. From where Jairus stood, it must have looked as though the delay killed her. That must be said plainly, because many lives feel like that, and pious words that hurry past it help no one. But Jesus had a greater purpose.

Do not trouble the Teacher. A teacher can heal the sick, but not raise the dead: kindly meant, entirely rational advice to let the rabbi get on.

Do not fear; only believe. Jesus answers at once. In Mark the verb means keep on believing (Mark 5:36); Luke gives it as a single plain command: believe. Jesus is not telling him to generate enough faith to raise the dead; that reading crushes bereaved people, and it is not what the sentence says. He is telling a man who has just been told it is over to keep holding on to the person beside him for another ten minutes. And the woman’s healing was for Jairus too: he has just watched, at his own cost, what this man does for someone who had run out of options.

And she will be well. Only Luke adds this. “Well” (sōthēsetai) means saved, the same word as verse 48: the promise of Jesus, given after the worst news.

Only one voice has been proved right. Death sends its messengers to every house: it is over, do not trouble him any more. Only one voice has answered them and been proved right: he went himself into the house of death, and on the third morning the women were asked why they sought the living among the dead (24:5). Because he lives, his word to Jairus is his word at every believer’s graveside: “Do not fear; only believe.” And when you are the one bringing bad news to someone, bring Christ’s word with it.

Why does God seem to delay when I pray? Scripture never pretends that God’s delays are easy; the psalms cry, “How long, O LORD?” (Psalm 13:1). But the story of Jairus, like that of Lazarus (John 11:6, 15), shows that his delays are never neglect. He was not too late for Jairus; he was exactly on time for a greater miracle. Not every prayer is answered as Jairus’s was; but the one who makes you wait is the same one who loves you, and he has never once been late for his own purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, 'Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.' And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls the dead girl sleeping because, for him, death is a sleep from which he can wake her; the mourners laugh because they know she is dead.

Peter and John and James. The inner three, who will also see him in glory at the transfiguration (9:28) and, in Mark, on his face in Gethsemane (Mark 14:33), now see him raise the dead. Tenderly, the parents are included: this is their daughter, not a demonstration.

Weeping and mourning. The house is full of noise: family and, it seems, professional mourners; Matthew mentions the flute players (Matthew 9:23). Mourning (ekoptonto) means beating their breasts. According to a later rabbinic rule, even a poor family was expected to provide flute players and at least one wailing woman (see mourning customs).

Not dead but sleeping. Some argue that she was only in a coma. That cannot be what Luke, a doctor, means. The messenger reported a death, mourners do not come for the unconscious, the crowd knew she was dead, and Luke writes that “her spirit returned” (v. 55). Sleep is the condition from which you are expected to get up, and in Jesus’ vocabulary that is now what death is. That is how the New Testament will go on to speak of believers who die: those who have fallen asleep (John 11:11–14; Acts 7:60; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). The last enemy has become, for his people, a bed. It is a claim about himself: the one standing in the room can wake the dead.

They laughed at him. They laughed, knowing: the derision of people who were right about the facts. Within minutes, the girl they had come to mourn got up and walked.

Does sleeping mean that the dead are unconscious? No. Jesus means that her death is not final; she will wake. The word describes the body awaiting resurrection, not the soul. Those who die in the Lord are with him at once, conscious and at rest (23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). There is no soul sleep and no purgatory: the believer’s soul goes immediately into the presence of Christ, and the body sleeps in the grave until he raises it on the last day (Westminster Confession 32.1; 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1).

In everyday life. When you stand at the grave of a believer, grieve, but with hope, and use his word: “she is not dead but sleeping”. It is not a euphemism; it is a promise. And if people laugh at your hope, do not be surprised. They laughed at him.

verseByVerse.quote: But taking her by the hand he called, saying, 'Child, arise.' And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With a touch and a word Jesus raises the girl from death, shows she is truly alive by having her fed, and refuses to make her a spectacle.

But taking her by the hand. As with the leper and the bier at Nain, he touches what the law says will defile him (Numbers 19:11), and death gives way.

Child, arise. A family word. Mark preserves it in Aramaic, Talitha cumi (Mark 5:41), the kind of phrase a mother might use in the morning: little girl, get up. The greatest power in the universe is exercised in the tone of voice used to wake a child for school.

And her spirit returned. Only Luke says this. Her spirit had left her body at death (23:46; Acts 7:59) and came back: a clear statement that she had been dead, and that the human spirit lives on after death. And she got up at once.

Something to eat. The detail that rings true, not the kind a legend-maker tends to add. Having conquered death in a Galilean bedroom, the Son of God’s first instruction is: get her something to eat. She was really alive, in a real body, and hungry. After the resurrection Jesus himself would eat to show he was not a ghost (24:41–43). The one who commands wind, abyss and grave notices that nobody has thought about her supper. After the great moments, someone has to think about the meal: be the one who notices.

Tell no one. Everyone would know she was alive, but they were not to spread the story: he refuses to be turned into a spectacle (compare 5:14).

In the flow. This raising closes the four miracles of 8:22–56 at the deepest point, and chapter 9 presses the disciples’ question until Peter answers it (9:20). A girl raised to die again points ahead to the one who will rise, never to die again (24:6; Romans 6:9).

The hand that took a dead girl’s fingers. That hand, in a Galilean bedroom, was itself nailed to a cross, laid still in a tomb and raised on the third day, and it holds “the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:18). One word from him on the last day will call every sleeping believer out of the dust, and the Lord who remembered a hungry girl’s supper will sit them down at the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Almighty over the grave, and thinking of our hunger: that is our Lord.

Can a thinking person believe this really happened? The mourners knew dead girls do not get up; that is why they laughed. The real question is whether God has come among us in Jesus; if he has, and Jesus himself rose from the dead, one girl raised in Galilee is no strain at all. Luke, a careful doctor, tells us he investigated everything from the beginning and wrote from those who were eyewitnesses (1:1–4), while people who had been in Galilee could still be asked. The deeper reluctance is often not the evidence but the cost: if this happened, Jesus has a claim on my life.

Why tell these parents to tell no one, when he told the Gerasene to declare it? The Gerasene lived in Gentile territory, where Jesus was not staying and where no crowd was waiting for a Jewish king. In Galilee, such news would bring crowds wanting a wonder-worker or a political Messiah, and Jesus’ hour had not yet come. He was not hiding his glory but guarding his mission: the full truth of who he is could be told rightly only after the cross and resurrection, and then to the ends of the earth.

Will Jesus raise my loved one who has died in him? Yes. This girl was raised to die again; what Christ promises his people is far greater. On the last day, “all who are in the tombs will hear his voice” (John 5:28–29), and those who belong to him will be raised imperishable, in bodies like his glorious body (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Philippians 3:21). The same hand that took this girl’s will take theirs. Meanwhile, their spirits are with him. Grieve for them, but grieve as one who knows that the Lord who says “arise” has never yet been disobeyed.

parallels.desc: the child’s life came into him again

8.text: <sup>1</sup> Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, <sup>2</sup> and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, <sup>3</sup> and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means. <sup>4</sup> And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable, <sup>5</sup> “A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it. <sup>6</sup> And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. <sup>7</sup> And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. <sup>8</sup> And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.” As he said these things, he called out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>9</sup> And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant, <sup>10</sup> he said, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’ <sup>11</sup> Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. <sup>12</sup> The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved. <sup>13</sup> And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away. <sup>14</sup> And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature. <sup>15</sup> As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience. <sup>16</sup> “No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. <sup>17</sup> For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light. <sup>18</sup> Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.” <sup>19</sup> Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. <sup>20</sup> And he was told, “Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.” <sup>21</sup> But he answered them, “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.” <sup>22</sup> One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, “Let us go across to the other side of the lake.” So they set out, <sup>23</sup> and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger. <sup>24</sup> And they went and woke him, saying, “Master, Master, we are perishing!” And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm. <sup>25</sup> He said to them, “Where is your faith?” And they were afraid, and they marveled, saying to one another, “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?” <sup>26</sup> Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. <sup>27</sup> When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs. <sup>28</sup> When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.” <sup>29</sup> For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.) <sup>30</sup> Jesus then asked him, “What is your name?” And he said, “Legion,” for many demons had entered him. <sup>31</sup> And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss. <sup>32</sup> Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. <sup>33</sup> Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned. <sup>34</sup> When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. <sup>35</sup> Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. <sup>36</sup> And those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. <sup>37</sup> Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned. <sup>38</sup> The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, <sup>39</sup> “Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.” And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him. <sup>40</sup> Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. <sup>41</sup> And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus' feet, he implored him to come to his house, <sup>42</sup> for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him. <sup>43</sup> And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. <sup>44</sup> She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased. <sup>45</sup> And Jesus said, “Who was it that touched me?” When all denied it, Peter said, “Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!” <sup>46</sup> But Jesus said, “Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.” <sup>47</sup> And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. <sup>48</sup> And he said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.” <sup>49</sup> While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, “Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.” <sup>50</sup> But Jesus on hearing this answered him, “Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.” <sup>51</sup> And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. <sup>52</sup> And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, “Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.” <sup>53</sup> And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead. <sup>54</sup> But taking her by the hand he called, saying, “Child, arise.” <sup>55</sup> And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. <sup>56</sup> And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.

keyVerse.quote: Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?
keyVerse.note: The disciples’ question gathers up the whole chapter. Its first half teaches how to hear the word of God; its second shows whose word it is, for wind, demons, disease and death all obey him. The rest of Luke answers the question, and the answer is the reason to take care how we hear.

8.reflection:
Look at the four soils in verses 11–15. Which of them describes how you have heard God’s word over the past year? What tends to trample, scorch or choke it in your life, and what would holding it fast look like this week?

The disciples obeyed Jesus and sailed straight into a storm (vv. 22–25). How does his question, “Where is your faith?”, speak to a storm you or someone you know is in now? What do you already know about him that the storm tempts you to forget?

The Gerasenes asked Jesus to leave a man they had given up on (vv. 34–37), and Jesus stopped a crowd for a woman nobody would touch (vv. 43–48). Who are the people your town or your church has quietly written off, and what step of love could you take toward one of them?

Jesus told Jairus, “Do not fear; only believe”, after the worst news had come (v. 50). How does this story shape the way we pray when God seems to delay, and the way we grieve for believers who have died?

9.title: The Turning Point: Cross, Glory, and the Road to Jerusalem
9.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 closes Jesus’ ministry in Galilee (4:14–9:50) and opens the long road to Jerusalem (9:51). It is the turning point of the Gospel: the question of who Jesus is receives its answer, and the answer turns at once toward the cross.

The message. Jesus is the Christ of God, the Father’s chosen Son, and his road to glory runs through the cross; so to follow him is to walk that road behind him. Herod asks, “who is this?” (v. 9); Peter answers, “The Christ of God” (v. 20); the Father says, “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” (v. 35). And what the disciples must hear above all is what nobody wants to hear: the Son of Man must suffer, be killed and be raised, and whoever comes after him takes up his cross daily.

Why it was said. Luke’s readers trusted a crucified Messiah, which the world thought absurd, and it was costing them (see the introduction). Here they see that the cross was not a disaster that overtook Jesus but the road he chose with open eyes, and that the cost of following is the cost he named at the start. And the slow, quarrelsome Twelve show that he works through people who are nowhere near ready.

How the chapter makes its case. The Twelve go out with his power and nothing in their pockets, and Herod asks who this is (vv. 1–9). Jesus feeds five thousand in the wilderness, as God once fed Israel (vv. 10–17). Peter confesses him as the Christ, and Jesus at once names the cross, his own and his followers’ (vv. 18–27). On the mountain his glory shines, Moses and Elijah speak of the exodus he will accomplish at Jerusalem, and the Father commands, “listen to him” (vv. 28–36). Below, the disciples fail a desperate father, cannot take in the second warning, argue about greatness and shut out an outsider (vv. 37–50). Then Jesus sets his face to go to Jerusalem, refuses fire on a Samaritan village, and tells three would-be followers that nothing may come before him (vv. 51–62).

Where it leads. The face that shone on the mountain is set like a flint toward Jerusalem, where it will be blindfolded and struck; the hands that fed thousands will be handed over into the hands of men. He goes not as a victim but to accomplish a new exodus. The cross is the road to the glory, and the glory shows what the cross achieves: the Son who hid his splendour for us never once looked back, so that people who look back a thousand times are counted fit for the kingdom in him.

For us. Answer his question for yourself: “But who do you say that I am?” Then follow him on his terms, self dethroned, the cross taken up today, the least welcomed, the fire refused. And when you fail as the Twelve failed, look at the one walking ahead of you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Twelve Sent Out; Herod's Perplexity
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus shares his own authority with weak men and sends them out with nothing but his word, and the news forces the question the whole chapter answers: who is this? He gives the Twelve power over demons and disease and sends them to proclaim the kingdom and to heal (vv. 1–2). They go without provisions, depending on God through those who receive them (vv. 3–4), and a town that refuses them is solemnly left to God (v. 5). They go, and the work is done everywhere (v. 6). Then the news reaches Herod, who beheaded John and now asks, “who is this about whom I hear such things?” (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology:
An apostle is one who is sent. The authority the Twelve carry is the authority Jesus has used since chapter 4, lent to them for their errand, and Acts will show the same word going on through his people.

It is given to men who are far from ready, and the errand keeps word and deed together (on both, see the note on vv. 1–2).
verseByVerse.examples:
Taking nothing for the road is not a travel policy for every age but a lesson in dependence, and staying in the first house guards the message too (see the note on vv. 3–4).

Herod is a warning that the right question is not enough (see the note on vv. 7–9).

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus shares his own power and authority with the Twelve and sends them to announce God’s kingdom and to show it by healing.

He called the twelve together. Chosen in 6:13 and trained by being with him through chapters 6–8, they are now sent.

Power and authority. Two different words. Power (dynamis) is the ability to do a thing; authority (exousia) is the right to do it. A burglar has the power to open your door and no authority; a magistrate has the authority to arrest and may lack the strength. The Twelve are given both, and earned neither. What they took into those villages was put into their hands that morning by someone who had it to give, which is still the only way anyone has ever had anything worth carrying.

Demons and diseases. Since chapter 4 Luke has shown Jesus casting out demons and healing diseases, always keeping the two apart (4:31–41). Now he hands that work on, and look who receives it: men who will shortly argue about which of them is greatest (v. 46), fail to cast out a demon (v. 40), want to burn a Samaritan village (v. 54), and desert him in a garden. He does not wait until they are ready. He never has.

He sent them out to proclaim and to heal. Sent out (apesteilen) is the root of our word apostle, one who is sent: not a rank but an errand. And the errand has two halves held together, announcement and demonstration, the healings confirming that the kingdom had come. A ministry that heals and says nothing has withheld the reason; a ministry that talks and touches nothing has announced a kingdom that apparently changes nothing.

Power that is his to give. No prophet could hand on power as his own. When Elisha asked for a double portion of his master’s spirit, Elijah could only say that he had asked a hard thing, which God alone could grant (2 Kings 2:9–10). Jesus gives power and authority over all demons simply because it is his to give, a claim no mere servant of God could make. What he lends here for a short mission in Galilee he will pour out from his throne as power from on high (24:49).

In everyday life. If you have felt unqualified to do anything for God, notice that the Twelve were unqualified too, and that whatever he calls you to, he equips you for. Take the task in front of you this week, the conversation, the class, the visit, and go, depending on him.

Does this authority belong to the church today? It was given to the Twelve for their mission, and its signs confirmed their message (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many Christians believe it continues; the more likely reading is that the sign gifts belonged to the apostolic age, while the commission to proclaim the kingdom goes on in every generation. That does not mean God has stopped healing. He heals today, often through medicine and sometimes beyond it, in answer to the prayers of his people (James 5:14–15). What has ceased, on the reading this commentary takes, is not his power or his willingness to answer prayer, but the gift given to particular people to heal at will as a sign authenticating new revelation. Christians who see it differently are brothers to be loved, not opponents. Either way, pray for the sick in faith, use the doctors God has given, and leave the outcome in his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Twelve are to travel with nothing, trusting God to provide through those who welcome them, and are not to trade up their lodging.

Take nothing for your journey. Five items, staff, bag, bread, money and a spare tunic, cover between them security, supply and comfort, and he takes all five away.

No staff. Mark says take only a staff (Mark 6:8). Perhaps Mark means “take the one you have”, while Luke and Matthew mean “do not acquire another”. Either way the point is the same: the list is not a dress code but an attitude. Take no extra provisions, and do not equip yourself against the possibility that God will not provide.

Nor bread, nor money. Not to beg, but to receive what God provided. Sent to preach the kingdom with no food and no money, every one of them will be hungry within a day and dependent on somebody who has not yet heard the message.

Whatever house you enter, stay there. A travelling teacher who attracted interest could expect better offers as the week went on, and the rule forbids trading up. A messenger whose comfort depends on pleasing a wealthy host will be tempted to say what the host wants to hear. It is also simple courtesy: do not humiliate the first family who took you in.

Sent as he was sent. The list strips the apostles down to the shape of their Lord’s own life. He had no house and would soon say that “the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (9:58); he was supported by the gifts of others (8:3); he went from village to village trusting his Father for the day’s bread. So the message of a King who became poor is carried by men who are visibly poor, and their emptiness puts his fullness on display. And when he asked them later whether they had lacked anything, they said, “Nothing” (22:35). He feeds the birds of the air, and he has never yet let a servant on his errand go hungry beyond what was good for him.

In everyday life. Ask what in your life is extra equipment against the possibility that God will not come through: the savings you trust more than him, the back-up plan that makes obedience unnecessary. And if someone shows you hospitality this week, receive it graciously and do not compare it with what others might have given.

What it does not mean. These orders were never meant to bind every missionary for ever: later Jesus told the same men to take a moneybag and knapsack (22:35–36). They fit this short, urgent mission in Galilee. What remains is the posture: urgency, simplicity, contentment and dependence on God.

Should churches pay their ministers and missionaries? Yes. Jesus’ instruction assumes that those who receive the message will provide for the messenger, and he says elsewhere that the labourer deserves his wages (10:7); Paul argues the same at length (1 Corinthians 9:3–14; 1 Timothy 5:17–18). A church should support its pastor and missionaries generously, so that they are free from anxiety; and those who serve should be content, and never preach for gain (1 Peter 5:2).
verseByVerse.note: The “bag” was a traveller’s pack for supplies; a second tunic was a spare.

verseByVerse.quote: And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A town that refuses the messengers is to be solemnly left to God’s judgment, and the messengers are to move on. Rejection is treated not as a possibility to pray against but as a certainty to prepare for: men with power over demons are told that some towns will simply not have them.

Shake off the dust from your feet. Jews coming home from Gentile lands are said to have shaken the dust of pagan roads from their feet before entering the holy land. Used of Jewish villages, the gesture is startling: a town of Israelites that refuses the kingdom of God is treated as though it stood outside the land. What marks out God’s people is no longer belonging to the nation but receiving the message. Paul would do the same at Pisidian Antioch and at Corinth (Acts 13:51; 18:6).

As a testimony against them. A warning now, and a witness at the judgment (10:10–16). The messengers have done their part; the town must answer to God for what it heard.

The Lord who weeps over the town. The command comes from the Lord who will weep over Jerusalem because it did not know the time of its visitation (19:41–44). He grieves over the towns that refuse more than his messengers ever will. But he is also their Judge, and refusing his messengers is refusing him: “The one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me” (10:16). A village that shuts its door on twelve Galileans has shut it on the Son of God.

In everyday life. With people who do not want to hear, two instincts are common and both are wrong: to keep pressing, as though a refusal were a problem of technique, until the gospel has become an irritation; or to shrug and conclude it never mattered. The dust does neither. It takes the refusal with complete seriousness, and then leaves without bitterness for the next village. If you have been carrying guilt for someone who has heard and refused, hand the weight back to God: your part was to tell them; changing the heart is his.

What it does not mean. Not personal contempt or revenge, and not a curse, but a solemn warning, which might still bring them to repentance.

So should I stop talking to my unbelieving friend about Christ? Not necessarily, and almost never withdraw from the friendship. The disciples were passing through towns on a short mission; most of us live alongside the same people for years. What changes after a clear refusal is usually the method, not the love. Stop pressing an argument he has heard and declined. Keep being his friend, keep praying for him, live the gospel in front of him, and be ready to speak again when he asks or when God opens a door (Colossians 4:5–6; 1 Peter 3:15). A refusal today is not a verdict for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And they departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Twelve obey, and the work of the kingdom is done through ordinary men in village after village. One verse covers the whole mission: they went, they preached, they healed, everywhere.

What is not here. No account of how it felt to set out with no money, or of the first refusal or the first demon. The orders to take nothing were the real conditions under which twelve ordinary men walked into real villages, and it worked: from the inside, ordinary hard work with no guarantee; from the outside, the kingdom of God arriving in villages that had waited centuries.

Preaching the gospel and healing everywhere. Evangelising (euangelizomenoi), Luke’s favourite word. The proclamation is named first, as in verse 2 and at 4:43, where Jesus said preaching was what he was sent for. “Everywhere” is emphatic, at the end of the sentence: they did not concentrate on the promising places.

His work in their hands. Luke opens his second volume by calling this Gospel an account of “all that Jesus began to do and teach” (Acts 1:1), as though Acts were what he went on doing, from heaven, through his servants. The healings in these villages were his healings; the Twelve were the hands. That is why their success can be told in a sentence.

What if my service for God feels ordinary and unseen? Then you are where the Twelve were. Most of what God does through his people is never written up. Each one’s work will be revealed on the day (1 Corinthians 3:13), and even a cup of cold water given in his name will not lose its reward (Matthew 10:42). God sees the Sunday school class taught for twenty years, the elderly neighbour visited weekly, the prayer list kept. The summary will come later, written by him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead, by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the prophets of old had risen. Herod said, 'John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?' And he sought to see him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
News of the mission reaches the ruler who killed John, and he asks the question the whole chapter answers: who is this?

Herod the tetrarch heard. This is Antipas, the son of Herod the Great, who held Galilee and Perea (3:1). Tetrarch is a lesser title; he wanted to be called king and Rome never allowed it. He was perplexed (diēporei): thoroughly at a loss, unable to find a way through.

John had been raised from the dead. The three theories, which the disciples will report again (v. 19), are all serious ones; Elijah was the forerunner Malachi promised (Malachi 4:5). All of them honour Jesus, and none is right: every one makes him one more prophet, and every one is too small.

John I beheaded. Luke does not tell the story of John’s death, which Mark tells at length (Mark 6:17–29). He records only Herod’s own words, the three he would least want quoted. Not “John was executed”, but “John I beheaded.” Whatever else this man is, he is not lying to himself about what he did, and if Mark’s account is any guide, he was haunted by it (Mark 6:16).

But who is this about whom I hear such things? The right question, the great question of the chapter and of the Gospel. The disciples asked it in the boat (8:25), and now a murderer in a palace asks it, correctly and urgently. Herod asks it; Peter will answer it (v. 20); the Father will give the final answer (v. 35).

Greater than John, greater than Elijah. Jesus is not John come back; John said that one mightier than he was coming, the strap of whose sandals he was not worthy to untie (3:16). He is not Elijah; Elijah’s promised return had already come in John, who went before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah (1:17). He is not one of the old prophets; they spoke the word of the LORD, and he is the one of whom the Father will say, “This is my Son, my Chosen One” (9:35). Herod had killed the greatest man born of women (7:28), and still had not met the one John came to announce.

He sought to see him. There is the tragedy. Herod wanted to see Jesus out of curiosity, not faith, and eventually he got what he asked for. At the trial he “was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him” (23:8). And Jesus did not answer him a word (23:9). Herod is the only person in Luke’s account of the trials to whom Jesus says nothing at all.

In everyday life. If you have been interested in Christ for a long time, ask the harder question: what am I going to do about the answer? Jesus still receives anyone who comes to him today.

Why did Jesus not answer Herod? Because Herod had already had his answer and refused it. He had heard John preach, and liked to listen to him (Mark 6:20), and then killed him rather than lose face. What he wanted at the trial was a show, not a Saviour, and Jesus’ silence was a judgment: there comes a point where more words would only be entertainment. That is a solemn warning to anyone who treats Christ as a subject of interest rather than a Lord to be obeyed. Seek him while he may be found (Isaiah 55:6).
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee. Luke records that he later saw Jesus at his trial.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Jesus Feeds the Five Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Lord who welcomes the crowd feeds it himself, as God fed Israel in the wilderness, and he does it through his disciples’ empty hands. He takes the Twelve away to rest, and gladly welcomes the crowd that follows (vv. 10–11). The disciples sensibly want the people sent away; he tells them to feed them, and all they have is five loaves and two fish (vv. 12–13). He seats the crowd in companies, takes, blesses, breaks and gives, and the disciples carry the bread out (vv. 14–16). All are satisfied, and twelve baskets are left over (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The feeding recalls Israel in the wilderness (see the notes on v. 12 and vv. 14–15), and looks forward to the feast Isaiah promised (see the note on v. 17); the Lord’s Supper is a foretaste of that table.

The four verbs, took, blessed, broke and gave, return at the Last Supper and at Emmaus (see the note on v. 16). The baskets left over show that his kingdom does not give minimum rations.
verseByVerse.examples:
Sending people away is the reasonable answer in many situations; the question is whether the need has been brought to Jesus before anyone decides (see the note on v. 12).

The loaves really are too little (see the note on v. 13), and guarding time for rest is right, but the plan is not the master when real need is standing in front of us (see the note on vv. 10–11).

verseByVerse.quote: On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus takes his tired apostles away to rest, and when the crowds wreck the plan, he welcomes them gladly.

On their return. They report back to him, because every ministry answers to the Lord who gave it. Then he withdraws with them for rest and private teaching; Mark gives his words: “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while” (Mark 6:31).

To a town called Bethsaida. Bethsaida lay at the top of the lake, near where the Jordan runs in, in Philip’s territory and beyond Herod’s reach. The feeding took place in a deserted place near it (v. 12).

The crowds followed. The rest lasts as long as it takes a crowd to work out where the boat is going; Mark says they got there first.

He welcomed them. Only Luke says this. Welcomed means received gladly: not tolerated, not endured. He met the people who had wrecked his plan as though they had been invited, and taught and healed them until the day was nearly over (v. 12).

Weary himself, he welcomed them. The Lord who invites the weary to come to him and find rest (Matthew 11:28) was himself weary, and gave up his rest to welcome a crowd. Every one of us who has come to him has come uninvited, at an inconvenient time, and been received gladly. His welcome is the gospel.

So should I never protect my rest? You should protect it; Jesus did, withdrawing again and again (5:16; 6:12). Rest is God’s gift and command. But the plan is not the master: with Jesus the rhythm is real right up to the moment the need is standing in front of him, and then it gives way, every time. When what you had prayerfully arranged is taken from you by people in need, the question is whether they are met as an intrusion or as guests. Guard your time in the ordinary run of things; when the need is genuine and in front of you, let love decide, and trust God to give you the rest you missed another way.
verseByVerse.note: Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the lake.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the day began to wear away, and the twelve came and said to him, 'Send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As night comes on in the wilderness, the disciples sensibly want the crowd sent away, forgetting who is standing beside them.

The only miracle in all four Gospels. Apart from the resurrection, the feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels (Matthew 14; Mark 6; John 6).

Send the crowd away. The light is going: thousands of people in open country, hours from anywhere, with night coming. The suggestion is not hard-hearted but responsible, twelve men facing a practical problem their teacher appears not to have noticed, and they are right about everything except who is standing beside them. John tells us Jesus already knew what he would do (John 6:6).

A desolate place. A wilderness, and Israel had been here before. “Can God spread a table in the wilderness?” was the people’s question in the desert, asked in unbelief (Psalm 78:19), and the answer was manna every morning for forty years (Exodus 16). Now the question returns from twelve tired men, and the God who answered it then is standing in front of them in a human body. Moses prayed and God sent bread; Jesus will take the bread into his own hands.

Experience has a short half-life. These men have just come back from casting out demons and healing the sick with nothing in their pockets, and their instinct now is to count resources and organise a dispersal. Experience of God’s provision fades quickly in all of us. Our arithmetic has never once included all of him.

Is it ever right to say no to a need? Yes. No church and no Christian can meet every need, and Jesus himself sometimes moved on when crowds wanted more (4:42–43). Limits, and referring people to others better placed to help, are not unbelief. The question this passage puts is whether we have brought the need to Jesus before we decided. Sometimes, after prayer, the answer is that this is not ours to carry. Sometimes he hands it back and says, “You give them something to eat.” The sin is not in saying no, but in leaving him out of the arithmetic.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, 'You give them something to eat.' They said, 'We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus hands the impossible need back to his disciples, and they rightly see that what they have is nowhere near enough.

You give them something to eat. “You” is emphatic. He hands the problem back, and there is no way the Twelve can obey in their own strength. They had just been preaching and healing in his power; could they not trust him for this?

Five loaves and two fish. Their answer is an inventory. John tells us these came from a boy, barley loaves, the bread of the poor, and two small fish (John 6:9). It is one packed lunch.

Unless we are to go and buy. There is an edge in that clause. Mark supplies their figure: two hundred denarii, about two-thirds of a labourer’s annual wage (Mark 6:37), and John adds that even that would not give each of them a little (John 6:7). They have costed it, and they are right: no amount of faith changes that sum, and Jesus never suggests otherwise. The command is not to be optimistic about the bread but to put it in his hands anyway. Nothing in this passage is multiplied before it is handed over.

Greater than Elisha. A man once brought Elisha twenty loaves of barley, and the prophet said, “Give to the men, that they may eat”; his servant answered, “How can I set this before a hundred men?” And the word of the LORD was that they would eat and have some left (2 Kings 4:42–44). The echo is plain: an order to give, an objection about numbers, food left over. But Elisha fed a hundred with twenty loaves on a word from the LORD. Jesus feeds five thousand men with five, and the word is his own.

What if what I have really is too little? It is too little, and that is not the problem. The question is never whether it is enough, but whether you will put it into his hands (1 Corinthians 1:27–29).

verseByVerse.quote: For there were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, 'Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.' And they did so, and had them all sit down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus has the vast crowd seated in ordered companies, as guests at a banquet, and the disciples obey before they can see where the food will come from.

About five thousand men. Men (andres); Matthew adds “besides women and children” (Matthew 14:21). The real number in that field was perhaps fifteen or twenty thousand people in all.

Groups of about fifty. And they did so. Consider what that commits the Twelve to: organising thousands, in failing light, into a hundred companies, with five loaves in a bag and no explanation. They have to seat the whole crowd before they know there is anything to serve, and they do it. The word for sit down is literally recline, as at a banquet.

Why groups of fifty? One reason is practical: twelve men can serve a hundred defined companies in order, with nobody missed, as they never could a mob. The other is older. When Israel came out of Egypt and was fed in the wilderness, Moses organised the people in ordered companies, with chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties and of tens (Exodus 18:21, 25). A crowd in a desolate place, arranged in fifties, about to be fed by God, is not an image any Jew would fail to recognise. Jesus is the new Moses, feeding the new Israel in the wilderness, and he is greater than Moses, because Moses did not make the manna.

A picture of the church. He did not feed a mass. He fed people in groups small enough to see each other’s faces, sharing out of the same basket: an early picture of what the church would look like.

Why does God ask me to obey before I see how it will work? Because that is what faith is: “the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). Abraham “went out, not knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8). If God always showed us the outcome first, we would be trusting the outcome, not him. He gives light for the next step, and the next step is usually something ordinary, like seating people on the grass. Do that, and leave the bread to him.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As host of the meal, Jesus takes, blesses, breaks and gives the bread, and his disciples carry it to the crowd.

Taking the five loaves. Four verbs follow, he took, he blessed, he broke, he gave, as a Jewish head of household did at the start of a meal. He looked up to heaven, to his Father, the giver of every gift. Five small loaves, held up in two hands before a hungry multitude, and a blessing spoken over them by the one through whom every field of barley in Galilee was made. He gives thanks over the actual, insufficient five, and it is in the breaking and the giving that there turns out to be more. The pile never visibly grows; it simply does not run out.

To set before the crowd. He could have handed it out himself. Instead the bread goes from his hands into theirs, and from theirs to the people, so that the men who had said “Send the crowd away” spend the next hour walking up and down a hillside giving away food they did not have. This is the pattern of ministry: we receive from Christ and give to others. We do not make the bread; we hand it out.

He broke and gave. Luke will use these four verbs twice more. At the Last Supper Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it and gave it to them (22:19). And on the first Easter evening, at a table in a village house, the stranger who had walked seven miles with two downcast disciples “took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them”, and their eyes were opened and they recognised him (24:30–31). The hands on this hillside are the hands they would know again, and the hands that broke the bread would themselves be broken, so that the bread of life could be given to the world.

In everyday life. Give thanks before it is enough. Before your next meal, before your next week of work, before you face a need too big for you, take what you have, look up, and thank God for it. Then hand it on. Everything you have to give others has come first from his hands.

Is the feeding the Lord’s Supper? No, but it points towards it. The feeding was a meal in the wilderness for a crowd; the Supper is the ordinance Christ gave his church, a remembrance of his death and a means of grace in which, by faith, believers feed on him spiritually (1 Corinthians 10:16; 11:23–26; 1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7; Westminster Confession 29.7). Luke uses the same four actions so that we see the connection: the one who fed the five thousand gives himself as the bread of life (John 6:35). When you come to his Table, you come to the same host, and he still takes, blesses, breaks and gives.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus says the blessing as the head of a Jewish household did at a meal.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone is fed to the full, and more is left at the end than there was at the start.

All ate and were satisfied. All: down to the last group of fifty at the far edge of the field. Were satisfied (echortasthēsan) is a strong word, used of animals grazed to the full, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for the satisfaction God gives: “I will satisfy her poor with bread” (Psalm 132:15); “he satisfies the longing soul, and the hungry soul he fills with good things” (Psalm 107:9).

Twelve baskets of broken pieces. Not crumbs, but kophinoi, the stiff wicker baskets a traveller carried. Twelve is the number of the tribes: enough for all Israel. And it is the number of the men who had said it could not be done: one basket each, carried back by the very people who had costed it and said no. He has never yet been handed something too small to work with, and never yet run short at the far end of the field.

Nothing wasted. The one who had just fed thousands from a boy’s lunch had the leftovers gathered (John 6:12). Extravagance and carefulness sit together without the slightest tension.

In the flow. Luke goes straight from the baskets to Peter’s confession, leaving out the long stretch of Mark between (Mark 6:45–8:26), so that Herod’s question, “who is this?” (v. 9), is followed first by a sign and then by an answer (v. 20).

The bread of life. The next day, John tells us, Jesus explained: “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). The miracle points to Jesus himself, who gives himself to satisfy the deepest hunger of the soul. And it is a foretaste of the great feast of the Messiah’s kingdom, when people will come from east and west and recline at table in the kingdom of God (13:29; 14:15), the feast the LORD spreads for all peoples, where he swallows up death for ever (Isaiah 25:6–8). A hillside full of satisfied people is a small, real sample of that table.

Was it really a miracle? Some explain it as a sharing miracle, the crowd moved by the boy’s example to bring out food they had hidden. But all four Gospels record a miracle: the disciples distributed food from five loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets of fragments were left over. Jesus himself later recalled it as something he had done (Mark 8:19).

Why am I not satisfied, if Christ satisfies? Many Christians feel a restlessness that seems to contradict this verse. Partly we try to feed on other things, and they do not fill. Partly our satisfaction in Christ is real now but not yet complete; we taste, and long for more (1 Peter 2:3). Even the hunger is a gift, a sign that we were made for him. Come back to him: in his word, in prayer, at his Table, among his people. And wait for the day when we shall hunger no more (Revelation 7:16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — Peter's Confession and the Cost of Discipleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is the Christ of God, and the Christ goes to a cross, so those who follow him must take up theirs. Out of his prayer comes the question; the crowds’ answers are all too small, and Peter names him “The Christ of God” (vv. 18–20). Jesus silences the title until he has filled it: the Son of Man must suffer, be killed and be raised (vv. 21–22). Then he tells everyone the terms: deny yourself, take up your cross daily, follow (vv. 23–24), for the whole world is no price for yourself, and the one now despised will come in glory (vv. 25–26). Some standing there will see the kingdom before they die (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology:
Peter’s confession is right, and Jesus at once fills the title with its true meaning: the Christ of God is the suffering, dying and rising Son of Man. On that title, and on the word must (dei), see the note on vv. 21–22.

The promise that some would see the kingdom before they died was kept within the lifetime of those who heard it, beginning eight days later on the mountain (see the note on v. 27).
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke’s word daily brings the cross into an ordinary week, and self-denial must be guarded from twisting (see the note on vv. 23–24).

The question about gaining the whole world is set at the highest price on purpose, and the warning speaks of shame because most Western believers are tempted to be embarrassed by Christ rather than to renounce him (see the note on vv. 25–26).

verseByVerse.quote: Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. And he asked them, 'Who do the crowds say that I am?' And they answered, 'John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen.' Then he said to them, 'But who do you say that I am?' And Peter answered, 'The Christ of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of Jesus’ prayer comes the question of the whole Gospel, and Peter answers it rightly: Jesus is the Christ, God’s promised King.

Praying alone. Jesus was in prayer, with the disciples nearby. Luke leaves out the setting (Caesarea Philippi, Mark 8:27), and he alone tells us Jesus was praying, as he does at turning point after turning point (3:21; 6:12). The most important question in the book comes out of a conversation with the Father.

Who do the crowds say that I am? The answers are the three that reached Herod’s court (vv. 7–8): John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the old prophets risen. Every answer is respectful, and every one is wrong in the same way: it fits him into a category that already exists, a great man in a great tradition. The modern answers are much the same: a great moral teacher, a prophet, a spiritual genius. They are compliments, and they are all too small, because no mere teacher accepts what Jesus is about to accept, to be confessed as God’s own Anointed.

But who do you say that I am? The Greek puts the pronoun first and hard: you, what do you say? It is the pivot of the Gospel, and it cannot be answered by a survey. Everything so far has been evidence; the question is what has been made of it. Every person must answer it.

The Christ of God. The Christ is the Messiah, the Anointed (Christos is the Greek for Messiah): the king Israel had been promised since David. Kings and priests were anointed with oil to show that God had set them apart (1 Samuel 16:13); to call Jesus the Christ of God is to say that God has appointed him to rule and to save his people (2:26; 23:35). Peter has stopped putting him in the line of the prophets and named him as the one the whole line was pointing at. Matthew records the fuller confession and Jesus’ blessing (Matthew 16:16–19).

Right word, wrong picture. The confession is correct, and Luke moves straight past it, because being right about the title is not the same as understanding it. In Mark’s account, within moments of getting it right Peter is arguing with it (Mark 8:32). That is most people’s first real confession: the word is true, and what it means is learned later, usually at a cost.

How did Peter know? Matthew gives Jesus’ answer: “flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17). Peter had seen the same evidence as the crowds, and God opened his eyes. That is still how anyone comes to say “Jesus is Lord”: only by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). If you can say it from the heart, it is God’s gift, and a reason for thanks rather than pride.

What if I am not sure what I believe about Jesus? Then do what Peter did: stay close to him and look at the evidence. Read one of the Gospels through, asking at every page who this is. Pray honestly, even if your prayer is, “If you are there, show me.” Speak to a Christian you trust. Jesus did not ask the question to shame his disciples but to bring them to the answer, and he has not stopped asking it. The crowds had opinions; Peter had a confession. The difference is not cleverness but coming close.
verseByVerse.note: Luke leaves out the setting (Caesarea Philippi) but notes that Jesus was praying. “Christ” means anointed one, the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one, saying, 'The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus silences the title until he has filled it with its true meaning: God’s Christ must suffer, be killed and be raised. The cross is not a plan that went wrong but what God appointed.

Tell this to no one. He strictly charged and commanded them: two forceful verbs. Why silence a true confession? Because for many in Galilee, Messiah meant a son of David who would raise an army, break Rome and restore the kingdom; after the feeding a crowd tried to make him king by force (John 6:15). A public claim would have started a movement he had not come to lead. So the word is held back until it can carry the meaning he gives it in the very next sentence.

The Son of Man. He at once calls himself the Son of Man, his own preferred title, which is not, as it sounds in English, a modest way of saying a human being. Its background is Daniel 7:13–14, the heavenly figure who comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom. Luke lets the two sides of the title meet at the trial, where the Son of Man who must suffer tells the council that from now on he will be seated at the right hand of the power of God (22:69). The title of glory is the name of the one who goes to the cross.

Must suffer many things. The first prediction of his death comes straight after the confession: yes, I am the Christ, and the Christ must suffer. Must (dei) means it has to happen because God has planned it and written it in Scripture (24:26, 44–46). Luke uses it at every hinge of this Gospel: a boy who must be in his Father’s house (2:49), a preacher who must go to the next town (4:43), and now this.

Rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes. Together they formed the Sanhedrin, the nation’s council. He would be rejected not by Rome but by the men who had the Scriptures.

Killed, and raised. From the first time he tells them, death and resurrection come in the same sentence, as again at 18:31–33. The disciples will still be devastated, because they did not understand it and were afraid to ask (v. 45). Luke does not record Peter’s rebuke and Jesus’ “Get behind me, Satan!” (Mark 8:32–33), perhaps to spare Peter, or to keep the focus on the teaching.

Why must the Christ suffer? Because there was no other way to save sinners.
