God’s justice required that sin be punished, and his love purposed to save; at the cross both were satisfied, when the Son of Man bore in his own body the penalty his people deserved (Isaiah 53:5–6; Romans 3:25–26; 1 Peter 2:24). The “must” is not fate imposed on Jesus from outside. It is the eternal plan of the Father, Son and Spirit, written in Scripture, which the Son freely embraced: no one takes his life from him; he lays it down of his own accord (John 10:18). So the cross is not an angry Father punishing an unwilling victim. The Judge, in the person of his own Son, takes the penalty he himself requires, and that is why it is both just and astonishing love (1 John 4:10).

In everyday life. Check the picture of Jesus you carry around. Is it a Christ who exists to make your life go well, or the Christ of God who must suffer and calls you to follow? When suffering comes, it is not proof that he has failed you. It is the road he walked first.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to all, 'If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever wants to follow Jesus must dethrone self and walk behind him under a cross, every day.

And he said to all. Not advanced material for the Twelve but the terms of entry. “If anyone would come after me”: would means wants to, wills to. It is a choice, and three clauses follow.

Let him deny himself. Not “deny himself things”, giving up sugar or television, but “deny himself”: say no to self as the centre and master of life. The verb (aparneomai) is the one Luke uses of Peter in the courtyard (22:34, 61); to deny the self is to say of your own claims what Peter said of Jesus: “I do not know him.” It is not self-hatred, and not the erasure of a personality God made. It is taking self off the throne, so that my wishes no longer have the last word. When what I want and what Christ says pull apart, his word decides, and I let it, even when no one would ever know (Galatians 2:20).

And take up his cross daily. Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution, and everyone hearing this had seen it. The phrase meant one thing: a man going to his death. So it is not merely “bear your hardships”; a difficult marriage or a chronic illness is real, and Scripture says much about it, but it is not this. To take up the cross is to accept rejection, shame and even death for Jesus’ sake. Only Luke adds “daily” (compare Matthew 16:24; Mark 8:34): he takes the most final image there is and makes it a routine, so it is not reserved for martyrs. The cross becomes a way of life, dying to self in a thousand daily choices, for Christ.

And follow me. To Jerusalem, to the cross, and beyond. Self-denial and the cross are not the goal; he is. The point of putting the self down is to walk after him.

Whoever would save his life will lose it. Life (psychē) here is the self, the whole person. A life organised round its own preservation, guarded against every cost of following Jesus, is being lost in the very act of being protected. To lose it for his sake is to hand it over to him, whatever it costs, and the life handed over is the one kept for ever. There is no third option, and the man who declines to choose has chosen.

Behind Jesus. Luke gives this saying a picture later. On the road to Golgotha the soldiers seized Simon of Cyrene and laid the cross on him, to carry it behind Jesus (23:26). But look at the order of the procession. Jesus goes first, to the place where the real dying is done, and the cross Simon carried was the one on which Jesus, not Simon, would die. Every disciple’s daily cross is carried behind that one, on a road whose end has already been reached by the one in front.

In everyday life. Name one way you can say no to yourself for Christ’s sake today: telling the truth when a lie would protect you, or serving someone who will not thank you. Small crosses, carried daily in the strength of the Spirit who raised Jesus, are how the self is dethroned; and on the days you drop yours, the cross that saves you is still his.

What it does not mean. Not salvation by self-denial; only Christ’s cross atones. Nor seeking suffering for its own sake. But the life that belongs to Christ takes the shape of his cross.

Does this mean I cannot enjoy anything? No. God “richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17). Self-denial is the refusal to let the self be king over his gifts. A Christian may enjoy a meal, a holiday, a career, a marriage, and enjoy them more than others, because he receives them from God’s hand and is ready to give them up if Christ asks. What he may not do is make any of them his master. The question is not “do I have good things?” but “who rules over them?”
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution. Only Luke adds “daily.”

verseByVerse.quote: For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To gain everything and lose yourself is a trade that makes no sense, and to be ashamed of Jesus now is to meet his shame when he comes in glory.

What does it profit … and loses or forfeits himself? A commercial question in commercial words: profit, gains, forfeits. On one side of the scale he sets the whole world; on the other, one item, yourself. Luke says “himself” where Mark says “his soul” (Mark 8:36): not a religious part of a person, but the man, the self who was going to enjoy it all. The trade is not merely bad; it makes no sense. The buyer has purchased everything and disposed of the only person who could have had it.

The prices people actually pay. If the trade fails at the highest price, it fails at every price below it, and the prices most people pay are small: a working life arranged around security, decisions taken to keep a reputation intact, a marriage kept comfortable by never saying the true thing.

Ashamed of me and of my words. He chose “ashamed” rather than “denies”, because the pressure on disciples was often not violence but scorn. Very few people in a Western country will be asked to renounce Christ; a great many are embarrassed by him, and especially by his words. It is one thing to hold a private faith and quite another to be the person at the table who believes what he said about sin, or judgment, or himself.

When he comes in his glory. Measure for measure: at the judgment Jesus will disown those who disowned him (12:8–9). And the glory is threefold, his own, his Father’s and the angels’: Jesus claims to share the Father’s glory. The one about to be rejected will return as the glorious Judge, and the man it is now embarrassing to be associated with will arrive in company like that.

Worth more than the world. Luke’s readers have seen this trade offered once before. When the devil showed Jesus every kingdom of the world in a moment, he offered the lot for one act of worship (4:5–7). Jesus refused. He would not gain the world by disobeying his Father; he would gain it by giving up his life. Now he is the heir of all things, holding by the cross what Satan offered without it. The one who tells us not to make the trade refused it for us, and is himself worth more than everything on the other side of the scale.

In everyday life. Where are you tempted to be ashamed of Jesus? In the moment of going quiet at a dinner table, what is being weighed is the opinion of a roomful of people against the opinion of the Son of Man in the glory of the Father. He was not ashamed of us: he “endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2). Next time the conversation turns, ask God for courage to say one true sentence about him.

If I have sometimes been ashamed of Jesus, will he disown me? This verse describes a settled refusal to own him, not a moment of weakness. Peter denied him three times and was restored (22:61–62; John 21:15–19). “If we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful” (2 Timothy 2:12–13). The answer to shame is not despair but to turn back to him, as Peter did. And if this verse troubles you, the trouble itself is a good sign: those who are settled in being ashamed of him are not usually grieved by it.

verseByVerse.quote: But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus promises that some of those listening will see the kingdom of God before they die, and eight days later three of them begin to.

Some standing here. Sceptics have built a case on this sentence: Jesus told the people in front of him that some would live to see the kingdom arrive; they all died; so, it is said, he was mistaken.

Until they see the kingdom of God. Luke leaves out Mark’s “come with power” (Mark 9:1): they will simply see the kingdom. Three answers are given. The weakest takes it as the second coming and strains the words. A much better one takes the kingdom to mean what Luke consistently means, the reign of God breaking in. But the strongest answer is the one Luke supplies straight away: about eight days after these sayings Jesus took Peter and John and James up the mountain (v. 28). All three of the first Gospels put the transfiguration immediately after this promise. The fulfilment begins there, a preview of the kingdom, and continues in the resurrection, the ascension, Pentecost (Acts 2:41), the spread of the gospel to Rome and the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, all within the lifetime of some of them.

A mercy as well as a fulfilment. He has just told them all to pick up a cross. Then he lets three men see, for a few minutes, what is on the other side of it. That is how it still works. Nobody gets the mountain permanently, and nobody is asked to walk to Jerusalem without ever having seen anything.

Is the kingdom here now, or still to come? Both. In Jesus’ works, his death and resurrection, and the gift of the Spirit, God’s reign broke into the world, and every believer has been transferred into it (Colossians 1:13). But it has not yet come in its fullness; that awaits Christ’s return in glory, when every enemy is put under his feet and the dead are raised (1 Corinthians 15:24–26). We live between the two, citizens of a kingdom that is real now and will be visible then, and so Christians can be joyful and longing at the same time.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For a few minutes three disciples see who Jesus truly is, and heaven tells them to listen to him, above all about the cross. While he prays, his face is changed and his clothing flashes white (vv. 28–29). Moses and Elijah, the Law and the Prophets, appear in glory and speak of the exodus he is about to accomplish at Jerusalem (vv. 30–31). Half awake, Peter tries to keep the moment with three tents (vv. 32–33). Then the cloud of God’s presence covers them, the Father names his Son, his Chosen One, and commands, “listen to him!”, and Jesus is left alone (vv. 34–36).
verseByVerse.theology:
The transfiguration shows who Jesus is and what his kingdom will be. The disciples see not a form he puts on but the radiance of who he always is (see the note on vv. 28–29).

Moses and Elijah speak with him about the cross, the greater exodus to which everything they did had pointed (see the note on vv. 30–31). On “my Chosen One” and the one command in the scene, “listen to him”, see the note on vv. 34–36.
verseByVerse.examples:
Peter’s tents show a familiar temptation: to hold on to a moment of glory and try to preserve it (see the note on vv. 32–33).

The response the Father asks for is not to build but to listen (see the note on vv. 34–36). And the timing is a kindness (see the note on v. 27).

verseByVerse.quote: Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Jesus prays on the mountain, the glory that is his own shines out through his body before three witnesses.

About eight days after. Luke ties the scene to the confession and the first prediction of the cross. Matthew and Mark say “after six days”; Luke’s “about” marks a rough count, and a week counted with its first and last days included covers the same span.

Peter and John and James. The inner three (8:51), who were in the room when Jairus’s daughter was raised, and who, in Mark’s account, are taken deeper into the garden at Gethsemane (Mark 14:33). They see him in glory and they see him in anguish, and the second scene cannot be understood without the first.

Up on the mountain to pray. Only Luke says why he went: not to be transfigured, but to pray, and it happened while he was praying, as the voice at the baptism came while he was praying (3:21–22).

The appearance of his face was altered. Mark and Matthew say he was transfigured (metemorphōthē, the word behind metamorphosis). Luke, writing for Greek readers used to stories of gods changing shape, perhaps avoids it for that reason, and describes what was seen. Matthew says “his face shone like the sun” (Matthew 17:2). Moses’ face shone after being with God (Exodus 34:29–35), but Moses reflected a borrowed glory; Jesus’ glory was his own, shining from within.

Not added, but uncovered. His clothing became dazzling white (exastraptōn), flashing like lightning. Nothing was added to him; the covering came off something that was there all along. The glory that filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:35) was, that day, standing on a hillside in a human body, praying, and for a few minutes the body did not hide it.

Where did the glory come from? From who he is. Jesus is the eternal Son, “the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature” (Hebrews 1:3). In becoming man he did not stop being God; he veiled his glory in our flesh (Philippians 2:6–7; John 1:14). It is also a preview of the glory he would enter after his suffering (24:26), and of the glorified body believers will share, when he transforms our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).

The glory he hid for us. The carpenter from Nazareth is the Lord of glory. He did not keep it shining. He let the veil fall back, walked down the hill and went to Jerusalem, where the face that shone was blindfolded and struck (22:63–64), as he had said it would be spat upon (18:32). That is the wonder: not only that the glory was there, but that he hid it for us, until the morning it could shine unhidden and draw us, beholding him, into the same likeness (2 Corinthians 3:18).

In everyday life. You will not shine like the sun, but prayer, with your eyes on him in his word, is where the Spirit changes us, usually so slowly that only others notice: a temper a little shorter-lived, a fear a little quieter, a face turned more often towards him.
verseByVerse.note: “About eight days” counts inclusively; Matthew and Mark say “after six days.” Only Luke says Jesus went up to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses and Elijah appear in glory and talk with Jesus about his coming death at Jerusalem, which Luke calls his exodus. Heaven interprets the cross before it happens: it will be God’s great rescue of his people.

Moses and Elijah. Moses, who gave the law, and Elijah, first among the prophets: the whole Old Testament on a hillside, bearing witness to Jesus (24:27, 44). Both are named in the closing words of the Old Testament (Malachi 4:4–5). Both had met God on the same mountain, Moses at Sinai and Elijah at Horeb, each hidden in a cleft or a cave while the glory passed by (Exodus 33:22; 1 Kings 19:9–13). Moses asked to see God’s glory and was shown only his back; Elijah, in despair, was met not in wind or fire but in a low whisper. Now they appear in glory, standing in the light, talking with him.

His departure. Only Luke tells us what they talked about, and his word is startling: exodos, exodus. It can simply mean death, departure from life (2 Peter 1:15). But Moses led the first exodus, and now the word is applied, in his hearing, to a death in Jerusalem. Jesus will lead a new and greater exodus, through his death, resurrection and ascension, bringing his people out of a slavery deeper than Egypt’s. Everyone who practises sin is a slave to sin (John 8:34): sin is not only something we do but a master we cannot dismiss, holding us under guilt and death. The exodus at Jerusalem breaks that master’s grip, so that the Son sets us free indeed (John 8:36).

Which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. Accomplish (plēroun) means to fulfil, complete. His death is not something that will happen to him, but a work he will finish. Jerusalem is the goal of the whole Gospel (v. 51; 13:33).

In glory, and talking of Calvary. Moses and Elijah are in glory, and they are not talking about glory. With the light of heaven on them, what they discuss is Calvary. The greatest of the saints in heaven are absorbed in the cross, and so shall we be, for ever: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain” (Revelation 5:12). And because of his exodus, a believer’s death too becomes a departure out of bondage into the presence of God.

How did the disciples know who Moses and Elijah were? The text does not say; most likely it was given with the vision itself, or by what they heard them say.

Does this show the dead are conscious? It shows that Moses and Elijah were alive with God, centuries after they left the earth, and that they knew and cared about the work of Christ. That fits the rest of Scripture: God is not the God of the dead but of the living, for all live to him (20:38), and those who die in the Lord are with him at once (23:43; Philippians 1:23). There is no soul sleep. But this is no precedent for contact with the dead, which Scripture forbids (Deuteronomy 18:10–12; compare 16:27–31). This was God’s doing, once, on a holy mountain, for his Son’s sake.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “departure” is exodus: his death, resurrection and ascension as a new rescue of God’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, 'Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah'—not knowing what he said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The drowsy disciples wake to see his glory, and Peter, overwhelmed, tries to make the moment last by building shelters.

Heavy with sleep. They almost missed it, and only Luke records it: the Son of God is shining, and the disciples are struggling to stay awake, as they will in Gethsemane, sleeping for sorrow (22:45). There is no rebuke. It is simply what we are like.

They saw his glory. Luke is careful to say so, because the testimony rests on these men. Peter would later write: “we were eyewitnesses of his majesty … we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain” (2 Peter 1:16–18).

Let us make three tents. Booths or shelters, probably with the Feast of Booths in mind, when Israel lived in shelters for a week to remember the wilderness, a feast that looked forward to God dwelling with his people. Luke notes that Peter speaks as Moses and Elijah are parting from Jesus: the tents are a way of making them stay. The proposal goes wrong twice. Three tents make three equals, Jesus level with Moses and Elijah; and a camp on the mountain means no road to Jerusalem, where the exodus they had just been discussing was to be accomplished. The answer from the cloud leaves Jesus standing alone.

Not knowing what he said. Candid and gentle: Peter does what people do in the presence of something overwhelming, which is to talk, and to propose a project.

The tent God had already pitched. Peter offers to make a dwelling for Jesus, and does not see that Jesus is the dwelling. John says that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”, using the verb for pitching a tent, and adds, “we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). The fulfilment of the Feast of Booths is standing in front of Peter, shining. The tent of meeting, where God met with his people in the wilderness, has come in person, and the glory Peter wanted to shelter is the glory that shelters Peter.

In everyday life. If you are living on the memory of a past spiritual high, thank God for it, and then ask what obedience he is calling you to in the valley this week. And if your prayers often fight sleep, take comfort: so did Peter’s. Keep coming.

Why can we not stay on the mountain? Because the glory was given for the road, not instead of it. Christians have high moments, a conference, a season of revival, a time of deep closeness to God in prayer, and they are real gifts. But they are not meant to be housed and preserved, and trying to recreate them leads to disappointment or worse. The way to the final glory runs through faithful ordinary obedience, through suffering, through the cross. The mountain strengthens you for that; it does not excuse you from it. And one day there will be a dwelling that does not end, when God himself makes his home with his people (Revelation 21:3).

verseByVerse.quote: As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, 'This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!' And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself, in the cloud of his presence, names Jesus as his chosen Son and commands the disciples to listen to him.

A cloud came and overshadowed them. Peter is interrupted mid-sentence. This is not weather but the cloud of God’s presence, the cloud of Sinai and of the tabernacle (Exodus 24:15–18; 40:34–35), unseen in Israel for centuries. Luke’s verb is the one he used at the annunciation: “the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (1:35). And only Luke says they entered the cloud, and were afraid as they did: everything Israel knew said that men do not walk into that and come out.

A voice out of the cloud. At the baptism the words were spoken to Jesus himself (3:22); here they are spoken to the three disciples, about him. “This is my Son”: not one of three, but the Son, the answer to Peter’s three tents.

My Chosen One. The title echoes Isaiah 42:1, where God presents his servant, whom he upholds, his chosen, in whom his soul delights. Jesus is the chosen Servant of the Lord, who will suffer (Isaiah 53). The rulers will mock this very title at the cross: “if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One” (23:35).

Listen to him! The only command in the scene: not look, not build, but listen. It echoes Deuteronomy 18:15: “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you … it is to him you shall listen.” Jesus is that prophet, greater than Moses. And the command is aimed with precision at three men who have spent eight days failing to accept one thing he said: that the Son of Man must suffer and be killed and be raised. Listen to him, above all when he speaks of the cross.

Jesus was found alone. The cloud lifts, and there is one figure, not three. The Law and the Prophets have stepped back, as every other voice in history steps back before his, and what is left standing in the ordinary light is a man they are going to follow down the hill to Jerusalem.

They kept silent. Jesus had ordered them to tell no one until he had risen (Mark 9:9). Before the cross, the glory they had seen would only have fed the wrong hopes.

How do I listen to him today? Through his word. The voice on the mountain turned the three from Moses and Elijah to Jesus alone, and Scripture does the same: the Son who spoke on earth now speaks through the Scriptures his Spirit inspired (Hebrews 1:1–2; 2 Timothy 3:16). There is no need for a new voice from a cloud, and we should not seek one; the canon is closed, and Scripture is sufficient. Christians who believe God still gives prophetic words usually agree that any such word must be tested by Scripture and can never add to it, and that shared conviction matters more than the disagreement. Listen when you read the Bible, slowly and with prayer, and when it is faithfully preached. Listen especially to the parts you would rather not hear, as the three needed to hear about the cross. And listen in order to obey, for hearing in the Bible always means doing.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “my Beloved”, as in Mark, and the KJV and NKJV follow them (“my beloved Son”). “Chosen One” is very likely what Luke wrote, since a copyist would more readily change it to match Mark than the other way round.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “my Beloved” for “my Chosen One.”

parallels.desc: it is to him you shall listen
my chosen, in whom my soul delights

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–50 — Healing, Humility, and the Second Passion Prediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the foot of the mountain the disciples’ weakness shows that everything depends on Jesus, and that his greatness is the greatness of one who stoops. The disciples cannot free a father’s only son; Jesus grieves over a faithless generation, heals the boy and gives him back (vv. 37–43). While the crowd marvels, he warns them again that he will be handed over, and they cannot take it in (vv. 44–45). They argue about who is greatest, and he sets a child beside him (vv. 46–48); they try to stop a man working in his name, and he forbids them (vv. 49–50).
verseByVerse.theology:
The disciples’ failure, after their success in verses 1–6, shows that the authority they had been given was never their own (see the note on vv. 39–40; Matthew 17:20).

The second prediction contains a bitter play on words, and Luke’s note that the meaning was concealed holds two things together (see the note on vv. 44–45).

The saying that whoever is not against you is for you seems to clash with 11:23 (see the note on vv. 49–50).
verseByVerse.examples:
The child beside Jesus challenges any measure of greatness by influence, platform or numbers (see the note on v. 48).

The father’s report that the disciples could not help is an honest record of failure, and a comfort of a hard kind: the church’s work has always included things that did not work. And John’s complaint that the man did not follow with us names an instinct every group knows (see the note on vv. 49–50).

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, 'Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Coming down from glory, Jesus meets a desperate father who asks only that he look at his only son.

Down from the mountain. From glory to need, the contrast Moses walked into when he came down Sinai with the words of God and found the people round a golden calf (Exodus 32). Jesus comes down with the Father’s voice still in the disciples’ ears, and finds a boy in convulsions and a ministry that has failed. That descent is where nearly all Christian work is done: the next morning, at the bottom of the hill, among people with a problem that will not wait.

Look at my son. A father shouting over a crowd does not ask for a miracle; he asks Jesus to look at the boy, to look upon him with favour and compassion. He has stopped expecting anything and is asking for attention.

My only child. Once more Luke alone has the word “only”, as with the widow’s only son at Nain (7:12) and Jairus’s only daughter (8:42). No other children, and in that world no future for the family either. Luke does not give his name: a father who has lived for years with a child destroyed in front of him at unpredictable intervals, and who has come to a preacher’s followers and been let down. Anyone who has cared for a severely ill or disabled child will recognise the exhaustion in the request.

The God who looks. The father asks what the desperate have always asked of God: look. Hannah prayed that the LORD would look on the affliction of his servant (1 Samuel 1:11), and Luke’s verb here is the one Mary used when she sang that God had looked on the humble estate of his servant (1:48). The father asks it of Jesus to his face, which is what the incarnation has made possible: the God who looks down from heaven has come close enough to be stopped on a hillside and asked to turn his eyes on one boy, and he does.

Does God see my child? Yes. The God who heard Hagar’s son crying under a bush in the wilderness (Genesis 21:17), and who looked on this boy through the eyes of his Son, sees every child and every parent. If you are caring for a child who is ill, disabled or far from God, you may feel unseen by everyone, including the church. Jesus is not like the crowd. Bring your child to him in prayer, as this father did, even if all you can manage is, “Lord, look at my son.” And ask your church family for help; they are meant to carry this with you (Galatians 6:2).

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father describes a spirit that is destroying his son, and admits that Jesus’ disciples could do nothing about it.

A spirit seizes him. The father’s description is clinical: sudden onset, a cry, convulsion, foaming, and then the flattened exhaustion afterwards. The symptoms resemble epilepsy, but the cause was demonic (v. 42). It shatters him (syntribon: crushes, bruises, breaks), and even between seizures it will hardly let him go. Satan’s aim is destruction.

Ill or possessed? Were these pre-scientific people simply calling a disease of the brain a devil? The answer comes from Luke himself, the last man in the New Testament who can be accused of not knowing the difference. He is a physician with a clinical eye: the woman who had spent all she had on doctors (8:43), the high fever (4:38), the sweat like drops of blood (22:44; those verses are missing from some early manuscripts, but the other examples stand without them). And he consistently keeps the two categories apart. They brought Jesus those “sick with various diseases”, and “demons also came out of many” (4:40–41); a crowd came to be healed of their diseases, and those troubled by unclean spirits were cured (6:17–18). Jesus speaks the same way: “I cast out demons and perform cures” (13:32). A man who thought every convulsion was a devil would not write like that. Luke reports the symptoms as symptoms, and then tells us that in this boy something else was behind them.

Two errors. Luke’s care rules out two harmful errors. The first makes every seizure, every darkness of the mind, a work of the enemy, a cruelty this Gospel forbids by listing sickness and spirits as different things. A Christian with epilepsy is not in the devil’s grip; he needs good medicine and the love of his church, not an interrogation about hidden sin. The second is the fashionable error, that “demon” was merely the old word for a disorder we can now diagnose. But in two verses’ time Jesus rebukes the thing, and it obeys and comes out. You do not reprimand a neurological condition and have it answer you.

But they could not. The honest report of a ministry failure, by the man it failed. Jesus had given the disciples authority over all demons (v. 1), and they had come back full of what they had done (v. 10), and it was real. Here, at the bottom of the mountain, with a father watching, nothing worked.

What his servants could not do. The failure throws the whole weight of the scene onto one person: the nine had real authority, and it failed, and the father’s hope now rests on Jesus alone. Every gift Christ gives his people remains his gift, and never becomes a power they own. What cannot fail in this story is not the ministry but the Master.

In everyday life. Past success is no guarantee of present power. Every work of God needs fresh dependence on him, so do not walk into this week on the strength of last week’s fruit. Pray before you begin, every time.

Why could the disciples not cast it out? Jesus calls it faithlessness (v. 41), and in Mark he adds that “this kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer” (Mark 9:29; some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add “and fasting”, but the earliest do not). The authority they had been given was real, but it was borrowed, and they had stopped depending on the one who gave it.

What should I do when the church fails someone? Admit it honestly, as this father’s words force the disciples to. Churches and Christians do fail people, in counsel, in care, in prayer, in noticing. The answer is not to pretend otherwise, nor to give up on Christ because his people failed. When the disciples could not help, the father took his son to Jesus himself. If you have been let down by Christians, do not let their failure keep you from the Lord. And if you are the one who failed, take it back to him in prayer, and learn dependence.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, 'O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.' While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marveling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus grieves over the unbelief around him, yet at once heals the boy and gives him back to his father, and everyone sees the majesty of God.

O faithless and twisted generation. One of the sharpest things Jesus says in this Gospel, aimed not at the father, who came and told the truth, but at a generation: the crowd, the disciples, the whole scene at the foot of the mountain. Twisted (diestrammenē) means perverse, crooked: the word Moses used of Israel in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 32:5).

How long am I to be with you and bear with you? Not simply anger, but the sound of a man carrying something heavy: the weariness of the holy Son among unbelievers, come down from the light of his Father’s presence into a valley where nothing works.

Bring your son here. Then, without pausing, compassion. He names the faithlessness and heals the boy anyway; he does not make the father’s help wait on the crowd improving.

Its last attack. While the boy was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. The thing is at its worst in the final seconds before it is finished, as anyone knows who has watched a besetting sin or a long oppression flare up hardest just as ground is being taken.

Gave him back to his father. Luke tells it more briefly than Mark, but ends on this, almost the phrase used at Nain, where Jesus “gave him to his mother” (7:15). Luke will not report a miracle as an event when it can be reported as a gift.

The majesty of God. Majesty (megaleiotēti), greatness, magnificence, is the word Peter uses for what he saw at the transfiguration (2 Peter 1:16). The majesty seen on the mountain is now seen in the valley: in a boy who could stand up, in the arms of a father who had stopped hoping.

He hands sons back to fathers. The splendour that shone beside Moses and Elijah stooped to lift a broken boy into his father’s arms. That is the greatness of our God: not only that he rules the universe, but that he hands sons back to fathers, and at the cost of his own Son is bringing many sons to glory (Hebrews 2:10).

Does Jesus lose patience with me? He grieves over unbelief, and says so; we should not pretend he is indifferent to it. But look at what he does with his weariness: “Bring your son here.” His patience is not endless in the sense that sin does not matter to him; it is endless in the sense that he goes on bearing with his people until he has finished his work in them. The same Lord who sighed over a faithless generation went to the cross for it. If you fear you have exhausted his patience, the very fear shows his Spirit is still at work. Bring your need to him.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.' But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the crowd is marvelling, Jesus tells his disciples plainly that he will be handed over to men, and they cannot take it in and are afraid to ask.

Let these words sink into your ears. Literally, “put these words into your ears.” At the height of the crowd’s enthusiasm for his power (v. 43) he speaks of his weakness, so that his disciples are not swept up in it. He is asking them to store something they will need later and cannot use yet.

Delivered into the hands of men. Delivered (paradidosthai) means handed over, betrayed: the word that will be used of Judas throughout the passion, and the word Isaiah’s Greek text uses of the Servant handed over because of their sins (Isaiah 53:12). And there is a bitter play on words: the Son of Man into the hands of men. The one who heals by his hands will be handed into human hands.

It was concealed from them. They could not reconcile a suffering Messiah with what they believed, and only Luke adds that it was concealed. By whom? Luke does not say, probably on purpose, and two things are true at once. There is a hiddenness God appoints, not as punishment, but because the time for understanding had not yet come: the Emmaus pair’s eyes were kept from recognising him (24:16) until they were opened after the resurrection (24:31, 45). And there is a hiddenness the disciples made for themselves, for Luke shows straight afterwards what they were thinking about instead: which of them was greatest.

Afraid to ask. This is their own part, and they were very likely afraid of the answer. A person may fail to understand because he is truly stuck, or because he has grasped enough to know he does not want the rest. They had understood more than they wanted to (Mark 8:32).

He walked toward it with open eyes. The hands that had just lifted a broken boy would be handed over into the hands of men, and he told his friends so while the crowd was still marvelling. He was not caught by the cross. We understand now what they could not: that the handing over was love, that the Father “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32), and that the one men handed over now holds us, and will not hand us over to anyone.

In everyday life. The question that most needs asking is often the one nobody will raise, because everyone suspects what the answer will cost. Ask it, in prayer and to people who know the Scriptures.

Why would God hide the meaning from them? For a time, and for their good: they could not yet bear the full truth of the cross. There are things in his word you may not understand yet, and some will become clear only through later experience, or in glory. That is no excuse for not asking; the disciples’ fear was their own fault. But it is a comfort when understanding is slow: he will finish teaching you.

parallels.desc: they understood none of these things

verseByVerse.quote: An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fresh from hearing that he will be betrayed, the disciples argue about rank, and Jesus answers by standing a child beside himself.

Which of them was the greatest. He has just told them he will be handed over, and what fills the silence is an argument about rank. Luke sets the two side by side without comment, and the same argument will arise at the Last Supper (22:24).

What were they arguing about? The timing suggests an answer. Three of them had just been up a mountain and come back different, and would not say why (v. 36). Peter had been the one to name him the Christ. The nine had failed with the demon. There was material for a dispute, and it was fresh. It happened in the hours after the glory, among people who had been let in on something, which is exactly where this sin lives. Nobody argues about greatness who has not first been given something.

Knowing the reasoning of their hearts. They did not tell him. He knew what they were thinking (5:22; 6:8), as the one who “knew what was in man” (John 2:25), reading the inner life of twelve people at once, including what they would not have admitted to each other.

A child by his side. He does not answer the argument or lecture them on humility. He takes a child (paidion, a young one, small enough to be taken) and stands the child beside himself, in the place of honour. Twelve grown men are ranking themselves, and he, on his way to be handed over, places beside himself the one person present with no rank whatsoever. That is the kind of King he is.

In everyday life. Your place beside Christ is a gift no one can outrank. Notice this week when you mentally rank yourself against someone, a colleague, a fellow church member, a sibling. Confess it to God plainly, and then do something to honour the person you were measuring yourself against.

Is it wrong to want to do well? No. Paul tells us to run to win the prize and to work heartily (1 Corinthians 9:24; Colossians 3:23), and ambition for God’s glory and the good of others is a virtue. What Jesus exposes here is the desire to be thought greater than others: comparison, rank, the need to be ahead. Can you rejoice when someone else is honoured, chosen or more fruitful than you (Romans 12:15)? Do you want to be great, or do you want Christ to be great? Pride hides easily in spiritual success, so watch especially after God has blessed you.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to them, 'Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
To welcome the least for Jesus’ sake is to welcome Jesus himself and the Father who sent him, and true greatness lies in becoming least.

Receives this child. A first-century child was loved, but in law and society had no standing and no capacity to confer honour on anybody. “Receives” is the language of hospitality: to welcome, to take somebody in. So the question is not “who is willing to be like a child?” (that comes at 18:17), but “who will you make room for, when the person can do nothing for you?”

Him who sent me. The child stands for Christ, and Christ for the Father who sent him, so that the person with the least standing in the room is joined, in two links, to the throne of God. This is where Christ has chosen to be found (compare 14:21), and the welcome of the least is the shape of God’s own hospitality.

The one who is great. He does not abolish greatness; he turns the way it is measured upside down. Not the one who seeks to be great, but the one who becomes small: who welcomes the unimportant and serves without seeking recognition (22:26–27). He who was the greatest became the least of all, the servant of all, so that the least might be made great in him.

Making it concrete. The test is how we treat those who cannot advance or repay us: the person who cleans the building, the member of the congregation whose conversation goes nowhere, the child in the room, who has nothing and is watching. Whatever is said to them is said to Christ, and whatever is given them goes to the Father.

Does this mean children’s work in the church matters? Very much. Those who welcome, teach and care for children in Christ’s name are receiving Christ himself, though their work is often unseen and rarely thanked. The crèche rota and the Sunday school are not lesser ministries for those not gifted enough to preach. And the principle reaches further: the disabled, the elderly with dementia, the newcomer who does not fit, the person with nothing to give. A church’s greatness is measured by how it receives those who can do nothing for it.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, 'Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.' But Jesus said to him, 'Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus forbids his disciples to stop someone working in his name merely because he is not one of their group. The name, not the group, does the work.

We saw someone. Nobody had asked John anything. Jesus has just said the least is the greatest, and John at once produces an incident in which the disciples enforced a boundary. The man was casting out demons successfully, where they had just failed (v. 40), and doing it “in your name”: not as a rival, but under the authority of Jesus.

He does not follow with us. The only objection is John’s own: not one of our group. Not “he does not follow you”, but “us”: the pride of the argument about greatness, now as group pride.

Not against you. The correction is immediate and generous. Anyone genuinely working in Jesus’ name against Satan is on the same side. What is corrected is a thoroughly religious instinct: the assumption that the boundary of my group is the boundary of the kingdom, and that work God does outside it is at best suspect and at worst competition.

The name that does the work. When Eldad and Medad prophesied in the camp, outside the circle at the tent, Joshua begged Moses to stop them, and Moses answered that he wished all the LORD’s people were prophets (Numbers 11:26–29). John plays Joshua here. But the power at work is not Moses’ spirit shared out; it is Jesus’ own name. The name, not the group, does the work, and the name belongs to him.

Against or with? Two chapters later Jesus says what sounds like the opposite: “Whoever is not with me is against me” (11:23). The difference is in the pronouns. There the subject is a person’s own relation to Christ, where there is no neutral ground. Here it is one servant’s judgment of another, where we are to give the benefit of the doubt. So this verse is a rule for how to view others, and 11:23 a test for oneself. About my own standing before Christ, assume nothing; about another man doing good in his name, assume the best.

In the flow. In a few verses the disciples fail to cast out a demon (v. 40), argue about greatness (v. 46), try to stop an outsider (v. 49), and will soon want fire on a Samaritan village (v. 54): men just shown the glory of Christ are absorbed in their own standing. In the very next verse Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem (v. 51). The road to the cross is the answer to their pride, and he travels it first.

In everyday life. Rejoice when Christ is served by believers outside your own circle. Pick out a church in your town that is not yours but preaches Christ faithfully, and pray for it this week. And watch for the moment when you are more pleased that your group succeeds than that Christ is honoured.

What it does not mean. Using the name of Jesus does not make a man a true believer, and this is no licence to treat doctrine as unimportant (Matthew 7:22–23; Acts 19:13–16; Galatians 1:8). The issue here is group loyalty, not the truth of the gospel.

How do I tell a fellow worker from a false teacher? Ask what he says about Christ and the gospel, not whether he belongs to your group. Does he confess Jesus as Lord and God, crucified for sinners and risen (1 John 4:2–3; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4)? Does he preach salvation by grace through faith, not by works (Galatians 1:6–9)? Do his life and teaching honour Christ? Where those are present, rejoice in his work, even if he baptises differently, governs his church differently or sings different songs. Where the gospel itself is denied, the name of Jesus is being used, not served, and love requires us to say so.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 51–62 — The Face Set Toward Jerusalem; The Cost of Following
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus turns resolutely toward Jerusalem and the cross, and following him means walking behind him with nothing put ahead of him. Knowing what waits there, he sets his face to go (v. 51). A Samaritan village refuses him, and he rebukes not the village but the disciples who want fire from heaven (vv. 52–56). Three would-be followers meet him on the road. One learns that the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (vv. 57–58); two ask to do something “first”, and hear that not even a father’s burial or a farewell at home may come before him (vv. 59–62).
verseByVerse.theology:
Luke gives ten chapters to the journey, and the journey is a picture of discipleship: to follow Jesus is to be on the road to Jerusalem, and so to the cross.

“Leave the dead to bury their own dead” is one of the most startling sayings in the Gospels, because burying a father was a sacred duty; on the one word it refuses, see the note on vv. 59–60, and on “fit for the kingdom”, vv. 61–62.

And the fire James and John wanted is answered by the direction Jesus is walking (see the note on vv. 54–56).
verseByVerse.examples:
The three would-be followers show three ways of not following (see the note on vv. 61–62).

Luke does not tell us what any of them decided, and a comfortable church needs the first exchange plainly (see the note on vv. 57–58).

verseByVerse.quote: When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing exactly what waits for him, Jesus resolutely turns toward Jerusalem, and at the first village he is refused for it.

The journey to Jerusalem. Here Luke’s long account of the journey begins, running some ten chapters to the gates of the city (19:28; see the introduction). Everything from here on happens on a road with one destination, and much of what only Luke records is here: the good Samaritan, the prodigal son, Zacchaeus.

For him to be taken up. “When the days drew near” is literally “when the days were being fulfilled”: the time is being counted, and it is running out on purpose. Taken up (analēmpsis) is a noun used nowhere else in the New Testament. It reaches past the cross to the ascension (Acts 1:2, 11, 22): the death, the rising and the going home to the Father, in one word.

He set his face. A Hebrew way of speaking, which Luke repeats in verse 53. In the prophets, to set one’s face is the posture of a man sent with a hard commission: Ezekiel was told to set his face toward Jerusalem and preach against its sanctuaries (Ezekiel 21:2). Above all it is the Servant’s resolve in Isaiah, who sets his face like a flint in the same breath as he gives his back to those who strike and does not hide his face from spitting (Isaiah 50:6–7). So the face turned to Jerusalem already knows what waits there. He is not swept toward the cross by events; he turns and starts walking. Our salvation rests not on our resolve but on his.

Messengers ahead of him. To arrange food and lodging. The direct route from Galilee to Jerusalem ran through Samaria; some Jews went round it, adding days, though Josephus says Galilean pilgrims usually took the direct road. Jesus goes straight through.

A village of the Samaritans. The Samaritans descended from northern Israelites who intermarried with peoples settled there after the Assyrian conquest in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:24–41). Their Scriptures were the five books of Moses alone, and their holy mountain was Gerizim, not Jerusalem (John 4:20). The hostility was ancient and mutual.

They did not receive him. He was going to worship at the temple they rejected, and Samaritans were often hostile to Jewish pilgrims passing through, so the refusal is not personal. And there is an irony in it: at the very start of the journey to the cross, what he is rejected for is going to the cross.

In everyday life. Is there a hard thing God has made clear you must do? His face was set for you first, and his Spirit steadies yours: set your face, and do not wait for it to become easy. And when obedience costs you a welcome somewhere, remember that it cost him a bed at the start of the road.

Did Jesus know everything that would happen in Jerusalem? Yes. He had already told the disciples twice (vv. 22, 44), and he would tell them again in detail: “he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon” (18:32). He did not go to Jerusalem hoping for the best. He went as the Lamb who knew the altar. Every step south was taken with full knowledge, and every step was chosen. He was not a victim of circumstances but the willing Saviour.
verseByVerse.note: Here Luke’s long account of the journey to Jerusalem begins. “Taken up” points to the ascension. Samaritans lived between Galilee and Judea and were often hostile to pilgrims heading to Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: I have set my face like a flint
Jews have no dealings with Samaritans

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, 'Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?' But he turned and rebuked them. And they went on to another village.
verseByVerse.commentary:
James and John want to call down fire on the village, and Jesus rebukes them: this is the time for grace, not judgment.

Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them? Jesus called James and John Sons of Thunder (Mark 3:17), and here we see why. They ask permission; there is even deference in “do you want us to?”, which makes it more disturbing, because they expect the answer might be yes. Their precedent is scriptural. Elijah, in this same region, called down fire from heaven on soldiers sent by the king of Samaria to arrest him (2 Kings 1:9–16). These two have just come down a mountain where they saw Elijah in glory, and they had been given power (v. 1). They are reasoning from the Bible, and reasoning badly, because the situation is not the same at all. Elijah faced armed men sent by an idolatrous king to seize a prophet; James and John face a village that declined to provide beds.

He turned and rebuked them. And they went on. Luke records no word to the village at all; the rebuke goes to the disciples. This is not the time for judgment but for grace. The day of vengeance has not yet come: at Nazareth Jesus stopped reading Isaiah just before those words (4:19). No fire, no argument, no curse. They walked on to another village.

The fire that did come. Jesus would later send his gospel to Samaria (Acts 1:8), where it was received with great joy, and John himself went there with Peter to lay hands on Samaritan believers so that they received the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:5–8, 14–17). Something did come down on Samaria from heaven: not fire, but the Spirit. The Lord who could have called down fire chose instead to bear the fire of God’s wrath himself, on the cross, so that Samaritans and Galileans and we ourselves might receive his Spirit. The man who wanted to burn a Samaritan village lived to pray for Samaritans to receive the Spirit.

In everyday life. When people reject you or the gospel, resist the desire for revenge: the Lord who could have sent fire on you sent the gospel instead. When you enjoy imagining the downfall of someone who has mocked your faith or hurt you, turn the thought into a prayer for them. And be careful of using Bible verses to justify the anger you already feel.

Will God never judge, then? He will. The day of vengeance is real, and Jesus speaks of it often (17:26–30; 21:22). Those who finally reject him will face God’s just and eternal judgment (2 Thessalonians 1:7–9). But judgment belongs to God, not to us, and to the last day, not to this one. “Now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2). Our task is to warn, to plead and to pray, never to wish destruction on those who reject us: “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord” (Romans 12:19).

Doesn’t religion make people violent? This passage takes the objection more seriously than most objectors do. Here are two of Jesus’ closest friends, fresh from a mountaintop, with a precedent from Scripture in hand, asking permission to burn a village. Religious certainty can do that. But the theologian William Cavanaugh has argued that the line between “religious” and “secular” violence is far harder to draw than we assume, and the last century’s worst killing was done in the name of nation, race and class, by regimes that had abolished God. Whatever a heart treats as ultimate, it will one day be tempted to defend with fire. So the real question is not whether you have a faith but what stands at its centre. James and John wanted fire to fall on their enemies. The one they followed rebuked them, and on the night men came to arrest him, he healed the ear of one of them (22:51). A Christian who calls down fire has not taken Jesus too seriously; he has not taken him seriously enough (see also the note on 12:51).

Textual note. Some manuscripts add “as Elijah did”, and others add Jesus’ words: “You do not know what manner of spirit you are of; for the Son of Man came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them.” These words are absent from the earliest and best manuscripts, which is why modern versions put them in a footnote and one Bible may be shorter than another here. They are almost certainly not what Luke wrote: a scribe appears to have supplied a rebuke Luke deliberately left unstated, and once written in a margin it moved into the text. Yet the added sentence is entirely true, and true from Luke’s own pages: “The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (19:10) is in this Gospel in Jesus’ own words, and within one chapter the hero of his most famous story will be a Samaritan (10:33). The copyist guessed the theology exactly right. He simply had no business putting his guess into the Gospel.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “as Elijah did,” and a further saying: “You do not know what manner of spirit you are of; for the Son of Man came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them.”

verseByVerse.quote: As they were going along the road, someone said to him, 'I will follow you wherever you go.' And Jesus said to him, 'Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
To an eager volunteer Jesus tells the truth: following him means giving up home and security, as he has.

Three would-be followers. Three short encounters on the road (vv. 57–62) cover between them most of the ways a person fails to follow.

Wherever you go. Nobody called this man. He volunteers everything, sincerely, perhaps impulsively. Matthew tells us he was a scribe (Matthew 8:19), used to attaching himself to a teacher. Does he know where Jesus is going? To Jerusalem, to the cross.

Foxes have holes … but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. Not a refusal but a disclosure: Jesus does not take advantage of enthusiasm. The animals of the land he made have somewhere to sleep. He had left his home in Nazareth, and had just been refused lodging in Samaria; the man has said “wherever you go” on a road where the last village would not have him. The Lord of heaven and earth, for whom all things were made, had nowhere to lay his head, and on the cross he bowed his head (John 19:30) in the only rest the world gave him. Following him means giving up security and comfort. Count the cost first (14:28).

What a comfortable church needs to hear. A certain kind of preaching promises that coming to Christ secures a settled, prosperous life. The one making this offer had nowhere to sleep and was walking towards an execution, and he told the volunteer so before he signed. Luke does not tell us what any of the three decided; the question is left standing for the reader.

In everyday life. Before you make a large promise to God, count what it may cost, and then make it anyway, leaning on his grace rather than your enthusiasm. And if you are helping someone come to faith, tell them honestly about the road.

Must every Christian give up their home? No. Jesus’ followers included people with houses, like Martha (10:38), and Peter kept his house in Capernaum. Jesus was not laying down a rule that disciples must be homeless, but telling a volunteer the truth about the road. What every disciple must do is hold home, comfort and security loosely, ready to lose them if following Christ requires it, as many believers around the world do today. A Christian may have a home; he may not make it his foundation. The question is whether you would still follow if it cost you the house.

verseByVerse.quote: To another he said, 'Follow me.' But he said, 'Lord, let me first go and bury my father.' And Jesus said to him, 'Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls a man to follow him now, and refuses to let even the sacred duty of a father’s burial come first.

Follow me. This one is called, with the two words said to Levi at the tax booth (5:27) and, in Mark, to fishermen at a lakeside (Mark 1:17).

Lord, let me first go and bury my father. The most reasonable sentence in the chapter. Burying a father was a sacred duty in Judaism, so important that, according to later Jewish writings, it overrode other religious obligations, like reciting the Shema. A son who did not bury his father had failed to honour him. Whatever the exact situation (see below), the man puts something else first, and that is why the answer lands as it does. Jesus is not being cold about a coffin. He is refusing one word, and the word is “first”.

Leave the dead to bury their own dead. A deliberately paradoxical saying: let the spiritually dead bury the physically dead. The village will manage the funeral; it cannot manage the proclamation. The kingdom is more urgent than even the most sacred family duty. He did not come to bury the dead but to raise them, and his call goes out to the spiritually dead with power to make them live.

Go and proclaim. The commission explains the severity: he is not told to abandon his family for nothing, but given an urgent errand.

The Lord who has the right to come first. The fifth commandment, to honour father and mother, stands under the first, to have no other gods, and here Jesus claims the place the first gives to God: no duty, however sacred, may stand in front of following him. That is the honest answer to the objection that this sounds like a cult leader cutting a man off from his family. From any mere man it would be. The demand is right only if the one making it is God, which is what this chapter has been showing. And the one who claims it honoured his own Father perfectly, all the way to Gethsemane: “not my will, but yours, be done” (22:42). His claim is the call of the Son who first put his Father before his own life.

In everyday life. What do you want to do first, before following Jesus fully? There will always be one more reasonable thing to finish first, and it is because such things are reasonable that they delay us so well. Name your “first”, and give it to him. Whatever you put first is your real lord.

What it does not mean. No Christian may use this to neglect his parents or stay away from funerals; Jesus condemned the Pharisees for using religion to avoid caring for parents (Mark 7:9–13). And if you have lately buried a parent, nothing here faults your grief or your care: Jesus himself wept at a friend’s tomb (John 11:35).

What if my family really does need me? Then caring for them may be exactly the way you follow Christ. Providing for your family and honouring your parents are Christian duties (1 Timothy 5:4, 8), and Jesus provided for his own mother from the cross (John 19:26–27). The man in this passage was not caring for his father; he was using him as a reason to delay obeying Christ. Duty done for Christ is following; duty used against Christ is the “first” that he refuses.

Uncertain wording. Was the father already dead? The words could mean either. But in that world burial happened the same day, or the next at the latest; if the father had just died, the son would be at the tomb, not standing on a road listening to a travelling preacher. More likely the father was still alive and the man meant: let me wait until he has died. That would be a request to put off following for years, until the duty was done, the inheritance settled, and he was free to go with nothing owing. Either way the point stands: he wanted something else first.
verseByVerse.note: Burying a father was a sacred duty; the man may have meant waiting until his father died.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet another said, 'I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.' Jesus said to him, 'No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Following Jesus allows no backward look: he must come before even a farewell at home.

Let me first say farewell. The third man volunteers like the first and asks for a delay like the second, and his request is the smallest: to go home and say goodbye.

The precedent of Elisha. When Elijah threw his cloak over Elisha at the plough, Elisha asked to kiss his father and his mother goodbye, and Elijah allowed it (1 Kings 19:19–21). He went back, burned his ploughing equipment, and followed. So the man is asking for what the prophet allowed, and this time the answer is no. Jesus demands more than Elijah, because he is more than Elijah.

Hand to the plow. Elisha destroyed the plough; this man wants to keep the option of the house. The ancient plough was light and single-handled, steered by eye on a fixed point ahead, and a ploughman who turns to look behind loses the line in a moment. A divided heart, half looking back to the old life, cannot plough straight for the kingdom. Lot’s wife looked back (Genesis 19:26; Luke 17:32). The issue is not affection for home but that the eyes are not on the work.

Fit for the kingdom. Fit (euthetos) means suitable, useful, well placed for a purpose. Not that he cannot be saved, but that half-hearted discipleship is useless for kingdom work.

The three obstacles. Comfort (v. 58), duty (v. 60) and family affection (v. 61): all good things, and none can come before Christ. The first would not count the cost; the second and third both said “first”. None of them is told he cannot come.

In the flow. The chapter that began with the Twelve sent out with nothing ends with three would-be followers learning that nothing may come before him. The next chapter sends out seventy-two more (10:1; some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read seventy).

One man never looked back. One man in this chapter put his hand to the plough and never looked back. Through the refusal of a Samaritan village, the failure of his friends and the darkness of the cross, he kept his eyes on Jerusalem until the work was done, and his last word there was a prayer of trust: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit” (23:46). Because he did not turn back, the furrow is cut: his unbroken obedience is counted as ours, and people who have looked back a thousand times are counted fit in him.

The tyranny of keeping your options open. Our culture has turned the backward look into a way of life: the dating app kept after the third date, the job search open in another tab, every commitment provisional in case something better appears. The American writer Pete Davis called it Infinite Browsing Mode, keeping every door open because closing any of them feels like a loss. It promises freedom and delivers a strange paralysis, a life spent in the corridor, never quite inside any room. Jesus is telling the third man the truth about how a furrow is cut and how a life is made: by putting your hand to something and not looking round. But the gospel goes deeper than good advice about commitment. We can give ourselves to Christ without reserve because he gave himself to us first, with no exit clause, all the way to a cross. He did not keep his options open. That is why we can close ours, and find that the narrow road is the one with room in it.

In everyday life. Is there an option you are keeping open, a relationship, a habit, a way back, in case following him does not work out? Close it this week, as Elisha burned his plough.

Is it wrong to miss my old life? Not in itself. Feelings of loss are human, and Christ is not offended by honest grief over what following him has cost. The danger is the backward look that wants to return, the heart that keeps the old life as an option in case Christ does not prove worth it. Paul counted everything as loss compared with knowing Christ, forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead (Philippians 3:8, 13–14). The cure for looking back is not trying harder not to look, but fixing your eyes on what is ahead: on “Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith” (Hebrews 12:2).
verseByVerse.note: A ploughman had to keep his eyes forward to cut a straight furrow.

parallels.desc: Elisha asks to kiss his parents goodbye

9.text: <sup>1</sup> And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, <sup>2</sup> and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. <sup>3</sup> And he said to them, “Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. <sup>4</sup> And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart. <sup>5</sup> And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.” <sup>6</sup> And they departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere. <sup>7</sup> Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead, <sup>8</sup> by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the prophets of old had risen. <sup>9</sup> Herod said, “John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?” And he sought to see him. <sup>10</sup> On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. <sup>11</sup> When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing. <sup>12</sup> Now the day began to wear away, and the twelve came and said to him, “Send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.” <sup>13</sup> But he said to them, “You give them something to eat.” They said, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.” <sup>14</sup> For there were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, “Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.” <sup>15</sup> And they did so, and had them all sit down. <sup>16</sup> And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd. <sup>17</sup> And they all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces. <sup>18</sup> Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. And he asked them, “Who do the crowds say that I am?” <sup>19</sup> And they answered, “John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen.” <sup>20</sup> Then he said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” And Peter answered, “The Christ of God.” <sup>21</sup> And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one, <sup>22</sup> saying, “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.” <sup>23</sup> And he said to all, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. <sup>24</sup> For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it. <sup>25</sup> For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? <sup>26</sup> For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. <sup>27</sup> But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” <sup>28</sup> Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. <sup>29</sup> And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white. <sup>30</sup> And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, <sup>31</sup> who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. <sup>32</sup> Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. <sup>33</sup> And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah”—not knowing what he said. <sup>34</sup> As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. <sup>35</sup> And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” <sup>36</sup> And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen. <sup>37</sup> On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. <sup>38</sup> And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, “Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child. <sup>39</sup> And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. <sup>40</sup> And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.” <sup>41</sup> Jesus answered, “O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.” <sup>42</sup> While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. <sup>43</sup> And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marveling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples, <sup>44</sup> “Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.” <sup>45</sup> But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying. <sup>46</sup> An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. <sup>47</sup> But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side <sup>48</sup> and said to them, “Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.” <sup>49</sup> John answered, “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.” <sup>50</sup> But Jesus said to him, “Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.” <sup>51</sup> When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. <sup>52</sup> And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. <sup>53</sup> But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem. <sup>54</sup> And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, “Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” <sup>55</sup> But he turned and rebuked them. <sup>56</sup> And they went on to another village. <sup>57</sup> As they were going along the road, someone said to him, “I will follow you wherever you go.” <sup>58</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” <sup>59</sup> To another he said, “Follow me.” But he said, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.” <sup>60</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” <sup>61</sup> Yet another said, “I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.” <sup>62</sup> Jesus said to him, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

keyVerse.quote: And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!”
keyVerse.note: Herod asks who Jesus is (v. 9) and Peter answers rightly (v. 20), but here the Father gives the last word: Jesus is his own Son, the chosen Servant, above Moses and Elijah. The one command in the scene is aimed at disciples who did not want to hear about the cross, and it gathers up the chapter: listen to him when he says the Son of Man must suffer, and when he says, “take up his cross daily and follow me.”

9.reflection:
The crowds called Jesus a prophet; Peter called him “The Christ of God” (vv. 18–20). What smaller answers do people around you give about Jesus, and how would you explain, from this chapter, why they are too small? What difference does your own answer make on an ordinary Monday?

Jesus tells everyone to deny himself and take up his cross daily (vv. 23–26). In your life, what would that look like this week, and where are you most tempted to go quiet because you are ashamed of him or his words?

On the mountain Moses and Elijah spoke of Jesus’ “departure” at Jerusalem, and the Father said, “listen to him!” (vv. 30–35). Why do you think the disciples found it so hard to hear what Jesus said about the cross (vv. 44–45)? Which of his words do you find hardest to listen to?

In verses 46–62 the disciples argue about rank, shut out an outsider and want fire on a village, and three would-be followers each want something “first”. Which of these responses do you recognise in yourself or your church, and how does Jesus setting his face toward Jerusalem answer it?

10.title: The Seventy-Two, the Samaritan, and the Better Part
10.overview:
