Where we are. Chapter 10 is the first stage of the long journey to Jerusalem (9:51–19:27). Jesus has set his face toward the cross; now he sends a wider circle ahead of him and teaches what belonging to his kingdom means.

The message. The kingdom of God has come near in Jesus, and everything depends on how you receive him. Refusing him is the gravest thing a town or a person can do (vv. 1–16). The kingdom’s true joy is not power but belonging, names written in heaven (vv. 17–24). It cannot be earned by keeping the law, and the law may not be shrunk to fit us (vv. 25–37). And its life begins not in anxious serving but at Jesus’ feet, receiving (vv. 38–42).

Why it was said. Luke’s largely Gentile readers (see the introduction) needed to know that the mission which reached them was Jesus’ own, pointed at the nations from the first, and that a Samaritan could be the hero and a woman a disciple. And every reader shares the lawyer’s instinct, to ask how little love we can get away with, and Martha’s, to serve the Lord until we forget to listen to him.

How the chapter makes its case. The sending (vv. 1–16) shows the kingdom arriving through vulnerable, urgent messengers: to reject them is to reject Christ and the Father. Their return (vv. 17–24) shows that small mission from heaven’s side, Satan falling, and turns their joy from what they can do to what has been done for them, as Jesus exults in the Father’s gracious will. A lawyer’s question (vv. 25–37) brings in the law’s two great commands, and the Samaritan shows how far the second reaches. Martha and Mary (vv. 38–42) answer the first: love for God begins at his feet.

Where it leads. Every scene points to Jesus. The kingdom is near because he is near; only he saw Satan fall, knows whose names are written, and makes the Father known. He alone would keep the law he hands back to the lawyer, and the Samaritan who stops on the bloody road, binds the wounds at his own cost and promises to return is the outline of the one telling the story, on his way to Jerusalem to pay for us. The good portion Mary chose is the Lord himself.

For us. Pray for labourers, and expect to be sent. Do not measure yourself by results; rejoice that your name is written. Stop asking who your neighbour is, and go and be one. And before you serve, sit down and listen. The one who asks all this has already crossed the road to you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Jesus Sends Out the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom of God has come near in Jesus, and how people receive his messengers is how they receive him. He sends seventy-two ahead of him in pairs, telling them first to pray for more labourers and warning them that they go as lambs among wolves (vv. 1–3). They travel light and in haste, offer peace to every house, stay where they are welcomed, heal the sick and announce the kingdom (vv. 4–9). A town that refuses them still hears the announcement on the way out, and faces a judgment heavier than Sodom’s (vv. 10–12); Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, which saw most of his works, a heavier one than Tyre and Sidon’s (vv. 13–15). For whoever rejects the messengers rejects Christ, and the Father who sent him (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Verse 16 governs all Christian mission, and its authority belongs to the message, not to the messenger (see the note on v. 16).

The woes teach that judgment is weighed by the light received (see the notes on vv. 10–12 and 13–15).
verseByVerse.examples: The word to Chorazin, and the comparison with Sodom (see the notes on vv. 10–12 and 13–15), bite hardest on anyone with a Bible on the shelf and a lifetime of sermons behind him.

verseByVerse.quote: After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. And he said to them, 'The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sends a wider circle ahead of him, and the first thing he tells them to do is pray for more workers. Only Luke records this second sending: the mission is not for the Twelve alone, and the harvest belongs to the Lord who sends.

Seventy-two others. The Twelve were sent in chapter 9; now a larger group goes out as Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem. The number has Old Testament echoes. The elders Moses appointed to carry a burden he could not carry alone numbered seventy, but two more left in the camp prophesied anyway (Numbers 11:16, 26); and the table of nations in Genesis 10 comes to seventy in the Hebrew and seventy-two in the Greek. Twelve for the tribes of Israel; seventy-two for the whole earth. This mission is pointed outward.

Two by two. Not only for company, though that helps on a dark road. Under the law a matter was established by two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and what these men carry is testimony. Pairs are harder to discredit and harder to discourage (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10).

Where he himself was about to go. They are an advance party, like John the Baptist preparing the way: the messenger arrives first, and the Lord follows into the place the message has opened. No believer ever goes anywhere for Christ where Christ is not already on his way.

The harvest is plentiful. We picture evangelism as a thin crop in a resistant field. Jesus says the field is not the problem; it is ready (John 4:35–38). Harvest is also, in the prophets and in John’s preaching, a picture of the end (3:17), so the image carries both urgency and hope: the crop is ripe, and ripe crops do not wait.

Pray earnestly. Faced with a shortage of workers, he does not first say “go” but “pray”, to men he is about to send out that very hour. The verb (deēthēte) means beg, plead, and the one begged owns the field: “the Lord of the harvest”, “his harvest”. The labour shortage is finally his problem, and he has told us how to raise it with him. “Send out” (ekballō) is often used for driving out, even of demons, and probably keeps some of its force: workers often have to be pushed into the harvest, by a God who overcomes their reluctance, rearranges their lives and sometimes uses hardship to get them moving.

The Lord appointed. Luke calls Jesus simply “the Lord” as the chapter opens. The harvest the Father owns is the harvest the Son has come to gather, and no one goes into it whom he has not appointed: mission begins in his choice, not our enthusiasm. He went into the field first, the true seed that fell into the ground and died so that it might bear much fruit (John 12:24). Every labourer since follows him into a harvest he has already secured, and the gathering in will be his glory, not ours.

What does praying for labourers look like in practice? Name real places and people: your church’s need for teachers and youth leaders, a missionary you know, an unreached people group, your own street. Pray for preachers and church planters, and for ordinary believers who will speak of Christ at work and at home. Pray for your own children and grandchildren to be among those sent, which is harder than it sounds. Hold your hands open while you pray, because the Lord of the harvest may answer by sending you, to the next room or the next continent.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “seventy” here and at v. 17, and they divide almost evenly, so translations differ. Nothing much hangs on it: the Old Testament supplies both figures, and a copyist who knew one could easily have changed the other to match.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read seventy. The number may recall the nations listed in Genesis 10, or the seventy elders who helped Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sends his messengers out defenceless and in haste, wholly dependent on God, because the task is urgent and he is their Shepherd.

Lambs in the midst of wolves. He says it as he sends them. A lamb among wolves is not an underdog with a fighting chance; it is food, and no shepherd ever put one there on purpose, which is exactly what he says he is doing. The whole security of the arrangement lies in the one doing the sending.

No moneybag, no knapsack. The list is close to the Twelve’s (9:3); “no sandals” probably means no spare pair. No wallet, no bag, no change of shoes for a journey on foot: total dependence on God, shown as plainly as possible. They will eat because God has gone before them into the houses.

Greet no one on the road. A roadside greeting could be a long exchange of embraces, family news and invitations to stay. Elisha, sending Gehazi urgently to a dead child, told him not to greet anyone on the way (2 Kings 4:29). This is a rule not about manners but about urgency: the courtesies of the road must not eat the daylight.

The design, not a fault. The mission is meant to be vulnerable, because it is the way he is going himself. These men go ahead of a Lord who has set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51) and has twice told them he must suffer (9:22, 44). The lambs walk the road of the Shepherd who will lay down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). A church that has made itself safe, powerful and protected has stepped off his road; the gospel of a crucified Lord has always travelled best in the hands of people who could be hurt.

In everyday life. Take the thing God has plainly given you to do, a conversation you owe a friend, a reconciliation, a call to a lonely relative, and ask what courtesies, hobbies and screens keep eating the daylight. And if you feel exposed as a Christian at work or at home, you were never promised the wolves would be tame. You were promised a Shepherd.

Does this mean Christian workers today should go without money or supplies? No. These instructions were for one short, urgent mission inside Israel, where hospitality to travelling teachers was expected, and Jesus later reverses them: “now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack” (22:35–36). Paul travelled with funds, received gifts and sometimes worked with his hands. What carries over is not the packing list but the posture: go in dependence on God, do not let comfort set the terms of obedience, and do not let lesser things crowd out what is urgent.
verseByVerse.note: Travellers’ greetings could be long and elaborate; there was no time for them.

parallels.desc: if you meet anyone, do not greet him

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house!’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The messengers offer Christ’s peace to every house and stay content with whoever receives it. That peace settles on a heart God has prepared or comes back unspent, and those who carry it are rightly supported by those they serve.

Peace be to this house! The greeting (shalom) means wholeness, a life not at war with God or with itself. From a man sent by Jesus it is not a pleasantry but the peace the angels sang over Bethlehem (2:14), and the next sentence treats it as something that goes somewhere, settles or does not, and can come back.

A son of peace. A Hebrew idiom: a person who belongs to the peace being offered and is ready for it, prepared before the messengers arrived. Evangelism is not manufacturing interest out of nothing; much of the work is finding the one whose heart God has made ready, as the Lord opened Lydia’s heart before Paul finished speaking (Acts 16:14).

It will return to you. Nothing is lost. Like the dove that found no place to rest and came back to Noah’s hand (Genesis 8:9), a blessing refused comes back to the one who offered it: a quiet mercy for every believer who has spoken, been rebuffed, and felt he had spent something he could not get back.

Remain in the same house. The rule is the Twelve’s, for the same reason: a messenger who moves to a better house has begun working for comfort, and one who depends on an important host’s goodwill will sooner or later soften his message to keep it.

The laborer deserves his wages. Paul quotes this saying as Scripture, beside the law not to muzzle an ox (1 Timothy 5:18; Deuteronomy 25:4): within the apostles’ lifetime a saying of Jesus stood beside the Law of Moses under the heading “the Scripture says”. Those who work for the gospel have a right to be supported by those they serve (1 Corinthians 9:14). It is not charity; it is wages earned.

Peace to you. The peace is his before it is theirs. The crowds will shout it as he rides into Jerusalem (19:38), he will weep that the city did not know the things that make for peace (19:42), and on the evening of the resurrection he will stand among frightened disciples and say, “Peace to you!” (24:36). The seventy-two speak a peace they cannot yet explain; one day he will speak it himself, risen, to men who had failed him. It was bought by the one who made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), and every time it rests on a son of peace, a war that began in Eden ends in one more heart.

Should I give to my church if I am not sure the money is well used? Give, and gladly: supporting those who teach you is obedience to Christ, not a favour to an institution (Galatians 6:6). But you are not asked to give blindly. A faithful church is open about its finances; if you have real concerns, raise them with the elders, privately and kindly. What you should not do is let vague suspicion become a permanent excuse for keeping back what Jesus says the labourer deserves.
verseByVerse.note: A “son of peace” means a person open to God’s peace.

verseByVerse.quote: Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. Heal the sick in it and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where the messengers are welcomed, they accept what is offered, heal the sick and announce that God’s kingdom has come near.

Eat what is set before you. More than manners is at stake. These Jewish men may have entered homes where not every kitchen kept the food laws, which marked Israel off from the nations at every meal. Many readers think Luke, writing for a Gentile church, sees where that leads: in his second volume Peter will be told, “What God has made clean, do not call common” (Acts 10:14–15), and within days he will be in a Roman centurion’s house. Paul gives the same rule (1 Corinthians 10:27). And to eat what a poor household sets before you, without inspecting it, is to accept the person; anyone fed by people who had very little knows that scrutinising the meal would have been the one unforgivable thing.

Heal the sick. Healing is not a tactic to win a hearing; healing and word are one announcement made in two ways, that the King has arrived. Wherever he goes, sickness and death begin to retreat: the first light of the morning in which he will wipe away every tear and death shall be no more (Revelation 21:4).

Has come near. Not that the kingdom will come, but that it has come near. The verb (ēngiken) describes something that has happened and still stands: it has drawn near and is at the door, and 11:20 will say plainly that it has come. God’s kingdom is his rule putting the world right: sin forgiven, sickness healed, the devil’s grip broken. It is near because the King is near, on his way through these very towns (v. 1): close enough to be reached, and demanding a response.

Is “heal the sick” a command to the church today? It belonged to this mission, whose signs confirmed the kingdom’s arrival in Jesus. Many Christians, Pentecostal and charismatic believers among them, hold that such healing gifts continue, and they should be heard charitably; this commentary takes the view called cessationism, judging it the more likely reading, that the sign gifts belonged to the foundational time when Christ and his apostles were establishing the word (Hebrews 2:3–4). But God still heals. The church still prays for the sick, the elders anointing and praying in faith (James 5:14–15), and God often answers, through medicine and sometimes beyond it. And the heart of the command, the message that the kingdom has come near, goes on until he returns.

parallels.desc: eat whatever is set before you

verseByVerse.quote: But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say, ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near.’ I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A town that refuses the messengers is solemnly warned, hears the offer once more, and faces a judgment heavier than Sodom’s, because it has refused more light.

Even the dust of your town. They are not to leave quietly but to make a public announcement in the street, the last thing a rejected messenger would want to do. The gesture is the Twelve’s (9:5): the dust a devout Jew shook off on returning from pagan ground. Performed in an Israelite street, it says that by refusing the King this town has put itself outside God’s people; being born in Israel no longer decides who is inside.

Nevertheless know this. Almost word for word what they say to the towns that receive them (v. 9); the only difference is the “nevertheless”. So the last thing a rejecting town hears is not a curse but the offer repeated, a final warning that is still an invitation. The kingdom came as near to that town as to the village that took the messengers in, but having it near is not the same as receiving it. It walked up the street.

More bearable for Sodom. Sodom is the Bible’s byword for a place beyond saving (Genesis 19), and a Galilean village that turned away two travelling preachers will fare worse, not because refusing hospitality is worse than Sodom’s sins, but because nobody ever announced the kingdom in Sodom’s streets or healed her sick in the market square. These towns had it, in daylight, and preferred not to. “On that day”, the day of judgment, verdicts are weighed: there are degrees of punishment according to privilege and knowledge (12:47–48; Matthew 11:22–24; Romans 2:12). Every sentence is just, and sentences differ, because the Judge knows exactly what each person was given.

The Judge who held back the fire. The one who speaks of Sodom was himself refused by a Samaritan village a few verses earlier, and when James and John asked to call fire down on it, he rebuked them (9:52–55). He is not soft on judgment; he claims to know what the last day holds for every town in Galilee. But he will not bring that day early. He sends the offer instead, because the Judge of that day is first on his way to Jerusalem, to bear judgment himself.

Is it right for Christians to walk away from people who reject the gospel? The gesture was a solemn act by commissioned messengers on a short, urgent mission, not a licence to write people off. We still warn plainly, and we may move on from those who will not hear when others are waiting (Acts 13:51; 18:6). But we keep praying and leave the door open, because Paul himself had once been on the rejecting side. With friends and family, keep loving, keep living the gospel, and speak again when God gives an opening. Judgment belongs to God, not to our frustration.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The towns that saw most of Jesus’ mighty works and stayed unchanged face the heaviest judgment of all. Judgment is measured by what people were given, and few were given more.

Woe to you, Chorazin! Among the most severe words in Luke, and they fall not on Rome or the Sanhedrin but on three small towns at the north end of the Sea of Galilee, where he had done most of his work. Chorazin appears in the New Testament only here and in Matthew 11:21, and no miracle done there is recorded; yet Jesus speaks of “the mighty works done in you” as though everyone knew (John 21:25).

Tyre and Sidon. Wealthy pagan ports, denounced by the prophets for pride and cruelty (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28); a Galilean would have filed them under hopeless. Sackcloth and ashes were the marks of repentance, as when the king of Nineveh came down from his throne (Jonah 3:6). And Jesus says they would have repented long ago: he knows what people would have done in circumstances they were never given.

And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? Capernaum was his base after Nazareth threw him out (4:31): there he taught in the synagogue, healed Peter’s mother-in-law, and emptied a street of its sick in one evening. Yet the most privileged village in Galilee is addressed in the taunt Isaiah aimed at the king of Babylon, the Bible’s great example of proud rebellion, who said in his heart “I will ascend to heaven” and was told “you are brought down to Sheol” (Isaiah 14:13–15). Hades is the Greek name for Sheol, the realm of the dead; here it is the place of judgment. Chorazin and Capernaum are ruins today, and even the site of Bethsaida is disputed.

The mighty works done in you. Everything turns on whose works they were. The miracles of Galilee were the signs Isaiah said would mark God’s own coming to save: the blind seeing, the lame leaping, the deaf hearing (Isaiah 35:4–6), the credentials Jesus pointed John the Baptist to (7:22). These towns had watched the Lord arrive in their streets and gone on as before. The measure of judgment is nearness to Christ himself, and few towns on earth had stood nearer.

Woes from the one who wept. They are spoken by the one who wept over Jerusalem (19:41), not as a judge glad to be rid of a case but as one whose love was spurned, and who goes on to Jerusalem to die for sinners no better than Chorazin. The Lord who weighs light so exactly gave the greatest light of all, himself, and still says to every town and every heart: come.

In everyday life. If you grew up hearing the gospel, ask honestly whether you have more light than you are walking in. Capernaum’s danger was not open hostility but a town that had seen it all and stayed the same. If you ask because you fear you have grown cold, take heart: Capernaum never asked. Numbness in grief, illness or depression is not the hardness Jesus condemns here, and a heart that grieves over its own dullness is already being stirred by him.

If Tyre and Sidon would have repented, why did God not send them these miracles? God gives light as he wills, and owes it to no one: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy” (Romans 9:15–16). We are not told why he chose Galilee and not Phoenicia, but we are told enough not to accuse him. Those who received more are judged more strictly, and those who had less are judged by what they had. The towns that saw and did not repent are condemned for their own refusal, not for a decree they were trying to obey. “The secret things belong to the LORD our God” (Deuteronomy 29:29); what is revealed is that the light came, and they would not walk in it.
verseByVerse.note: Chorazin and Bethsaida were towns near Capernaum at the north end of the lake. Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities. Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: 'The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
To hear or reject Christ’s messengers is to hear or reject Christ himself, and the Father who sent him. One sentence holds the whole doctrine of Christian mission.

The one who hears you hears me. Follow the chain backwards: the Father sends the Son, the Son sends the seventy-two, so what is done to them is done to the Son, and to the Father. When Saul persecuted the church, the risen Lord asked him, “why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). An authorised envoy carried his sender’s standing; the rabbis said a man’s representative is as the man himself. Jesus puts ordinary men, with no money, no bag and no spare sandals, in that position, joined by a direct line to the throne of heaven.

A comfort and a weight. A believer stammering through the gospel to a colleague is not sharing a personal opinion; if the colleague hears, he has heard Christ. That is the comfort. The weight is that there is no neutral response to the gospel faithfully spoken, and the person declining is not declining you. The refusal is no verdict on you, and nothing to be casual about.

The authority of preaching. When the word of God is faithfully preached, Christ himself speaks: “how are they to hear without someone preaching?” (Romans 10:14–17); “we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us” (2 Corinthians 5:20). The preacher is not the source of the authority, but his message, if true to Scripture, carries Christ’s. The Second Helvetic Confession (1566) puts it boldly: “The preaching of the word of God is the word of God.”

Carried by such as us. The Father sent the Son, and the Son has never stopped sending. How kind of God, that the voice which called the worlds into being should be willing to be carried by such as us, and should count the welcome given to his smallest messenger as a welcome given to himself.

What it does not mean. Without its one limit the verse becomes a tool for tyrants, and it has been misused to shield leaders from criticism. The authority belongs to what the messenger says from Christ, not to whatever he happens to want. A sermon carries Christ’s authority exactly as far as it says what Scripture says, and the Bereans were commended for checking Paul against it (Acts 17:11).

How do I tell when a preacher is speaking with Christ’s authority? Open your Bible during the sermon and ask whether the point is actually in the passage. Where it plainly is, receive it as Christ’s word to you, however unwelcome or plainly delivered. Where he adds his own views on politics, schooling or methods, weigh them as one man’s counsel. If he contradicts Scripture, speak to him privately, and if necessary to the elders. The authority is in the word, not the voice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — The Return of the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The greatest joy is not what we can do for God but what he has done for us, and Jesus himself shares that joy with the Father. The seventy-two come back amazed that demons obeyed them; Jesus tells them he saw Satan fall, and confirms their authority (vv. 17–19), but turns their joy to their names written in heaven (v. 20). Then, in one of the few places Luke tells us what Jesus felt, he exults in the Holy Spirit, thanks the Father for revealing these things to little children, and claims that only he can make the Father known (vv. 21–22). Privately he tells his disciples how blessed they are: they see what prophets and kings longed to see (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology:
Father, Son and Spirit meet in one sentence at v. 21 (see the note on vv. 21–22). The joy of God overflows into the mission and into those who share it.

Verses 21–22 are among the highest claims Jesus makes in the first three Gospels (see the note on vv. 21–22). The dividing line is whether a man will come with empty hands.
verseByVerse.examples:
The register of names in heaven belongs in the hands of every believer who measures himself by usefulness (see the note on v. 20).

And verses 23–24 rebuke the boredom of long familiarity (see the note on vv. 23–24).

verseByVerse.quote: The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, 'Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!' And he said to them, 'I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventy-two’s small mission was part of Satan’s downfall, and Jesus saw it happen.

The seventy-two returned with joy. Joy runs through Luke, from the angels’ “good news of great joy” (2:10) to the disciples’ return to Jerusalem “with great joy” (24:52); here it is the joy of men who have seen God at work through their own unremarkable hands. And “even” gives them away: they expected the preaching and the healings to work (v. 9), but not that demons would obey them. Yet they say carefully how it happened: “in your name”. Whatever the exhilaration, they know whose authority it was.

I saw Satan fall. It may look back to Satan’s first fall (Isaiah 14:12 is often read this way), or forward to the cross and the final defeat (Revelation 12:9–11). But the context favours what has just happened: they came back talking about demons submitting, and his answer begins “I saw”. He is telling them what their tour looked like from where he stood. The kingdom of God is overthrowing the kingdom of Satan (11:20–22), and the decisive blow would fall at the cross, when the ruler of this world was cast out (John 12:31) and the powers were disarmed and put to open shame (Colossians 2:15). Like lightning: sudden, not a slow retreat; and downward, so whatever height the adversary held, he is not holding it.

The Son who made him fall. The Son who saw Satan fall is the Son who made him fall: he went to the cross, where the serpent bruised his heel, and crushed the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). So there is no ordinary Christian work. Seventy-two men had spent their tour in small towns nobody has heard of, saying an unimpressive sentence to farmers, and the Son of God, watching the same tour, saw the ruler of this world come down out of the sky. There is only work whose real size cannot be seen by those doing it.

If Satan is defeated, why is there still so much evil? Because he is defeated but not yet destroyed. The decisive battle was won at the cross, and his final end in the lake of fire is certain (Revelation 20:10). Meanwhile he is like an enemy whose capital has fallen, still dangerous in retreat. He prowls like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8), and we resist him, firm in faith. But he cannot take back one person Christ has rescued, and every time the gospel is believed his kingdom shrinks again. We fight from victory, not toward it.

parallels.desc: how you are fallen from heaven

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gives his messengers authority over all the enemy’s power, and promises that nothing can finally harm them. The promise is victory over evil, not immunity from pain.

Serpents and scorpions. The language comes from Psalm 91:13: “You will tread on the lion and the adder.” Serpents and scorpions are biblical shorthand for hostile and demonic power, reaching back to the serpent in the garden (Genesis 3:15), and the next clause names the enemy: Satan.

Nothing shall hurt you. Read as bodily immunity, the phrase is contradicted by almost everyone who first heard it. James was killed with the sword (Acts 12:2); Stephen was stoned; Paul was beaten and shipwrecked, though he once shook a viper into the fire unharmed (Acts 28:3–6), which shows that God can preserve, not that he always will. Luke puts both halves in one breath: “some of you they will put to death”, but “not a hair of your head will perish” (21:16–18). The enemy cannot finally destroy them; nothing can separate them from the love of God (Romans 8:35–39).

He trod on the serpent first. He gives authority over serpents because he has already trodden on the serpent. In the wilderness he would not use the promise to save himself; on the cross he would not come down to save himself; and so he saved us. “Nothing shall hurt you” is a promise only he could make, because he let everything hurt him, and rose. Our safety is his wounds.

What it does not mean. Set beside the longer ending of Mark (Mark 16:18; those verses are missing from the earliest manuscripts), this verse has been made the charter of snake-handling churches, where people have died. But Jesus is describing authority over demons, not inviting anyone to pick up vipers. And Psalm 91 is the very psalm the devil quoted in the wilderness, urging Jesus to throw himself from the temple, and Jesus refused: “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” (4:9–12). To engineer a danger to make God prove a promise is not faith; Jesus called it temptation.

In everyday life. If you are troubled by fear of curses, spirits or the occult, or haunted by a dark past, take your stand on Christ’s finished work, renounce any involvement plainly, and pray in his name; you do not need to perform anything.

Does every believer have this authority over the enemy? Every believer is protected by Christ: “he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4), and “the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). We resist the devil by faith, prayer and the word, and he flees (James 4:7). But the particular commission and signs belonged to the seventy-two’s mission, and a Christian needs no formulas, shouted commands or rituals to be safe. Jesus himself at once points away from the power to the greater thing (v. 20).

parallels.desc: you will tread on the lion and the adder

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The deepest joy is not in what we can do for God but in belonging to him: our names are written in heaven.

Do not rejoice in this. He does not call the joy wrong, only misdirected. It was about what they could do, and a joy resting on results comes and goes with them: there will be days like the one at the foot of the mountain, when the disciples tried and nothing happened (9:40), and the results are not in your hands. Spiritual power can also feed pride: some on the last day will say, “did we not … cast out demons in your name?”, and be told, “I never knew you” (Matthew 7:22–23). Power in ministry proves nothing about the heart.

Your names are written in heaven. The tense means written and still written. The image is a citizen register, the roll of those who belong to a city: the book of life (Exodus 32:32; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 20:12). It is the reverse of what they were celebrating at every point. The authority was given for a task; the name is written for good. The authority varies with the day; the writing was done before they were sent and is not under review. The authority is theirs to exercise; the name was entered by someone else. And it is written in heaven, the one place no enemy can reach.

Election. Election is God’s choosing of particular people for himself, an act of love whose reason lies in him, not in them. The names were written before the foundation of the world (Revelation 17:8; Ephesians 1:4). Joy rests on grace, not on performance.

Who can read the register? Only someone who has seen it. Having said, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (v. 18), Jesus now speaks of what is written in heaven as a man speaks of a room he has lived in. No prophet ever told anyone his name was entered there. The Son can, because he came from the Father and knows the Father’s book, and because he is going up to Jerusalem to die for those whose names are in it. The seventy-two hear their eternal standing from the lips of the one on whom it rests.

Written in his blood, kept by his life. Before the seventy-two were born, before the mountains were brought forth, a hand wrote their names in the book of the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 13:8), written in his blood and kept by his life. No failure on earth reaches that page, and the God who wrote it does not erase.

For those who measure themselves by usefulness. This verse is for the minister whose standing before God seems to rise and fall with the size of the congregation, the parent who reads his children’s faith as a report card on his own, the Christian ill for two years who quietly suspects he has become surplus. The thing worth rejoicing in was never the doing. It is a name, already written, in a book they cannot reach and cannot lose.

How can I know my name is written there? Not by trying to read the book, which God has not opened to us, but by looking at the Christ he offers you: whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). If you have turned from sin and are trusting Christ alone, your trust is itself the sign of the writing, because no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). The fruit of the Spirit, love for other believers, and a growing hatred of sin confirm it (1 John 3:14). If you are unsure, do not stare inward: come to him now. Nobody who comes is found missing from the roll.

parallels.desc: blot me out of your book

verseByVerse.quote: In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, 'I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus rejoices that the Father reveals himself to the humble, and claims that only he, the Son, can make the Father known.

He rejoiced in the Holy Spirit. Luke seldom tells us what Jesus felt, and here he stops to do it. The verb (ēgalliasato) means not quiet contentment but exultation, the verb of Mary’s song, my spirit rejoices in God my Saviour (1:47). Only Luke says it happened in the Holy Spirit: the Son, filled with joy by the Spirit, speaks to the Father, three persons, one delight. And the occasion is a group of nobodies coming home from a preaching tour.

Lord of heaven and earth. “Father” is the word of a son at home; “Lord of heaven and earth” is the title of the King of all things. Jesus holds intimacy and sovereignty in one breath, and teaches us to do the same.

Hidden and revealed. He thanks the Father for a hiding as well as a revealing, and that must be faced, not explained away. “These things” are what the seventy-two have just seen: Satan falling, the kingdom arriving, and whose name it came in. The wise are the professionally religious, men with the texts, the training and the standing, who have watched it all and concluded he is a problem. The little children (nēpioi, infants) are fishermen and farmers who could not have argued a point of law. Learning is not the fault, but it gives a person one more thing to rely on instead of God, and pride blinds (1 Corinthians 1:18–31).

Your gracious will. “Gracious will” (eudokia) is good pleasure, the word of the angels’ song of “peace among those with whom he is pleased” (2:14). Jesus does not merely accept the Father’s arrangement; he delights in it. The Lord of heaven and earth owes his light to no one, and the Son bows before that freedom with joy, not with questions.

All things have been handed over to me. Scholars have long called this passage the Johannine thunderbolt, because it sounds exactly like John’s Gospel (Johannine means “of John”). “All things”: not authority in some defined area, but everything. Then he describes a knowing only two share: the Father knows the Son, the Son knows the Father, and nobody else knows either except by the Son’s choosing. Only God can know God fully, so this is not a teacher who understands God better than others but a claim to stand inside the life of God, on the near side of a door only he can open. And he opens it, as a gift no one earns or works out (John 6:44; 14:6; 17:6). That last clause makes this prayer joy rather than terror.

A joy that has never stopped. Beneath the noise of the world there is a joy that has never stopped: the Father delighting in the Son, the Son exulting in the Father, the Spirit filling the Son with gladness. For one hour on a Galilean road that joy broke the surface. The Lord of heaven and earth did not need us to complete his happiness. He opened the door anyway, and the gladness of God himself is the house we are brought into.

Why would God hide things from clever people? Jesus is not ranking intelligence or rewarding the incurious; he is describing a posture. Augustine knew this from the inside. In his Confessions he tells how the Platonist philosophers taught him much about God and the eternal Word, yet could not show him what he lacked: that the Word became flesh and humbled himself. He could see the homeland from a distant height, he said, but not the road to it, and the road was humility. A child does not reach the truth by climbing; he receives it. Were salvation given to the brilliant, it would be one more achievement to boast of; instead the cleverest person in the room comes in by the same low door as everyone else, which is where God himself came in, at Bethlehem.

Does God, then, choose who will understand? Jesus says so plainly, and the Reformed reading takes his words at face value: understanding is God’s gift, given by his gracious will, and no one can boast of having worked it out. Christians in the Arminian tradition (named after the Dutch theologian Jacobus Arminius) read them differently, holding that God’s choosing follows his foreknowledge of who will believe, and they love these words too; but the plainest sense lays the reason in the Father’s gracious will. Yet those who reject Jesus are responsible for it (vv. 13–16), and the invitation is to all: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden (Matthew 11:28), which in Matthew follows these very words. Both are true. If you want to know God, that desire is already the Son at work, so come.

Can people of other religions know God without Christ? They may know that God exists, for creation declares his power (Romans 1:20), and their consciences bear witness. But they do not know him as Father, and cannot be saved by that knowledge. Saving knowledge of God comes only through the Son: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). That is not narrowness for its own sake but the shape of reality, and it is why the church must go and tell, because the Son is willing to reveal the Father to anyone, from any nation, who comes to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then turning to the disciples he said privately, 'Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples are more blessed than the greatest saints of old: they see in Jesus what prophets and kings longed to see.

Blessed are the eyes! Not “blessed are you” for being perceptive, but “blessed are the eyes”, for what is in front of them. The blessing is entirely a matter of where they stand in history, which they did nothing to arrange.

Many prophets and kings. Put names to that. Abraham, promised that all nations would be blessed through his offspring, died with one son of the promise and a burial plot, yet rejoiced to see Christ’s day (John 8:56). David, promised a son whose throne would stand for ever, went to his grave a thousand years before the child was born. Isaiah described the Servant’s wounds seven centuries early and never met him. Daniel saw one like a son of man receive an everlasting kingdom, and was told to seal the book. They all “died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13). And a group of Galilean labourers had been eating with him.

My eyes have seen your salvation. At the end of that long line one man was allowed to see. Simeon took the infant in his arms and said he could depart in peace, for his eyes had seen God’s salvation (2:29–30). Salvation was a child he could hold, and that is what the disciples’ blessed eyes are looking at: not an experience or a doctrine, but a Person. Everything the prophets and kings strained toward has a face, turned toward these men as he speaks. Nor were the old saints disappointed in the end: Moses stood with him on the mountain and spoke of his departure (9:30–31), and all of them now see face to face what they longed for. We live in the age every saint of old leaned toward. Blessed are our eyes.

The boredom of proximity. A boredom can settle on people long in church, the gospel a known quantity and the Bible a familiar book: not usually unbelief, but what happens when something extraordinary has been close at hand for years. Yet we have what even the disciples lacked before the cross: the finished account of the death and the rising, the whole of Scripture, and the Spirit given. Daniel was told to seal up his book; ours lies open on the kitchen table.

Were the Old Testament believers worse off in salvation? No. They were saved by the same Christ, through faith in the promise, as we are through faith in the fulfilment (Romans 4; Hebrews 11). What they lacked was not salvation but sight: they saw the dawn from far off, and we stand in the morning. Our advantage is in clarity and fullness, which makes us more grateful, not more proud.

In the flow. In the very next verse one of the wise and understanding stands up, a lawyer who knows the Scriptures and still asks how to earn life (v. 25), and the prayer of v. 21 comes true in front of the reader.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–37 — The Parable of the Good Samaritan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No one can earn eternal life by keeping the law, and no one may shrink the law to make it keepable; its true reach is shown by a Samaritan who stopped. A lawyer tests Jesus with the greatest question there is, and answers it himself from Scripture: love God with all you are, and your neighbour as yourself (vv. 25–28). Wanting to justify himself, he asks where “neighbour” ends (v. 29). Jesus tells of a man left half dead, passed by a priest and a Levite and rescued at great cost by the man the lawyer would least want to admire (vv. 30–35). Then he turns the question round, not who is my neighbour but who proved to be one, and does not lower the command by an inch (vv. 36–37).
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus uses the law here as it was meant to be used: not as a ladder to climb up to life but as a mirror that shows us our sin (see the note on vv. 27–28).

The priest and the Levite are offered no excuse (see the note on vv. 30–32). On the parable’s main meaning, and how it also shows the mercy of Christ, see the box “Where Christians differ: Christ the Samaritan?” at the end of the note on vv. 33–35.
verseByVerse.examples:
The Samaritan’s care is costly and specific (see the note on vv. 33–35). “Go, and do likewise” means that kind of schedule-wrecking, wallet-opening mercy, not a feeling or a good intention.

Read honestly, that is unbearable (on why it is still good news, see the note on vv. 36–37).

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying, 'Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?' He said to him, 'What is written in the Law? How do you read it?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A lawyer asks Jesus how to earn eternal life, and Jesus turns the test into a question about how the man himself reads Scripture.

A lawyer stood up. Not a courtroom advocate but an expert in the law of Moses, a scribe, trained in what God had said and what it required. Luke gives his motive before he speaks: not an enquiry but a public examination of a Galilean teacher with no formal qualifications. He stands, a respectful posture; the purpose is not respectful.

Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? The greatest question there is (the rich ruler will ask it in the same words, 18:18), but the wording gives the man away. “What shall I do?” assumes that eternal life is achieved by an action, and he wants the specification. Yet he asks to inherit, and an inheritance is the one thing nobody works for: it comes by belonging to a family. He has put a doing-word and a receiving-word in one sentence and not noticed. The inheritance he wants to earn is held out by the Father to children who cannot earn it: “if children, then heirs, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17). The Son came down to make outsiders sons, and the eternal life no one can buy is the gift of his own life, shared.

What is written in the Law? How do you read it? Jesus answers with two respectful questions, inviting an expert to show what he knows. But “what is written” asks for the text, and “how do you read it” asks for the man. People who disagree about Scripture usually have the same words in front of them; what differs is the reading, and a reading is never neutral. It is done by someone who wants some things to be true and others not. So in a handful of words the examination has moved. The lawyer came to test Jesus on the content of the law; he is about to be tested on what he has been doing with it.

Beginning with Moses. Luke ends his Gospel with the same Teacher on the Emmaus road, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, interpreting the things concerning himself in all the Scriptures (24:27). The lawyer is about to read Moses accurately and still miss the one standing in front of him, the only man who would ever do what Moses commands. A reading of the law can be correct in every word and still be wrong at the centre.

In the flow. The lawyer’s answer in v. 27 sets out the plan of the rest of the chapter. Love for your neighbour is shown on the Jericho road (vv. 30–37); love for the Lord your God, at Jesus’ feet in Bethany (vv. 38–42). In both, the one who gets it right is the one nobody expected: a Samaritan, and a woman sitting in a student’s place.

What does eternal life mean here? Not simply living for ever, which in one sense everyone will do, in joy or in judgment, but the life of the age to come, the life of God’s kingdom, beginning now and completed at the resurrection: “this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). So the lawyer is really asking how to belong to God for ever, and the answer will turn out to be a Person, not a performance.
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered, 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.' And he said to him, 'You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law’s whole demand is love for God with all we are and for our neighbour as ourselves, and anyone who truly kept it would live.

You shall love the Lord your God. The lawyer joins Deuteronomy 6:5, from the Shema, which every Jew recited daily, and Leviticus 19:18, a single line in a chapter of assorted laws, into one command, as Jesus himself did (Mark 12:29–31). He has seen what holds the law together. The four terms are not separate compartments but a way of saying “all of you”, nothing held back: affections, life, effort and thinking.

Do this, and you will live. An echo of Leviticus 18:5: “if a person does them, he shall live by them.” Is Jesus telling a man he can earn eternal life by keeping the law? Taken at face value the sentence is true: anyone who loved God with all his heart, soul, strength and mind, and his neighbour as himself, without a lapse from first breath to last, would live. The catch is not in the offer but in the doer, and no such doer has ever lived, apart from the man saying it. He did this, and he lived; and then he gave his life away, so that those who had not done this might live in him.

Law and gospel. So Jesus uses the law as it was meant to be used: not as a way to earn life but as a mirror that convicts of sin. “Through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20); “the law was our guardian until Christ came” (Galatians 3:24). It brings a man to the end of himself so that he will look elsewhere; the lawyer, instead, will look for a smaller law (v. 29). The law demands perfect love because God is holy (Leviticus 19:2), and Christ’s perfect obedience is counted to those who trust him: “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). God treats them as though Christ’s record were their own, and lays their sin on him (2 Corinthians 5:21).

What it means to love God. Love for God is neither a feeling summoned on demand nor a duty ticked off on Sundays, but treasuring him above everything. No heart is empty of such love: Timothy Keller often pointed out that if God is not what we love most, something else will be, a career, a child, a reputation, and whatever holds that place will rule us and in the end let us down. Love is not produced by command but drawn out by what it sees, and the heart has never been shown anything lovelier than Christ, who loved his Father with all his heart and then gave himself for people who had not loved God at all. “He who is forgiven little, loves little” (7:47); the more you see what your forgiveness cost him, the more your love will grow. So this week, before you pray, spend five minutes with one scene of Christ in the Gospels, and ask not “Do I love him enough?” but “What has he done for me?”

In everyday life. Because Christ kept these commands for you, you can measure yourself honestly against them rather than against other people. Have you loved God with all your heart today, or with a corner of it? Where not, do not reach for a smaller definition; go back to the one who kept them, and ask for grace to love a little more.

If no one can keep the law, why should Christians still try to obey it? Because the law that could never save us now describes the life Christ has saved us into. Once we are justified by faith, the same commands become the shape of gratitude, and the Spirit writes them on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; Romans 8:4). We obey not to be accepted but because we are accepted, and our imperfect obedience pleases the Father for Christ’s sake. The law still shows us our sin daily and sends us back to Christ, and it still shows us the path of love. A Christian does not throw away the map because he has stopped trying to earn the journey.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, 'And who is my neighbor?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wanting to declare himself in the right, the lawyer looks for a limit to the word “neighbour”. One of the world’s best-known stories begins with a question asked by a man looking for somewhere to hide.

Desiring to justify himself. Luke gives the motive again, and this time the whole chapter turns on it. To justify is to declare someone in the right, as a judge does at the end of a case. The lawyer wants to pronounce that verdict over himself, to come out of this conversation still able to say he had done what was required. It is the instinct of the human heart: to define God’s law in a way we can keep. Jesus will later tell the Pharisees, “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts” (16:15).

And who is my neighbor? It sounds like precision. But if “neighbour” can be defined, it has edges; if it has edges, there are people outside them; and a man can love everyone inside the line and walk past the rest with a clear conscience. Not “whom should I love?” but “whom am I permitted not to?”

A live question. Teachers discussing Leviticus 19:18 leaned on its phrase “the sons of your own people”, so “neighbour” was generally taken to mean a fellow Israelite; the sect at Qumran made it a rule to love the sons of light and hate the sons of darkness. The instinct presents itself as realism: nobody can help everybody, so a line has to be drawn. Jesus is about to tell a story in which the line the lawyer most wanted, the racial and religious one, is crossed by the man he least wanted to admire.

The one who could have justified him. The God who is love never asked who his neighbour was; he crossed every line to make himself ours. A few chapters on, a tax collector who could only beat his breast and ask for mercy went home justified, and the Pharisee who listed his record did not (18:9–14). The lawyer is trying to do for himself the one thing that can only be done for him, in the presence of the one person who can do it. Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem to become the righteousness sinners cannot produce. The man looking for a smaller law is standing beside the Lord who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5).

parallels.desc: those who justify yourselves before men

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus replied, 'A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Jesus’ story a man lies stripped and half dead, and two servants of God’s temple see him and pass by. Only Luke records the parable, and its fame has cost it the shock it was built to deliver; its details give the shock back.

Going down to Jericho. We are told nothing about the man: no name, trade, nationality or religion. The lawyer asked for a category, and the first thing the story refuses him is a category. The road was notorious: some seventeen miles (27 km), dropping over three thousand feet (900 m) through limestone gorges and blind bends. Jerome, living nearby centuries later, says it was still called the red or bloody ascent.

Stripped and half dead. Clothing showed a man’s nationality and status, and speech the rest; naked and silent, he is unclassifiable: a human being in a ditch, and no way to tell whether he is one of ours.

By chance a priest. Why did he pass? Fear of the robbers, perhaps; or ritual purity, since touching a corpse made a priest unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11–13); or simple indifference. Jesus gives no reasons; excuses do not matter. But he was going down, away from Jerusalem toward Jericho, where many priests are said to have lived between their weeks of service: his duty was behind him. And the very law he may have been keeping commands a man to help even his enemy’s fallen animal (Exodus 23:4–5).

So likewise a Levite. Levites assisted the priests in the temple: religious, respectable, knowledgeable about the law. Of this man Luke adds that he “came to the place”. He got closer, looked from nearer, and crossed anyway.

The shape of the story. Such stories often ran in threes, and after a priest and a Levite the natural third man was an ordinary Israelite: the establishment fails and the common man does right. What arrives instead breaks the pattern.

The same road, later. On his last journey Jesus climbs this very road through Jericho toward Jerusalem (18:35–19:28). A blind beggar shouts from the roadside and the crowd tells him to be quiet; Jesus stops and gives him his sight (18:35–43). In Jericho he stops under a tree for a man the whole town had written off (19:1–10). The one telling this story does not pass by on the other side. He stops for the man at the edge of the road, on his way up to die.

In everyday life. Whom have you passed by on the other side? The colleague whose marriage is falling apart, the neighbour whose bins have not moved in a week, the widow who sits alone at church. A busy schedule of good things makes a convenient other side of the road; but the Lord who stopped for a blind beggar on his way to die did not pass you by, and he can make room in your week for them.

Is it always wrong to pass by someone in need? No. There are real dangers, prior duties and needs you cannot meet, and sometimes the loving thing is to call for help rather than stop yourself; a woman alone at night is not commanded to pull over on a dark road. But the priest and Levite had no reasons Jesus thought worth mentioning; they did not want the cost. The test is honest: am I unable, or merely unwilling? Has God put this person in my path, and is there something I can actually do? If so, the ditch is my business.
verseByVerse.note: The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho drops over 3,000 feet in about 17 miles through barren, rocky country, and was notorious for robbers. Touching a dead body made a priest unclean.

parallels.desc: no priest shall make himself unclean for the dead

verseByVerse.quote: But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who stops is a despised Samaritan: moved with compassion, he gives his own time, goods and money to save someone who would have counted him an enemy.

But a Samaritan. The hostility was ancient, mutual and violent. Samaritans came from the remnant of the northern kingdom mixed with settlers brought in after the Assyrian conquest; their temple on Mount Gerizim had stood until a Jewish army destroyed it, and Jews regarded them as heretics and half-breeds. Within living memory, Josephus says, Samaritans had scattered human bones in the temple courts at Passover. Jews had no dealings with Samaritans (John 4:9), and only a chapter earlier a Samaritan village had refused Jesus a bed (9:52–54). This is the man Jesus makes the hero.

He had compassion. All three saw; only one had compassion. The verb (esplanchnisthē) comes from the word for the inward organs: compassion felt in the body. Luke uses it of Jesus seeing the widow at Nain (7:13), of the father seeing the prodigal (15:20), and here. The difference is not in the seeing but in what the seeing was allowed to do.

Oil and wine. Jesus itemises the care: bandages from whatever cloth he had, and oil and wine, the standard treatment, wine to cleanse and oil to soothe, his own travelling supplies, now gone. There may be a quiet irony: oil and wine were also offerings in the temple the priest had just left. The Samaritan poured them out in the true worship, for “I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6).

On his own animal. So the Samaritan walked, at an injured man’s pace, in robber country, and spent the night at the inn nursing a stranger. In the morning he paid two denarii, two days’ wages for a labourer, board for perhaps a fortnight, and promised to repay whatever more was spent; without payment a penniless guest might have been held as a debtor. He has written a blank cheque, in a foreign town, for an unconscious man of the race that despises him, and bound himself to return.

Whom they called a Samaritan. The despised Samaritan is the clearest picture in the Gospels of the despised Saviour, “despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3), whom they called a Samaritan (John 8:48). Every act of mercy we do is a faint echo of the mercy that found us on the road.

What if helping someone could be dangerous or be taken advantage of? Love sometimes takes real risks, but wisdom is not its enemy. The Samaritan did not hand the man his purse; he paid the innkeeper and arranged care, both generous and sensible. You may help through the right channels, involve others, set limits that protect your family, and decline to fund what would harm someone. What love may not do is use prudence as a disguise for indifference. Ask: what would genuinely help this person, and what part of it can I carry?

Where Christians differ: Christ the Samaritan? From the early church onward (Origen, Augustine), many read the parable as an allegory of salvation: the man is Adam, the robbers the devil, the priest and Levite the law and the prophets, the Samaritan Christ, the inn the church, the two denarii the two commandments of love, and the return the second coming. This commentary’s view: the parable’s primary meaning, given by Jesus himself, is ethical: go and do likewise (v. 37). It answers the lawyer’s question, who is my neighbour?, and reading every detail as a code goes beyond the text. Yet there is a true echo: Christ is the supreme neighbour, who came to us when we were his enemies, half dead in our sins, and gave himself to save us (Romans 5:8–10). The parable both commands love and points to the love that makes it possible, and every Christian’s mercy flows from his.
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans and Jews despised each other. Oil soothed wounds and wine cleaned them. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; two could cover some days at an inn.

parallels.desc: the captives clothed, anointed and carried on donkeys to Jericho

verseByVerse.quote: Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?' He said, 'The one who showed him mercy.' And Jesus said to him, 'You go, and do likewise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turns the lawyer’s question round: what matters is not who qualifies as my neighbour but whether I will be one, to anyone in need.

Which of these three … proved to be a neighbor? This is the parable’s most important move. The lawyer’s question put the other person under examination and the questioner safely in the chair; Jesus’ question puts the questioner in the road and asks what he did. The issue is no longer the boundary of obligation but what kind of man is walking past. Neighbourliness is defined not by the other person’s status but by my compassion.

The one who showed him mercy. He seems unable to say it. The answer is one word, the Samaritan, and he uses a whole phrase instead. Luke leaves it exposed: a man who has understood the story perfectly and cannot get the word out of his mouth.

You go, and do likewise. And there the parable stops, which is unbearable if you have been reading honestly. Go and be the Samaritan: cross a racial hatred, spend your own money, take on an open-ended liability for a stranger who can never repay you. Anyone who finds that manageable has not understood it; anyone who has understood it stands where the lawyer stands, looking for somewhere to put his feet.

Who is telling the story. Now it matters who is telling the story. One person has kept this command whole. He came down a far longer road than the one to Jericho, to where we lay stripped and half dead and in no condition to ask. He bound up the wounds at his own expense. He paid what we could not, and he has promised to come back. And he is on the road to Jerusalem as he speaks, to settle the account himself.

The name that stuck in his throat. The lawyer could not bring himself to say the name of the one who showed mercy. God has said it for ever. To his Son, who humbled himself to the point of death on a cross for people who had despised him, he has given “the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:8–10). The word that stuck in the lawyer’s throat will be on every tongue in heaven, a name of mercy.

Mercy received, then mercy passed on. The order is never mercy shown to earn mercy, but mercy received and then passed on: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). “Go, and do likewise” remains binding, but it is addressed to people already picked up out of a ditch, which makes it good news, not a sentence.

Does this mean I must help everyone in need? The parable defines a neighbour as one who shows mercy to the person in front of him, whoever he is. It does not tell us how to meet every need in the world, nor is it a programme for the state. You cannot help everyone, and God does not ask you to. But it forbids us to decide that someone in real need, whom God has put in our path, is not our concern because of who he is. Begin with the household of faith and those nearest you (Galatians 6:10), and let your circle of mercy keep widening.

Can’t anyone be a good Samaritan without Jesus? Many who do not believe show striking kindness, and Christians should honour it gladly as God’s common goodness in his world. But the lawyer asked how to inherit eternal life, and the standard Jesus sets is mercy without limit, to anyone, every time, from the heart. Nobody, believer or not, has kept that. So the parable does not divide the kind from the unkind. It shows everyone that they need a Neighbour who kept it for them, and a new heart that begins to love like him (Ezekiel 36:26).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Listening to Jesus comes before serving him, and it is the one thing that can never be lost. Martha welcomes him into her house, while her sister Mary takes a disciple’s place at his feet, a place not normally open to a woman (vv. 38–39). Martha’s good service turns into anxiety and grievance, and she accuses her sister and finally Jesus of not caring (v. 40). He answers her tenderly and without lowering the truth: one thing is necessary, and Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken from her (vv. 41–42).
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus does not send Mary back to the kitchen; he defends her right to receive what he is giving, and so welcomes women as full disciples.

The good portion lasts (see the note on vv. 41–42): the word Mary takes in is “the living and abiding word of God” (1 Peter 1:23). What lasts is what is truly necessary, and it must not be crowded out by what merely feels urgent.
verseByVerse.examples:
The scene does not set serving against listening; it puts them in order, listening first (see the note on vv. 41–42). Martha’s work was needed. What was not needed was for it to be done by a woman who had stopped sitting down.

Many who serve have prayed her prayer, “do you not care?” (on how Jesus answers it, see the note on v. 40).

verseByVerse.quote: Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Martha welcomes Jesus into her home, and her sister Mary takes the place of a disciple at his feet. After the parable about doing comes a story about listening (see “In the flow” in the note on vv. 25–26).

A village. Luke does not name it. John does: Bethany, two miles from Jerusalem, the home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus (John 11:1; 12:1–3).

Martha welcomed him. It is her house; Luke says so, which is unusual enough to notice. Where hospitality was a sacred obligation, a travelling teacher and his disciples, perhaps thirteen or more people, meant a great deal of work, and Martha opened her door to them all. She is not a woman lacking spiritual interest. She is the one who let him in.

Mary sat and listened. Sitting at the feet is the posture of a disciple under a rabbi; Paul was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). Women were taught the law as it applied to their duties, but the formal place of a student under a teacher was for men. Mary sat down in that place, Jesus let her, and within minutes he will defend her right to be there. And the tense means she kept on listening.

At the Lord’s feet. Luke keeps bringing people here: a sinful woman weeping (7:38), the freed demoniac clothed and in his right mind (8:35), Jairus (8:41), a healed Samaritan giving thanks (17:16). Mary sits where the forgiven, the rescued and the grateful sit. We know of no rabbi who said that listening to him was the one thing necessary; this Teacher will say it within the hour (v. 42), and only the Lord could say it truly. How gracious of the Son of God, on his way to the cross, to stop in a village house and give himself to whoever would sit and listen.

In everyday life. If you are a woman who has been told, in so many words, that deep study of Scripture is not really for you, know that Jesus defended your seat.

Does Mary’s place at Jesus’ feet mean women may hold every office in the church? It means women are full disciples, called to learn, to know the Scriptures deeply and to sit under Christ’s word as fully as any man: a revolution in its day, and Luke’s point. Who may serve as an elder or preach to the gathered church is answered elsewhere, where the New Testament reserves that office to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7). This commentary holds that complementarian view (men and women equal in worth, with some roles given differently), because Paul grounds it in creation rather than local custom (1 Timothy 2:13), and understands headship as self-giving service, never domination. Many faithful Christians read those passages differently and welcome women as pastors, and they deserve to be heard with respect. Mary’s example rebukes any church that keeps women from learning deeply. It does not settle the eldership question either way.
verseByVerse.note: John places Martha and Mary in Bethany, near Jerusalem. Sitting at a teacher’s feet was the place of a disciple.

verseByVerse.quote: But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, 'Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Martha’s good service turns into anxiety and resentment, until she accuses even the Lord of not caring.

Distracted with much serving. Distracted means pulled away, dragged in different directions (periespato): less busy than torn. And what tears her is much serving, diakonia, the word that will become the church’s term for ministry. Her service was good and necessary. The problem is not that she chose work over devotion but what the work has become inside her: it has pulled her away from Jesus.

Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Three steps, each further than the last: she interrupts his teaching, accuses her sister in front of the guests, and accuses him. “Do you not care?” is not a request but a charge, almost the words the disciples threw at him in the storm: “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” (Mark 4:38). From serving him to reproaching him: the distance was crossed in an afternoon, in a kitchen, doing a good thing. “Tell her then to help me”: she does not even ask him to intervene; she tells him what to say. Busy, worried people often judge those who are not as busy.

Not hard on her. Every word is what an exhausted person says, and she is not wrong about the facts. A service that began as a gift has turned, somewhere between the door and the fire, into a grievance, and the sign is that she is keeping score. Service can quietly become a way of earning a place, a bid for thanks or proof that we matter, and then everyone not helping feels like a threat. “Do you not care?” is what resentment sounds like when it finally reaches God. And he does not rebuke her for the tone; he answers what is underneath it.

The guest who serves. Martha thinks the serving in this house runs one way, from her kitchen to his table. At the last supper Jesus will say, “I am among you as the one who serves” (22:27), and he promises that at his return the master will dress himself for service and wait on his servants at table (12:37). When this Lord comes into a house, he comes chiefly to give, and his hosts’ first duty is to receive. The Lord whom Martha accused of not caring was on his way to the clearest proof of care the world has ever seen.

In everyday life. Busyness has a way of turning into resentment: the sigh as you clear up after the church lunch, the mental list of who never helps. Those are signals, not proofs that you are wrong to serve. Stop, sit down for five minutes with him, and let him take the score card out of your hand.

Is it wrong to complain to God? Not to bring him your distress: the psalms are full of honest lament, “How long, O LORD?”, and he invites us to cast all our anxieties on him, because he cares for us (1 Peter 5:7). What Martha shows is the moment honest weariness hardens into accusation, when “do you not care” is said as a verdict rather than a cry. Tell him the truth about how you feel, and then let him tell you the truth about himself. He does care, which is precisely why he will not simply give Martha what she asks.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord answered her, 'Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gently tells Martha that listening to him is the one necessary thing, and that what Mary has chosen will never be taken from her.

Martha, Martha. The doubled name is not impatience. Luke records it at other moments: “Simon, Simon” (22:31); “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem” (13:34); “Saul, Saul” (Acts 9:4). It is the address of someone who sees the whole of a person and is about to say what she needs and will not enjoy: a gentle rebuke, from love.

Anxious and troubled. Two verbs, and neither is “busy”. Anxious is merimnas, the worry Jesus forbids in 12:22–26 and the root of the cares that choke the word (8:14). Troubled (thorybazē) means agitated, in an uproar. He is diagnosing not her workload but a heart not resting in God.

One thing is necessary. Not just one dish, but the one thing that matters most: listening to Jesus. David knew it: “One thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD” (Psalm 27:4). David’s “one thing” was the LORD himself. Here it is to sit at Jesus’ feet, and he says it without apology, standing where the LORD stands in the psalm.

The good portion. Portion (meris) is a share, used of a helping at table (Genesis 43:34) and of the LORD as his people’s inheritance (Psalm 16:5): Martha is in the kitchen dividing up portions, and Mary has taken the one that matters. The dinner will be eaten by nightfall; the word Mary is taking in is permanent.

It will not be taken away. The good portion is a Person, and nothing can take him away: “The LORD is my portion,” says my soul, “therefore I will hope in him” (Lamentations 3:24). He is the inheritance of everyone who sits at his feet, and Mary’s portion is offered to us.

What it does not mean. Not a rebuke of practical service: Luke has just praised a man who bandaged a stranger and paid his bills. Nor a recommendation of the monastery over the kitchen. It is a statement about order. Listening to Jesus comes first and is the source of true service; service without listening becomes anxious and resentful.

Why does rest feel like falling behind? Martha would fit easily into our world, with more labour-saving machines than any generation and less rest, and busyness worn as a badge of importance. Underneath lies something older. If my worth depends on what I produce, sitting still is dangerous, because while I sit I am worth nothing; so a day off feels like guilt and an empty evening like failure. Mary is not being lazy. She has stopped trying to justify her existence by her output. Religion and the secular gospel of achievement agree: work, and then you may rest. The gospel reverses the order. Christ has done the work that matters and finished it, and the first thing he asks of the busy is to sit down and receive.
