Only those who know they are already loved can really stop, and only they can go back to the kitchen without a score card.

With young children, a job and an elderly parent, how can I possibly sit at his feet? The good portion is not measured in hours, and Jesus is not asking a mother of three to keep a monk’s timetable. It is a matter of where your heart rests. Take what you can: ten minutes with a Psalm before the house wakes, a passage at breakfast, a sermon while you drive, a prayer at the sink. Guard the Lord’s Day as a time to receive. And let the busy hours themselves be done at his feet, done for him and in dependence on him. Little and real is better than much and anxious.

Textual note. If your Bible has a footnote here, some manuscripts read “few things are necessary, or only one”. The shorter reading is very likely original, and the sense is unaffected.

parallels.desc: one thing have I asked of the LORD
the LORD is my chosen portion

10.text: <sup>1</sup> After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. <sup>2</sup> And he said to them, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest. <sup>3</sup> Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. <sup>4</sup> Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road. <sup>5</sup> Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house!’ <sup>6</sup> And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. <sup>7</sup> And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house. <sup>8</sup> Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. <sup>9</sup> Heal the sick in it and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’ <sup>10</sup> But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say, <sup>11</sup> ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near.’ <sup>12</sup> I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town. <sup>13</sup> “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. <sup>14</sup> But it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. <sup>15</sup> And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades. <sup>16</sup> “The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.” <sup>17</sup> The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!” <sup>18</sup> And he said to them, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. <sup>19</sup> Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you. <sup>20</sup> Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” <sup>21</sup> In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. <sup>22</sup> All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” <sup>23</sup> Then turning to the disciples he said privately, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! <sup>24</sup> For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.” <sup>25</sup> And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>26</sup> He said to him, “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?” <sup>27</sup> And he answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.” <sup>28</sup> And he said to him, “You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.” <sup>29</sup> But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” <sup>30</sup> Jesus replied, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. <sup>31</sup> Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. <sup>32</sup> So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. <sup>33</sup> But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. <sup>34</sup> He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. <sup>35</sup> And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’ <sup>36</sup> Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?” <sup>37</sup> He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” And Jesus said to him, “You go, and do likewise.” <sup>38</sup> Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. <sup>39</sup> And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching. <sup>40</sup> But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.” <sup>41</sup> But the Lord answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, <sup>42</sup> but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.”

keyVerse.quote: Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.
keyVerse.note: Each scene of the chapter asks what we do with the Lord who has come near, and this answer gathers them up. The seventy-two are told to rejoice not in what they can do but in what has been given them (v. 20), and the lawyer who wants to do something to inherit life is shown he cannot (v. 25); here the one necessary thing is to receive from Jesus himself a portion no one can take away. All true going, loving and serving flows from that place at his feet.

10.reflection:
Jesus tells the seventy-two to pray for labourers before he sends them, and sends them as lambs among wolves (vv. 2–3). How does knowing that the harvest is the Lord’s change the way you pray, and the way you face hostility to your faith? Whom could you pray for by name this week?

Jesus turns his disciples’ joy from what they could do to the fact that their names are written in heaven (v. 20). When does your sense of standing with God rise and fall with your usefulness or results? What would it look like to rest in what he has done instead?

The lawyer asked, “And who is my neighbor?” to find out whom he could leave out (v. 29). What lines do we draw today, and who in your own path are you most tempted to pass by? How does seeing Jesus as the one who stopped for you change your answer?

Martha served Jesus and ended up accusing him (v. 40); Mary sat and listened (v. 39). What most often pulls you away from his feet, and what one practical change would make room for the good portion this week?

11.title: Prayer, Darkness, and the Woes of the Pharisees
11.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 11 comes early in the long journey to Jerusalem (9:51–19:27). Mary has just chosen the one thing needed by sitting at Jesus’ feet (10:38–42); now his disciples, watching him pray, ask him to teach them.

The message. God can be known as Father, and everything turns on whether we know him so or only know about him. To those who ask, he is a Father more generous than any on earth, and his best gift is his own Spirit. In Jesus his kingdom has broken into the strong man’s house, and no one can stand neutral before it. And religion that keeps the outside clean while the heart stays greedy and proud is under his woe, however correct it looks.

Why it was said. Luke’s readers needed to learn to pray as Jesus’ disciples, sure that the God they prayed to was generous (see the introduction). They also lived among respectable religion that rejected Jesus, and among people who wanted more proof first; this chapter shows both responses were there from the start, and why.

How the chapter makes its case. The order is not random. Prayer comes first (vv. 1–13): the Lord’s Prayer, the friend at midnight, and the promise of the Spirit. Then conflict (vv. 14–28): Jesus’ exorcisms are the finger of God, the stronger one has come, there is no neutral ground, a swept house must be occupied, and the true blessing is to hear God’s word and keep it. Then the sign (vv. 29–36): this generation gets only the sign of Jonah, and the trouble is not the lamp but the eye. Finally the table (vv. 37–54): six woes on Pharisees and lawyers, and the hunt begins. Prayer is life with the Father; the conflict shows his kingdom at work in Jesus; the woes show what religion becomes when the form remains and the Father is not known.

Where it leads. The Son who prays hands us his own word for God, and keeps hold of it on the cross. The one greater than Solomon and Jonah will give the sign of Jonah in full, going down into death and coming back. He walks toward the ambush with his eyes open, so that people who had only known about God might call him Father.

For us. Pray boldly and persistently, as a child who belongs at the table, and ask above all for the Spirit. Do not wait on the fence for more proof. And let the woes search you: they are the sins of people who know their Bibles, and the cure is not more polish but the one who cleans from the inside and moves in.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Prayer is a child speaking to his Father, and Jesus himself gives his disciples the words. Seeing him pray, they ask to be taught (v. 1). He gives them one word of address, “Father”, which is the heart of it, and five requests in a deliberate order (vv. 2–4). God comes first: that his name be honoured and his kingdom come. Then our needs: bread for today, forgiveness for the past, protection for what lies ahead. Luke’s form is shorter than Matthew’s (Matthew 6:9–13; on the two forms, see the note on v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology:
“Father” is the revolution in this prayer (see the note on v. 2).

The first two petitions put God’s honour and God’s reign before every need, and they cannot be prayed without cost (see the note on v. 2). The request for bread is deliberately small (see vv. 3–4).
verseByVerse.examples: The word “for” in the forgiveness petition must not become a bargain, and “lead us not into temptation” is not a fear that God might make us sin (on both, see the note on vv. 3–4).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, 'Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing Jesus pray, a disciple asks to be taught, and Jesus’ answer gives his followers a prayer of their own. Prayer has to be learned, and the best teacher is the one who prays perfectly.

Jesus was praying. The order matters: he prays, they watch, and then one of them asks. Luke shows Jesus at prayer more than any other Gospel: at the baptism (3:21), all night before choosing the Twelve (6:12), on the mountain where his face changed (9:28–29). Men who had grown up saying prayers several times a day watched the way this man prayed and concluded they did not know how.

Lord, teach us to pray. They had watched him still a storm, feed thousands and raise the dead, yet what a disciple asks to be taught is how to talk to his Father. Prayer does not come naturally to sinners.

As John taught his disciples. Teachers and movements had characteristic prayers that marked out what a group was for, and John had given his. Jesus’ disciples want a prayer that belongs to them and expresses who they are as his.

The one who taught us is praying still. The Son of God, who had the Father’s presence every moment, still went away to pray. He prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (22:32), and he lives now to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25). Our stumbling words reach the Father on the strength of his.

Why does prayer feel so hard? For most Christians prayer is the part that never quite settles: the first thing to go in a busy week and the last to come back. It is the one Christian activity with no audience and no visible result in the moment; our flesh resists dependence; and the enemy hates it. The answer is not a technique, nor more determination. It is what this disciple did: to say to the one person who can do anything about it that he does not know how. Then start small and keep going, using the words Jesus gives.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers commonly gave their disciples a characteristic prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus teaches his disciples to come to God as their Father, and to ask first that God be honoured and his reign come. The whole prayer rests on its first word.

When you pray, say. Luke’s version is shorter than Matthew’s (Matthew 6:9–13), with five petitions to Matthew’s seven; Jesus probably taught it more than once. Is it a form to recite or a pattern to follow? Both. Christians may pray these words together, so long as they pray them from the heart and not as empty repetition (Matthew 6:7). And they shape all our other prayers: praise before petition, God’s glory before our needs, forgiveness alongside bread.

Father. One word, and it was a revolution: simply “Father”, without “our” or “in heaven”. The Old Testament calls God Father perhaps a dozen times, nearly always of Israel as a nation (Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16), and an individual almost never addresses him so in prayer. Behind Luke’s Greek very probably stands the Aramaic Abba, the word Jesus uses in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). It is not baby-talk; grown men used it of their fathers. But it is family vocabulary, and there is little or no evidence that Jews of the period prayed to God with it. He hands it to them as the first word.

Hallowed be your name. “Hallowed” (hagiasthētō) means treated as holy. In Hebrew thought a name is the person as he is known: God himself as he has revealed himself. So the petition asks that he be known and reverenced as what he actually is, first by the one praying and then by everybody else (Ezekiel 36:23), in a world that has trampled his name. The person praying volunteers to be part of the answer.

Your kingdom come. The central petition, and the shortest. God’s reign, which has come in Jesus (11:20), is still to come in fullness (22:18); the early church prayed Maranatha, “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22). No one can pray it and stay in charge of his own life. To ask for God’s rule to come is to ask for my own to end; each time I pray it honestly, I step down from the throne a little.

The Son’s own word, opened to us. Paul says what has happened: “you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15). Adoption is God taking into his family people who were not his children by nature, and giving them everything a son has: his name, free access to the Father, a share in the inheritance (Galatians 4:4–7).

He kept hold of the word. The God whose name the seraphim cry “Holy, holy, holy” has let us call him Father. It cost the Son everything to open that word to us, and Luke lets us hear him keep hold of it to the end: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (23:46). He held on to it through the darkness of bearing our sin, so that rebels might sit at the Father’s table and say it after him.

What it looks like to hallow his name. Begin with him. Before your list, spend a minute telling God what he is like: faithful, patient, holy, kind. Use his name with care. Not as an exclamation, and not as a stamp on your own plans (“the Lord told me”) when he has not said so. Let your life carry his name well. Because of the hypocrisy of God’s people, “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles” (Romans 2:24). Honesty on a tax return and patience with a difficult child are how the people around you learn what he is like. Want his reputation more than yours. When the credit goes to someone else, let it go if his name is honoured. And when you fail, do not despair. On the way to the cross the Son prayed, “Father, glorify your name” (John 12:28), and he hallowed it perfectly in your place. You honour the name as a forgiven child who bears it, not as a servant trying to earn it.

What if my earthly father was absent or cruel? Then the word may at first bring pain rather than comfort. But Jesus is not asking you to picture God as your father was. He is showing you what fatherhood was always meant to be, and what your father failed to be: the Father from whom every family is named (Ephesians 3:14–15), faithful, patient, never abusive, never absent. Many with wounded histories have found that saying “Father” to God slowly heals what an earthly father broke. Read how Jesus speaks of him, and let that, not your memory, fill the word.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, fill Luke’s version out to match Matthew’s; the earliest do not.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s version of the Lord’s Prayer is shorter than Matthew’s; the ESV notes that some manuscripts add phrases from Matthew’s form. “Hallowed” means treated as holy.

parallels.desc: I will vindicate the holiness of my great name

verseByVerse.quote: Give us each day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having put God first, the prayer brings him our whole life: bread for today, forgiveness for the past, and protection for what lies ahead. All three are asked for daily, and for “us”.

Our daily bread. The word behind “daily” is epiousios, so rare that Origen, a native speaker, thought the evangelists had coined it; it may mean “for today”, or “necessary”, or “for the coming day”. The point is daily dependence, as Israel gathered manna day by day (Exodus 16:4): enough for today, asked again tomorrow (Proverbs 30:8). Hoarded manna rotted overnight (Exodus 16:19–20), so that Israel had to come afresh every morning; anyone who wishes God would settle his finances once and for all is asking for something this prayer will not give. “Each day” is only in Luke. And the words are “us” and “our”: we pray for others’ bread as well as our own.

Forgive us our sins. Matthew has “debts”; Luke has “sins”, probably to make the meaning clear for Gentile readers. We need it as much as bread, every day. Sin is a debt: the obedience and honour we owe God and have not paid.

For we ourselves forgive. Here Luke keeps the image of debt. The word “for” must not become a bargain: God’s forgiveness is not purchased by ours, and this prayer has just called him Father, which no one earns. Our forgiving is a sign that his forgiveness has reached us, not a payment for it. A man who has grasped what has been cancelled on his own account cannot keep a ledger open against his neighbour; if he can, he may not have understood the first half of the sentence (Matthew 6:14–15; 18:21–35). The verb means we go on forgiving, as a settled habit, and “everyone” means no exceptions.

Lead us not into temptation. The word (peirasmos) covers both testing and enticement; it is the one used of Jesus in the wilderness (4:13). God tempts no one to sin (James 1:13), yet trials come under his hand. On the Mount of Olives Jesus will twice tell his disciples to pray that they may not enter into temptation (22:40, 46), and within hours Peter falls. So the prayer is: Father, I am weak; do not bring me to a test I cannot bear, or let me fall when tested (1 Corinthians 10:13). Matthew adds: “but deliver us from evil.”

The one who forgives. The man teaching this petition has already said to a paralysed man, “your sins are forgiven you”, and proved it by making him walk (5:20–24). He never needed to pray “forgive us our sins” for himself; he “bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24), so the debt we ask to be forgiven has already been paid. At the cross Luke alone records him doing what the second half of the petition says, under the greatest wrong ever done: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (23:34). Some early manuscripts lack this prayer, but it is widely accepted as genuine and most Bibles print it. And he went into the wilderness and the garden in our place, met the tempter at his strongest, and did not fall.

In everyday life. Name to your Father the particular situation where you know you are weak, the screen late at night, the colleague who provokes you, the shop where you overspend; pray specifically not to be led there, and then do not walk into it.

Should Christians save and plan, if we pray for daily bread? Yes. Joseph stored grain for seven years of famine; the ant prepares her bread in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8); believers are to provide for their households (1 Timothy 5:8). This petition does not forbid savings, insurance or a pension. It forbids trusting them. The man with a full barn still prays for daily bread, because the barn, the health to use it and the next breath are all from God (12:16–21).

Does forgiving mean I must trust again or pretend it did not happen? No. Forgiveness means you release the debt: you give up the right to repay, and hand the case to God, who judges justly (Romans 12:19). It does not mean the wrong was small, that consequences vanish, or that trust is instantly restored; trust is rebuilt slowly, by changed behaviour. A victim of abuse may forgive and still rightly report the crime, keep away from the abuser and protect others; forgiveness never requires anyone to remain in danger, and abuse is never to be tolerated. If the feelings lag behind, keep praying this prayer; forgiveness is often a decision renewed many times before the heart catches up.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–13 — Ask, and It Will Be Given
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is not a reluctant neighbour to be worn down but a Father more generous than any on earth, so keep asking. Two pictures follow the prayer, and both argue from the lesser to the greater. If a sleepy friend will get up at midnight and give bread to a shameless knocker, how much more will God (vv. 5–8). So keep asking, seeking and knocking, for everyone who asks receives (vv. 9–10). And if a sinful father would never hand his child a snake for a fish, how much more will the heavenly Father give good gifts, the best of them being the Holy Spirit (vv. 11–13). That answer meets the honest problem of prayers that seem unanswered.
verseByVerse.theology:
The promise is not a blank cheque (see the note on vv. 9–10), and a refused request does not mean the Father is deaf (see the note on vv. 11–13).

Where Matthew has “good things” (Matthew 7:11), Luke has “the Holy Spirit” (see the note on vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.examples:
The man at midnight is not asking for himself (see the note on vv. 5–6).

For anyone praying about something that has not moved in years, see what the Father promises to everyone who asks (vv. 11–13).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus pictures prayer as a man in need going at midnight to a friend’s door, sure he will be heard, to ask for bread for someone else.

A friend at midnight. Only Luke records this parable. A Galilean peasant home was often a single room: the family asleep together on a raised platform, and one door barred at night with a heavy beam. Bread was baked in the morning, so by midnight most houses had none, and neighbours knew who had baked.

Nothing to set before him. Hospitality was a sacred obligation, and many students of village life think a traveller arriving at night was in a sense the whole community’s guest. So the man banging on the door is doing what any neighbour would expect, and his request is modest: three small loaves, enough for one meal, and “lend”: he will return them.

A friend’s door. He presumes on a friendship at the worst possible hour, which is precisely what friendship is for. That is Jesus’ picture of prayer: not a subject petitioning a distant monarch through the correct channels, but a man in the dark, out of bread, with somebody depending on him, walking round to a house where he knows he will be heard.

You give them something to eat. The disciples had already stood where this man stands. With five thousand hungry people and five loaves, Jesus told them: “You give them something to eat” (9:13). Then he took the loaves, looked up to heaven, blessed and broke them, and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd (9:16). That is the shape of all Christian giving: empty hands, a Lord who looks up to his Father, and bread passed on.

Asking for someone else. He is not asking for himself. He is in the position of everyone who has tried to help another and found himself empty: the parent with a child in trouble, the friend sitting with someone grieving, the Sunday school teacher on Saturday night. “I have nothing to set before him” is not a reason to give up. It is the reason to knock.
verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to a traveller was a sacred duty; villagers baked daily, and a household might have nothing left at night.

verseByVerse.quote: and he will answer from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’? I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If even a sleepy neighbour will get up and give to a shameless knocker, how much more will God, who never sleeps, give to his children. The man in bed is not a picture of God but a contrast with him.

Do not bother me. The excuses are entirely accurate: in a one-room house, unbarring the door and stepping over the children will wake everyone. But “I cannot” means “I will not”. Yet even this man gets up. How much more will God, who will neither slumber nor sleep (Psalm 121:4).

Because of his impudence. Impudence is shamelessness (anaideia). Whoever’s shamelessness it is (see “Uncertain wording” below), the parable lands in the same place: how much more the Father, who is neither asleep nor inconvenienced, and who has tied his own name to keeping his word (Psalm 23:3; Ezekiel 36:22).

Borrowed boldness. Boldness at God’s door is not cheek; it is borrowed. Only the Son has an unbarred right to his Father’s house (2:49), and he hands his disciples his own word for God, “Father”, as the first word of their prayers. A sinner may knock without shame at midnight for the same reason a son may walk into his father’s house at any hour: the Son has brought him in and stands beside him at the door. The sleeper gave three loaves to save his face; our Father gave his own Son to save us, and a giver like that does not grudge bread at midnight.

Most prayer dies of good manners. It is possible to be so respectful of God that nothing is ever actually asked for, and this parable was told to kill that. We do not have to wear God down; but we should pray with the boldness of a man banging on a door in the dark because he has nothing and knows where the bread is (18:1–8).

If God already knows what I need and wants to give it, why keep asking? Because prayer is not information for God; it is fellowship with him. He has chosen to work through his people’s prayers, as a father delights to hear his children ask for a gift he has already bought. Persistent prayer also changes us: it clarifies what we want, exposes motives and deepens dependence. And Scripture commands it: “pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17). We keep knocking not to change his mind but because he has told us to, and because he is worth talking to.

Uncertain wording. Whose “impudence” is meant is argued over. The traditional reading makes it the asker’s: his brazen persistence wins, which fits what follows (v. 9), and the ESV notes that the word can be rendered “persistence”. A second reading gives it to the sleeper, who gets up to avoid the disgrace of being the man who had bread and would not open the door. The asker’s shameless boldness is the likelier sense, but the lesson does not depend on deciding.
verseByVerse.note: A peasant family slept together in one room; opening the barred door would wake everyone. The ESV notes that “impudence” can also be rendered “persistence.”

verseByVerse.quote: And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep on asking, seeking and knocking, because the Father has promised that everyone who asks receives. One well-worded request does not close the matter.

Ask, seek, knock. Three verbs, rising in intensity. Ask: make the request. Seek: search with effort. Knock: stand at a closed door and stay there, as the man in the parable did. Each is in a form that means keep on, and three promises answer them: given, found, opened. And they are for everyone who asks, not a spiritual elite.

The honest problem. A great many people have read this verse and then buried someone they prayed for, and a Christian who has asked for years for a child to come home may fairly ask what is going on. Three things must be said. First, Scripture never treats this as a blank cheque: “if we ask anything according to his will he hears us” (1 John 5:14); “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4:3). Second, Jesus himself prayed a prayer that was not granted in the form he asked: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me” (22:42). Third, and this carries the weight, Jesus answers the question himself, at once, with a father and a child (vv. 11–13).

We were sought first. The God who says “ask”, “seek”, “knock” is not hiding behind his door. In Luke the great Seeker is God himself: the shepherd after the lost sheep, the woman sweeping for the lost coin, the Son of Man who came to seek and to save the lost (15:4–10; 19:10). We seek because we were sought first, by a Father who did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32).

In everyday life. No child of this Father is scolded for coming back to the door. If a prayer you prayed for years has been answered with a no, bring that grief to him honestly as well. Asking again is not unbelief; it is exactly what he told you to do.

verseByVerse.quote: What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
No earthly father tricks his child with something harmful, so the heavenly Father, who is perfectly good, will give his best gift, the Holy Spirit, to those who ask him. This is Jesus’ own answer to the pain of prayers that seem to go unanswered.

A serpent for a fish, a scorpion for an egg. A second argument from the lesser to the greater. Both pairs are chosen with care: it is often said that a fish and a water snake look roughly alike, and that a pale scorpion with its legs and tail curled in might pass for an egg. The picture is not a father refusing his son but one handing him something that looks like what he wanted and will hurt him. Every parent listening knows that nobody does that.

You then, who are evil. An aside, dropped in as an agreed fact. He is talking to ordinary decent parents, and takes it as common ground that they are sinful (Romans 3:10–12). Even so, they would not hand a child a scorpion.

How much more will the heavenly Father. Here is the answer to the hardest question a praying person meets, why some requests are refused, and Jesus does not answer by adding conditions to the promise. He describes the one who keeps it. A request denied does not mean the Father is deaf; it means he has seen a snake where the child saw a fish. That does not make unanswered prayer painless. It removes the one conclusion that would be unbearable: that the silence means indifference.

The Holy Spirit. Matthew’s version ends with “good things” (Matthew 7:11). Luke has “the Holy Spirit”, and so tells you what “good things” finally means. The best thing the Father has to give is himself, present in a Person: to dwell in his children, make them holy, help them pray (Romans 8:26) and empower them for witness (Acts 1:8). Whatever else is given or withheld, the gift promised to everyone who asks is God himself, the one gift that can never turn out wrong.

The promise of the Father. He gave the Son, the best of heaven, for children who were evil; he gives the Spirit to all who ask. Luke follows this promise to its fulfilment. The risen Jesus sends the promise of his Father upon his disciples (24:49), and at Pentecost Peter says that Jesus, exalted at the right hand of God, has poured out the Spirit (Acts 2:33). To ask the Father for the Spirit is to ask for what Christ died and rose to give.

Is it not harsh to call loving parents evil? Only if “evil” meant “as wicked as possible”. Jesus means that even our best love grows from hearts curved in on ourselves: we love our children, and also love being needed and getting our own way with them. The decent parent and the scoundrel need the same Saviour (Romans 3:23). And the phrase is meant not to crush parents but to lift our eyes: if love mixed with sin still gives good gifts, think what love without any sin will give.

If every believer already has the Spirit, why ask? This is not a promise of a second blessing, a later, separate experience of the Spirit that only some believers receive, as some traditions teach; many who hold that view love the Spirit deeply, but Luke’s words here do not require it. Every believer receives the Spirit at conversion (Romans 8:9; Galatians 3:2). We ask now for his ongoing work: to be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner being (Ephesians 3:16), for his fruit, and for his help in our weakness. You will never ask for that and be handed a scorpion.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add a bread-and-stone example, as in Matthew 7:9. It was probably added to match Matthew.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add a bread-and-stone example, as in Matthew.

parallels.desc: the gift of the Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–28 — Jesus and Beelzebul; True Blessedness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus’ power over demons shows that God’s kingdom has arrived, and no one can stay neutral toward him. He frees a mute man, and his critics answer in two ways still common today: they blame the devil, or they demand more proof (vv. 14–16). Jesus shows the charge to be absurd and inconsistent (vv. 17–19): his works are the finger of God, and the kingdom has come (v. 20). One stronger has overpowered Satan and is carrying off his goods, which are people (vv. 21–22). So there is no neutral ground (v. 23), and a life swept clean but left empty is not safe (vv. 24–26). The true blessing is open to all: to hear God’s word and keep it (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology:
The returning spirit is a warning against a cleaned-up life that has not received new life from God (see the note on vv. 24–26).

The saying that whoever is not with him is against him does not contradict 9:50 (see the note on v. 23).
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman’s blessing on Jesus’ mother is well meant, and Jesus redirects it (see the note on vv. 27–28).

And anyone whose Christianity consists mainly of things he has stopped doing should turn the swept house into a question (see the note on vv. 24–26).

verseByVerse.quote: Now he was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marveled. But some of them said, 'He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons,' while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus frees a man from a demon that kept him mute, and while the crowd marvels, his critics either blame the devil or demand more proof. The rest of the chapter grows from this one exorcism.

A demon that was mute. The demon made the man mute; Matthew adds that he was blind as well (Matthew 12:22). Jesus has just promised the Holy Spirit to those who ask (v. 13); now God’s power is at work in him, and religious men call it the devil’s. The chapter will end with them lying in wait for him (vv. 53–54).

The people marveled. Wonder, which is not the same as faith. Then come the critics’ two responses, still the commonest among those who do not want to accept him.

By Beelzebul. The charge concedes a good deal. Nobody disputes that the man is speaking or suggests a trick; they admit the miracle and blame it on another source. Later Jewish writings against Jesus did the same, calling him a sorcerer rather than denying his deeds (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 43a). Baal-zebub was the god of Ekron whom a king of Israel once consulted instead of the LORD (2 Kings 1:2–3), and by the first century Beelzebul was a title for the chief of the demons (on the name, see “Uncertain wording” below). So the charge is as serious as it can be, said of a man who has just given a mute person his voice back.

A sign from heaven. The second response is subtler, and worse: a real sign, from the sky, on their terms. Demanding more evidence while standing in front of the evidence is a way of postponing a decision indefinitely while appearing reasonable. Luke says they did it to test him, which is what Jesus refused, in the wilderness, to do to his Father (4:12).

A tongue set free. Isaiah had said that when God came to save, the tongue of the mute would sing for joy (Isaiah 35:4–6), and Jesus pointed John the Baptist to such works as his credentials (7:22). The critics are deciding what to do with the God of Isaiah’s promise standing in front of them, and they call him the devil.

Is it wrong to want evidence for faith? No. Christianity is not a leap in the dark; God has given abundant evidence, and Luke wrote his Gospel so that Theophilus might have certainty (1:4). The risen Jesus was seen by many witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Honest questions are welcome. What Jesus refuses is the demand that God perform on our terms after he has already spoken. If you are genuinely seeking, read the Gospels themselves and ask God to show you the truth. If you find you would not believe whatever you were shown, the problem is not the evidence.

Was this not simply an illness that ancient people blamed on demons? Luke, a physician (Colossians 4:14), does not blame every illness on demons. He distinguishes healing the sick from casting out demons (4:40–41; 6:18; 13:32), and he records Zechariah struck mute by God with no demon involved (1:20). So he is reporting a real distinction, not a primitive habit of mind. And the hostile witnesses who were there did not call it an illness; they argued about whose power cured it.

Uncertain wording. The meaning of the name Beelzebul is not certain. Baal-zebub in 2 Kings 1 means “lord of flies”, perhaps a Hebrew mockery of a pagan title; the spelling with -zebul may mean something like “lord of the dwelling” or “exalted lord”. What is clear is how Jesus’ hearers used it: as a name for “the prince of demons” (v. 15), that is, Satan (v. 18).
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, 'Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus shows that the charge is absurd, since Satan would not wreck his own work, and inconsistent, since the critics do not say the same of their own exorcists. The objection was a conclusion looking for a reason.

Knowing their thoughts. Whether or not the charges were said to his face, Jesus answers what is in the room, as Luke keeps noting (5:22; 6:8; 9:47). Solomon confessed that only the LORD knows what is in every human heart (1 Kings 8:39). Accused of serving the prince of demons, he shows whose knowledge he has.

A kingdom divided. The first answer: the charge is illogical. He starts from what nobody would dispute in politics or family life. If the prince of demons is expelling demons, he is dismantling his own operation, and no commander destroys his own positions. Something is assumed along the way that is easy to miss: Jesus takes it as given that the kingdom of darkness is a kingdom, organised, unified, under command, and never working against its own aims (4:5–6). He says it in passing, as too obvious to argue.

By whom do your sons cast them out? The second answer is inconsistency. Jewish exorcists were active at the time (Acts 19:13–14), and the Pharisees did not call their work satanic. So “they will be your judges”: your own people’s practice condemns your double standard. An objection a man does not apply consistently is not his real reason. He reached his conclusion first and built the argument afterwards to justify it. That is a hard word for anyone who has found a convincing reason for refusing what he did not want to accept.

In everyday life. Look for the double standard in how you weigh other people’s ministries: the church across town whose fruit you dismiss while excusing the same weaknesses in your own, the preacher you criticise for what you praise in your favourite.
verseByVerse.note: Other Jewish exorcists were active at the time; “your sons” means the critics’ own followers.

verseByVerse.quote: But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ exorcisms are God’s own hand at work, as in the exodus, and they prove that God’s reign has already arrived. The people accusing him are standing in it.

The finger of God. Matthew reads “by the Spirit of God” (Matthew 12:28); Luke keeps the Exodus wording, which would have rung like a bell in that crowd. Pharaoh’s magicians, beaten by the plague of gnats, told Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8:19), and the tablets of stone were “written with the finger of God” (Exodus 31:18). So the phrase carries deliverance from slavery and the giving of the covenant, and Jesus applies it to one mute man set free, before men who have just accused him of witchcraft. Like the plagues, his exorcisms are God liberating his people from a tyrant.

The kingdom of God has come upon you. Has arrived, has overtaken you (ephthasen): not merely near, as the seventy-two announced (10:9), but here. The kingdom is God reigning, and where the King acts, the reign is present, which is why the evidence for its arrival is not a throne or an army but a man who can suddenly talk. And it has come “upon you”, the people accusing him.

The finger that wrote the law. The finger that wrote the law on stone and humbled Pharaoh touched a mute man in Galilee, and he spoke. That same power raised Christ from the dead (Ephesians 1:19–20). The tyrant who held the world has met the finger of God, and the finger of God has a human hand.

In everyday life. When you face a temptation that has mastered you for years, remember that the finger of God is stronger than that habit. And when you pray for someone bound by addiction or despair, pray as one who believes the King has already invaded the enemy’s territory.

Has the kingdom come, or is it still coming? Both. God’s reign has broken in, yet it has not come in its fullness: we still pray “Your kingdom come” (v. 2), and we still live among sickness, sin and death. This is the already and not yet of the kingdom. It came in the King’s first coming; it grows as the gospel spreads and hearts bow to him; and it will be complete when he returns and every enemy is put under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:24–26). Every demon driven out by the finger of God was a pledge of the day when the devil himself is thrown down for good (Revelation 20:10).

Where is the kingdom of God today, if not in exorcisms and healings? Wherever Christ reigns. Whenever a sinner repents and believes, a captive is set free; the kingdom is there when the word is faithfully preached and obeyed, and whenever a believer forgives, gives, or resists sin in Christ’s strength. Look for it where people bow to Jesus, and pray for it there first.
verseByVerse.note: “The finger of God” is what Pharaoh’s magicians said of the plague of gnats, which they could not copy.

verseByVerse.quote: When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his spoil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan holds people as a strong man guards his goods, but Jesus is the stronger one who has overpowered him and is setting his captives free. This short parable interprets everything Jesus has just done.

A strong man, fully armed. The strong man is Satan: not weak or asleep but fully armed, in his own house, guarding property he regards as his. His captives cannot escape by their own strength. The human race was not neutral territory awaiting instruction. It was occupied.

One stronger than he. The stronger one is Jesus: John promised that one mightier than he was coming (3:16), and in Nazareth Jesus announced liberty to the captives (4:18). “Attacks”: the initiative is his. “Overcomes”: not a contest but a result. The victory began in the wilderness (4:1–13), continued in the exorcisms, and was won at the cross, where he “disarmed the rulers and authorities” (Colossians 2:15) and destroyed the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14–15).

The armor in which he trusted. The man is not merely beaten but disarmed, and what is removed is also his confidence.

Divides his spoil. The property is not merely recovered but given away. Isaiah said of the Servant: “he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death” (Isaiah 53:12). And the goods in this parable are not gold. What is carried out of the strong man’s house is a human being who could not speak.

No struggle recorded. No exorcism in this Gospel is a struggle. He speaks and it is over; the demons do not fight him, they beg (8:28, 31). The strong man never lands a blow until the cross, where the blow he landed was his own undoing. We were the goods in his palace, safe in his keeping and hopeless in our chains. Then one stronger came, walked into the house of death, broke its doors, and carried us out on his shoulders.

Can the strong man move back into a believer? No. A believer belongs to Christ and is the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19); he has been delivered from the domain of darkness (Colossians 1:13). The strong man cannot move back into a house the stronger one now owns. Christians can be tempted, deceived and oppressed by the devil, and must resist him (Ephesians 6:10–18), but not owned. A believer troubled by dark thoughts or fears need not look for an exorcist. Confess any sin, renounce any occult involvement, and stand on what Christ has done.

parallels.desc: he shall divide the spoil with the strong

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can stay neutral about Jesus: whoever does not side with him and join his work is against him. The middle ground is abolished in one sentence.

Whoever is not with me is against me. Those who wanted a further sign would have thought themselves open-minded, merely waiting for more evidence. Jesus tells them there is no such position: in the war between Christ and Satan there is no neutral ground.

Whoever does not gather with me scatters. “Gather” and “scatter” are harvest words, and Luke has already named the harvest: plentiful, with few labourers (10:2). Scattering needs no malice, only absence: grain left ungathered is lost whether trampled or simply not picked up.

In everyday life. Ask what you are actually doing for the harvest: praying for the lost by name, supporting gospel work, speaking of Christ when the door opens, welcoming newcomers at church. Sympathetic spectating is not a third option.

But did Jesus not say the opposite in 9:50? Two chapters ago John, having stopped a man casting out demons in Jesus’ name, was told: “Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you” (9:50). The two sit together once you watch the pronouns. There, the subject was “you”: the disciples’ judgment of a stranger. Here it is “me”: a person’s own standing before Christ. They run in opposite directions on purpose. About somebody else, doing good in Christ’s name outside your circle: assume the best, and do not stop him. About yourself, in relation to Christ: assume nothing, because neutrality is not on offer. Generous outward, rigorous inward. Reverse those two and you get exactly the religion Jesus is about to spend the rest of the chapter dismantling.

Is it not narrow to say there is no neutral ground? A shepherd who says each sheep is either in the fold or out on the hills is not being narrow, only accurate, and Jesus can say it because of who he is. If he were one teacher among many, neutrality would be reasonable. But he has just shown himself the stronger one who sets captives free (v. 22), and in front of a rescuer there is no polite middle position. And it offends most not the irreligious but respectable men who thought waiting for more evidence a safe place to stand. The same Jesus who will not allow neutrality welcomes anyone, of any past, who comes to his side.

parallels.desc: the one who is not against you is for you

verseByVerse.quote: 'When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A life cleaned up but left empty is not safe: evil returns stronger unless Christ himself comes to live there. Following the point about neutrality, this strange little story warns that deliverance from evil is not enough by itself.

Waterless places. Desert places were widely thought to be the haunt of demons (Isaiah 13:21; 34:14). And note the pronoun the spirit uses when it decides to return: “my house”. It has been evicted and has not conceded ownership.

Swept and put in order. That is good news, which makes the story so unsettling: this life has visibly improved, the mess dealt with, the habits sorted out. One word is missing, which Matthew supplies: “empty” (Matthew 12:44). Reformed, but not occupied.

Seven other spirits. Seven is the Bible’s number for completeness: the man is now wholly taken over. The house was not merely available. It had been made attractive.

Worse than the first. The warning is aimed at something religion produces in quantity: reformation without regeneration. Reformation is a person changing his habits; regeneration is God giving him new life from within, the new birth without which no one can see the kingdom of God (John 3:3–6). A man gives up the drink or the temper, and everyone says he is better, which makes it harder to see that nobody has moved in. An empty swept house is not a neutral state on the way to something better; it is a vacancy, advertised. It applied to a generation stirred by John and Jesus but never committed to him (Matthew 12:45), and to anyone who makes a fresh start without Christ.

The remedy is occupation. The remedy is not more sweeping but occupation, by the stronger one who walks into an occupied house and takes it (v. 22). The Gerasene man was not left empty; he was found “sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind” (8:35). Christ does not merely clean the house; he moves in. The Father and the Son make their home with those who love him (John 14:23), and no spirit, however many it brings, can drive out the stronger one who lives there.

In everyday life. When you put off an old habit, ask what you are putting on in its place: prayer where there was the screen, generosity where there was grasping, fellowship where there was isolation. And ask the Father for the Spirit he promises to those who ask (v. 13).

Can a Christian be repossessed? No: what Christ has taken he keeps (John 10:28; see the note on vv. 21–22). This parable describes a life cleaned up but left empty, someone reformed but not converted. But the warning is still for church members, because it is possible to sit in church for years, clean and orderly, without ever having received Christ. If you fear that you are that empty house, the fear is itself a hopeful sign, since an empty house does not worry about who lives in it; turn to Christ now, and he will come in.
verseByVerse.note: Waterless places were thought to be the haunt of demons.

verseByVerse.quote: As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, 'Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed!' But he said, 'Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greater than the honour of being Jesus’ mother is the blessing open to everyone: to hear the word of God and keep it. Jesus does not deny the woman’s praise; he widens it to the whole crowd.

A woman in the crowd raised her voice. Only Luke records this very human interruption: in the middle of an argument about demons and kingdoms, a woman shouts a blessing on his mother.

Blessed is the womb! A common way to praise a son was to praise his mother. It is well meant, and true. Elizabeth said something very like it, filled with the Holy Spirit (1:42), and Mary herself sang that all generations would call her blessed (1:48).

Blessed rather. “Rather” (menoun) means “yes, but more than that”: a redirection, not a contradiction. Jesus refuses the assumption under the compliment, that blessedness is physical nearness to him. One womb bore him; what he offers instead is open to anybody, in any century: hear the word of God and keep it. It is the same point as 8:21.

Mary heard and kept. Mary is the outstanding example of the very thing he commends: “let it be to me according to your word” (1:38). Elizabeth called her blessed because she believed (1:45), and twice Luke tells us she treasured these things in her heart (2:19, 51). What made her blessed was not the biology, which nobody can share, but the faith, which everybody can.

The word of God, from his lips. In Luke the word of God is what Jesus himself speaks (5:1; 8:11). So when he says “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God”, he is not pointing away from himself. The woman praised the body that bore him; he points her to the voice that is speaking to her, and the way into Mary’s blessedness is to listen to her Son. How generous is this Lord, who will not let the greatest blessing be one woman’s privilege. Mary bore the Word made flesh; every believer receives the same Word by faith and carries him in the heart.

In everyday life. The practical question after any sermon or Bible reading is not how near you have been to the word but what you will keep: hold on to the one thing God said to you, and do it this week (see the note on 8:15).

Where Christians differ: devotion to Mary. Roman Catholic and Orthodox devotion gives Mary a unique place of honour and intercession: praying to her, and, in Catholic teaching, calling her Queen of Heaven and Mediatrix (one who shares in bringing Christ’s grace to us). They distinguish this honour from the worship due to God alone, and many of them love Christ deeply; the difference is real, and it can be stated without contempt. This commentary’s view: Jesus himself redirects attention from his mother’s physical role to the blessing of obedience, which she shares with all believers. Mary is rightly called blessed, and is a great example of faith. But she is not to be prayed to or venerated. Christ alone stands between God and men as mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), and Mary herself rejoiced in God as her Saviour (1:47).

parallels.desc: all generations will call me blessed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–36 — The Sign of Jonah; The Light in You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The evidence is already enough; what is lacking is not light but eyes willing to see it. As the crowds grow, Jesus refuses evidence on demand and offers only the sign of Jonah: a prophet given back from the deep, with a call to repent (vv. 29–30). Two pagan witnesses, the queen of the South and the men of Nineveh, answered far smaller light and will condemn this generation, for something greater than Solomon and Jonah is here (vv. 31–32). The lamp has not been hidden, so the trouble lies in the eye (vv. 33–34), and the gravest danger is that the light a person steers by is darkness (vv. 35–36).
verseByVerse.theology:
The queen and the Ninevites answered far smaller light (see the note on vv. 31–32).

The eye sayings are about the heart (see the note on vv. 33–34).
verseByVerse.examples: The warning that the light in you may be darkness is aimed first at religious people, and the promise after it is warm (see the note on vv. 35–36).

verseByVerse.quote: When the crowds were increasing, he began to say, 'This generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus refuses to perform proof on demand; the only sign this generation will be given is the sign of Jonah. As Jonah, given back from the deep, called Nineveh to repent, so the Son of Man will be God’s sign and summons to them.

This generation is an evil generation. Luke marks the moment: the crowds were increasing, and that is when he said it. Popularity never once altered what Jesus told people. This generation is evil because it does not repent, despite seeing God’s works.

It seeks for a sign. They had asked for a sign from heaven (v. 16). He refuses, though he has spent the chapter performing signs: a mute man is standing there talking. What is refused is evidence on demand, made to order, for people who have already decided what would count. A sign given to someone resolved not to believe becomes one more thing to explain away (v. 15).

The sign of Jonah. Jonah became a sign to the Ninevites in two ways, and both are true. The first is the man and his message: a foreigner with one sentence of judgment walked into Nineveh, and the city repented in sackcloth (Jonah 3:4–9). They saw no wonder; they heard a word. The second is where he had been: he arrived as a man who had gone down into the deep and been given back after three days (Jonah 1:17). Matthew spells that out (Matthew 12:40); Luke leaves the reader who knows Jonah to see it.

So will the Son of Man be. Luke shows at the end how the sign is given: the risen Jesus tells his disciples that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations (24:46–47). The sign this generation is promised is an empty grave outside Jerusalem and the word that goes out from it to the world, and it is enough.

Christ ran toward us. The sign of Jonah is mercy all the way down. Jonah went down into the deep because he ran from God; Christ went down into death because he ran toward us, bearing the judgment Nineveh deserved and we deserve. And on the third day he came back, rejoicing, to preach peace to the very city that rejected him.

If God wanted to be believed, why not simply prove it? Many ask this sincerely: write it across the sky, and I will believe. But proof that would satisfy the request would have to leave no room to say no, and a God who compelled belief like that would have our submission but never our trust, as a regime gets obedience from a crowd that has seen the tanks. Love cannot be forced, not even by evidence. The crowd around Jesus had plenty of evidence; what they wanted was a sign on their own terms, with themselves on the bench. God’s answer is stranger and better than writing in the sky: a man who goes down into death for his enemies and comes back. That is real evidence, an empty tomb in a city full of hostile witnesses, but it does not bully you. It is a love that waits to be answered.

How was Jesus three days and three nights in the earth if he died on Friday and rose on Sunday? The phrase is Matthew’s (Matthew 12:40), not Luke’s, but readers often ask. In Jewish reckoning any part of a day counted as a day and night. Esther called for a three-day fast, night and day, and went in to the king on the third day (Esther 4:16; 5:1); an Egyptian had not eaten for three days and three nights, and it was the third day (1 Samuel 30:12–13). Friday, Saturday and Sunday make three days: an idiom, not a stopwatch.

verseByVerse.quote: The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A pagan queen and a pagan city answered far smaller light, and at the judgment they will condemn those who ignored one greater than Solomon and Jonah. The more light a person is given, the stricter the judgment.

The queen of the South. Two witnesses are called, both chosen to sting: a pagan queen and a pagan city. The queen of Sheba, probably from south-west Arabia, travelled well over a thousand miles on a rumour, under no obligation to anybody’s God, and said the half had not been told her (1 Kings 10:1–7). She crossed that distance to hear Solomon; they had a greater one in their midst and would not listen.

Something greater than Solomon is here. The Greek says “something greater”, not “someone greater”. That is broader and stranger: the kingdom and the wisdom of God, present in the person of Jesus. The wisest man who ever lived is outranked by Wisdom itself, standing in the street. He is the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30), “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).

The men of Nineveh. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, the empire that had destroyed the northern kingdom and deported its tribes, and whose armies were remembered for cruelty long afterward. They were a byword for a people beyond hope. They repented at the preaching of a man who did not want to be there, who had run in the opposite direction, preached judgment with no promise of mercy, and was furious when it worked (Jonah 3:5–10; 4:1).

Something greater than Jonah is here. Jonah was swallowed by the deep and given back; the one who will actually break death is speaking. He says “behold”, and leaves it there. Israel’s prophets pointed away from themselves to the LORD; this one points to himself. If pagans repented at Jonah’s preaching, how much more should Israel repent at his?

The point. Sheba had a rumour, Nineveh one sentence from an unwilling foreigner; the men listening to Jesus have him. The more light, the stricter the judgment (10:13–15): a pagan queen who crossed deserts for a rumour of wisdom will stand up beside people who could not be troubled to cross a room. And this greater one has not stayed in a distant palace for us to travel to. He came all the way to us.

Will the queen of Sheba and the Ninevites be in heaven? Jesus does not say. His point is not their final destiny but their response: they answered far smaller light with seriousness, and that will expose those who answered the greatest light with indifference. The Ninevites’ repentance turned away a temporal judgment (Jonah 3:10); whether any came to saving faith is known to God. What is certain is that no one is saved apart from the grace of God revealed in Christ, and that we, who have heard him, have no excuse.
verseByVerse.note: The queen of the South is the queen of Sheba, probably in south-west Arabia. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The light has not been hidden; whether a person sees it depends on the eye, on whether the heart is single toward God or grasping. The problem with this generation is not lack of light but lack of sight.

A lamp on a stand. The saying was used before (8:16), and here it has a different edge. No one lights an oil lamp to hide it. Something greater than Solomon and Jonah is the lamp, and it has not been hidden: it has stood in the middle of Galilee, healing people in daylight.

Your eye is the lamp of your body. The lamp on the stand is outside; now there is a lamp inside, the eye. As a window lights a house, the eye lets light into the body; spiritually, it is the heart’s ability to perceive God’s truth. A blocked window leaves the house dark, however strong the sun outside.

Healthy or bad. A healthy eye is single, undivided and open-handed, fixed on God, and the light comes in. A bad eye is grasping, envious and calculating (see “Uncertain wording” below), and that condition determines what light can get in. This is not about eyesight or intellect.

A blocked window. That explains the whole chapter. The men in front of him are not short of information; the block is not ignorance but what they want. What a person wants to be true affects what he is able to see, and nobody ever thinks that is happening to him. Yet the God who said “Let light shine out of darkness” is the God who opens blind eyes to see it (2 Corinthians 4:6). The light and the sight are both his gifts.

How can I tell if my eye is bad? Watch for the things that make Scripture suddenly unclear to you. When a plain passage about money, sex or forgiveness seems strangely complicated, ask whether the difficulty is in the text or in what obeying it would cost. Notice envy, which turns other people’s blessings into grievances, and greed, which makes generosity feel foolish. Then ask God to heal your sight: “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). A single eye is not a perfect one; it is one turned wholly toward God and willing to see.

Uncertain wording. The two words for the eye carry more than one sense, and it is not certain which Jesus meant to stress. “Healthy” (haplous) literally means single: sound, undivided, sincere, and in the usage of the day also generous. “Bad” (ponēros) means evil or diseased, and in Jewish idiom an evil eye meant a grudging, envious, tight-fisted disposition (Deuteronomy 15:9; Matthew 20:15). The likely meaning holds these together: an eye fixed undivided on God and open-handed toward others, against one that is divided and grasping.
verseByVerse.note: A “bad” eye was an idiom for stinginess or an evil desire.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gravest danger is to be sure you see while the very light you steer by is darkness; the promise is a life opened wholly to God’s light, bright enough for others to see by. The warning is aimed first at religious people.

Lest the light in you be darkness. Few warnings in Luke should trouble a religious person more. A man in the dark usually knows it. The danger here is that the thing you navigate by is itself darkness, like a faulty compass that takes you further off the harder you try. “Be careful” means inspect the instrument. The Pharisees thought they saw (John 9:39–41).

Who is it for? The context answers. Luke goes straight from this saying to a Pharisee’s dinner table and six woes. The men being warned are the most religiously informed in the country, who tithed their garden herbs and built their lives around getting this right. So those at greatest risk are the ones closest to the truth for longest: long church attendance, real biblical knowledge, doctrine they could defend. All of it can be light, or the darkness a man steers by, and from inside the two feel identical.

Wholly bright. Then, after the warning, the promise, and it is unexpectedly warm. “Having no part dark” is the condition: not a life with most of the rooms lit and one door kept shut, but the whole of it, with nothing held back, no dark corner reserved. And the result, like a lamp with its rays, is not a person who has achieved something impressive but one who has become useful: someone others can see by.

Having no part dark. Only one life has met that condition in full. His eye was single toward his Father from first to last, and on the mountain, as he prayed, his clothing became dazzling white (9:29). What he offers the Pharisees is not a technique for self-inspection but himself, the light by which every other light is tested.

Into the darkness for us. The light that searches us is the light that saves us. The Lord who warned that a man’s light may be darkness went himself into the darkness that fell over the whole land as he hung on the cross (23:44), so that people steering by broken compasses might be brought out into his day.

If I cannot tell from the inside, how can I ever be sure? Not by staring inward, but by letting something outside you test you. Measure yourself by Scripture, not by your feelings or your church’s customs. Invite honest friends to tell you what they see. Look at fruit: does your knowledge make you humbler and kinder, or prouder and colder? And above all, pray as David did: “Search me, O God, and know my heart! … And see if there be any grievous way in me” (Psalm 139:23–24). The man who asks God to show him his darkness is not the man this verse describes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–54 — Woes to the Pharisees and Lawyers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Religion that keeps the outside clean while the heart stays greedy and proud stands under God’s woe, and it hardens against the one who exposes it. At a Pharisee’s table Jesus skips the ritual handwashing and answers his host’s astonishment with a cup clean outside and full of greed within (vv. 37–41). Then come six woes (on the word, see the note on v. 42). Three fall on the Pharisees, who tithe herbs and neglect justice and the love of God, love the best seats, and are unmarked graves (vv. 42–44). Three fall on the lawyers, who load burdens they will not touch, build the tombs of murdered prophets, and have taken away the key of knowledge (vv. 45–52). The meal ends with the scribes and Pharisees lying in wait to catch him in his words (vv. 53–54).
verseByVerse.theology:
The tithing woe is about a swap nobody makes on purpose (see the note on v. 42).

The heaviest woe is the key of knowledge (see the note on v. 52).
verseByVerse.examples: The burdens woe puts a test to every teacher (see the note on vv. 45–46). And the tomb-building woe explains why every generation admires the awkward prophets of the past and finds its own intolerable (see the note on vv. 47–48).

verseByVerse.quote: While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus accepts a Pharisee’s invitation and pointedly does not perform the ritual washing before the meal, which opens his challenge to religion that tends only the outside. Whatever he says next, he says as a guest who came when he was asked.

A Pharisee asked him to dine. Luke records three such meals (7:36; here; 14:1), and at every one the host is challenged. He is not denouncing enemies from a safe distance but eating their food.

He reclined at table. Reclining was the posture of a formal meal with guests, so the whole exchange took place in front of the Pharisee’s friends.

He did not first wash. The washing was not hygiene but a purity ritual (Mark 7:3–4), to remove ceremonial defilement picked up in the day. The law of Moses required such washings only of priests handling holy things; this was the tradition of the elders. The Pharisees applied the priestly standard to everybody, all the time, a serious ambition: they wanted the whole nation to live as though serving in the temple.

Deliberate. Probably. His disciples had done the same in front of a delegation from Jerusalem, and he had defended them (Mark 7:1–5). He is not being careless or rude, but declining, before witnesses, to endorse a system.

The only clean person in the room. The Holy One of Israel sat down unwashed at a Pharisee’s table, and he was the only clean person there. He came to make the unclean clean, not by water poured on hands, but by his blood poured out for sinners, which cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). In Luke he is forever at someone’s table: Levi’s (5:29), Simon the Pharisee’s (7:36), Zacchaeus’s (19:5–7). He accepts Pharisees’ invitations as he accepts sinners’, because both need him. And the guest at their tables is the host of a greater one, where people will come from east and west and recline at table in the kingdom of God (13:29).

Should a Christian accept invitations from people who disapprove of him? Jesus did, again and again, knowing the hostility at the table. Accept them where you can and be a gracious guest; meals are one of the best places for real conversation. But do not buy peace by pretending to agree with what you believe is wrong. Jesus was courteous enough to come and honest enough to speak.
verseByVerse.note: The washing was a ritual of purity before a meal, not hygiene.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said to him, 'Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God made the inside as well as the outside, so outward purity over a greedy heart is worthless to him; a heart he has made clean shows it by giving. Jesus answers his host’s unspoken criticism with the cup and dish on the table in front of them.

The outside of the cup. The Pharisees had detailed rules for washing vessels (Mark 7:4), and rabbinic discussions later written down in the Mishnah debate whether the inside and outside of a cup could be clean or unclean independently. Jesus takes their own debating point and turns it on them.

Full of greed and wickedness. A cup polished outside and filthy within is not partly clean; the polish makes it worse, because it gets the cup put back on the table. “Greed” (harpagē) is plunder, robbery: a startling charge against the most scrupulous men in the country. They are taking what belongs to others.

You fools! “Fools” (aphrones) means senseless. The argument is from creation: the same God made the visible and the invisible parts of a man, and he sees the inside (1 Samuel 16:7).

Give as alms. The inside is full of greed, and the remedy for greed is not scouring the cup but giving away what was grasped (Micah 6:8; on the wording, see “Uncertain wording” below). Jesus treats the tight fist as the real disease and the careful observance as its cover. Then “everything is clean for you”: when the heart is right, the ritual rules do not matter. Mark notes that in teaching like this Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19).

The Maker at the table. The guest asking whether the Maker of the outside did not make the inside also is the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3). He is not guessing what God sees in a man; he is looking. And he still stayed for the meal. He cleans from the inside out, and what he cleans he fills with his own generosity: the generosity of the one who, though he was rich, yet for your sake became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9).

In everyday life. The Maker who sees your heart came to give you a new one, so you can afford to look honestly: lay your bank statement alongside your church attendance and ask which one tells the truer story about your heart. Then give something away this week that you would rather keep.

If Jesus warns against calling a brother a fool, how can he say it here? There (Matthew 5:22) he forbids the angry insult that despises a person. Here, as the prophets did, he gives the Lord’s verdict on teachers who ignore the God who made the inside (v. 40). He is the Judge and sees hearts; we do not. So we may name folly in what people teach and do, but we must never use contempt as a weapon against a person, and never imagine that our anger shares his perfect knowledge.

Does this mean that almsgiving cleanses a person? No. Jesus is not teaching salvation by charity, but telling men obsessed with outward purity what God calls clean. Only the blood of Christ cleanses a sinner before God; but a heart he has cleansed will show it by opening its hands.

Uncertain wording. “Give as alms those things that are within” is a difficult sentence, and translators differ. It has been read as “give the contents of your cups and dishes as alms” or as “give from within, from the heart”. The likeliest sense is the first: give the food and wealth the cup and dish stand for to the poor, instead of grasping them. Both make the same point.

parallels.desc: to the pure, all things are pure
