verseByVerse.quote: 'But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to those who are scrupulous over small duties while neglecting justice and the love of God, the great things the small ones were meant to serve. Jesus does not scorn the small duties; he condemns the swap.

Woe to you Pharisees! Six woes follow, three on the Pharisees (vv. 42–44) and three on the lawyers (vv. 46–52). “Woe” (ouai) is not a curse or an insult. It is the prophets’ word, a cry of lament as much as a verdict: the sound a man makes watching somebody walk toward a cliff. Jesus will weep over Jerusalem later (19:41), and the woe and the weeping come from the same heart.

Mint and rue. The law required a tithe of the produce of the field (Deuteronomy 14:22–23), and said nothing explicit about a pot of mint by the door. The Pharisees tithed the garden herbs too, counting out every tenth leaf. Luke names rue, a herb the later rabbinic rules in the Mishnah did not even require to be tithed (Shebiith 9:1), so this was devotion going beyond what their own tradition asked. There is something admirable in taking God that seriously.

Justice and the love of God. The men counting mint leaves were failing at the weightier matters (Matthew 23:23). Justice: fair dealing with others, especially the poor. The love of God: loving him with the whole heart. The two great commandments (10:27).

Without neglecting the others. Jesus does not abolish the herb-tithing; they were right to do it. What he condemns is the swap: small, achievable duties quietly put in place of large, demanding ones.

How the trade happens. Nobody decides to swap justice for mint. The measurable duty satisfies: it can be completed and checked off. Justice and the love of God can never be checked off, and a man who spends his religious energy on things that finish will run out before he reaches the things that do not. Attendance and reading plans are countable; opinions on secondary matters can be defended. Whether I am just, and whether I love God, can be neither counted nor settled by argument, and they are the two things this verse says were being neglected.

Both, in one life. One man did the weightier matters and the smaller ones together. Jesus kept his Father’s law down to its details, and in the same life proclaimed good news to the poor and liberty to the oppressed (4:18), and loved his Father with the whole heart from boyhood to the cross. The Pharisees at this table were looking at what they had neglected, sitting across from them in a body.

In everyday life. Keep your quiet time, your giving and your church commitments; then ask whether anyone you dealt with today was treated unjustly by you, and whether you loved God at your desk as well as in your pew. Often you did not. Then go back to Christ, who kept both for you: his obedience is counted as yours, and your imperfect love is accepted for his sake.

What does justice look like for an ordinary Christian? Paying workers and bills fairly and on time. Telling the truth in business and on forms. Refusing to exploit anyone’s weakness or poverty. Speaking up for the person being treated unfairly at work or in church, especially the one with no voice. And caring about the poor with your money and your time, not just your opinions (Proverbs 31:8–9). Justice is love in the shape of fairness, and it is checked daily, not annually.

Where Christians differ: the tithe today. Some teach that Christians must give a tenth of their income, as a binding law. Others say the tithe belonged to the old covenant, and the New Testament gives no fixed percentage. This commentary’s view: the New Testament does not command a tithe for Christians, but calls for generous, cheerful, proportionate, sacrificial giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8–9). Jesus was speaking here to Jews under the law, before the cross. A tenth is a wise starting point, and many will give more. The heart matters more than the percentage, and the point of this verse is the weightier matters: justice and the love of God.
verseByVerse.note: The law required a tithe of produce; the Pharisees extended it to garden herbs such as mint and rue.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to those who love to be seen and honoured for their religion, for human praise is all the reward they will get. The seats are not condemned; the appetite is.

The best seat. The best seat in the synagogue was probably a bench at the front, facing the congregation, near the chest where the scrolls were kept: to sit there was to be seen by everyone, in the act of being religious. Greetings in the marketplaces were the elaborate public respect paid to a recognised teacher in the open square.

The word is “love”. Somebody has to sit at the front; what is diagnosed is an appetite, love of prominence and recognition (Matthew 6:1–5; 23:5–7).

The second audience. A man who loves the front seat now has two audiences, God and other people, and the people stand between him and God. Every religious act can be rewarded by God or by human praise, and the praise arrives at once: “they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:2). It is a woe, not a scolding, because it defeats itself unseen: once the praise is paid, no reward is left to come.

The lowest place. At another Pharisee’s table Jesus tells guests to take the lowest seat, for “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (14:7–11). He was describing his own road: laid in a manger (2:7), numbered with criminals at the end (22:37). And God has given him the highest place there is.

He never needed a greeting. Before Jesus had preached a sermon, a voice from heaven said: “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased” (3:22). He never needed a greeting in the marketplace, because he had that, and everyone who is in him is wrapped in the same pleasure. Beside that honour every bench at the front of every building on earth is a small thing.

What if I recognise this in myself? The desire to be well thought of is not cured by pretending not to have it; public modesty about one’s own achievements is one of the front seats. Nor is the remedy trying harder to be humble. It is that a man who already has the approval he most needs stops shopping for the substitute. The prayer Jesus taught begins with the word “Father”, and a person who has heard that word settle on him has considerably less use for a bench at the front. Practise doing some good things in secret, where only he sees (Matthew 6:4), and let him be enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to religious leaders who look entirely safe while passing spiritual death to those who trust them, without either side knowing it. The danger lies precisely in the respectability.

Unmarked graves. Touching a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16), barring him from worship, so graves were whitewashed each spring before Passover so that pilgrims could go round them (compare Matthew 23:27; see burial customs and tombs). An unmarked grave is one a man walks straight over, and finds out afterward, if ever.

Deadly in three ways. First, they are graves: whatever is on the surface, the contents are dead. Second, they defile: the self-appointed guardians of purity were in fact sources of defilement to the people they taught. Third, and worst, nobody can tell. The damage is done precisely because they look safe.

Not obvious hypocrites. Obvious hypocrites are less dangerous, because everybody eventually spots them. These are respected men, whose seriousness about God is genuine and whose lives are outwardly admirable, quietly transmitting something that kills. A young believer takes his cue from the most impressive religious person he knows, and if that person has rules without justice and knowledge without love, he will catch it without knowing.

The one who touched the dead. Under the law, contact with death spread uncleanness to whatever it touched. In Luke, when Jesus is involved, the movement runs the other way. At Nain he touched the bier, and the dead young man sat up and began to speak (7:14–15); in Jairus’s house he took a dead girl by the hand, and her spirit returned (8:54–55). These Pharisees passed death on unawares; Jesus touches death, and passes on life. There was once a grave that defiled no one, because it could not hold its occupant. He entered the place of death and came out on the third day, and he turns tombs into doorways.

How do I protect myself and my children from unmarked graves? Test every teacher, however respected, by Scripture and by fruit (Matthew 7:15–20; 1 John 4:1). Watch whether a ministry produces love, humility and joy in Christ, or fear, pride and harshness. Be wary of anyone who cannot be questioned. Do not take your whole picture of the Christian life from one impressive person; let your children see many ordinary faithful believers. And where you find real spiritual abuse, name it and bring it into the light; protecting victims always matters more than protecting a reputation.
verseByVerse.note: Touching a grave made a person unclean; an unmarked grave defiled people without their knowing it.

parallels.desc: whoever touches a grave is unclean

verseByVerse.quote: One of the lawyers answered him, 'Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.' And he said, 'Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to teachers who load people with religious demands and will not lift a finger to help them carry the load. A lawyer’s protest does not stop the woes; it doubles them.

You insult us also. The lawyers, experts in the law of Moses, were often Pharisees too. He does not say “that is untrue” but “you insult us”, which concedes the accuracy and objects to the tone, one of the commonest defences against a word that cannot be answered.

Burdens hard to bear. The picture is of pack animals and their drivers. These men had built an elaborate structure of rulings around the law, specifying exactly how each command was to be kept, and the ordinary Israelite was expected to carry it. Peter would later call it a yoke “that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear” (Acts 15:10).

Not with one of your fingers. Either they found clever ways round their own rules or, the heavier charge, did nothing to help others carry them, never asking whether a man with a farm and five children could do it. Set that against Jesus, who two chapters later lays his hands on a woman bent double for eighteen years and straightens her, and is rebuked for doing it on the Sabbath (13:10–17). The lawyers would not move a finger toward the load. He puts his hands on it.

In everyday life. Christ has put his hands on your load; lift a finger for theirs: the young mother overwhelmed by advice, the new believer drowning in expectations, the friend who feels he can never do enough.

Does this mean Christian teachers should not preach high standards? No. Jesus set the highest standard of all, but his standards come with grace to keep them and forgiveness for failing them, and he himself carried the heaviest load. The test for anyone who teaches is simple and uncomfortable: does what you say make it harder or easier for an ordinary struggling believer to get up on Monday? High standards can be preached in a way that lifts people or flattens them, and the difference is usually whether the preacher gets under the load himself and points people to Christ who bears it.
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honouring the prophets of the past while rejecting God’s messenger in front of you is not repentance but agreement with those who killed them. The sons finish what the fathers began.

You build the tombs of the prophets. Building and beautifying prophets’ tombs was a genuine piety of the period. It looked like the most respectful thing imaginable, even like repentance. Jesus calls it complicity.

Witnesses who consent. There is a bitter play in it: the fathers put the prophets in the ground, and the sons put up the masonry over them. They honour dead prophets and reject the living one, as their fathers did. Tomb-building is a way of being on the right side of a controversy that is safely over. A dead prophet has stopped saying the things that got him killed; meanwhile a living one is sitting at their table telling them their religion is an unmarked grave, and they are about to arrange his death. A man who says he would never have joined the mob, while queuing to join this one, has not broken with his fathers. He has simply arrived late.

A tomb that could not be kept. The one Prophet whose tomb they would most like to build could not be kept in one: the stone was rolled away, and “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22). We do not build monuments to a dead Christ. We worship a living one.

The pattern in every generation. Every generation admires the reformers and martyrs of the past, whose battles are settled, and finds their like in its own congregation intolerable. A dead prophet asks only for a gift towards his monument; a live one asks for repentance.

Are there prophets today whom we must heed? Not in the sense of new revelation: the prophets and apostles laid the foundation once for all, and the canon of Scripture is closed (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 1:1–2). But God still sends people who apply his word to us with uncomfortable accuracy: the pastor who preaches on the sin our church tolerates, the friend who tells us the truth. The test is not whether they claim a new word from God, but whether what they say is what Scripture says. When it is, we must not honour the Bible on the shelf while silencing the person reading it to us. Some Christians believe God still gives prophetic words today; most of them agree that nothing said now can add to Scripture or correct it, and that is the point that matters here.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute,’ so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The generation that rejects God’s final messenger fills up the guilt of all who killed his prophets, and the reckoning will fall on it. It is the climax of a long history of rejection.

Prophets and apostles. God, in his wisdom, sends messengers, and his people kill them. Note the word “apostles”: Jesus is looking at the men who will be sent after him, and some will be killed: Stephen (Acts 7:58–60), James (Acts 12:2). (On the source of the saying, see “Uncertain wording” below.)

The blood of all the prophets. The generation that rejects the Messiah finishes what its ancestors began, and so brings their guilt to its full measure (Matthew 23:32).

From Abel to Zechariah. The two names are the bookends of the Hebrew Bible. Abel is the first murder, in Genesis (Genesis 4:8). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court, on the king’s orders, for rebuking the people (2 Chronicles 24:20–22); his is the last murder of a prophet recorded in Chronicles, which stands last in the Hebrew ordering of the books. So from the first page to the last, the whole of the Old Testament. As he died, Zechariah said: “May the LORD see and avenge!”

Required of this generation. This was fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (19:41–44; 21:20–24), within forty years of these words.

A better word than the blood of Abel. Abel’s blood cried out from the ground; Zechariah’s prayed that the LORD would see and avenge. There is another blood, shed by this same generation, that “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). It cries not for vengeance but for pardon. “Father, forgive them,” said the one whose blood it was. The account of all the prophets’ blood was settled in full, and for everyone who trusts him it is settled in mercy.

What it does not mean. Verses like this have been quarried for centuries to justify appalling treatment of Jewish people. But this is addressed not to a nation or a race but to the scribes and lawyers in that room. The speaker is a Jew, as are his disciples and every prophet he names, and he will weep over this city, not gloat (19:41). To turn a Jewish prophet’s rebuke of Jewish leaders for killing Jewish prophets into a charge against Jewish people as such is to end up standing exactly where the men being rebuked are standing. Christians owe Jewish people love, gratitude for the Messiah who came from them, and the gospel offered humbly.

In everyday life. Each time you hear a clear word and set it aside, it becomes easier to do again. Name the truth you have been putting off, and, since the blood that speaks pardon still pleads for you, obey it before the week is out.

Is God punishing men for what their ancestors did? Scripture appears to forbid exactly that: “The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father” (Ezekiel 18:20); “nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers” (Deuteronomy 24:16). But Jesus has already said why this is not inherited guilt: “you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers” (v. 48). Nothing is charged to these men that they have not personally ratified. The guilt is incurred by choosing, with eyes open, to do the identical thing. And the reckoning falls here because this is the generation to whom the Son himself has come, the one to whom every murdered prophet was pointing. The account closes not because they are worse than their ancestors but because they have more light and are about to do worse with it. The judgment is proportional to the privilege, exactly as at Chorazin (10:13–15).

Uncertain wording. Two things here are not certain. First, the quotation from “the Wisdom of God” matches no known book exactly. The likeliest explanation is that Jesus is speaking as the Wisdom of God, the one who sent the prophets; Matthew puts the words directly in his mouth, “I send you prophets” (Matthew 23:34). Second, Matthew calls this Zechariah the son of Barachiah (Matthew 23:35), while 2 Chronicles 24:20 names his father as Jehoiada; Luke gives no father’s name. Jehoiada may have been his grandfather, or the name may reflect a confusion with the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1). This is a real difficulty, and believers who hold Scripture true admit that no answer is certain. Either way, Jesus means the last prophet’s murder in the Hebrew Bible’s order, as Abel’s was the first.
verseByVerse.note: Abel is the first murder in Scripture; Zechariah’s is the last in the Hebrew Bible’s order, which ends with Chronicles.

parallels.desc: Zechariah stoned in the temple court

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heaviest woe falls on teachers who hid the way to knowing God: they never went in themselves, and they blocked those who were going in. They held the key by office and used it to lock the door.

The key of knowledge. Behind the door is the knowledge of God: not information about him, but knowing him, which the Scriptures exist to produce. These men held the key by office. The key is the right understanding of Scripture, which points to Christ (24:27, 44–45; John 5:39), and they have taken it away, locking with their traditions the door God had opened.

You did not enter yourselves. They had the key and never used it; they did not come to Jesus. A lifetime handling the Scriptures of the living God, and they never went in; it is possible in every generation.

You hindered those who were entering. People were already on their way in, and these men got in the way: by burying the law under rulings no ordinary person could carry (v. 46), by making the way in a matter of outward ritual rather than of the heart (v. 39), and by teaching so that God came out looking like the sort of person they were. That last does the real damage: a teacher chiefly transmits not doctrine but an impression of God, and people believe the impression long after they have forgotten the doctrine.

He opened the Scriptures. The lawyers took away the key; Christ turns it. On the evening of his resurrection he opened the Scriptures on the Emmaus road until their hearts burned (24:32), and then opened the minds of the rest to understand them (24:45). No keyholder on earth can lock out a sinner whom he has let in.

How do I know whether my teaching opens or shuts the door? Ask whether people leave your teaching seeing Christ more clearly, and wanting him more. Ask whether you point to the cross and the empty tomb, or mainly to rules and techniques. Ask whether struggling people find in you a way in or a wall. And be in the room yourself: the surest way to open the door for others is to be someone who has gone through it and is still delighting in what is inside.

verseByVerse.quote: As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The meal ends not in repentance but in an ambush, as the scribes and Pharisees begin hunting for words to use against Jesus. From here the opposition is a hunt with a purpose.

To press him hard. The dinner produced not repentance, nor even argument, but something colder. “Press him hard” (deinōs enechein) means to be bitterly hostile, and they provoke him to speak, firing questions as a witness is pressed until he says something usable.

Lying in wait. The vocabulary of an ambush. Respectable men follow a guest out of a house to get a sentence they can use, as they will in Jerusalem (20:20–26). This is a turning point: the hunt will run without interruption to a trial and a cross.

Truth softens or sets. God’s word, spoken plainly by a guest at their own table, hardened them. That is not a failure of the message. Pharaoh’s heart set harder with every plague; Isaiah was told that this people would hear and not understand (Isaiah 6:9–10). The truth is never neutral. It softens a heart or hardens it, depending on the heart it lands on.

Walking into the trap on purpose. The scene leads straight into Luke 12, where Jesus’ first words to his disciples are “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy”, and “do not fear those who kill the body” (12:1–4). The journey to Jerusalem now has hunters following it, and Jesus walks on toward the cross with his eyes open. They never could catch him in his words, because he never spoke a false word. When at last they took him, it was not because he slipped, but because he gave himself up, the Good Shepherd laying down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). The hunters thought they had trapped him; in fact he walked into the trap on purpose, to spring it on death itself, and to rescue the very men who were hunting him.

Why does the same word soften some and harden others? Because the word meets hearts in different conditions, and because God in his sovereign mercy opens some hearts (Acts 16:14) and in his justice leaves others to the hardness they have chosen (Romans 9:18). No one who hardens himself can blame God; no one who is softened can boast. When the word cuts, do not reach for a reason to resent the one who spoke it. Bring the wound to God and ask him to soften you. A heart that asks to be softened is already being softened.

parallels.desc: to trap him in his talk

11.text: <sup>1</sup> Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.” <sup>2</sup> And he said to them, “When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. <sup>3</sup> Give us each day our daily bread, <sup>4</sup> and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.’” <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, <sup>6</sup> for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’; <sup>7</sup> and he will answer from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’? <sup>8</sup> I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs. <sup>9</sup> And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. <sup>10</sup> For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. <sup>11</sup> What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; <sup>12</sup> or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? <sup>13</sup> If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” <sup>14</sup> Now he was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marveled. <sup>15</sup> But some of them said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons,” <sup>16</sup> while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven. <sup>17</sup> But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. <sup>18</sup> And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. <sup>19</sup> And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. <sup>20</sup> But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. <sup>21</sup> When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; <sup>22</sup> but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his spoil. <sup>23</sup> Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. <sup>24</sup> “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ <sup>25</sup> And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. <sup>26</sup> Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.” <sup>27</sup> As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed!” <sup>28</sup> But he said, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!” <sup>29</sup> When the crowds were increasing, he began to say, “This generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. <sup>30</sup> For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation. <sup>31</sup> The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. <sup>32</sup> The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here. <sup>33</sup> “No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. <sup>34</sup> Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness. <sup>35</sup> Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. <sup>36</sup> If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.” <sup>37</sup> While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. <sup>38</sup> The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner. <sup>39</sup> And the Lord said to him, “Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. <sup>40</sup> You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? <sup>41</sup> But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you. <sup>42</sup> “But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. <sup>43</sup> Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces. <sup>44</sup> Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.” <sup>45</sup> One of the lawyers answered him, “Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.” <sup>46</sup> And he said, “Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers. <sup>47</sup> Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. <sup>48</sup> So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs. <sup>49</sup> Therefore also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute,’ <sup>50</sup> so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, <sup>51</sup> from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation. <sup>52</sup> Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.” <sup>53</sup> As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, <sup>54</sup> lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.

keyVerse.quote: If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!
keyVerse.note: This verse gathers up the chapter’s teaching on prayer: God is not a reluctant neighbour but a Father, better than the best earthly father, and his greatest gift is himself, the Holy Spirit. It also exposes, by contrast, the rest of the chapter, where men who knew all about God accused his Son and never asked. The gift promised here is what Christ died and rose to pour out (24:49; Acts 2:33).

11.reflection:
Jesus teaches us to begin prayer with one word, “Father” (v. 2). What difference does it make to pray as a child rather than as a servant or a stranger? What makes that word hard or easy for you to say?

The friend at midnight is asking bread for someone else, and he will not stop knocking (vv. 5–10). Who are you trying to help with nothing to set before them? How do verses 11–13 help when a prayer you have prayed for years has not been answered as you hoped?

Jesus says there is no neutral ground (v. 23), and that a life swept clean but left empty is not safe (vv. 24–26). Why is “I am waiting for more evidence” not as safe a place to stand as it sounds? What is the difference between cleaning up a life and Christ living in it?

The woes fall on people who knew the Bible well and took religion seriously (vv. 37–52). Which of them, tithing herbs while neglecting justice, loving the front seat, loading burdens, or shutting the door on others, is the most likely danger in your church, or in you? How does knowing God as Father free us from them?

12.title: Fear, Greed, Anxiety, and the Coming Fire
12.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 12 belongs to the long journey to Jerusalem (9:51–19:27) and follows straight on from the dinner where Jesus pronounced woes on the Pharisees and lawyers, who are now lying in wait for him (11:53–54). The crowd has grown to many thousands, and Jesus speaks mostly to his disciples while it listens.

The message. Live your whole life in the open before God, in the light of his coming, and without fear, because the God you must answer to is your Father. Three rivals compete for a disciple’s heart: the fear of people, the grip of possessions, and the drowsiness that forgets the Master is coming. Jesus answers each with the same God: the one to be feared above all, who counts the hairs of your head; who calls the hoarder a fool and is glad to give his little flock the kingdom; who will return at an hour no one expects, and serve the servants he finds waiting.

Why it was said. The disciples were a little flock in a hostile land, soon to be dragged before synagogues and rulers; many were poor and might well go hungry; and their Master was about to leave them for a long night. Luke’s readers knew all three: opposition, poverty and the long wait for Christ’s return (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Fear first (vv. 1–12): hypocrisy is the mask fear wears, but everything hidden will be revealed; fear God and you need fear nothing else, for he forgets no sparrow, and the Son and the Spirit stand with those who confess him. Then possessions (vv. 13–34): a quarrel over an inheritance prompts the parable of the rich fool, who died the night he planned bigger barns; then the cure for anxiety, ravens and lilies, a Father who knows, a kingdom given, and treasure in heaven. Then readiness (vv. 35–48): servants with lamps lit, a thief at an unknown hour, and a steward judged by what he did with the delay. Last, urgency (vv. 49–59): a fire, a baptism, a divided household, and a crowd that reads the sky but not the time, urged to settle with God on the road, before they reach the Judge.

Where it leads. At the heart of the chapter are a Master who comes home and ties on an apron to wait on his servants (v. 37), and a Son who longs to be plunged into the baptism of his death (v. 50). The one who warns of the Judge is the one who will pay the debt, so that those who settle with him on the road find not a prison but a Father’s table.

For us. Ask which of the three rules you: the fear of what people think, the security of what you own, or the quiet assumption that the Master is delayed. Then hear the tenderest words in the chapter: “Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (v. 32).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Fear God, Not Man; Acknowledge Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Live in the open before God and fear him alone, for he is the Father who counts your hairs, and his Spirit will give you words. With the crowd pressing in, Jesus warns his disciples first against hypocrisy, the mask worn for fear of people, which cannot last, because everything hidden will be revealed (vv. 1–3). The cure is the right fear: those who kill the body can do no more, so fear God, and then fear nothing, because he forgets no sparrow (vv. 4–7). The stakes are eternal: confess Christ before men and he will confess you before the angels (vv. 8–9). The hardest saying, the blasphemy against the Spirit (v. 10), is followed at once by the promise that the same Spirit will give the words in the hour of trial (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
The word for hell is Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom, where children had been burned in sacrifice to Molech (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31). On who has authority to cast into it, and why the same God does not forget a sparrow, see the notes on vv. 4–5 and 6–7.

The blasphemy against the Spirit must be read in its context, the charge that Jesus cast out demons by Beelzebul (see the note on v. 10).
verseByVerse.examples:
The saying about inner rooms and housetops cuts both ways (see the note on v. 3).

The confession sayings are not a performance test (see the note on vv. 8–9), and the promise of words in the hour of trial is not a promise of acquittal (see the note on vv. 11–12).

verseByVerse.quote: In the meantime, when so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first, 'Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ first warning to his own disciples is against hypocrisy, because it spreads quietly and cannot stay hidden: one day everything will be seen.

The setting. The teaching follows straight on from a dinner that ended with the Pharisees and lawyers lying in wait to catch him in something he might say (11:53–54). Luke’s word for the crowd is myriads, and people are being walked on: the height of his popularity, with his enemies at his heels. Yet in the crush he turns from the thousands to the handful, because he has just watched what religion had done to the men at that table.

The leaven of the Pharisees. Leaven was not a sachet of yeast but a lump of dough kept back from the last batch, left to sour, and worked into the new one: small, invisible once mixed in, and changing everything it touches (1 Corinthians 5:6). Every Jewish household searched out and removed all leaven before Passover (Exodus 12:15, 19), so the word already meant something to be cleared out of the house, not lived with. Hypocrisy, too, starts small and spreads through a life and a community.

Which is hypocrisy. Luke alone gives Jesus’ own definition. A hypokritēs was a stage actor, speaking his lines from behind a mask. Hypocrisy is not failing to live up to what you believe, which is the condition of every honest Christian. It is playing a part: pretending to be what you are not.

Nothing is covered up. The first argument is practical. He does not say hypocrisy is wrong, though it is; he says it does not work. The performance has a closing date, and at the judgment everything behind the mask will be public (8:17). That is frightening or liberating, depending on whether a person is keeping up a false front.

The eyes that see through every mask. The one who says this is the one who will do it: when the Lord comes, he “will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart” (1 Corinthians 4:5). Luke has shown him doing it already: he knew the thoughts of the scribes before they spoke (5:22), and read the heart of the Pharisee at whose table a sinful woman wept (7:39–40). This is the Judge himself telling his friends what his eyes will one day uncover, while there is still time to come out from behind the mask and be forgiven.

Found out long ago, and covered. The Lord who warns us against masks wore none: what he said in the temple he said in the garden. And he came to save hypocrites, knowing everything behind every mask and loving us still. On the day when all is revealed, those who are in him will not be found out. They were found out long ago, at the cross, and covered.

If I struggle with sin I have not overcome, am I a hypocrite? No. A hypocrite is not a person who fails but a person who pretends. The believer who fights a sin, confesses it to God and perhaps to a trusted friend, and keeps getting up again is not acting a part; he is being honest about a war. Hypocrisy begins when you cultivate an image you know is false, and condemn in others what you excuse in yourself. The cure is to walk in the light (1 John 1:7): honest before God, honest with someone, and humble about yourself. And the deepest cure is the gospel itself. Hypocrisy runs on the need to be approved, and a person who knows he is fully known by God and still loved in Christ no longer needs a mask (Romans 8:33–34).
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) works invisibly through the whole lump; here it pictures hypocrisy.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is said in the most private place will one day be heard in the most public one. The saying is a warning to the hypocrite and an encouragement to the quiet witness.

The inner rooms and the housetops. The private rooms are the inner rooms, the windowless storeroom at the back of a house where nobody could overhear. The housetops were flat, and where the roofs adjoined, a man standing on his could be heard by the whole street; it was where public announcements were made. What is said in the first will be repeated from the second (compare Matthew 12:36).

It cuts both ways. In context the primary force is the warning: everything a man is when nobody is watching, the private appetites, the things said about people not in the room, will be read out. But it is also an encouragement. Much of what the disciples say for Christ will be said quietly, in rooms with no audience; it is being heard, and will be preached to the world.

Not done in a corner. The rooms where Jesus taught the Twelve were small: a boat, a house, an upper room. Within weeks of his resurrection what had been said to a handful was proclaimed to thousands, and Paul could tell King Agrippa that none of it had been done in a corner (Acts 26:26). The bargain to betray him was struck in private, away from the crowd (22:3–6), and God turned what that whispered plot led to, the cross, into the most public news in the world, announced from every housetop as the place where sinners find mercy.

In everyday life. Speak in private as a child whose Father hears it all: the comment about someone you would never make to their face, the message you would hate to see forwarded. And take courage: the God who hears every whisper in every inner room is not a spy but a Father, who hears the gossip and the groaning alike, the curse and the prayer too deep for words. Everything hidden will be revealed, and for those who are his, the last thing revealed will be how much they were loved.

Will my forgiven sins be broadcast at the judgment? Scripture’s emphasis for believers is that their sins are blotted out, cast into the depths of the sea, remembered no more (Hebrews 8:12; Micah 7:19). Whatever is opened on that day will be opened as the record of grace, not as evidence for condemnation, because there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). The warning presses on the hidden life being kept from God now. Bring it into the light today, in confession, and it will never be used against you.
verseByVerse.note: Flat roofs were public places; announcements were made from them.

verseByVerse.quote: 'I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let the fear of people rule you, because the worst they can do ends at death; fear God, whose authority reaches beyond it. Jesus says this to his friends, and he says it to set them free.

I tell you, my friends. Only here in the first three Gospels does Jesus call his disciples “my friends” (compare John 15:14–15), and he does it just before preparing them for persecution.

Nothing more that they can do. Hypocrisy often comes from fear of people, and Jesus goes to the root. Persecution will come, but the worst it can do is kill the body; then it has nothing left, because death is not the end.

Authority to cast into hell. Luke’s word is not merely power but authority (exousia), the lawful right to rule what lies beyond death. Some have taken this to be the devil, but Satan is never handed the keys of anyone’s final destiny, and believers are told to resist him (James 4:7), not to fear him. The one whose authority runs past the grave is God. Hell is geenna, Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, which his hearers could have pointed at; Jesus uses it of the place of final, conscious punishment.

Fear him. The fear of God drives out the fear of people: the LORD of hosts, him you shall regard as holy, let him be your fear (Isaiah 8:12–13); “the fear of man lays a snare” (Proverbs 29:25). And this awe is the beginning of wisdom. The God who has authority to cast into hell sent his Son into the place of judgment for us. The fire that we feared fell on him; the One with authority over death went down into it and came out holding its keys (Revelation 1:18). So the God we fear is the God we flee to.

The road to Jerusalem. The man who says this is walking to Jerusalem to be killed (9:51), and he lived by this saying first. When Pharisees warned him that Herod wanted to kill him, he sent back word that he would go on, today and tomorrow, and finish his course (13:31–33). When they did their worst, they could kill his body and seal a tomb, and after that they had nothing more that they could do. Every tyranny runs on the fear of what can be done to a body; this sentence cuts the supply line, and invites his friends to stand where he stands.

In everyday life. Whose opinion do you fear most? Your manager’s, your family’s, the group chat’s? Name the person whose disapproval most shapes what you say about Christ. Then put that fear next to the fear of God, and watch it shrink to its true size.

Are Christians meant to be afraid of God? This is spoken to “my friends”. The fear of God is not cringing terror for his children, but reverent awe of the one who holds all power, including over eternity: fear the right one most. Its effect is the opposite of paralysis: a man who fears God properly has been made unafraid of everything else, because the worst any human power can do to him has been put in its true proportion. A child can be in awe of his father’s strength and run into his arms in the same moment. That is why the next thing Jesus says is “fear not”.

How can a God of love have authority to cast into hell? Because love that is not also just would not be good. A God who looked at cruelty, abuse and contempt for himself and did nothing would not be loving; he would be indifferent. Jesus, the kindest man who ever lived, speaks more plainly about hell than anyone in Scripture, and here as a warning to his friends. Hell is God’s final, just answer to sin that was never brought to him for mercy (Romans 2:5–6). And the same God has opened the way of escape at his own cost, so that no one who flees to his Son will be condemned (John 3:16–18).
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” renders Gehenna.

verseByVerse.quote: Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God to be feared is the God who counts the hairs of your head, so his children need fear nothing else. If he forgets no sparrow, he will not forget you.

Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Two verses after “fear him” comes “fear not”, and the bridge between them is a bird nobody wanted. Sparrows were the cheapest meat in the market, food for the very poor. Matthew gives the price as two sparrows for a penny (Matthew 10:29); Luke says five for two pennies, which suggests that a buyer of four got the fifth thrown in free, the one with no value at all.

Not one of them is forgotten. Including that one. Not that God feeds them or values them, but that none is forgotten, the language of memory: even the bird thrown in free is registered.

The hairs of your head. The Greek tense means they have been counted and the count still stands: a figure that changes daily and is never out of date. That God knows it shows not that the number matters but that his attention to you is complete.

Fear not. The God to be feared (v. 5) is the God who cares. Jesus has just conceded that they can kill you, yet even then your body is not outside his care. Nothing happens to you that he does not know and allow, and he works all of it for the good of those who love him (Romans 8:28). The one to be feared and the one who counts the hairs are the same person, and the second fact is what makes the first bearable.

Priced at Calvary. How does a disciple know he is worth more than many sparrows? The sparrow’s value was fixed in the market; ours was fixed at the cross: “you were ransomed … not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Our worth is not something we bring to God. It is what he has decided to spend on us, and he spent his Son. A dying thief, worth less than the fifth sparrow to the world that crucified him, said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (23:42), and the Son of God answered with paradise. He has never forgotten one sinner who called on him.

If God cares so closely, why did he let this happen to me? Jesus does not promise that sparrows never fall; Matthew says “not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father” (Matthew 10:29). The promise is not that nothing painful will happen, but that nothing will happen unknown, unnoticed or outside his purpose. You may not see the reason this side of glory, and Scripture does not ask you to pretend the pain is small; it asks you to trust the character of a Father who counts hairs, who did not spare his own Son, and who will one day wipe every tear away. Bring the question to him honestly; the psalms give you words for it.
verseByVerse.note: Sparrows were the cheapest birds sold for food; Matthew says two for a penny, Luke five for two, as if the fifth came free.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever openly owns Jesus before people, he will own as his before God; whoever disowns him, he will disown. There are two courtrooms, and what happens in the second corresponds to what happened in the first.

Acknowledges me. The word means confesses, openly declares loyalty; the unusual construction, “confesses in me”, suggests declaring an allegiance, not merely stating a fact. And both halves are public: before men, then before the angels of God.

Before the angels of God. At the judgment Jesus is the judge, and his word, “this one belongs to me”, decides eternal destiny. Whatever is said for him in a difficult room is said again, by him, in front of the angels; and whoever denies him here will be denied there (compare 9:26).

What it does not mean. Not that a single failure means final rejection: Peter denied Jesus three times in public (22:57–62) and was recommissioned on a beach (John 21:15–19). The warning is against a settled refusal to own him over a life, and the warning itself is one of the means God uses to keep us faithful. He was not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11), though we have so often been ashamed of him.

The smaller moments. Nor should the warning be softened. Few Western Christians will stand in a court; the moments that count are smaller: the conversation at work where it would be easier to say nothing, the family gathering where silence is taken for agreement, the friendship of a decade in which the most important fact about your life has never been mentioned. None is a courtroom denial, but a man can spend his whole life quietly declining to be identified with Christ, without ever once deciding to deny him.

If I stayed silent when I should have spoken, have I denied Christ? Probably you failed, as Peter did, and the answer is the same as his: go back to the Lord, confess it, and be restored. The look that made Peter weep was mercy (22:61–62). A single silence is not a settled life of denial. Ask God for the next opportunity, and take it. Often the best repair is to go back and say, “I wanted to tell you what Christ means to me, and I did not.” That is how a failure becomes a confession.

verseByVerse.quote: And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every word spoken against Jesus can be forgiven, but not the settled refusal of the Spirit who points to him, because that refuses the only way to forgiveness. Few verses have caused sincere Christians more terror, and it must be handled slowly.

A word against the Son of Man. That this is forgivable is an extraordinary concession. Men can insult him, mock him, misjudge him, and be forgiven if they repent: Paul once blasphemed Jesus and persecuted the church (1 Timothy 1:13), and Peter denied him. Both were forgiven.

Blasphemy against the Spirit. The context unlocks the verse. In Mark and Matthew this saying comes straight after the accusation that Jesus cast out demons by Satan (Mark 3:28–30; Matthew 12:31–32), and Luke has just given us that accusation (11:15). Men had watched the Spirit work through Jesus in the open and called it the devil: “for they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit’” (Mark 3:30). That is the sin: not a word said in a bad moment, but a deliberate, settled rejection of the Spirit’s testimony to Christ, in full knowledge, calling God’s light darkness. Luke places it between the call to acknowledge Christ (vv. 8–9) and the promise of the Spirit’s help (vv. 11–12): a disciple who fails under pressure, as Peter would, can be forgiven; those who hear the Spirit’s witness to Christ through these disciples and finally refuse it are refusing the only voice that leads to pardon.

Why can it not be forgiven? Not because grace is insufficient, but because the Spirit is the one who brings people to repentance by convicting of sin and pointing to Christ (John 16:8–14). It is not that someone wants to repent and cannot be forgiven, but that he no longer wants to repent. A man who has finally refused the Spirit is not troubled; he does not lie awake over the question.

Spoken against, and praying. Why can a word against the Son of Man be forgiven at all? Because he came to be spoken against: appointed for a sign that is opposed (2:34), called a glutton and a drunkard (7:34), accused of working by Beelzebul (11:15); and from the cross he prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (23:34). The forgiveness held out to his slanderers was bought by the one they slandered. That is also why the other sin is beyond forgiveness: it refuses the Spirit who points to that blood, and there is no other blood to flee to.

Baptised in the name they had spoken against. Glory to the Spirit who does not give up easily. Fifty days after a Jerusalem crowd called for the death of the Son of Man, he cut men to the heart (Acts 2:23, 36–41), and about three thousand were baptised in the name of the one they had spoken against. The God who warns of the one sin never forgiven has forgiven every sin of everyone who comes to Christ.

The anxiety is the disproof. If you are reading this with your stomach tight, that is proof that you have not committed it: the Spirit does not trouble hearts he has stopped working on. The unforgivable sin has never once been committed by a person who wanted to be forgiven. If you know someone haunted by this verse, do not leave them with it: sit with them, read John 6:37 aloud together, and remind them that the door is open.

What about blasphemous thoughts that come into my mind against my will? Many tender believers are tormented by sudden, horrible thoughts about God or the Spirit, which they hate even as they arrive. Those thoughts are not the sin Jesus describes; they are temptations or intrusive thoughts, and the distress they cause shows your heart is on God’s side. Do not argue with them endlessly; bring them to Christ, tell him you hate them, and turn your attention to his promises. If they are persistent and consuming, speak to a wise pastor and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up; there is no shame in either.

Where Christians differ, and a pastoral word. Some have taught that the unforgivable sin is a specific act, such as suicide or a particular blasphemous word. This commentary’s view: it is not a single act or careless word, but a final, hardened rejection of the Spirit’s witness to Christ. Anyone who is worried that they have committed it has not, because the very worry shows the Spirit is still at work in them. Those who have committed it do not care. And a family grieving a suicide should hear plainly that Scripture nowhere calls that tragedy the unforgivable sin; a true believer who dies in such darkness is still held by Christ, from whose hand no one can snatch his sheep (John 10:28).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When disciples are put on trial for Christ, they need not dread what to say, because the Holy Spirit will give them the words in that hour. The Spirit who is blasphemed by unbelievers (v. 10) stands beside believers.

When they bring you. Not “if”, but “when”. Luke’s second volume shows it again and again: Peter and John before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4), Stephen before the council (Acts 7), Paul before governors and a king (Acts 24–26).

How you should defend yourself. The word (apologēsēsthe), from which we get apologetics, was the set term for a courtroom defence speech. Men trained for years to make one well; the disciples are told not to worry about it.

In that very hour. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke boldly before the council, and they were astonished at uneducated, common men (Acts 4:8–13). Stephen spoke with a wisdom they could not withstand (Acts 6:10).

The Son of Man standing. Stephen made his defence under this promise, and at the end of it he saw “the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:56): the one who promised to acknowledge his confessors before the angels (12:8) was on his feet for the first martyr. Later Jesus repeats the promise in his own name: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict” (21:15). He gives the words, and watches from the throne.

What it does not mean. It is not a licence for unprepared preaching. The situation is arrest and interrogation, not a man who has not opened his Bible all week and intends to trust the Spirit on Sunday; Paul told Timothy to do his best to present himself to God as one approved, rightly handling the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15). Nor is it a promise that the defence will succeed. Stephen spoke under exactly this promise and was stoned. What is promised is not acquittal but the right words.

The ordinary comfort. The dread of not knowing what to say, at a hospital bedside or in front of someone hostile, keeps many Christians quiet. The promise is not that you will be eloquent. It is that in the hour, and not before it, you will not be alone in the room. Christ himself stood silent before his accusers so that we might never stand alone before ours.

In the flow. The chapter’s first movement began with the mask worn for fear of what people think (v. 1) and ends with the last fear that keeps a disciple quiet. The Father counts the hairs, the Son confesses his own before the angels, and the Spirit gives the words: the whole Trinity stands behind a frightened witness.

In everyday life. Pray for persecuted Christians standing trial today, that the Spirit would give them words; find one name or country and pray for it specifically.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Parable of the Rich Fool
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A life does not consist in what it owns, and whoever stores up for himself without being rich toward God is a fool. A man interrupts teaching about hell and martyrdom to ask Jesus to make his brother share the family estate; Jesus refuses to arbitrate and warns the whole crowd against all covetousness (vv. 13–15). The parable that follows shows covetousness in a respectable man: the land gave the harvest, he forgot the Giver, talked only to himself, and told his soul that grain would satisfy it (vv. 16–19). God’s first word to him is “Fool!”; his soul is demanded that night, and his goods pass to others (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology:
The fool of the Psalms is the one who says in his heart that there is no God (Psalm 14:1; see the note on vv. 20–21).

The alternative Jesus names is not poverty but being rich toward God (see the note on vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.examples: The man’s problem was not his abundance but his accounting (see the note on vv. 18–19), and the question left hanging, “whose will they be”, answers itself (see vv. 20–21).

verseByVerse.quote: Someone in the crowd said to him, 'Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.' But he said to him, 'Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you?' And he said to them, 'Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus refuses to be drawn into a quarrel over an inheritance and goes to its root: the craving for more, which mistakes possessions for life. From here to verse 34 the chapter turns from the fear of people to the other great ruler of the heart, the grip of possessions.

Tell my brother. Jesus has been talking about hell and martyrdom, and a man wants help with a family estate. It was not an unreasonable request: rabbis were sometimes asked to settle inheritance disputes, and the law gave the eldest son a double portion (Deuteronomy 21:17; see inheritance). But he does not ask Jesus to settle the dispute; he says “tell my brother”. He has already reached his verdict and wants it enforced.

Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you? The address is cool, “man”, not “friend”, and the refusal is flat. There is an echo of what was said to Moses when he intervened between two Hebrews in Egypt: “Who made you a prince and a judge over us?” (Exodus 2:14). He never enquires whether the grievance is just. He refuses because this is not what he came to do: to act as referee over one man’s estate would have made him a hired official in a family quarrel, when he is the Lord of both brothers, come to deal with the heart. The man’s real problem is not his brother but his greed.

All covetousness. He refuses the case, diagnoses the plaintiff, and speaks to the whole crowd. Covetousness (pleonexia) is the desire for more, and “all covetousness” includes the respectable kinds, such as the reasonable-sounding insistence on getting everything one is owed. The tenth commandment forbids it (Exodus 20:17), and Paul calls it idolatry (Colossians 3:5). The man may have been in the right; what Jesus saw was a man who could not let go.

Judge of the living and the dead. The man’s question, “who made me a judge”, has an answer he did not know: God did. Peter would tell Cornelius that Jesus is “the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead” (Acts 10:42). He will not sit as arbitrator over one field, because he will one day sit as Judge over both brothers and every field on earth. He who owned everything became poor, so that brothers who quarrel over fields might become fellow heirs of a kingdom.

What your life consists in. Hardly anyone would say his life consists in his possessions; we only want to be secure, or to give the children a good start. Those are good things. But Timothy Keller, in Counterfeit Gods, pointed out that the idols that rule us are usually good things we have turned into ultimate things, and you can tell which ones by how we react when they are threatened. Whatever you are sure would make you safe, if only you had a little more, is what your life has come to consist in, and it can never give you enough. Jesus says life is something else: not what you hold but who holds you. He came that we “may have life and have it abundantly” (John 10:10; compare 14:6). The one who is in Christ already has the one possession that cannot be required of him tonight (v. 20), because it is a person, and that person will never die again.

In everyday life. Where this saying applies: the quiet resentment over who got what in a will, the endless browsing for the next upgrade, the sense that a little more would finally be enough. The next time you think a little more would settle it, ask what you expect it to give you, and thank Christ that in him you already have it. Where applying it would be wrong: using it to shame a widow for seeking what she needs to live, or to tell a poor family that wanting a decent wage is covetous. Greed is the grip, not the need.

Is it wrong to seek justice in a money dispute? Not in itself. Scripture values justice, and Paul used his right as a Roman citizen to appeal to Caesar (Acts 25:11); sometimes a fair settlement should be sought, especially to protect the vulnerable. But Jesus’ warning cuts close to every inheritance quarrel: what is happening in your heart? Is the money worth the brother? Christians should be slow to take one another to court (1 Corinthians 6:1–8), quick to seek reconciliation, and willing, sometimes, to be wronged rather than lose a relationship. Where you must pursue a claim, pursue it without bitterness, and be ready to let go of more than you think you can.
verseByVerse.note: Rabbis were sometimes asked to settle inheritance disputes. The law gave the eldest son a double share.

parallels.desc: a double portion to the firstborn

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable, saying, 'The land of a rich man produced plentifully, and he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parable begins with a man given a harvest he did not make, who talks it over with nobody but himself. The trouble is not the harvest but the forgotten Giver.

The land produced. Only Luke records this parable, and the way it opens matters: not “a rich man made a fortune”, but “the land of a rich man produced”. He may have ploughed and sown well, but the harvest came out of soil he did not make, watered by rain he did not arrange (Acts 14:17). It is why firstfruits were brought to the temple and the edges of the field left for the poor (Leviticus 19:9–10). It is the first thing the man will forget.

He thought to himself. Literally “he dialogued with himself”: not with God, his neighbours, his wife or the labourers who brought the harvest in. The whole discussion of an enormous surplus takes place inside one skull.

What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops? His problem is real. He is not a fraud or an oppressor; the parable gives him no vices at all. He asks a sensible question and gives it the wrong answer. The right one stood in his own Scriptures: he could have shared with the poor (3:11), and there were poor people within a mile of that farm. Listen to the pronoun: “my crops”. In his soliloquy he will say “I” or “my” again and again, and nobody mentions God until God himself speaks.

Twelve baskets left over. The man telling this story lived the opposite way: he talked with his Father before great decisions (6:12), and in a deserted place took five loaves and two fish, gave thanks, and fed about five thousand men, with twelve baskets left over (9:17). The rich fool’s surplus went into barns; Jesus’ surplus went into baskets for others.

In everyday life. The pay rise, the bonus, the inheritance, the unexpected refund: before it is absorbed into a larger lifestyle, stop and ask God and someone wise what it is for.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records this parable of the rich fool.

parallels.desc: I must leave it to the man who comes after me

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rich man stores everything for himself and tells his soul it is satisfied, as if grain could feed a soul. This is the sentence the parable is built to reach.

Larger barns. The solution is rational and revealing. A surplus can be distributed or stored; he never considers the first, and demolishes serviceable buildings to build larger ones. And the ownership has quietly changed: it began as the land producing (v. 16); it is now “my barns”, “my grain”, “my goods”.

I will say to my soul. Having talked to himself for two verses, he addresses the only one left to talk to, his own soul, and tells it that its needs have been met. Every clause offers the wrong kind of thing. “Ample goods”: quantity, offered as an answer to a soul. “Laid up for many years”: a guarantee about a future he does not own. “Relax, eat, drink, be merry”: real goods, not one of which a soul can live on (compare Isaiah 22:13). He treats the ache of his soul as if more supplies could cure it. And he went to bed satisfied.

Something for the soul to eat. The man is right that his soul needs feeding, and wrong about the menu. Jesus never mocks the soul’s hunger; he came to meet it. He tells of a father who kills the fattened calf so that a lost son may eat (15:23), and at the last takes bread and says, “This is my body, which is given for you” (22:19). The barn-builder says to his soul, “you have ample goods laid up”; Christ says, I have been given for you. One is a store that will belong to someone else by morning; the other is a gift that death cannot recall. Blessed be the God who made the soul too large for any barn. He “has put eternity into man’s heart” (Ecclesiastes 3:11), so that no harvest could ever be enough, and then filled the emptiness with himself: whoever comes to him shall not hunger (John 6:35).

Was his sin saving and planning ahead? No. Scripture commends the ant that stores up food in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8), and a man who does not provide for his family has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). His sin was not the barns but the heart: his future taken for granted and God left out. Saving for old age is wise; living as if the savings were your life is folly.

Is it wrong to look forward to retirement? Not at all; rest after a lifetime of work is a good gift. But the rich fool planned to stop being useful and start consuming, and a Christian’s later years can be some of his most fruitful: time to pray, to serve the church, to help grandchildren and neighbours, to give generously, to mentor younger believers. Enjoy rest with thanks, and keep asking how you can be rich toward God with the time and money you have saved.

parallels.desc: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die

verseByVerse.quote: But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’ So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls the man a fool, demands his life that night, and leaves his stores to others: so it is with everyone who gathers for himself and is not rich toward God.

Fool. God’s first word in the parable follows straight on the man’s “be merry”. He is not called wicked but a fool, and in the Bible that is not an insult about intelligence. “The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 14:1): not a philosophical position but a working assumption. This clever, prudent farmer simply made every plan as if God did not exist and as if he would never die. Then God speaks one sentence, and every plan is finished: he rules the calendar we write our plans in (James 4:13–15).

This night. Required (apaitousin) is a financial word: demanded back, as a loan is recalled. The soul he was addressing as his own had been on loan the whole time, and it is being called in tonight. He said “many years”; God says “this night”.

And the things you have prepared, whose will they be? The question is left unanswered because everyone knows the answer: somebody else’s. He cannot take any of it with him (Psalm 49:16–17; Ecclesiastes 2:18–19; 1 Timothy 6:7). By morning his harvest belonged to people he had not thought about once, perhaps to the very kind of inheritance dispute that began this conversation (v. 13).

Into your hands. Set beside this night the night at the end of Luke’s Gospel. The rich fool’s soul is demanded back; he had no say. Jesus, dying, cried out, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (23:46). Nobody collected his life like a debt. He gave it, into a Father’s hands, for fools like this one. And because he did, Stephen under the stones could pray, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59). For those in Christ the night the soul is called in is not a creditor at the door. It is a Son receiving his own.

What does being rich toward God look like? “For himself” is the diagnosis; “rich toward God” is the alternative, and it is not poverty: the man was rich in the wrong direction (compare v. 33; 1 Timothy 6:17–19). It begins with knowing God himself as your treasure, and then it shows in how you use everything else: giving regularly and generously to the church and to gospel work; caring for the poor and the stranger; being hospitable; supporting family members in need; holding your possessions as a steward, ready to release them. It includes being rich in good works: time, attention and love spent on others. A poor widow with two small coins can be richer toward God than a millionaire (21:1–4).

When work becomes a religion. Few of us build barns, but many of us build careers, and the logic is the same. The writer Derek Thompson called it workism: the belief that work is not only how we earn a living but the centre of our identity and the purpose of our lives. It looks like diligence, but a career asked to be a saviour makes ruthless demands. You are only as worthy as your last result; rest feels like failure (see the note on 10:41–42) and retirement like a small death. It cannot forgive you when you fail it, and it cannot go with you on the night your soul is required. The gospel does not answer by making us careless about work. It takes the weight of our souls off it. Someone whose treasure is already in God can work hard, even ambitiously, for the good of others, and lose the job without losing himself. His name does not need to be on the barn, because it is already written in heaven (10:20).

Is it not harsh to call a hard-working man a fool? Not when you see what the fault is: Jesus finds no fault with his farming. The folly is that he rested everything on the one thing he could not control, the length of his life. That is the heart’s oldest idol: the belief that enough in the barn means I am safe and need no one, not even God. Religious people can build the same barn out of a record of good works. For the man in the story the word came too late. For us, hearing the parable while it is still today, it comes in time, and that is a mercy (2 Corinthians 6:2).
verseByVerse.note: In the Bible a fool is not unintelligent but one who lives as if there were no God.

parallels.desc: the fool says in his heart, “There is no God”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Your Father knows what you need and is glad to give you the kingdom, so do not live anxious, but seek his kingdom and put your treasure where he is. The “therefore” ties this to the barns: the poor can be as gripped by possessions through worry as the rich fool was through hoarding (vv. 22–23). Jesus argues from the least regarded creatures, ravens God feeds and wild flowers he dresses for a week (vv. 24, 27–28), and from the uselessness of worry, which cannot add an hour to life (vv. 25–26). The nations worry because they have no Father; the disciples have one (vv. 29–30). So they are to seek his kingdom, which he delights to give (vv. 31–32), and to give generously, because the heart follows its treasure (vv. 33–34).
verseByVerse.theology:
The argument from ravens and lilies is not an argument for passivity (see the note on vv. 22–24).

On “O you of little faith”, see the note on vv. 27–28; on why the nations are anxious and the Father’s children need not be, vv. 29–30.
verseByVerse.examples:
Knowing that worry achieves nothing does not cure it; what the argument does is change the question (see the note on vv. 25–26).

The command to sell possessions is not a metaphor, but it is not a rule about percentages either (see the note on vv. 33–34).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his disciples, 'Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not live anxious about food and clothing: the God who gave you life and feeds the birds nobody wants will feed you.

Therefore. A man has just died with full storehouses, and the lesson for disciples who had nothing to store is not “store less” but “worry less”. The rich fool trusted his possessions; the poor can be as preoccupied with them through anxiety. Both try to secure a life by managing supplies.

Your life, your body. Anxious (merimnate) means divided in mind, distracted: Martha’s word (10:41), and the cares that choke the word in the parable of the soils (8:14). This is spoken to people who might actually go hungry. Yet life is more than food: if the Creator has already given the great things, a living soul and a body, he will hardly withhold the small ones that keep them going. And life is not the sum of what sustains it: a man can have all the food and clothing he needs and be, as the last parable showed, a fool who dies that night.

Consider the ravens. Ravens were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:15), scavengers, the least regarded; Matthew says “birds of the air” (Matthew 6:26), but Luke names the bird nobody wanted. A psalm says it: “He gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that cry” (Psalm 147:9).
