Yet God feeds them. Without a barn between them, unlike the rich fool. If God feeds the birds nobody wants, how much more will he feed his children, whose value the price of his Son has proved.

Nowhere to lay his head. The one who says this lived it. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (9:58). He was supported by women who gave out of their means (8:3), and in the wilderness, starving, he refused to turn a stone into bread for himself (4:4). He is not a rich man advising the poor, but the poorest man in the company, inviting them into the trust he lived in.

What it does not mean. Not that we should stop working or planning. The ravens are set against the rich fool’s barns, not against the farmer’s plough: the birds still go out after their food (compare 2 Thessalonians 3:10). The verse is against the belief that security comes from how much is stored up.

In everyday life. This applies to the late-night spiral about bills you have already planned for, and the constant checking of a balance that has not changed. It would be wrong to apply it by telling a family with no food to stop worrying instead of helping them. The church is often the Father’s answer to the raven’s cry.

Is anxiety a sin, then, and is every anxious believer of little faith? Jesus is speaking to worry that springs from not trusting the Father. But some anxiety has roots in the body and the mind, and it is a real illness. Elijah despaired (1 Kings 19:4), the psalmist wrestled with his troubled soul (Psalm 77), and they were not cast off. Talking to your pastor and seeking out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up, is not a lack of faith, and neither is receiving treatment if the doctor recommends it. The command still invites every anxious believer to bring the fear to the Father who knows what we need (v. 30).
verseByVerse.note: Ravens were unclean birds, yet God feeds them.

parallels.desc: he gives to the young ravens that cry

verseByVerse.quote: And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Worry cannot add a single hour to your life, so it achieves nothing, and it shows that your life is in God’s hands, not yours.

Which of you by being anxious? Now he argues from results. Anxiety feels like responsible preparation, but what has it ever produced? Nobody has ever lengthened his life by worrying (on the wording, see below); if anything, worry shortens it.

As small a thing as that. He calls adding an hour to a life a small thing, which inverts the whole scale: to a person at a bedside an extra hour is worth everything, but to God it is small. And if a man cannot do even that, then his life, with the food and clothing it needs, is plainly in God’s hands and not his own. Worry does not change tomorrow; it only spoils today, and it forgets the God who controls what we cannot.

Clearing the ground. This is less a comfort than a demolition: anxiety is a machine that burns enormous fuel and produces nothing. That clears the ground for the right question: not “how do I stop worrying?” but “what am I going to trust instead?” The answer is not a technique. It is a Father.

When the days drew near. Jesus measured his own life not by hours he could add but by an hour his Father had set. He set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51); in the garden he prayed, “not my will, but yours, be done” (22:42); and to the men with swords he said, “this is your hour, and the power of darkness” (22:53). He walked unhurried into the darkest hour there has ever been, because his times were in his Father’s hand. Our times are in his hand, and his hand was pierced for us.

In everyday life. Take the thing you are anxious about and divide it into two lists: what I can do today, and what only God can do. Do the first list. Pray over the second, item by item, and then deliberately give thanks for one thing.

What is the difference between worry and responsible concern? Concern looks at a real problem, does what can be done, and leaves the rest with God. Worry keeps turning the problem over long after anything can be done, and treats the turning as if it were doing something. Paul’s cure is specific: “do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6–7). Do the next thing, pray about the rest, and give thanks.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “span of life” (hēlikia) can mean either length of life or bodily height, and the measure added is literally a cubit (about eighteen inches; see cubit). So the phrase can be read “a single cubit to his stature”, as the ESV notes. Most translations prefer span of life, which suits a passage about staying alive. Either way, nobody has managed it by worrying.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “a single hour to his span of life” can also be read “a single cubit to his stature.”

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith!
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God dresses wild flowers more splendidly than Solomon, though they are burned within the week, he will surely clothe his children; worry shows how little we trust him.

Consider the lilies. Wild flowers of the Galilean hillsides (on the word, see below). Toiling and spinning were the two halves of a household’s labour: men toiled in the field, women spun thread for cloth. The flowers do neither.

Even Solomon. Solomon is the highest available standard, the king whose court left a foreign queen breathless (1 Kings 10:4–5). And a weed on a hillside beats him: dressed by nobody, and gone in a fortnight.

Thrown into the oven. The hillsides dried out, and the stalks were gathered as fuel for a peasant’s clay oven. God takes trouble over the appearance of something that will heat somebody’s bread within the week. He delights in beauty, and has determined to make his people beautiful for ever: the God who paints the hillsides for a single week has clothed his people in the righteousness of Christ, a garment of salvation that will never wear out or be thrown in the oven.

O you of little faith. The rebuke is gentle, and it is a rebuke. “Little-faith ones” is one word in the Greek, used by Jesus only of disciples; nobody is called little-faith who has none. He traces the worry not to their circumstances but to too little trust in their Father. That does not make an anxious believer faithless (see the note on vv. 22–24); but underneath most ordinary worry lies a belief about God: that he might forget me, or not care, or not be able. So the deepest cure is knowing him better, because those who know his name put their trust in him (Psalm 9:10).

Greater than Solomon. A chapter earlier Jesus told this crowd that “something greater than Solomon is here” (11:31). The greater than Solomon was dressed in splendid clothing by Herod’s soldiers to mock him (23:11), and at the cross they divided his garments by casting lots (23:34). The King who robes the hillsides went to his death with less covering than a wildflower, and when he says “how much more will he clothe you”, he speaks as the one who would be stripped to keep that promise.

How can little faith grow? Not by staring at your faith, but by looking at God. Faith grows as it feeds on his promises and remembers his faithfulness: read the Psalms that recount what he has done, keep a record of answered prayer, sit under the preaching of his word, take small steps of obedience that require trust, and watch him keep his word. Pray as the father of the boy with the unclean spirit did: “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). Jesus did not reject that prayer. He answered it.

Uncertain wording. Which flower Jesus meant is not known. The word (krinon) was used loosely of bright wild flowers; suggestions include the scarlet anemone and wild irises. The point does not depend on the species.
verseByVerse.note: Dry grass was used as fuel for clay ovens.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried. For all the nations of the world seek after these things, and your Father knows that you need them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not chase after food and drink as the anxious world does, because you have a Father who knows you need them.

Nor be worried. The word (meteōrizesthe) was used of a ship tossed on the swell or something suspended in mid-air (it gives English meteor): anxious suspense, unanchored, going wherever the next wave puts you.

All the nations of the world. “The nations” is the standard Jewish term for the Gentiles, used here as description, not insult. The pagan world had gods of harvest and weather to be managed, none reliable, so provision had to be negotiated without end. In that setting anxiety is rational: if nobody is certainly looking after you, somebody had better.

Your Father knows. “Your Father”: the name he taught them to pray with (11:2). “Knows”: so it need not be brought to his attention, and much anxious praying is really lobbying, as though the case had not yet been properly presented. “That you need them”: the needs are not dismissed as unspiritual. The gods of the nations had to be bargained with; our Father gives freely, and delights to.

Revealed by the Son. The difference between the nations and the little band around Jesus is that the disciples had been brought to know God as Father. No one knows who the Father is except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (10:22). The anxious pagan could not say “your Father”. The Son came to make orphans into sons: God sent forth his Son to redeem, so that we might receive adoption as sons and cry, Abba! Father! (Galatians 4:4–6). Adoption takes a stranger into God’s family for ever, with a son’s name, access and inheritance, not for any merit but because he is joined to the Son (Galatians 4:7).

If my Father already knows, why pray about my needs? Because he tells us to ask: “Give us each day our daily bread” (11:3). Prayer is not briefing God; it is trusting him out loud. Asking keeps us dependent and turns anxiety into conversation. The pagan asks in order to persuade a reluctant power; the Christian asks as a child whose Father already knows and already cares.

verseByVerse.quote: Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you. 'Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make God’s kingdom your pursuit and trust him with the rest, because your Father has gladly chosen to give you the kingdom itself.

Instead, seek his kingdom. He has just said the nations seek after food and drink, and uses the same verb: go after this instead (Matthew adds “and his righteousness”, Matthew 6:33). The alternative to anxiety is not seeking nothing but a different pursuit, and the man chasing the kingdom grows calmer because his mind is on something sure.

Added to you. Food and clothing are added as extras: not what the disciple is seeking, but not withheld either. It is not a promise that a Christian will never be hungry; Paul knew what it was to be in need (Philippians 4:12). What is promised is that the Father who knows will not forget, not that provision will always look like comfort.

Fear not, little flock. Only Luke records these tender words. “Little flock” is an honest name: a small, vulnerable group in an occupied province, like sheep among wolves (10:3). He does not tell them they are stronger than they look, but who the shepherd is, with all the weight of Psalm 23, of Isaiah 40:11, where he gathers the lambs in his arms, and of Ezekiel 34, where God himself searches for his sheep.

Your Father’s good pleasure. It was his glad decision (eudokēsen), the same verb as at the Jordan: “with you I am well pleased” (3:22). The Father’s delight in his Son and his delight in giving the kingdom to the Son’s little flock are one delight, and at the last supper Jesus tells the Twelve, “I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom” (22:29). The gift is not a wage but the kingdom, the whole of it, the thing they had been told to seek, handed over to a frightened handful because their Father enjoyed doing it. If he gives you the kingdom, will he not give you bread? “He who did not spare his own Son … how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32).

So what does seeking the kingdom look like on an ordinary day? Mostly it looks like the day you already have, lived under a different King: honest work done as for the Lord, patience with a tired spouse and time for a child, giving first and spending carefully, forgiveness when wronged and confession when you fail, gathering with his people on the Lord’s Day and sharing Christ when the door opens. It rarely feels dramatic: it is ordinary walking in God’s will, one decision at a time, with his kingdom, not your comfort, as the question you ask first.

In everyday life. It applies to the choice between a promotion that would swallow your family and church life and a slower path that keeps them. It does not mean thinking you must leave your job for full-time ministry to really seek the kingdom, or neglecting your family’s needs for a church project. The kingdom is sought in the ordinary calling God has given you.

parallels.desc: he will tend his flock like a shepherd
the kingdom given to the saints

verseByVerse.quote: Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give your possessions to the needy and so store up treasure in heaven that nothing can take, because your heart follows your treasure.

Sell your possessions. The command is not a metaphor; some early Christians did exactly this (Acts 2:44–45; 4:34–37). But must every Christian sell everything? Luke answers across his two volumes. Zacchaeus gives away half his goods, and salvation has come to his house (19:8–9). The women of 8:3 supported the ministry out of means they still had. And Peter’s rebuke to Ananias turns on this: “While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own?” (Acts 5:4). So the command is not a rule about percentages but a transfer of ownership: whatever is still in the disciple’s hands is at the Master’s disposal. For one man that means selling the lot, as for the rich ruler whose possessions owned him (18:22); for another an open house or a quietly emptied account. It can never mean a Christian who has drawn a line and considers the rest his own.

Moneybags that do not grow old. Leather purses wore out, and wealth stored as fine clothing could be eaten by moths or stolen. He is against not investment but bad investment. What is given to God and the poor is stored up in heaven (1 Timothy 6:18–19), and treasure in heaven is mostly ordinary: kindness, generosity and faithful work done for Christ.

Where your treasure is. We assume the heart chooses and the money follows; he says the heart goes to where the treasure already is. So the affections can be steered: a man who cannot make himself care about something can move his money into it and find, months later, that his heart has followed. And what you actually love shows not in the confession of faith but in the bank statement and the diary.

Where Christ is. Why should the heart want to go there? Because that is where the Lord is: “seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians 3:1). Treasure in heaven is not a private account in the sky but everything given away for love of him, laid up with the one who gave himself away first. The heart that follows its treasure upward arrives not at a vault but at a person.

In everyday life. Ask about the possession you could not bear to lose, the room full of things unused for years. Do not apply it by selling the family home without your spouse’s agreement, giving away what your children need, or treating a tired single mother’s modest savings as a sin. Hold everything open-handed, and let love, not guilt, decide what goes.

How much should I give, and to whom? The New Testament sets no fixed figure, but it asks for regular, proportionate, cheerful and sacrificial giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 9:7). Begin with your own church, which feeds you; then the needy around you, especially fellow believers (Galatians 6:10); then gospel work further afield. Many find a tenth a wise starting point and grow from there. Give in a way that costs you something, planned and quiet. If you are in debt or poverty, give what you can with a glad heart; the widow’s two coins counted most of all.

In the flow. The section began with a man wanting more from his brother (v. 13) and ends with Jesus telling his disciples to give away. A heart whose treasure is in heaven looks for the one who is coming from there, and so the servants waiting for their master come next.
verseByVerse.note: Wealth was often stored as fine clothing, which moths could eat.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Live every day ready for your Lord’s return, faithfully doing the work he left you, because he will come unexpectedly. Servants wait through the night, belts fastened and lamps lit, for a master coming home from a wedding, and he rewards them by waiting on them himself (vv. 35–38). A householder caught by a thief shows that the hour cannot be known, so readiness must be constant (vv. 39–40). When Peter asks whom this is for, Jesus answers with a steward set over the household: the faithful one is given charge of everything (vv. 41–44), the one who abuses the delay is judged (vv. 45–46), and judgment fits what each knew and was given (vv. 47–48).
verseByVerse.theology:
The master who serves his watching servants overturns every ancient picture of authority, and it is the pattern of Christ’s whole ministry: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45).

The steward (oikonomos) owns nothing and holds the keys (see the note on vv. 41–42), and his reward is a larger trust, not retirement (see vv. 43–44). And the hidden hour is part of the design (see the note on vv. 39–40).
verseByVerse.examples:
The bad servant’s ruin begins with a private conclusion that his master is delayed (see the note on vv. 45–46).

The two beatings show that judgment has degrees, and the closing principle falls hardest on the well-taught (see the note on vv. 47–48).

verseByVerse.quote: 'Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, and be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast, so that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Disciples are to live ready for their Lord’s return, like servants dressed for work with lamps lit, waiting to open the door the moment he knocks. Those whose treasure is in heaven (v. 34) are already leaning toward the day it is opened.

Stay dressed for action. Literally “let your loins stay girded”, as the ESV notes. A long outer robe had to be pulled up and tucked into the belt for running, working or fighting (see clothing); to be girded was to be ready to move. Israel ate the first Passover with belts fastened, sandals on and staff in hand (Exodus 12:11), dressed to leave a country that night.

Lamps burning. An oil lamp kept burning through the dark hours needed somebody awake to trim the wick and top up the oil. Readiness is not achieved once and possessed; it is maintained, hourly, by somebody who has not gone to sleep.

From the wedding feast. A wedding feast could run for days, so the servants have no timetable, only a duty that continues regardless.

The door at once. Their readiness comes down to one modest test: not whether they achieved anything impressive in his absence, but whether, when he knocked, somebody on the other side of the door was still expecting him.

The exodus he accomplished. On the mountain Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about his departure, literally his exodus, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (9:31). The disciples dress like Israel on the Passover night because a greater exodus is under way, and its Lamb is the one speaking (1 Corinthians 5:7). The fastened belt is not the dress of people hoping to be rescued. It is the dress of people whose ransom has been paid and whose departure is certain. The long night of waiting has a morning, and the knock will be the voice of the Bridegroom.

What does being ready actually mean? Not constant alarm, or giving up ordinary work to watch the sky. It means being a true believer, trusting Christ now, with nothing between you and him that you would be ashamed for him to find; keeping short accounts with God and others, confessing sin quickly and putting wrongs right; and being about your Master’s business, faithful in the work, the family and the church he has given you. A ready servant may be found asleep in bed at night; what matters is that he is the Master’s, and expecting him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the literal wording, “Let your loins stay girded”: the long robe tucked into the belt for work.

parallels.desc: your belt fastened, ready to leave

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master who finds his servants awake will overturn every custom and serve them at his own table: that is how Christ will receive those who wait for him.

He will come and serve them. Nothing in the ancient world prepares anybody for this. The master ties up his own robe, the same girding the servants were told to do in v. 35, sits them at his table, and waits on them. That whole society rested on the line between those who recline and those who serve; a master returning at midnight expects his meal (17:7–8). The “Truly, I say to you” admits how hard this is to believe.

The second watch, or the third. Whether Luke counts the night in Roman four watches or Jewish three, these fall in its depths: the hardest time to stay awake and the least expected time to come. That is where most Christian waiting is done: not in the first years but in year twenty, in the dark, with no sign of anything, holding a lamp.

Picture or promise? Both, and Luke shows it. At the Supper Jesus says it about himself in plain words: “who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves” (22:27). On the same night John records him rising from the meal, tying a towel round himself, and washing his disciples’ feet (John 13:4–5), girded, exactly as here. The image is no exaggeration: it is what he is like. The King of kings, before whom angels veil their faces, will tie up his robe and bring the dishes to tired servants who managed to stay awake. He has served us once already, at the cross, with his own body and blood, and the hands that pass the bread at the feast will still bear the marks of that first service.

In everyday life. If you are in the dead middle of a long night, a long illness, a long wait for a prodigal, a long season of dryness, keep your lamp lit for one more hour. Do the next small faithful thing. The Master who is coming is not a harsh inspector but the one who will tie on an apron and serve you.

Will Christ really serve us in heaven, rather than we serving him? Both. His servants will worship him (Revelation 22:3), and we will gladly serve him for ever. But the deepest truth of the kingdom is that he serves us first and always: he feeds us at his table, wipes away our tears, and gives us himself. Our service is only ever a response to his. Heaven is not the place where Christ finally gets the reward of being waited on by us, but where we discover the full extent of how he loves to give.
verseByVerse.note: The second and third watches covered the middle of the night.

parallels.desc: he dressed himself and washed their feet

verseByVerse.quote: But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have left his house to be broken into. You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one knows when the Son of Man will come, so the only way to be ready is to be ready all the time.

The thief. The picture changes: the master coming home from a wedding becomes a burglary. It is the same event, welcome in one picture and dreaded in the other, and the whole difference is whether the person inside is ready.

Broken into. Literally “dug through”: a thief made a hole in a mud-brick wall. The householder is not blamed for sleeping at night; he is caught out because the one thing he needed, the hour, was the one thing unavailable.

An hour you do not expect. Christ is not a thief, but his coming will be as unexpected: “the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5:2; Revelation 16:15). The image is about the timing, never his character, and no one knows the day (Mark 13:32).

Why the hour is hidden. If the hour were knowable, readiness could be scheduled, and everyone would schedule it late, as the servant in the next parable does. The hour is hidden on purpose, to make readiness a way of living rather than a task done nearer the time. And there is mercy in it: no Christian is asked to be ready later, only now, which is the only thing anybody can actually do.

The time of your visitation. His first coming was already being missed: weeping over Jerusalem, he would say “you did not know the time of your visitation” (19:44). The city that read the prophets every Sabbath slept through the arrival of its King. But shepherds keeping watch by night heard the news first (2:8–11), and Simeon and Anna were among those waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (2:25, 38). The Lord who came once to a sleeping city and a few watchers is telling his friends which kind of household to be. We do not know the hour, but we know the One who is coming, and to those who love his appearing, his coming will be no thief’s surprise but a homecoming.

Will Christ come secretly first and take believers away before the end? This commentary holds that he will not. Many earnest believers have been taught that Christ will first remove his church secretly before a great tribulation, and they long for his appearing as sincerely as anyone; this is a difference among brothers, not a test of faith. The New Testament describes one visible, public return of Christ at the end of the age, when the dead are raised, believers are gathered to him, and the world is judged (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). His coming is unexpected in its timing, like a thief, but not hidden in its manner: “every eye will see him” (Revelation 1:7). That is why the call is simply to be ready, all the time, for the day itself.
verseByVerse.note: Houses had walls of mud brick that a thief could dig through.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said, 'Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all?' And the Lord said, 'Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the proper time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked whether the warning is for the apostles or for everyone, Jesus answers that it falls especially on those set over others, whose task is to feed the household faithfully.

Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all? It is just the kind of question Peter asks. Probably he means: is the standard the same for the Twelve as for the crowd, or is there a separate arrangement for us?

Who then is the faithful and wise manager? Jesus answers with another parable, this one for people with responsibility over others: yes, it applies especially to you, Peter, but not in the direction the question hoped. The manager is an oikonomos, a steward, often himself a trusted slave, placed over the whole household and its supplies (16:1). He held the keys and the accounts, owned nothing, and could be dismissed. The word is used of church leaders: “stewards of the mysteries of God”, of whom it is required that they be found faithful (1 Corinthians 4:1–2; Titus 1:7).

Their portion of food. His one named duty is not to increase the estate but to feed the household: Christian leadership as Jesus states it, feeding God’s household with his word, faithfully and at the right time. It is the commission Peter will be given on a beach three times over (John 21:15–17), and hand on to the elders (1 Peter 5:2; Acts 20:28).

Faithful and wise. Faithful: trustworthy with what is not his. Wise: knowing what the household needs and when. A reliable man with no judgment will feed them the wrong thing, and a shrewd one who cannot be trusted will feed himself. And he is not asked to produce food from nowhere, only to distribute what the master has provided, on time.

A Son over the house. “Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant … but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son” (Hebrews 3:5–6). Jesus is the steward who never once fed himself from the stores: he taught daily in the temple (19:47), and on his last night, with the cross hours away, he was still setting food before his disciples (22:14–20). Every pastor and parent who feeds others is handing out what he provided, and will answer to him.

If I am not a church leader, is this for me? Yes, in its own measure. Every Christian is a steward of something: a family, a Sunday school class, a friend who looks to you, gifts and money and time (1 Peter 4:10). Parents especially are given the task of feeding their children with God’s word at the proper time. The questions are the same as for a pastor: am I faithful with what is not mine, and wise about what the people in my care need now?
verseByVerse.note: A household manager was often a trusted slave put in charge of the other servants.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant found faithfully at his work when the master comes will be blessed with charge of everything the master has.

So doing. The blessing is attached not to results but to still working faithfully at the thing he was left to do, on the day the master happens to arrive. The steward answers not for the size of the household but for whether the food went out on time. The aim is not a heroic finish but an unbroken habit.

All his possessions. The reward for having been trusted with a job is a bigger job: not a pension or an easier post, but more responsibility, permanently (19:17). Faithful servants will share Christ’s reign (22:29–30; 2 Timothy 2:12). Scripture gives few details, but it means real work in a renewed creation, every gift used with no sin to spoil it and no death to cut it short (Revelation 22:3–5). The steward began with no property and ends with the run of the estate, all of it entrusted, none of it his by right. That is what being an heir means: “heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17). The God who could have run his household without us chose to entrust it to us, and then to make the stewards heirs.

In everyday life. What the Master has given you to do is probably not glamorous: the nappies, the spreadsheet, the hospital visit, the Bible study preparation, the care of an ageing parent. Do today’s portion of it faithfully, and stop measuring yourself by results he has not asked you for.

Are rewards in heaven earned? No. Every reward is grace upon grace: God gives the gifts, the strength to use them, and then rewards the use as if it were ours (1 Corinthians 4:7; 15:10). Salvation itself is never earned; it rests on Christ alone. But Scripture does promise real, differing rewards to faithful servants, and Jesus means us to be encouraged by them. There will be no envy in heaven, because every servant will be full, and every crown will be cast at his feet (Revelation 4:10).

verseByVerse.quote: But if that servant says to himself, ‘My master is delayed in coming,’ and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant who decides his master is delayed, and so mistreats others and indulges himself, will be caught unprepared and judged with the unfaithful.

My master is delayed. Everything that follows comes out of one sentence, said to himself: no rebellion, just a private conclusion about a timetable. And it is accurate; the master is delayed. What is wrong is what the servant does with it. People begin to think he will never come (2 Peter 3:3–4), and live accordingly.

To beat and to get drunk. These are the two directions in which a leader goes bad. He turns on the household, using authority given to feed his fellow servants to hit them; in religious office that seldom involves fists, but the pulpit used to settle a score, or discipline that is really about control. And he turns to himself: “eat and drink and get drunk” echoes the rich fool, and the food he was appointed to distribute (v. 42) goes down his own throat. A man who expects his employer within the hour does not start drinking the cellar.

Cut him in pieces. The verdict is not in doubt, whatever the exact sense of the phrase (see below). The household is God’s: to mistreat those he has entrusted to you is to sin against him (Ezekiel 34:2–10). The servant held the keys and the office, but the judgment puts him with those who never trusted the master, which is where he had really stood all along.

The Master beaten in his own house. The parable came true against Jesus himself within months. In the high priest’s house his guards blindfolded the Lord of the household and beat him (22:63–64). He did not return the blows; he went on to the cross for servants like them. The judgment here is the verdict of one who knows in his own body what it is to be struck by those who should have served.

In everyday life. Ask where the long delay has made you careless: in your use of authority at home or work, in your appetites, in what you excuse because judgment feels far away. If you lead anyone, ask the people under you whether you serve them or use them, listen, and bring what you hear to the Master who forgives servants who confess (1 John 1:9).

Is this servant a true believer who loses his salvation? Luke’s own word answers it. He is put with the unfaithful, the apistoi, which also means unbelievers: he ends among the people who never trusted the master, because that is what he was. He is a professing servant whose conduct shows he never truly knew his master; Matthew says he is put with the hypocrites (Matthew 24:51). “Cut in pieces” is a picture of severe judgment, not of a believer’s fall from grace. A true servant may fail and be disciplined, but those who belong to Christ endure to the end because he keeps them.

What should a church do about a leader who abuses those in his care? Take it seriously and act, because Jesus does. Abuse of any kind, physical, sexual, emotional or spiritual, must never be tolerated or covered up to protect a ministry’s reputation. Crimes should be reported to the civil authorities; victims should be believed, protected and cared for; and the leader should be removed from office while the matter is examined honestly (1 Timothy 5:19–20). A church that protects the powerful at the expense of the vulnerable has taken the side of the servant in this parable.

Uncertain wording. “Cut him in pieces” translates a word (dichotomēsei) that literally means cut in two, a known ancient punishment. Some take it as a vivid figure for the severest punishment; others suggest “cut him off”, cast him out, which suits the next phrase. Either way it is final judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required, and from him to whom they entrusted much, they will demand the more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s judgment is exactly fair: the more a person knew and was given, the more he will be held to account.

A severe beating, a light beating. Two servants, the same offence, different sentences, and the difference is what each knew. Deliberate disobedience in full knowledge brings the greater judgment. Judgment has degrees: it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon than for the Galilean towns that watched him work (10:13–14). Perfect justice fits the punishment to what each knew (Romans 2:12). But the second servant is not acquitted. Ignorance reduces the sentence; it does not produce innocence.

Much was given. The passive “was given” is the reverent way of saying God gave, so every item is a deposit, not an achievement: a Christian upbringing, an open Bible in your own language, a church down the road, years of clear preaching, health, money, time. Each raises the bar, for teachers above all (James 3:1), and for Christians in wealthy and free countries.

An account, not a shelter. This falls hardest on the well-taught: the man who has heard the gospel plainly for four decades and done nothing about it is not in the safer category; he is nearer the severe beating than the light one. A lifetime of good sermons is not a shelter but an account he must answer for. The believer who has heard much and, however haltingly, keeps turning to Christ is not that servant; his account was settled at the cross.

By his stripes. Both servants deserve a beating, and there is no third servant who does not. The gospel answers not with a lighter sentence but with a substitute. Pilate, finding no guilt in Jesus, still said, “I will therefore punish and release him” (23:16), and the flogging followed (Mark 15:15). The one who knew his Father’s will perfectly and did all of it took the stripes owed to servants who knew and did not: wounded for our transgressions, so that by his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). He did not merely suffer alongside sinners; he stood in their place and bore the penalty, so that it will never be laid on them (1 Peter 2:24).

In everyday life. You have been given much, and you will never use it perfectly. Christ did his Father’s will perfectly in your place; his obedience is counted as yours, and for his sake your faltering service is accepted. Name three things you have been given that most of the world has not, and ask of each: what does my Master want me to do with it this week?

Does this mean people who never heard the gospel will be saved by their ignorance? No. The servant who did not know still receives a beating; ignorance lessens judgment but does not remove guilt, because all have sinned against the light of creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 2:14–15). Salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–15), which is exactly why the church must send preachers. God will judge everyone with perfect fairness, according to what they knew. Infants who die in infancy, who cannot hear or believe, are in the hands of a merciful God, and we may trust that his elect among them are saved by Christ through the Spirit. Parents who have lost a little one may rest their grief on the kindness of the Saviour who took children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16).

Should I avoid learning more of the Bible so as to be judged less? That would be to choose darkness so as not to be blamed for it, which is itself a sin against light. The goal is not to know less but to obey what you know. The God who requires much gives grace to do it, and a believer who keeps learning and obeying, however imperfectly, is not storing up judgment but growing in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 49–59 — Fire, Division, and the Urgent Hour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus’ coming is a crisis no one can stay neutral about, so read the time you are living in and get right with God now. He longs for the fire he came to cast, but first he must go through the baptism of his death, and he is pressed until it is done (vv. 49–50). He brings peace with God, yet divides even households by their response to him (vv. 51–53). Then he turns to the crowds: they read the weather well and will not read the present time (vv. 54–56). They can judge for themselves what is right (v. 57), and must settle with their accuser on the road, before they reach the Judge (vv. 58–59).
verseByVerse.theology:
The distress of 12:50 is not a man hanging back from the cross (see the note on vv. 49–50).

The charge of hypocrisy at 12:56 is precise (see the note on vv. 54–56), and the call to judge for themselves is not an invitation to decide what suits them (see the note on v. 57).
verseByVerse.examples:
The division saying speaks to anyone whose family went cold at their conversion (see the note on vv. 51–53).

Every generation is expert at reading something (see the note on vv. 54–56). And the last penny is an illustration of urgency, not a doctrine of purgatory (see the note on vv. 58–59).

verseByVerse.quote: 'I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus longs for the fire he came to bring, but first he must be plunged into the suffering of his death, and he is pressed until it is done. For two verses Luke lets us hear what it was like inside him.

Fire on the earth. Fire pictures judgment (3:9, 17), purifying (Malachi 3:2–3), and the Holy Spirit: John announced that the Messiah would baptise with the Holy Spirit and with fire (3:16), and Acts opens with tongues as of fire resting on the waiting disciples (Acts 2:3). The same fire refines and consumes, depending on what it lands on.

A baptism. The word means to be plunged, submerged, and it is not the Jordan, which is behind him. In the Psalms the waters are often death: “all your breakers and your waves have gone over me” (Psalm 42:7). He is talking about his death (Mark 10:38) and calling it a drowning: on the cross he would go under the full weight of God’s holy anger against the sins of his people, as a man goes under a flood, because the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:6).

How great is my distress. Distress means gripped, hemmed in (synechomai); Luke uses it of a high fever (4:38) and of an army closing on a city (19:43). It anticipates Gethsemane (22:42–44, though verses 43–44 are missing from some early manuscripts; the agony itself is plain in 22:42).

Pentecost waits on Golgotha. Read the two verses together: the fire he longs for cannot be lit until the baptism of Calvary is finished, and he is pressed between them. This is not a man hanging back: he wanted the cross over, not to escape it but to reach a people set alight by the Spirit he would pour out. The breakers and waves went over him so that they would never go over us. He went down into the flood alone, and stands now on its far shore with all whom he carried through. The fire he longed to kindle has never gone out.

In the flow. His death at Jerusalem makes the chapter’s warnings urgent: people will divide over him (vv. 51–53), and the crowds must read the times and settle with God while they are still on the road (vv. 54–59).

Does this baptism tell us anything about Christian baptism? Indirectly, yes. Jesus calls his death a baptism, and Paul says that believers are baptised into his death, buried with him and raised to walk in newness of life (Romans 6:3–4). That is why this commentary holds believer’s baptism by immersion: going under the water pictures union with Christ in the death he describes here, and coming up pictures resurrection, and in the New Testament baptism follows repentance and faith (Acts 2:38, 41). Our paedobaptist brothers, who baptise the infants of believers as members of God’s covenant people, much as Israel’s sons were circumcised, see the same union signified in the baptism of infants, and we honour their faith. But the reality behind every baptism is this one, which Jesus endured alone.

Uncertain wording. “Would that it were already kindled” renders a compressed, awkward exclamation; word for word it runs “and what do I wish, if it is already kindled?” Most translations take it, as the ESV does, as a wish; some read a question. The sense is not in doubt: he longs for the fire.
verseByVerse.note: Fire can picture judgment or purifying; “baptism” here pictures being overwhelmed by suffering.

parallels.desc: the baptism with which I am baptized

verseByVerse.quote: Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus brings peace with God, but not the world’s peace: people divide over him, even within one household.

Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? It is meant to shock, since the angels announced “on earth peace” over the fields outside Bethlehem (2:14), and Zechariah sang that he would guide our feet into the way of peace (1:79). Jesus does bring real peace: peace with God, which every human being most needs and cannot manufacture (Romans 5:1), and peace among those who belong to him. What he never promised is the peace of the world, a peace kept by leaving the truth alone, which lasts only as long as nobody asks who he is.

Rather division. His coming divides people by their response to him. Simeon said it over the infant: “this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many”, and a sword would pierce through his mother’s own soul (2:34–35). The division would cut even his own mother, and he never asks a disciple to stand where he has not stood.

Five divided. Five is a household: father, mother, son, daughter, and the son’s wife living with them. Three against two, then two against three: the same fracture from both sides, because in a divided house both halves feel like the ones being left. The source is Micah 7:6, a society coming apart in a time of judgment, where a man’s enemies are the men of his own house. Now it will happen because of loyalty to him. Every pair is named in both directions: there is no suggestion that the believing half will find it easy or behave well.

A household that can never be divided. The Prince of Peace accepted being the cause of division, because the only lasting peace is peace with God. His own family once thought he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21), and still he gathers into his family everyone who does his Father’s will. In him the lonely believer has a household that can never be divided.

What it does not mean. Not that the disciple should go looking for a quarrel or leave his family to fend for itself. Paul tells believers to live at peace with everyone as far as it depends on them (Romans 12:18), and a great deal of family division is caused by Christians being insufferable rather than by Christ. But when others reject Christ, conflict may come, and loyalty to Christ must come first (14:26).

The mercy of a warning. Jesus does not say the division is good; he says it in advance, which is the mercy in it. A Christian whose family went cold at his conversion often concludes that he handled it badly. When everything has been done gently and the division comes anyway, it is not evidence of failure. It is the thing he warned about, happening.

In everyday life. This applies to the parent who disowns a child for being baptised, or the spouse who mocks every prayer. It does not excuse rudeness or neglect, or cutting off a family that simply finds your faith strange. Ask whether the offence is Christ, or you.

How do I love a family that opposes my faith? Honour your parents in everything that does not require disobeying Christ. Be the kindest person at the family table, and let your life speak before your words. Do not preach at every gathering; do answer honestly when asked. Pray for them, sometimes for decades, keep the door open, and refuse bitterness. Where there is real danger or abuse, you may need distance for safety, and that is not unloving. And remember that God has often used one believer’s patient faithfulness to bring a whole household to Christ (Acts 16:31–34).

Is this not the trouble with religion, that it divides people? Every strong conviction divides, the sceptic’s included. The real question is what a conviction does to those who disagree with it. The Christ who divides is the one who prayed for the men crucifying him (23:34) and told his followers to love their enemies (6:27). A faith whose centre is a man laying down his life for those who rejected him gives no licence to hate anyone, and Christians who have used it that way have betrayed him.

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: He also said to the crowds, 'When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, ‘A shower is coming.’ And so it happens. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat,’ and it happens. You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowds read the weather well but refuse to read the far plainer signs that God’s decisive time has come in Jesus.

A cloud rising in the west. West of Israel is the Mediterranean: cloud building over the sea meant rain, as Elijah’s servant saw from Carmel (1 Kings 18:44). South is the Negev and the desert; a south wind meant scorching heat that could strip a crop in a day. Two signs, two confident readings, and Jesus grants that they are right: their instincts about the sky are reliable and hard-won.

You hypocrites. The charge is precise. Because they choose where to look, it is hypocrisy and not an honest mistake: a man who reads the sky every morning and cannot read what is standing in front of him has made a choice, and is pretending it was a limitation.

The present time. “The present time” (kairos) is this decisive moment, the time of God’s visitation. And Jesus does not expect them to have read a secret sign, but the whole visible situation: a preacher healing in the streets, demons evicted, the poor told good news, thousands following, and the religious authorities plotting a death. The Messiah was among them, and he had said so in plain words at Nazareth: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (4:21). God has never been unclear about his visitations; the clouds of mercy have been rising over this world since the manger. But they would not read it, and he will weep over Jerusalem because it did not know the time of its visitation (19:44).

Turning it on ourselves. Every generation is expert at reading something: markets, politics, the mood of a culture, a career. The person who can tell you exactly where the country is heading has often never asked what God is doing in his own lifetime, or his own house. The evidence is not usually missing. What is missing is the decision to read it.

In everyday life. Can you read the signs of what God is doing? Take ten minutes and ask: where has God been at work in my life in the last year, in a trial, an answered prayer, a conviction that will not go away? The Spirit who gave you eyes for his Son will teach you to read it.

Does this mean I should try to match news events to Bible prophecy? Not in the way that often happens. Jesus’ point is that the decisive time had already arrived in his coming. The present time, for us, is the age between his first and second comings: the day of salvation, when the gospel goes to the nations and his return is always near. No one can set the date, though Scripture names things that will come first (2 Thessalonians 2:3). Reading the times means responding to God with repentance, faith and readiness, not building charts of headlines.
verseByVerse.note: Clouds from the west came off the Mediterranean with rain; the south wind blew hot off the desert.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd already has enough light to reach the right verdict about Jesus; what is lacking is the will to reach it.

Judge for yourselves. He has just told them they can read the sky and will not read the times; now he asks why they do not work it out themselves. The verb is the one for reaching a verdict, and “for yourselves” puts the responsibility where the crowd would least like it. They had spent the chapter asking him to settle things: my inheritance (v. 13), a sign (11:16), whether this parable is for us (v. 41). He hands the decision back to them. You have the evidence; use your own judgment honestly, and you will see who I am and what you must do.

What it does not mean. It is not an invitation to decide for themselves what is true: a man can be entirely convinced and entirely wrong (Proverbs 14:12; Jeremiah 17:9). The question is narrower and harder: given the evidence you can already read, the conscience you have, the Scriptures you possess, why have you not drawn the obvious conclusion? Very often, because the conclusion would cost something. The crowd’s problem is not a shortage of light but an unwillingness to act on it.

Who do you say that I am? The verdict Jesus wants them to reach is a verdict about him. He had put that question to his disciples in private, and Peter answered, “The Christ of God” (9:20). Nothing of the evidence was hidden from the crowd. And there is a strange mercy in the question. The one who will one day judge them is asking them to judge him first, while a right verdict can still save them.

In everyday life. Is there a question you keep postponing, whether to be baptised, whether to make things right with someone, whether to give up a known sin, because you are waiting for someone to tell you? You already know, and the Spirit who gives willing hearts will help you. Do it this week.

Should I not rely on my pastor and church to tell me what is right? Listen to them, gratefully: God gives teachers to the church, and you should be humble enough to be taught (Hebrews 13:17). But no teacher can believe for you, repent for you or obey for you. On the plain things, who Jesus is, what sin is, what he commands, you already know enough to act. Take your questions to your pastor, but do not hide behind them.

verseByVerse.quote: As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are all on the way to God’s court with a debt we cannot pay, and now, on the road, is the time to be reconciled to him. In context (vv. 54–57), the lawsuit is a picture of the coming judgment.

Settle on the way. A man is walking to court with his accuser, with a debt he cannot pay and the case certain to go against him. The road is the last stretch of time in which anything can be done. “Make an effort” is a strong verb: put yourself into it.

Judge, officer, prison. Three handovers in a row, down to debtors’ prison. On the road he is a man who can negotiate. In the courtroom he is a case.

The very last penny. The penny is the lepton, the smallest coin in circulation.

Not one penny left to pay. The Lord who warns of the debtors’ prison stood up at Nazareth and read that he had been anointed to proclaim liberty to the captives and the year of the Lord’s favour (4:18–19). He has not shortened anyone’s sentence; he has opened the doors. Luke answered the question of the debt itself in a house where a woman wept over Jesus’ feet: when the debtors could not pay, “he cancelled the debt of both” (7:41–42). The record of debt that stood against us was not put on an instalment plan but set aside, nailed to the cross (Colossians 2:14). So settle now, while it is still called today, and know that the settlement is an amnesty purchased at the Judge’s own expense. There is not one penny left to pay for the forgiven. It is finished.

How do I settle with God? Not by offering to pay, because the debt is beyond you, and not by promising to do better, because that adds nothing to what is owed. You settle by agreeing with God about your sin, turning from it, and trusting Jesus Christ, who died to pay that debt in full and rose again. Tell him so, in your own words, today. Then you are no longer on the way to court as a debtor; you are walking home as a child. If you are already his, the parable also applies between people: settle your quarrels quickly (Matthew 5:23–25).

In everyday life. This presses on anyone who has put off the question of God for years, assuming there will be time later. It must not be used to frighten an assured believer into thinking he must keep paying for forgiven sin, or to pressure someone into a settlement that lets an abuser off.

Three reasons the purgatory reading fails. With its parallel in Matthew 5:26, this clause has been cited for purgatory, since “until” seems to promise a way out at the end of the paying. But first, this is practical advice about a lawsuit, and a doctrine cannot be built on the incidental details of an illustration: pushed that way, the persistent widow would make God a judge who grants justice only to stop being pestered (18:1–8). Second, nobody earned wages in a debtors’ prison, so not getting out until the last penny is paid is the ordinary way of saying not getting out at all. Third, it would reverse the passage’s point: if there were a way to pay later, the advice to settle on the road would be optional.

Where Christians differ: purgatory. Roman Catholic teaching has sometimes cited this verse in support of purgatory, a place where souls pay for their sins after death before entering heaven. This commentary’s view: the parable is about urgent reconciliation before judgment, not about a process of purification after death. Christ’s one offering has cleared the believer’s account completely (Colossians 2:13–14; Hebrews 10:14), and the believer who dies goes at once to be with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). For those who reject Christ, the debt can never be paid.
verseByVerse.note: The “penny” was the smallest coin in circulation.

12.text: <sup>1</sup> In the meantime, when so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. <sup>2</sup> Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. <sup>3</sup> Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops. <sup>4</sup> “I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. <sup>5</sup> But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him! <sup>6</sup> Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. <sup>7</sup> Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows. <sup>8</sup> “And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, <sup>9</sup> but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God. <sup>10</sup> And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. <sup>11</sup> And when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, <sup>12</sup> for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.” <sup>13</sup> Someone in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” <sup>14</sup> But he said to him, “Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you?” <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.” <sup>16</sup> And he told them a parable, saying, “The land of a rich man produced plentifully, <sup>17</sup> and he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?’ <sup>18</sup> And he said, ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. <sup>19</sup> And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.’ <sup>20</sup> But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’ <sup>21</sup> So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.” <sup>22</sup> And he said to his disciples, “Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. <sup>23</sup> For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. <sup>24</sup> Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds! <sup>25</sup> And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? <sup>26</sup> If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest? <sup>27</sup> Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. <sup>28</sup> But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith! <sup>29</sup> And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried. <sup>30</sup> For all the nations of the world seek after these things, and your Father knows that you need them. <sup>31</sup> Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you. <sup>32</sup> “Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom. <sup>33</sup> Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. <sup>34</sup> For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. <sup>35</sup> “Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, <sup>36</sup> and be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast, so that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks. <sup>37</sup> Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. <sup>38</sup> If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants! <sup>39</sup> But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have left his house to be broken into. <sup>40</sup> You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.” <sup>41</sup> Peter said, “Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all?” <sup>42</sup> And the Lord said, “Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the proper time? <sup>43</sup> Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. <sup>44</sup> Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions. <sup>45</sup> But if that servant says to himself, ‘My master is delayed in coming,’ and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, <sup>46</sup> the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful. <sup>47</sup> And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. <sup>48</sup> But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required, and from him to whom they entrusted much, they will demand the more. <sup>49</sup> “I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! <sup>50</sup> I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished! <sup>51</sup> Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. <sup>52</sup> For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. <sup>53</sup> They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.” <sup>54</sup> He also said to the crowds, “When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, ‘A shower is coming.’ And so it happens. <sup>55</sup> And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat,’ and it happens. <sup>56</sup> You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time? <sup>57</sup> “And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? <sup>58</sup> As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. <sup>59</sup> I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.”

keyVerse.quote: Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
keyVerse.note: Here the chapter’s fears meet their answer. The disciples are told not to fear those who can kill the body, not to grasp at possessions and not to worry about food, and this verse gives the reason: the little flock has a Father who delights to give it the kingdom itself. The God who did not spare his Son will not withhold bread, and those who have been given the kingdom are free to sell, give, confess and wait.

12.reflection:
Jesus traces hypocrisy to the fear of people and answers it with the fear of God and the God who counts the hairs of our heads (vv. 1–7). Whose opinion most shapes what you say, or do not say, about Christ? How does knowing God as both Judge and Father change that?

The rich fool talked only to himself and told his soul it had enough (vv. 16–21). What “barns” do people around you trust for security, and which are you tempted to trust? What would being rich toward God look like for you this month?

Jesus answers anxiety not with a technique but with a Father who knows what we need and is glad to give the kingdom (vv. 22–32). Which of his arguments, the ravens, the lilies, the hour you cannot add or the Father’s good pleasure, speaks most to your worries, and why?

The servants are ready when the master knocks, and he serves them (vv. 35–48). What would being ready look like in your ordinary week? How does the picture of Christ tying on an apron change the way you think about his return?

13.title: Repent or Perish; the Narrow Door; Jerusalem's Lament
13.overview:
Where we are. Jesus is on the long journey to Jerusalem (9:51–19:27). Chapter 12 ended with a call to read the signs of the times and settle with your accuser before you reach the judge (12:54–59); chapter 13 presses that urgency home, and its last words turn towards the city where the journey ends.

The message. Time is short and grace is still open: repent now. Disasters are not God’s verdict on their victims but a summons to everyone still alive; God’s patience is real, but it has an end; the door into his kingdom is narrow, and it will be shut. Yet the one who warns is the one who frees, pleads and longs: he straightens a woman Satan has bound, asks for one more year for a barren tree, and grieves over the city that will kill him.

Why it was said. The crowds assumed that suffering marked out the guilty, and that being Abraham’s children, having eaten with Jesus and heard him teach, would be enough. Luke’s readers, many of them Gentiles (see the introduction), needed to know both that they had a real place at the feast and that privilege saves no one. Every reader who watches the news and quietly feels safe needs the same word.

How the chapter makes its case. Two disasters, a massacre and an accident, receive the same answer: “unless you repent, you will all likewise perish” (vv. 1–5). The barren fig tree shows why judgment waits, and that it will not wait for ever (vv. 6–9). The healing on the Sabbath shows what the kingdom is: Satan’s captive set free, and a religion that cannot rejoice exposed (vv. 10–17). The mustard seed and the leaven promise that this small beginning will fill the world (vv. 18–21). Asked whether few will be saved, Jesus tells his hearers to strive to enter by the narrow door before it shuts, for being near him is not the same as belonging to him, and the table will be filled from every nation (vv. 22–30). Finally he refuses to be hurried by Herod and laments over Jerusalem (vv. 31–35).

Where it leads. Everything in the chapter leans towards the cross. The sinless Galilean will die at Pilate’s hands at Passover; the vinedresser who stood between the tree and the axe will take the axe himself; the hen will spread her wings and take what was coming for her chicks. The door is narrow because it is a person, and the chapter ends not with the door slammed but with the word “until”.

For us. Stop measuring yourself against those who suffer, and use the year you have been given: turn to Christ now, and keep turning. Look round for the bent and overlooked, rejoice when God sets someone free, and pray like the vinedresser for those who still bear no fruit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Repent or Perish; the Barren Fig Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Disasters are no verdict on their victims, but they are a summons to everyone still alive: repent while there is time. Jesus refuses the crowd’s assumption that the Galileans Pilate killed were worse sinners (vv. 1–3), adds an accident at Siloam and gives the same answer word for word (vv. 4–5), and then shows why the axe has not yet fallen. A fig tree given every advantage has borne nothing for years; the vinedresser accepts the verdict but pleads for one more year and sets to work on it, and the reprieve has an end (vv. 6–9).
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus does not say that God never punishes; he says these deaths are not the special punishment of especially sinful people. All are sinners, all will die, and all need to repent (see the note on vv. 1–3).

The fig tree and the vineyard were familiar pictures of Israel (Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 8:13; Hosea 9:10). Who stands between the tree and the axe is treated at vv. 8–9. But the extra time has a limit.
verseByVerse.examples:
This passage forbids two things people say (see the note on vv. 4–5, with what may be said to the grieving).

The vinedresser is also a model for patient labour with an apparently hopeless case, a child who will not turn or a church that has not grown (see the note on vv. 8–9).

verseByVerse.quote: There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. And he answered them, 'Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When disaster falls on others, the question is not what they did to deserve it but whether you are ready to meet God. Jesus will not read the victims’ deaths as a verdict on their lives; he turns the news into a summons to repent.

The Galileans and Pilate. The incident is recorded nowhere else, the kind of local atrocity that left no trace in the histories, though it fits the brutal Pilate whom Josephus describes. Some Galileans were killed in the temple courts while offering sacrifices, probably at Passover, when laymen slaughtered their own lambs: men killed at the altar, in the act of worship, by the governor of a pagan empire.

Why do they raise it? Jesus has just urged the crowds to be reconciled to God before judgment (12:54–59), and some respond with a news item. Why, Luke does not say. They may be testing him: condemn Pilate and he is a rebel; say nothing and he has no sympathy for his own people. But his answer shows what they were actually thinking.

Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? He brings the assumption into the open before they can say it: the manner of a man’s death is a comment on his life. It was the working theology of the ancient world. Job’s friends spent most of a book on it (Job 4:7), and the disciples will ask it about a blind man: “who sinned, this man or his parents” (John 9:2)? It is the natural conclusion of anyone who believes God is just and in charge, and it is wrong. It is also attractive: if the dead deserved it, the living can feel safe, because a good enough life would keep the sword and the tower away. It is religion used as a way of staying in control, and Jesus takes it out of their hands.

Unless you repent. Then the turn nobody was ready for. The living are in the same position, and the only difference between them and the men on that temple pavement is timing. They brought a question about somebody else’s guilt, and he hands it back with their own name on it. “Likewise” may also be meant literally: some forty years later many Jews died at Roman hands in the temple courts during the siege of Jerusalem.

What does perish mean here? More than dying, since the Galileans have already died and his hearers will die whatever they do. To perish is to be lost before God: to die unreconciled and come under his judgment for ever (in John 3:16 perishing is the opposite of eternal life). What happened to those men’s bodies, sudden, unprepared and final, pictures what will happen to every soul that meets God without repentance. That is why the warning is urgent and not merely sad.

What is repentance? Turning from sin to God. It sees sin as God sees it, an offence against him and not only harm to ourselves, and grieves over it; it lays hold of God’s mercy in Christ, since sorrow with no hope in it only drives a sinner further from God; and by grace it leaves the sin behind and sets out on a new obedience (Westminster Confession 15.2; 1689 London Baptist Confession 15.3). It is not a single event at conversion but the shape of the whole Christian life, and while you are still breathing it is never too late to begin.

The same governor, the same feast. Within months another Galilean would die at Pilate’s hands at Passover time, and he is the one answering the question. Three times Pilate found no guilt in him (23:4, 14, 22). He was not a worse sinner than all the Galileans; he was the one sinless Galilean. His blood was not mingled with the sacrifices; it was the sacrifice, shed so that those who repent will never perish. The one who said “unless you repent” is the one who makes repentance possible, and who receives every repenting sinner with joy.

The secular way of saying they had it coming. We still say it when the news breaks, only in new words: he smoked, she should not have walked home that way, they built on a flood plain. Where the ancients said sin, we say lifestyle and risk factors. Jesus lets neither version stand. He does not deny that choices have consequences; he denies that our carefulness makes us safe. Then he offers what the reflex was looking for in the wrong place: not a promise that no tower will ever fall on us, but that those who turn to him will not perish when it does.

In everyday life. Watch for the reflex next time the news breaks: the faint relief that it was over there, the quick search for what they did differently. Let it send you instead to the one honest prayer the news can produce: Lord, I am no safer than they were; have mercy on me.
verseByVerse.note: This massacre is not recorded elsewhere, but it fits what is known of Pilate’s brutality. Many assumed disaster was punishment for a particular sin.

parallels.desc: who that was innocent ever perished? see: John 9:1–3 = who sinned, this man or his parents?

verseByVerse.quote: Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whether evil is done by people or simply happens, it is no measure of the victims’ guilt, and it calls every survivor to repent. Jesus adds an accident to the massacre and gives the same answer word for word (vv. 3, 5): death comes to everyone, often without warning, and the only safety is repentance.

The tower in Siloam. The first case was murder; this one is an accident. Siloam was the area round the pool at the south end of Jerusalem (John 9:7); perhaps a tower in the wall gave way on eighteen people. Between them the two cases cover the whole field: evil done by human beings, and evil that nobody did.

Were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? Offenders means debtors (opheiletai), the word Jesus taught them to use in prayer (11:4). Were they greater debtors to God? The question assumes that God keeps an account of sin, and that the falling tower was him collecting on eighteen unusually large debts. Jesus agrees that there is an account. He denies that the tower tells us anything about theirs.

Disasters and God. God is sovereign over all things, including disasters (Amos 3:6; Isaiah 45:7), but Scripture does not teach that every disaster punishes the particular sins of those who suffer.
