Since Adam sinned, death has been in God’s world and the ground has been cursed (Genesis 3:17–19; Romans 5:12); towers fall and bodies fail because the whole creation groans under that sentence (Romans 8:20–22), not because each victim earned his own blow. So when a wall comes down on a school, or a diagnosis arrives, refuse both of the sentences people offer: “they must have done something”, which Jesus denies twice and which must never be said to the bereaved, and “God had nothing to do with it”, which he does not say either.

Esteemed stricken. One death would be read exactly as Jesus forbids these to be read. At the cross the rulers sneered, “He saved others; let him save himself” (23:35), and Isaiah had foreseen the misreading: “we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted” (Isaiah 53:4). He was crushed by the will of God, not for his own sins, for he had none, but for ours. His is the one death where God’s judgment truly can be read, and there it fell on the one man who had not deserved it.

So what may be said to the grieving? Very little about the dead, and a great deal to the living. The honest answer to “why them?” is that we are not told, so do not offer explanations God has not given, or hurry anyone through their grief. Sit with them, weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15), pray with them, and speak of the God who is not distant from suffering because his Son entered it. Jesus’ word here, that our footing is no firmer than theirs, is usually a word for the preacher and for your own heart before it is a word for a widow.

And what about my own suffering? Is God punishing me? If you are in Christ, no. The punishment your sins deserved was laid on him, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). God does discipline his children, but as a father training them, not a judge sentencing them, for their holiness and good (Hebrews 12:5–11). You may not be able to say what a particular trouble is for, but you can say what it is not: God paying you back. It may be a call to search your heart, and it is always an invitation to draw near.
verseByVerse.note: Siloam was the area around the pool of Siloam in the south of Jerusalem; the tower’s collapse is otherwise unknown.

parallels.desc: not wishing that any should perish

verseByVerse.quote: And he told this parable: 'A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. And he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
God looks for fruit from those he has given every advantage, and a life that bears none cannot stand for ever. Only Luke records this parable; it explains why the axe has not yet fallen, and why it will.

A fig tree in a vineyard. A fig tree planted in a vineyard stands in prime cultivated ground: it has had every advantage. Anyone who knew the prophets would recognise the images: Israel is the vineyard where God looked for grapes and found wild grapes (Isaiah 5:1–7), and the fig tree in which he came looking and found nothing (Jeremiah 8:13; Micah 7:1).

Found none. Fruit means righteousness, justice, repentance and faith, the fruits in keeping with repentance that John demanded (3:8): not leaves, not size, but the only thing a fig tree is for.

For three years now. Not impatience. The law required that the fruit of the first three years be left untouched in any case (Leviticus 19:23), so the owner may have waited those years and then come three more. Some see a reference to the length of Jesus’ ministry, though that is uncertain. Certainly this man has given the tree every year it was owed and several it was not.

Cut it down. The charge is not that it has done harm, but that it is using up the ground (katargei, wasting, exhausting it). A fruitless tree draws water out of good soil and takes the light: what it takes could have fed a fruitful one.

He came seeking fruit. In a later vineyard story the owner sends servant after servant and at last says, “I will send my beloved son” (20:13). The owner who comes looking on this fig tree is God, and in the man telling the parable he had come in person, going through the towns of Israel looking for repentance and faith, until he wept over the city that would not have him (19:41). And the God who seeks fruit is the God who gives the sap, the sun and the soil, so that every fig his people ever bear is grown from his own goodness and offered back to his glory.

What fruit is God looking for in me? Not a performance or a quota of activity, but the life that grows from a heart turned to God: repentance, trust in Christ, and the fruit of the Spirit that follows (Galatians 5:22–23), with honest dealings and mercy to the poor (3:10–14). Fruit is quiet and grows over time. You will often see it more clearly in others than in yourself, and a believer who fears he has none is often bearing more than he knows. The barren tree is not a struggling Christian; it is a life that has had every privilege and given nothing back to God at all.
verseByVerse.note: Fig trees were often planted in vineyards. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.

parallels.desc: the vineyard that yielded wild grapes

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered him, ‘Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The barren tree is spared another year only because someone pleads for it and works on it, and even that reprieve has an end.

This year also. The vinedresser does not dispute the verdict. He accepts the whole case and asks for time: a picture of intercession and of God’s patience (2 Peter 3:9). It is hard not to see the storyteller in him: the one who stands between the tree and the axe is standing in that crowd.

Dig around it. “Let it alone” is only half his sentence. He will dig round the roots, breaking up compacted ground so water can reach them, and dung it: heavy, unglamorous labour on a tree that has given him nothing for three years, and he volunteers for it.

Well and good. The sentence in Greek is broken off: “if it bears fruit next year”, and then nothing. The translators supply “well and good”; Jesus leaves a silence. And if not, judgment is delayed, not cancelled: the vinedresser himself names the limit.

The point. The parable ends without telling us what happened, because the hearers must decide. The disasters said the axe is real; this parable says who is holding it back. A gospel that is all axe produces terror; one that is all delay produces a man still intending to repent in fifteen years’ time. Jesus gives both together.

The axe fell on him. The Son of God came down into the vineyard and took up the spade himself. And when the axe did fall, it fell on him: the one truly fruitful tree was cut down, hanged on a tree and made a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), so that barren trees might be spared and made fruitful. Every year of grace you have had was bought by his blood and asked for by his prayers (Hebrews 7:25).

In everyday life. This may be your extra year, and God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance (Romans 2:4). If there is a sin you have been meaning to deal with, or a call to Christ you have been answering with “later”, the parable says: now, while the ground is being dug for you.

How do I pray for someone who seems hopeless? Like the vinedresser: neither writing the tree off nor pretending there is fruit, but asking for another year and going to get the spade. Pray specifically and persistently for the child who will not turn, the friend who shrugs, the church that has not grown, and add whatever digging is yours: the patient kindness, the honest conversation, the invitation, the Bible left open. The results belong to God; the asking and the labour belong to us.

Does this mean a Christian can be cut down and lost? The parable is spoken first to Israel, and then to everyone who has privilege without fruit: the person who has heard the gospel all his life and never truly turned. It does not teach that those who belong to Christ can be cut off: his sheep will never perish (John 10:28), and he who began a good work will complete it (Philippians 1:6). But a fruitless profession is not safe, because fruit is the evidence of life (Matthew 7:16–20). If the warning troubles you, that is not the axe at your root but the vinedresser’s spade, and the right response is to turn to Christ now.

parallels.desc: God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — A Woman with a Disabling Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus sets free a woman Satan has bound, and shows that the Sabbath was made for exactly such mercy. In a synagogue he sees a woman bent double for eighteen years, still coming to worship; he calls her, lays his hands on her, and she stands straight and glorifies God (vv. 10–13). The synagogue ruler, counting a healing as work, scolds the crowd (v. 14). Jesus answers from their own practice: if they untie an ox to water it, a daughter of Abraham must be loosed from Satan’s bond on the Sabbath day (vv. 15–16). His opponents are shamed, and the people rejoice (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology:
Luke does not call the woman possessed, but Jesus says Satan had bound her (see the notes on vv. 10–11 and vv. 15–16). Jesus calls her “a daughter of Abraham”, inside the covenant (v. 16).

His argument comes from their own practice, and makes the Sabbath the most fitting day of all to set a captive free (this is treated fully at vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.examples:
The ruler’s real failure was that he did not see her (see the note on v. 14, with “How do I know if I am like this man?”).

And shame need not be the end (see the note on v. 17).

verseByVerse.quote: Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a synagogue on the Sabbath Jesus finds a woman whom Satan has kept bent double for eighteen years, still coming to worship and asking for nothing.

In one of the synagogues. Only Luke records this healing, and it is the last time in this Gospel that Jesus is recorded teaching in a synagogue. The synagogues are closing their doors to him.

A disabling spirit. Literally “a spirit of weakness”. Her condition was caused by Satan (v. 16), though she is not described as possessed and no demon is cast out: a physical condition with something darker behind it, Satan making use of the sickness of a fallen world.

Bent over. Luke the doctor (Colossians 4:14) describes it precisely: perhaps a fusion of the spine. For eighteen years she could hardly have seen the sky or looked another adult in the face without twisting her whole body.

Still coming to worship. Eighteen years bent double, in a culture that read affliction as a verdict, and she is still in the synagogue. She asks for nothing; she may have stopped expecting anything. She had become the settled furniture of the place, the bent woman everybody knew and nobody expected to change. But the Lord sees the ones who have stopped expecting to be seen: eighteen years did not exhaust his attention, and a crowded room did not hide her from him.

The first synagogue and the last. Luke opened Jesus’ ministry in the synagogue at Nazareth, where he read that he had been anointed “to set at liberty those who are oppressed” (4:18). Now, in the last synagogue scene, the promise is kept for one person nobody else had looked at. The synagogue had read the Scriptures over her for eighteen years. What it had not had, until this Sabbath, was the one the Scriptures were about, standing in the room.

In everyday life. Look round your own church for the person who has become furniture: the one with the long illness, the one who comes alone, the one nobody expects to change. Jesus saw her. Ask him for eyes like his.

Is sickness caused by Satan? Luke says this woman’s condition came from a spirit, and Jesus calls her one “whom Satan bound” (v. 16). But Scripture never teaches that every illness is demonic: the man born blind was not (John 9:3), and Paul’s thorn was a messenger of Satan that God used for his good (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). A believer cannot be owned by Satan, though God may permit him to be afflicted. The ordinary response to illness is prayer and medicine, not exorcism.

parallels.desc: another synagogue healing on the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her, 'Woman, you are freed from your disability.' And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unasked, Jesus calls the woman, declares her free and lays his hands on her, and at once she stands straight and praises God.

He saw her and called her. She did not ask. He saw her, folded double and probably out of everyone’s sightline; the same verb is used of him seeing the widow at Nain (7:13), and there too the seeing led straight to action. He called her over, so she had to cross the room, slowly, bent, with every eye following her. He took the initiative, as he always does with those he saves.

You are freed. Literally, you have been released, and the release stands (apolelysai): the vocabulary of untying, which Jesus will use three verses later of the ox. Not “be healed”, but the knot undone.

He laid his hands on her. Eighteen years, and it takes one sentence and a pair of hands. A healing touch, and a human one, which nobody may have given her for a long time. “The LORD lifts up those who are bowed down” (Psalm 146:8).

She glorified God. The tense suggests she kept on doing it. For eighteen years she had not been able to lift her face towards heaven in a building built for lifting faces towards heaven, and the first use she made of standing upright was worship.

A knot tied for eighteen years. He saw her before she saw him, called her before she asked, and undid in a moment a knot Satan had tied for eighteen years. One day the whole bent creation will stand up straight at his word.

Why does Jesus heal some and not others, and should I expect healing? His healings are signs that the kingdom has come and that the one who will undo every curse is here. He did not heal every sick person in Israel, and he does not promise every believer healing in this life; Paul left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). God still heals, in answer to prayer and through medicine, and we should ask him freely (James 5:14–15). But the miraculous gifts that marked the apostles were signs for the founding of the church, and we hold, charitably, that they are not given in the same way now, since the apostles and prophets were the church’s foundation, laid once (Ephesians 2:20). Many faithful Christians in Pentecostal and charismatic churches believe these gifts continue, and we gladly own them as brothers and sisters. What every believer is promised is the final straightening: a resurrection body with nothing bent in it (Philippians 3:21). Ask boldly, and rest in that.

parallels.desc: the LORD lifts up those who are bowed down

verseByVerse.quote: But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people, 'There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where everyone else sees a woman set free, the synagogue ruler sees only a rule broken. He counts mercy as forbidden work.

The ruler of the synagogue. The man responsible for organising its services (8:41). A woman has just stood upright for the first time in eighteen years and is praising God in his synagogue, and he is angry.

To the people. He does not speak to Jesus, who did it, but to the people, and in effect to her: public instruction aimed sideways, like the sermon everyone knows is about one person. It is cowardice dressed as teaching.

Six days. He is quoting the fourth commandment (Exodus 20:9), and he is right that the Sabbath forbids work. What he has done is classify a healing as work.

Come on those days. His ruling collapses at once. He tells a woman who has not been healed on any working day for nearly two decades to come back on Monday, as though healing were a service with opening hours. The real failure is not exactly legalism. He did not see her. A daughter of Abraham stood up straight in his building, and what registered was a diary problem.

Lord of the Sabbath. He talks as if a healer had opened a clinic on the wrong day. But “the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath” (6:5): the commandment the ruler quotes was given by the God whose Son was standing in his synagogue, doing the very work the day had always pointed to.

In everyday life. If you have a grievance with someone, take it to that person, not sideways to everyone else (Matthew 18:15).

How do I know if I am like this man? Religion can watch God act and think first about procedure, and from the inside that feels not like hardness but like carefulness. What is your first reaction when God moves in an unexpected way: in a person you had written off, in a church tradition not your own, in a service that ran late? Gladness, or a list of objections? Order matters, and Scripture asks for it (1 Corinthians 14:40). But when your love for the way things are done is stronger than your joy that a sinner is helped, the rule has taken the place of the Lord who gave it.
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Lord answered him, 'You hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
If it is right to untie a thirsty animal on the Sabbath, freeing a daughter of Abraham from Satan’s bonds is exactly what the day is for.

You hypocrites! The plural is deliberate. One man spoke; Jesus answers a whole way of thinking, and everyone in the room who agreed.

Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? The argument is unanswerable because everybody present did it. An animal tied in a stall cannot reach water, and no farmer would leave a beast thirsty from Friday evening to Saturday evening. The traditions later written down by the rabbis allowed livestock to be untied, led out and watered on the Sabbath, because mercy to a beast was not counted as work. So they already hold that a knot may be untied on the Sabbath to relieve suffering. Jesus asks them only to apply the rule they use every week.

Ought not this woman. Now the comparison, the sharpest thing in the chapter. Ought (edei) is the word Luke uses again and again for what God’s plan requires: it was not merely permitted to heal her; it was required. And “this woman” is set over against “his ox or his donkey”: the animal has an owner who will take trouble for it. Is she to have less?

A daughter of Abraham. The phrase occurs nowhere else in the Gospels. Everyone in that synagogue would have called himself a son of Abraham (compare Zacchaeus, 19:9); the title is handed to a bent, unnamed woman, and it means she is inside the covenant with every right that carries. Of more value than an ox.

Whom Satan bound. He names who tied the knot: the strong man of chapter 11, whom a stronger one overpowers (11:21–22). This is not only an illness. Satan has held her like occupied ground, and now he is being driven out. Her eighteen years are set against the ox’s one thirsty day.

Be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day? A play on words: you untie your animals; should I not untie this woman? And his last words are the ones they thought were the problem: “on the Sabbath day”. Not in spite of the Sabbath, but on it. The Sabbath remembered God’s freeing Israel from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15), so it is the most fitting day of all to free a captive of Satan. The Sabbath finds its fulfilment in the freedom Christ brings.

A day of untying. The first day of the week has been a day of untying ever since Christ rose on it, having broken the bonds of death itself. He counts a bent daughter of Abraham worth more than every ox in Israel, and he paid for his people’s release with his own life.

Where Christians differ: does the Sabbath still bind Christians? Many, following the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the fourth commandment remains, moved by Christ’s resurrection to the first day, so that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, kept holy for worship and works of necessity and mercy (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8). Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, the true rest, so that no day binds the conscience in itself (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5), while Christians gladly gather on the Lord’s Day as the apostles did. This commentary’s view: the second view fits the New Testament best: the Lord’s Day is a gift to be kept gladly, not a Sabbath law moved to Sunday, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it. The Westminster and 1689 view is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. Both agree on what this passage teaches: the day of rest is a day of mercy, kindness never breaks it, and its meaning is found in Christ, who gives rest to the weary (Matthew 11:28).
verseByVerse.note: Even the strictest rules allowed livestock to be watered on the Sabbath.

parallels.desc: he also is a son of Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same act of mercy shames Jesus’ opponents and fills the ordinary people with joy.

Put to shame. “Adversaries” is a word for opponents in a lawsuit, and it is plural: the synagogue ruler was one of a group. They had no answer: not shouted down, but shown up, as all who set themselves against the Lord are put to shame (Isaiah 45:16).

All the people rejoiced. The ordinary people, with nothing invested in a ruling about Sabbath work, saw it rightly. The word for “glorious things” (endoxois) is used in the Greek of God’s mighty acts at the exodus (Exodus 34:10): something of the weight of God has been visible in their synagogue, and they know it.

Two responses to one event. They all saw a woman folded double for eighteen years stand up; what divided them was what they brought into the building. That is the pattern for the rest of this Gospel: the same act of God gladdens one man and humiliates another, as on the descent from the Mount of Olives, where the disciples praise God and Pharisees tell him to rebuke them (19:37–39). He is “appointed for the fall and rising of many” (2:34).

Is there hope for the man who was put to shame? Yes. Shame is what a person feels when he has been shown to be wrong, and for anyone willing to take it, it is the last stop before repentance. Luke does not tell us what the synagogue ruler did next; the door was still open when the paragraph closed. If Christ has shown you up, in your pride or your hardness, the shame is meant not to drive you away from him but to bring you to him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–30 — Mustard Seed, Leaven, and the Narrow Door
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom that frees one bent woman will fill the world, yet no one enters it by being near; each must go in by the narrow door while it is open. The mustard seed and the leaven show its small, hidden beginnings and its certain growth, outward until the nations shelter in it and inward until all is changed (vv. 18–21). When someone asks whether few will be saved (vv. 22–23), Jesus answers the asker instead: strive to enter (v. 24), for the master will shut the door, and those who only ate in his presence will be left outside (vv. 25–27), while people from every quarter sit at table with Abraham (vv. 28–30).
verseByVerse.theology:
The question about the number of the saved is put in the third person, about other people, and Jesus turns it back on the crowd (vv. 22–23). The striving he commands is not a way of earning entry (see the note on v. 24).

The words “I do not know where you come from” are not a lapse of memory (see the note on vv. 25–27). And the table they miss is full, with guests from east and west (see the note on vv. 28–30).
verseByVerse.examples:
Everything the people outside plead is true and beside the point (see the note on vv. 25–27).

In Luke the door is a Person (see “How do I know I am inside?” in the note on v. 24).

verseByVerse.quote: He said therefore, 'What is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom of God begins so small that it is easily despised, yet it will grow until the nations find shelter in it.

He said therefore. The “therefore” ties this to the healing. One freed woman, one village synagogue, one argument won against a minor official, and the establishment more hostile than it was that morning: if this is the kingdom of God arriving, it does not look like much. His answer is that the kingdom is here, that its beginnings are small, and that it will grow.

A grain of mustard seed. The mustard seed was proverbially tiny, the standard picture of the negligible (17:6). The kingdom began with one man from Nazareth and a handful of followers. And it is sown “in his garden”, deliberately: somebody put a thing that small into the ground, as if it could possibly be worth the effort.

Became a tree. The mustard plant by the Sea of Galilee can grow ten feet (3 m) tall, large enough for birds to perch in. Calling it a tree is a stretch, and is meant to be.

The birds of the air. The image is Ezekiel’s and Daniel’s, and there it means a kingdom under whose shelter the nations live (Daniel 4:12, 21; Ezekiel 31:6). So Jesus takes the picture of the imperial cedar and puts it on a garden herb. That is the joke, and it is also how God works. The empires start large and end in ruins. This starts with a seed you could lose in the palm of your hand, and the nations end up living in it. Every believer in every land is a bird in that tree.

The tender sprig. Ezekiel’s nesting birds are a promise about a king: the Lord takes a tender sprig from the broken royal house of David, plants it on a high mountain, and birds of every sort nest under it (Ezekiel 17:22–23). The kingdom grows from small to great because its King did, growing up like a root out of dry ground (Isaiah 53:2): a carpenter’s son, a teacher with a few fishermen, a body in a borrowed tomb. The one telling this parable is the sprig the parable is about.

In everyday life. Do not despise small beginnings (Zechariah 4:10). The Sunday school class of six, the Bible study with three, the conversation over a fence: these are mustard seeds, and the Gardener knows what he has planted. Sow, and leave the growing to him.

Does this mean my church should be large? No. The parable is about the kingdom across the whole sweep of history, not a promise that every congregation will grow big; many faithful churches stay small for generations, and many large ones are not faithful. If the church in your own country seems to be shrinking, the parable takes in the whole world and the whole age: in the last century the gospel has spread across Africa, Asia and Latin America faster than at almost any time in history. What it forbids is despising the small and hidden as if God could not be at work there. The measure of a church is whether Christ is preached and his people are being changed. Small faithfulness is part of the great tree.
verseByVerse.note: Mustard seed was proverbially tiny; the plant can grow taller than a man.

verseByVerse.quote: And again he said, 'To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom works like yeast in dough: hidden, quiet and from within, until it has changed the whole.

Like leaven. This ought to bring a reader up short. One chapter ago, from this same speaker, leaven was the picture of everything that ruins: “the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy” (12:1). Israel scoured it out of the house before Passover (Exodus 12:15), and Paul means malice and evil by it (1 Corinthians 5:6–8). Here, unusually, it is a picture of the kingdom.

Why is leaven good here when it is bad elsewhere? Because the image is about the way leaven works, not about whether what it carries is good or evil. Some have concluded that Jesus is warning of corruption spreading quietly through the church, but his words rule that out: he says the kingdom of God is like leaven, the very wording he has just used of the mustard seed, as the matching half of a pair. Turn the second into a warning and you break the pair. What makes yeast a good image for hypocrisy, that it is small, hidden, works from the inside and does not stop until the whole batch is changed, makes it a good image for the kingdom. At 12:1 something false permeates a community; here something true permeates the world.

A man in the first parable, a woman in the second. Luke often sets a man beside a woman, as with Simeon and Anna. And the woman hid it: the kingdom works from within.

Three measures. About 50 pounds (22 kg) of flour, enough to feed a hundred people, about what Sarah baked for her heavenly visitors (Genesis 18:6). The comedy is deliberate: a pinch of yeast, invisible the moment it goes in, and a mountain of dough; and the pinch wins.

All leavened. The whole lump is transformed: the answer to anyone who has compared the size of the world with the size of the church and concluded that the arithmetic is hopeless.

The two parables together. The seed is seen from outside: something small becomes a thing the birds can find. The leaven is seen from inside: something small changes every part. One is the kingdom’s reach, the other its depth.

Christ in you. The New Testament names the hidden thing: not a rule laid on the outside but the King himself living within by his Spirit, “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Colossians 1:26–27). The risen Jesus poured out the Spirit (Acts 2:33) on about a hundred and twenty in one city (Acts 1:15), and by the last page of Acts the kingdom of God is being proclaimed in Rome (Acts 28:31). Nobody watching that upper room could have seen the dough rise. It rose. The kingdom entered the world hidden in a virgin’s womb, grew in obscurity in Nazareth, was buried in a tomb, and has been rising ever since.

What it does not mean. Not necessarily that the whole world will become Christian before Christ returns, the hope some godly Reformed teachers have held. The parables promise growth and transformation, not universal conversion, and other passages speak of persecution and falling away until the end (18:8; 21:12; 2 Timothy 3:1–5).

How does the kingdom work in me like leaven? Quietly and thoroughly. Christ does not stay in one compartment of a life. He begins with the heart and works outward into habits, words, money, marriage and work, usually slower than we want and deeper than we notice. You can no more watch it week by week than watch dough rise, but look back over years and you will often find that what once ruled you no longer does. The one who hid the yeast will not stop until the whole is leavened (Philippians 1:6). So do the hidden work faithfully: the honest day’s labour, the kind word at home, the prayer no one hears. That is how the gospel moves through a street, an office and a family.
verseByVerse.note: Three measures of flour is a very large batch, about what Sarah baked for her three guests.

verseByVerse.quote: He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem. And someone said to him, 'Lord, will those who are saved be few?' And he said to them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked whether only a few will be saved, Jesus will not feed curiosity about other people; he turns the question on the one asking.

Toward Jerusalem. Luke has been noting the direction of travel since 9:51. The question about how many will be saved is put to the one person on that road who knows, because he is going to Jerusalem to save them.

Lord, will those who are saved be few? A live question in the schools: Jewish teachers debated how many of Israel would have a share in the age to come. Some said all Israel would be saved, with a few named exceptions; others were considerably tighter. And look at how it is framed: a question about a number, and a number relating to other people. The man asking has left himself out of the count.

No number given. Wherever curiosity presses for what God has not told, the times and seasons, who is greatest, what will happen to that man, Jesus turns the question back on the asker. And he answers “them”, plural: the whole crowd, and the question becomes personal. The Lord of the harvest knows the number of his own, every name written in the book of life before the foundation of the world. He does not need our arithmetic.

So will few be saved, or many? Scripture gives two answers that sound opposite and are both true. Seen from the road, the way is narrow, and in any generation those who find it are few compared with the crowd on the broad road (Matthew 7:13–14). Seen from the end, John sees “a great multitude that no one could number”, from every nation, tribe, people and language (Revelation 7:9), and not one the Father has given the Son will be lost (John 6:37–39). But you will not be in that number by being in a majority, a family or a church. Jesus’ answer is not a statistic. It is: make sure you are one of them.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not ask how many will be saved; make every effort to go in yourself, through the one narrow door, while it is still open.

The door. It leads into the kingdom feast (vv. 28–29), and the master who shuts it is Jesus himself (vv. 25–27). The way in is through him: “I am the door” (John 10:9).

Strive. Agōnizesthe is what an athlete does in the games (hence agony): to strain, to exert everything, as though something depended on it. Something does.

The door is narrow. Not locked, not hidden, not high. Narrow: which says nothing about how hard it is to open and everything about how much can be carried through it. Not your own righteousness, nor your pride, nor the sin you mean to keep. It is wide enough for any sinner and too narrow for any sinner’s baggage.

Will not be able. Not because they wanted Christ and were refused, but because they came too late (v. 25), or on their own terms. Plenty of people intend to go through later, and he is telling them that later is a door that shuts.

He made himself narrow. The door is narrow because it is a person, and he made himself narrow for us, stripped of glory and stretched on a cross, so that the way into the Father’s house might be opened to sinners from every corner of the earth.

In everyday life. If you have been meaning to settle things with God, do not let another week pass. And if you are inside, keep striving in the Spirit’s strength, for the door is the beginning of the road. But your welcome does not hang on your striving: Christ obeyed perfectly in your place, and for his sake the Father accepts your faltering steps.

If I must strive, am I not earning my way in after all? No; look at what the striving is for. Not “strive to become worthy” or “strive until you have done enough”, but “strive to enter”. The effort is not payment offered at the door but the urgency of a man who will not be talked out of going through it. Everything in Luke pushes against the earning reading: the tax collector who can only beat his breast goes home justified (18:13–14), and the dying criminal with nothing to offer is promised Paradise that very day (23:43). This is the striving of the drowning man for the rope, not of the labourer for his wages.

How do I know I am inside? The door is not a standard you climb to but a Person you come to, and Luke has been showing us the entering all along in ordinary people: the centurion who asks Jesus only to say the word (7:7), the woman told that her faith has saved her (7:50), the leper who came back (17:19), the blind man who would not stop shouting (18:38–39). Not one was admitted for being impressive. Each came to Jesus himself, with nothing, and would not be turned aside. If that is what you are doing, you are not outside knocking (John 6:37). And doubt is not the same as being outside: a true believer may wait long and conflict with many difficulties before he has assurance (Westminster Confession 18.3; 1689 London Baptist Confession 18.3). Look not first at the strength of your faith but at the Christ it holds. Come to him again today with nothing in your hands, and assurance usually grows as you keep coming, see the Spirit’s fruit slowly appear, and rest on his promise rather than your feelings.

verseByVerse.quote: When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us,’ then he will answer you, ‘I do not know where you come from.’ Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’ But he will say, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of evil!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once the door is shut, having been near Jesus will count for nothing; only belonging to him will.

The door shut. The scene moves to a house at night, and the decisive action has already happened: this is the day of judgment (Matthew 25:10). The master shut the door once, at a time of his choosing, as any householder does at the end of the day.

Lord, open to us. They call him “Lord”, but too late (6:46). They are at the right house, asking the right person.

I do not know where you come from. Not a failure of memory: as God he knows everything about everyone (Psalm 139:1–4). To know, in the Hebrew idiom, is relational: God knew Israel among all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2), and “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19). “Where you come from” asks whose are you, what is your connection to this house? There is none: they were never his (Matthew 7:23).

We ate and drank. Every word of the plea is true: they had eaten in his company and heard him teach in their streets. And it is beside the point, for every claim is about having been near him. Nobody says “we trusted you”.

Workers of evil. The words are from Psalm 6:8, and they land hardest on those closest to religion in any generation: “I was at that church for thirty years; I sat under good preaching; I took communion.” All true, and all a description of where a man stood rather than what he did about it. They thought of themselves as guests; he calls them workers of evil, because a life never brought to him for cleansing is a life of unforgiven sin, however respectable it looked (Isaiah 64:6).

Now he knocks. Today the scene runs the other way: the Lord who will one day shut the door now says, “Behold, I stand at the door and knock” (Revelation 3:20). Those who knock too late are those who would not open while he knocked.

In everyday life. Take one familiar thing this week, the grace before a meal, the hymn you sing without thinking, and stop inside it long enough to speak to him rather than about him. And pray that children who have grown up near the gospel will come to belong.

I have been in church all my life. Should this frighten me? It should make you honest, not hopeless. The question is not how long you have been near Jesus but whether you have come to him, owning your sin and trusting him alone to save you. If you have, a lifetime in church is a great mercy. If you are not sure, do not settle it by reviewing your attendance: go to him now, in your own words, and ask him to receive you. The people in this parable are not those who came and were refused, but those who never came and assumed that being near was enough.

parallels.desc: depart from me, all you workers of evil

verseByVerse.quote: In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out. And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who trusted in their privilege will find themselves shut out, while people from every nation sit down at God’s feast.

Weeping and gnashing of teeth. Grief, and anguish with perhaps rage still in it: the misery of those shut out of the kingdom (Matthew 8:12; 13:42).

Abraham and all the prophets. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are the forebears Jesus’ hearers were proud of. And the torment Jesus names is what they see: exclusion means knowing exactly what has been lost and who is at the table.

Cast out. The shock: Abraham’s children shut out, because they did not share Abraham’s faith. Not pagans, but men whose whole assurance rested on their descent, an assurance John had demolished when he warned them not to say that they had Abraham as their father (3:8).

From east and west. From all four points of the compass: the Gentiles, from every nation (Isaiah 49:12; Psalm 107:3). The table is full, and full of people nobody in that synagogue expected to see there.

Recline at table. The messianic banquet (Isaiah 25:6–8; Revelation 19:9), where Gentiles sit with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matthew 8:11): not a snack at the door but a place at the table, with nothing more to do but enjoy the host.

Last who will be first. The great reversal: Gentiles, last in privilege, first in the kingdom; many in Israel, first in privilege, last. It has been Luke’s theme since Mary’s song (1:52). But it is not a general maxim about the underdog: the order is set by grace, and those most confident of their standing are the last to ask for mercy, though asking is the only way in.

At my table in my kingdom. Luke tells us whose table it is. Every meal in this Gospel has Jesus at its centre, and at the Last Supper he promises the Twelve that they will “eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (22:30). The feast with Abraham is his feast. Blessed be the Host who was himself shut out for us, crucified outside the city gate (Hebrews 13:12), so that strangers from east and west might sit down with Abraham and never be sent away. Not one seat will stand empty, and at that feast death itself is swallowed up for ever.

In everyday life. Thank God for every advantage you have had, then come to him as though you had none. Be glad, not jealous, when someone from far off is welcomed to the table, and look round your church for the newcomer, a guest of the same King.

Who are the first who will be last today? Anyone whose confidence rests on what he has rather than on Christ: a Christian upbringing, a good church, a long record of service, sound doctrine held at arm’s length. These are gifts, and the first in privilege can be first in the kingdom too, if they come as beggars; but privilege trusted becomes a wall. The last who will be first are those who knew they had no claim at all: the convert from a wrecked life, the believer in a land that heard the gospel only yesterday, the child with simple faith.

Where Christians differ: when is the feast spread? Some place it in a thousand-year reign on earth after Christ returns. This commentary’s view: it is the feast of the new creation after his one visible return, because the New Testament joins that return directly to the resurrection, the judgment and the new heavens and earth (John 5:28–29; 2 Peter 3:10–13). Both wait for the same feast and the same Host.

Where Christians differ: is the punishment conscious and lasting? Some evangelicals, reading the Bible’s language of destruction (Matthew 10:28), hold that the lost are finally destroyed and cease to exist, and they hold it earnestly. Most Christians through history have held that the punishment of the lost is conscious and without end. This commentary’s view: the punishment is conscious and lasting. This picture is of people who are present and aware of what they have lost, and Jesus elsewhere speaks of eternal punishment in the same breath as eternal life (Matthew 25:46), so that whatever one lasts, the other does. Hell is not annihilation but exclusion from the joy of God’s presence under his just judgment (2 Thessalonians 1:9). It is a terrible truth, and Jesus speaks it with tears, not relish.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined at a banquet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus goes to Jerusalem to die on his Father’s timetable, not Herod’s, and grieves over the city that will kill him. Warned that Herod wants to kill him, he calls Herod a fox and sends back a schedule Herod does not set: he will finish his work, for a prophet must perish in Jerusalem (vv. 31–33). Then he speaks to the city itself, longing to gather its children as a hen gathers her brood, and pronouncing its house forsaken until it says, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” (vv. 34–35).
verseByVerse.theology:
“Your house is forsaken”: the temple God called “my house” is handed back to them, because its owner is leaving (see the note on v. 35, with Ezekiel’s departing glory).

But the sentence ends with “until”, and its last line is a welcome (see v. 35, and the question there on a future turning of Israel to Christ).
verseByVerse.examples: The lament is the model of grief for those who hear the gospel and turn away. It is not anger but refused love, and every parent praying for a child who will not turn, and every pastor who has watched someone come close and walk away, has tasted something of it.

verseByVerse.quote: At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, 'Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.' And he said to them, 'Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.’ Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No threat from Herod can hurry or halt Jesus: he will finish his work on God’s timetable and die where the prophets died, in Jerusalem.

Get away from here. It is the only time in the Gospels that Pharisees warn Jesus of danger, and their motive is uncertain. Not all were hostile (Luke records three who invite him to dinner), but the warning may be a manoeuvre to drive him towards Judea, where his real opponents waited. Luke does not say, and it is better not to decide.

Herod wants to kill you. The threat is credible: this is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea, who had beheaded John (9:9).

Go and tell that fox. In Jewish usage a fox was the small, destructive predator, set against the lion: Herod is being called a nuisance rather than a power. Which is what he was. Rome never let him be king, and he would end his days exiled to Gaul.

The third day I finish my course. The reply is a timetable, and it belongs to somebody else: a short time set by God, not by Herod, ending in the completion his work would reach at his death and resurrection in Jerusalem (Hebrews 2:10). The verb comes from the same family of words as “It is finished” (John 19:30).

I must go on my way. There is the “must” again (dei), what God’s plan requires, which has driven this Gospel since a boy in the temple said he must be in his Father’s house (2:49). Herod’s threats cannot change God’s plan.

Away from Jerusalem. Bitter irony. Jerusalem had a long history of killing the prophets (Jeremiah 26:20–23): the city that exists to bring men to God has a settled record of killing the men God sends. So this prophet is safe from Herod; his death is appointed for another place.

Never the victim of a schedule he did not set. Herod schemed, Pilate washed his hands, the crowds shouted, and through it all the Son walked steadily to the hour appointed by his Father, to lay down his life of his own accord and take it up again (John 10:18). The Lord who is not afraid of foxes holds every one of his people in the same unhurried, unbreakable hand.

What if someone is threatening me? Jesus did not ignore the danger, and he did not run from his calling either. He went on doing the work God had given him, in the place God had given it, until the time God had set. Take sensible precautions, seek help, and where there is abuse or real danger, go to those who can protect you; Scripture never asks you to stay under violence. But do not let fear decide your obedience. Your days are written in God’s book before one of them came to be (Psalm 139:16), and no Herod can add a minute to them or take one away.

Did Jesus insult a ruler? He spoke as a prophet with authority over Herod, giving God’s verdict on a cunning and destructive man. It is not a pattern for speaking of rulers with contempt: Paul apologised for speaking against the high priest (Acts 23:5), and Peter tells believers to honour the emperor (1 Peter 2:17). We may and sometimes must speak plainly about injustice, and never be ruled by fear of the powerful. But our ordinary duty is to pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2) and speak of them with respect, even when we oppose what they do.

Uncertain wording. “Today and tomorrow and the third day” is probably a Semitic way of saying “a short while, and then the end”, not a count of three literal days, and v. 33 repeats it to a different point: he will keep travelling until he reaches the city. How exactly the two sayings fit together is debated. And teleioumai can mean “I finish” (ESV, “I finish my course”) or “I am brought to completion”. Either way the meaning is clear: his work and his journey both end, on God’s schedule, in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, who had executed John. A fox was a picture of cunning and destructiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus grieves over Jerusalem, which has refused God’s messengers again and again, and longs to shelter its people as a hen shelters her chicks.

O Jerusalem, Jerusalem. The double address shows deep emotion, grief and love, the same tone as “Martha, Martha” and “Simon, Simon” (10:41; 22:31). It is what he says when he sees the whole of someone and grieves.

The city that kills the prophets. This is what the city does, as a settled practice, and the charge is historical. Zechariah was stoned in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:21); Jeremiah was thrown into a cistern to die (Jeremiah 38:6). And it is about to kill the greatest of the prophets.

How often. This is the phrase that matters. Jesus had visited Jerusalem several times (John 2:13; 5:1; 7:10), but “how often” is the language of someone who has been trying for a very long time, with every prophet who was sent and killed behind it. The one speaking is the one who sent them: Jesus speaks as God, who longed to gather his people.

As a hen. Luke sets this lament straight after the message to “that fox”: a fox is on the prowl, and a hen stands between it and her chicks. In the Old Testament God shelters his people under his wings (Ruth 2:12; Psalm 91:4), often as an eagle (Deuteronomy 32:11). But a hen has no talons and cannot fight. The way she saves her chicks is by spreading her wings and staying where she is, taking on herself what was coming for them. That is the image he chose for himself, on the road to a city that was going to kill him.

You were not willing. Every verb before these words is his: “would I have gathered”. The willingness was entirely on one side and the refusal on the other. Not unable: not willing, and that is the only thing standing between those chicks and those wings.

Then he came himself. Glory to the Lord God of Israel, who sent prophet after prophet into a city that killed them, and then came himself, grieving on the road. “How often” is the voice of a love that kept count of every rejection and kept on calling. His wings are spread still, and no chick that ran under them has ever been turned away.

In everyday life. Let the tears of Jesus shape the way you speak about those who reject him: not with contempt or indifference, but with longing. Pray for the people you know who have refused him, by name, with something of his grief. And if there is any part of your own life you have been unwilling to bring under his wings, bring it today.

If God is sovereign, how can his tears be real? Because he means what he says. God truly delights in mercy, truly calls and truly grieves when his call is refused, and none of that is pretence, though he has also purposed what will come to pass. Scripture asks us to believe both: no one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6:44), and whoever refuses Christ does so freely and is answerable for it. The tears of Jesus are the clearest window we have into the heart of God towards sinners.

Can I still come? Yes. If you fear you have refused him too long, the fear itself is a sign he is still gathering you. The finally lost are not those who wanted to come and were turned away, but those who would not. Come today, and you will find room under his wings.

Where Christians differ: God’s will and human refusal. Arminians, Christians who follow the Dutch theologian Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609), many of them deeply devoted to Christ, take this verse to show that God wills all to be saved but that human free will can finally resist his saving purpose. This commentary’s view: Scripture teaches both that God is sovereign in salvation (John 6:37, 44; Ephesians 1:11) and that he sincerely calls sinners and grieves over their refusal (Ezekiel 18:23, 32; 33:11). Reformed theology distinguishes God’s revealed will, what he commands and desires (that people repent and come), from his secret decree, what he has determined will happen. Jesus’ lament is genuine: God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. The responsibility for refusal lies entirely with those who refuse. Both truths stand; we should not cancel one by the other.

parallels.desc: under his wings you will find refuge

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, your house is forsaken. And I tell you, you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Jerusalem would not be gathered, God abandons its temple to judgment, and the city will not see Jesus again until it welcomes him.

Your house is forsaken. “Your house”: it had never been theirs. The prophets called it “my house”, a house of prayer (Isaiah 56:7), as Jesus will say in that very building (19:46). To call it “your house” instead of “my house” is to say that its owner has moved out (Jeremiah 12:7; 22:5). The sentence was carried out in AD 70, when Roman armies burned the temple (19:43–44; 21:6).

Israel had seen this before. Ezekiel watched the glory of God leave the temple for the mountain on the east (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23), and the building was flattened a few years later. And the glory that left in Ezekiel’s day had come back in person, a baby carried into the temple in Simeon’s arms (2:27–32), and was now being refused.

Until you say. The quotation is Psalm 118:26, sung by pilgrims arriving for the feasts, and the crowds will sing it over him as he comes down the Mount of Olives (19:38). But within the week the city handed him over, so many see the deeper fulfilment at his return. He came once to die, and he is coming again to reign.

The shape of the sentence. The chapter opened with blood in the temple courts and a barren tree granted one more year; now the year is running out for the city itself. Yet Luke ends not on the axe but on “until”. Jesus pronounced a terrible sentence over the city he was born to save, and left a door open in its last line. The words that follow are not a list of conditions but a welcome, the one thing that city never gave him.

Does this mean a future turning of Israel to Christ? Paul teaches that all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:25–27), which many understand as a future conversion of large numbers of the Jewish people before Christ returns. Others take it of the full number of God’s elect, Jew and Gentile. Either way, the verse holds out hope as well as judgment.

How should Christians think about the Jewish people today? With love, gratitude and longing. “Salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22): the patriarchs, the covenants, the Scriptures and the Messiah himself came through them (Romans 9:4–5). Paul had unceasing anguish for his kinsmen and prayed for their salvation (Romans 9:2–3; 10:1). Contempt for Jewish people denies the gospel; it does not defend it. Yet the way of salvation is the same for Jew and Gentile: faith in Jesus the Messiah, the only name under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). So we pray, we love, and we tell the good news, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
this house shall become a desolation

13.text: <sup>1</sup> There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. <sup>2</sup> And he answered them, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? <sup>3</sup> No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. <sup>4</sup> Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? <sup>5</sup> No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.” <sup>6</sup> And he told this parable: “A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. <sup>7</sup> And he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?’ <sup>8</sup> And he answered him, ‘Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. <sup>9</sup> Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.’” <sup>10</sup> Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. <sup>11</sup> And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself. <sup>12</sup> When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her, “Woman, you are freed from your disability.” <sup>13</sup> And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God. <sup>14</sup> But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people, “There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.” <sup>15</sup> Then the Lord answered him, “You hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? <sup>16</sup> And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?” <sup>17</sup> As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him. <sup>18</sup> He said therefore, “What is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? <sup>19</sup> It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.” <sup>20</sup> And again he said, “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? <sup>21</sup> It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.” <sup>22</sup> He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem. <sup>23</sup> And someone said to him, “Lord, will those who are saved be few?” And he said to them, <sup>24</sup> “Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able. <sup>25</sup> When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us,’ then he will answer you, ‘I do not know where you come from.’ <sup>26</sup> Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’ <sup>27</sup> But he will say, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of evil!’ <sup>28</sup> In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out. <sup>29</sup> And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. <sup>30</sup> And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.” <sup>31</sup> At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, “Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.” <sup>32</sup> And he said to them, “Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.’ <sup>33</sup> Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem. <sup>34</sup> O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! <sup>35</sup> Behold, your house is forsaken. And I tell you, you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’”

keyVerse.quote: No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.
keyVerse.note: Spoken twice, word for word (vv. 3, 5), this sentence sets the tone for the whole chapter: the barren tree’s last year, the narrow door that will be shut and the city that would not be gathered all press the same call. It turns every question about other people’s guilt back on the one asking. And it comes from the one who would himself die at Pilate’s hands, so that those who repent will never perish.

13.reflection:
When disaster strikes other people, what explanations do those around you reach for, and what do they reveal (vv. 1–5)? How does Jesus’ answer change the way you watch the news, and the way you comfort someone who is grieving?

The vinedresser accepts the verdict on the barren tree but asks for one more year and sets to work on it (vv. 6–9). What does this show about God’s patience and Christ’s intercession? Who are you praying for in this way, and what digging might be yours to do?

The synagogue ruler saw a rule broken where everyone else saw a woman set free (vv. 10–17). Where are we tempted to care more about how things are done than about people being helped? Who in your church has become part of the furniture?

Those left outside could say, “We ate and drank in your presence” (v. 26). What is the difference between being near Jesus and belonging to him? How might verse 34 encourage someone who fears they have refused him too long?

14.title: The Banquet, the Invitation, and the Cost
14.overview:
Where we are. On the long journey to Jerusalem (9:51–19:27), Jesus has just said that many will come from east and west to the kingdom’s table while some who ate with him are shut out (13:28–29). Chapter 14 sits him at an actual table, then puts him back on the road.

The message. God’s kingdom is a feast given free to those who cannot repay, and coming to it costs everything. The Host fills his house with the poor and the broken; the only people left outside were invited and had something better to do. But he asks to be loved above every gift he gives, above family and self, with a cross carried behind him and everything held open-handed. Grace and cost are not two messages but one: the feast is free, and it is worth everything.

Why it was said. At the table sat respectable men who scrambled for honour, entertained those who could repay, and spoke warmly of a kingdom far off; on the road walked keen crowds who had not counted the cost. Luke’s readers, many of them Gentiles from the “highways and hedges” (see the introduction), needed to know both their welcome and its cost.

How the chapter makes its case. At a Sabbath dinner Jesus heals a man with dropsy and silences the experts (vv. 1–6). Watching the guests jostle for seats, he teaches that God humbles the self-exalting and exalts the humble (vv. 7–11), and tells his host to invite those who cannot repay (vv. 12–14). In the parable of the great banquet the invited send polite excuses, and the house is filled from the back streets and the hedgerows (vv. 15–24). Then he names the cost to the crowds, love above all, a cross and everything a person has, and a builder, a king and tasteless salt show why it must be counted (vv. 25–35).

Where it leads. Every part of the chapter is lived first by the one telling it. He took the lowest place, a cross between two criminals, and God exalted him; his body and blood made everything ready. He counted the cost before he set out for Jerusalem, and carried the cross behind which we carry ours. The King who could have marched against us sent his Son to make peace.

For us. Take the low seat and let God do the honouring; set your table for people who cannot pay you back; come to the feast today, as poor as you are. And count the cost honestly, not to prove you can afford it, but to surrender everything to the King who has already made peace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Human need is never out of season: Jesus does on the day of rest the work the day was made to celebrate, and exposes rules that bend for ourselves but not for the suffering. At a leading Pharisee’s Sabbath dinner he is watched closely, and a man with dropsy is set before him (vv. 1–2). He asks the lawyers the question they hoped to catch him on; they will not answer, and he heals the man and sends him away (vv. 3–4). Then he points to what any of them would do at once for a son or an ox in a well, and they cannot reply (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: The argument has the same shape as the one in the previous chapter (13:15), but it is sharper, and they are beaten by their own practice (this is treated fully at vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus heals before he argues (see the note on vv. 3–4).

The double standard being exposed is a common one: rules applied strictly to other people and generously to oneself and one’s own (see “Where is my real theology?” at vv. 5–6).

verseByVerse.quote: One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, they were watching him carefully. And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus accepts a seat at a table where he is watched as a suspect, and a suffering man has been put in his path.

At a Pharisee’s table. The third such invitation Luke records (7:36; 11:37); every one ends in confrontation, and he kept going. “A ruler of the Pharisees” is a leading Pharisee, and Sabbath meals, prepared the day before, were the week’s occasion for entertaining.

They were watching him carefully. The verb is used of watching with a purpose, as the plotters watched the gates day and night to kill Paul (Acts 9:24). It is surveillance (6:7): the guests’ real business is to collect evidence.

Dropsy. Swelling from fluid build-up (oedema), a sign of serious illness of the heart, liver or kidneys; the term (hydrōpikos) is a physician’s word found nowhere else in the Greek Bible, and only Luke records this healing. The sufferer is swollen with water yet desperately thirsty, and Greek moralists used the illness as an image of insatiable greed, craving the very thing that is killing him. The rest of the chapter is about people at a table who cannot stop wanting the best seat.

Was he planted there? He was “before him”, prominently placed, at a formal dinner in a private house, where a sick man would not normally be. Luke does not say how he got there, but he may well have been put there to test Jesus. If so, the only person in the room treated as a person that evening was the one the others were using.

No table too hostile. He came into a world that watched him carefully in order to kill him, and he kept coming, until the meal at which he gave himself as bread for the world. There is no table so hostile that his kindness cannot enter it.

Why did Jesus keep accepting invitations from people who opposed him? Because he came to seek and to save the lost, and the self-righteous are lost too (19:10). He ate with tax collectors and with Pharisees alike. That does not mean we must put ourselves under abuse or keep going where we are only mocked. But hostility is not, on its own, a reason to withdraw: those who watch you most critically may most need to see Christ in you up close.
verseByVerse.note: Dropsy is swelling of the body from fluid build-up, a sign of serious illness.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, 'Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?' But they remained silent. Then he took him and healed him and sent him away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus brings the hidden question into the open and answers it by healing the man. His mercy will not wait for his critics’ permission.

Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees. Nobody has said anything; he is answering their unspoken thoughts. They have set the trap; he asks the question himself, out loud, before touching anybody, in the technical language of their own debates, “is it lawful”, and puts it to the experts for a ruling. If they say yes, they cannot object; if no, they show themselves heartless.

They remained silent. They cannot say yes, because their position depends on saying no; they cannot say no, with a swollen man standing in the room. But silence is not neutral. It is a decision, taken in front of a suffering man.

Took, healed, sent away. He laid hold of a diseased body in front of men obsessed with ritual purity, healed him, and sent him away, a mercy of its own: the man need not stand there for the argument to come, and whatever he was brought for, he will not be used for it. Jesus asked the question no one wanted asked, and answered it with his hands.

When should I speak up rather than stay silent? When someone is being wronged or a plain truth of God denied, and you are in a position to say something, silence is not safe ground. You need not speak about everything, and wisdom chooses its moment (Proverbs 26:4–5). But ask honestly why you are quiet. If the answer is that speaking would cost you the approval of the room or your standing at work, that is the silence Jesus exposed here. Say the true and kind thing, briefly and without heat, and leave the outcome to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out?' And they could not reply to these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They would rescue a son or an ox at once on the Sabbath, so they have no ground for objecting to mercy shown to a man. The day of rest was made for exactly this kind of rescue.

Which of you … will not immediately pull him out? As in the previous chapter, the argument runs from what they already do to what they will not allow, but it is sharper. There the animal was merely thirsty (13:15); here something is drowning, and nobody stands at the wellhead consulting a ruling. Many Jews of the day would rescue a son or an animal on the Sabbath; only the strictest, such as the community at Qumran, forbade lifting a beast out of a pit on that day.

A son or an ox. A deliberately shocking pair. If you would break the Sabbath for your child, and for your livestock, why is a man with dropsy in a lower category than both? And there is a quiet irony: a man with dropsy was full of water; a man in a well is surrounded by it.

They could not reply. The second silence of the evening (v. 4), and this time it is inability rather than choice: he has simply described what every man in the room would do.

The day made for release. Israel kept the day remembering that the LORD had brought them out of slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). Jesus came announcing liberty to the captives (4:18), and a chapter earlier loosed a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound (13:16). The Lord of the Sabbath (6:5) is doing on the day of rest what the day was meant to celebrate.

He went down into the well. The Son of God did not merely reach down into the well; he went down into it, into the pit of our sin and death, drew us out and set our feet upon a rock (Psalm 40:2). He did it immediately, without waiting for us to deserve it.

Where is my real theology? Our real theology is in what we do without thinking, and a bad doctrine is quickly exposed by asking where its holder makes an exception for himself. Where are you strict with others and generous with yourself: about lateness, money, speech, forgiveness? Where your rules bend for you, you will find what you actually believe.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Many, following the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, to be kept for worship and for works of necessity and mercy (Westminster 21.8; 1689 22.8). Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, so that no day in itself binds the conscience (Colossians 2:16–17), while gladly gathering on the Lord’s Day. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Matthew 11:28), and the Lord’s Day is a gift, set apart gladly for worship, fellowship and rest, not a law about work; no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5), and the Westminster and 1689 view is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. On this passage both agree: works of mercy are always right on the day of rest, and human need is never an interruption to be ignored.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “a donkey” for “a son”, the more expected pair. “Son or ox” is the more surprising reading, the kind a copyist would smooth away rather than invent, and very probably what Luke wrote.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “a donkey” for “a son.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — Places of Honour; Inviting the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s table runs on grace, not on rank or repayment, so do not grasp for honour and do not give in order to get. Watching the guests choose the best couches, Jesus tells of a guest sent down in shame to the lowest place and another called up higher (vv. 7–10), and states the rule by which God runs his world: the self-exalting will be humbled and the humble exalted (v. 11). Then he turns to his host: invite the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind, who cannot repay you, and God will repay you at the resurrection of the just (vv. 12–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The reversal of honour runs through Luke (1:52; 14:11; 18:14), and the accounts are settled at the resurrection of the just, not in this life. Why the parable cannot be obeyed as a technique is treated at vv. 10–11. And the one who said this was on his way to the lowest place of all, the cross, from which God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:8–9).
verseByVerse.examples: The instruction to the host is not a ban on family meals (see the question at the end of the note on vv. 12–14). The host who invites only those who will invite him back has traded, not given. The host who invites those who cannot repay imitates the God who invites sinners with nothing to offer, and God himself will repay him at the resurrection (v. 14).

verseByVerse.quote: Now he told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honor, saying to them, 'When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him, and he who invited you both will come and say to you, ‘Give your place to this person,’ and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not seize the place of honour for yourself, because the one who seats the guests may move you down in front of everyone.

He noticed how they chose the places of honour. The Pharisees watched Jesus; Jesus watched them working out how important they were. Guests reclined on couches ranked by closeness to the host, so choosing your couch was announcing your estimate of yourself, in a culture where honour was gained and lost in front of witnesses.

A parable. It opens as etiquette, the sort of thing a wise uncle might say, and ends by revealing who runs the seating plan of the universe.

Give your place to this person. Important guests might well arrive late, so the scene would have made everyone wince. The man must get up in front of everybody, and by then the middle places are taken, so he walks the length of the room to the very bottom, and the shame lasts all evening. Proverbs had said it: “it is better to be told, ‘Come up here,’ than to be put lower in the presence of a noble” (Proverbs 25:6–7).

Someone more distinguished than you. There was such a guest at that table, and nobody offered him their couch: the one whom David called Lord (20:41–44). Luke does not even tell us where he reclined. He had every right to the top couch and was the only man in the room who did not need it, because his honour came from his Father and could not be added to or taken away by the seating plan (John 5:41–44).

Is it wrong to want to be recognised? The desire to be honoured is not itself evil: God made us for glory, and he promises honour to those who seek it by patient well-doing (Romans 2:7). What Jesus condemns is seizing it, ranking yourself above others. The question is whose honour you want. Live for the room’s estimate and you will always be anxious about the next guest through the door; live for God’s, and you can sit anywhere and let him do the honouring in his own time.
verseByVerse.note: Places at a banquet were ranked by closeness to the host.

parallels.desc: better to be told, “Come up here,” than to be put lower

verseByVerse.quote: But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at table with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
