Take the lowest place, because God humbles those who exalt themselves and exalts the humble. What sounds like social advice is the way God runs his world.

Go and sit in the lowest place. If the advice stopped here it would be shrewd manoeuvring: take the bottom seat as a tactic and enjoy being moved up. The next verse closes that trap.

Humbled and exalted. Jesus need not say who does the humbling and the exalting: it is God, whose way with the world Mary sang (1:52) and Jesus repeats (18:14).

Why humility is accuracy. So the parable cannot be obeyed as a technique, only by somebody who has stopped competing because he knows his standing. The man in the low seat is simply accurate: he is at the table by invitation, not by merit, and that is why he is free. A person who is not defending a position cannot be demoted from it.

“Friend, move up higher.” The one who said this lived it: he humbled himself to the cross and was highly exalted (Philippians 2:5–11). He was on his way to the lowest place there is, a cross between two criminals, and from there he answered as only the Host can: “today you will be with me in paradise” (23:43). He went to the bottom of the table so that every sinner could hear, “Friend, move up higher.”

In everyday life. Let someone else have the parking space, the last word, the credit for the idea, and do one piece of good this week that nobody will ever know was yours.

What it does not mean. Not false humility: taking the lowest place in order to be promoted is pride in disguise. True humility is not thinking less of yourself, but thinking of yourself less, and leaving your honour to God (1 Peter 5:5–6).

Does humility mean I should never accept a responsibility or say I can do something well? No. Refusing a task God plainly calls you to is not modesty but disobedience. Paul could say he worked harder than all the apostles, and add at once that it was the grace of God with him (1 Corinthians 15:10). Humility is honest about gifts, because it knows they are gifts (1 Corinthians 4:7); it serves without needing the credit and rejoices when others are honoured. You may sit at the head of the table if the host puts you there. Just do not put yourself there.

verseByVerse.quote: He said also to the man who had invited him, 'When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give to those who cannot pay you back, and God himself will repay you at the resurrection.

He said also to the man who had invited him. Jesus turns to the host at his own table, having eaten his food: one of the least comfortable moments in the Gospels.

Friends, brothers, relatives, rich neighbours. The whole ordinary guest list of any household. In that culture an invitation created a debt, repaid by a return invitation of matching quality: a transaction, not grace (6:32–34).

The poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind. People often excluded from religious gatherings (Qumran barred the lame and blind from its meals), and the opposite of the first four: they cannot invite anyone back. Not that they are more deserving: their inability to repay is the qualification. They are the very people God will bring to his banquet (v. 21).

The resurrection of the just. The raising of the righteous to life at the last day (Acts 24:15; John 5:29). The repayment is not cancelled but moved: God himself takes on the debt, a far surer promise than a rich neighbour’s return invitation.

The guest list of his own ministry. Luke’s reader has heard this list before: “the blind receive their sight, the lame walk … the poor have good news preached to them” (7:22). The host is told to set his table the way Jesus has set his ministry, for these are the people the Messiah was anointed to reach (4:18). The whole of salvation is a feast given to those who cannot repay, by a God who needs nothing from us and delights to give, and every table that welcomes them is a small copy of his.

In everyday life. God fed you when you could not repay. Whom could you invite who could never invite you back? Start with one name: the widower from church, the international student, the struggling family, the man nobody sits with.

So am I forbidden to have my family round for Christmas dinner? No. A dozen verses on, Jesus says that a disciple must hate his father and mother (v. 26), the Hebrew way of stating a comparison as if it were absolute. The same way of speaking is at work here: not “never invite your friends”, but “do not let your table be only that”. Jesus himself ate with friends, at Levi’s feast and in Martha’s house. The question is not whether the family may come on Sunday, but whether anyone else ever does.

Does giving in hope of a heavenly reward spoil it? No. Jesus himself sets the reward before us (Hebrews 11:6). What spoils giving is wanting the return from people: thanks, status, an invitation back. To look to God for your reward is to give freely to people, since you need nothing from them. And the reward is grace, not wages: God crowns in his children what his Spirit has worked in them, and its greatest part is the Giver himself.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture a meal created an obligation to invite in return.

parallels.desc: the Levite, sojourner, fatherless and widow shall eat

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — The Parable of the Great Banquet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The feast of the kingdom is ready now, and the only people missing from it will be those who had something better to do. A guest speaks warmly of eating bread in the kingdom one day (v. 15); Jesus answers with a banquet already prepared, whose invited guests send polite excuses about a field, oxen and a marriage (vv. 16–20). The angry master does not cancel the feast but fills it, first from the streets and lanes of the city with the poor and the broken, then from the highways and hedges, urging people in until his house is full (vv. 21–24).
verseByVerse.theology: The master’s anger does not cancel the feast; it redirects it (see the note on v. 21). The servant brings in the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame, the very guests Jesus had told the host to invite (v. 13), and then goes beyond the town to the highways and hedges (see the note on vv. 22–24). The original guests are shut out by their own choice.
verseByVerse.examples: “Still there is room”, and the words “compel people to come in” press on the church an urgency of love, not force (see the note on vv. 22–24, and the box “Where Christians differ: compel them to come in” at the end of it).

verseByVerse.quote: When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him, 'Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A guest speaks a true blessing about the kingdom to come, and with it steers the talk away from the table in front of him.

Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God! Entirely correct: the messianic banquet was Israel’s settled hope, the feast of rich food for all peoples when death is swallowed up for ever (Isaiah 25:6–8; 13:29). He assumes he will be there.

Why does Jesus answer a true remark with a warning? Listen again: it is a blessing about people in general and about the future, and it puts nobody on the spot. Jesus has just spoken about this table, tonight: stop grasping for seats, and fill your tables with people who cannot repay. What comes back is a warm sentiment about a banquet in the age to come, the religious equivalent of “what a wonderful idea in principle”. The man wants to talk about who will one day sit at the kingdom’s table; he is about to be told that the invitations have already gone out and the replies are coming in now.

The bread was already at the table. The guest spoke of eating bread in the kingdom as something far off, across the table from the one who would give that bread. On the night he was betrayed Jesus would take bread and say, “This is my body, which is given for you”, and promise that his disciples would eat and drink at his table in his kingdom (22:19, 30). The blessing the man admired from a distance was sitting opposite him.

In everyday life. Watch for the moments when you change the subject to something true and general because the specific was getting close: a sermon applied to someone else, a talk about the church’s needs that never reaches your diary.

parallels.desc: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to him, 'A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has prepared the feast of his kingdom, and the summons now goes out: everything is ready, come.

A great banquet. The host is God, preparing the feast of the kingdom. A formal banquet, it seems, involved two invitations: the first well in advance, so that the host knew the numbers before he killed the animals; the second on the day, when everything was ready. These guests said yes weeks ago, and the host has bought and slaughtered on the strength of it, as Israel had been invited long ago through the prophets, and had said yes.

He sent his servant. Sent on foot to men who outrank him, with words not his own. Many see in him Jesus himself, and after him those who preach the kingdom. He does not prepare the feast and cannot add to it; the message that it is ready is his whole commission.

Everything is now ready. Not “would you consider coming?” The work is done, the cost met, the table laid; only the guests are missing. That is the gospel in a sentence: it does not first ask us to do something but announces that something has been done, and asks only whether we will come and sit down.

What made everything ready. When Jesus told this parable the costliest part of the preparation was still ahead of him at Jerusalem: not animals killed for a dinner, but the Son himself given up. The one carrying the summons is the one whose body and blood would lay the table, and by Pentecost nothing remained to be done (Acts 2:38–39). The Father planned the feast before the foundation of the world, the Son paid for it with his own blood and cried “It is finished”, and the Spirit goes out still with the summons.

In everyday life. When you speak of Christ, remember what you carry: not a programme of self-improvement but news. You are a servant with a message, not a salesman with a pitch.

What does it mean for me to come? To come is to trust Christ: to stop relying on anything you bring and rely on what he has done. It is not first a matter of feelings or of cleaning yourself up; the guests at this feast are fed, not inspected. Turn from your sin, rest on Christ, and tell God in your own words that you have nothing, asking him to receive you for his Son’s sake. And having come, keep coming: to his word, his table and his people. The banquet is ready today, and the invitation is addressed to you.
verseByVerse.note: Guests were invited ahead of time and then summoned when the meal was ready.

verseByVerse.quote: But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused.’ And another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused.’ And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The invited guests turn the feast down politely, with good things as their excuse.

They all alike began to make excuses. With one accord, as though it had been arranged. These men had already accepted, and to refuse now was a grave insult. Three excuses are given as samples, and not one is disreputable.

A field. Possessions: nobody bought land unseen, and the field would still be there tomorrow.

Five yoke of oxen. Business: ten oxen mean a wealthy man, and you would test them before buying, not on the evening of a feast.

A wife. Family, and blunter: the first two say “please have me excused”; this one simply states it. He may be leaning on the law that excused a newly married man from war for a year (Deuteronomy 24:5), but a banquet is not a war, and that law protected a marriage; it did not excuse a man from a feast.

Not now. Possessions, work and family are all good things, and here they become excuses for refusing God’s invitation (8:14; 9:57–62). Nobody says “I do not want to come.” They express regret and stay at home, which is how the gospel is very often refused: not “I refuse Christ”, but “not now, there is something I have to deal with first”, said politely for forty years. It is not a postponement. It is the refusal. And behind each excuse sits a heart that has made a good thing into the thing it cannot do without: a gift allowed to take the Giver’s place.

The one who let nothing keep him away. Against these excuses stands the man telling the story, his face set for Jerusalem (9:51). Jesus had a mother, brothers, a trade and a home town, and none of them became his apology. He came to the feast his Father appointed, and it was the cross, where he made a place for the very people who had refused him. Every one of us once sent our apology to that table, and the Host sent the invitation again; every guest who will finally sit there is there because one man never sent an excuse.

But surely my family and work are things God gave me? They are, and that is what makes them dangerous as excuses. God gives fields, oxen and wives to be enjoyed with thanksgiving under him (1 Timothy 4:4). Coming to Christ does not take them away; it puts them in their place, and they are better there. The trouble begins when a gift is used to keep the Giver at arm’s length. If your reason for not coming to Christ, or not following him fully, is something good, you are where these men were. Bring the field and the oxen and the marriage with you to the feast; do not send them as your apology.
verseByVerse.note: The law excused a newly married man from war for a year, but not from a feast.

parallels.desc: a newly married man free at home one year

verseByVerse.quote: So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is rightly angry when his invitation is refused, but his anger fills the feast instead of cancelling it.

The master of the house became angry. Not the petulance of a man whose party has been spoiled: he had his guests’ word and spent accordingly, and what has been refused is a gift already paid for, refused unanimously and casually.

Streets and lanes. The anger redirects the banquet, quickly, because the food is ready: to the thoroughfares and back alleys where the outcasts lived, the tax collectors, sinners and poor whom the religious elite kept out.

Bring in the poor. Exactly the list of verse 13: God does what Jesus told the host to do, a quiet rebuke to a room that had just let the instruction pass. The people who cannot repay him are not a second-best arrangement; they were always the guest list he wanted.

Where Jesus had been eating. The men at that dinner knew where Jesus went when he was not at their tables: Levi’s great feast with a large company of tax collectors (5:29), and soon the grumble again, “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (15:2). The servant in the back streets pictures what they had watched him do all along: calling sinners to repentance (5:32). The King of glory fills his house with beggars and calls them his guests, and the joy of the feast is that every person there knows he had no right to be.

In everyday life. Who in your town, or on the edges of your congregation, is sure that church is not for them? You were brought in from the lanes yourself. Make your church a place where the poor and broken are not tolerated but wanted.

Is God really angry with people who decline his invitation? Yes, and it would be a lesser God who were not. His anger is no outburst but the settled response of holy love to generosity treated as an inconvenience, sobering for anyone treating the gospel as an offer with no deadline. Yet it does not cancel the feast; it sends the servant out again, to people nobody else wanted. God’s anger at refusal and his eagerness to fill his house stand together.

What if I feel too broken to belong at God’s table? Then you are exactly the guest this verse describes. The poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame were not brought in because they had recovered, but as they were. In this parable a sense of unworthiness is not a barrier; it is the mark of those who are carried in. Come as you are, and he will make you what he wants you to be.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servant said, ‘Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.’ And the master said to the servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is still room, so the invitation goes out beyond the town, urgently, until God’s house is full; only those who refused it will miss the feast.

Still there is room. The most hopeful sentence in the parable. Every street has been swept, and the hall is not full: God’s house was built larger than anyone expected.

Highways and hedges. Now he is sent outside the town, to the roads and the hedgerows where vagrants sheltered: people with no address, suggesting the Gentiles. This is the mission of Acts, to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8; 13:46).

Compel people to come in. “Compel” means urge strongly. A man summoned from a hedgerow to a nobleman’s banquet would assume a mistake, and need pressing before he believed the invitation was meant for him. The compulsion in view is a servant taking a beggar by the arm and saying: “no, truly, he means you.”

None of those men. Those who refused will be shut out (13:28), by their own choice. In the last line the “you” is plural, so it is not spoken to the one servant: Jesus steps out of the parable and speaks to the dinner party he is sitting at.

Grace ran out to the hedgerows. That outward sweep began with Christ: Simeon called the baby “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (2:30–32), and the risen Lord said that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations (24:47). “Still there is room”: no words are more welcome to a sinner. The Father’s house has many rooms, and the Son has gone to prepare them (John 14:2). His grace has run out to the hedgerows and found us there, and no refusal will stop it until the house is full (John 6:37–39).

In everyday life. Name to yourself the person you have assumed would never be interested, beyond the hedges of your usual circle, and tell them, kindly and plainly, that the invitation is for them.

How do I urge someone without being pushy? Urgency and respect belong together. Do not be embarrassed to ask someone to come, more than once if need be, or to tell them the invitation is truly for them, especially if they think they are too far gone. But never manipulate, bully, or use pressure that bypasses the conscience; God opens hearts, and we only persuade (Acts 16:14). Pray before you speak, listen as much as you talk, and let your life make the invitation believable. Love presses; it does not coerce.

Where Christians differ: compel them to come in. Augustine used this verse to justify the state forcing heretics (the Donatists) back into the church, and it was later used to defend forced conversions and persecution. This commentary’s view: this is a grievous misreading. The compulsion is the urgency of love and persuasion, not force; faith cannot be coerced. The gospel is to be pressed on people earnestly, but never by violence (2 Corinthians 5:11, 20). Everyone actually compelled in this parable thought himself too far outside to be wanted; the only people who stay out were invited politely and had other plans. Nobody is dragged to this table against their will.
verseByVerse.note: “Compel” means press them to come: the invitation is so generous it must be urged.

parallels.desc: we are turning to the Gentiles

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Coming to the free feast means giving Christ everything, so count the cost before you start. Jesus turns to the enthusiastic crowds and names it three times: he must be loved above family and life itself (vv. 25–26), followed with a cross (v. 27), and given all a person has (v. 33). Between these, a builder and a king sit down to calculate, the one so as not to be mocked for an unfinished tower, the other so as to ask for peace before an army twice his size arrives (vv. 28–32). Salt that has lost its taste is fit for nothing: let anyone with ears hear (vv. 34–35).
verseByVerse.theology:
These words are spoken to people already following and already enthusiastic (see “He is not recruiting” at vv. 28–30).

The king’s parable adds what the builder lacks: a way out (this is treated fully at vv. 31–32). And “renounce” means to let go (v. 33).
verseByVerse.examples:
Most of the time loving Christ makes a person a better son, husband and father (see “When does the conflict actually come?” at vv. 25–26). When the two claims cannot both be honoured, the cost is real, and the grief is no sign of having done wrong; but the command never licenses coldness. You go on loving your family, usually better than before, and simply stop letting their approval decide what you do with Christ.

The salt saying closes the chapter (see the note on vv. 34–35).

verseByVerse.quote: Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them, 'If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can follow Jesus who does not love him more than family, and more than life itself.

Great crowds accompanied him. He stops the procession to say one of the hardest things in the Gospel, which is not what a man does who is trying to keep a crowd: he wants disciples. On the road to Jerusalem (13:22), where many hoped the kingdom was about to appear (19:11), he tells them what following him will cost. The parable has shown that the feast is free; these verses show what it means to come in. The invitation costs the guest nothing, and coming to the Host costs him everything else, because the one who gives the feast asks to be loved above every gift he gives.

Does not hate. “Hate” here is a Hebrew idiom for loving less. Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and the very next verse says that Leah was hated (Genesis 29:30–31). Matthew gives the plainer form: “whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37).

Yes, and even his own life. The closest relationships are named one by one, so no one can think his case the exception, and last the hardest of all: a man’s own self.

He cannot be my disciple. Not “may not be a very good disciple”, but “cannot be”. No prophet ever said, “love me more than your mother.” Moses said, “love the LORD your God with all your heart” (Deuteronomy 6:5). Jesus puts himself where Moses put God: either he is God, or this is outrageous.

What a disciple is. Not the advanced class of keen Christians: a learner, an apprentice (mathētēs), and in Acts the ordinary name for every believer (Acts 11:26). A rabbi’s disciple lived with his teacher, walked behind him, and copied how he prayed, worked and treated people, until he became like him. In that sense everyone is somebody’s disciple, apprenticed to some voice (a parent, a profession, the people whose approval we cannot do without) that shapes us over the years into its image. Jesus asks to be the voice above every other.

Unlike the rabbis. A student usually chose his rabbi; Jesus says, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). Students outgrew their rabbis; his never graduate, “for you have one teacher” (Matthew 23:8). And this Teacher went to school first: “he learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8), all the way to a cross, for the very disciples who would run from it.

He gave up his first place. Only one who is God can ask for this, and only one who loves like God would deserve it. Christ asks for first place because he gave up his first place, and every one of our loves came from him: to put him first is to love them at their source.

In everyday life. Spend time with your Teacher in a Gospel each day, and before the next real decision ask not “What do I want?” but “What has my Teacher shown me?”

The idol in the family photograph. Of all the loves Jesus names, family is the one our culture finds hardest to criticise. Many who have let go of God have kept a religion of the home: my children are the meaning of my life, I would do anything for them. Much of it is beautiful, but a family asked to be God buckles under the weight. The child who is my reason for living cannot be allowed to fail, move far away or believe differently, and my love becomes a demand that he justify my existence. Jesus asks for first place not so that we will love our families less but so that they are set free from having to save us. A parent whose life is secure in Christ can let a child disappoint him, and a husband who is not looking to his wife for salvation can finally love her as she is. Only a Saviour who needs nothing from our families can teach us to love them without devouring them.

Is this not a convenient softening? Is the idiom a rescue operation for a hard saying? No; it is the only reading the rest of Scripture allows. The same Lord upheld the fifth commandment with unusual severity. When the scribes devised Corban, a way of declaring money dedicated to God so that it need not support aged parents, Jesus said they were making void the word of God by their tradition (Mark 7:9–13): precisely what a literal reading of this verse would license. He kept the commandment himself at the last possible moment, giving his mother into John’s care from the cross (John 19:26–27). And Paul says that anyone who does not provide for his household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8).

When does the conflict actually come? Most of the time there is no conflict: loving Christ makes a man a better son, husband and father. The verse speaks to the moment when both claims cannot be honoured: a convert whose family cuts him off; a wife whose husband demands that she stop going to church; a son told to join a dishonest business. Then Jesus must win, gently and without contempt, and with the door kept open. And where a family relationship involves abuse, putting Christ first never means submitting to it; it may mean seeking safety and help.
verseByVerse.note: “Hate” here is a Hebrew idiom for loving less. Matthew’s parallel says “loves father or mother more than me.”

parallels.desc: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah — “Leah was hated”

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To follow Jesus is to accept, for his sake, the rejection and shame of a condemned man, as a way of life.

Bear his own cross. He said it before, after Peter’s confession, adding “daily” (9:23). Here the verb is “bear”, the sustained business of walking under a load, and it is “his own” cross: each carries the one with his name on it.

What the image meant. To that crowd it was no worn metaphor but a man already sentenced, carrying the beam of his own execution through jeering streets: finality, since nobody carrying a crossbeam is coming back; shame, since crucifixion was designed to degrade; and submission, since he has stopped fighting. To bear your cross is to accept rejection, shame and death for Jesus’ sake.

And come after me. The cross is carried behind someone: the disciple walks where Jesus has walked. This is the second “cannot be my disciple” (v. 26): there is no discipleship without a cross.

Behind Jesus. Luke shows the verse acted out: Simon of Cyrene, with the cross laid on him, to carry it behind Jesus (23:26). But that day Jesus went in front to his own death, on the very beam Simon carried. Every disciple’s cross is carried behind the one cross that saves: ours is borne in his company; his was borne for us. And every one is carried behind a risen Lord who has walked the road to the end and out the other side.

In everyday life. Name the place where following Jesus costs you something this week, and, in the strength he gives, do not quietly lay that cross down.

Is my cross the illness or difficulty I have? Not exactly. Every Christian suffers the ordinary troubles of a fallen world, and God uses them; but the cross Jesus means is what comes to you because you follow him: the career move declined because it meant dishonesty, the friendships lost because you would not join in, the mockery at work, the sin you go on refusing year after year, the persecution that in many lands means prison or death. A cross is chosen in the sense that you could put it down by abandoning Christ. Bearing it means you will not.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution.

verseByVerse.quote: For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before you follow Jesus, reckon honestly what it will cost, so that you do not start with enthusiasm and give up halfway.

Desiring to build a tower. A tower might guard a vineyard (Isaiah 5:2) or be a farm building, an ordinary landowner’s project. “Sit down”: stop and do the arithmetic before the first stone is laid.

Not able to finish. The failure is public and permanent, an abandoned foundation visible from the road, like the hearers who receive the word with joy and fall away in the time of testing (8:13).

He is not recruiting. With a great crowd attached, he tells them to stop and calculate whether they can afford it: the opposite of every technique for gathering a following, and a rebuke to any appeal that hides the cost until the decision is made.

The builder who finished. The one telling this parable had counted his own cost: “the third day I finish my course” (13:32), his face set to Jerusalem knowing what was there (18:31–33). At the cross the mockers thought they were looking at an abandoned foundation: “He saved others; let him save himself” (23:35). They were watching the last stone go in, and three days later our redemption stood complete. No disciple’s tower is safe because the disciple is a good builder, but because the Lord who lays the foundation of his people never began anything he could not finish.

In everyday life. When you speak of Christ, tell the cost honestly as well as the joy. And if you have stalled halfway, with a foundation laid years ago and little built since, come back to him today. He finishes what he starts.

If I must count the cost, how can anyone afford it? No one can pay it in his own strength, and that is part of what the counting reveals, as the next parable shows. The cost is real, but the one who calls also supplies. “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6), and those who build on him are kept by his power, not their own (1 Peter 1:5). The counting is not meant to deter anybody, but to make the commitment real, so that what begins gets finished, and the tower is a witness rather than a joke.
verseByVerse.note: A tower might guard a vineyard or a farm.

verseByVerse.quote: Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A king facing an army twice his size must reckon whether he can win, and if he cannot, ask for peace while there is still time.

Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war …? A second parable, and a greater matter: from a half-built shed to an army, from money to survival. “Sit down first” again, and do the sum: ten thousand against twenty thousand, not hopeless, but the kind of arithmetic that makes an honest man face a hard conclusion.

He sends a delegation. Here the parables part. The builder can only finish or be mocked; the king has a third option: “while the other is yet a great way off”, he sends envoys and asks for terms.

Two readings, both true. First, as with the tower: count the cost. Second, God is the king coming against you with superior force: make peace with him now, while he is far off, by surrendering everything (12:58).

Who is the greater king? In a chapter about the cost of following Jesus, the man facing a force twice his size is not being invited to conclude that he can manage it with effort. He cannot; nobody can. What is left is the delegation, while there is still distance between you, and that is not defeat but the only wise move on the board. The disaster is the man who marches out because he never sat down and did the sum. That is what counting the cost is for: not to establish that you can afford discipleship, but to bring you to the point of sending the delegation.

What are the terms of peace? Astonishingly generous. The King who could have crushed us demands no reparations; he sent his own Son and has made the peace himself. “In Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them”, and he has sent ambassadors to plead: “be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:19–20). The terms are unconditional surrender to his Son and trust in what his Son has done. We give up our arms; he gives us his friendship. To a proud heart that sounds like humiliation, but no more than a drowning man letting go of the wreckage to take the rope. Being justified by faith, “we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). To be justified means to be declared righteous by God the Judge: not made sinless overnight, but counted right with him because Christ’s obedience and death are credited to us (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). There is no stronger King, and none more willing to receive those who lay down their arms.

In everyday life. Where are you still at war with God: a command you resent, a providence you will not accept? Send the delegation today; tell him you give it up, and ask for his peace.

verseByVerse.quote: So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can be Christ’s disciple who keeps anything back from him.

So therefore. This is the cost both parables told us to count, and the third “cannot be my disciple” (vv. 26, 27, 33): Christ comes above family, above self, and above possessions.

Renounce. The verb (apotassetai) meant to say goodbye, as of the man who wanted to say farewell at home (9:61): a man releasing his hold on what he is leaving. It does not necessarily mean literally selling everything; it means giving up ownership of everything to Christ.

All that he has. Not only property but reputation, plans, rights and the future a man has drawn up. What you are most certain God would never ask of you is what this verse is about.

The one who let go first. Jesus asks for nothing he did not give up himself: he had nowhere to lay his head (9:58), and at the end even his clothes were divided by lot (23:34). He renounced all that he had, not to buy a disciple’s freedom from possessions but to buy the disciple. What we renounce is nothing beside what we receive, for he is the treasure for which a wise man sells everything with joy.

The freedom of letting go. There is mercy in the severity: a man who has let go of everything cannot be robbed or blackmailed, or moved from the low seat, because he has nothing to defend.

In everyday life. Name in prayer what you have not yet surrendered: savings, retirement plans, your children’s futures, your reputation, your time, and live this week as its steward. You will not let go perfectly, but the one who renounced all for you did, and for his sake your faltering surrender is accepted.

Must I sell everything I own? No; Luke will not allow that reading. Zacchaeus gives half and is told salvation has come to his house (19:8–9). The women of 8:3 funded the ministry out of means they must still have had. Peter’s rebuke to Ananias turns on the fact that the property was his to keep (Acts 5:4). Some are called to give up a great deal literally; all are called to stop holding, keeping everything open-handed, as stewards and not owners, ready to give whatever he asks. The test is not what percentage you give but whether anything you have is off limits to him.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A disciple who will not pay the cost is like salt that has lost its taste: still called salt, and good for nothing.

Salt is good. Salt kept meat and seasoned food, and was even put to use on the land.

If salt has lost its taste. Not salt that has disappeared, but salt still in the jar, still the right colour, still called salt, which has stopped working (on how this could happen, see the box below).

Not even for the manure pile. Luke’s detail is the sharpest of the three Gospels: even the dunghill will not take it.

It is thrown away. So with the half-committed disciple: not wicked, simply useless for the one thing that was the point of him, keeping the appearance and losing the function. Discipleship that is not costly is not discipleship, and a church that has lost its distinctiveness is useless to the world.

He who has ears to hear, let him hear. The same words followed the parable of the soils (8:8): hearing that takes the word in and acts on it. They hand the chapter back to the reader. A cost has been counted or not; a table serves people who can repay or people who cannot; a seat has been grasped or given up. What is left is the hearing.

Peter was not thrown out. The Lord who warned about salt thrown away said to Peter on the night of his denial, “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (22:32). Peter wept bitterly, and was turned again and sent to strengthen his brothers. Christ keeps his own by his intercession, and the savour he gives he does not let go.

I feel I have lost my saltiness. Is there hope? Yes. That you feel it and care is a sign that the Spirit is still at work in you; salt that has truly lost its savour does not grieve over it. Return to Christ, confess where you have grown cold or compromised, and ask him to restore the joy of your salvation (Psalm 51:12). Saltiness is not manufactured by trying harder to be different; it comes from closeness to Christ, and returns as you return to him: to his word, to prayer, to his people, and to the cost you had begun to avoid.

Where Christians differ: can a true Christian lose his saltiness and be thrown away? Arminian Christians, who hold that a true believer can finally fall away, read the verse that way and press its warning with real seriousness. This commentary’s view: Jesus is warning those who follow at a distance without counting the cost. A disciple in name who will not carry his cross shows that he never truly had the salt (1 John 2:19; John 15:6). Those whom Christ has truly made his own he keeps to the end (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6). The warning is real, and it is one of the very means by which Christ keeps his true disciples faithful: they hear it, and they hold on to him.

Uncertain wording. “Has lost its taste” translates a verb that elsewhere means “to become foolish” (mōrainō), and how salt could lose its saltiness is not certain, since pure salt does not. The usual explanation is that much salt in Palestine, gathered by the Dead Sea, was mixed with gypsum and other minerals, so that damp could leach out the true salt and leave a tasteless white powder, thrown onto paths. Others suggest salt blocks used in ovens, or that Jesus deliberately describes something impossible. It is also uncertain how salt served “for the soil or for the manure pile”, whether as fertiliser in small amounts or to slow the rotting of dung. Whichever picture lies behind it, the meaning is clear: salt that no longer does what salt is for is worthless.
verseByVerse.note: Impure salt could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

14.text: <sup>1</sup> One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, they were watching him carefully. <sup>2</sup> And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy. <sup>3</sup> And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?” <sup>4</sup> But they remained silent. Then he took him and healed him and sent him away. <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out?” <sup>6</sup> And they could not reply to these things. <sup>7</sup> Now he told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honor, saying to them, <sup>8</sup> “When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him, <sup>9</sup> and he who invited you both will come and say to you, ‘Give your place to this person,’ and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place. <sup>10</sup> But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at table with you. <sup>11</sup> For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” <sup>12</sup> He said also to the man who had invited him, “When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. <sup>13</sup> But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, <sup>14</sup> and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.” <sup>15</sup> When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him, “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” <sup>16</sup> But he said to him, “A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. <sup>17</sup> And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’ <sup>18</sup> But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused.’ <sup>19</sup> And another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused.’ <sup>20</sup> And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’ <sup>21</sup> So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.’ <sup>22</sup> And the servant said, ‘Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.’ <sup>23</sup> And the master said to the servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. <sup>24</sup> For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.’” <sup>25</sup> Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them, <sup>26</sup> “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. <sup>27</sup> Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. <sup>28</sup> For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? <sup>29</sup> Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, <sup>30</sup> saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’ <sup>31</sup> Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? <sup>32</sup> And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. <sup>33</sup> So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple. <sup>34</sup> “Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? <sup>35</sup> It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

keyVerse.quote: And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’
keyVerse.note: This is the gospel in one sentence and the hinge of the chapter: the feast is not earned by the guests but prepared by the Host, and the only question left is whether they will come. Around it the chapter explains who comes (the poor who cannot repay, vv. 13, 21), who stays away (those with better things to do, vv. 18–20), and what coming means (a Host loved above everything, vv. 25–33). What made everything ready was still ahead of Jesus at Jerusalem: his own body, given for us.

14.reflection:
The guests at the Pharisee’s table watched Jesus, competed for seats and invited those who could invite them back (vv. 1–14). Where do you see the same instincts in your own heart, at work, at church or at home? What does Jesus’ teaching on honour set you free from?

Jesus tells his host to invite those who cannot repay (vv. 12–14), and the master in the parable fills his house with exactly those people (v. 21). Whom could you, or your church, welcome who could never return the favour? What keeps us from doing it?

Every excuse in vv. 18–20 is about something good. Which good things most often become reasons for putting Christ off, or for following him only half way? How does “everything is now ready” (v. 17), and what it cost to make it ready, answer them?

Jesus tells keen crowds to sit down and count the cost (vv. 25–33). How should that shape the way we speak of Christ to others? And how does the king who sends a delegation (vv. 31–32) turn counting the cost into good news rather than a burden?

15.title: Lost and Found: The Three Parables of Grace
15.overview:
Where we are. Jesus is on the long road to Jerusalem (9:51), and he has just told of a banquet thrown open to “the poor and crippled and blind and lame” (14:21). Chapter 15 shows such guests arriving: tax collectors and sinners crowding in to hear him, while the religious men who should have been first at the feast stand back and complain.

The message. God goes looking for the lost, and when one is found he rejoices. Jesus does not deny the charge that he “receives sinners and eats with them” (v. 2); he explains it. He welcomes sinners because this is what God is like: the shepherd who searches until he finds, the woman who sweeps until she hears the coin, the father who runs down the road. And the chapter leaves its hearers with a question: will they share his joy, or stand outside it?

Why it was said. The Pharisees and scribes believed that holiness meant keeping your distance from people like these, and that a teacher who ate with them must be lax himself (on the Pharisees and tax collectors, see the introduction). Jesus answers their grumbling not with a rebuke but with stories built to win their agreement and then turn it on them.

How the chapter makes its case. Luke calls the three stories one parable (v. 3). A shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to search for one, carries it home and calls in the neighbours (vv. 3–7). A woman lights a lamp and sweeps her dark house for one coin, and does the same (vv. 8–10). Each time Jesus draws the lesson: there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. The stories narrow, one in a hundred, one in ten, one in two, and they deepen: a sheep wanders, a coin simply lies where it fell, a son leaves on purpose. The younger son demands his inheritance, wastes it, and comes home to a father who runs to him, embraces him before he can confess, and restores him with robe, ring, sandals and feast (vv. 11–24). The elder son, who never left, refuses to go in, and his father comes out and pleads with him (vv. 25–32). He stands for the grumblers of verse 2, and Jesus never says whether he went in.

Where it leads. The one telling these stories is the seeker in them. He “came to seek and to save the lost” (19:10), and he was walking to Jerusalem, where the cost of the father’s welcome would be met. The only Son who could truly say “I never disobeyed your command” did not resent the feast for sinners. He died to provide it.

For us. The chapter finds every reader somewhere: in the far country, on the road home with a speech prepared, or out in the yard, resentful of grace given to others. Wherever you are, the Father is coming out to meet you. Come home, and come in to the feast.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Parable of the Lost Sheep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus welcomes sinners because God goes after the lost and rejoices when he finds them. Two verses set the scene for the whole chapter: sinners keep coming to hear Jesus, and the religious leaders grumble that he eats with them (vv. 1–2). His answer is three stories that Luke calls one parable (v. 3), each about something lost and each ending in a party. The first puts his critics inside the story: any of them would search for a lost sheep until he found it and carry it home rejoicing (vv. 3–5). Heaven rejoices in just that way over one sinner who repents, so why object when Jesus does (vv. 6–7)?
verseByVerse.theology:
The shepherd seeks the sheep; the sheep does not seek the shepherd (see the note on vv. 3–5). That is the pattern of grace: “no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44).

The phrase “ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance” can be read two ways, and serious readers hold both. It may simply mean those already safe in the fold, or, read against the chapter’s ending, it may be ironic (see the note on vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.examples:
The ninety-nine are safe in the shepherd’s care while he searches, and a church that begrudges the energy spent on the lost has forgotten that it was once the one (see “What about the ninety-nine?” at vv. 3–5).

The men it was told to were sure they were among the ninety-nine, and the parable was built so that they would agree with every word of it right up to the moment they saw it was about them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, 'This man receives sinners and eats with them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sinners kept coming to Jesus and he welcomed them to his table, and the religious leaders grumbled that no holy man would do such a thing. Without meaning to, they put the gospel into words.

All drawing near. The form of the verb suggests they kept coming: a settled pattern, not one occasion. Tax collectors were Jews who collected Rome’s revenue, regarded as traitors as well as extortioners. “Sinners” is broader: the openly immoral, but also, to the scrupulous, anybody who did not keep the purity code. And they came to hear him, not for bread or healing: something in him made sinners feel welcome.

Grumbled. Muttered among themselves (diegongyzon): the word the Greek Old Testament uses of Israel grumbling in the wilderness about the water and the bread (Exodus 15:24; 16:7–8). They do not argue with him. It is the muttering of people who have decided not to listen.

Receives sinners and eats with them. Meant as an accusation, and completely accurate. Receives (prosdechetai) means welcomes, and to eat with a man was to accept him and tie your reputation to his. The offence was not that he preached to sinners but that he sat down with them. Their complaint is the gospel, and the most wonderful thing about him: Jesus receives sinners.

The holy one at the sinners’ table. The scandal only makes sense if Jesus is who Luke says he is. A lax teacher eating with sinners would have surprised nobody. This is the one whom even the demons named “the Holy One of God” (4:34), whose touch made a leper clean instead of making himself unclean (5:13). The Pharisees thought a holy man must be protected from sinners. Jesus is the holiness from which sinners need no protection, because it heals what it touches. He did not keep his distance from us; he came and sat at our table, and then spread his own table and invited us to it.

Does receiving sinners mean Jesus approves of sin? No. He receives sinners in order to save them, and the word that runs through the chapter is repentance (vv. 7, 10). The doctor sits with the sick because he means to heal them (5:31–32). Jesus never told a sinner that what he had done did not matter; he forgave sins and called sinners to follow him, as he did Levi (5:27–28). His welcome is not approval of the old life but the open door out of it. That is the pattern for his church: a table open to any sinner, and a gospel that calls every sinner home.

So should Christians spend time with people whose lives are a mess? Yes, gladly, as Jesus did, with the aim of drawing them to him: real friendship, meals and patience, not a project kept at arm’s length. It also takes wisdom. You go as one who belongs to Christ, not to join in the sin, and if a friendship is pulling you away from him rather than drawing them towards him, something needs to change (1 Corinthians 15:33). But the danger in most churches is not that we are too close to sinners. It is that we are as far from them as the Pharisees were.
verseByVerse.note: Eating together signalled acceptance; that was the offence.

verseByVerse.quote: So he told them this parable: 'What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Any shepherd would search for one lost sheep until he found it and carry it home gladly, and that is how God seeks the lost. Jesus wins his critics’ agreement before they see that the story describes what they are objecting to.

What man of you. The question puts his critics inside the story and compels agreement: any shepherd would do this. That is the trap: their own instinct, applied to the welcome they object to. Shepherding was humble, dirty work, which later rabbinic writings list among the suspect trades, yet Jesus asks these respectable men to imagine being shepherds, and God himself is the shepherd of Israel (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34).

Leave the ninety-nine in the open country. One per cent, hardly worth worrying about, you might think. But a sheep that has strayed rarely finds its own way back. The ninety-nine are in pasture, presumably with other shepherds, so this is not the recklessness it sounds.

Go after the one that is lost, until he finds it. “Until he finds it” sets the only limit on the search: not until dark, not until it seems hopeless. This is the love God promised through Ezekiel, when he said he himself would search for his sheep (Ezekiel 34:11, 16), and the mission Jesus will name at Zacchaeus’ door: “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (19:10).

He lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. A frightened, exhausted sheep, it is often said, will lie down and refuse to move, so the shepherd hoists it across his neck and carries it home over the same country he searched. No scolding, no punishment: the whole weight of the animal that caused the trouble is on his shoulders, and he is glad all the way home. Isaiah had seen it: “he will gather the lambs in his arms” (Isaiah 40:11). And the shoulders that carried us home are the shoulders that carried a cross.

In everyday life. Somewhere near you is a sheep who has wandered: a friend who has stopped coming to church, a child who has turned away. Go after them, in prayer first and then in person, gently, without scolding. A phone call, a meal, a note: the shepherd’s work is often as plain as that.

If the shepherd does all the work, what do I do? You are found. The sheep does nothing except get lost and be carried, and that is a true picture of salvation: God seeks us before we seek him, and “we love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Our repentance and faith are real, and we must turn to him, but that is the sheep’s response to the shepherd’s arms, not its own way home. If you are still lost, know that he is the one who goes looking. Cry out to him, and you will find you have been sought.

What about the ninety-nine? Does God care less about faithful believers? No. They are not abandoned but left safe in the pasture. The parable does not rank the sheep; it shows how much one lost sheep matters to a shepherd who loves them all. If you have been in the fold for years and feel overlooked, remember that you were once the one he went after. The shepherd who carried you home has not put you down.

parallels.desc: I myself will search for my sheep
he will carry them in his bosom

verseByVerse.quote: And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.’ Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finding the lost ends in a party, and heaven rejoices like that over every sinner who repents.

Calls together his friends. Joy must be shared, so he throws a party over one sheep in a hundred, perhaps at a cost greater than the sheep was worth. Celebration is what finding produces.

Over one sinner who repents. The word “repents” appears here for the first time in the chapter, in Jesus’ explanation, not in the story. In the story the sheep is found; in reality the sinner repents. They are the same event seen from two sides.

The party at Jesus’ table. So the meals the Pharisees complained about are this party. When Jesus sat down with tax collectors he was doing on earth what heaven was doing over the same people, and the grumblers stood at the edge of heaven’s celebration calling it a scandal.

Does God really feel joy? Yes. The LORD your God “will rejoice over you with gladness … he will exult over you with loud singing” (Zephaniah 3:17). His joy is not needy or fluctuating like ours; he is eternally blessed in himself. But he truly delights in mercy (Micah 7:18). If you have come to Christ, you were the cause of God’s rejoicing. That is not sentiment but what Jesus said.

Where Christians differ: the ninety-nine. Some take the “ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance” simply as those already safe in the fold. Others take it as irony aimed at the grumblers. This commentary’s view: it is irony. There are no righteous people who need no repentance (Romans 3:10, 23), but that is exactly how the grumblers saw themselves (18:9), and by the end of the chapter Jesus will paint one of them as an older brother refusing to come in. Nobody who believes he needs no repentance has yet given heaven anything to celebrate. The first reading is still true in itself: the found are safe, and the shepherd still loves them (see “What about the ninety-nine?” at vv. 3–5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — The Parable of the Lost Coin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lost cannot find themselves, so God searches until they are found, and every finding fills his presence with joy. The second story moves indoors: God, just pictured as a shepherd, is now a woman with a lamp and a broom in a dark house, hunting for a coin that can do nothing at all to be found (vv. 8–9). Jesus’ lesson repeats the first with one change of tense: the joy is not only coming but happening now, before the angels of God, every time one sinner repents (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The angels are “ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14). They are not detached from the gospel. The finding of one lost sinner is gladness in the presence where they stand, and they know what was lost.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman’s method is a pattern for prayer and pastoral work that will not give up. She lights the lamp, she sweeps away what covers the coin, and she keeps at it. The sweeping is the least glamorous part, and it is the part that finds the coin.

The coin’s helplessness is a comfort. Anyone who has watched someone they love become unable to help themselves, through addiction, illness of the mind or a hardness they cannot break, is looking at the coin. It cannot call out or move towards the light, and that changes nothing about the search.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman searches her dark house for one lost coin until she finds it, and calls her neighbours to rejoice: God seeks the lost as carefully as that. And the coin, unlike the sheep, can do nothing at all to be found.

What woman. The second parable moves indoors, and the seeker is a woman. Luke often sets a story about a man beside one about a woman, as with the mustard seed and the leaven (13:18–21). God, just pictured as a shepherd, is now a woman searching her house on her hands and knees.

Ten silver coins. Each was a drachma, roughly a day’s wage. The ten may have been her savings, or coins worn as her security and the sign of her marriage. Either way, losing one was a real loss for a poor woman.

Light a lamp and sweep the house. A poor house had few or no windows and a beaten earth floor, so even at midday the corners were dark: hence the lamp. She sweeps and listens for the clink, because in that gloom you might well hear a coin before you saw it, and she keeps on “until she finds it”: the shepherd’s refusal to stop, and then the shepherd’s party.

The difference. A sheep wanders by its own folly; a son will walk away deliberately; a coin cannot do anything at all. It lies where it fell, in the dark, and is simply lost, and then simply found, and everything in between was done by somebody with a lamp.

Salvation has come to this house. The grumblers did not have to imagine a searcher going through a house. A few chapters on, Jesus will stop under a tree in Jericho, call a chief tax collector by name and say, “I must stay at your house today” (19:5), and the crowd will grumble with the very verb of this chapter (19:7). The seeking in these parables is what Jesus was doing, house by house, in the towns where they lived.

In everyday life. If you feel as helpless as a coin under the furniture, unable to do anything to get yourself found, take heart: that is precisely the kind of lost thing this woman went looking for.

Is it right to picture God as a woman? The parable pictures God’s searching love through a woman’s action, as Scripture elsewhere compares his care to a mother’s (Isaiah 49:15; 66:13), and Jesus has just compared himself to a hen (13:34). These images of what God does are precious. But Scripture never addresses God as mother or calls him “she”. He reveals himself as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and we name him as he has named himself, rejoicing in every likeness Scripture gives and still praying, as Jesus taught us, “Our Father”.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that each coin was a drachma, roughly equal to a denarius, about a day’s wage. Houses were dark, with small windows and earthen floors.

verseByVerse.quote: Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every time one sinner repents, God himself rejoices, and the angels see it. The joy is not only coming at the end; it is happening now.

Joy before the angels. Jesus draws the same lesson as from the sheep, with two changes. The time: over the sheep “there will be” joy; here “there is” joy, now, every time. And the place: “before the angels of God”, the joy of God himself, with the angels looking on.

Whose joy are they watching? The wording does not say, but the parables have told us: the shepherd rejoiced, the woman rejoiced, and a father is about to run down a road and kill the best animal on the farm. Every seeker in this chapter is God, and every one is delighted. Somewhere a man nobody has heard of, at the end of a life he is ashamed of, turns round, and God is so pleased that the angels stop and watch.

Over one sinner who repents. The arithmetic never changes: one sheep in a hundred, one coin in ten, one sinner of no importance to anybody. The God before whom the seraphim cover their faces bends down to delight in one sinner turning home. That is a long way from the God the grumblers were defending, and from the God many people privately imagine: correct, grudging and disappointed. There is no reluctant pardon anywhere in the chapter, no probation in which the found thing has to prove itself. There is a search, and then there is a party.

Do the angels know when someone is saved? The verse says there is joy in their presence, and Scripture shows angels longing to look into the gospel (1 Peter 1:12) and serving those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), so it is natural to think they share heaven’s gladness. But we should not speculate beyond what is written. The point is the God before whom they stand: the joy that fills heaven at a sinner’s repentance is first and most of all his.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–32 — The Parable of the Prodigal Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God welcomes home sinners who have wasted everything, and pleads with the self-righteous to share his joy. The story is about a father and two sons. The younger demands his share, wastes it in a far country and ends among the pigs (vv. 11–16), until he comes to himself and heads home with a speech prepared (vv. 17–19). The father runs to him, embraces him before he can confess, and restores him with robe, ring, sandals and a feast (vv. 20–24). The second half belongs to the elder son, who never left, refuses to go in, and hears his father plead with him in the yard (vv. 25–32). The ending is left open for the grumblers to finish.
verseByVerse.theology:
The father’s running and the feast both protect the son (see the notes on v. 20 and vv. 23–24).

Some have argued that because the parable has no sacrifice, no blood and no mediator, the doctrine of atonement was a later invention. But the father does not forgive at no cost (see “Who paid for the calf?” and the box “Where Christians differ: forgiveness without a cross?” in the note on vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.examples:
The boy came home because he was hungry, and the father does not interrogate the motive (see the question at the end of the note on vv. 17–19). Luke shows the same thing elsewhere: the tax collector who could not lift his eyes went home justified (18:13–14), and the criminal on the cross came with a few hours left and nothing else to try (23:42–43).

The elder brother is the parable’s real target (see the notes on vv. 29–30 and on the open ending at vv. 31–32).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, 'There was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’ And he divided his property between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A son asks for his inheritance while his father is still alive, wanting his father’s goods without his father, and the father lets him have it. Here is the root of all sin: taking God’s gifts and wanting to live without him.

There was a man who had two sons. Only Luke records this parable. It is announced as being about two sons, though usually preached as though it were about one. The younger stands for the tax collectors and sinners (v. 1), the older for the Pharisees and scribes (v. 2), and the father for God. The new thing is a son who never left and is still lost: through him the parable speaks to the grumblers, not only about them, and leaves them an open ending (see “The open ending” at vv. 31–32).

Give me the share. The shock of that sentence is the doorway into the parable. A father normally divided his property at death, and the younger son would receive one-third, since the elder received a double portion (Deuteronomy 21:17; see inheritance and the firstborn). A father could distribute property early, but it was not the son’s place to ask. To ask now was, as many have put it, like saying: “I wish you were dead; I want your things, not you.” And the words are careful: “the share of property that is coming to me”. He asks not for a gift but for what he considers already owed.

He divided his property between them. Astonishingly, the father agrees, without a recorded word or condition. He does not force his son to stay. And note “between them”: the elder son receives his share too, which will matter when he complains that he has never been given anything. This is what every sinner does to God: takes his gifts, life, health and abilities, and wants to live without him. Sin does break God’s rules (1 John 3:4), but underneath the broken rule lies a broken relationship: a Father turned away from, his gifts kept and his company refused.

The Son who tells of the Father. It matters who is telling this story. Jesus had said that no one knows who the Father is except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (10:22). Here the Son draws the portrait to explain his own behaviour: he receives sinners because this is what the Father is like. Watch Jesus at a table with tax collectors and you are watching the father of the parable at the gate.

In everyday life. Look at the good things in your hands today, your health, your money, your time, your mind, and ask whether you are using them with God or without him. The request of verse 12 is rarely made out loud. It is made in the way we spend a Saturday.

Why does God let people walk away from him? The father does not hold his son by force, and God does not drag sinners into his house against their will. He lets people have what they insist on, and sometimes that is the most terrible judgment there is (Romans 1:24). But the letting go is not indifference: the father’s eyes are on the road from the day the boy leaves. God’s patience gives a sinner room to discover what the far country is really like, and his providence, as the next verses show, is at work even there. If someone you love has walked away, the parable does not tell you to stop loving or praying. It tells you to keep watching the road.
verseByVerse.note: A father normally divided his property at death. The younger son would receive a third, because the elder son had a double share.

parallels.desc: a double portion to the firstborn

verseByVerse.quote: Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The son turns everything into cash, goes as far from his father as he can, and wastes it all. Freedom from his father became slavery to his appetites.

Gathered all he had. He did not even wait. Turning his share into cash probably meant selling family land, itself a shameful thing, for land in Israel was the family’s portion in the inheritance of God’s people, held in trust across generations (Leviticus 25:23–28). The whole district would soon have known what the boy thought of his father.

A far country. Probably Gentile land, as the pigs suggest, far from his father, his people and his God. Distance was the point: nobody there had heard of his father, and nobody would report on him.

Squandered in reckless living. Squandered means scattered (dieskorpisen), like seed thrown to the wind. Reckless (asōtōs) describes a wasteful life with no brake on it, not one particular vice. His brother will say “with prostitutes” (v. 30); the story never confirms it.

Two sons, two prayers. Luke sets another Son beside this one. The younger son’s first words are “give me” (v. 12): the Father’s goods, without the Father. The Son who tells the story will kneel on the Mount of Olives and pray, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (22:42), and his last words on the cross will be, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit” (23:46). One son took his share and spent it on himself. The other gave up everything that was his and spent himself on his Father’s will, so that sons like the first could come home.

What is my far country? It may not involve travel at all. It is anywhere you go to be out of your Father’s sight, or so you think: the screen at midnight, the second life at a conference, the hidden spending, the resentment nursed in private. It always begins with wanting the gifts without the Giver, and it always promises freedom. Name it honestly before God. The first step home is admitting where you are.
verseByVerse.note: A far country is Gentile land.

parallels.desc: a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Famine strikes, and the son sinks so low that he feeds a Gentile’s pigs and envies them their food. The far country that welcomed his money gives him nothing once it is gone.

A severe famine. He chose the far country and the spending; he did not choose the famine. Sin puts a man where events he cannot control can destroy him, and they do not ask his permission.

He hired himself out. The verb means he attached himself, clung. This is a starving man fastening himself to a Gentile who does not want him, and the employer’s response reads as a way of getting rid of him.

To feed pigs. Pigs were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:7), and a rabbinic saying curses the man who raises them. A Jew feeding pigs for a Gentile had fallen as low as a person could go: cut off from his people, his worship and his God.

Longing to be fed with the pods. Probably carob pods, fed to animals and eaten by the very poorest in hard times. He cannot get even those: he is not eating them; he is longing to. He left home with a third of an estate, and now ranks below the livestock.

No one gave him anything. The far country is generous to a man with a purse and has never once fed anybody without one.

He has filled the hungry. Luke’s Gospel has been listening for this hunger since its first chapter. Mary sang of a God who “has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty” (1:53), and in a desolate place Jesus fed five thousand until all were satisfied (9:17). The far country gives the hungry nothing; the Son who tells this story is the one in whom God fills them. The pigsty is exactly where his kind of mercy is aimed.

In everyday life. If someone you love is in the pigsty, do not be in a hurry to rescue them from every consequence. Pray that the famine will do its work, and be ready for the day they come to themselves.

Is God behind the famine? God rules over famines as over everything (Psalm 105:16), and here the hardship is the very thing that turns the son homeward. That does not make every hardship a punishment for a specific sin, as Jesus has just insisted (13:1–5). But the bottom of the pit is never outside God’s reach, and he often uses empty hands to make a sinner look up. If you are at the bottom now, your misery may be the severe mercy that brings you home. Do not waste it.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean under the law; a Jew feeding pigs for a Gentile had sunk as low as possible. The pods were probably carob pods, used as animal feed.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.'’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hunger brings the son to his senses: he remembers his father’s goodness, owns his sin against God and his father, and sets off home. He has understood his guilt, but not yet his father.

When he came to himself. He came to his senses, for since the request of verse 12 he had not been in his right mind. Sin is a kind of madness that believes lies: that God is holding out on us, that the far country gives life, that we would be freer without him. The Lord calls it forsaking the fountain of living waters for broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13). Repentance begins with seeing things as they really are: where I am, and where I could be.

More than enough bread. He remembers that even the lowest workers on the estate have more than enough: the one thing he had never valued. God’s kindness draws sinners back (Romans 2:4), and every homeward thought a sinner ever had was first a gift from him.

I will arise and go to my father. Repentance is a decision followed by action: turning round, going back.

Against heaven and before you. “Against heaven” means against God, for all sin is first against God (Psalm 51:4). He does not blame the famine, his friends or his father. He names it as sin, not misfortune.

No longer worthy. True: he has forfeited every right. Hired servants were day labourers with no place in the family, paid at the end of each day (see wages). He plans to work off his debt. His repentance is real, but he has entirely misunderstood his father.

Sin against heaven, pardon on earth. If sin is first against heaven, only heaven can forgive it, and the scribes in Luke knew it: “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (5:21). Jesus answered them by healing a paralysed man, “that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins” (5:24).
