The confession this boy rehearses is the confession sinners were bringing to Jesus, and they were receiving from him what only heaven could give.

In everyday life. Make your confession to God specific: not “I have not been very good”, but the thing itself, by name. And if you are rehearsing a hired servant’s speech, planning how to make it up to God, he is not looking for a labourer. He is looking for his son.

Was his repentance real if he only came home because he was hungry? This troubles many honest Christians. The text is candid: the boy came home not because he missed his father but because he was starving. So a reader looks at his own conversion and goes cold: “I turned to God when my marriage collapsed; I prayed because the results came back. Was any of that real?” Nobody’s repentance is pure at the outset. Hunger is very often the first grace, the mercy that makes a man look up when comfort never would have. What matters is not the elegance of the motive that got you onto the road, but whose house you are walking towards. Motives are purified on the way, as the father’s embrace is about to show.
verseByVerse.note: Hired servants were day labourers, with no place in the family.

parallels.desc: against you, you only, have I sinned

verseByVerse.quote: And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father has been watching for his son, and when he sees him far off he runs to him and embraces him before a word of confession is spoken. This is the centre of the parable and the answer to the grumblers.

He arose and came. He did what he said. Luke gives the journey half a sentence; what it cost to walk back into that village smelling of pigs is not described.

A long way off. That tells you what the father had been doing. You do not recognise a figure at that distance unless you have been looking for a long time. The old man had been watching a road for a boy who had every reason never to appear on it, and he saw his son before his son saw him.

And felt compassion. He was moved in his innermost being (esplanchnisthē): the word used of Jesus at Nain (7:13) and of the good Samaritan (10:33).

And ran. The most shocking thing in the parable. In that culture, it is widely thought, it was undignified for an older man to run: he would have to hitch up his robe and show his legs. So the father makes a fool of himself in front of the whole village. Some have also suggested that a son who had lost his inheritance among Gentiles could be cut off by the village; the father reaches him first, taking the shame on himself and protecting his son.

Embraced him and kissed him. Literally “fell on his neck”, as Esau embraced Jacob (Genesis 33:4). The boy is filthy and ceremonially unclean, and the father has him by the neck and kisses him again and again (the Greek verb is a strengthened one), the sign of reconciliation (2 Samuel 14:33), before the son can say a word.

The God who runs. God is not a reluctant judge who must be persuaded to forgive, but a father who runs to meet repentant sinners. He does not run because he takes sin lightly. He is the holy God before whom Isaiah cried out that he was lost (Isaiah 6:5), and that is what makes the running so astonishing: the one who has every right to keep his distance is the one who closes it. The God of all majesty set aside his dignity and ran. And behind the running lies a greater shame borne for us: the Son of God, stripped and lifted up outside the city, “despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2), so that the Father could embrace sinners without compromising his holiness.

In everyday life. If you have been putting off coming back to God until you have cleaned yourself up, look at this verse: the Father is already running. And when someone who has hurt you comes back, go out quickly to meet them, as you were met.

If we invented God, would we have invented this one? Sigmund Freud argued that religion is wish-fulfilment: we project onto the sky the strong father we needed as children. Some religion fits that well enough. But try projecting this father. No patriarch of that world would have dreamed him up; a man of standing was honoured for waiting with dignity while the offender came crawling. Nor would a modern wish invent him, for he is not the easygoing grandfather who never much minded what we did. This father minds terribly, and runs anyway. Projections flatter us. The God of the Bible keeps turning out to be both holier and more tender than anyone was hoping for, and the cost of his tenderness falls on himself. The father on the road is not the God we would have made. He is the God who made us, and came looking.

If God runs to forgive, does it matter how I live? It matters more, not less. The son who has been met on the road like this does not go back to the pigs; he has found his father’s heart, and the far country has lost its charm. Grace truly received changes what we love (Titus 2:11–12). “Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!” (Romans 6:1–2). The father’s running is not permission to leave again. It is the most powerful reason never to want to.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture it was thought undignified for an older man to run.

parallels.desc: Esau ran to meet him and embraced him
you who once were far off

verseByVerse.quote: And the son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The son still makes his confession after the embrace, but he leaves out his offer to work as a hired servant. Grace does not make confession unnecessary; it makes bargaining impossible.

What he says, and what he does not. Both his statements are entirely true, but his father’s mercy came first: the embrace before the confession, the love before the coming. And he leaves out the last line of his prepared speech: “Treat me as one of your hired servants” (v. 19). You cannot earn your way back to a father who has already forgiven you. He comes as a son, or not at all.

Who makes the unworthy worthy? The boy is right: he is not worthy. The parable does not explain how a holy Father can call such a son his son without pretending that nothing happened, and it does not need to, because the one telling it was on his way to Jerusalem. There he would be “numbered with the transgressors” (22:37) and die between two criminals, the only Son who was ever worthy. The welcome at the gate costs the son nothing because it cost the Son everything. Sinners who say “not worthy” are received as sons in him.

Why confess, if I am already forgiven? Because confession is not payment; it is honesty. The son still says the words; what he does not get to do is set the terms of his return. For the believer, daily confession is not earning back a lost sonship but a child being truthful with his Father, and receiving again the assurance of a pardon already given (1 John 1:9). The one thing a returning sinner has to bring is an honest account of himself. Everything else in this scene is supplied by somebody else.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts add here the line “Treat me as one of your hired servants”, but most scholars think a copyist brought it in from verse 19.

verseByVerse.quote: But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without even answering the confession, the father restores his son completely, with robe, ring and sandals: honour, authority and freedom. There is no probation; the boy is a son of the house again at the gate.

Bring quickly. “Quickly” comes first and sets the pace: no delay, no probation, and nobody is sent to wash first. Timothy Keller, in The Prodigal God, pointed out that “prodigal” means recklessly extravagant, spending until nothing is left, and that in this story the word fits the father better than either son: the younger son spent his father’s money on himself, but the father spends his honour, his best robe and his fattened calf on a son who deserves none of it.

The best robe. Literally “the first robe”: the finest in the house, perhaps the father’s own. It covered his rags and showed the village that he was restored to honour. The parable is about the Father’s joy over a returning sinner (vv. 7, 10), not about how forgiveness is achieved. But the Old Testament pictures God clothing his people with salvation (Isaiah 61:10; Zechariah 3:3–5), and the New Testament shows him clothing sinners with Christ himself (Galatians 3:27), so Christians have rightly heard in the robe an echo of the righteousness God gives in Christ, an echo that comes from the rest of Scripture, not from the parable alone. When God justifies a sinner, he declares him righteous, not because he has become good, but because Christ’s perfect obedience is counted as his, like a robe put over rags (2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). Anyone entering the room afterwards would see a son of the house, and nothing else.

A ring. Probably a signet ring, used to seal documents, giving him authority to act on his father’s behalf, as Pharaoh’s ring did for Joseph (Genesis 41:42). It is handed to the one member of the family who has shown beyond argument that he cannot be trusted with money.

Shoes on his feet. Sandals were a mark of the free; slaves often went barefoot. He had come to ask for a place among the hired men. Before he can propose it, his father has put shoes on him.

Three gifts at the gate. The father does not restore him gradually as he proves himself, but completely, before the boy has done one honest day’s work, and then lets him live as what he has been declared to be. If you are in Christ, that is you: not a hired servant on probation, anxiously working to stay in favour, but a son in the robe, the ring and the sandals. The Son was stripped so that we might be clothed; he was treated as a slave so that we might wear the sandals of sons. Every gift at that gate was paid for by the Father’s own Son.

Is the prodigal a believer who fell away? The parable answers the complaint about tax collectors and sinners (vv. 1–2), and the younger son stands for sinners coming home to God. He is a son throughout; the father calls him “my son” (v. 24). It may comfort a believer who has wandered for a season, but it does not teach that sonship can be lost and regained. If you are a Christian who has drifted, the way back is the same road: come to yourself, confess, and go home. You will find your Father has not changed.
verseByVerse.note: The robe honoured him, the ring gave him authority, and sandals marked a son, not a barefoot slave.

parallels.desc: Pharaoh gives Joseph his ring and garments

verseByVerse.quote: And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.’ And they began to celebrate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father throws a feast for the whole village, because the son he had lost as dead is alive and home. It is the party of the first two stories.

The fattened calf. A peasant household rarely ate meat, and a fattened calf was kept back for a single great occasion, with enough meat for a large gathering, perhaps the whole village. So the father calls in the village that had watched the boy leave, and that too protects his son: everyone who comes to the meal has, by coming, accepted the father’s verdict on him. It is very hard to shun a man you have eaten fatted calf for.

Let us eat and celebrate. Eating together is the very thing the Pharisees complained about (v. 2): Jesus eats with sinners because God celebrates their return.

This my son was dead, and is alive again. The boy had just said he was no longer worthy to be called a son; the father does not argue the point but simply uses the word. “Dead” and “alive” are the language of resurrection. A son who had done what this one did may well have been reckoned dead to the family, and the father takes that language and reverses it. Coming home to God is passing from death to life, God’s own work of making the dead alive (Ephesians 2:1–5), and repentance is the first sign of it.

They began to celebrate. Luke says “began”: the celebration is still going on in the last verse, with music audible from the field, and one son standing outside it.

Who paid for the calf? Not the boy, who came up the road with nothing but the smell of pigs on him. Everything comes from the father’s own resources, and he never mentions the cost. The cross is where the bill was met: God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood”, to show his righteousness, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:25–26). Propitiation is the sacrifice that bears the full weight of God’s holy anger against sin and so turns it away. Christ is both the sacrifice that pays for the feast and the host who welcomes us to it. The boy came home to a feast because the Son would go to a cross.

In everyday life. Make your church and your home places where returning sinners are celebrated, not merely tolerated. When someone is baptised, or comes back after years away, show up, rejoice, and eat with them. And if you have never quite believed that God is glad you are his, read verse 24 again, with your own name in it.

Where Christians differ: forgiveness without a cross? Some have argued that this parable shows God forgives freely, with no need for atonement: the father simply forgives, and there is no sacrifice. This commentary’s view: a parable teaches one main point, not every doctrine. This one shows God’s welcome to repentant sinners, in answer to the Pharisees; it does not explain how forgiveness is possible for a holy God. The rest of Scripture does: Jesus came to give his life as a ransom (Mark 10:45), his blood is poured out for the forgiveness of sins (22:20; Matthew 26:28), and Luke ends with the Christ who must suffer so that forgiveness may be proclaimed (24:46–47). The father’s running, at cost to his own honour, hints at the cost God himself bore, and the one telling the story was on his way to Jerusalem to die.
verseByVerse.note: A fattened calf was kept for the greatest celebrations.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elder son comes in from the field, hears the celebration and, instead of going in, stops a servant to ask what is happening. Now comes the Pharisees’ part of the story, and the first sign of the distance between this son and his father.

In the field. The older son is the Pharisees’ picture (v. 2): working, dutiful, as always, not a bad son by any ordinary measure. He is out working while his brother is being kissed at the gate.

He heard music and dancing. Nobody sent for him; he learns of the feast by getting close enough to hear the band. And he does not go in and ask his father; he stops outside and questions a servant, treating his own home as somewhere he needs to be briefed about before entering.

Your brother has come. The servant says “your brother” without hesitation; the elder son will refuse the word. The answer is simple and accurate, and it contains every fact the elder brother will later distort.

Safe and sound. Healthy, whole (hygiainonta). The stated cause of the celebration is not that the brother has proved himself but simply that he is home and well. A servant who has been in that house all his life has understood the father exactly. The son in the yard is about to show that he never has.

The brother who went looking. The elder son will not say “brother”, and he never went out to look for the boy. The parable leaves that gap, and the one telling it fills it. He is the Son who left his Father’s side to find his lost brothers, and “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11). Where the elder son counted the cost of the calf, this Son paid the cost of the feast. That is not a hidden meaning but the contrast the story invites. And “safe and sound” is his report on all his people: he will bring every one the Father gave him through the far country and the dark, and present them whole before the Father’s face, without a single one missing.

Can someone be in the church and still outside the feast? Yes, and this is the most searching part of the chapter. The older son lives on the estate, works the fields and keeps the rules, and he does not know his father’s heart. It is possible to grow up in a Christian home, serve faithfully for decades, hold sound doctrine, and still relate to God as an employer rather than a Father, and to grace as something for other people. The test is not how long you have been in the field but whether the music of grace makes you glad. And if you fear you are the older brother, the fear itself is a good sign: the son in the story felt none, and the Father has come out to plead with you to come in.

verseByVerse.quote: But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elder son angrily refuses to join the feast, and his father comes out to plead with him. God pleads with the self-righteous as truly as he runs to the prodigal.

Angry and refused to go in. He grows angry, like the grumbling Pharisees (v. 2), and the tense of the second verb suggests he kept refusing. With the guests soon aware he was outside, it was a public insult as great as his brother’s demand: the younger son shamed his father by leaving, the elder by standing in the yard.

His father came out. For the second time in one day the old man goes out to a son who has humiliated him. He does not send a servant; he leaves his own celebration, and the love that ran down the road walks out into the dark yard. Entreated (parekalei) means urged, begged. The father, who has every right to order his son indoors, stands outside asking, and through this very parable Jesus is pleading with the Pharisees.

In everyday life. If you are standing in the yard about something, resentful of how God has blessed someone else, angry that grace has gone where you think it should not, recognise the father’s voice pleading with you, and go in. And if you love someone who is standing outside, go out to them as the father did, gently and more than once.

Is God kind to sinners and severe to the religious? Not in this parable. The father goes out to both, and the second time is harder, because this son does not want to be found. And there is a warning in the staging. Standing in the yard feels like taking a position. It usually is just standing in a yard, in the dark, near a house where people are happy, waiting to be persuaded to enjoy something you have already decided not to enjoy. The father will not force him in. The door is open, the music is audible, the invitation has been delivered in person, and after that the yard is a choice.

verseByVerse.quote: but he answered his father, ‘Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elder son’s answer shows his heart: he has served his father like a slave, resents his generosity, and will not call the sinner his brother. He was as lost as his brother, though he never left home.

Look, these many years I have served you. He does not even say “Father”, the word with which the younger son began his confession. “Served” (douleuō) means “I have slaved for you”: the whole tragedy in one verb. He has been a son for the entire story and has experienced it as employment. The younger son wanted to come back as a hired servant; the older son had been living like one all along.

I never disobeyed. Outward obedience, like the rich ruler’s (18:21) and Paul’s before his conversion (Philippians 3:6), with a heart far from his father.

A young goat. He wanted to celebrate, but with his friends, not his father. A young goat is a modest animal, a small grievance carefully preserved, and the complaint does not stand: his share of the estate had been made over to him in verse 12. He had been living on his own property, asking permission he did not need, and resenting a father who had already given him everything. Self-righteousness always resents grace.

This son of yours. Not “my brother”: the servant managed the word without effort; the elder son cuts the boy out of his own family. And he puts the worst construction on it, “with prostitutes”, though verse 13 says only “reckless living”. Resentment fills in the blanks in the worst available way and calls it honesty. “You killed the fattened calf for him!” is the Pharisees’ complaint, “This man receives sinners”: not about justice, but about somebody else’s welcome.

A friend of tax collectors and sinners. The elder son will not call the sinner “brother”. Jesus’ enemies had already given him the opposite name: “Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!” (7:34). He let the name stand. Where the elder son kept the record of his brother’s sins, Jesus took sinners as his friends and carried the record of their sins away. The name the grumblers threw at him is the best news the far country has ever heard.

The Son who never disobeyed. The Father bears with the insults of both his sons, the one who wished him dead and the one who served him as a slave, and he gives himself to his children. And the true Son, who alone could say “I never disobeyed your command” and say it truly, did not resent the Father’s welcome of sinners. He died to make it possible.

In everyday life. If there is someone whose sins you rehearse, aloud or in your head, call them “brother” or “sister” in your prayers this week, and ask God to bless them.

How do I know if I am an older brother? You keep score of your service and feel God owes you. You find obedience a grind, done for reward rather than love. You resent it when God is generous to people with worse records. You remember other people’s sins in detail and find it hard to call them “brother”. You enjoy your friends more than your Father. The cure is not to try harder at being a good son, but to see that you, too, have needed grace every day, and that everything the Father has was always yours as a gift.

Is it not unfair that the son who wasted everything gets the party? Only if the party were wages. Nothing was taken from the older son: every goat on the farm was already his (v. 31). Grace is unfair to no one; it only gives more than anyone deserves. Strict fairness would leave both sons outside, one for his rebellion and the other for his contempt, for “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). Nor is justice ignored: at the cross God bore the cost of the welcome himself, so that he is both just and the one who justifies (Romans 3:26).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The father answers tenderly: his elder son has always had his father and everything he owns, and his brother’s return had to be celebrated. Whether the son went in, Jesus does not say.

Son. Child (teknon): after everything said in the yard, the father’s first word is an endearment.

Always with me. Everything he wanted, he already had: his father’s presence, and the whole estate. He has had for years the one thing his brother threw away, and has been counting goats, as the Pharisees had the covenants and the temple (Romans 9:4–5) and lived as servants, not sons. The sharpest thing in the parable is not aimed at the disreputable: a man can live in his Father’s house for decades, keep every rule, resent the whole arrangement, and never once take anything from a storehouse he has always owned.

It was fitting. It was necessary (edei), the word Luke uses all through his Gospel for what God’s purpose requires. A party was the only right response.

This your brother. Not “this son of yours” but “your brother”: the father hands the word back, corrected. The relationship in dispute now is not between the father and the younger boy but between the two brothers.

The open ending. Jesus does not say whether the older son went in, because the Pharisees and scribes listening had to decide: would they come in and rejoice that sinners were coming home, or stay outside? Both sons had wanted the father’s goods more than the father, one by breaking the rules and the other by keeping them. Jesus has put the grumblers of verse 2 on the doorstep of a lit house, with the music still playing, and left them there. The ending was theirs to write. It still is.

The same must. Luke’s readers know this necessity from the lips of Jesus: “The Son of Man must suffer many things” (9:22), and, after the resurrection, “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (24:26). The party over a returning sinner is necessary as the cross is: both are what God’s purpose of mercy requires, and because the Son had to die, the feast can be held at all.

The music has not stopped. “All that is mine is yours”: the Father said it to a resentful son in the dark, and he says it to every child he has brought in. The Father who ran to the younger son and walked out to the elder is the God who “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” and with him graciously gives us all things (Romans 8:32). His house is never full of servants only. It is full of children, every one an heir, and the music has not stopped.

What does “all that is mine is yours” mean for me as a Christian? That in Christ you are an heir, not a hired hand. All things are yours, Paul says, whether the world or life or death or the present or the future, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (1 Corinthians 3:21–23). The Father’s presence, his promises, his Spirit and an inheritance kept in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4) are already yours, not as wages but as a son’s portion. So pray as a child who has access, give as one who cannot be impoverished, and serve as one who is already loved.

parallels.desc: to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants

15.text: <sup>1</sup> Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. <sup>2</sup> And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” <sup>3</sup> So he told them this parable: <sup>4</sup> “What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? <sup>5</sup> And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. <sup>6</sup> And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.’ <sup>7</sup> Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance. <sup>8</sup> “Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? <sup>9</sup> And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.’ <sup>10</sup> Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.” <sup>11</sup> And he said, “There was a man who had two sons. <sup>12</sup> And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’ And he divided his property between them. <sup>13</sup> Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living. <sup>14</sup> And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. <sup>15</sup> So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. <sup>16</sup> And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything. <sup>17</sup> “But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! <sup>18</sup> I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. <sup>19</sup> I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”’ <sup>20</sup> And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him. <sup>21</sup> And the son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ <sup>22</sup> But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. <sup>23</sup> And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. <sup>24</sup> For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.’ And they began to celebrate. <sup>25</sup> “Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. <sup>26</sup> And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. <sup>27</sup> And he said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.’ <sup>28</sup> But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him, <sup>29</sup> but he answered his father, ‘Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. <sup>30</sup> But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!’ <sup>31</sup> And he said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. <sup>32</sup> It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.’”

keyVerse.quote: And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.
keyVerse.note: This is the answer to the grumblers’ complaint in verse 2, drawn in a single picture. The father has been watching the road, and he closes the distance himself, at the cost of his own dignity, before his son has said a word. Jesus receives sinners because this is what God is like, and the one who tells the story would soon bear a far greater shame to bring sinners home.

15.reflection:
The Pharisees meant “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (v. 2) as an accusation. Why is it good news? Who are the people your church would find it hardest to welcome to its table?

The sheep, the coin and the son are lost in different ways: by wandering, through no will of their own, and on purpose. Which picture best describes how you were lost, or how someone you are praying for is lost now? What does each story show about the One who searches?

The father runs and embraces his son before he can finish his confession (vv. 20–22). How does that change the way you come to God after you have sinned? Do you ever come with a “hired servant’s speech”?

The elder son never left home, yet stands outside the feast (vv. 25–32). Where do you see his attitude in yourself: keeping score, resenting grace to others, serving God as an employer? What would it mean for you to go in?

16.title: Money, the Law, and the Great Divide
16.overview:
Where we are. On the road to Jerusalem (9:51), having answered the grumbling Pharisees with three stories of the lost being found (chapter 15), Jesus turns to his disciples, with the Pharisees listening, and speaks about money, and through money about the heart.

The message. What you do with money shows which master you serve, and the time to use it for God is now. Everything we hold is God’s and ours only for a while; death will call in the account and fix our place for ever. So be as shrewd about eternity as the world is about money, and never let money become your lord. And do not wait for a louder warning: God has already said all we need in his word.

Why it was said. Many read wealth as a sign of God’s approval, and the Pharisees, “lovers of money” (v. 14), sneered at this teaching (see the introduction). Jesus speaks to people who thought themselves right with God while they stepped over the poor, and to disciples who could learn the same.

How the chapter makes its case. Two stories frame it. A dishonest manager about to lose his post uses what he still controls to secure a welcome (vv. 1–7). Jesus seems to commend a fraudster, but the praise is for his foresight, not his dishonesty, and it shames the sons of light (v. 8): use money for eternity, be faithful in that small, borrowed thing, and serve God, not money (vv. 9–13). To the sneering Pharisees he answers that God reads the heart, that the Law still stands to the last dot, and that their easy divorces show how they bend it (vv. 14–18). The second story, the only parable in which Jesus names a character, shows where a life spent on oneself ends, and warns that those who will not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead (vv. 19–31).

Where it leads. That last line is a prophecy: someone did rise, and many still would not believe. But the one telling these stories is the faithful Steward who lost nothing his Father gave him, the Servant who refused every offer mammon made, and the help promised in Lazarus’s name, who came to the gate where we lay and took our wounds on himself.

For us. Look at your bank statement and your gate, and ask what they say about your master. Use what you have for God and for people while there is time, and listen to the Scriptures you already hold: they point to the One who rose.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Parable of the Dishonest Manager
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything you have is on loan from God and the time to use it is short, so be at least as shrewd about eternity as the world is about money. A manager about to lose his post uses the gap between dismissal and audit to turn his master’s debtors into friends who will take him in (vv. 1–7). Jesus praises not his dishonesty but his foresight, and turns it on the sons of light (v. 8): use the money that will fail to make friends who will welcome you into the eternal dwellings (v. 9). Faithfulness with that small, borrowed thing shows what God can trust you with (vv. 10–12), because money is no neutral tool but a rival master, and no one can serve both (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology:
The commendation is careful: what is praised is his shrewdness, not his dishonesty (see the note on v. 8).

The three descriptions of money in verses 10 to 12 each cut it down to size, and the promise on the other side is easily missed: “the true riches”, and “that which is your own” (this is treated fully at vv. 10–12).
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 9 has been read as though a man could purchase his welcome into heaven. The verse answers that in three words: “when it fails” (see the note on v. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: He also said to the disciples, 'There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. And he called him and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything we hold belongs to Someone else, and the account is about to be called in. The parable opens with a steward caught wasting his master’s goods and told that his time is up.

The setting. Chapter 15 answered the grumbling Pharisees; this chapter is spoken to the disciples, though the Pharisees are still listening (v. 14). The manager is wasting (diaskorpizōn) his master’s possessions, the verb used of the younger son squandering his inheritance (15:13). The prodigal was welcomed home by a father; the manager will have to find a welcome by his wits.

A manager. The oikonomos ran a large estate, usually as a slave or freedman: he kept the accounts, made contracts and collected rents in his master’s name. With absentee landlords common in the region, he could do great damage before anybody opened the books.

Wasting his possessions. By incompetence or dishonesty, the property was leaking away. Luke never says whether the charges were true, but the manager does not dispute them, and his immediate plans for unemployment answer the question well enough.

Turn in the account. The dismissal comes first and the audit second: he is finished, and the paperwork is a formality. That gives him a gap. He is no longer trusted but not yet stripped of authority; the debtors have not been told; his master’s seal is still in his hand. The whole parable turns on that interval, and so does the application.

The Steward who lost nothing. Set beside this manager the one telling the story. Jesus too was entrusted with his Father’s house: “this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me” (John 6:39). Stewards in Scripture are so often found wanting; this one never was, and when charges were brought against him at the end, they were false (23:2, 14). He rendered his account in full, with nails in his hands, and it is the account God now reads over the wasteful stewards who trust him. We scattered our Master’s goods; he gathered us, and the audit we dreaded has become the place where his perfect record is read out in our name.

Who is the manager meant to be? Not a code for one group, whether Pharisees, Israel’s leaders or disciples, but a picture of every human being before God. Your money, body, time, gifts and years belong to God, and you are their steward (1 Corinthians 4:2, 7). The notice has already been served: “it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment” (Hebrews 9:27). The only open question is what you will do with the time in between.
verseByVerse.note: A manager (steward) ran an estate for his master, often with wide powers to make deals in his name.

verseByVerse.quote: And the manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Facing ruin, the manager thinks ahead and sees that when his post is gone, all that will matter is who will take him in.

The manager said to himself. Luke takes us inside a man’s head for the third time: the rich fool talking to his soul (12:17), the prodigal coming to himself in the pigsty (15:17). Each is at the end of his options; but this man, unlike the rich fool, thinks ahead.

Not strong enough to dig. Two doors, both shut. He cannot dig and is ashamed to beg: the first is a limitation, the second a decision. His pride survives his disgrace intact.

I have decided. The tense suggests a flash of clarity. He is not buying money; he does not embezzle for himself. He wants houses, an open door, a place at a table when he has nothing. At the last possible moment he has worked out that when wealth goes only relationships are left, and that wealth, while he still controls it, can be turned into them. It took a dismissal notice to make him see it.

Who will receive me? His question was answered a chapter earlier, in the Pharisees’ complaint: “This man receives sinners” (15:2). The man with nothing left to trade does not have to buy his way into a house: there is one who receives people precisely when they come with nothing. The manager schemes for a welcome because he does not know the Host; the sinners at Jesus’ table had found one without scheming at all.

Is it wrong to plan for my future, or to save for retirement? No. The manager is held up as an example of planning, not blamed for it. Scripture commends the ant that stores in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8) and calls a man who will not provide for his household worse than an unbeliever (1 Timothy 5:8); the rich fool was condemned not for his barns but for not being rich toward God (12:21). The question is not whether you plan but how far ahead. Most people plan carefully for thirty years and not at all for eternity. Prudent saving is stewardship; a pension that has become your security in place of God is idolatry, and only you and he know which yours is.

verseByVerse.quote: So, summoning his master's debtors one by one, he said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of oil.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.’ Then he said to another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and write eighty.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Using the authority he still holds, the manager quickly slashes what his master’s debtors owe, so that each of them now owes him.

One by one. And quickly, before the news gets out. These are probably tenant farmers who paid rent in produce, or merchants who had bought on credit: serious contracts, not petty debts.

A hundred measures of oil. Perhaps 3,000 litres of olive oil, the yield of some 150 olive trees; a hundred measures of wheat was the crop of something like a hundred acres. Each debt represents years of a labourer’s wages.

Write fifty. The debtor writes it himself, on his own bond, so the document looks legitimate and carries no trace of the manager. On one common estimate the fifty measures of oil taken off were worth about 500 denarii, more than a year and a half’s wages, and the twenty measures of wheat (“write eighty”) about the same. Each debtor now owes the manager a very large favour.

Was it dishonest? The reductions are curiously uneven, half the oil and a fifth of the wheat, so some scholars suggest he removed something that varied by commodity: his own commission, a steward’s customary surcharge, or interest the law forbade charging fellow Jews (Deuteronomy 23:19). On that reading he waives his own fee to buy goodwill. But Jesus calls him dishonest (v. 8), and the simplest reading is that he cheated his master to put the debtors in his debt. It cannot be settled with certainty, and the parable does not need it to be. What Jesus commends is neither the honesty nor the dishonesty, but the shape of what he did: he took a resource about to stop being his and spent it, at once, on the only thing that would still exist after the deadline. “Sit down quickly”: part of his prudence is speed.

Five hundred, fifty, and nothing. Luke’s reader has met two debtors before. At a Pharisee’s table Jesus told of a moneylender whose debtors owed five hundred denarii and fifty, and when they could not pay, “he cancelled the debt of both” (7:41–42). The manager trims a bill by roughly the larger sum to buy himself a welcome. Jesus is the creditor in person, and he does not trim. He cancels, for people who could never return the favour. The manager wrote fifty to buy friends; Christ wrote nothing, because he paid everything, and called us his friends (John 15:15).

In everyday life. A man who learns that his firm is closing updates his CV that night. What have you been treating as if there were all the time in the world: a reconciliation postponed, a sin you meant to deal with, a conversation about Christ you meant to have? The manager had hours; you do not know how long you have, and that is a kindness as well as a warning.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the size of these debts: a hundred measures of oil was about 800–900 gallons, a hundred measures of wheat about 1,000–1,200 bushels. Cutting them won the debtors’ gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus praises the manager’s foresight, not his fraud, and turns it into a rebuke: worldly people act more wisely for this life than God’s people do for eternity.

The master commended. The surprise of the parable, and the sentence is careful. He is still the dishonest manager, literally the steward of unrighteousness; the praise does not clear his name. What is praised is that he acted phronimōs: with the practical intelligence that sees a situation clearly and acts on it. A commander can admire an enemy’s manoeuvre without approving of the war.

The sons of this world. Here is the sting, aimed at his own people. “The sons of this world” live for this age; “the sons of light” are God’s people (John 12:36; Ephesians 5:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:5), a title some devout groups claimed. Jesus grants the title and then says the other side is better at reading a situation and acting in time.

Sons of the light. Nobody is a son of light by nature. Zechariah sang of the sunrise from on high, given to those who sit in darkness (1:78–79), and Simeon held that light in his arms (2:32): a son of light is someone on whom Christ has risen, and who knows the light is shining now and will not wait. The wisest Son of Light who ever lived did not merely see a crisis coming; he walked into it on purpose. He set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51), knowing the hour and the cost, and spent everything he had, his reputation, his body, his life, on the one thing that would still exist after the deadline: a people for his Father.

What it does not mean. Jesus is not commending dishonesty, or teaching that the end justifies the means. A parable can use a bad man to make a good point, as with the unjust judge (18:1–8). The argument runs from the lesser to the greater: if even a scoundrel acts decisively to secure a few years of comfort, how much more should the sons of light act for eternity.

How would I actually be shrewd about eternity? Set your giving before you see what is left, not after. Choose a church, a house and a job with an eye on what they will do to your soul and your children’s, not only on salary and schools. Invest in people, friendships with believers, hospitality, the young, because people are the only part of this world that goes on into the next. And deal with sin today rather than meaning to, because the window is not as wide as it seems.

Uncertain wording. Who is “the master” who commends him? The Greek ho kyrios can mean “the master” or “the Lord”, and it is not certain where the story ends and Jesus’ comment begins. Most likely it is the rich man, since Jesus speaks in his own voice in verse 9 (“And I tell you”); some take it as the Lord himself. Either way, the foresight is praised, not the dishonesty.
verseByVerse.note: The master praises the manager’s shrewdness, not his dishonesty.

verseByVerse.quote: And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Use money, which will soon be worthless to you, for what will last: give it in ways that make friends for eternity.

Unrighteous wealth. The hardest sentence in the chapter. Literally “the mammon of unrighteousness”, mammon being a Semitic word for money or possessions: not necessarily wealth gained dishonestly, but the money of this unrighteous world, where nobody’s money is clean all the way back. Jesus says: use it to make friends, by giving to the poor and supporting the work of God.

So that when it fails. When money runs out, or when you die and it is useless to you. A currency guaranteed to become worthless is not the purchase price of eternity.

The eternal dwellings. The manager made friends who would receive him into their houses; you can make friends who will welcome you into eternal homes. Whoever “they” are (see below), the point is the same: use money now with an eye on eternity, and lay up treasure in heaven (12:33).

Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. Luke’s second volume shows who stands at that door. As the stones fell on Stephen, he saw the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God and prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:56, 59). The friends made by generosity may be glad to see us, but the welcome belongs to the risen Christ, and he receives his people as a host, not as a creditor collecting on an investment. We spend the mammon that fails; he spent the riches that never fail, and spent them on us.

What it does not mean. Not that you can buy your way into heaven, and Luke will not let the verse be read that way. The tax collector who could offer nothing but his beaten breast went home justified (18:13–14); the dying criminal bought nothing and was promised Paradise that day (23:43); and in this very chapter a rich man’s fortune cannot buy one drop of water. Salvation is by grace, but true faith is generous: generosity is the evidence of faith, not the price of heaven, and how a man treats his wealth shows which master owns him (v. 13).

So how much should I give, and to whom? Scripture sets no fixed percentage for the Christian, but it sets a direction and a spirit. Give regularly and in proportion to what you have received (1 Corinthians 16:2), cheerfully, not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7); give first to the ministry of the word in your own church (Galatians 6:6) and to the poor, especially fellow believers (Galatians 6:10). Many find a tenth a sensible starting place, not a ceiling. The test of this verse: ten years from now, will there be people, in heaven or on the way there, partly because of what you did with your money? If you cannot say yes, start this month with something that costs you.

Uncertain wording. Who are “they” who receive you? The Greek does not say. Some take it of the friends themselves, those you helped or who came to faith through the gospel you supported, glad at the door of the next life to see their benefactor arrive. Some take it of angels, who carry Lazarus a few verses later (v. 22). Many take “they” as a reverent Jewish way of saying that God will receive you, without naming him, as at 12:20, where the Greek literally reads “they require your soul”. The point does not depend on the choice.
verseByVerse.note: “Unrighteous wealth” renders mammon, a Semitic word for money or possessions.

parallels.desc: rich in good works, storing up treasure

verseByVerse.quote: 'One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? And if you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who will give you that which is your own?
verseByVerse.commentary:
How you handle money, a small thing that is not even yours, shows whether God can trust you with the true riches that will be yours for ever.

Faithful in a very little. The parable is finished and the application widens. Character does not change with scale: how a man handles a small thing is not a warm-up for a large one but a sample of it.

Dishonest in a very little. We easily believe we would be generous if we had more, honest if the stakes were higher; Jesus says the evidence is already in. The expense claim rounded up, the hours padded, the change not returned, the excuse not quite true: none of these is small in what it reveals.

Who will entrust to you the true riches? Three descriptions cut money down to size. It is unrighteous wealth, the currency of a fallen world. It is “a very little”, an extraordinary thing to say to people for whom money meant eating or not eating; yet compared with eternal things, any sum is small. And it is “another’s” (v. 12). Set against it are the true riches of the kingdom: God’s word, his grace, responsibility in his kingdom, eternal reward. How we handle money tests whether we can be trusted with greater things.

That which is another’s. Money belongs to God, and you are the steward of the parable, running an estate you did not buy, with the audit coming. Then the promise, easily missed under the warnings: “that which is your own”. Something is coming that will truly be yours, an inheritance imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4). Everything held now is on loan; what is being trained for cannot be taken away, and the training ground is a bank account.

Subject to them in Nazareth. Of Jesus between twelve and about thirty Luke tells us only that he went down with his parents to Nazareth and was submissive to them (2:51–52). Those were the very little years. When they were over, before a single miracle, the Father spoke from heaven: “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased” (3:22). The one who says “faithful in a very little” had been faithful in a very little for most of his life.

Why would God care so much about money? He owns the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10) and needs none of yours. He watches what a man does with a small sum of somebody else’s, because that is the surest evidence of what he would do with anything. Money is concentrated life: hours of work, security, pleasure and power in a form you can count. What you do with it shows what you love, and God cares very much about what you love.

Does this mean I earn my place in heaven by being faithful? No. “That which is your own” is an inheritance, and an inheritance is never earned by the heir. But God is pleased to reward the faithfulness his grace produces, and Scripture speaks plainly of differing rewards (19:17; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15). The believer is not saved by his faithfulness but for it, and then, in a kindness almost embarrassing, rewarded for what God himself worked in him. As Augustine said, when God crowns our merits he crowns nothing but his own gifts.

In everyday life. The Son faithful in the hidden years at Nazareth was faithful for you, and his Spirit now makes you faithful in small things. This week, put right one small dishonesty you have let stand: the overcharge, the borrowed thing not returned, the claim not quite accurate. Nobody else may notice; that is exactly why it matters.

verseByVerse.quote: No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Money is not merely a tool but a rival master, and no one can give himself to God and to money at once.

No servant can serve two masters. The servant is a household slave (oiketēs). A man may hold two jobs, but a slave’s whole time, body and will belonged to his owner. So this is not advice about priorities but a statement about what is possible.

Hate the one and love the other. “Hate” and “love” is the Hebrew way of saying that one is put before the other (14:26): one will always come first. But the strength of the language is deliberate: the divided man does not end up mildly disappointing one master; he ends up with something like contempt for him.

You cannot serve God and money. Money is again mammon, treated almost as a name: not a thing you own but someone who owns you, a rival lord with demands and slaves, promising security, power and happiness, the things only God can give. Then the flat impossibility: not “should not”, but “you cannot”.

Him only shall you serve. One man made this choice without wavering. In the wilderness the devil offered Jesus the authority and glory of all the kingdoms of the world if he would worship him, and Jesus answered: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve” (4:5–8). Every promise mammon makes was laid before him at once, and he refused it, hungry and alone. The one who says you cannot serve two masters is the one Servant who never tried.

Not slaves but friends. There is a Master worth serving with everything, and he is not a hard one. Mammon takes everything and gives back anxiety; this Lord gave everything and gives back rest. He was sold by a disciple who chose the other master (22:5). He let himself be bought so that we might be bought back, and the slaves of mammon he redeems he does not take as slaves but calls his friends.

The conflict that rarely surfaces. Most people serving money would sincerely say they love God. The truth shows when the two masters give conflicting orders: the promotion that means leaving a faithful church, the giving that means a smaller car. God first and money a firm second is not a way of serving both. It is serving one of them, by a man who has not noticed which.

How do I know which master I serve? Ask what you worry about, because worry is the prayer we pray to the god we fear will fail us. Ask what you would find hardest to give up if God asked; whether your giving is the first line of the budget or the last; whether money or God decides where you live and which church you attend; how you feel when the markets fall. A Christian may feel the loss; but if a bad month on the statement shakes your peace more than a month without prayer, mammon has a stronger claim on you than you thought.

Is it wrong to be rich? No. Abraham was very rich, and he is the host at the banquet a few verses later; Joseph of Arimathea was rich and a disciple (Matthew 27:57). Paul tells the rich not to set their hopes on uncertain riches but on God, and to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–18). It is not wrong to have money; it is fatal to serve it. But Jesus speaks of the danger of wealth far more than of its blessing, because wealth makes that service so easy to slide into and so hard to notice.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “money” renders mammon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — The Law, the Kingdom, and Human Exaltation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Men may admire you, but God reads the heart, and his word stands even when you bend it. The Pharisees, who loved money, sneer at Jesus’ teaching, and he goes past the ridicule to what lies beneath it: they justify themselves before men, but what men exalt God abhors (vv. 14–15). They claim the Law as their ground, yet the Law and the Prophets pointed to the kingdom now being preached, which people are pressing into (v. 16), and the Law has not lost a single dot (v. 17). The divorce saying is not a change of subject but an example: their easy divorces show that they were loosening the Law, not keeping it (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Since John announced the King, the kingdom is entered with urgency, and the most unlikely people are pressing in (see the note on v. 16). Because the Law still stands, God’s design for marriage in Genesis 2:24 still binds, and the kingdom does not relax it (see the note on v. 18).
verseByVerse.examples: Read alone, Luke’s flat saying would make every divorce and remarriage adultery. On the exceptions Matthew and Paul record, and on those already divorced and remarried, see the note on v. 18 and the box “Where Christians differ: may a divorced person ever remarry?” at the end of it.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him. And he said to them, 'You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees sneered because they loved money, and Jesus tells them that God, who sees the heart, loathes the very things that win human admiration.

Lovers of money. Literally “silver-lovers” (philargyroi), a blunt thing to say of the most respected religious men in the country. Not all Pharisees were wealthy, but the love of money did not feel like a vice: the covenant promised full barns to the obedient (Deuteronomy 28:1–14), and it was a short step to reading the balance sheet as a certificate of righteousness.

They ridiculed him. They turned up their noses: a poor teacher from Galilee, telling them about money! That gives them away. They do not argue from Scripture; they sneer, as people often do when something has landed and cannot be answered. Ridicule lets a whole room off the hook by making the speaker faintly absurd.

Justify yourselves before men. Jesus goes straight past the laughter. To justify yourself before men is the exhausting work of keeping up other people’s good opinion, the opposite of the tax collector who will stand at the back of the temple two chapters later, with no audience and no defence, and go home justified by God (18:14). These men were their own defence counsel before a human jury; God is the Judge, and the verdict he gives the tax collector rests on mercy, not on a record (18:13).

But God knows your hearts. “Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). The audience and God are two different courts, and only one of them is final.

An abomination. A heavy word (bdelygma), the Greek Old Testament’s standard term for idols; Proverbs calls everyone arrogant in heart an abomination to the LORD (Proverbs 16:5). So what this society most admires, success, honour, religious reputation, when it flows from pride, belongs with the idols. And the Lord they sneered at was exalted by God to the highest place precisely because he refused every exaltation among men (Philippians 2:8–9). What men despised, God crowned.

The one who reads hearts. Again and again Luke says that Jesus knew their thoughts (5:22; 6:8; 9:47). The one who says “God knows your hearts” is reading theirs as he says it. They were being judged not by a Galilean teacher’s opinion but by the searching gaze of God in the face of a man.

Does God hate success, then? No. God gives wealth, skill and honour, and Scripture praises the man skilful in his work (Proverbs 22:29). The abomination is pride: success turned into a throne, the applause of men taken for the verdict of heaven. The same promotion can be received with gratitude by one man and worshipped by another. The question is what you are leaning on, and whose praise you are living for (John 5:44).

Is it wrong to care what people think of me? Not entirely. “A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches” (Proverbs 22:1), and an elder must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7). But reputation is a by-product of faithfulness, not its goal. The danger begins when the audience becomes the judge: when you would rather be thought generous than be generous. A simple test is what you do when no one will ever know. Jesus told us to give, pray and fast in secret, and promised that the Father who sees in secret will reward (Matthew 6:4).

parallels.desc: the LORD looks on the heart

verseByVerse.quote: 'The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The age of promise ran until John; now the kingdom it promised is being preached, and people are pressing to get in.

In the flow. Verses 16 to 18 are not stray sayings but answer men who justify themselves (v. 15) by the Law: it pointed to the kingdom now preached (v. 16), it still stands and judges (v. 17), and their divorce rulings show how they bend it (v. 18). The rich man’s story then ends on the same words, “They have Moses and the Prophets” (v. 29): the Scriptures these men claimed will testify against them if they will not hear.

The Law and the Prophets were until John. “The Law and the Prophets” is the whole Old Testament, and Jesus dates its era. Not abolished at John, as the next verse insists, but the time of promise has closed, because what it pointed to has come. John stands where the two eras join, which is why none born of women is greater than he, and yet the least in the kingdom of God is greater (7:28).

The good news of the kingdom. The time of fulfilment has begun. The kingdom of God is his rule breaking into the world in Jesus, to forgive sinners, heal what sin has spoiled and gather a people who live gladly under him (17:20–21; Colossians 1:13). The verb is euangelizetai, the gospel is preached: the kingdom is not a programme for us to implement but a report of what God has done, and its centre is a person. At Nazareth Jesus read Isaiah’s words about the one anointed to preach good news to the poor, rolled up the scroll and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (4:18–21). The era of promise ended because the Promised One was standing in the room. What kings and prophets longed to see is now preached in every village (10:24).

Everyone forces his way into it. On the likeliest reading (see below), since John announced the King the kingdom is entered the way a man presses through a closing door, with the urgency of 13:24: “Strive to enter through the narrow door.” And there is a quiet rebuke in “everyone”: tax collectors and sinners are pushing in through a door these men are standing beside, discussing.

Does this mean I get into the kingdom by my own effort? No. Good news is received, not earned. The striving is not effort that earns entry but the urgency of a man who will let nothing, pride, fear of people or pleasure, keep him from the gift; those who press in have stopped trusting their own righteousness. And behind every human pressing in is the God who draws: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). The urgency is ours; the power is his.

Uncertain wording. “Everyone forces his way into it” is difficult, because the Greek verb (biazetai) can be read more than one way. It may mean that everyone is pressing urgently to enter, as the tax collectors and sinners are doing. It may mean that everyone is being urged in, like the guests compelled in from the highways (14:23); the ESV notes this in its margin. Or, as in Matthew 11:12, it may speak of the kingdom suffering violence from its opponents. In Luke’s context the first seems most likely.

verseByVerse.quote: But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new era does not cancel God’s law: heaven and earth will pass away before the smallest stroke of it fails.

One dot of the Law. Straight after saying an era has ended, Jesus says the Law is untouchable: heaven and earth are less secure than what God has written. The dot is the keraia, literally a little horn, the tiny stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another.

How the law continues. The two verses are held together by one word: fulfilment. Jesus came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17–18). Its era has closed, but it has not been cancelled; it has been kept, by the man saying this. Its moral demands remain, its ceremonies find their reality in him (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1), and its promises are kept in him. The Passover lamb, the scapegoat, the bread in the holy place, the blood on the mercy seat: not one was a wasted pen stroke, because all were sketches of him. And the moral law, which condemned us to the last dot, was kept to the last dot by the Son, and its curse borne by him to the last drop.

Must Christians, then, keep the Old Testament law? Reformed Christians distinguish three kinds of law. The ceremonial laws, sacrifices, food laws and festivals, are fulfilled in Christ and no longer bind us (Hebrews 9–10). The civil laws were given to Israel as a nation and expired with it, though the principles of justice behind them (their general equity) still teach wisdom (the Westminster Confession 19.4; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.4). The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still guides believers, not as a way to earn God’s favour but as the shape of the life he has given us (Westminster 19.5–6; 1689 19.5–6). Not a dot fails, because Christ fulfils all of it, some by completing it and some by writing it on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).

Two opposite errors. One man reads verse 16 and concludes that grace has made the moral law a historical curiosity; verse 17 exists to stop him. Another reads verse 17 and concludes that nothing has changed and he must still produce a righteousness of his own; verse 16 exists to stop him. The kingdom is preached as good news, and entered by people pressing in with nothing in their hands.

Why does Jesus turn straight from the law to divorce? The subject has not changed: verse 18 is an example of verse 17, the point at which their tradition had quietly loosened the Law (on the school of Hillel, see “Why here?” at v. 18).

In everyday life. When a commandment is inconvenient this week, notice the instinct to treat it as a dot that surely does not matter: a small lie, a small lust, a small theft of time. Then remember the One who kept every dot for you, and keep it for love of him.
verseByVerse.note: The “dot” is a tiny stroke of a letter.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In God’s eyes marriage is for life, so to discard a spouse and marry another is adultery, whatever a human ruling allows. Jesus gives it as an example of the Law the Pharisees claimed to keep and were in fact loosening.

Why here? An example of the permanence of God’s law (v. 17), aimed at the Pharisees, who used the law to allow easy divorce. Deuteronomy 24:1 let a man divorce his wife if he found some indecency in her, and the school of Hillel read that so broadly that a burnt dinner could count; Rabbi Akiva later added finding a prettier woman. They justified themselves (v. 15) by quoting Moses while breaking God’s intent for marriage. There may also be a pointed reference to Herod Antipas, who had divorced his wife to marry Herodias, his brother’s wife, and imprisoned John for saying so (3:19–20).

Divorces his wife and marries another. In God’s eyes the bond still holds, so remarriage is adultery (Mark 10:11–12). Divorce in that world was a man’s prerogative: he wrote the certificate, and she was put out. The man who discards his wife for another has not left a contract but broken a covenant made before God: Malachi calls her “your wife by covenant”, with the LORD as witness between them (Malachi 2:14).

Marries a woman divorced. The second husband too. The sin reaches everyone who treats the first marriage as though it had never been.

The exceptions. Luke, like Mark, gives the saying flat. Matthew records the same teaching twice, both times with an exception for sexual immorality (Matthew 5:32; 19:9), and Paul adds a second case: if an unbelieving spouse insists on leaving, the believer is not enslaved (1 Corinthians 7:15). Luke gives the rule, not the rulings on particular cases: marriage is for life, and the exceptions are narrow doors in a solid wall, not the wall itself.

When our marriages break, his does not. Behind this hard saying stands a Bridegroom who has never once divorced his bride. Israel went after other lovers, and the LORD said through Hosea that he would betroth her to himself for ever (Hosea 2:19). The church is no better, and he gave himself up for her, to present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). When our marriages are broken, his is not. He hates the breaking of covenant because he is faithful, and he is faithful to us.

What about the person already divorced and remarried on no ground the New Testament allows? This question keeps people out of church: is every day of the new marriage a fresh sin, and the only repentance to break the second home apart? No. Jesus tells the woman at the well that she has had five husbands (John 4:18); he calls them husbands, names the truth exactly, and does not tell her to go back and unpick it. A second marriage, once made, is a real marriage: not an ongoing act of adultery but a covenant with real obligations to a real spouse and children. Past sin is to be confessed and forgiven like every other sin, and left at the cross, not dragged out and re-committed every morning. If that is your history, the word to you is not “go back”. It is: be washed, and be faithful now.

Such were some of you. Paul lists adulterers among those who will not inherit the kingdom, then adds a sentence that has rescued many consciences: “And such were some of you” (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). The Lord who drew the line on marriage is the Lord in whose name the adulterer is washed. The fence stands where Jesus put it, chiefly to protect the wife who could be dismissed with nothing; but the gospel does not lock a man outside his own forgiveness.

What if my spouse is abusing me? Then this verse is not a chain to keep you in danger. Abuse is never to be tolerated, in the church or in the home, and nothing in Jesus’ words requires a husband or wife to stay under the same roof as someone who threatens, beats or terrorises them. Get yourself and your children to safety; tell your elders and, where a crime has been committed, the police (Romans 13:4). Separation for protection is not the sin this verse condemns. Whether persistent, unrepentant abuse has broken the marriage in the way Scripture recognises, by the abuser’s wilful abandonment of every duty of the covenant, is to be weighed carefully with faithful elders, and many Reformed churches have judged that it can. What is never right is to tell a victim that God wants her to stay and suffer. Jesus’ words protect the vulnerable; they were never meant to be turned against them.

Is there a way back if I was the one who sinned in my divorce? Yes, as for every other sin: confess it to God without excuse, put right what can be put right, and receive his forgiveness fully. That may mean seeking reconciliation with a former spouse if both are unmarried and it is possible; it will certainly mean honesty, humility and faithfulness to the obligations you still have, especially to your children. It does not mean living for ever under a cloud. David, who took another man’s wife and killed him to cover it, wrote the psalm the church still prays: “wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Psalm 51:7).

Where Christians differ: may a divorced person ever remarry? Some Christians hold that there is no ground for remarriage while a former spouse lives, reading this verse without exceptions. Others allow divorce and remarriage on wider grounds, such as incompatibility or the breakdown of love. This commentary’s view: the position of the Westminster Confession (24.5–6) is best: marriage is for life, and divorce is always a tragedy; but adultery, and wilful desertion that cannot be remedied by the church or the civil authority, are grounds on which the innocent party may divorce and, after the divorce, remarry as if the offending party were dead. Jesus himself allows divorce for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9) and Paul for desertion by an unbeliever (1 Corinthians 7:15); Luke gives the principle, and Matthew and Paul its exceptions. Persistent, serious abuse can amount to such desertion, and the elders help judge each case; the abused should seek safety at once, and abuse is never to be tolerated. Those who have sinned in divorce and remarriage can find full forgiveness in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–31 — The Rich Man and Lazarus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What we do with what we have in this life is settled for ever at death, and God has already given us all the warning we need. A rich man dressed and fed like a king passes a starving, sick beggar at his gate every day (vv. 19–21). At death their places are reversed: Lazarus is carried to Abraham’s side, the place of honour at the feast, and the rich man is in torment (vv. 22–23). Nothing he says shows he has learned anything, and a chasm fixed by God now lies between them (vv. 24–26). He asks for Lazarus to warn his brothers, but they have Moses and the Prophets, and those who will not hear them would not be convinced even by someone risen from the dead (vv. 27–31). It is the fullest picture of life after death in the first three Gospels.
verseByVerse.theology: The story teaches that there is conscious existence after death, before the resurrection, that the punishment of the wicked is real torment, and that the separation is fixed in both directions (see the notes on vv. 22–23 and v. 26, and the box “Where Christians differ: parable or history?” at the end of the note on vv. 22–23).
verseByVerse.examples:
The story does not teach that poverty saves and wealth damns (see “What it does not mean” at vv. 19–21).

The rich man had heard the Law and the Prophets read every Sabbath of his life; the problem was never a shortage of evidence (see the notes on vv. 27–29 and vv. 30–31).

verseByVerse.quote: 'There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A rich man lives in daily luxury while a starving, sick beggar lies ignored at his gate. The story, found only in Luke, sets out the two lives before it turns to their two deaths.

Why this story here. It shows the danger of wealth (v. 13), the reversal promised in the beatitudes and woes (6:20–26) and the sufficiency of Scripture (vv. 29–31), and it answers the sneering Pharisees, who thought money a sign of God’s favour: here is a man who had all of it.

Purple and fine linen. Every detail is a price tag. Purple dye came from the murex shellfish, thousands to a garment, so costly that some societies kept it for royalty; fine linen was a luxury cloth. And he is unnamed (tradition calls him Dives, Latin for “rich”): the man who had every name worth having in this life has none before God.

Feasted sumptuously every day. Not on feast days, when ordinary people ate meat, but every day, and with display: he made merry, splendidly.

At his gate was laid. Perhaps somebody put him there because he could not move himself. And this is the gateway of a great house: the rich man could hardly enter or leave without passing him.

Named Lazarus. Apart from Abraham, the only character in Jesus’ parables to be given a name. Lazarus, from Eleazar, means “God helps” or “God has helped”. No one else did. God knows the poor by name, and the name is the parable’s single hint about where this man’s hope lay.

What fell from the table. Covered with sores, perhaps from malnutrition, he wants not a place at the table but the scraps that fall to the floor, like the prodigal longing for the pigs’ pods (15:16). Even those were not given to him.

Even the dogs. Most likely not a comfort but scavenging street dogs, unclean animals, reaching him when no human being will, and he too weak to keep them off: the final degradation.
