God has visited his people. The one telling the story is the help the name promises. When Jesus raised a widow’s only son at the gate of Nain, the crowd said, “God has visited his people” (7:16). No one at the rich man’s gate helps Lazarus, but the man speaking had been stopping at gates all over Galilee, touching lepers and feeding the hungry: the hope hidden in the beggar’s name was walking the roads of Israel. He came out to where we lay, covered with sores we could not heal, and he did not pass them like a rich man. He took them on himself: “with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). The God who helps is not a hint in a name. He is a Man with scars.

The rich man’s sin. Not that he was rich, nor that he did anything to Lazarus. He did nothing. He walked past the poor man every day. His sin was neglect, the failure to love his neighbour, and behind it the failure to love God, because a man who loves God cannot step over his image every morning.

What it does not mean. Read carelessly, this is a story in which poverty saves and wealth damns, since Lazarus is not said to have believed anything and the rich man is accused of no crime. But the beatitude at 6:20 blesses the poor because empty hands are where faith is usually found, not because an empty purse is a ticket, and Abraham, in this very parable, was a wealthy man. What condemns the rich man is not his purple but the gate he walked past daily. What saves Lazarus is not his sores but the God who knew his name.

Who is the Lazarus at my gate? Usually someone you pass so often you have stopped seeing him: the homeless man outside the station, but just as often the widow two doors down who has not had a visitor in a month, the colleague whose marriage is collapsing, the asylum-seeking family at the back of church, the believer who cannot pay the gas bill. Your gate is wherever your daily path brings you within reach of real need. God does not ask you to meet every need in the world. He asks you not to step over the one he has laid where you will see him.

Should I give to every beggar who asks? Not necessarily; wisdom is not the opposite of love. Cash for someone feeding an addiction may not help him, and Scripture expects the able to work (2 Thessalonians 3:10). But the rich man’s problem was no giving and no seeing. Never walk past without at least seeing the person: a word, a name asked, a meal bought, a referral to a church or charity that can do more. And support, regularly, those who do this work well. Love may be wise; it may not be blind.
verseByVerse.note: Purple dye was costly and fine linen a luxury: the clothing of the very rich. Lazarus, the Greek form of Eleazar, means “God has helped”; he is the only character in Jesus’ parables, apart from Abraham, who is given a name.

parallels.desc: whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor

verseByVerse.quote: The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At death the two men’s places are reversed: Lazarus is carried to the place of honour beside Abraham, and the rich man wakes in torment.

The poor man died. No burial is mentioned. He most likely went into a pauper’s grave, and the parable passes over it, because something else was happening that nobody could see.

Carried by the angels. As in verse 20, everything is done for him: laid at a gate by men, carried through death by angels. “Abraham’s side” is literally “Abraham’s bosom”, the language of a banquet, where the guest in the place of honour reclined beside the host (John 13:23). It pictures paradise, the messianic banquet where many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (13:28–29). So the beggar who longed for what fell from a table is now in the place of honour at the greatest table there is. And the true Host of that banquet, Christ himself, went down into death, so that for those who are his it would no longer be a pit but a doorway.

In Hades. The Greek term for the realm of the dead (the Hebrew Sheol); here, the place of punishment for the wicked. Torment (basanois) is agony, and it is conscious: he sees, recognises, suffers and will shortly argue. The reversal is complete. “He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty” (1:53).

He lifted up his eyes. The first person he picks out is Lazarus, the one face he had trained himself not to register, every day, for years. And he knows his name. He had always known it.

Hades and Abraham’s side. Hades here is the place of the dead before the final judgment, not yet the lake of fire; Abraham’s side is the blessedness of believers with God, the Paradise promised to the dying thief that very day (23:43). The souls of the righteous are received into the highest heavens to behold the face of God, and the souls of the wicked are cast into hell, reserved to the judgment of the great day (Westminster 32.1). Then the bodies are raised, and soul and body together enter their final state.

When a Christian dies, does he sleep until the resurrection? No. The body sleeps in the grave, which is why the New Testament can call death falling asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14); the soul does not. Lazarus is carried at once to Abraham’s side; the thief is with Christ today; Paul says to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Your believing mother, your child who trusted Jesus, the friend you buried last year: they are not unconscious or waiting in some grey place, but with Christ, awake, at rest and rejoicing, awaiting only the resurrection of their bodies.

Is there a purgatory, a place where souls are cleansed before heaven? No. Lazarus goes straight from the gate to the banquet; the story has no third place. Christ’s blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7), and “by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). Nothing remains to be paid off. Believers are made perfect in holiness at death and pass immediately into glory (Westminster 32.1; 1689 31.1). Purgatory would add our sufferings to Christ’s sacrifice, as though his were not enough. It was.

In everyday life. Two funerals: one with no mourners and angels in attendance, one with every honour and none of the things that mattered. Which is your life preparing? And if you are grieving a believer this week, read this verse again. They were carried.

Where Christians differ: parable or history? And what happens after death? Some take this as a literal description of the afterlife; others as a parable using popular imagery, not to be pressed for details. It begins like other parables, “There was a rich man”, but names Lazarus, which no other parable does. Some, holding soul sleep (the view that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection) or annihilationism (that the lost finally cease to exist), deny that the dead have conscious existence, or that the lost suffer for ever; among them are Christians who love Scripture and hold these views sincerely. This commentary’s view: it is a parable, and its details (seeing across the chasm, speaking, a drop of water) are pictures, not a map of the afterlife. But Jesus would not use a picture that taught falsehood. The story teaches clearly that at death there is conscious existence, that immediately after death the righteous are comforted and the wicked suffer, that there is a fixed separation, and that destiny is settled at death. The fuller picture comes at the resurrection and final judgment, when Hades itself gives up its dead (Revelation 20:13–15) and the lost go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life (Matthew 25:46). The punishment is conscious and it is without end.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Abraham’s side” is literally “Abraham’s bosom”, the place of honour beside the host at a banquet. Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame.’ But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even in torment the rich man has not changed, and Abraham reminds him that he chose his comforts in this life, which is why the places are now reversed.

Father Abraham, have mercy on me. Two things show he has not changed. The first is “Father Abraham”: he pleads descent, as John the Baptist had warned against: “do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father’” (3:8). Ancestry is his only claim. And “have mercy”: he never showed mercy to Lazarus, and now he begs for it.

Send Lazarus. The second is worse. He knows the name, sees the man in the place of honour beside Abraham, and his instinct is to have him fetched like a servant to bring water. Even now Lazarus is someone who ought to run his errands. Nothing has been learned. Hell does not change a man; it shows what he is.

Cool my tongue. He who feasted every day begs for a single drop of water, the mirror image of the scraps Lazarus longed for from his table, and even that is refused.

In this flame. Fire is a picture of the suffering of the lost, used by John the Baptist and by Jesus himself (3:17; Mark 9:43–48). Whether or not the flame is physical, what it pictures is real, and Jesus chose the most terrible image available because nothing less would be true.

Child, remember. Abraham’s answer opens tenderly, with no cruelty and no gloating. But the answer is no, and it turns on one word: “remember”. Abraham produces no list of sins; he asks the man to recall his own life.

Your good things. “Your” is exact. He chose his comfort in this life as his portion: “woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation” (6:24). He lived for himself, got what he lived for, and it lasted exactly as long as he did. Lazarus received bad things, and his good things never came in this life; he was not saved because he was poor, but his name suggests he trusted God.

Comforted here. The reversal is the whole case against the rich man, without a charge read out. The tragedy is not that he enjoyed good things, but that he wanted so little. He could have had God himself as his portion, as the psalmist did (Psalm 16:5; 73:26), and he settled for linen and dinners, a portion that ended with his last breath.

A son of Abraham. The rich man rests his claim on Abraham. Jesus in Luke makes children of Abraham another way. He freed a woman bent double for eighteen years and called her a daughter of Abraham (13:16). He went into the house of a chief tax collector and said, “Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham” (19:9). The children Abraham actually welcomes are the ones Christ has found, freed and brought to his side.

Christ received our bad things. There was One who did cry out in anguish and thirst, and whose cry was answered with mockery and sour wine (23:36). He drank the cup of wrath to its last drop, so that no one who trusts in him will ever beg for a drop of water in the flame. The rich man received his good things in his lifetime; Christ received our bad things in his, so that we might be comforted for ever. He is the portion that cannot be used up.

How can heaven be happy if people we love are in hell? Scripture gives no formula for one of the hardest questions a Christian carries. But in the parable Abraham is neither cruel nor tormented: he speaks with tenderness and in perfect agreement with God’s justice. In glory we will see as God sees and love what he loves; no one will be in hell whom God has wronged, and no one in heaven will doubt that the Judge of all the earth has done right (Genesis 18:25). Until then, the question should drive us to pray and speak to those we love while the door is open, trusting that God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4).

Isn’t heaven just a way of keeping the poor quiet? Karl Marx called religion “the opium of the people”: a drug that numbs the oppressed with dreams of another world so that they stop demanding justice in this one. Some churches deserved the charge. But here the life to come is not a sedative for the man at the gate; it is an alarm for the man in the house. Jesus uses eternity not to tell Lazarus to be content but to tell the comfortable that what they do with the poor at their door will be weighed for ever. God’s judgment makes injustice impossible to shrug off, because nothing done to the least is forgotten. If death ends the story, the man in purple simply won. The gospel does not ask the poor to wait quietly. It gives them a Lord who was laid in a manger at birth and in a borrowed grave at death, who knows every Lazarus by name, and who will not let the dogs have the last word.

parallels.desc: men whose portion is in this life

verseByVerse.quote: And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, in order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
After death no one can cross between comfort and torment: God has fixed the boundary, and destiny is settled.

A great chasm has been fixed. A second reason for refusing, not about what the man deserves but about what is possible. “Has been fixed”: established and still standing, and it was God who fixed it.

None may cross. The barrier works both ways, so no one crosses from here, not even out of compassion. It is not that mercy is unwilling to reach him; the door is now shut, by God, and neither pity on one side nor pleading on the other can open it.

No second chance. After death, destiny is fixed: “it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment” (Hebrews 9:27). The same sentence in Hebrews goes straight on to Christ: “so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him” (Hebrews 9:28). Men die once; Christ was offered once; and that single offering is why the time before the chasm is fixed is a time of open mercy. Behold, now is the favourable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2).

The same chasm. This is why the parable sits in a chapter about money. In verses 19 to 21 there was a gulf too, and it was a gate: the space between the rich man and Lazarus, which he could have crossed any day of his life. He never did. Now he is on the far side of a chasm he cannot cross, and it is the same chasm. There was one chasm wider than this, and only one person has ever crossed it: the gulf between a holy God and a sinful race, which nothing we could build would bridge. The Son came down across it, took flesh, and bore in his body the wrath that fixes chasms, so that the door could be opened from heaven’s side.

What about people who never heard the gospel, or who died as infants? The parable warns people who had Moses and the Prophets and would not listen. Salvation is only through conscious faith in Christ (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–17), which is why the church sends preachers rather than waiting for a second hearing after death. Those who never heard are judged by the light they had, and all have sinned against that light (Romans 1:20; 2:12). Infants who die in infancy are a different case: Scripture gives grounds for hope, and the confessions teach that elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where and how he pleases (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 10.3; the Westminster Confession 10.3). If you have lost a little one, you may rest your grief on the Lord who called the infants to himself (18:15–16). Neither case offers a second chance after death.

Is never-ending punishment not out of all proportion to one lifetime of sin? Only if sin is measured by how long it lasted. A wrong is weighed by the one it is against: striking a stranger is serious; striking a king was treason. Sin is rebellion against the infinitely holy God, and its guilt is measured by his majesty (Psalm 51:4). Nor do the lost become penitent: the rich man in the flame still gives orders about Lazarus and asks for relief, never for God. Hell is God’s righteous judgment, giving the lost, justly and for ever, the life without him that they chose (Romans 2:5–8). And the one who spoke of it most plainly went to the cross to save sinners from it. The door is open today.

parallels.desc: to die once, and after that comes judgment

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father's house— for I have five brothers—so that he may warn them, lest they also come into this place of torment.’ But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rich man wants Lazarus sent to warn his brothers, but Abraham answers that they already have God’s word in Scripture, and it is enough.

My father’s house. His concern for his family is real, and this is usually read as the one decent thing he does. But it is still “send him”: twice now Lazarus is an errand boy. And he is to go to his father’s house, where the brothers are presumably still feasting and stepping over somebody at the gate.

Five brothers. They live as he lived. To warn (diamartyrētai) is to testify solemnly. And there is a faint excuse in the request, as if he had never been warned properly. Abraham’s answer meets it exactly.

They have Moses and the Prophets. The Old Testament Scriptures: the brothers have been warned. The Law of Moses commands that the poor be provided for and the corners of the field left for them (Leviticus 19:9–10; Deuteronomy 15:7–11), and the Prophets return to it again and again (Amos 6:4–7; Isaiah 58:6–7). Beyond care for the poor, the Scriptures call to repentance and faith in the Messiah they promise.

Let them hear them. Listen and obey. The rich man would have heard the Law read Sabbath after Sabbath, walked home past Lazarus and had dinner. Nobody in that house lacks information. He wants something more compelling than the word of God; Abraham replies that the word is enough, and the problem was never the evidence.

Listen to him. In Luke, Moses and the Prophets speak of one person. On the mountain of the transfiguration Moses and Elijah stood with Jesus and spoke of his departure at Jerusalem, and a voice from the cloud said, “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” (9:30–35). After the resurrection he interpreted to his disciples in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (24:27). To hear Moses and the Prophets rightly is to hear them pointing to Christ. The brothers had a Bible whose whole message was the one telling this story.

The sufficiency of Scripture. God’s word is enough to bring people to repentance and salvation. The sacred writings are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus, and all Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work (2 Timothy 3:15–17). The whole counsel of God is either set down in Scripture or deduced from it, and nothing is ever to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit or traditions of men (Westminster Confession 1.6).

Should I look for visions, dreams or messages from the dead to guide me? No. The story gives no warrant for contact with the dead, which Scripture forbids (Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Isaiah 8:19); the request is refused because the living have the Scriptures. God has spoken, finally and fully, in his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and the canon of his word is closed. Christians differ over whether God still gives prophecy or dreams, but even those who believe he does agree that nothing may be added to Scripture or set above it. If you want to hear God speak, open the Bible: he will never say anything elsewhere that contradicts it, or anything outside it that you need more.

In everyday life. You have more than the five brothers had: the Gospels and the letters as well. Are you waiting for something more before you obey: a sign, a feeling, a clearer word? Take the next plain command you find on the page this week and do it, trusting the Spirit who speaks there to give what he asks.
verseByVerse.note: “Moses and the Prophets” means the Old Testament Scriptures.

parallels.desc: if you believed Moses, you would believe me

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’ He said to him, ‘If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unbelief lacks not evidence but a willing heart: those who will not hear Scripture would not be convinced even by someone rising from the dead.

No, father Abraham. He contradicts Abraham flatly, remarkable from where he stands and entirely in character: he has managed people all his life and is still doing it.

If someone goes to them from the dead. The rich man’s theory is that more evidence would make people believe. It sounds reasonable, and most Christians have thought it about somebody they love.

If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets. Where a heart is set against God’s word, more evidence rarely moves it, because the resistance is not only in the mind. Miracles do not create faith in a heart that has decided against it; they only add to its guilt.

Neither will they be convinced. A haunting prophecy. Somebody did rise from the dead soon after, and the leaders who had heard this teaching were not convinced. Matthew tells us they paid the soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matthew 28:11–15). And in John’s Gospel, when another Lazarus was raised from the dead at Bethany, the chief priests responded by planning to kill him and Jesus too (John 11:43–53; 12:10–11). The test was run. It went exactly as he said.

How faith actually comes. “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17), by the work of the Spirit. The spiritually dead come to life not because a ghost visits them but because God speaks through his word and opens their hearts, as he opened Lydia’s (Acts 16:14). That is why the church preaches rather than performs: the power is in the message, because the Spirit works with the word.

Someone has risen from the dead. Not a beggar sent back on an errand, but the Lord of glory, who now holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). The rich man asked for a messenger; God sent his Son, and raised him on the third day, just as the Scriptures had said (24:46). He stands at the gate of every hearer of this story, not as a beggar, but as a King with his hands full of mercy.

Should I pray for a sign for a relative who will not believe? Pray for him, constantly and by name, and above all that God would open his heart to the word, because that is how God saves; a sign without a new heart would only harden him, as this verse warns. So put the word in front of him: your life, which he reads first, your words about Christ, a Gospel to read, an invitation to hear the Bible preached. And do not despair if nothing seems to happen. The Spirit is not in a hurry, and many who resisted for decades were finally won by a verse they had heard a hundred times.

parallels.desc: after Lazarus of Bethany is raised, they plot to kill Jesus

16.text: <sup>1</sup> He also said to the disciples, “There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. <sup>2</sup> And he called him and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’ <sup>3</sup> And the manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. <sup>4</sup> I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses.’ <sup>5</sup> So, summoning his master's debtors one by one, he said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’ <sup>6</sup> He said, ‘A hundred measures of oil.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.’ <sup>7</sup> Then he said to another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and write eighty.’ <sup>8</sup> The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light. <sup>9</sup> And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings. <sup>10</sup> “One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. <sup>11</sup> If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? <sup>12</sup> And if you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who will give you that which is your own? <sup>13</sup> No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.” <sup>14</sup> The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him. <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God. <sup>16</sup> “The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it. <sup>17</sup> But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void. <sup>18</sup> “Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery. <sup>19</sup> “There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. <sup>20</sup> And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, <sup>21</sup> who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores. <sup>22</sup> The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, <sup>23</sup> and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side. <sup>24</sup> And he called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame.’ <sup>25</sup> But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish. <sup>26</sup> And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, in order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us.’ <sup>27</sup> And he said, ‘Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father's house— <sup>28</sup> for I have five brothers—so that he may warn them, lest they also come into this place of torment.’ <sup>29</sup> But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.’ <sup>30</sup> And he said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’ <sup>31</sup> He said to him, ‘If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.’”

keyVerse.quote: No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the chapter. The manager’s story shows how to use money for what lasts, and the rich man’s story shows where serving it ends; between them stands this flat impossibility. The one who said it had refused every offer mammon could make (4:5–8), and he is the Master worth serving with everything.

16.reflection:
The manager acted decisively because he knew his time was short (vv. 3–8). What would it look like for you to be as shrewd about eternity as people around you are about careers and pensions? Where have you been living as if there were all the time in the world?

Jesus calls money “a very little” and “that which is another’s” (vv. 10–12), yet says it shows whether we can be trusted with true riches. What do your small honesties and your giving reveal about which master you serve (v. 13)?

The rich man’s sin was not his wealth but the beggar he walked past every day (vv. 19–21). Who is at your gate, someone you pass so often you have stopped seeing them? What one step could you take this week?

Abraham says the brothers have Moses and the Prophets, and that a resurrection would not convince those who will not hear them (vv. 29–31). Why is Scripture enough? How should that shape the way we pray and speak for the people we love who do not yet believe?

17.title: Forgiveness, Faith, Gratitude, and the Coming Son of Man
17.overview:
Where we are. Jesus is still on the road to Jerusalem (9:51; 17:11). Having warned the money-loving Pharisees with the rich man and Lazarus (chapter 16), he turns to his disciples, and the chapter moves from the life of the church to the end of the world, with the same Lord ruling both.

The message. Belong to the King with your whole heart turned towards him. Disciples are to guard the weak, forgive without counting, trust a great God with small faith, and claim no credit when they have obeyed. And the kingdom, which has already come in Jesus and will come in a day as sudden as lightning, is not a date to be calculated but a King to be faced. One thread runs through it all, the way a person faces: the Samaritan turns back to Christ, and Lot’s wife looks back to the world.

Why it was said. The disciples were a small company following their Master towards a cross, soon to live together without him in sight, wronging and forgiving one another and tempted to think that service earns credit. The Pharisees wanted a timetable for the kingdom (v. 20). Both needed the same correction: what matters is not when, but who (on Samaritans and Pharisees, see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Four short sayings press the disciples (vv. 1–10): do not trip the little ones, rebuke and forgive a brother seven times a day, trust God with mustard-seed faith, and when you have done all, say you have only done your duty. Then a story shows what faith looks like (vv. 11–19): ten lepers obey Christ’s word and are cleansed, but only a Samaritan turns back to give thanks at his feet, and only he hears, “your faith has made you well.” Jesus answers the Pharisees’ question about when by pointing to who: the kingdom is in their midst (vv. 20–21). Then he tells the disciples that his return will be as public as lightning, that he must suffer first, and that it will break in on ordinary life as the flood and the fire did, dividing even two in one bed (vv. 22–37).

Where it leads. The King stands in the middle of the chapter, unrecognised by the men asking when he will come. He is the one Servant who did all that was commanded, the Lord whose word cleanses lepers on a distant road, the one at whose feet a Samaritan gives praise to God, and the Son of Man who “must suffer many things” (v. 25) before he comes in glory. Lot’s wife looked back to the place of judgment because her heart was there; Jesus set his face towards Jerusalem and the cross (9:51) because his heart was with us.

For us. Ask which way you are facing. Turn back to Christ with your thanks, keep forgiving as you have been forgiven, serve without keeping accounts, and live each ordinary day as someone who would be glad to see him come that evening.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Stumbling Blocks, Forgiveness, Faith, and Duty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Life in Christ’s company is lived in complete dependence on him, with no claim on him. Four short teachings press the disciples on different parts of their calling: do not trip the weak (vv. 1–2); rebuke and forgive the brother who falls, without counting (vv. 3–4); trust God for the faith to do it, since even the smallest real faith rests on his power (vv. 5–6); and when it is done, claim no credit, because a servant who has done his duty has put no one in his debt (vv. 7–10). Each makes the disciple lean harder on his Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
The forgiveness teaching echoes the Lord’s Prayer: “forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us” (11:4). This does not make forgiveness a condition of justification; it describes what justification does to a heart. Those forgiven much love much (7:47).

The servant parable checks the pride that obedience produces, and it speaks of the best possible day, when everything commanded has been done (see the note on vv. 9–10, with what it does not mean).
verseByVerse.examples:
Forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same act (see “What if he never says he repents?” at vv. 3–4).

The servant parable can sting anyone who has served for years without thanks; it is not the whole picture (see the note on vv. 7–8).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his disciples, 'Temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come! It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Snares are certain in a fallen world, but whoever trips one of Christ’s little ones into sin faces a judgment worse than drowning. Turning from the Pharisees to his disciples, Jesus begins a set of sayings for a community learning to live while its Lord walks towards the cross.

Temptations to sin. Snares, stumbling blocks (skandala). The oldest sense was the trigger of a trap: anything that trips a person into sin or out of faith. Jesus does not promise a church in which nobody is ever tripped up.

Woe to the one. That snares are bound to come excuses nobody; each person who causes another to fall is accountable. Luke’s woe is the prophets’ word, a cry of grief as much as a verdict. Judas was the stumbling block God had foretold, and still the Son of Man said “woe to that man by whom he is betrayed” (22:22). Peter holds both truths in one sentence: Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”, and lawless men crucified him (Acts 2:23).

A millstone. Deliberately extreme. A millstone was the heavy upper stone of a mill, far too heavy to struggle free of, and for a Jew drowning with it carried a particular horror: a body that could never be buried. And this is the better outcome.

These little ones. The phrase includes children but reaches wider: the young in faith, the tax collectors and sinners who have just come to Jesus (15:1), anyone whose hold is not yet firm and who is watching somebody stronger to learn how this is done. He measures the danger to them in millstones and seas, because to him they are not little at all.

The weight falls on the influential. Nobody trips a person who is not following him, so this is a word for parents, teachers, leaders, and anyone admired by a younger believer. To ruin your own soul is a catastrophe; to ruin somebody else’s is worse.

The Shepherd’s anger. Through Ezekiel the LORD charged the shepherds of Israel that they had not strengthened the weak or brought back the strayed, and so the sheep were scattered (Ezekiel 34:4–5). Then he promised to come himself (34:16), and Luke has just shown him carrying one sheep home on his shoulders (15:4–6). So the millstone is not a harsh teacher’s temper but the anger of the Shepherd himself, who has come at great cost for the weak, against anyone who would drive them off again.

In everyday life. Think of three people who watch you: a child, a new Christian, a colleague who knows you go to church. What have they learned about Christ from you this month? If one of those lessons is false, correct it in front of them.

How might I cause someone to stumble without meaning to? Most stumbling blocks are not set deliberately. A church leader whose private life contradicts his preaching. A parent who teaches prayer and never prays, or mocks other Christians at the dinner table. A mature believer who flaunts a freedom, in drink, entertainment or speech, before someone just escaped from that very thing (Romans 14:13–21). Harsh legalism trips people too, by teaching them that God is impossible to please. And in its gravest form it is the abuse of a child or a vulnerable person by someone they trusted, which has driven many out of the faith and is exactly what this millstone is for. Such abuse must be reported, never hidden to protect a church’s name.

What if I have caused someone to stumble? Then repent, and do not let the millstone become despair: the warning is meant to bring disciples to their senses, not to push them past forgiveness. Confess it to God; where possible go to the person, own it without excuse, and ask how you can help put it right; then live differently in front of them. Peter denied his Lord three times in front of servants who were watching, and was restored to feed the very lambs (John 21:15–17). The blood of Christ covers the sins of influence too.
verseByVerse.note: The millstone is the heavy upper stone of a mill.

verseByVerse.quote: Pay attention to yourselves! If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch yourself first; then lovingly confront a brother who sins, and forgive him every time he repents, without keeping count.

Pay attention to yourselves! Watch your own example and your own heart. The words look both ways: back to the millstone, since the surest way not to trip a weaker believer is to watch your own feet, and on to the rebuke, which a man who has just examined himself gives differently.

If your brother sins, rebuke him. Love does not ignore sin: a fellow believer who sins should be lovingly confronted, privately first (Matthew 18:15; Galatians 6:1). The rebuke is not optional, and it is not unkind.

If he repents, forgive him. The goal is restoration, not humiliation; a rebuke that does not hope for repentance is only an attack.

Seven times in the day. Seven is the number of completeness: not a limit, but limitless forgiveness, like the seventy-seven times Jesus gives Peter (Matthew 18:21–22; older versions read seventy times seven). Seven times in one day is deliberately absurd, meant to stop us counting: anyone who apologises seven times before evening is by ordinary judgment not sincere, and Jesus chooses that case on purpose. The test is not whether the repentance convinces us, but whether we forgive as a settled rule or only until our patience runs out.

Forgiveness from a forgiving Lord. The command comes not from a teacher of ethics but from the one who said of a weeping woman, “her sins, which are many, are forgiven” (7:47), and who “receives sinners and eats with them” (15:2). He forgives at his own cost, from a cross, for people who were still driving the nails. So seven times a day is not a quota laid on a reluctant heart but the overflow of a Lord whose own forgiving has never run dry, passed on by people who know they are the larger debtor.

What it does not mean. Forgiveness does not mean pretending wrong was not wrong, or always restoring full trust at once, or removing all consequences. A treasurer who stole may be forgiven and still not be given the chequebook again. But forgiveness means letting go of the debt and of revenge, and being ready to restore the relationship.

How do I rebuke a brother without crushing him? Begin with the log in your own eye (Matthew 7:3–5): are you angry, have you done the same, is this really sin or only something that annoys you? Go to him, not about him: privately, soon and in person, not in a message he must read alone at midnight. Name the thing, not the man. “What you said about her in front of them was untrue, and it hurt her” can be heard; “you are a liar” cannot. Ask, and listen: you may not have the whole story, and you may end up apologising. Have the pardon ready, so that the moment he says “I repent” you can tell him it is finished. Paul’s word is “restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted” (Galatians 6:1). After the third denial “the Lord turned and looked at Peter” (22:61), and that look broke him without destroying him. Christ has dealt with your sin without crushing you, and that is the only safe place to speak from.

What if he never says he repents? Luke leaves this case open, and it is where most real wounds live. Forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same act. Forgiveness is what you do before God with your own heart: releasing the debt, refusing to nurse the injury, declining to make yourself the creditor. Jesus prays for this from the cross for men who had not repented (23:34; the prayer is missing from some early manuscripts, but many scholars judge it genuine). Reconciliation is the restored relationship, and that takes two; Jesus attaches it to “if he repents”. You can be commanded to forgive on your own, but not to reconcile on your own. That protects both people: it frees the one who was wronged from having to pretend nothing happened, or from endless re-injury in the name of grace; and it keeps the one who did wrong from being written off, because he remains someone Christ came for.

And if the sin is serious and goes on? This private rebuke is the first step Jesus describes more fully in Matthew 18:15–17, where unrepentant sin is taken to one or two others and then to the church. Forgiveness in your heart does not mean the church must look away. And where the sin is a crime, abuse of a spouse or a child, or anything that endangers others, forgiving does not mean staying silent or staying in danger. Report it, protect the vulnerable, and let the elders and the civil authorities do their work. You can release your own claim to revenge and still insist that justice be done.

In everyday life. You will not find seven pardons a day in yourself; the Spirit of the Lord who forgave you is the one who gives them. Name in prayer the brother or sister you need to confront lovingly, or forgive again, and ask God to show you your own part. Then either go and speak, gently and privately, or tell him plainly: “I forgive you, and I will not bring it up again.” The gravest danger in a long unrepented offence is not that the other man stays hard. It is that you do.

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles said to the Lord, 'Increase our faith!' And the Lord said, 'If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked for more faith, Jesus answers that the smallest real faith is enough, because its power lies in the God it trusts. The apostles have just been told to forgive a brother seven times in a day, and their response is that they have not got enough of whatever it takes: an honest request, and a good prayer.

Asked of the right Lord. Luke’s wording is careful: the apostles said to “the Lord”, the title the Greek Old Testament gives to God. They bring a request only God can grant. Faith is not a quantity a man can raise in himself; it is given, and in Luke it is Jesus who guards it. On the night of his arrest he will tell Peter that Satan has demanded to sift him like wheat, “but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (22:31–32). Peter’s faith faltered that night, and it did not fail, because it hung on the prayer of his Lord.

A grain of mustard seed. They wanted more; quantity was never the issue. The mustard seed was proverbially tiny (Mark 4:31). What matters is not how big the faith is but whom it trusts: tiny faith in a great God can do great things.

This mulberry tree … planted in the sea. The mulberry, or sycamine, the black mulberry of Palestine, has a deep, spreading root system and was very hard to uproot, and the sea is where nothing grows: a tree that cannot be moved, put where it cannot live. Faith does the impossible, because God does. The mustard seed does not move the tree; the One it trusts does, the One who takes the deep-rooted tree of our sin and casts it into the depths of the sea (Micah 7:19). Forgiving seven times a day may feel like uprooting a mulberry tree; faith in God makes it possible.

What it does not mean. The verse has been turned into a promise that enough faith secures whatever is asked. On that reading the tree stays rooted because you did not believe hard enough, and so, it follows, did the tumour and the sick child. That has been preached to many people at the worst hour of their lives, and it cannot be got out of this text. The apostles have not asked for power to work wonders. They have asked for help to forgive, and the mulberry tree is his answer about that.

My prayer was not answered. Was my faith too small? No. If your faith was the size of a mustard seed, it was enough, because the power never lay in your faith but in God. Luke has already recorded the one prayer in history offered in perfect faith: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me” (22:42). The cup was not removed, and nobody will suggest the faith in Gethsemane was too small; nor, in the whole of Acts, do men who heal the lame and raise the dead ever move a tree. When God does not do what we asked, it is not because we failed a test of believing hard enough, but because our Father, who loves us and knows what we do not, has a better purpose, as he had for Paul, whose thorn was not removed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). Faith is not the confidence that God will do what I want. It is trust that he is good and wise, and the willingness to keep obeying while I wait.

So how does my faith grow? By looking at the One you trust, not by trying to feel more certain. Faith comes from hearing the word of Christ (Romans 10:17), so read and hear it. It grows by use, like a muscle: the next time you forgive when it is hard, or give when it is costly, you will find that God was there. It grows in the fellowship of believers and at the Lord’s Table, where Christ is set before us. And it grows by asking: “Increase our faith!” is a prayer God loves to answer.
verseByVerse.note: The mulberry (sycamine) tree has a deep, spreading root system.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Will any one of you who has a servant plowing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’? Will he not rather say to him, ‘Prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you will eat and drink’?
verseByVerse.commentary:
No master serves his slave first: a servant who comes in from the field simply goes on serving. Jesus pictures a household everyone knew in order to say something hard about deserving (vv. 9–10).

A servant plowing. The question expects the answer no, and every man listening would have given it. Picture a small farm: a farmer with one slave, who ploughs by day and works in the house in the evening. When he comes in, supper has not been made, because he is the one who makes it. To “recline at table” is the posture of a guest at a formal meal: no master would treat his slave as an honoured visitor in his own house.

Prepare supper for me. The slave’s duty continued; that is how a household ran, and everybody knew it. “Dress properly” is, in the ESV margin, “gird yourself”: tuck up the robe for work, as the servants waiting for their master did in chapter 12.

Afterward you will eat. Easy to miss under the severity: the servant is not going hungry; he eats second. The hard word about deserving is spoken inside a picture where the servant is fed.

The Master who took the servant’s place. Luke makes sure the reader meets this household again. At the Last Supper the disciples argue about which of them is the greatest, and Jesus answers in the very terms of this parable: “who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves” (22:27). The Lord of the household, who had every right to sit, took the servant’s place, and the next day his service went to the uttermost, his body given for the very servants who had argued over seats (22:19). No earthly master ever behaved like that; only the King of glory would.

For the one who serves unseen. The scene will sting anyone who has spent years serving in a church without acknowledgement and recognises this household exactly: the work simply expected, the meal made after everybody else has eaten. Jesus is not telling such a person that this is all there is. This same Gospel has already given a second picture of the household, and it is the ending: a master who comes home and serves his watching servants at his own table (12:37).

Does Jesus approve of slavery here? No. He uses the household as his listeners knew it to make a point about God, just as he uses a dishonest manager and an unjust judge without approving of them. Slavery was a fact of life in that world. The Old Testament regulated a form of servitude rather than abolishing it, and that is a real difficulty for modern readers; but its laws protected the servant, and the gospel set to work on the institution from inside: Paul tells a master to receive his runaway slave no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16), and the Bible condemns man-stealing outright (1 Timothy 1:10; Exodus 21:16). The parable’s subject is not human employment but the relation of a creature to his Creator, who owns us by right and whom we can never put in our debt.

verseByVerse.quote: Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even on the day a disciple has done everything commanded, he has earned nothing: obedience is what we owe God, and any reward is grace.

Does he thank the servant? No, not because thanks would be wrong, but because thanks are for something over and above. A servant doing only what was required puts no one in his debt.

When you have done all. Note the condition. This is the sentence for the day a man has done everything, with nothing outstanding, and no ordinary sinner has ever had that day (Romans 3:23). Even then there would be no credit.

Unworthy servants. Unworthy (achreioi) means unprofitable, owed nothing. It does not mean worthless in God’s sight; the parable is about what is owed, not about how much God loves his servants. It means having no claim on the Master: at the end of the accounting there is nothing on the credit side that God did not first supply.

Only our duty. Obedience to God is our duty, not a favour to him. We cannot put God in our debt: “who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?” (Romans 11:35). This destroys the idea of earning salvation or merit by good works. Any reward he gives is grace, undeserved favour; Paul draws exactly that line between wage and gift: “to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due” (Romans 4:4).

Why this parable sits here. The chapter has just demanded three enormous things: do not trip the weak, forgive seven times a day, exercise the faith you have. A disciple who manages any of that will feel the thought rise that God now owes him a little. That thought is the target: the oldest religion in the world, the hope of putting God in our debt, and it lives most comfortably in the busiest servants of the church. The irreligious man thinks he owes God nothing; the religious man is tempted to think God owes him something; the gospel undoes both.

The one Servant who did all. The sentence imagines a man who has done all that he was commanded, and Scripture knows only one. The Son of whom the Father said, “with you I am well pleased” (3:22), prayed in the garden, “not my will, but yours, be done” (22:42). He alone could have come in from the field with nothing outstanding and claimed the wage. He did not claim it for himself. He “was numbered with the transgressors” (22:37), so that his obedience might be counted as theirs, servants who had no credit of their own.

What it does not mean. This saying has been used to flatten people who were already flat. It does not mean God is indifferent to what his servants do. The same Lord will serve his watching servants (12:37) and set the faithful man over ten cities (19:17). Nothing is owed as a wage, yet the Master rewards his servants anyway, as a gift; as Augustine put it, when God crowns our merits he crowns nothing but his own gifts.

Then why bother working hard for God? Because love does not work for wages. A son helps his father not to be paid but because he is a son and loves him. Freed from the need to earn, the Christian can serve with joy instead of anxiety, and God, who owes us nothing, has promised to reward even a cup of cold water given in Christ’s name (Matthew 10:42). We work hard because we are already accepted, not in order to be.

In everyday life. Catch the quiet bookkeeping in your heart this week: “I have served on the rota for three years, I tithe, I gave up that job for the church, surely God will see me right.” Name it, and hand the ledger back to him. Then do your duty gladly, as one already accepted for Christ’s sake, and when a blessing comes, receive it as a gift, not a payment.

Where Christians differ: merit. Medieval theology developed a doctrine of merit, including works of supererogation, good works beyond what is required, which built up a treasury of merit in the church that could be applied to others. This commentary’s view: this verse refutes it. No one can do more than duty requires. Even after doing everything, we are unworthy servants. Reward is grace. The Reformers saw it clearly: we cannot by our best works merit pardon of sin or eternal life, and when we have done all we can, we have done but our duty and are unprofitable servants (the Westminster Confession 16.5; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 16.5, which echoes this very verse).

parallels.desc: who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Many receive gifts from Christ; the one who is saved is the one who turns back to the Giver. On the border of Galilee and Samaria ten lepers stand at a distance, as the law required (Leviticus 13:45–46), and cry for mercy (vv. 11–13). Jesus does not touch them; he sends them to the priests for the inspection given to those already healed (Leviticus 14), and as they go they are cleansed (v. 14). The nine go on, doing what they were told. One, a Samaritan, turns back and falls at his feet (vv. 15–16). Jesus asks where the nine are (vv. 17–18) and tells the foreigner that his faith has made him well (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology:
The story shows the difference between receiving a benefit from God and responding to God himself. All ten received cleansing; only one came back to the Giver (on the nine, see the note on vv. 17–18).

Luke shows Samaritans in a good light three times: the good Samaritan (10:33), this leper, and Samaria as the first step beyond Jerusalem in Acts (1:8; 8:5). On the man the temple fenced out, see v. 18.
verseByVerse.examples: The nine were ordinary, not villains. A family prays for a sick child and the child recovers, and within weeks thankfulness has given way to relief and normal life. The story calls ordinary people to come back.

verseByVerse.quote: On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance
verseByVerse.commentary:
On his way to the cross, Jesus is met by ten lepers, outcasts whom the law kept at a distance. Only Luke records this healing.

On the way to Jerusalem, between Samaria and Galilee. The journey continues (9:51), every step of it towards a cross. The border country, where Jewish Galilee met Samaritan territory, is a detail that will matter in five verses.

Ten lepers. They are outside the village, which is where the law required them to be. Leviticus put a man with the disease outside the camp, in torn clothes, with his hair loose, calling out “Unclean, unclean” as anyone approached (Leviticus 13:45–46). Leprosy then covered a range of skin conditions, but the consequence was the same: total exclusion from worship, from family, from work, from touch.

A colony of the excluded. Luke saves a detail for verse 16: one of the ten is a Samaritan. Jews and Samaritans did not eat, worship or share a cup together, but here they live together outside a village: shared misery has done to their divisions what no argument ever did.

At a distance. It is where each of them had perhaps been standing for years. The holy Son of God entered a world of lepers and became, on the cross, the one cast outside the camp (Hebrews 13:12–13), so that people who had stood at a distance all their lives could be brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13).

In everyday life. Ask who in your town stands at a distance: the long-term ill, the person with a disfiguring condition, the prisoner’s family, the one everyone avoids at the school gate. Then go nearer than is comfortable, because your Lord did.

Is leprosy a picture of sin? In a sense, yes, read carefully. The leper was not more sinful than his neighbours, and his disease was not necessarily a punishment for a particular sin (compare John 9:3, about a man born blind), though Scripture records cases where it was (Numbers 12:10; 2 Kings 5:27). But the law made leprosy a living parable of uncleanness: it spread, it disfigured, it cut a man off from God’s house and God’s people, and no one could cure it but God (2 Kings 5:7). That is what sin does to every one of us. And Jesus, who could not be made unclean by touching lepers, made them clean, which is exactly what he does with sinners.
verseByVerse.note: Lepers were required to keep their distance and cry out a warning.

parallels.desc: the leper must live alone, crying “Unclean”

verseByVerse.quote: and lifted up their voices, saying, 'Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.' When he saw them he said to them, 'Go and show yourselves to the priests.' And as they went they were cleansed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lepers cry for mercy, and Jesus answers with a command that can only be obeyed by trusting his word: as they go, they are cleansed.

Jesus, Master, have mercy on us. They shout, because the law kept them at a distance. “Master” is epistata, a word only Luke uses, and everywhere else in this Gospel it is on the lips of disciples (5:5; 8:24; 9:33). These men are not disciples, but they use it rightly. And they ask not for cleansing but for mercy, the cry that echoes through Luke (18:13, 38), and leave it to him to decide what mercy will mean.

Show yourselves to the priests. He does not touch them, as he had touched the leper in chapter 5; he gives them an errand. A priest had to declare a healed leper clean before he could rejoin society (Leviticus 14:2–32): it is the inspection you go for when the disease has gone. So ten men with visible leprosy are told to set off and be examined for its absence, before they are healed. Will they go, still leprous, trusting his word?

As they went. Not before they went, but as they obeyed. There would have been a stretch of that road during which they had obeyed and nothing whatever had changed. Faith acts on Christ’s word before seeing the result, like Naaman, who was healed when he obeyed and washed (2 Kings 5:14).

A word that is enough. Here is a Lord who does not need to touch, or wave a hand, or even be present: he speaks, and leprosy dissolves on a dusty road some distance away. It is the voice that said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.

In everyday life. Is there a plain command you are waiting to feel ready for: to forgive, to confess, to be baptised, to give, to speak to a neighbour about Christ? Start walking this week, on his word alone, and watch what he does on the road.

Does this mean I must obey before I am saved? No. Grace comes first: God gives life, and faith and obedience flow from it. These men did not earn their cleansing by walking; their walking was their faith, trusting a word already spoken. Faith always hears Christ’s word and acts as if it were true, because it is. You do not need to feel forgiven before you believe you are forgiven; you take him at his word, and the feelings come on the road.
verseByVerse.note: A priest had to declare a leper clean before he could rejoin the community.

parallels.desc: he shall be brought to the priest

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; and he fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks. Now he was a Samaritan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the ten, seeing that he is healed, turns back to worship at Jesus’ feet, and he is the last man anyone would have expected: a Samaritan.

Turned back. The other nine are usually called ungrateful, and it is not quite that simple. They were obeying: until a priest certified them they could not go home or touch their children. Nine men are hurrying towards what they have wanted for years, doing exactly what they were told. One of them turns round.

With a loud voice. As loudly as he had cried for mercy from a distance (v. 13): the same volume, redirected.

At Jesus’ feet, giving him thanks. The posture of worship as well as gratitude: he has worked out not only that a benefit came, but where from. Giving thanks (eucharistōn) is the word behind Eucharist, the church’s ancient name for the Lord’s Supper, the meal of thanksgiving, and here is that thanksgiving on the Samaritan border: a cleansed sinner on his face before the One who cleansed him.

Now he was a Samaritan. The punchline, delayed for effect: to many Jews a Samaritan was a heretic and a half-breed. The nine were going to the priests and the temple, the machinery of a religion this man was excluded from. So the outsider, who had no temple to report to and no certificate available to him, went to the only place that was open, and it turned out to be the right one. Jesus receives him without a word of reproach. In Christ there is neither Jew nor Samaritan; there is only a crowd of cleansed lepers at his feet, and the song never ends: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain” (Revelation 5:12).

In everyday life. Take one specific mercy from the last year and turn back with it: not a general thank you, but this one, named, out loud, to Christ. Then tell one other person what he did.

Why do outsiders so often respond better than insiders? Because they have nothing to lean on. The insider has his upbringing, his church, his knowledge, his standing, and it is very easy to receive a blessing and file it with the rest. The outsider knows he deserves nothing, so a gift astonishes him. That is why Jesus could say that tax collectors and prostitutes were going into the kingdom ahead of the religious (Matthew 21:31). The cure for a church full of insiders is not to become less churchly but to remember what we were, and where we would be if he had not turned to us first.
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans and Jews despised each other; shared misery had joined these ten.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus answered, 'Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus notices who comes back: all ten received the gift, but only the despised foreigner returned to the Giver.

Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Jesus notices our gratitude and our ingratitude. It is a rare moment in Luke, a note of something like disappointment at how he has been treated. He seldom voices it on his own behalf: when a Samaritan village would not receive him, he simply went on to another (9:53–56).

Every one of them got what he asked for. The healing was not withheld from the ungrateful. All ten were cleansed before any of them had shown what he would do about it. God “is kind to the ungrateful and the evil” (6:35).

Ordinary, not villains. The nine are down the road, doing what they were told, perhaps rushing home to their families, and that makes the question searching rather than merely sad. Nobody decided to be ungrateful. They received something enormous and moved straight on to the next necessary thing, and the next, until the healing was simply behind them. And Jesus does not say the nine failed to feel grateful; all ten were presumably delighted. He says nobody was found to return. Gratitude here is not a feeling but a change of course.

Except this foreigner. “Foreigner” (allogenēs) is a startling word: it names exactly what the stone barrier in the temple court was built to keep out: it is the word on the temple inscription, since dug up, that warned foreigners not to pass into the inner courts on pain of death. Jesus names this man by the very status the sign held against him. The only man in the story fenced out of the temple is the only one who came back to worship, to Jesus, the true temple.

The root of idolatry. Paul traces the whole downward slide of humanity to exactly this: although they knew God, they did not honour him as God or give thanks to him (Romans 1:21). Ingratitude is not a small fault of manners. It is the root of idolatry, the refusal to let the Giver be seen behind the gift.

Praise to God at the feet of Jesus. The man fell at Jesus’ feet and thanked him, and Jesus calls it returning to “give praise to God”. He does not redirect the worship, as Peter did when Cornelius fell at his feet (Acts 10:25–26). The LORD gives his glory to no other (Isaiah 42:8), and here a man gives God glory at the feet of Jesus, and Jesus calls it exactly that.

He counted to ten on that road. No mercy he gives is lost in a crowd. And when one turns round, “there is joy before the angels of God” (15:10). The Lord who asks where the nine are rejoices over the one, and his joy, not his disappointment, is the last word on that road.

Does God really mind if I forget to say thank you? Yes, because he loves you, not because he is touchy. A father minds when his child takes his gifts and never looks up, not because he needs the thanks but because the child is missing the father. Thanksgiving is how a gift becomes a meeting. And the habit protects us: the heart that gives thanks in everything (1 Thessalonians 5:18) is guarded against pride, which thinks it earned its blessings, and despair, which forgets it ever had any.

Thankful, but to whom? Gratitude has become respectable again: psychologists study it, and apps remind us to list three good things before bed. But it is curious to be told to feel thankful without being told whom to thank, for a gift implies a giver. G. K. Chesterton recalled a remark of the poet Dante Gabriel Rossetti, that the worst moment for the atheist is when he is really thankful and has nobody to thank. The nine lepers are the ancient version of a gratitude journal kept with no one in mind: glad, relieved, even thankful in a general way, and gone. Only the Samaritan follows the feeling back to its source. The gospel does not merely tell us to count our blessings; it shows us the face behind them, the one who spent his life on people who would mostly forget to come back, and at his feet gratitude finds where it was meant to go.

parallels.desc: they did not honour him as God or give thanks to him

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, 'Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus declares the Samaritan not only cleansed but saved: the faith that brought him back to Christ has made him whole. He is pronounced well by Jesus himself, before any priest has examined him.

Your faith has made you well. All ten were cleansed (vv. 14, 17), so what is left for this man to receive? The answer is in the verb. For “made you well” the ESV margin gives “has saved you”: sesōken. Luke has used the phrase twice before, and both times about something more than a body: to the woman weeping at his feet, who was forgiven (7:50), and to the woman who touched his garment (8:48). The word can mean healing or salvation, and Luke’s usage seems deliberate. Ten men were cleansed of leprosy. One was saved.

What his faith consisted of. Not much: he shouted for mercy from a distance with nine other men, obeyed an instruction that made no sense, and when he saw what had happened, turned round and went back to the one who did it. Saving faith is not a great achievement of the soul. It is an empty hand that comes back to Christ.

In the flow. A few verses earlier the apostles asked for more faith (v. 5) and were told that faith the size of a mustard seed is enough. Here is the proof: a Samaritan with almost nothing but a cry and an errand obeyed, and Jesus says that faith has saved him. Next the Pharisees will ask when the kingdom of God is coming (v. 20), while the one man who has found it is a foreigner at the King’s feet.

Can a person enjoy God’s blessings and still not be saved? Sadly, yes. Answered prayers, a healed body, a happy family, even religious experiences: all can be received from God by people who never bow to his Son (Matthew 7:22–23). The test is not what you have received but whether you have come back to the Giver. If you are uncertain, do what the Samaritan did. Do not wait to feel worthy. Turn round, go to Jesus, fall at his feet and thank him, and hear him say what he said to that man.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–37 — The Kingdom and the Coming of the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom has come in the King, and his return will be sudden, unmistakable and final, so be ready now. The Pharisees ask when the kingdom is coming, as though it were a datable event; Jesus answers that it cannot be tracked by signs, because it is already in their midst in him (vv. 20–21). He tells the disciples they will long for his presence but must not chase rumours, for his return will be as public as lightning, though first he must suffer (vv. 22–25). The days of Noah and Lot show a world caught in the middle of ordinary life (vv. 26–30), so let nothing turn the heart back (vv. 31–33), for that day will divide even those closest together (vv. 34–37).
verseByVerse.theology:
The kingdom has come in the person and work of Jesus, and it has not yet come in fullness (see the question at the end of the note on vv. 20–21).

On the verse 36 printed in some Bibles, see the textual note at the end of the note on vv. 34–37.
verseByVerse.examples:
A Christian can genuinely leave something behind and spend the rest of his life half-turned towards it, like Lot’s wife (see the note on vv. 31–32).

The disciples’ “Where, Lord?” is our instinct too (see the note on vv. 34–37).

verseByVerse.quote: Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them, 'The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, nor will they say, ‘Look, here it is!’ or ‘There!’ for behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom of God is not an event to be tracked down by watching for signs; it is already present, in the midst of the very men asking when it will come. Here the chapter turns from how disciples live to the end: Jesus answers the question about when by pointing to who.

When the kingdom would come. The question assumes a future event with a date that can be worked out, and askers who stand in no relation to it except waiting. Many in Israel expected a visible, political kingdom announced by signs: the defeat of Rome and the restoration of Israel.

Not in ways that can be observed. The word (paratērēsis) is used of a physician watching for symptoms or an astronomer observing the heavens. The kingdom is not invisible, but it is not tracked down by watching for clues, which is precisely what those who study prophecy to date the end have always done. Nor is it a place you can point to on a map, “Look, here it is!” If you need someone to show you where it is, it is not the kingdom.

In the midst of you. Jesus is speaking to Pharisees, men who had been lying in wait to catch him (11:53–54), in whose hearts the kingdom certainly was not. It is standing in the room (on the wording, see the note at the end).

The King in front of them. The kingdom is present in the person of Jesus, standing among them, and in his works: “if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (11:20). They are asking him when he will arrive. The rule of heaven, longed for by prophets and kings, did not come as a weather pattern or a political event but as a Man who could be touched, who ate with sinners and wept at graves. They were looking past him for signs, and he was the sign. And the kingdom is present wherever the King has taken his throne in human hearts by his Spirit.

Is the kingdom present or still to come? Both. It is in the midst of them, because the King is in the room; and at once Jesus speaks of the day of the Son of Man still to come (vv. 22–37). Theologians call this the already and the not yet. The King has come, won his decisive victory at the cross and the empty tomb, and reigns now from heaven; he will come again to raise the dead, judge the world and make all things new.

So is the kingdom of God a political programme? No. Christians should be good citizens, work for justice and love their neighbours in public life, and the gospel has transformed whole societies. But the kingdom is not built by votes, revolutions or legislation, and it is never identical with any nation, party or movement. “My kingdom is not of this world,” Jesus told Pilate (John 18:36). It comes where Christ is preached and believed, and it will come in fullness only when he returns. A church that confuses the kingdom with its politics will be disappointed by every election and lose its message.

Uncertain wording. The Greek entos hymōn can mean “within you”, as the King James Version renders it and the ESV margin notes, or “among you”, “in the midst of you”; some have suggested “within your reach”. The words alone do not settle it. The setting does: Jesus is answering Pharisees, not describing the inner life of believers, and he never speaks elsewhere of the kingdom as something inside every human heart. So most scholars prefer “in the midst of you” or “among you”. The verse has been carried off to mean that the kingdom is an inner spiritual light every person is born with, needing no king outside us; that cannot be got out of this text.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the alternative “the kingdom of God is within you”; “in the midst of you” fits the setting: the King stood among them.

parallels.desc: the kingdom has come upon you

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the disciples, 'The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you, ‘Look, there!’ or ‘Look, here!’ Do not go out or follow them. For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus has gone, his disciples will long to see him and be tempted by rumours of his return, but his coming will be as unmistakable as lightning across the sky. The audience has changed: this is not for the Pharisees but for the men who will still be here when he is not.

One of the days of the Son of Man. A tender sentence and a bleak one. After his departure, in persecution and waiting, his disciples will long for one of the days, an ordinary day of walking about with him, and they will not get it. He says so plainly.

Do not go out. Longing makes a person vulnerable: a man who badly wants Christ to appear is exactly the man who will travel to where somebody says he has (21:8). The instruction is blunt and doubled.

As the lightning flashes. Nobody has ever been told where the lightning was, or had to travel to see it. It fills the sky from one horizon to the other, and everybody sees it at once. His return will be sudden, visible to all, unmistakable: “every eye will see him” (Revelation 1:7). Anything that has to be pointed out is not it. Every claim that Christ has returned quietly, or secretly, or to a particular place or group, is refuted by this one sentence, spoken in advance so that his people would not spend the centuries chasing rumours.

He will not come quietly. The One who was laid unnoticed in a manger and led out of the city to die between criminals will come the second time in a glory that fills the sky. The longing of every lonely disciple will be answered in a single flash, and the face they waited for will be the one thing everyone sees.

For the believer who feels far from God. If you have known a season of unusual nearness to God and now do not, the longing is not a fault. Jesus names it and allows it; he does not offer a technique for recovering the feeling. He is not absent because you cannot feel him. He has promised to be with you always, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20), and the longing itself is a sign of his Spirit in you. Keep to the means he has given, his word, prayer, the Supper, the fellowship of his people, and wait for him. He will come.

What about people who predict the date of his return? Do not follow them. Jesus said that “concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only” (Matthew 24:36), and that it is not for us to know times or seasons (Acts 1:7). Every date ever set has passed, and many who trusted them were shipwrecked in faith. The right posture is not calculation but readiness: live every day so that you would be glad to see him come that evening. Watchfulness is a way of life, not a reading of the news.

verseByVerse.quote: But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the glory comes the cross: the Son of Man must first suffer and be rejected by his own generation. One sentence dropped into a discourse about the end changes the shape of everything around it.

He must suffer many things. “Must” is the divine necessity (dei) that has run through this Gospel since a boy in the temple said he must be in his Father’s house (2:49). The suffering is not a setback on the way to the glory: “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (24:26).

Rejected by this generation. Not Rome, though Rome will drive the nails, but “this generation”, his own people, including the Pharisees he was answering a few verses ago. Luke has recorded the prediction twice already (9:22, 44).
