He knew the scourge and the spittle and the nails, and he did not slow his pace: the Lord of glory chose rejection by his own generation so that a rejected generation could be received by his Father.

Why put it here at all? The disciples have just heard of a day of sky-filling glory, and a man can build a very attractive religion out of that alone. Jesus will not let the second coming be detached from the first. The Son of Man who comes like lightning is the same man who is going to be spat at, flogged and hung up outside a city wall, and he is going to be that first. Any hope of his return that skips the cross has the wrong person coming back.

In everyday life. It is possible to be thrilled by prophecy and unmoved by Calvary. If you think more often about the end of the world than about the cross, read Luke 22 and 23 in a single sitting this week, and ask the Spirit to move you by the suffering as much as by the glory. And if you are suffering for Christ, remember the order: first the cross, then the crown, for him and for you.

Why must he suffer? Why could God not simply forgive? Because God is just as well as merciful, and he cannot pretend sin does not matter without ceasing to be good. At the cross the Son bore the penalty our sins deserved, so that God could be both “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). To justify means to declare righteous, as a judge acquits: God counts the believer right with him because the penalty for his sin has been paid in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:21). He “was pierced for our transgressions”, and the punishment that brought us peace was laid on him (Isaiah 53:5). The “must” is not a cruel necessity imposed on an unwilling Son; it is the plan of the Father and the Son together, freely embraced in love for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of Man will come on a world absorbed in ordinary life, as the flood came on Noah’s generation, who had been warned and paid no attention.

The days of Noah. From Genesis 6–7, and Jesus treats the flood as real history. Notice what he does not say about Noah’s generation. Genesis is not gentle about them: the earth was corrupt and filled with violence, and every intention of the thoughts of their hearts was only evil continually (Genesis 6:5, 11). Jesus could have made that the point. He does not.

Eating and drinking and marrying. Four activities, and not one of them is a sin: ordinary life in a village. The problem was that they were absorbed in it and ignored God’s warnings through Noah, “a herald of righteousness” (2 Peter 2:5), living as if judgment would never come. They had a preacher and a boat going up in their own neighbourhood, and they went on eating and drinking, not because they had weighed the evidence, but because life was going on as it always had. Nobody in Noah’s village decided to drown. They simply had a normal week, and then another, until the last one.

Until the day. The ark was probably years in the building, in public. Then one day Noah went inside, and “the LORD shut him in” (Genesis 7:16), and the day he went in was the day it came. Luke does not soften “destroyed them all”, and he uses the identical phrase about Sodom two verses later.

The Son of Man in the place of the LORD. In Genesis it is the LORD who sees the earth’s corruption, sends the waters and shuts the door of the ark. Jesus calls the coming judgment “the days of the Son of Man”, his own days: he is claiming the part God played in Noah’s generation. That is why the warning is mercy: the Judge has come first to give it himself. And he is the ark as well, the refuge God has provided from the wrath to come, who took the waters of judgment over his own head so that those inside him would rise above them.

In everyday life. Look at your week: is there one hour in it given to getting ready for that day? And if you know someone who is not in the ark, do what Noah did: keep building and keep preaching.

Is it wrong, then, to enjoy ordinary life? No. Eating, drinking and marriage are good gifts of God, to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4–5), and Jesus himself came eating and drinking (7:34). Noah did not stop eating; he believed God’s word and built accordingly. Enjoy your meals, your marriage, your work, before God and with an eye on the door; just do not let them become a reason to ignore the one who gave them, or the day he has appointed.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot—they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all— so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sodom too was busy buying, planting and building on its last morning; so the day of the Son of Man will fall suddenly on a world going about its business.

The days of Lot. Jesus adds a second example, from Genesis 19, because the first could be dismissed. Noah’s flood was at the dawn of history; Sodom was a real town, in country Jesus’ hearers could have walked to.

Buying and selling, planting and building. Again not one is wicked: the busyness of a prosperous city with no thought of God. Planting and building are the most hopeful things a person can do, because both invest in a future, and that is what makes the list so bleak. On its last morning, Sodom was a town where people were putting in orchards and laying foundations.

What Jesus selects. Sodom is a byword for a particular sin, and elsewhere Scripture names its pride, excess of food, prosperous ease and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49). Jesus mentions none of it. What he selects is the property market and the planting season.

The day when Lot went out. As with Noah, the rescue of the righteous and the arrival of the judgment fall on the same day. Genesis is explicit that the angels could do nothing until Lot was out: “Escape there quickly, for I can do nothing till you arrive there” (Genesis 19:22). Then fire and sulfur, sudden and complete: the phrase “destroyed them all” is the same as for the flood, and the point is the same. No one in the city expected it that morning, and no one escaped who had not left.

When the Son of Man is revealed. Revealed means unveiled (apokalyptetai). He will not arrive from somewhere else, like a visitor; he is not absent now, merely unseen, reigning at the Father’s right hand. The day does not change where he is. It changes what can be seen, and the judgment will be as sudden and complete as Sodom’s. For those who love him, that day is not a terror but the unveiling of the One they have trusted without seeing, and they will be like him (1 John 3:2).

In everyday life. When you sign a contract, plant a garden or plan an extension this year, add a sentence to the plan: “If the Lord wills” (James 4:15). It changes nothing in the paperwork and everything in the heart.

How can a loving God destroy whole cities? Because his love is holy love, not indifference. A judge who shrugged at violence and cruelty would not be kind but complicit, and the outcry against Sodom had reached heaven (Genesis 18:20–21). Even so, God did not rush. He listened to Abraham plead, agreed to spare the city for the sake of ten righteous people (Genesis 18:32), and in the end led Lot out by the hand. He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11), and the Jesus who warns of the fire went to the cross so that people from the worst of cities could be spared it.

Will Christians be taken out of the world before the judgment, like Lot? Lot was rescued on the very day the fire fell, not years before; Noah entered the ark on the day the flood came. Many faithful Christians expect a rapture before a time of tribulation, and they love the Lord’s appearing as much as anyone. But the pattern here points to one public day on which his people are gathered to him and the world is judged (2 Thessalonians 1:6–10; see the note on vv. 34–37). Believers are not promised escape from suffering before that day; Jesus told them to expect tribulation (John 16:33). They are promised that not one of them will be lost. The Lord who took Lot by the hand will not forget a single one of his own.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. Remember Lot's wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On that day nothing left behind will be worth a single step back; remember Lot’s wife, who was brought out of Sodom but left her heart there.

On the housetop. Roofs were flat and often reached by an outside stair: he must leave with what he is wearing. Similar words in 21:21 and Mark 13:15–16 concern the flight from Jerusalem before its fall in AD 70; here the warning takes the same form but is about the last day. On the day of Christ’s coming there will be no time to save possessions, and no point. Attachment to things will be fatal.

In the field. Nothing behind a disciple is worth a step backwards, not even the field-worker’s instinct to go back and fetch one thing first. Jesus has already said that no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (9:62); here the same warning is applied to the final day.

Remember Lot’s wife. One of the shortest verses in Luke, and he does not need to tell the story. She had been brought out by the hand: the angels seized Lot and his wife and daughters and set them outside the city, “the LORD being merciful to him” (Genesis 19:16). She was rescued, past the point of danger. And she looked back to Sodom as she fled, and became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26). It sounds like a small thing punished enormously, but it was probably not mere curiosity: everything she had was in that town, and to turn round was to have her heart still in it. She was out of Sodom, and Sodom was not out of her.

Half-turned. You can meet a Christian who has genuinely left something behind and spends the rest of his life half-turned towards it: the career surrendered and still mourned, the relationship broken off and still visited in the imagination, the old life renounced and remembered fondly. He is walking forward, but not looking forward. Jesus does not say “remember Sodom”, but remember the woman who got out and did not get away.

The face that was set. Luke has already shown us the opposite of Lot’s wife, and it is Jesus himself. “When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem” (9:51), and nothing on the road turned it. Lot’s wife turned back towards the place of judgment because her heart was there. Jesus walked forward into the place of judgment because his heart was with the people he came to save. She looked back and was lost; he did not look back, and the lost are saved by it.

In everyday life. Name what you are tempted to look back to. Then tell God what it is, ask his Spirit to break its pull, and do one thing this week that puts it further behind you.

Can a true believer be lost like Lot’s wife? No one whom Christ has truly saved will finally perish (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6); God keeps his own to the end. But that promise does not make warnings like this unnecessary. They are among the very means by which God keeps us, waking us up when our hearts drift back. Lot’s wife shows what an outward rescue without an inward change looks like: someone who left Sodom with her feet but not with her heart. If this verse troubles you, that is a mercy. Turn your face to Christ, and keep it there.
verseByVerse.note: Lot’s wife looked back and was turned into a pillar of salt.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Clinging to your life is the way to lose it; letting it go into Christ’s hands is the only way to keep it. He has said this before, after Peter’s confession (9:24). Here it follows a man on a roof told to leave his goods and a woman remembered for looking back: the principle is the same, but the application has moved from a lifetime to a moment.

Seeks to preserve. To secure as one’s own possession. The man on the roof and Lot’s wife both try to keep hold of a life being taken away, and the holding on loses it. It describes how things are, not only how they ought to be: the parent who holds a child too tightly loses him; the person who cannot bear to be disliked ends up with no friendships of any weight; the man who protects his reputation above everything is eventually left with nothing but a reputation.

Whoever loses his life will keep it. “Keep” means preserve alive, keep living (zōogonēsei). Giving up your life to Christ is not a heroic sacrifice with nothing on the other side but the only route by which anything survives at all. The man who lets go is not choosing loss over gain; he is putting his life into the only hands that can keep it.

He saved others. Luke will show this sentence carried out to the letter. At the cross the rulers sneered, “He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One!” (23:35). Every voice at Golgotha urged him to preserve his life, and he would not; he committed even his spirit into his Father’s hands (23:46). The man who refused to save himself is the reason anyone else is saved, and the one life that was wholly given up is the life that was given back on the third day.

What does losing my life look like for an ordinary Christian? Rarely martyrdom, though for millions it has been. More often it is the daily surrender of what you would hold on to: obedience that costs a promotion, truth that costs a friend, money given away, a home opened when you would rather close the door, being known as a Christian at work. And at the end, dying in faith, letting go of everything into the hands of Christ. None of it is wasted; all of it is kept alive in him.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. There will be two women grinding together. One will be taken and the other left.' And they said to him, 'Where, Lord?' He said to them, 'Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
That night will divide people who lived side by side, and what decides it is not where anyone is but how each stands with the Son of Man.

Two in one bed; two women grinding. The coming of the Son of Man will divide those who were closest, outwardly the same and inwardly different. Two women at a small hand mill sat opposite each other, a task often done at dawn. One scene is at night and one by day: he may come at any hour, and from each pair one is taken.

Taken and left. The verb for “taken” can also mean “received” (John 14:3), so the word alone does not settle it; the context must, and in the examples of Noah and Lot it was the judgment that did the taking (vv. 27, 29).

Where, Lord? The disciples’ instinct, and ours. They have just been told that two people in one bed will be separated for ever, and what they want to know is the geography.

The vultures. A proverb (the ESV margin gives “eagles”; one Greek word covered both), and it tells them nothing about location, deliberately: “where” is the wrong question. As certainly as vultures gather round a dead body, judgment will fall wherever there is spiritual death, as visibly as vultures circling, and nobody will have to be told where. Those taken are taken to judgment.

The child set for the fall and rising. What divides the two in one bed is nothing the eye can see. Luke announced it at the beginning, when old Simeon took the baby in his arms and said, “Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel” (2:34), and Jesus has said it himself: he came to bring not peace but division, even within one house (12:51–53). The separation of that night will bring into the open a dividing line that already runs through households now: how each person stands with him.

The same night brings the Bridegroom. The night that brings the vultures brings the Bridegroom. For those who are his there is no terror in that separation; not one of his own will be overlooked in the dark, because the Shepherd knows every one of his sheep by name. And the Judge at whose coming the earth will tremble is the Saviour who was judged in their place, so that the day which divides the world will unite his people with him for ever.

Then what do I make of the catching up in 1 Thessalonians 4? It is real and glorious, but it is not secret: a cry of command, the voice of an archangel and the trumpet of God (1 Thessalonians 4:16). At Christ’s one return the dead in Christ rise and the living are caught up to meet him in the air, as citizens go out to meet a king and escort him into the city. Believers are not left behind, nor taken away years early; they are gathered to their Lord on the day the whole world sees him.

Will my believing spouse or parent save me on that day? No. Two in one bed, two at one mill: the nearest relationships on earth, and one is taken and the other left. You can sleep beside a believer, work beside one, be raised by one, and still be lost. Faith is personal: each must come to Christ himself. That is not a cold truth but an urgent invitation: if you have been sheltering under someone else’s faith, come to Christ for yourself today. And if you love someone who is not yet his, pray, and speak, while it is still today.

Where Christians differ: one taken, one left. Dispensationalists (who divide God’s dealings into distinct eras and keep Israel and the church apart) teach that one will be taken describes the secret rapture of believers before a tribulation, as in the novels and films about being left behind, reading it alongside the catching up of believers to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17) and his promise to take them to himself (John 14:3). This commentary’s view: those who hold that view are brothers whose hope in Christ’s coming is real; but in context, the comparisons with Noah and Lot (vv. 26–30) show that those taken are taken in judgment, like those swept away by the flood, while those left are like Noah and Lot, spared. And the vultures (v. 37) show that being taken means death. There is no secret rapture here. Christ’s coming will be visible like lightning (v. 24), and will bring both the gathering of his people and judgment, at one public return. The point is the same on any reading: be ready. Scripture names things that will come first (2 Thessalonians 2:3), but no date is given, and the day will come suddenly on all who are not watching.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 36: “Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left.” The KJV includes it, but the line is absent from the earliest manuscripts of Luke and was probably copied in from the parallel in Matthew 24:40. Modern versions put it in a footnote and keep the old numbering, which is why the gap is visible in some Bibles. Nothing has been hidden, and no teaching of Scripture depends on it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 36, “Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left,” and that “vultures” may also be rendered “eagles.”

17.text: <sup>1</sup> And he said to his disciples, “Temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come! <sup>2</sup> It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin. <sup>3</sup> Pay attention to yourselves! If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, <sup>4</sup> and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.” <sup>5</sup> The apostles said to the Lord, “Increase our faith!” <sup>6</sup> And the Lord said, “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you. <sup>7</sup> “Will any one of you who has a servant plowing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’? <sup>8</sup> Will he not rather say to him, ‘Prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you will eat and drink’? <sup>9</sup> Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? <sup>10</sup> So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.’” <sup>11</sup> On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. <sup>12</sup> And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance <sup>13</sup> and lifted up their voices, saying, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” <sup>14</sup> When he saw them he said to them, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” And as they went they were cleansed. <sup>15</sup> Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; <sup>16</sup> and he fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks. Now he was a Samaritan. <sup>17</sup> Then Jesus answered, “Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? <sup>18</sup> Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?” <sup>19</sup> And he said to him, “Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.” <sup>20</sup> Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them, “The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, <sup>21</sup> nor will they say, ‘Look, here it is!’ or ‘There!’ for behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.” <sup>22</sup> And he said to the disciples, “The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. <sup>23</sup> And they will say to you, ‘Look, there!’ or ‘Look, here!’ Do not go out or follow them. <sup>24</sup> For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day. <sup>25</sup> But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation. <sup>26</sup> Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. <sup>27</sup> They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all. <sup>28</sup> Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot—they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, <sup>29</sup> but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all— <sup>30</sup> so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed. <sup>31</sup> On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. <sup>32</sup> Remember Lot's wife. <sup>33</sup> Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it. <sup>34</sup> I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. <sup>35</sup> There will be two women grinding together. One will be taken and the other left.” <sup>37</sup> And they said to him, “Where, Lord?” He said to them, “Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.”

keyVerse.quote: Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; and he fell on his face at Jesus’ feet, giving him thanks.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on which way a person faces, and this is the man who turned round. All ten received the gift, but only one came back to the Giver, gave God praise at Jesus’ feet, and heard that his faith had made him well. Lot’s wife is his opposite: rescued, yet looking back to the world (v. 32).

17.reflection:
Jesus tells us to rebuke a brother who sins and to forgive him every time he repents, even seven times in a day (vv. 3–4). Which do you find harder, the rebuke or the forgiveness? How does remembering how much you have been forgiven change both?

The apostles ask for more faith, and Jesus answers that the size of faith matters less than the God it trusts (vv. 5–6). How has this saying been misused, and how might it encourage someone whose prayers have not been answered as they hoped?

All ten lepers were cleansed, but only the Samaritan turned back to give thanks, and only to him did Jesus say, “your faith has made you well” (vv. 15–19). What blessings have you received and simply moved on from? What would it look like to turn back with one of them this week?

Jesus compares his coming to the days of Noah and Lot, when people were absorbed in ordinary, good things, and then says, “Remember Lot’s wife” (vv. 26–32). What are you most tempted to look back to, and how can we help one another keep our faces turned towards Christ?

18.title: Prayer, Humility, Children, Wealth, and Sight
18.overview:
Where we are. Jesus is still on the road to Jerusalem (9:51), and this chapter brings him to Jericho, the last town before the climb to the city. It follows straight on from his warning that the Son of Man will come suddenly after a long wait (17:22–37).

The message. God gives his kingdom to people who come to him with empty hands. Those who come with nothing but their need are filled; those sure they already have what is required go away with nothing.

Why it was said. Luke tells us. Jesus told the first parable so that his disciples would always pray and not lose heart while they waited for his return (v. 1), and the second to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and despised others (v. 9). Both dangers were real for the disciples walking with him to the cross, and for the churches Luke wrote for (on Pharisees and tax collectors, see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. It is built on pairs, and in each pair the unexpected person receives. A persistent widow and an unjust judge show that God, his opposite, will give his chosen ones justice (vv. 1–8). A Pharisee and a tax collector pray in the temple, and only the sinner who asks for mercy goes home justified (vv. 9–14). The disciples would send infants away; Jesus says the kingdom belongs to such (vv. 15–17). A rich ruler who has kept the commandments goes away very sad, while disciples who have left everything are promised many times more (vv. 18–30). At the centre stands the answer to “Then who can be saved?”: “What is impossible with man is possible with God” (v. 27). The Twelve cannot understand the third prediction of the cross (vv. 31–34), while a blind beggar who will not be silenced sees exactly who Jesus is (vv. 35–43).

Where it leads. The chapter shows how God does the impossible: the Son of Man goes up to Jerusalem to be mocked, killed and raised (vv. 31–33). He is the true sacrifice the tax collector asked God to accept, the Chosen One in whom the elect are heard, the only man who truly kept the commandments the ruler claimed, and the Son of David who stops on the way to his cross for one blind beggar.

For us. Come as the widow, the tax collector, the infant and the beggar came: with empty hands, and still asking. Let go of whatever keeps your hands full, and keep praying until he comes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Persistent Widow and the Unjust Judge
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people must keep praying and never give up, because the God they cry to is nothing like a reluctant judge. Luke gives the point before the story starts (v. 1). A judge who neither fears God nor respects man faces a widow with no husband, no money and no standing, and gives her justice only to stop her wearing him down (vv. 2–5). The argument runs by contrast: if even he acts, how much more will God act for his chosen ones who cry to him day and night (vv. 6–7). Justice is certain; the question left open is whether the Son of Man will find faith when he comes (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer is not a way of overcoming God’s reluctance: the judge is the contrast, not the model (this is treated fully at vv. 6–7).

“Speedily” does not promise a quick answer by our clocks (see the note on v. 8).
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable ends by turning the question round: will the Son of Man find faith in us (see the note on v. 8)?

There is a word here for the believer whose daily prayer has quietly collapsed, who prays in a crisis but thinks regular prayer pointless since God knows what he needs. Persistent prayer is not meant to inform God. It keeps the heart turned towards the only Source of help.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. He said, 'In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus wants his disciples to keep praying and never give up, and he says so before the story begins.

The link. Jesus has just warned of a long wait before the Son of Man comes without warning (17:22–37). How should his disciples live in the meantime? By prayer.

Always to pray and not lose heart. Losing heart (enkakein) means growing weary, giving out. The alternative to persistent prayer is not some other spiritual activity; it is quitting. And the command itself reveals God: the Lord of heaven wants to be asked. He has not left a universe running without him; he has opened his door to the weak and told them to keep knocking.

Neither feared God nor respected man. The Old Testament asks two things of a judge: that he fear God and that he regard the people in front of him (2 Chronicles 19:6–7). This man has neither, and Luke says so twice, here and in the man’s own mouth (v. 4). He is in the story to be the opposite of God.

The teacher who never stopped praying. The one who tells this parable is the most persistent man of prayer in the Gospels. Luke, more than any other Gospel writer, shows him praying (3:21; 5:16; 6:12; 9:29), and he will die praying (23:46). He asks his disciples to walk a road he walked every day, and never once gave up.

In everyday life. Most of us do not stop praying by a decision. We drift, and one day the old request is simply no longer on our lips: the prodigal, the illness, the marriage, the salvation of a parent. This parable is Jesus coming after that drift. The request you quietly let go of is allowed back, and he is the one inviting it.

What does “always to pray” actually mean? Not doing nothing but pray, since Jesus also worked, ate, slept and taught, but never giving up, and living in a settled habit of turning to God: “pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17). In practice that means fixed times, morning and evening, to bring your needs and other people’s to God; short prayers through the day as things happen; and refusing to drop a request because the answer is slow. It is not a feeling of constant devotion but a direction of the heart that keeps coming back.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a widow in that city who kept coming to him and saying, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’ For a while he refused, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect man, yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A defenceless widow keeps demanding justice until a judge who cares for nothing gives it, simply to be rid of her. Justice is done in that city for the worst possible reason: one powerless woman would not go away.

A widow. In the Bible a widow is the standing example of someone defenceless: no husband to represent her, no money for a bribe, little standing in court. So the law singled her out for protection: God “executes justice for the fatherless and the widow” (Deuteronomy 10:18). The one case this judge is most obliged to hear is the one he refuses.

Kept coming. The tense means continual coming; persistence was her only weapon. She asks not for charity or revenge but for justice, a verdict rather than a favour, because she believes she is in the right.

He said to himself. In his own head the judge repeats the narrator’s verdict on him almost word for word, untroubled by what he is. He gives in not from justice, compassion or conscience, but to make it stop.

The widows’ Lord. Luke keeps putting widows in front of Jesus, and every time he is this judge’s opposite. At Nain he saw a widow following her only son’s bier, had compassion on her, and gave the boy back to his mother (7:12–15). He will single out a poor widow’s two small coins (21:1–4) and warn against the scribes who “devour widows’ houses” (20:47). The God who executes justice for the widow has come into Israel’s towns in person, and he needs no beating down: at Nain he saw the widow before she had said a word.

In everyday life. If you are fighting a long battle for justice, against an employer, a landlord, an ex-spouse, a system that will not listen, take the widow as your companion. Pursue what is right by every honest means, and bring the case to the higher court every day.

Does God answer only if I nag him? No, and the next verses say so. God is not the judge. The widow had to wear down a man who did not care; you come to a Father who does. Persistence in prayer is not a technique for overcoming God’s reluctance, because he has none, and the Son who prayed through the nights on earth always lives to make intercession for his people (Hebrews 7:25). It is what faith looks like while it waits: it keeps coming because it believes there is Someone worth coming to. Nor do many words earn a hearing (Matthew 6:7). Pray often, not because God is hard of hearing, but because you are dependent, and he loves to be asked.

Uncertain wording. “Beat me down” is a boxer’s verb, literally to strike under the eye; Paul uses it of disciplining his own body (1 Corinthians 9:27). It is not certain whether the judge means that she will wear him out, that she will shame him in public, or, half in jest, that she will end up hitting him. Most take it as a vivid way of saying “wear me out”.
verseByVerse.note: Widows had no one to plead their case; the law singled them out for protection.

parallels.desc: you shall not mistreat any widow

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said, 'Hear what the unrighteous judge says. And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If even a corrupt judge gives justice in the end, how much more will God give it to his chosen people who cry to him.

Hear what the unrighteous judge says. Jesus tells them to listen to the villain. This is an argument from the lesser to the greater, like the father who gives good gifts (11:13). It does not say, God is reluctant, so keep pestering him, but: if even a man like that gives justice in the end, how much more will the God who loves you.

Will not God give justice. Every term is set against the judge. He had no fear of God; this is God, who is just and who cares. The widow was a stranger to him; these are his elect (eklektōn), the people he has bound himself to, against whom no charge can stand because God himself justifies them (Romans 8:33). He hears each cry in the night as if it were the only one: not a judge to be beaten down, but the Father who runs to meet his child (15:20).

Who cry to him day and night? She was a nuisance at his door; they “cry to him day and night”, the language of the Psalms and of a people in exile, with a strong verb. It is the sound people make when something is badly wrong and they know whom to shout at: God’s people suffering in a hostile world, longing for justice and for Christ’s return, like the martyrs under the altar crying “how long?” (Revelation 6:10).

Will he delay long over them? Jesus raises the delay himself and does not pretend it is not there: the widow has been coming a long time, and the elect cry day and night. What he denies is that it means God does not care, which was the judge’s only reason. To people whose prayers have gone unanswered for years he says: whatever the reason for your wait, it is not that one, because the one you are asking chose you. God is patient (2 Peter 3:9), but he will not abandon his people.

Chosen in the Chosen One. Luke uses the word “elect” sparingly, and first of Christ. On the mountain the Father’s voice said of Jesus, “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” (9:35). The elect are chosen in that Chosen One and loved with the Father’s love for his Son. Their cry is heard because it comes through him, and their vindication is sure because his was: the one the rulers mocked as a Chosen One who could not save himself (23:35) was raised and seated at the Father’s right hand.

What does “elect” mean, and why mention it here? The elect are those God chose in Christ before the foundation of the world, not because of anything in them but out of sheer love (Ephesians 1:4–5). Many Christians, often called Arminian, understand election as God choosing those he foresaw would believe; Reformed churches, with this commentary, read Ephesians 1 as resting it on his free love alone, and both find in it a reason to pray with confidence. Here it is the strongest ground for confident prayer: God set his love on you before you existed, and he will not ignore you now. Election is not a puzzle to make you anxious; it is a pillow for a weary pray-er. If you are crying to him day and night for his justice and his kingdom, that cry is itself the mark of his chosen.

Uncertain wording. “Will he delay long over them?” renders a compressed Greek phrase (makrothymei ep’ autois) whose verb usually means to be patient or slow to anger. It can be read as a question (will he keep them waiting?), as a statement (he is patient with them), or as a clause tied to their crying (even while he bears long with them). The likely sense, as in the ESV, is a question expecting the answer no, which verse 8 gives.
verseByVerse.note: The argument runs from the lesser to the greater: if even this judge acts, how much more God.

parallels.desc: I cry out day and night before you

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will certainly give his people justice; the open question is whether the Son of Man will find them still trusting and praying when he comes.

Speedily. The word seems not to fit real life, for many have prayed for the same thing for a decade or more. It does not promise a quick answer by our clocks: “with the Lord one day is as a thousand years” (2 Peter 3:8). It means that when God moves he does not drag his feet, and that nothing is being held up by reluctance at his end.

What the elect are crying for. Not relief but justice, and justice is exactly what the coming of the Son of Man brings. The one who was denied justice in Pilate’s court will return as Judge. Some prayers are answered in this life; every prayer of God’s people is answered at that day, and none of them a minute late.

Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth? The parable ends with the reverse of the question we arrive with. We ask whether God will keep faith with us; he settles that flatly and asks whether he will find faith in us. The Greek has “the faith”: the persistent, praying faith the widow has just shown. Everything turns on “nevertheless”. Justice is certain; whether those waiting for it will keep praying is left open, put to each reader. It is the very danger the parable was told to address: not that God will fail to answer, but that we stop asking.

He will find what he planted. When the Son of Man comes, he is looking for faith: the widow still knocking, the old saint still praying for her grandchildren, the persecuted church still crying “how long”. And the faith he looks for is the faith he gives, kept alive by the Spirit he sends and the intercession he makes, for he is the founder and perfecter of our faith (Hebrews 12:2). When he comes, he will find what he planted.

For the one who has prayed for years. If you are still praying after many years, and have concluded that the long silence means you are ignored, read the last line again. What he says he will be looking for when he comes is the very thing you are doing.

Does this mean true believers might lose their faith? No. Those whom God has truly called he keeps to the end (John 6:39; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5), but he keeps them through means, and a searching question like this is one of them. It is meant not to make the elect doubt their election but to keep them praying; a believer who answers, Lord, keep me faithful, is doing what the question was asked to produce. Those who finally fall away show that they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). Those who keep crying day and night are the faith he will find.

Uncertain wording. “Speedily” translates en tachei, which can mean “soon” or “suddenly”, swift once it begins, and interpreters divide. Since the parable openly admits a long wait (vv. 1, 7), the second sense fits well: when God acts for his people, finally at Christ’s return, he will act swiftly and decisively. Either way, the delay is never reluctance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — The Pharisee and the Tax Collector
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God declares right with himself the sinner who asks for mercy, not the respectable man who trusts his own record. Luke names the target first: “some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt” (v. 9). Two men go up to pray, a serious keeper of the law and a man who collected taxes for the occupying power from his own people (v. 10). The Pharisee thanks God for himself and measures himself against others (vv. 11–12); the tax collector will not lift his eyes and asks only for mercy (v. 13). Then Jesus gives a verdict no one expected: the sinner goes home justified, and the other does not (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Here, in a parable, is justification by faith alone. The tax collector brings nothing but his need, asks God to be propitiated (see the note on v. 13), and goes home justified (see the note on v. 14).
verseByVerse.examples:
The Pharisee’s religion needed somebody underneath him (see “This tax collector” at vv. 11–12), and the same thing can happen in any church.

In a small group one man shares requests that are articulate, theologically careful and mostly about what he is doing for God. A woman prays, “Lord, I do not know what to say; I am a mess; have mercy.” Prayer is not measured by eloquence but by honesty about need, and one of those two is much closer to going home justified.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt: 'Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus aims this parable at people who trust their own goodness and despise others, and he sets two very different men side by side in the temple. It is one of the clearest pictures of justification in the Gospels.

Trusted in themselves. The first parable was about persistence in prayer; this one is about humility, and again Luke names the target first: trusting in one’s own goodness to be right with God. If my standing with God rests on my own record, I must measure that record against something, and the easiest measure is other people.

Treated others with contempt. Despised, counted as nothing. It follows from the first clause as effect from cause: a man who is sure of himself by comparison needs somebody to be worse. And Luke says not “to the Pharisees” but “to some who”: a description rather than a party.

Two men went up. Probably at an hour of prayer, during the morning or afternoon sacrifice (Acts 3:1). And God built the temple not to display the righteous but to receive the guilty, with an altar of sacrifice at its heart.

A Pharisee and a tax collector. The pairing is as wide as first-century Judaism could make it. A Pharisee was not a hypocrite in the popular sense but a serious man who organised his life around the whole law, by any ordinary measure the best sort of person available. A tax collector took money from his own people for the occupying power and lived on what he could collect above the assessment (3:12). Everyone listening is sure which of them goes home right with God, which is why the last verse comes as such a shock.

The friend of sinners. The posture Jesus is exposing is the one he met wherever he went (7:34; 15:2), and the contempt that looked down on tax collectors fell, sooner or later, on the one who sat beside them. Luke uses the same verb of Herod and his soldiers, who “treated him with contempt and mocked him” (23:11). The Son of God took his place among the despised, and was despised with them, so that the despised could be received by God.

Who are the Pharisees today? Not a group across the street, but the person in any church who trusts in his own record and measures himself against others, and very often the person reading this. The trap is that this parable can produce a new kind of Pharisee: God, I thank you that I am not like that Pharisee. It is aimed at a posture of the heart, and the only safe place to stand while reading it is where the tax collector stood.
verseByVerse.note: Pharisees were respected for their devotion to the law; tax collectors were despised as collaborators and cheats. Public prayers were offered at the temple morning and afternoon.

parallels.desc: the hour of prayer, the ninth hour

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisee, standing by himself, prayed thus: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisee’s prayer is really about himself: he thanks God that he is better than other people and lists what he does beyond the law. He asks for nothing, because he thinks he needs nothing.

God, I thank you. The opening is correct; it begins exactly as a good prayer should. But he thanks God for himself, not for God’s mercy, and says “I” five times in two verses.

Another thanksgiving. Luke has recorded a very different prayer that began the same way. When the seventy-two came back, Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children” (10:21). Same opening, opposite directions: one looks up in delight at what God gives the small, the other down in satisfaction at what he has made of himself.

Not like other men... or even like this tax collector. Then the prayer becomes a list of other people, notorious sinners beside whom he naturally comes off well. And the fourth category is standing in the same courtyard: he has looked, identified him, and put him in the prayer with contempt.

I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all. The law required one fast a year, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29); strict Pharisees fasted on Mondays and Thursdays. The tithe was on farm produce, but he tithes everything that passes through his hands, probably even produce he had bought, which the grower should already have tithed (compare 11:42). This is not fraud: he does more than God asked.

The problem. He was probably telling the truth about his outward life. His problem was not insincerity, and not his deeds, but his heart: he trusted in them, compared himself with others rather than with God, and despised sinners. He came to the temple sure that God owed him something, and left the same. The temple was built for sinners who need mercy, and he asked for none.

He never once prayed it. Only one Man could have prayed the Pharisee’s prayer honestly, “I am not like other men”: Jesus, “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26). And he never once prayed it. Instead he was baptised in the line of sinners and numbered with the transgressors. The only one with a true credit balance gave it away to men with nothing, and went to the cross with our debts on his account.

Is it wrong to thank God that I am not living in some sin? Not in itself. If God has kept you from drunkenness or adultery, that is his grace, worth thanking him for. The difference is where the thanks points. Grateful humility says, but for the grace of God, there go I, and it makes you gentler with the fallen; the Pharisee’s thanks said, look at me, and it made him harder. Thanksgiving that ends with you feeling superior to someone has become the Pharisee’s prayer. Paul, who could list more virtues than this man (Philippians 3:4–6), counted them all as loss and called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15).

Uncertain wording. “Standing by himself” could also be “prayed to himself”, because the Greek phrase (pros heauton) may go with either verb. With “standing”, he stood apart, perhaps so as not to be defiled by others; with “prayed”, he prayed silently, or with himself in view. Either fits the man, whose words show plainly that the prayer was about himself.
verseByVerse.note: The law required only one yearly fast (the Day of Atonement); the Pharisee fasted twice a week and tithed even what the law did not require.

verseByVerse.quote: But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tax collector brings nothing but his sin, and asks God to turn away his anger and show him mercy. His posture, his gesture and his six words are the whole gospel from the sinner’s side.

Standing far off, eyes lowered. He comes only as far into the court as he thinks a man like him may come. Both men stand apart from the crowd, for opposite reasons: the Pharisee thinks himself above the others, the tax collector unworthy to be among them. And he cannot do the ordinary thing, standing with eyes and hands raised to heaven: “O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you” (Ezra 9:6).

Beat his breast. A sign of deep grief, and apparently unusual for a man in that culture: it belonged chiefly to mourning, to funerals. Luke records it once more, of the crowd walking home from Golgotha (23:48). He beats his heart, the source of his sin.

Be merciful to me. “Be merciful” (hilasthēti) is not the ordinary word for mercy. It means “be propitiated”, and belongs with the word for the mercy seat, where the blood of atonement was sprinkled (Hebrews 9:5; Romans 3:25). Propitiation is the turning away of God’s just anger against sin by a sacrifice that meets it, and the wonder of the gospel is that the offended God provides the sacrifice himself: “he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 4:10). The tax collector is not asking God to overlook anything but to accept atonement for him and turn away his wrath, standing in the temple, very possibly at the hour when a lamb was being offered.

The sinner. Not “a sinner” but “the sinner”, as if he were the only one: what a man says when he has stopped comparing. The Pharisee saw four categories of people and himself above them; this man cannot see anybody else in the building. He makes no promises, to leave his trade or repay what he took, though he might have thought them the price of being heard. He asks for mercy and stops talking.

No prayer surer of an answer. God answered him, though not by the animal on that day’s altar. The true sacrifice, and the true mercy seat where God’s anger is turned away, was Jesus himself, on his way to Jerusalem as he told the parable. Every sinner who beats his breast and asks for mercy is asking for the cross, and the cross has already been given. No prayer has ever been surer of an answer than a sinner’s plea for what God has already provided.

So does repentance not involve change? It does, and the change will come: Zacchaeus, another tax collector, will restore fourfold in the next chapter (19:8). But the change is the fruit of mercy, not its price. A man does not clean himself up in order to come to God; he comes to God to be cleaned. If you are waiting until you have sorted yourself out before you pray this prayer, you have reversed the gospel. Come as you are, and let the God who justifies you begin to make you new.
verseByVerse.note: Beating the breast was a sign of deep grief or remorse.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tax collector, not the Pharisee, went home right with God, for God brings down those who exalt themselves and lifts up those who humble themselves. The verdict rests on Jesus’ own authority: “I tell you.”

Went down to his house justified. A courtroom word: declared right with God, acquitted. Not made morally perfect, but declared righteous by God the Judge, and the Greek tense means it is done and it stands. A man who had defrauded his neighbours for a living left the temple with a standing before God that the most religious man in the country lacked, having offered nothing but an accurate description of himself and a plea for mercy.

Rather than the other. Not “more than”: the Pharisee was not justified, because he trusted in his good works. He went home exactly as he came, the quiet tragedy of the parable.

Everyone who exalts himself. The principle of 14:11, the passive verbs leaving God unnamed as the one who humbles and lifts up. It must not become a technique: a man who humbles himself in order to be exalted is still exalting himself. The tax collector was not performing humility but telling the truth about himself, the only humility that has ever done anybody any good.

The doctrine of justification. Here, some twenty years before Paul wrote a word about it, is the doctrine he would set out: a person is “justified by faith apart from works of the law” (Romans 3:28), and God “justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5). The tax collector contributes nothing and receives a verdict. It is the strangest courtroom in the world: the guilty man goes free and the Judge pays.

The one who went lowest. The saying has one perfect fulfilment, and it is Christ, who did not humble himself as a technique either. Though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and humbled himself to the point of death on a cross; therefore “God has highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:6–9). The tax collector goes down to his house lifted up because the Son went further down than any sinner, and was raised higher than every name.

Two ways of being your own saviour. Many modern people hold one belief more firmly than any creed: what really counts is being a good person. The secular moralist shares the Pharisee’s premise: my standing rests on my record, which looks best beside someone else’s, and today the list may read bigots, hypocrites and people who vote the other way. The psychologist Jonathan Haidt has argued that morality binds us into teams and blinds us to our own faults, and our politics, more and more a contest of contempt, bears him out. You can keep yourself at the centre by breaking the rules, like the tax collector, or by keeping them, like the Pharisee, and Jesus overturns both: rule-breakers are not told they are fine, and the decent are told that their goodness, trusted in, has become the wall between them and God. The way home is the same for both: stop comparing, and ask for mercy as the sinner.

Is it fair that the fraud goes home justified and the decent man does not? It would be unfair if justification were a prize for the best life, but it is a pardon, and a pardon can only be received by someone who admits he needs one. The Pharisee was not turned away for being too good; he received nothing because he asked for nothing. Nor was the tax collector let off lightly: his sin would be paid for in full, by the Son of God on the cross (Romans 3:25–26). Grace never pretends the standard is lower than it is; at the cross God meets it himself, for anyone, decent or not, who stops pretending.

Can I be sure I am justified? Yes. Justification is not a feeling, or a grade that rises and falls with your performance; it is God’s verdict, and he does not revise it. If you have come as the tax collector did, with nothing but your sin and his mercy in Christ, you went home justified too, and no charge can stand against you (Romans 8:33–34). When your sense of it wavers, especially after you sin, pray the same prayer again: the verdict rests on Christ’s righteousness, not yours, and his does not waver.

Where Christians differ: how are we justified? Roman Catholic teaching (Council of Trent, 1547) holds that justification is a process in which God makes us inwardly righteous by infusing grace, received through baptism and increased by good works and the sacraments; it can be lost through mortal sin and restored through penance. This commentary’s view: the Reformers rightly taught that justification is God’s legal declaration that a sinner is righteous, on the basis of Christ’s righteousness imputed (credited) to him, received by faith alone (Romans 4:3–8; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). The tax collector went home justified that day, at once, not after a long process of becoming righteous. Good works follow as the fruit of justification, never as its ground.
verseByVerse.note: “Justified” means declared right with God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom belongs to those who come with nothing, as an infant comes. Parents bring babies for Jesus to touch, and the disciples, protecting his time, turn them away (v. 15). Jesus calls the little ones to himself and forbids anyone to hinder them, using the word Luke uses again in Acts when the Ethiopian asks what prevents him from being baptised (Acts 8:36), the word for keeping out someone who should be let in (v. 16). The kingdom belongs to such, and no one enters it except by receiving it as a child receives (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Does this passage support the baptism of infants? See the box “Where Christians differ: does this passage support infant baptism?” at the end of the note on vv. 16–17 (and see on Acts 2:39). What it does say, with force, both sides agree on: no one enters the kingdom by contributing.
verseByVerse.examples:
The crowd will use the same verb of rebuke against a blind beggar later in this chapter (see the note on vv. 38–39).

When a family brings a newborn into church and asks for prayer, this passage gives the content: the child is being brought to Jesus, as these infants were, and his posture is welcome, not reluctance.

verseByVerse.quote: Now they were bringing even infants to him that he might touch them. And when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Parents bring even babies for Jesus to bless, and his disciples, meaning well, try to send them away. Straight after the tax collector, the scene shows again that the kingdom belongs to those who come with nothing.

Even infants. Babies in arms (brephē, compare 1:41), where Matthew and Mark use the broader word. Here Luke rejoins the order Mark follows (Mark 10:13).

That he might touch them. To bless them, as Jewish parents brought children to rabbis and elders for a blessing. Luke says nothing of the parents except what they wanted: contact, a conviction that whatever was in this man was worth getting their children within arm’s length of.

They rebuked them. Not cruelty. The pressure on him is enormous and the time visibly short (17:25), a queue of mothers has formed with babies who cannot understand a word, and the disciples are protecting his time. But the verb is a strong one, used of Jesus silencing a demon (4:35), and they are about to be corrected in front of the parents.

The baby who became the one they came to. Luke used the same word of the baby Jesus wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger (2:12, 16), and weeks later that baby was carried into the temple and lifted into old Simeon’s arms (2:28). Now the one carried in as a baby is the one to whom babies are carried. The Son of God passed through infancy on purpose, so infancy is not a waiting-room outside his concern; it is ground he has walked.

The judgment that never feels like a fault. The people with nothing to contribute are still the ones edged out of the schedule, not by hard men but by conscientious ones with much to get through. Children in a church service, the elderly and the disabled are easily treated as interruptions to the real ministry. Jesus treats them as the ministry. On his way to the cross, carrying the weight of the world’s salvation, the Lord of glory stopped to call infants to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus called them to him, saying, 'Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus welcomes the infants and declares that his kingdom belongs to people like them, who can only receive it as a gift. No one, of any age, enters it any other way.

But Jesus called them to him. The children, or possibly the parents; the wording allows either, and one comes with the other. “Do not hinder them” is the language for keeping out somebody who should be let in: nothing must stand between a child and Jesus.

Come to me. Jesus places the door of the kingdom not at the temple or the teachers of the law but at himself, and in the same breath gives them the kingdom. Coming to Jesus and receiving God’s kingdom are, on his own lips, one movement. Moses and John the Baptist pointed beyond themselves; Jesus points to himself, and calls the smallest people in the land to the place where the kingdom is given.

To such belongs the kingdom. Not that the kingdom is like them, nor that they may come in later: it belongs to them, and “to such” widens it past these babies to everyone of that kind, dependent, helpless, receiving as a gift.

Like a child. Not because children are innocent; anyone who has raised one knows better, and Scripture nowhere claims it (Psalm 51:5). What an infant in that world had was nothing: no legal standing, no achievements, no capacity to give anything back. It could only be carried and received. To receive the kingdom like a child is to come with no credentials, no negotiating position, and nothing whatever to bring.

Between the tax collector and the ruler. The kingdom is received, not achieved, and this saying sits between a tax collector who had nothing and a ruler who had a great deal. One verse after Jesus says the kingdom belongs to people who cannot do anything, the ruler will ask “what must I do”.

How does a grown-up receive like a child? You cannot make yourself small again, but you can stop pretending to be big. Come without credentials. Leave the record of your service and of your sins alike at the door, and pray the tax collector’s prayer (v. 13). Take him at his word. A child does not ask his father for a guarantee. When Jesus says “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37), believe that it includes you. Ask for what you need. Children ask all day, and the Father is glad to give (11:11–13). Keep receiving. The kingdom is not entered like a child and then run like an adult; every morning you are carried again. Behind all of it stands the Son himself, who lived his whole life receiving from his Father’s hand and in Gethsemane still prayed “Abba, Father” (Mark 14:36). And it is “your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (12:32). A gift is the only way it has ever been given.

Isn’t faith something we are meant to grow out of? Immanuel Kant defined enlightenment as the courage to use your own understanding without another’s guidance, and most of us have absorbed some version of it: to be grown up is to be independent, and faith is a comfort blanket a mature culture should put down. Jesus turns the picture over. The child is praised not for believing easily but for receiving, for having nothing to bring. And the dream of needing nobody is less grown up than it sounds: it is a toddler’s cry, I can do it myself, and life exposes it in a hospital bed or beside a grave. There is a childishness that refuses to grow up, and a childlikeness that has grown up enough to admit it is not God. Only the second can receive a kingdom, because only empty hands can be filled.

What of little children who die? Scripture gives no age of accountability and no explicit promise. But Luke’s own scene gives good ground for hope: these are infants who could profess nothing, and Jesus says the kingdom belongs to such. David, burying a baby son, said he would go to him (2 Samuel 12:23), and Abraham’s question still stands: “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25). The Westminster Confession (10.3) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (10.3) both state that elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when, where and how he pleases. Salvation is still by grace through Christ alone, but grieving parents may entrust their child to the one who called little ones to himself, and many believers have found in this very verse the strength to bury a baby with hope. Jesus wept at a friend’s grave (John 11:35); grief like this is not a failure of faith, and he does not hurry it.

How do we bring our children to Jesus today? Pray for them and with them every day, from before they can understand. Read them the Bible and tell them the stories of Jesus. Bring them to church, and let them see you love it. Live the gospel in front of them, including saying sorry when you sin against them. Talk naturally about God at the table and in the car (Deuteronomy 6:7). And when they come to trust Christ, as you pray they will, do not tell them they are too young to mean it. Their faith may be small and simple; so is everybody’s, at first.

Where Christians differ: does this passage support infant baptism? It is often brought to the question, and honestly it neither settles it nor is irrelevant to it. Those who baptise infants point out that Jesus takes up children who offer nothing, declares the kingdom theirs, and blesses them, and that God has dealt with families as units since Abraham, putting the covenant sign on children long before they could profess anything (Genesis 17:7; Acts 2:39). Those who baptise only believers answer, fairly, that he blesses these infants and does not baptise them, and that every baptism recorded in Acts follows a profession of faith. This commentary’s view: the passage shows Christ’s welcome for children and the need to bring them to him, but it does not mention baptism and cannot settle that question. The New Testament pattern of baptism following repentance and faith fits the credobaptist position, baptism for those who profess faith (Acts 2:38, 41; 8:12), held charitably. What it does say, with force, is what both sides agree on: no one comes into this kingdom by contributing, and every adult who enters comes in on precisely the same terms as the baby in his mother’s arms. Brothers who baptise their infants do so out of a sincere desire to bring their children to Christ, and they are honoured here.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eternal life cannot be earned, only received from God, and nothing may be held back from Christ. A rich, respected ruler asks a sincere question in the wrong shape: what must I do to inherit? (vv. 18–19). Jesus points him to commandments he believes he has kept (vv. 20–21), then lays his finger on the one thing he loves more than God, and the man goes away very sad (vv. 22–23). The camel and the needle (vv. 24–25) bring the despairing question, “Then who can be saved?”, and Jesus answers with the gospel: what is impossible with man is possible with God (vv. 26–27). Those who have left all for him lose nothing (vv. 28–30).
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus is not prescribing poverty for every disciple (see the note on vv. 22–23). He is testing this man at the one point where the first commandment would cost him.

The crowd’s dismay (“Then who can be saved?”) shows they assumed wealth was a sign of God’s favour. Jesus’ answer is the pivot of the chapter (see the note on vv. 26–27).
verseByVerse.examples:
Peter’s “we have left our homes” is better heard as a question than a boast, and the answer is generous but qualified (see the note on vv. 28–30).

A church member may serve faithfully on every committee and give generously, and still have one area he has never let Christ touch. The ruler was exemplary by most measures. The issue was not what he had done but what he would not surrender.

verseByVerse.quote: And a ruler asked him, 'Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?' And Jesus said to him, 'Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A sincere, successful man asks what he must do to earn eternal life, and Jesus makes him weigh what he means by “good”.

A ruler. After the infants who receive comes a man who wants to achieve. A ruler is a man of official standing, perhaps a synagogue leader; Matthew tells us he was young (Matthew 19:20), and he was rich (v. 23). Mark says he ran up and knelt (Mark 10:17), which is not the behaviour of a man laying a trap. Whatever is wrong here, insincerity is not it.

Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life? The shape of the question is the whole problem. It is the lawyer’s question (10:25), and it joins two words that do not belong together, “do” and “inherit”: an inheritance is the one thing nobody works for. And he asks it one verse after Jesus said the kingdom belongs to infants.

Why do you call me good? “No one is good except God alone.” Jesus makes the ruler weigh his own word: either it was flattery, or he has said far more than he intended. And if only God is good, the ruler is not good either. That is why Jesus starts here: a man who uses the word that easily assumes people can be good, and counts himself among them. Everything that follows will test that.

Is Jesus denying that he is good, or that he is God? Neither. The title is true: Jesus is good because he is God, and without sin (Hebrews 4:15). His question presses the man to think about what he is saying: if only God is good, and you call me good, what do you think I am?
verseByVerse.note: Luke calls him a ruler; Matthew adds that he was young.

verseByVerse.quote: You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery, Do not murder, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother.’' And he said, 'All these I have kept from my youth.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus points the ruler to commandments that can be seen from outside, and the man claims to have kept them all, not seeing how deep the law goes.

You know the commandments. Jesus teaches him nothing new. All five commandments come from the second table of the Ten Commandments, which governs how we treat our neighbour, and all can be seen from outside. Missing is the first table, about God himself: other gods, idols, the name, the Sabbath. Missing too is the tenth, “you shall not covet”, the one commandment that is entirely inward. That is where the ruler’s problem lies: his wealth is his god (Exodus 20:3), and he covets. Verse 22 will fill in the omission.

All these I have kept from my youth. Sincere, and outwardly perhaps true; nothing suggests he is lying. By any measure a community could apply he is an exemplary man, which is why the passage is uncomfortable. He is a warning not about scandalous living but about a life that passes every test a person can be set; a man who has passed every test he knows about will not go looking for the one he has not been given.

Another boy who kept the law. Luke has shown us one youth of whom the claim was simply true: at twelve the boy Jesus went down to Nazareth and was submissive to his parents (2:51). He honoured his father and mother as no son ever has, and loved his Father in heaven with his whole heart. The ruler’s record passed every outward test; Christ’s passed every test, the heart’s included, and the one man who could truly say “All these I have kept” was standing in front of the man who said it. And his obedience was not kept for himself. Every commandment he honoured, first table and second, outward and inward, from the manger to the cross, is counted to everyone who trusts him. The ruler offered his own righteousness and was found wanting; the believer offers nothing but Christ, and is found complete in him (Colossians 2:10).

In everyday life. Take the tenth commandment this week, “you shall not covet”, and watch your heart for seven days. You will quickly find that you have not kept all these from your youth, and you will find yourself where the tax collector stood, which is the best place to be: he went home justified.

Was the ruler really blameless? Only by outward measure. He has not understood that the law reaches the heart, where anger and lust break it (Matthew 5:21–28), and that no one keeps it as God requires (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:10–11). Unlike the tax collector, he has never seen himself as a sinner. Jesus’ next words expose his god (v. 22), and the answer to his need comes at verse 27: “What is impossible with man is possible with God.”

Why does Jesus point him to the law, if no one is saved by keeping it? Because the law is the mirror that shows us our need of a Saviour. “Through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20), and “the law was our guardian until Christ came” (Galatians 3:24). A man who thinks he is healthy will not go to a doctor, so the Physician first shows him his disease. That is still how God brings people to Christ: the commandments, rightly understood, strip away every claim of our own and leave us looking for mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus heard this, he said to him, 'One thing you still lack. Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.' But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus puts his finger on the one thing the ruler loves more than God, his wealth, and calls him to give it up and follow him, and the man cannot.

One thing you still lack. It sounds like a small balance on a settled account. It is not: his wealth had his heart, so he had broken the first commandment.

Sell all that you have. Not a universal rule for disciples: Jesus does not say it to Zacchaeus, who is also rich and gives away half (19:8–9), nor to the women who funded the ministry out of their means (8:3), nor to Martha, whose house he was glad of. The first table of the law, quietly left out two verses ago, is being applied: “You shall have no other gods before me,” and the man is asked to show that he has none, where it would cost him. It is a test designed for this one man, to show him what rules his heart.

Treasure in heaven. Not a loss, but an exchange (12:33). Everything he gives up is banked where moth and rust do not destroy.

Come, follow me. The real goal: not mainly a command about money but a call to discipleship, with an obstacle removed first. In the idol’s place Jesus puts not a further rule but himself. The whole heart that the first commandment claims for God, Jesus claims as the one to be followed, because to follow him is to have God as God. Eternal life is not found in the selling. It is found in the Person the selling would free him to follow.

Very sad. Deeply grieved (perilypos): the word is strong. He does not argue; he understood exactly what was offered and what it cost. He wanted eternal life, but not more than his money. Luke leaves him standing there, sad, in front of Jesus, unlike the tax collector and the disciples who left everything (5:11, 28).

He had already done it. Mark records that Jesus looked at this man and loved him (Mark 10:21), and he asked for everything because he was offering everything. The one who said “Sell all that you have” had already done it. He became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9), and at the end was stripped even of his clothes (23:34). He gave up all he had to purchase a people, and they are his treasure. Whatever he asks of us, he has already outgiven.

Must I sell everything to follow Jesus? Not necessarily, as Zacchaeus, Mary and Martha show. But you must be willing to, and you must give up whatever Jesus puts his finger on. For one person it is money; for another a relationship, a career, a reputation, a grudge, a habit. The question is not whether you have possessions but whether they have you. If Jesus asked for yours today, would you be sad, like the ruler, or glad, like the man who sold all he had to buy the field with the treasure (Matthew 13:44)? Whatever you cannot give up has become your god, and Jesus loves you too much to leave it there.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, seeing that he had become sad, said, 'How difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wealth makes it humanly impossible to enter God’s kingdom, because the kingdom is entered only with empty hands.

Jesus, seeing that he had become sad. Spoken over a man still standing there, by the one who would weep over Jerusalem for not knowing “the things that make for peace” (19:41–42). The Lord who will not lower the price takes no pleasure in the refusal; he tells the truth about riches with sorrow in his face, the only way it has ever been told well.

How difficult it is. Not because wealth is wicked or God objects to comfort, but because wealth is the most effective device ever invented for keeping hands full. A rich man’s difficulty is not that he loves money more than a poor man does; often he does not. It is that his life is arranged so that he never has to depend on anybody, and the kingdom is entered only by people who have run out of alternatives.

A camel through a needle. The image is deliberately absurd: the largest animal in the land, the smallest opening in common life. It is comic exaggeration, and the sentence means what it appears to mean: impossible.

Two softenings to set aside. One says the eye of the needle was a small gate in the Jerusalem wall; there is no evidence that any such gate existed, and the story appears no earlier than the Middle Ages. Another reads “rope” for “camel”, as a few late manuscripts do, but a rope will not go through a needle either.

With him, even the camel goes through. The needle’s eye is not too small for a camel because God is stingy about the entrance. It is exactly the right size for a person carrying nothing. And the Son became the poor man who went through the narrowest gate of all, the gate of death, carrying nothing but our sins, so that rich and poor alike could pass through after him.
