Is the camel me? By any global standard, almost everybody reading this is. A roof, more than one set of clothes, food for tomorrow, a phone and some money put by place you among the wealthiest people who have ever lived, so the danger in this verse is for you. The safeguard is not guilt but generosity and dependence: holding everything with an open hand, giving freely, and praying for daily bread as if you had none in the cupboard.
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who heard it said, 'Then who can be saved?' But he said, 'What is impossible with man is possible with God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one, rich or poor, can be saved by human effort, but God does what no one else can do.

Then who can be saved? Not the reaction a modern reader expects. We hear that it is hard for the rich and think wealth is a spiritual danger; they concluded that nobody could be saved at all, because they shared an assumption Luke has been dismantling since chapter 16, that prosperity was evidence of God’s approval. The rich could give alms, keep the law without economic pressure, and be visibly blessed. If they cannot be saved, who can?

The right question. Despairing and logical, it is at last the right question. The ruler asked, “what must I do?” The crowd asks who can be saved, which means saved by someone else.

Possible with God. One sentence, and it is the gospel. Jesus grants the objection: salvation is humanly impossible, for anyone, rich or poor. The camel does not get smaller and the needle does not get wider. What he adds is a different actor. Salvation is God’s work from start to finish: “by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8). The camel can go through the needle if God takes it through.

The pivot of the chapter. Everything before this has been preparing for it. The widow could not get justice; the judge gave it. The tax collector could not justify himself; God did it. The infants could not come; they were carried. And a rich man cannot enter the kingdom, and God can put him there. Salvation is not a difficult thing made possible by effort but an impossible thing done by somebody else. The impossible is his speciality, and every saved sinner is a monument to it.

How God does the impossible. Luke shows the answer in two steps, and both are Christ. A few verses on, Jesus tells the Twelve that he will be handed over, mocked, flogged and killed, and rise on the third day (vv. 31–33): that is the price of the impossible. And a chapter later a rich chief tax collector hears that today salvation has come to his house (19:9–10). What is possible with God arrives as the Son of Man, walking in through a rich man’s front door on his way to die.

In everyday life. Think of the person you have privately given up on. “Possible with God” is written over him too, and over every prayer you still pray for him. And when you look at your own heart and despair of ever changing, read the same sentence over yourself.

If salvation is God’s work, what part do I play? You repent and believe, but even that is his gift working in you. Faith is not your contribution that God rewards; it is the empty hand with which you receive what he gives. God does not drag people into the kingdom against their will; he changes the will, so that they come freely and gladly (John 6:44; Philippians 2:13). The Bible calls this the new birth, or regeneration: God gives a new heart that wants what the old one refused (Ezekiel 36:26; John 3:3–8). That is why no one in heaven will boast, and why you can pray with real hope for the hardest person you know. If God can bring a camel through a needle, he can save your brother.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said, 'See, we have left our homes and followed you.' And he said to them, 'Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever disciples give up for the kingdom, God repays many times over in this life, and with eternal life in the age to come. Jesus answers Peter’s anxious remark with a promise.

We have left our homes. This can sound like boasting, but Peter has just watched a man grieve because he could not give up his possessions, and his sentence is less a claim to merit than a question with the question mark missing: we did it; is it all right? And “our homes” is understated. Luke has recorded what they left: boats, nets, a tax booth (5:11, 28).

House or wife. Only Luke includes “wife” (also 14:26). Peter was married (4:38), and his wife later travelled with him (1 Corinthians 9:5). Leaving here means putting the kingdom first, sometimes literally leaving family behind for mission.

For the sake of the kingdom of God. This is no licence for abandoning a family: a man who will not provide for his own household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8).

Many times more in this time. Something is returned now, though not usually in the same currency. Mark names houses, brothers, mothers and children (Mark 10:30), a description of what the church turned out to be: a man who lost a family found himself in a hundred houses. But Mark adds two words Luke omits, “with persecutions”. The return is real, and not comfortable.

In the age to come. The answer to the ruler’s question (v. 18), and what he was left without. Those who give up everything for Christ gain eternal life, not as a wage for leaving but as the inheritance of those who have found the treasure worth more than everything else.

The Son who made a new family. Jesus asks nothing here he has not lived. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (9:58). When his mother and brothers came and could not reach him for the crowd, he said, “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it” (8:21). He left his home to make a household. The “many times more” that he promises is the family he himself gathered, brothers and sisters drawn round him to hear the word, and every convert who loses a home finds a place at his table.

What if following Christ has cost me my family? Then this promise is for you in particular. Many converts from other religions, and some from secular families, are cut off by parents or spouses for their faith. The church is meant to be the answer: real homes opened, real meals shared, real brothers and sisters who stand with you at weddings and funerals. If you are such a believer, tell your church what you have lost; if you are a member of a church, look for such believers and become their family. Keep praying for those who rejected you. Many have later come to faith themselves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–43 — Third Passion Prediction and the Blind Man at Jericho
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus goes up to Jerusalem to suffer as the prophets wrote, and while his closest friends cannot see it, a blind beggar sees who he is. The third and fullest passion prediction roots everything that is coming in what the prophets wrote (vv. 31–33), yet the Twelve understand none of it, and Luke says so three times (v. 34). Outside Jericho a blind beggar who has heard one sentence from a stranger calls Jesus “Son of David”, the first person in this Gospel to say it aloud (vv. 35–38). Those in front tell him to be quiet, and he cries out all the more, as the widow at the start of the chapter would have done (v. 39). Jesus stops, gives him his sight, and he follows, glorifying God (vv. 40–43).
verseByVerse.theology: Matthew and Mark place the healing as Jesus left Jericho, Luke as he drew near, and Matthew has two blind men where the others have one. On how these fit, see the note on vv. 35–37. Differences left unsmoothed are what honest reports look like.
verseByVerse.examples:
The slowness of the Twelve is a comfort to anyone who has read a passage many times and seen nothing (see the question at the end of the note on v. 34).

Then Jesus stopped for a beggar the crowd wanted silenced (see the notes on vv. 40–41 and vv. 42–43).

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the twelve, he said to them, 'See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon. And after flogging him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells the Twelve plainly that in Jerusalem he will be handed over, abused and killed, exactly as the prophets wrote, and that on the third day he will rise. It is the last and fullest of his formal announcements (9:22, 44; compare 17:25), and he takes the Twelve aside to give it.

Going up to Jerusalem. Pilgrims always went up to Jerusalem, which sits high; but Jesus’ face has been set that way since 9:51, and this is the last stretch. Straight after the promise of many times more and eternal life (v. 30), he shows what those gifts will cost, and who will pay.

Everything that is written. Only Luke adds this. What is coming is not a disaster overtaking a good plan but a text being brought to completion, Isaiah 53, Psalm 22 and much more, and Jesus will explain it after his resurrection, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets (24:25–27, 44–46).

Delivered over to the Gentiles. To Pilate and the Roman soldiers, which is new; the earlier predictions named the elders and chief priests. Under Roman rule the Jewish council could not lawfully put a man to death (John 18:31), so the leaders who rejected him would need the governor to do it.

Shamefully treated... flogging him. Insulted, outraged, abused. Isaiah’s Servant did not hide his face from disgrace and spitting (Isaiah 50:6), and the psalmist is mocked (Psalm 22:7–8). Much of the list is about humiliation rather than pain, and every item happened (22:63; 23:11, 36; Mark 14:65). The flogging was Roman scourging, with whips weighted with bone and metal, followed by crucifixion, the death Rome reserved for slaves and rebels.

On the third day. The promise of resurrection, as in the first prediction (9:22): whenever he lays out the whole road, he does not stop at the grave. Chapters 22 to 24 will carry out every word.

The turn in the verbs. Every verb in this list is passive or has somebody else as its subject: things done to a man who is not doing anything. Then the last clause turns: “he will rise”. Active, and his own. Everything up to the grave happens to him; what follows he does. The spit, the mockery, the whip and the nails were written down centuries before, and still he set his face to go up. The Son of God walked into the darkest chapter of the prophets with his eyes open, because on the far side of it was the third day, and on the far side of the third day was us.

In everyday life. Read Isaiah 53 this week, and then Luke 23, and mark every place where the one fulfils the other. Let the precision of it steady your faith: the God who kept these promises to the letter will keep every promise he has made to you.

If he knew all this, why did he go? Because he chose to. Of his own life he said, “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18). He “set his face to go to Jerusalem” (9:51), prayed in the garden, “not my will, but yours, be done” (22:42), and on the cross committed his own spirit into his Father’s hands (23:46). He went up not as a victim caught by events but as the Lamb walking to the altar, the Father’s will and his own love being one. He knew every blow in advance and went anyway, for the joy set before him (Hebrews 12:2), the joy of bringing many sons to glory (Hebrews 2:10). The prophecy is not a fate he was trapped in; it is a promise he came to keep.

verseByVerse.quote: But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Twelve understand none of it, because the meaning is hidden from them until the risen Christ opens their minds.

They understood none of these things. Three statements of one fact in one verse. Jesus has just told them plainly exactly what will happen, and twelve men who had been with him through his whole ministry took in nothing.

Hidden from them. A passive verb that leaves the one acting unnamed, as at 9:45: it points to God, and the hiding was for a time. The same Gospel ends with the risen Christ himself lifting it, when he opens their minds to understand the Scriptures (24:45). The cross is not explained by those who stand near it. It is explained by the one who hung on it, from the far side of the grave.

They did not grasp what was said. Not stupidity: they had a settled picture of the Messiah with no room in it for a crucifixion, and the words found nowhere to lodge. That is how most misunderstanding of Scripture works: we bring fixed expectations the words do not fit, without noticing we are bringing them.

A mercy to the reader. These men would shortly preach the resurrection, and the honest record of how slow they were is part of the case for their testimony: the early church would hardly invent a story in which its founders were told in advance and understood not a word.

Why do I read the Bible and sometimes get nothing from it? The disciples heard this from the Lord himself, three times, and it was hidden. Understanding came not by effort or proximity but after the resurrection, when he opened the Scriptures to them and then opened their minds (24:27, 45). So keep reading, and pray before you read: “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). Read with others, and sit under preaching. The Spirit who wrote the word is the one who gives light to it, and he delights to answer that prayer, often in a quiet moment long after the reading.

verseByVerse.quote: As he drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the roadside begging. And hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what this meant. They told him, 'Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Near Jericho a blind beggar hears that Jesus of Nazareth is passing by, and he will not let the moment pass. The crowd’s name for Jesus is accurate, but far too small.

As he drew near to Jericho. Jericho lay some 15 miles (about 25 km) from Jerusalem, down in the Jordan valley, the last town before the long climb to the city.

By the roadside begging. Pilgrims for Passover passed by in crowds, and were generous at festival time. For a blind beggar this road in this week was the best pitch of the year.

He inquired what this meant. He has to work out from sound alone that something is happening.

Jesus of Nazareth is passing by. “Passing by”: this was the man’s one chance, for as far as the Gospels tell us, Jesus never came that way again.

The man from Nazareth and the blind. The crowd’s label holds more than they knew. In the synagogue at Nazareth, at the start of his ministry, Jesus had read from Isaiah that the Spirit of the Lord had anointed him to proclaim recovering of sight to the blind, and had said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (4:18–21). Now the man from Nazareth is passing a blind beggar on the Jericho road, and the promise he read aloud is about to be kept.

One man or two, entering or leaving? Luke says the healing happened as Jesus drew near to Jericho, before he entered the town (19:1); Matthew and Mark say it was as he was going out (Matthew 20:29; Mark 10:46). Matthew also reports two blind men where Mark and Luke report one, and only Mark gives a name. The number and the name are the easy half: none of the three says only one, and one never denies two. Mark gives not just a name but a father’s name, Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus, which is how you identify a man his readers could go and ask; he had probably become known in the church, and Mark and Luke tell of that one man, while Matthew notes there were two. The harder half is probably explained by the ground itself. There were two Jerichos in the first century, roughly a mile apart. The ancient city stood as a ruin on its old mound; Herod the Great had built a splendid new town to the south with his winter palace, and the road ran between them. A traveller there was leaving one Jericho and approaching the other within minutes. Matthew and Mark may date the event by the town at Jesus’ back, Luke by the town ahead; if so, both are true of one man on one road on one afternoon. It is a likely explanation rather than a proven one, and others have been offered; believers who hold Scripture true can say so honestly and leave the detail open.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 17 miles by road east-north-east of Jerusalem. Mark names the man Bartimaeus; Matthew mentions two men.

verseByVerse.quote: And he cried out, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!' And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, 'Son of David, have mercy on me!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blind man calls Jesus the promised King and begs for mercy, and when the crowd tries to silence him he shouts all the louder.

Son of David. Told “Jesus of Nazareth”, he answers “Son of David”, a messianic title, the promised king from David’s line (2 Samuel 7:12–16), and the first time in Luke’s Gospel that any human being has used it of him aloud, and it comes from a blind beggar in the dust outside a town. He knows what the Messiah was to do: give sight to the blind (Isaiah 35:5; 61:1).

The blind who see. Twelve men who could see understood none of it (v. 34); a man who cannot see, working from a sentence shouted at him by a stranger, gets the identity right. Luke has put the two side by side on purpose.

Have mercy on me! The tax collector’s prayer again (v. 13), in substance if not in the same Greek word: a beggar with no claim, only need. He asks for mercy and leaves it to Jesus to decide what form it takes.

Those who were in front rebuked him. The verb Luke used of the disciples turning away the infants (v. 15): the people nearest Jesus repeat what the disciples were just corrected for.

All the more. He does not lower his voice; he raises it, because this is the only chance he is going to get. He has the widow’s persistence (vv. 1–8).

The King on the roadside. David’s greater Son does not rule from a distance. He rules from a roadside, from a cross, from the right hand of God, and everywhere he hears the cry of the poor.

What if the people around me discourage me from coming to Jesus? Cry out all the more, as he did. It may be friends who mock, family who think you have gone too far, a culture that calls faith foolish, or, sadly, people in the church who make the needy feel unwelcome. Jesus is not like the people at the front; he hears the voice they tried to silence. And if you are one of those at the front, near Jesus, make sure you are not the one standing between him and someone crying for mercy.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stopped and commanded him to be brought to him. And when he came near, he asked him, 'What do you want me to do for you?' He said, 'Lord, let me recover my sight.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stops on his way to the cross for one beggar, and asks him to say what he wants.

And Jesus stopped. He is on the last stretch of the road to Jerusalem, with the mockery, the flogging and the death ahead of him, and he stops, because somebody is shouting. The Son of Man’s whole progress towards his passion halts outside Jericho for one beggar the people at the front had tried to silence.

Commanded him to be brought. Those who tried to silence him now bring him (Mark 10:49).

What do you want me to do for you? On the face of it an unnecessary question, since anybody could name the need. Partly, being asked is itself a dignity: this man has spent years being talked about over his head, and it may have been long since anyone in that town put a question to him. But mostly a request has to be made; Jesus will not heal him over his head either. The mercy he shouted for has to become a specific thing he is prepared to ask for out loud, in front of the crowd that had just told him to be quiet.

Lord, let me recover my sight. He asks plainly, without hedging or wondering whether it is too much. Set that beside the ruler at verse 18: the ruler wanted to do something; the blind man asks Jesus to do something for him.

Still asked from the throne. He still stops. He has never once been too busy, never once walked past, never once told a crying sinner to be quiet. The question asked on the Jericho road is still asked from the throne. The same Jesus sits at the right hand of God, a high priest who can sympathise with our weaknesses, and the throne he sits on is a throne of grace, where the needy receive mercy and find help in time of need (Hebrews 4:15–16). The King of kings hears the specific request of the smallest of his people, the eyes, the rent, the son, the fear, and none is beneath his attention.

If God knows what I need, why should I ask? Because he wants us to. “You do not have, because you do not ask” (James 4:2). Asking is not informing God but trusting him, and it brings our needs out of the vague background of worry into the light of his face. Jesus knew what the blind man wanted and still made him say it, because the asking was part of the healing. So be specific in prayer: name the thing. “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matthew 6:8), and he still loves to hear you say it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, 'Recover your sight; your faith has made you well.' And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Jesus’ word the blind man sees and is saved, and he follows Jesus up the road, glorifying God. The chapter that began with a widow being ignored ends with a whole crowd giving praise.

Recover your sight. A word of command, no touch, no procedure, and it is done.

Your faith has made you well. Literally “has saved you” (sesōken), the phrase Luke keeps for moments when more than the body is healed, spoken also to the sinful woman (7:50), the woman with the bleeding (8:48), and the Samaritan leper (17:19). The verb means both healed and saved: something has happened here that is more than a pair of eyes.

What his faith was. There was not much of it: he had heard a name, shouted a title, refused to be silenced, and asked for the obvious thing, and Jesus calls it faith and says it has saved him.

And followed him. At once, though not told to; Jesus had sent others home (8:39). His new eyes fix on Jesus, and the first road he walks is the one up to Jerusalem. The rich ruler would not follow (v. 22); the beggar does.

Glorifying God. As the Samaritan did (17:15). The gift turns into worship, directed to God through the One who gave it.

All the people. His healing leads others to praise, including the people who had told him to be quiet. Throughout the chapter, those who come with nothing receive everything (see “The pivot of the chapter” at vv. 26–27).

Never too hurried for a sinner. The Son of Man had set out for a city where he would be handed over and killed, and his friends had not understood a word of it. On the way he gave a beggar his eyes and gained a follower. That is the grace of God in Christ: unhurried towards the cross, and never too hurried for a sinner on the way to it.

In everyday life. Tell someone this week what Christ has done for you, simply, like a man describing the day he first saw. And follow him where he is going, even when the road leads up to Jerusalem.

Does Jesus still heal the blind today? He can, and God still answers prayer for the sick, sometimes wonderfully. But this healing was a sign of who Jesus is, the Messiah who opens blind eyes as Isaiah promised, and Scripture does not promise that every prayer for healing will be granted now. The gifts of miraculous healing given to the apostles confirmed their message (Hebrews 2:3–4) and are not, in our judgment, the normal pattern for the church today (a cessationist view, held charitably towards brothers who see it differently), though God remains free to heal as he pleases, and we should pray for the sick in faith (James 5:14–15). Many faithful Pentecostal and charismatic believers expect such gifts today and pray accordingly; the difference is over the normal pattern, not over God’s power. The greater miracle, which he does every day, is the opening of blind hearts to see his glory. And the full healing of every believer’s body is certain, at the resurrection.

18.text: <sup>1</sup> And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. <sup>2</sup> He said, “In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man. <sup>3</sup> And there was a widow in that city who kept coming to him and saying, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’ <sup>4</sup> For a while he refused, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect man, <sup>5</sup> yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming.’” <sup>6</sup> And the Lord said, “Hear what the unrighteous judge says. <sup>7</sup> And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them? <sup>8</sup> I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?” <sup>9</sup> He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt: <sup>10</sup> “Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. <sup>11</sup> The Pharisee, standing by himself, prayed thus: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. <sup>12</sup> I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get.’ <sup>13</sup> But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’ <sup>14</sup> I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.” <sup>15</sup> Now they were bringing even infants to him that he might touch them. And when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them. <sup>16</sup> But Jesus called them to him, saying, “Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. <sup>17</sup> Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.” <sup>18</sup> And a ruler asked him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>19</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. <sup>20</sup> You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery, Do not murder, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother.’” <sup>21</sup> And he said, “All these I have kept from my youth.” <sup>22</sup> When Jesus heard this, he said to him, “One thing you still lack. Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” <sup>23</sup> But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich. <sup>24</sup> Jesus, seeing that he had become sad, said, “How difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! <sup>25</sup> For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup> Those who heard it said, “Then who can be saved?” <sup>27</sup> But he said, “What is impossible with man is possible with God.” <sup>28</sup> And Peter said, “See, we have left our homes and followed you.” <sup>29</sup> And he said to them, “Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, <sup>30</sup> who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life.” <sup>31</sup> And taking the twelve, he said to them, “See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. <sup>32</sup> For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon. <sup>33</sup> And after flogging him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.” <sup>34</sup> But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said. <sup>35</sup> As he drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the roadside begging. <sup>36</sup> And hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what this meant. <sup>37</sup> They told him, “Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.” <sup>38</sup> And he cried out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>39</sup> And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>40</sup> And Jesus stopped and commanded him to be brought to him. And when he came near, he asked him, <sup>41</sup> “What do you want me to do for you?” He said, “Lord, let me recover my sight.” <sup>42</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Recover your sight; your faith has made you well.” <sup>43</sup> And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.

keyVerse.quote: What is impossible with man is possible with God.
keyVerse.note: This is the pivot of the chapter. The widow could not get justice, the tax collector could not justify himself, the infants could not come and the rich man could not enter, but God does what none of them can. And the chapter at once shows how he does it: the Son of Man goes up to Jerusalem to die and rise (vv. 31–33).

18.reflection:
Jesus told the parable of the widow so that his disciples would know they ought “always to pray and not lose heart” (v. 1). What request have you quietly stopped bringing to God, and what in this parable gives you courage to take it up again?

The Pharisee was probably telling the truth about his outward life, yet he went home unjustified (vv. 11–14). Whom are you most tempted to measure yourself against, and what would it look like to pray only the tax collector’s prayer?

Jesus put his finger on the one thing the ruler loved more than God (vv. 22–23). What would you find hardest to give up if he asked for it, and how does verse 27 bring hope to that struggle?

The disciples rebuked the parents, and the crowd rebuked the blind man (vv. 15, 39). Who in our church or neighbourhood might feel turned away from Jesus, and how can we become people who bring them to him instead?

19.title: Zacchaeus, the Minas, and the Triumphal Entry
19.overview:
Where we are. Luke 19 brings the long journey to Jerusalem, begun in 9:51, to its end. Jesus passes through Jericho, the last town before the climb, tells a parable on the road, and rides down the Mount of Olives into the city and its temple.

The message. The King has come, seeking the lost and claiming what is his, and everyone must decide whether they will have him. He goes looking for a despised tax collector and turns his life inside out with one welcome. He tells his followers that his kingdom comes by way of a departure and a return, with work to do in between and a reckoning at the end. And he enters his city as the humble King of Zechariah’s prophecy, weeping over the people who will not know him and clearing his Father’s house. Salvation and judgment arrive in the same person, on the same day.

Why it was said. The crowd on the road supposed “that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately” (v. 11). Passover was near, a blind man had just been healed at Jericho, and many hoped this Galilean would take David’s throne within the week. They also despised tax collectors and expected the Messiah to keep his distance from such men (see the introduction). Luke’s readers, living after the cross and the ascension, needed to know why the King had gone away, what he had left them to do, and why Jerusalem had refused him.

How the chapter makes its case. Zacchaeus shows the King’s purpose (vv. 1–10): a rich man, the camel of 18:25, goes through the eye of the needle, because “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (v. 10). The parable of the minas corrects the timetable (vv. 11–27): a nobleman receives his kingdom in a far country, then returns to reward his faithful servants, expose the idle one and judge the citizens who said, “We do not want this man to reign over us” (v. 14). Then the parable begins to be acted out. The King rides down the Mount of Olives on a colt to his disciples’ praise (vv. 28–40), weeps over the city that “did not know the time of your visitation” (vv. 41–44), and claims the temple as a house of prayer, where the leaders seek his death and cannot touch him (vv. 45–48).

Where it leads. The three scenes show three faces of one King: the Shepherd who stops under a tree for one lost man, the nobleman who must go away before he reigns, and the King on a donkey who comes in peace and weeps for those who refuse him. He is riding to the cross, where the peace his disciples sing of, “Peace in heaven” (v. 38), will be made in his blood. And from this same hill he will later be carried up to receive the kingdom (24:50–51; Acts 1:9–12).

For us. We live in the interval the parable describes. Christ has sought us, entrusted us with his gospel, and will return. Receive him with joy as Zacchaeus did, put what he has given you to work, and do not let the day of his visitation pass you by unrecognised.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus came to find the lost, and his welcome changes a man whom nobody else could change. A rich and hated chief tax collector, the kind of man Jesus has just said can enter the kingdom only by God’s doing (18:24–27), is trying to see Jesus (vv. 1–4); but it is Jesus who stops, calls him by name and claims his house (vv. 5–6). The crowd grumbles, while Zacchaeus, already welcomed, gives half his goods away and repays fourfold (vv. 7–8). Jesus explains it all: salvation has come to this house, for the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: The episode is a picture of sovereign grace: God acts first and freely. Jesus claims the house before any repentance has been spoken, and the repayment follows as the fruit of salvation, not the reason for it (on this and on the fourfold, see the note on vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.examples: The story is also addressed to the crowd. When a church receives a man with a known past, the financial wrongdoing, the trail of damage, it can welcome him into membership and still treat him as a man on trial. That is how the grumbling crowd in the street thought, not how the Lord thought when he went in to eat with Zacchaeus.

verseByVerse.quote: He entered Jericho and was passing through. And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, on his way to the cross, passes through Jericho, and Luke points to the man everyone thought furthest from the kingdom: a chief tax collector, and rich. Only Luke records the story.

Passing through. This is the last stop before the city. Jericho lies about fifteen miles (some 25 km) from Jerusalem, and from here the road climbs through the desert to the Mount of Olives. A blind beggar has just received his sight outside the town (18:35–43), so the crowd is large, loud and celebrating, and Passover is near. Jesus was not stopping; he was walking through Jericho on his way to a cross.

Jericho. Not a backwater but the city of palms, a winter resort for the wealthy on the trade route from the east. Herod the Great had built palaces there, and his son Archelaus rebuilt them, a fact that will matter for the parable (v. 12). The customs post was probably one of the most lucrative in the country. It was also the city whose walls fell to Joshua, whose name is the Hebrew form of Jesus. The first Joshua came to Jericho to destroy it; the second comes to save a man in it.

A man named Zacchaeus. Zacchaeus is a Hebrew name, Zakkai, meaning pure or innocent. The town had long since decided he was neither. He is about to become what his name said, but not by any effort of his own.

A chief tax collector. The title (architelōnēs) appears, so far as we know, nowhere else in surviving Greek literature. He held the contract for the district, with other collectors under him, and took a percentage of everything each of them took. To his neighbours he was a traitor working for the occupying power and a thief growing fat on his own people.

Rich. By this point in Luke the word has weight, because money is the very thing that should have shut him out. Three chapters back a rich man was in torment and a beggar at Abraham’s side (16:19–31). One chapter back a rich ruler who had kept the commandments went away very sad, held by his wealth, and Jesus said that what is impossible with man is possible with God (18:23–27). The next rich man is up a tree. Zacchaeus had broken the commandments for years, and his wealth was dirty as well as heavy: he is the camel going through the eye of the needle (18:25). The difference between him and the ruler is not that one was better, but that Jesus stopped at one man’s tree. Salvation is not the reward of the less sinful.

The impossible walks into Jericho. Luke answers the question of 18:26, “Then who can be saved?”, not with a statement about divine power in general but with Jesus himself, entering Jericho on foot. The God for whom all things are possible is here in person, on his way to the cross that will pay for everything Zacchaeus ever took. The Saviour comes to where he is, and the door that wealth had shut is opened from the other side.

In everyday life. Who is the person you would least expect to become a Christian? Pray for him or her by name this week, and refuse the quiet conclusion that anyone is beyond it, yourself included.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho, near the Jordan, was a rich town on a major trade route. A chief tax collector oversaw other collectors and profited from all of them.

parallels.desc: how difficult for those who have wealth

verseByVerse.quote: And he was seeking to see who Jesus was, but on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was about to pass that way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zacchaeus kept trying to see who Jesus was, and when the crowd shut him out he set aside his dignity, ran ahead and climbed a tree.

Seeking to see who Jesus was. The verb is continuous: he kept seeking. And it is the word Jesus will use of himself seven verses later: “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost”. Two searches are running in this story, and they meet under a tree. Perhaps he had heard that this teacher was called “a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (7:34); Luke does not say what drew him.

Small in stature. A short man can usually work his way to the front. A short and hated man, in the town where he holds the tax contract, will find that the people in front of him do not move. The crowd around Jesus can be the very thing that keeps people from him.

He ran on ahead. Grown men of position did not run in that culture, it is often pointed out: it meant hitching up the long robe, which is part of what makes the father’s run so striking (15:20). A rich and powerful man sprints down the road ahead of a procession.

A sycamore tree. Not the plane tree of northern Europe but the sycamore-fig, a broad tree with a short trunk and low branches, easy to climb. Climbing is a boy’s activity, and it puts him where the whole street can see him. He was willing to look ridiculous before the people who despised him, because there was somebody he had to see. Yet Christ had chosen the tree before the man chose to climb it. The one who laid out the road through Jericho knew which branches would hold a desperate tax collector that afternoon.

Does a person have to seek Jesus before Jesus will find him? No. Zacchaeus’s seeking is real, but it is the smaller search inside a larger one: Jesus had come to Jericho to find him (v. 10). No one seeks God on his own (Romans 3:11); when anyone begins to seek, it is because the Father is already drawing him (John 6:44). So the desire you feel to know Christ is not your achievement but the first sign that he is calling you. Follow it, and do not wait to be sure of your motives first.
verseByVerse.note: The sycamore here is the sycamore-fig, a tree with a short trunk and wide, low branches, easy to climb.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, 'Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.' So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stops, calls Zacchaeus by name and claims his house for the day, and Zacchaeus receives him with joy.

He looked up. Zacchaeus. Zacchaeus climbed up to see; he had not expected to be seen. The Lord of glory, who came down from heaven, looks up into the branches at a sinner. He knew the name, and nothing in the story explains how. The good shepherd “calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3). Jericho had called him many names, none of them kind; Jesus uses the one that means pure.

Hurry and come down. The urgency is on Jesus’ side. All through Luke the one who searches is the one who hurries: the shepherd, the woman sweeping for her coin, the father running down the road.

I must stay at your house today. “Must” is dei, “it is necessary”: Luke’s word at every turning point for what God’s plan requires, ever since a boy in the temple said he must be in his Father’s house (2:49). It has governed his preaching, his cross and his journey (4:43; 9:22; 13:33); here it governs an evening in a tax collector’s dining room. “Today” is sēmeron, Luke’s word for the present moment of salvation (2:11; 4:21; 23:43), and it returns four verses later. And Jesus does not ask; he announces. To stay in a man’s house was a public sign of friendship and acceptance, and of all the houses in Jericho he chooses the house of a notorious sinner.

Received him joyfully. Welcomed him as a guest, with the joy of the found, the joy of chapter 15 (15:5–7, 9, 32). The rich ruler went away sad; Zacchaeus receives Jesus with joy. Nothing has yet been said about sin or restitution; that will come, from Zacchaeus himself.

He knows your name. He knew it before the tree, before the road, before the world (Ephesians 1:4). He stopped where you were hiding and said that he must come in, today. There is no greater honour on earth than to have the Son of God insist on being your guest.

Why does Jesus invite himself? It is a mercy. A man in Zacchaeus’s position does not issue invitations; he has learned not to put himself where he can be refused. If Jesus had waited to be asked, he would have waited under that tree until dark. Grace does not wait for us to find the courage to invite it; it comes and says, “I must stay at your house today.” That is how every conversion begins: not with our invitation to Christ but with his claim on us.

parallels.desc: I will come in to him and eat with him

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw it, they all grumbled, 'He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.' And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, 'Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd condemns Jesus for eating with a sinner, but the sinner, welcomed first, stands up and gives his wealth away and repays those he cheated.

They all grumbled. Not only the scribes and Pharisees of 15:2 but the whole crowd, probably including people who had just praised God over a blind man (18:43). The verb is the one used of Israel murmuring in the wilderness. A crowd can rejoice at a miracle of power and resent a miracle of grace in the same hour.

The guest of a sinner. Accurate, and meant as an accusation: to eat in such a house was, in their eyes, to share its uncleanness and approve its owner. They were right that Jesus had joined himself to a sinner, and wrong about which way the defilement would run. He is not made unclean by Zacchaeus; Zacchaeus is made clean by him.

Zacchaeus stood. Probably rising at the meal, the posture of a formal declaration; Luke and the new disciple both call Jesus “Lord”. The grumbling outside has been heard inside, and Zacchaeus answers it not with argument but with a changed life.

The half of my goods. Far beyond anything the law required, and nobody asked for it. Jesus told the rich ruler to sell everything (18:22) and he could not; Zacchaeus gives half, unasked. One meal with Jesus has done what no law or lecture could: the man who spent his life taking cannot wait to give.

Fourfold. The “if” is probably not doubt; it is how a man speaks when he knows very well that he has cheated people. “Defrauded” is the word John the Baptist used to the soldiers: do not extort by false accusation (3:14). Fourfold is the law’s penalty for the worst case, a stolen sheep slaughtered or sold (Exodus 22:1); for fraud the law required only the sum plus a fifth (Leviticus 6:5). He sentences himself at one of the heaviest rates in the law. With half given away and fourfold paid from the rest, he would be left with little, and he does not care.

What it does not mean. Not that his giving earned his salvation. Salvation came to his house when Jesus came (v. 9); the vow is the fruit of a heart already changed by Jesus’ welcome, not the price of it (Ephesians 2:8–10). He could give so freely because a greater restitution was about to be made for him, on a cross. Nor must every Christian give away half his goods: Zacchaeus chose it freely, undoing a fortune built on theft. The test for every believer is a loosened grip on money and an open hand.

Shame has never made anyone generous. Our culture has rediscovered the crowd’s method: name the offender and wait for the pressure to work. Sometimes exposure does stop an abuse, and justice requires that wrongs be named. But shame tells a person what he is and leaves him there, behind his wall. Jericho had been grumbling at Zacchaeus for years, and he had only grown richer and more guarded. Shame can produce compliance, resentment or despair, never a glad, open hand. What opened his was being chosen, in front of everyone, by the one man in Jericho with every right to condemn him. The gospel does not lower the standard: Zacchaeus sentences himself at the law’s heaviest rate. But it puts the welcome before the change, so that the change comes from joy instead of fear. A church that wants to see people like Zacchaeus changed must first be willing to be grumbled at for eating with them.

Must a new Christian make restitution for past wrongs? Where it is possible, yes. Repentance includes putting right what we have wrongly taken or damaged (Exodus 22:1; Leviticus 6:1–5). It is not the ground of forgiveness, which is Christ’s blood alone, but how forgiven people behave. In practice: repay what you took, return what you kept, correct the false report, confess the lie to the person it harmed. Where the person cannot be found, or repayment is beyond you, give what you can to the poor, as Zacchaeus did, and leave the rest with God. Take wise counsel where restitution might harm others, as with a confession that would wound an innocent party.

Uncertain wording. Both verbs are present tense, “I give”, “I restore”, and some modern commentators read them as habitual: Zacchaeus protests that he already gives half and already repays, so the grumbling is unjust. The grammar allows it, but the passage points the other way. A chief tax collector who already did so would not have stayed rich (v. 2), and “today salvation has come to this house” is a strange thing to say to a man who had been fine all along. And the present tense is also the ordinary form of a promise made on the spot, as a man at the altar says, “I take you.” The likely meaning is a vow from this moment: “from now on, I give; from now on, I restore”.
verseByVerse.note: The law required a thief to repay a stolen sheep fourfold; for ordinary wrongs, the amount plus a fifth.

parallels.desc: restore it in full and add a fifth

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, 'Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus declares that salvation has arrived in Zacchaeus’s house, restores him to Abraham’s family, and explains why: finding the lost is the reason he came.

Today salvation has come to this house. One of Luke’s great todays, a spine through the Gospel: unto you is born this day a Saviour (2:11); “today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (4:21); this one; and, from a cross, “today you will be with me in paradise” (23:43). Notice what has arrived: not a verdict, though he is forgiven, but salvation, which came up the road that afternoon and is sitting at the table. Salvation is first a person. Simeon held a baby and said, “my eyes have seen your salvation” (2:30). To be saved is not to be handed a pardon at the door while Jesus walks on, but to have him: “whoever has the Son has life” (1 John 5:12).

A son of Abraham. A deliberate provocation, because it is what the grumblers would have denied. In the popular reckoning a tax collector had forfeited his place in Israel. Jesus hands him the title back, as he did for a woman bent double for eighteen years, “a daughter of Abraham” (13:16). And it is more than birth: Zacchaeus is now a son of Abraham by faith as well as by blood (Galatians 3:7; Romans 4:11–12).

To seek and to save the lost. The sentence that gathers up the whole Gospel answers the grumbling of v. 7: going to a sinner’s house is not an exception for a promising case but the stated purpose of his coming. He comes for sinners, not the righteous (5:32), and saves them by giving his life. The verbs are the shepherd’s from chapter 15 and the Lord’s through Ezekiel, who condemned Israel’s faithless shepherds and promised to shepherd his flock himself: “I will seek the lost” (Ezekiel 34:11–16). The Son of Man claims to do what the LORD promised to do: to be the divine Shepherd in person. Lost means missing from where one belongs, as a coin is lost from a purse. To be lost is to be missed, and heaven noticed Zacchaeus was gone.

He never came back empty-handed. Zacchaeus climbed a tree to look at somebody who had come to town looking for him: the gospel in one afternoon. The Shepherd of Israel left the ninety-nine, walked the road through Jericho and went up to a cross, so that the lost might be found and carried home. Blessed be the Son of Man, who came to seek and to save, and who never once came back from a search empty-handed.

In everyday life. If the Son of Man came to seek the lost, his people cannot be content to wait in the building for them to arrive. Who is the Zacchaeus in your street or office, the one others avoid? Go to their house, or invite them to yours, and let them see what grace looks like at a table.

Who are the lost? Everyone, until Christ finds them. The word does not describe a special class of very bad people but all of us apart from him (Isaiah 53:6). The grumblers were as lost as Zacchaeus, and further from being found, because they did not know it. If you know you are lost, you are exactly the kind of person he came for.

Does this mean his family and servants were saved with him? Salvation came to “this house”, and the wife, children and servants who had lived on the proceeds were brought near to grace. Blessing spreads through a believing household, but each person must still believe for himself. At Philippi the jailer was told, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household,” and then Paul spoke the word to all who were in his house, and the household believed and rejoiced (Acts 16:31–34). Faith is never inherited. Children of believers have great privileges, and parents should pray and expect great things, but each child must come to Christ personally.

Where Christians differ: whom should the church baptise? Paedobaptist churches, which baptise infants, see believers’ children as included in God’s covenant promise as Abraham’s were (Genesis 17:7; Acts 2:39). Others baptise only those who confess faith themselves. This commentary’s view: believer’s baptism, because in the New Testament baptism follows a person’s own repentance and faith (Acts 2:38, 41). Faithful Christians have long differed here, and this commentary honours brothers who baptise the children of believers.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–27 — The Parable of the Ten Minas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kingdom will come, but not yet: the King must go away to receive it, and his servants must work until he returns. The crowd near Jerusalem expected the kingdom at once (v. 11), so Jesus tells of a nobleman who goes to a far country to be made king, as Herod’s son Archelaus once did (v. 12). He leaves each of ten servants the same small sum to trade with (v. 13), while his citizens send word that they do not want him (v. 14). On his return two servants are rewarded beyond all proportion (vv. 15–19); the third, who hid his mina behind a false picture of his master, loses it (vv. 20–26); and the rebels are judged (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology:
The kingdom has not yet come in full: the King goes away and returns, and his servants work in between. The reward for faithfulness in a very little is out of all proportion, and it is more responsibility, not retirement (see the note on vv. 16–17).

“To everyone who has, more will be given” describes how entrusted things behave (see the note on vv. 24–26). Luke’s parable, unlike Matthew’s talents, adds one more question: whether you wanted the King at all.
verseByVerse.examples:
The third servant’s fear was not reverence, and his picture of a harsh master was false (see the note on vv. 20–21). He is called wicked for doing nothing (vv. 22–23). A life that has carefully avoided wrong has not on that account done what it was left here to do.

Verse 27 is spoken by a king inside a story borrowed from a tyrant’s homecoming, and its horror is meant (see the note on v. 27).

verseByVerse.quote: As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. He said therefore, 'A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the crowd expected the kingdom at once, Jesus tells a parable that puts a journey and a delay before the coronation: the King must go away to receive his kingdom, and then return.

He proceeded to tell a parable. Luke, unusually, gives two reasons. He was near to Jerusalem: it was Passover season, a man who had raised the dead was at the head of the procession, and every hope seemed about to be fulfilled. And they supposed the kingdom would appear immediately, throwing off Rome and taking David’s throne. They were wrong about the timing, in a way that would nearly destroy their hope within the week, so everything in the parable inserts a delay where they expected a coronation: a departure, a long absence, work to do, and an accounting on the return.

A nobleman went into a far country. Before there is a kingdom there is a journey, and the throne is granted somewhere else. When Herod the Great died in 4 BC, his son Archelaus travelled to Rome to have his kingship over Judea confirmed by Caesar, and a delegation of fifty Jews followed him to argue against it (Josephus, Antiquities 17). Archelaus came back with a lesser title, ethnarch rather than king, and ruled so brutally that Rome deposed him ten years later. He had also rebuilt the royal palace at Jericho, the very town Jesus is leaving, and many on that road would have remembered.

The meaning. Jesus is the nobleman. The King does not receive his kingdom in Jerusalem; he receives it in a far country, and comes back. Through his death, resurrection and ascension he went to the Father, and like the Son of Man in Daniel’s vision he came to the Ancient of Days and was given “dominion and glory and a kingdom” (Daniel 7:13–14). He reigns now from heaven, and he will return (Acts 1:9–11). There is no vote left on the throne of the universe: every Christian waits, not for a candidate who might be elected, but for a King already crowned.

An error of timing, not of hope. Jesus corrects one thing only: the kingdom will come in its fullness later than they think, and there is work to do meanwhile. The church has lost each half in turn. A Christianity that expects nothing has stopped believing there is a return; a Christianity that sets dates has generally stopped working while it waits. If prophecy charts have unsettled you, set them down: Jesus told this parable to cool date-setting. Your task is not to calculate the day but to be found faithful on it.

Where Christians differ: what kind of kingdom is the nobleman receiving? Premillennial readers (Christ returning before a thousand-year reign on earth) hold that the kingdom received in heaven is set up on earth only after his return, in a thousand-year reign in which the faithful servants govern actual cities. The amillennial view (taking the thousand years of Revelation 20 as a picture of Christ’s present reign) holds that the kingdom is received at the ascension and Christ reigns now, over his church and over all things for her sake (Ephesians 1:20–23); his return will bring not a further earthly stage but the final judgment and the new creation, in which his people share his reign for ever. This commentary’s view: the second reading fits the parable and the New Testament best. Jesus says the kingdom was given to him in the far country, not that it would begin later, and Peter declares at Pentecost that Jesus has already been exalted to David’s throne (Acts 2:30–36). The return is one public event that brings reward and judgment together, as the parable itself shows (vv. 15–27), not a secret coming before the end. Brothers who hold other views, including many who expect the church to be caught up before a time of tribulation, read these texts with equal love for Scripture and confess the same returning King.
verseByVerse.note: Local rulers went to Rome to have their kingdoms confirmed. Herod’s son Archelaus did so in 4 BC, and a Jewish delegation went after him to oppose it.

parallels.desc: will you at this time restore the kingdom?

verseByVerse.quote: Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Engage in business until I come.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The King leaves every servant the same small sum and one instruction: put it to work until I come.

Ten minas. They are his slaves, trusted to manage his affairs while he is away, and each receives one mina. That detail matters. In Matthew’s similar parable of the talents, the master gives different amounts, “to each according to his ability” (Matthew 25:15). Here everybody gets exactly the same. Where the sums differ, the story is partly about ability; where they are identical, the only thing left to compare is what each man did. The two parables are cousins, but Luke’s has no great unequal sums and adds rebel citizens; Jesus taught constantly and very likely reworked his material for the moment.

A mina. A mina was a hundred denarii, about a hundred days’ wages for a labourer. For a nobleman about to receive a kingdom it is a trifle: a test of faithfulness in small things (16:10).

What is the mina? The parable does not say. Because each servant receives the same, it most likely pictures what all disciples equally receive: the gospel, the knowledge of the King, and the calling to serve him while he is away. Gifts, money and opportunities that differ are better pictured by Matthew’s talents. No servant can say he was given nothing. Every believer has the gospel, and every believer is sent to trade with it.

Engage in business. Trade with it, put it to work; not “look after this.” “Until I come” is both a promise that he will and a statement that the trading has an end date: money, an instruction to risk it, and a return that is certain but unscheduled. That is the situation of the church. He does not say what business to engage in or how he will assess them; he gives them the money and goes. So the timid servant’s failure is not a broken rule but a refusal to believe the freedom was real, and that the master would be pleased with the attempt.

The commission of the departing King. Luke records what the real King said before he went to the far country. The risen Jesus showed his disciples from the Scriptures that the Christ must suffer and rise, and told them that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (24:46–47). Then he was carried up into heaven (24:51). That is what the trading looks like: a crucified and risen Lord’s gospel, put into ordinary hands, with orders to spend it everywhere until he comes back. The gospel that the angels long to look into (1 Peter 1:12) has been put into the hands of people like us, and it is enough to fill the world.

In everyday life. Think over what Christ has entrusted to you: the gospel, the people near you, the hours of this week, your money, a skill you take for granted. Pick one and ask what trading with it would look like before Sunday, asking the Spirit for courage to risk it. Do not wait for a perfect plan; the master did not give one.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a mina was about three months’ wages for a labourer.

verseByVerse.quote: But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’ When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the nobleman is away his own citizens reject his rule, but he receives the kingdom anyway, and on his return he first calls his servants to account.

But his citizens hated him. A second plot enters the parable. These are the nobleman’s own people, just as it was Archelaus’s own subjects who sent a delegation after him.

We do not want this man. He is walking towards the city that is about to say exactly this; within days its chief priests will say, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). They object not to his qualifications but to being ruled by him at all, the cry of every human heart since Eden that will not have God for its King. Today the cry is usually quieter: glad of his help, not of his rule. Yet no heart goes unruled. Career, approval, comfort or a person will take the throne he is refused, and none of those kings has ever died for its subjects.

Having received the kingdom. The objection was lodged and overruled far away, and the kingdom granted anyway. The nations rage, and the One who sits in the heavens laughs; he has set his King on Zion (Psalm 2:1–6). Every objection since has met the same answer: he has received the kingdom.

These servants to be called. The first thing he does on arriving with a kingdom is not to deal with the rebels but to send for his own servants. Judgment begins with the household of God (1 Peter 4:17), and all of us must stand before Christ’s judgment seat (2 Corinthians 5:10).

What it does not mean. The accounting is not a trial to decide whether the faithful servants belong to the master. They were his servants before he left, and no condemnation awaits those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). What is examined is what they did with what he gave them, and what is given is reward. That should make us serious, not afraid.

In everyday life. Where in your life are you saying, “I do not want this man to reign over me”? Rarely in words; usually in one room of the house kept locked: money, sexuality, a grudge, your ambitions, your time. Open the room to him today, while he is still asking.

Is it wrong to want rewards? No. Jesus offers them, and offers them to motivate us (6:23, 35; 12:33). The desire to hear him say “well done” is not selfish ambition but love wanting to please the one it loves. What would be wrong is to think we earn heaven, or to serve for the reward rather than for the Master. But the two do not compete: the reward is mostly the Master himself, his pleasure, his presence and a share in his work.

parallels.desc: we have no king but Caesar

verseByVerse.quote: The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten minas more.’ And he said to him, ‘Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first servant credits his master’s money with the gain, and the King praises his faithfulness in a very little with a reward out of all proportion.

Your mina has made ten minas. Not “I have made ten” but “your mina has made ten”. The servant reports a result without claiming it. Paul said the same: “it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Well done, good servant! The returning king’s first words in the parable. Before the rebels are dealt with, the man who traded faithfully hears his master say “good”, and there is no greater reward in heaven or on earth than that word from that mouth. He is praised not for being gifted but for being faithful in what the master calls “a very little”.

Ten cities. Now the disproportion, which is the whole point: not ten minas but cities, with people in them. The parable calls the mina small precisely to make the reward look absurd. And the reward is more responsibility: not rest, and not payment, but a larger share in the King’s rule. The popular picture of heaven is of idleness; Scripture’s runs the other way: his servants will worship him, and they will reign for ever and ever (Revelation 22:3–5; 2 Timothy 2:12). The life to come is not retirement, and the training for it is going on now.

The one Servant who earned the word. Only one servant has ever heard the Father’s approval on his own merit: “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased” (3:22). Every other “well done” is spoken over servants who have been joined to him. That is why the first servant says “your mina” and not “my work”: his trading was itself a gift, and his welcome rests on Another’s faithfulness.

In everyday life. This week will bring a lunch box packed, an email answered honestly, a child put to bed with a prayer, a lesson taught to six children. The King calls that very little, and he is watching it. And when something goes well, say aloud, “your mina did this”, and give him the credit.

Will we really rule cities? The parable uses the language of its story, but the reality behind it is that the redeemed will share in Christ’s reign over the new creation, with real responsibility, real work and real joy, when he makes all things new (Revelation 21:1–5; 22:5). It is wise not to build a map from a parable. What we are told is enough: faithfulness now is not wasted, and it is preparing you for something far greater than you can imagine.

verseByVerse.quote: And the second came, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made five minas.’ And he said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second servant gained half as much and is rewarded in proportion, with no rebuke and no comparison.

Five minas. Same sum, same absence, same instruction, half the result: less than the first, but still faithful. Over five cities: A reward proportioned to the return, and every bit as real. There are degrees of reward in the kingdom (1 Corinthians 3:12–15), but no disgrace in having fewer cities than the man next to you. The reply is shorter, with no “well done” recorded, but it is better not to press that. Luke is compressing, as he does everywhere, and the parable’s contrast is not between the ten and the five but between both of them and the man who hid his mina. Together they show the principle: the King rewards what was actually done, in proportion to it, without marking one servant against another.

He came. With a smaller result than the man before him, he came anyway and said, before the whole court, exactly what he had produced. The third servant will arrive with an explanation.

The Judge who counts small coins. The King who sets the five-mina servant over five cities without reproach is the same Lord who, in a few days, will watch a poor widow put in two small copper coins and say that she put in more than all of them (21:1–4). He measures what was given against what was held back, and he never confuses a small return with an unfaithful one.

What if I have done much less than other Christians I know? Then this verse is for you. You are not being measured against them. Faithfulness is judged by what you did with what you were given in the life God appointed you: your health, your circumstances, your years. A mother with three small children, a man caring for a dying parent, a believer with a long illness may trade quietly, and be over cities. Comparison is not the King’s method; do not make it yours. Bring him what you have, honestly, and expect his kindness.

verseByVerse.quote: Then another came, saying, ‘Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief; for I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third servant hands back the mina untouched and blames his master’s severity, but his excuse exposes his own heart.

Here is your mina. Luke calls him, literally, “the other one”. He has the mina, and that is what he thinks will save him: nothing lost, spent or risked. The others reported what the mina had made; he reports where he put it.

Laid away in a handkerchief. A cloth for wiping the face (soudarion), the word used of the cloth over Lazarus’s face (John 11:44). Burying money was the recognised secure method, and according to later rabbinic law a man who did so was not liable if it was stolen. A cloth was no such safeguard: he did not even take proper care of it.

A severe man. He offers it as an explanation; it is in fact an accusation. “Severe” is austēros, used of unripe, sour fruit and of a man with no give in him. The two charges that follow describe a profiteer, who collects where he has not invested and harvests fields he never planted. So the servant’s defence is that his master is grasping and unfair, and that his own inactivity was a rational response.

His fear was not reverence. It is not the fear of the Lord, though it can look like it. Reverence produces obedience; this produced nothing. He was too frightened to act, and called it caution; his fear was really unbelief. This is religion run on self-protection: not pleasing the master but staying out of trouble with him, which always does as little as it safely can.

His picture of the master was a slander. This master handed out money to ten men with no conditions, and has just given a servant ten cities for a mina. The servant has invented a harsh master to excuse his own doing nothing. A false view of God is never harmless, and very often it leads to a life of doing nothing for him.

The Master’s face. The servant called his master a man who takes what he did not deposit. The Son who told the story was on his way to Jerusalem to give, not to take: to pour out his blood for his people (22:20). Whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9), and nothing in that face is harsh. He wept over the city that rejected him and prayed for the men who crucified him.

What if I find myself afraid of God? The right fear is reverent awe of his holiness joined to trust in his mercy, and it draws you towards him (Psalm 130:4). The wrong fear sees a harsh taskmaster waiting to catch you out, and it drives you to hide. The cure is not to try harder but to look again at who he is, at the cross: a God who gives his Son for his enemies is not severe. As you see his love, fear of punishment gives way to the reverent, glad fear of a child (1 John 4:18).
verseByVerse.note: A handkerchief was not a safe place for money; burying it was safer.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him, ‘I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant! You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master convicts the idle servant by his own words: if he truly thought his master hard, he would at least have put the money in the bank.

With your own words. The servant has not stolen the money, wasted it or run off with it. He is called wicked for laying it away in a cloth: doing nothing with what God gives is sin. “You knew that I was a severe man?” is not an admission; the master argues from the servant’s own words: very well, suppose I am what you say.

Why then did you not put my money in the bank? There the trap closes. “Bank” is trapeza, the money-changer’s table, where deposits earned interest. It required no skill, no judgment and no courage. If the master really were a hard man, the sensible response would have been to make certain he got something. The one course his stated fear cannot justify is doing nothing. The fear was a cover story: he did nothing because he did not care about his master’s interests.

The Servant who left nothing undone. “Nothing bad was done” is the whole defence, and exactly what is condemned. Set beside him the one Servant who did not merely avoid sin. From the boy who must be in his Father’s house (2:49) to the man who committed his spirit into his Father’s hands (23:46), he did his Father’s will, and that whole-hearted obedience is counted to everyone who trusts him (Romans 5:19). Counted means credited to our account: the guilty pronounced righteous, not because they have become good but because Christ’s righteousness is reckoned to them (Romans 4:5). It is the only righteousness that will stand when the King asks what was done with his gift.

Is the third servant a believer who loses reward, or an unbeliever who is lost? Outwardly he belongs to the household: he was given a mina and called a servant. But his picture of the master as harsh shows that he never knew him, and in Matthew’s cousin-parable the worthless servant is cast into the outer darkness (Matthew 25:24–30). He represents those who are outwardly religious, perhaps in church for years, but never serve Christ because they never trusted him. Faithfulness is not the ground of salvation but the fruit of knowing a gracious master.

Then can a true Christian lose his salvation? No. Those whom God has justified he will also glorify (Romans 8:30), and no one can snatch Christ’s sheep out of his hand (John 10:28–29). The parable describes someone who was near the master and never knew him: a warning to search ourselves, not a threat hanging over those who trust Christ. A true believer may be weak, fearful and slow, and will still bring something, however small, because the Spirit is at work in him (Philippians 1:6). What the parable exposes is the settled heart that has never loved the master at all.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to those who stood by, ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’ And they said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten minas!’ ‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The idle servant’s mina goes to the most faithful, because in the King’s service gifts that are used grow and gifts that are buried are lost.

Take the mina from him. The idle man loses even what he had, and the best trader is trusted with it. The bystanders object, “Lord, he has ten minas!”, and most readers feel the same.

To everyone who has. Not a rule for distributing prizes but a description of how entrusted things behave. The saying has appeared before, attached to hearing: “Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given” (8:18). Ability grows by use. This is true of spiritual gifts, opportunities and understanding of God’s word: the one who obeys what he knows is given to know more.

From the one who has not. The third servant was still holding the mina when that was said. In the master’s reckoning a coin wrapped in a cloth is not a possession at all, and a man who hides what he was given loses even the ability to use it. Nothing is more perishable than an unexercised gift.

The enthroned King still gives. Exalted at the right hand of God, Jesus poured out the promised Holy Spirit on his waiting people at Pentecost (Acts 2:33). The nobleman who received a kingdom does not sit on it like a miser. Every increase of faith, understanding and fruitfulness in his servants is the overflow of his throne, and his treasury never runs low.

Is this the rich getting richer? No. The parable is not about money or social advantage; Luke has spent chapters warning the rich and lifting the poor (1:53; 6:20–24; 16:19–31). It is about the gifts of the King. In his kingdom those who use what he gives receive more of the same, and those who despise his gifts lose them. A poor widow who prays faithfully is the one who has; a wealthy churchgoer who buries the gospel is the one who has not.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parable ends with the King’s judgment on those who refused his reign: a terrible picture, meant as a final warning.

These enemies of mine. The citizens of v. 14 return. The servant was idle; they are open rebels.

Slaughter them before me. One of the hardest sentences in Luke, sometimes quoted as though Jesus commanded violence against opponents. But these are words spoken by a character in a story, not an instruction to disciples. The picture is borrowed from Archelaus, whose reprisals were remembered with horror. Not one command in this parable is addressed to the servants about the citizens; their whole task is to trade. Christians are never to take up the sword against those who reject Christ (22:49–51).

The horror is the point. Yet the horror of the image is not an embarrassment to be explained away. It pictures what it is to refuse a king who is coming back anyway, pointing first to the destruction of Jerusalem, which he will foretell with tears in a few minutes (vv. 41–44), and ultimately to the last judgment, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven and those who do not obey the gospel suffer “the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord” (2 Thessalonians 1:7–9).
