A judgment described this starkly by a man who will weep over the city fourteen verses later is not bloodlust. It is the last warning of someone who would give anything to be heard.

Three groups. Faithful servants rewarded, the unfaithful servant stripped, enemies destroyed: reward and judgment together, in one event, and no neutral fourth group. Everyone who hears of the King is trading for him, burying what he gave, or refusing his reign.

The rebels he visited first. Before grace found them, every one of his people was among those who said, “We do not want this man to reign over us.” The King who will summon rebels to judgment went first to a chief tax collector’s house, and was welcomed there with joy.

How can a loving Jesus speak of slaughter? Because love is not indifference. A King who did nothing about those who destroy his people would not be good. Final judgment is real and eternal, and Jesus speaks of it more than anyone in the Bible. But he is on his way to Jerusalem to bear judgment himself, so that rebels who come to him will never face it. The same Jesus prayed for the men who crucified him, “Father, forgive them” (23:34). Some early manuscripts lack that prayer, but many scholars judge it a true saying of Jesus, and most Bibles print it. The door is open now. The parable is spoken so that no one need be found among the enemies when he comes.

parallels.desc: kiss the Son, lest he be angry

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–44 — The Triumphal Entry and Jesus Weeping over Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus enters Jerusalem as the King who comes in peace, and the city that should have known him does not. He leads the climb from Jericho and sends for a colt, taking up Zechariah’s picture of the humble King (vv. 28–34). His disciples lay their cloaks on the road and praise God aloud, hailing “the King who comes in the name of the Lord” (vv. 35–38); when the Pharisees want them silenced, he answers that the stones would cry out (vv. 39–40). Then, with the city in full view, he weeps over it and foretells its destruction, because it did not know the time of its visitation (vv. 41–44).
verseByVerse.theology:
The disciples add one word to Psalm 118:26: “blessed is the King who comes” (see the note on v. 38, with why it is peace in heaven and not on earth).

If they were silent, the stones would cry out (see the note on vv. 39–40); and within a generation the stones of this city would lie in heaps (vv. 43–44).
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke’s word for the weeping is the loud one, used of Peter after the cock crowed (22:62; see the note on vv. 41–42).

A preacher on Palm Sunday may be tempted to stop at the shouting. The passage will not let him: the day is triumphant and heartbroken at once. On the visitation that saves and judges, see the note on vv. 43–44.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples, saying, 'Go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it here. If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you shall say this: ‘The Lord has need of it.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus leads the way up to Jerusalem and arranges his own entry, sending for the very animal Zechariah had named for the humble King.

He went on ahead. In front of them, leading, resolute, as when he set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51). Nobody is dragging him up that road. Jericho lies about 850 feet (260 m) below sea level and Jerusalem about 2,500 feet (760 m) above it, so the fifteen miles are a climb of some 3,400 feet (1,000 m) through the desert. He walks towards the place where the departure of his parable will begin.

Bethphage and Bethany. Villages on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem; Bethany was the home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus (John 11:1). Zechariah had prophesied that on the day of the LORD “his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives” (Zechariah 14:4).

A colt tied. The instructions are startlingly specific. Luke does not say whether this is prior arrangement or foreknowledge, but nothing about the next hour is improvised: Jesus is in control of his own entry into the city where he will die. Even the password, “The Lord has need of it”, uses ho kyrios, which to the owners could sound like simply “the master” but on Jesus’ lips means the Lord of all.

On which no one has ever yet sat. In Israel an animal never put to ordinary use was fit for sacred purposes, like the cows “on which there has never come a yoke” that drew the ark (1 Samuel 6:7). This colt is set apart for a holy use. It will carry the King.

The animal is the prophecy. A conquering king rode a horse, the animal of war. Zechariah had described the alternative: “Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9), and “he shall speak peace to the nations” (9:10). As far as the Gospels tell us, he has walked everywhere; on the one recorded occasion he rides, he chooses the very animal Zechariah named, a colt.

In everyday life. If the Lord has need of something you have, he owes you no other explanation, and he asks for ordinary things at short notice: your car on Sunday morning, your spare room, your evening for a grieving friend, your savings. Which of your possessions would you struggle to untie if two strangers came and said these words? That is the one to offer first.
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the Mount of Olives (Olivet), just east of Jerusalem. An animal never ridden was fit for a sacred purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them. And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, 'Why are you untying the colt?' And they said, 'The Lord has need of it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything happens just as Jesus said, and the owners yield their colt to the Lord who needs it.

Just as he had told them. Luke records the match on purpose, as he will with the upper room (22:13). For chapters the disciples have heard things they could neither understand nor test (18:31–34); here is a prediction they can check within the hour, and it holds to the last detail. The Lord who is right about a tethered colt can be trusted about a cross and an empty tomb.

Its owners said to them. The challenge came, precisely as he said. Only Luke mentions the owners, and the word is plural: kyrioi, literally “lords”. The lords of the colt ask, and the answer is that the Lord needs it: the lesser lords yield to the greater. The likeliest explanation of how it worked is the simplest: Jesus had friends in Bethany, and an arrangement had been made or the phrase was recognised.

The Lord who borrows. The one who owns the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10) sends two men to ask for the loan of a donkey. He was born in borrowed lodging, rode on a borrowed animal, ate his last meal in a borrowed room and was buried in a borrowed grave. He who was rich became poor for our sakes (2 Corinthians 8:9). The owner of all things became a borrower, so that we, who own nothing, might inherit all things with him.

Why would the Lord of all need anything? He does not need anything in the sense of lacking it: God is not “served by human hands, as though he needed anything” (Acts 17:25). His need here is the need of a King who has decided to use ordinary things and ordinary people in his work. That is the dignity he gives us. He could have summoned angels; he asked for a donkey from a family in that village; their name is not recorded, and their colt is in the Gospels for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it. And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples set Jesus on the colt and carpet the road with their cloaks, treating his ride into the city as a coronation.

They set Jesus on it. The cloaks go on first, because there is no saddle. And there is a royal echo: when David’s son Solomon was made king, he rode on David’s own mule to be anointed (1 Kings 1:33–40). The Son of David rides to his capital the same way.

Cloaks on the road. A gesture every Jew would recognise. When Jehu was proclaimed king, the officers “every man of them took his garment and put it under him on the bare steps”, and proclaimed, “Jehu is king” (2 Kings 9:13). Cloaks under the feet of a man are a coronation. Luke does not mention palm branches, and he does not need them.

What a cloak cost. To a poor Galilean his cloak was his blanket at night and often the most valuable thing he owned, so valuable that the law forbade a creditor to keep one overnight (Exodus 22:26–27). They lay it in the dust so that a donkey can walk over it.

Worship, not waste. Nothing is achieved by putting a coat under a colt; nobody got anything back but a dirty cloak. The gesture is pure declaration: this man is the King, and nothing I own is too good to be walked on by him. That is worship: not a transaction, but honour given because it is owed, like Mary of Bethany’s ointment (John 12:1–8).

On the road out. Within the week, other men will take his clothes from him and cast lots for them at the foot of a cross (23:34). On the road in, his people threw down everything they had so that he could pass over it. On the road out, the last garment he owned was divided by strangers. Of everyone in that procession, the only one who understood where it was going was the man on the donkey.

In everyday life. What is your cloak, the thing you value most that you could lay at his feet? Your reputation at work, your plans for retirement, your hold on a child who wants to go to the mission field. Worship is laying down something costly because he is King.

Why a donkey and not a warhorse? A horse would have announced the war against Rome that many in the crowd wanted. The donkey announces a King who comes in peace, whose victory will be won not by killing his enemies but by dying for them; his kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36). That is still how he comes: by the gentle power of the gospel, winning hearts rather than seizing territory.
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey

verseByVerse.quote: As he was drawing near—already on the way down the Mount of Olives—the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen,
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the city comes into view, the whole company of Jesus’ disciples breaks into loud praise to God for all the mighty works they have seen.

On the way down the Mount of Olives. At one point on the descent the whole city comes into view: the Kidron valley below, the wall opposite, and the temple platform filling the eye, its white stone and gold catching the light. That is where the shouting starts.

The whole multitude of his disciples. Matthew and Mark have the crowds; only Luke says it was his own followers: the many who had come with him from Galilee, the women who had provided for him, the healed and the forgiven. Their loud praise echoes his birth, when the shepherds returned “glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen” (2:20).

All the mighty works. They praise God for what they have watched him do: a widow’s son sitting up on his bier, a legion of demons driven out, five loaves and twelve baskets, a blind man at Jericho, very likely still with them and shouting loudest. They were wrong about the week ahead, but not about him. Every reason the disciples had on that hillside, we have, and the empty tomb besides.

The same hillside. Luke will bring his readers back to this slope. After his resurrection Jesus leads his disciples out as far as Bethany, blesses them, and is carried up into heaven from the mount called Olivet (24:50–51; Acts 1:9–12). Today the King comes down that hill to be crucified; then he will go up from it to the right hand of God. The road runs down to a cross and back up to a throne, over the same ground.

What if I do not feel like praising? Then do what they did: remember. Praise in Scripture is rarely a feeling first; it is a telling of what God has done, and feeling usually follows (Psalm 103:1–5). Begin with the mighty works you know for certain: the cross and the empty tomb, your own conversion, the prayers answered, the troubles survived. Say them aloud, or sing them with the church when you would rather stay silent. Praise without strong emotion is not dishonest. It is telling the truth about God.
verseByVerse.note: The road from the Mount of Olives descends into the Kidron Valley, with the city and temple in full view.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, 'Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples hail Jesus as the promised King and sing of peace in heaven, more truly than they know.

Blessed is the King. The line is Psalm 118:26, sung at the great festivals, probably to greet pilgrims arriving at Jerusalem. But the psalm reads, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD!” Luke’s disciples insert one word: “Blessed is the King who comes.” That is a claim about the man on the donkey, made in public, at Passover, in earshot of Jerusalem, and it is why the Pharisees object in the next verse.

The words he said they would say. Jesus had told Jerusalem, “you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’” (13:35). Now his own disciples say almost exactly that. Jerusalem will not say it this week; one day every tongue will.

Peace in heaven. Luke closes a circle he opened in his second chapter. Over a field outside Bethlehem the angels had sung, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased!” (2:14). Now human voices sing it back, with the terms reversed: the angels said peace on earth; the disciples say peace in heaven. Luke omits the word “Hosanna”, which his Gentile readers might not have understood, and gives us this instead.

In the flow. Only a day’s walk back Jesus told a parable to cool the hope that the kingdom would appear at once (v. 11), and now his disciples hail him as King. The shouting is true, and the parable never denied it; it told how his kingdom comes, by a journey to a far country, which for Jesus means the cross, the grave and the ascension, and then a return. The procession is the King setting out on that journey.

The singers do not know how right they are. They think they are escorting a king to a coronation; they are walking beside him to an altar, singing the anthem of a peace that will be made in blood on Friday afternoon and will hold for ever. He came once on a donkey, and he will come once more in a cloud with power and great glory (21:27). Between the two comings the hillside choir has never fallen silent, and every generation that takes up the line is right about him.

Why peace in heaven and not on earth? Because that is where things stand. There will be no peace on earth this week, only a mob, a trial, a scourging and an execution; the city of peace is about to reject it (v. 42). But the reconciliation between God and sinners is being accomplished by the very week that will look like total defeat: through the blood of his cross God made peace (Colossians 1:20). It means that God’s just anger against our sin has been dealt with, so that God is no longer against the sinner who trusts Christ. That is propitiation: Christ’s death turning God’s wrath away by taking it on himself (Romans 3:25). It is not first a calm feeling in us but a changed standing with God (Romans 5:1, 10). Peace on earth will follow, first in every heart that believes, and finally in a new creation without war.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
glory in the highest, peace on earth

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, 'Teacher, rebuke your disciples.' He answered, 'I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees want the praise stopped, but Jesus answers that it is so rightly his that creation itself would give it if his people fell silent.

Teacher, rebuke your disciples. It is the last time the Pharisees appear in Luke’s Gospel, and their final recorded words are a request to stop the worship. Their concern may have been partly genuine: a messianic acclamation at Passover, with Roman troops reinforced in the fortress overlooking the temple because festivals produced riots, was dangerous. But listen to the address. The disciples said “King”; the Pharisees say “Teacher”, and the whole dispute lies in the difference between those two words. They ask not that he deny the claim, only that nobody say it out loud.

The very stones would cry out. The praise is not whipped up by excitement; it is owed to him, and if these voices stop, the created order will take over. Creation was made by him and for him (Colossians 1:16). Yet he chose to be praised by the voices of Galilean fishermen and healed beggars, and by ours. Let not the stones take our place.

The stones as witnesses. Habakkuk, denouncing the man who builds by injustice, says “the stone will cry out from the wall” (Habakkuk 2:11). And Jesus is looking at a city of magnificent stonework. Four verses later he will say that not one stone will be left on another (v. 44), and within a generation their ruin will bear its own witness to him.

In everyday life. Where do you go quiet about Jesus because someone would rather you did: at a family meal, in an office, with a friend who has asked a direct question? Do not mistake the pressure for wisdom. You do not have to shout, and you are not left to your own nerve: the Holy Spirit teaches his people in that very hour what to say (12:12).

Is it wrong to worship loudly or emotionally? No. Jesus refused to silence it, and Scripture is full of shouting, clapping and singing with a loud voice (Psalm 47:1; 98:4). Nor is quiet worship less real. What matters is that praise is true, directed to Christ, and done decently and in order (1 Corinthians 14:40). The danger here is the person who is embarrassed that Jesus should be praised at all, or who would rather the claim that he is King were not made in public.

parallels.desc: the stone will cry out from the wall

verseByVerse.quote: And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, saying, 'Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the height of his welcome Jesus weeps aloud over Jerusalem, because the city has missed the peace he brings and is now blind to it.

He wept over it. At the summit of the greatest public acclaim he ever received, surrounded by people singing that he is King, he is crying. Only Luke records it. “Wept” is eklausen: not quiet tears but loud weeping, the word used of mourners at a funeral. He has lamented over this city before, in the saying about the hen and her brood (13:34); now the lament becomes tears. Not for himself, though he was riding to his death, but for the city that would reject him. The King who could have ridden in as a conqueror rode in weeping.

Would that you had known. In Greek the sentence breaks off unfinished, as speech does when the speaker cannot go on. “Even you”: of all cities, the city of David and the temple, whose name was popularly understood as city of peace, did not know the things that make for peace. They are Jesus himself, the King of peace riding on Zechariah’s donkey, and the peace with God he came to bring. On this day, the day of God’s visitation, the King has come, and the city does not know him.

Hidden from your eyes. He does not say they were never offered. They are hidden now, after all the city has seen and heard. Because the people had rejected the light, it was withdrawn from them: the judgment in which God gives people over to what they have chosen (8:10; John 12:37–40).

Who hid these things from their eyes? Luke’s phrase points to God, who hides in judgment what people have refused to see (10:21; Isaiah 6:9–10; Romans 11:7–10). Yet Jerusalem’s refusal was its own, and Jesus weeps over it. God’s hardening and their responsibility stand together, and so do God’s judgment and Christ’s tears. We are not given a formula but shown both in the face of one man on a donkey, which is enough to keep us from two errors: thinking God is helpless before human refusal, and thinking he is cold towards it.

In everyday life. Who do you know who is turning away from Christ: a child, a friend, a former churchgoer? Do you weep for them, or only worry, or have you quietly stopped thinking of them? Plead for them with God. And let Christ’s tears shape how you speak to them: not judgment with a hard face, but the warning and the invitation of a Saviour who wept.

Can a person today reach a point where it is too late? Scripture warns that a person can harden himself until God gives him over (Romans 1:24; Hebrews 3:12–15); that is why today matters. But anyone troubled by the fear that it is too late shows by that very concern that God is still at work in him. The hardened do not weep over their hardness. If you want Christ, come to him; he will never cast out anyone who comes (John 6:37).

Does this mean God is finished with the Jewish people? No. Jesus foretells the judgment of a city in that generation, not that no Jew can be saved. Within weeks thousands of Jews in this same city were converted at Pentecost (Acts 2:41), and Paul insists that “God has not rejected his people” (Romans 11:1–2). Jews, like Gentiles, are saved only by faith in Jesus the Messiah, and Christians should long and pray for their salvation, as Jesus wept for it.

Where Christians differ: what does Paul mean by “all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25–26)? Some expect a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return; others read “all Israel” as the full number of the elect from Israel and the nations. This commentary’s view: without pressing one reading, Romans 11 most naturally looks for a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ, within the one people of God (see the note on Romans 11).

parallels.desc: that I might weep day and night

verseByVerse.quote: For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side and tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. And they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus foretells the siege and destruction of Jerusalem, and gives one reason: the city did not recognise the day God came to it.

A barricade around you. Within one generation every clause happened. In AD 70 the Roman general Titus besieged Jerusalem and threw up a wall right round it, nearly five miles (7 km) long, in three days, so that no one could get out and no supplies could get in; Josephus, who was there, describes it. Some scholars think Luke wrote after the event and shaped the wording to fit it; but Jesus’ warnings against the temple appear in every Gospel, and the language is the prophets’ own language of siege (Isaiah 29:3; Ezekiel 4:2).

Hem you in. The siege lasted about five months. Josephus records people eating leather, and the dead thrown over the walls because they could not be buried. The verb in “tear you down to the ground” is used in the Greek Old Testament of infants dashed against the rock in a captured city (Psalm 137:9). Huge numbers were killed, and many thousands of survivors were sold into slavery.

Not one stone upon another. As Jesus will say of the temple (21:6). The temple was burned and dismantled, and some of the great stones thrown into the street below still lie at the foot of the temple mount, the paving cracked under them.

The time of your visitation. The only reason Jesus gives for the city’s fall. “Visitation” is episkopē, God coming to see about his people, the word of Zechariah’s song: “he has visited and redeemed his people” (1:68). In Scripture a visitation is an inspection as well as a rescue, and the coming that saves those who recognise it condemns those who do not. God came to Jerusalem, on a donkey, weeping, and the city did not recognise the day. God has not changed; there is simply no other Saviour to send.

A temple that can never fall. Not one of his warnings has failed, and not one of his promises will. The same Jesus who foretold the stones thrown down gave himself to be torn down in our place, so that all who know the day of his visitation will be built into a temple that can never fall, made of living stones (1 Peter 2:4–5).

Was AD 70 the final judgment? No, but it was a preview of it. The fall of Jerusalem was a real judgment in history on the generation that rejected the Messiah, told in the language of the prophets who foretold the fall of the first temple. It also pictures the last day, when Christ will return to judge the whole world (21:25–28; Acts 17:31): the first came on one city, the second will come on all. Nor does this give any Christian licence to despise the Jewish people. Jesus wept as he said it, and so should we.
verseByVerse.note: The Romans besieged Jerusalem in AD 70, building a siege wall round it, and destroyed the city and temple. A “visitation” is God coming in mercy or judgment.

parallels.desc: I will encircle you with towers

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–48 — The Cleansing of the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The King claims his Father’s house, and the leaders resolve to destroy him. Luke gives the clearing a single clause and gives his space to the words: two Scriptures set side by side say that God’s house was to be a house of prayer for all peoples, and it has become a den of robbers (vv. 45–46). Then Jesus stays, teaching every day in the court he has cleared, as its owner. The nation’s leaders seek his death but can do nothing, because the people hang on his words (vv. 47–48).
verseByVerse.theology: The clearing is a prophet’s sign of judgment, not an attempt at reform. Set side by side, the two texts say: you were called to be a house of prayer; you have become a den of robbers (on the exact charge, see vv. 45–46). The leaders want him dead and cannot touch him (see the note on vv. 47–48).
verseByVerse.examples:
The trade Jesus drove out served the temple’s worship. This was religious activity crowding out prayer, which is much harder to see from inside, and it blocked the door for those furthest from God.

A church known mainly for its events, café and programmes, good in themselves, may find that sustained prayer together has been crowded out. The question this passage puts to any congregation is not whether the activity is legitimate, but whether a stranger walking in could find room to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold, saying to them, 'It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus enters the temple as its Lord and drives out the traders, charging that the house meant to be a house of prayer for the nations has become a robbers’ hideout.

And he entered the temple. The prophet Malachi had said it: “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple”; “but who can endure the day of his coming?” (Malachi 3:1–2). He comes as its owner, not its visitor. Luke moves straight from the tears to the temple, without the fig tree that Mark includes (Mark 11:11–14), so that the King’s first act in Jerusalem is to clean his Father’s house.

Drive out those who sold. Luke’s account is the briefest of the four (compare Mark 11:15–17; John 2:15). The selling, in the Court of the Gentiles, was not in itself illegitimate: pilgrims needed sacrificial animals and the right coin for the temple tax, and the trade was probably controlled by the high-priestly families. But this service to pilgrims had taken over the one part of the temple where a non-Jew could come and pray.

A house of prayer. The first quotation is Isaiah 56:7, which in full says “my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples”. That is the promise the Court of the Gentiles existed to fulfil, and the cattle market was standing on it. And “my house”: Jesus claims it as his own.

A den of robbers. The second quotation is Jeremiah 7:11, and it is a bomb. Jeremiah preached it at the gate of the first temple to people who believed the building guaranteed their safety, chanting, “the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD”, while cheating and oppressing outside it. It went on to announce that God would do to that house what he did to Shiloh (Jeremiah 7:14), which was to destroy it. So Jesus, just after foretelling that not one stone will be left on another, quotes the sermon that foretold the previous temple’s destruction.

The exact charge. A den is not where robbers rob but where they retreat to feel safe afterwards. The temple had become a hiding place, a religious system people used to feel secure while their lives were indefensible, as religion has been used ever since.

He built it with his blood. Some twenty years earlier a boy in this temple had said he must be in his Father’s house (2:49). Now the Son returns as its Lord, clears its outer court for the nations, and within days gives his body to be broken for the very sins that had made it a den. The Son has made a house of prayer for all peoples, and he built it with his blood.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid every sale in a church building; the offence was commerce crowding out prayer in the one court open to the nations. And it was the Messiah acting with authority over his Father’s house, not a pattern for Christians to use force.

What does this mean for the church? The church is now God’s house, built of living stones (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:19–22), and the same two tests apply. Is it a house of prayer for all peoples, where the stranger is welcomed to seek God? Or is it a den, where people come to feel safe while refusing to repent? A church can fail either test without selling anything.

Was Jesus losing his temper? No. Luke gives the action one clause and most of his space to Scripture: this was the King’s judgment, not a fit of rage. And anger at what destroys people is part of love, not its opposite. A God unmoved by religion used to fleece pilgrims and shut out the nations would not be good. The same Jesus who drove out the traders had wept over the city only a little earlier (v. 41).

Where Christians differ: is this the clearing John describes? John places a clearing of the temple near the beginning of Jesus’ ministry (John 2:13–17), while Luke places this one in the final week. Some scholars think John placed the one event early for his own purposes; others see two separate events. This commentary’s view: two events is the likelier explanation: the Passovers differ, the words differ, and a trade driven out once would soon have crept back. Believers have held either view without doubting either Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him, but they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus teaches every day in the temple he has claimed, and the leaders who want him dead can do nothing, because the people hang on his words.

Teaching daily in the temple. Having driven out the sellers, he stays, teaching every day for the rest of the week (21:37–38), as an owner, not a protester. The cleansed temple becomes a place of teaching, and the Word of God himself is its teacher.

The principal men. The chief priests of the temple establishment, the scribes who were experts in the law, and the leading laymen: between them the entire leadership of the nation, the Sanhedrin.

Were seeking to destroy him. The plot that began in Galilee (6:11; 11:53–54) is now settled; only the method remains to be found.

Nothing they could do. The most powerful men in Jerusalem want a man dead and cannot touch him, not because he is hiding, but because he stands in the most public place in the city, every day, while the people hang on his words: literally hang from him (exekremato), leaning in, spellbound. They protected him, for now. What finally breaks the deadlock is not a change in the crowd but a man on the inside who offers to hand him over quietly (22:3–6).

He let them have him. The authorities did not overpower him. He walked into that city on a colt he had sent for, cleared the temple and taught in it daily under the eyes of men who could do nothing about it, until the hour came that he had been walking towards since chapter nine, and he let them have him. His death was not a defeat. It was an offering.

In the flow. The long journey begun in 9:51 ends here. In chapter 20 the leaders send trap after trap, and each answer leaves them silent (20:26, 40).

Why did the same crowd turn against him? Many hung on his words for the excitement of a prophet who confounded the leaders, without bowing to him as King, and when he did not overthrow Rome they turned (23:13–23). It may not have been exactly the same people, for the crowd before Pilate was stirred up by the leaders (Mark 15:11), but Luke shows the people as a whole drawn into the cry (23:13). Hanging on someone’s words for a week is not the same as building your life on them (6:46–49). The test is what you do when following him becomes costly.

19.text: <sup>1</sup> He entered Jericho and was passing through. <sup>2</sup> And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich. <sup>3</sup> And he was seeking to see who Jesus was, but on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. <sup>4</sup> So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was about to pass that way. <sup>5</sup> And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.” <sup>6</sup> So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully. <sup>7</sup> And when they saw it, they all grumbled, “He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.” <sup>8</sup> And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” <sup>9</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. <sup>10</sup> For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” <sup>11</sup> As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. <sup>12</sup> He said therefore, “A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return. <sup>13</sup> Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Engage in business until I come.’ <sup>14</sup> But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’ <sup>15</sup> When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business. <sup>16</sup> The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten minas more.’ <sup>17</sup> And he said to him, ‘Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’ <sup>18</sup> And the second came, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made five minas.’ <sup>19</sup> And he said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’ <sup>20</sup> Then another came, saying, ‘Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief; <sup>21</sup> for I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.’ <sup>22</sup> He said to him, ‘I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant! You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? <sup>23</sup> Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?’ <sup>24</sup> And he said to those who stood by, ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’ <sup>25</sup> And they said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten minas!’ <sup>26</sup> ‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. <sup>27</sup> But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.’” <sup>28</sup> And when he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. <sup>29</sup> When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples, <sup>30</sup> saying, “Go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it here. <sup>31</sup> If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you shall say this: ‘The Lord has need of it.’” <sup>32</sup> So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them. <sup>33</sup> And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, “Why are you untying the colt?” <sup>34</sup> And they said, “The Lord has need of it.” <sup>35</sup> And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it. <sup>36</sup> And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road. <sup>37</sup> As he was drawing near—already on the way down the Mount of Olives—the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen, <sup>38</sup> saying, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” <sup>39</sup> And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.” <sup>40</sup> He answered, “I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.” <sup>41</sup> And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, <sup>42</sup> saying, “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. <sup>43</sup> For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side <sup>44</sup> and tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. And they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation.” <sup>45</sup> And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold, <sup>46</sup> saying to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.” <sup>47</sup> And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him, <sup>48</sup> but they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.

keyVerse.quote: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.
keyVerse.note: Jesus’ own summary of why he came answers the grumbling at Zacchaeus’s door and explains the whole chapter. The King who stops for one lost man in Jericho is the same King who weeps over the lost city and rides on to the cross to save. It is also the theme of Luke’s whole Gospel.

19.reflection:
Zacchaeus was seeking to see Jesus, but Jesus had come to Jericho to find him (vv. 3–5, 10). How does it change the way you think about your own conversion, or about someone you are praying for, to know that Christ is the one who seeks first?

The crowd grumbled at Jesus for eating with a sinner, yet his welcome did what years of their contempt never did (vv. 7–8). Where are we tempted to use shame to change people? What would it look like for our church to welcome first?

In the parable every servant receives the same mina and the same instruction (v. 13), and the third servant hides his because he thinks his master is harsh (vv. 20–21). What has Christ entrusted to you, and how might a wrong picture of God be keeping you from putting it to work?

At the height of his welcome Jesus wept over Jerusalem because it did not know the time of its visitation (vv. 41–44). Who do you know who is turning away from Christ, and how should his tears shape the way we pray for them and speak to them?

20.title: Authority, Parables, and Traps in the Temple
20.overview:
Where we are. Luke 20 is one long day in the temple in the last week before the cross. Jesus has entered Jerusalem as King and cleared his Father’s house, and now he teaches there daily while the leaders look for a way to destroy him (19:45–48).

The message. Jesus is the beloved Son, with every right to the house he has claimed, and those who question his authority are tenants refusing the owner what is his. Each trap set for him becomes a window onto who he is: the Son sent last, the rejected stone God sets at the corner, the one who claims for God not a coin but the whole person, the one who speaks for the God of the living, and David’s Lord. No one can stay neutral before him.

Why it was said. The leaders feared for their position, the Passover crowds hung on his words, and Rome watched for any hint of revolt. Luke’s readers knew that the Messiah had been rejected by his nation’s teachers and executed under a Roman governor, and they lived under Caesar themselves (see the introduction). Luke shows them that the rejection was no sign of weakness in his case: he answered every challenge, and the leaders refused him with open eyes, as Scripture had foretold.

How the chapter makes its case. The leaders demand his credentials and are exposed by their silence about John (vv. 1–8). He answers them in a parable: the tenants will kill the owner’s beloved Son, but the rejected stone will become the cornerstone (vv. 9–19). Spies ask about tribute, and he gives Caesar his coin and God the person who bears God’s image (vv. 20–26). The Sadducees mock the resurrection with a riddle, and he proves it from Moses (vv. 27–40). Then he asks how David’s son can be David’s Lord (vv. 41–44), and warns against scribes who devour widows’ houses (vv. 45–47), just before a poor widow gives everything she has (21:1–4).

Where it leads. Jesus wins every argument and goes to the cross anyway, not because his case was weak but because he chose to. The parable is his own story, told to the men who will carry it out. But the God of the living raises his Son, sets the rejected stone at the corner, and seats David’s Lord at his right hand until every enemy, death the last, is under his feet (Acts 2:32–36).

For us. Every question we bring to Jesus becomes his question to us. Will we let the owner have his vineyard, and give God not a portion but ourselves? The Son sent last is still sent to us, and the stone the builders rejected is still the one place to build a life.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus’ authority comes from the same place as John’s, and men who will not face the truth about John cannot be handed the truth about Jesus. An official delegation demands to know who gave him the right to act as he has in the temple, a question built as a trap (vv. 1–2). Jesus answers with a question about John’s baptism, which is really the same question (vv. 3–4). Their huddle weighs only what is safe, not what is true (vv. 5–6), so they plead ignorance, and he declines to answer men who have refused the light they already had (vv. 7–8). The parable that follows answers anyone willing to hear.
verseByVerse.theology: The authority of Jesus is the central question of the Gospels, and the answer they avoid is that he acts as the Son sent by the Father. They refuse to judge John not because they cannot tell, but because they will not face the answer (see the note on vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.examples:
The manoeuvre survives in every institution, the church included, and it rarely feels like dishonesty from inside. It feels like responsibility: there is always a reason why the honest answer would be unhelpful just now (on how to test yourself, see the note on vv. 5–6).

Jesus is endlessly patient with people who honestly do not know (see the note on vv. 7–8).

verseByVerse.quote: One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, the chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up and said to him, 'Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nation’s rulers demand to know who gave Jesus the right to act as he has, and the question they ask in hostility is the one every reader must answer. They find him in the temple, preaching the gospel.

The setting. These are Jesus’ last days of public teaching. Having cleared the temple, he has stayed to teach in it, while the leaders look for a way to destroy him and cannot (19:45–48).

Preaching the gospel. They come for him in the middle of a sentence. The phrase is Luke’s own addition, his favourite word for announcing good news. Even in the last week, to the very people whose leaders would hand him over, it is gospel.

The chief priests and the scribes. Together with the elders, the chief priests and scribes made up the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council. This is an official delegation.

By what authority. “These things” needs no explaining: a king’s entry, the traders thrown out of courts the priests administered, and the teaching since. On its face the question is fair, for the temple was under the high priest’s authority. But both jaws of the trap are shut. If he claims human authority, they can show he has none; if he claims divine authority, they have a charge of blasphemy. And nobody asks whether what he did was right, or whether the trade had crowded out the prayer the court existed to serve. The question is only about his right to act, which is where an institution usually hides when it does not want to discuss whether the act was right.

Who gave Jesus his authority? The Father did, and the whole Gospel has been answering the question. The voice at his baptism called him the beloved Son (3:22). He forgave sins, and proved his authority to do it by healing a paralysed man (5:24). Demons, winds and death obeyed him. All things have been handed over to him by his Father (10:22), and after his resurrection he will say that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (Matthew 28:18). The One questioned by the Sanhedrin in the temple courts is the One before whom the Sanhedrin will one day stand to be judged. And if his authority is from God, his words are not advice to be weighed but commands to be obeyed, and his promises are as sure as God.

In everyday life. Every life has to settle what the Sanhedrin asked. Most of us accept his authority in general and quietly question it in particular: money, sexuality, time, speech, plans. Find the one area where you most often argue about his credentials when the real issue is that you do not want to change, and settle it with him today.
verseByVerse.note: The chief priests, scribes and elders together made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, 'I also will ask you a question. Now tell me, was the baptism of John from heaven or from man?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers with a question about John, not to dodge theirs but because it is the same question. Replying with a question was a normal move in rabbinic debate.

From heaven or from man? “From heaven” means from God. John’s ministry had raised the identical issue: a man with no priestly appointment or institutional backing, baptising in the Jordan and calling the nation to repent. By what authority? They had faced that question already and never answered it. A prophet’s ministry is either God’s or it is not, and everyone in Israel had already made a private judgment about John.

The connection runs deeper. John had said who Jesus was: “he who is mightier than I is coming” (3:16), and at the Jordan the voice from heaven had answered their question (3:21–22). If John’s baptism was from heaven, the man John pointed to needs no further credentials.

A generous question. This is not a clever deflection. Jesus offers them the answer in the one form they could accept without losing face, by working it out themselves: a route to the truth that does not require surrender in public. And he asks not about himself but about a matter they had had years to settle, on public evidence. Their difficulty was never a shortage of information about Jesus of Nazareth. It was what they had already done with the last man God sent.

Is it right for a Christian to answer a question with a question? Sometimes, when it is done as Jesus did it: not to dodge, but to bring the real issue into the light. Many hostile questions rest on a hidden assumption, and a good question can show it gently. If someone asks how you can believe in a God who allows suffering, you might ask what makes them so sure suffering is wrong. But Jesus also answered sincere questions directly and patiently. The skill is to tell the difference, and the aim is always to help the person to the truth, not to win.

verseByVerse.quote: And they discussed it with one another, saying, 'If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’ But if we say, ‘From man,’ all the people will stone us to death, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders ask themselves not what is true but what is safe, and find that every honest answer would expose them. Luke lets us hear the huddle.

Why did you not believe him? They see the difficulty at once, and it is not one of logic. They had rejected John (7:30). If John was from God, their refusal to receive him is a public fact requiring explanation.

Stone us to death. Only Luke says the fear was of stoning, the penalty for blasphemy and false prophecy. John had been killed by Herod, and the popular verdict on him had hardened into reverence for a martyr. To deny him in a temple court full of Passover pilgrims would have been physically dangerous. The people were convinced; the leaders were calculating.

Truth is missing. Not one clause of the deliberation considers what John’s baptism actually was. The leaders of God’s people, in the temple, weigh a question about a prophet and leave truth out entirely.

The listener in the huddle. They spoke among themselves, but not out of his hearing in any sense that mattered: Luke has shown again and again that Jesus knew the reasonings of scribes and Pharisees before they said a word (5:22; 6:8; 9:47). They were calculating in the presence of the Mightier One whom John had announced (3:16), the Son on whom the Spirit came down at John’s baptism. The truth they were avoiding stood a few feet away and could read them. He never once calculated. He said what was true in the temple, before the council and before Pilate, knowing it would cost him his life. Because he did not seek his own safety, we are safe in him.

How do I know if I am deciding by what is safe rather than what is true? Watch what moves first in you when a hard question arrives. If your first thought is “what will people think?” or “what will this cost me?”, you are in the huddle. Other signs: your answer changes with who is asking; you avoid the parts of Scripture that would settle a matter you would rather leave open; you say you are still thinking about it, for years. The remedy is to ask God, before anyone else, what is true, and then to trust him with the cost (Proverbs 29:25).

verseByVerse.quote: So they answered that they did not know where it came from. And Jesus said to them, 'Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders plead ignorance to escape the question, and Jesus will not hand a plain answer to men who have refused the light they already had.

They did not know. Almost certainly untrue, and everybody present knows it; but it commits them to nothing and cannot be attacked. Yet these are the official teachers of Israel, whose duty was to judge true and false prophets, and they have just declared in public that they cannot tell whether the greatest prophetic movement of their age was from God. A man who will not risk being wrong ends up unable to say anything at all.

Neither will I tell you. The refusal is not petulance. He had made them a real offer, and they declined it, not for want of information. God does not supply further light to people who have refused what they already have (8:18).

And yet he does answer. Not in a plain statement they can take to court, but in a story, in the very next breath, in which the owner sends his beloved son (v. 13): an answer only an honest heart can receive. His silence toward the scheming is never silence toward the seeking.

What about people who genuinely do not know? Jesus deals with them all through this Gospel with enormous patience: the centurion, the woman in the crowd, the thief on the cross, the disciples themselves, who ask badly and are answered anyway. The difference between them and those whose questions are a way of never arriving anywhere shows not in the difficulty of the question but in what happens to the answers: whether each one is weighed, or simply replaced by the next question. Jesus can be asked anything. What he will not do is join a conversation designed never to end. If you are honestly unsure, tell him so, and keep reading what he said. He has never turned away an honest seeker.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–19 — The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s leaders are tenants who have refused God his fruit for centuries and are about to kill his Son, but God will overrule them. Jesus tells the people a story built on Isaiah’s vineyard, so its meaning is plain (vv. 9–10). The owner sends servant after servant, each treated worse than the last (vv. 11–12). Last he sends his beloved son, and the tenants kill him to seize the inheritance, so the owner will destroy them and give the vineyard to others (vv. 13–16). Psalm 118 confirms it: the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone, and no one can stay neutral toward it (vv. 17–18). The leaders understand and try to seize him at once (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable is one of Luke’s plainest statements of Jesus’ divine sonship: the son is not one more servant but the heir. On “Perhaps they will respect him”, see the note on vv. 13–14.

The vineyard given to others is not a statement that God has finished with the Jewish people (see the note on vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus answers the crowd’s horror with Psalm 118:22 (v. 17), and v. 18 adds Isaiah’s and Daniel’s stones: no one walks past it (see the note on v. 18).

The leaders understood the parable at once and tried to arrest him that hour (see the note on v. 19).

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to tell the people this parable: 'A man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants and went into another country for a long while. When the time came, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells the people the story of Israel as God’s vineyard, let out to tenants who refuse the owner his fruit. The council has just refused to answer him, so he tells the crowd a story about its leaders, in their hearing, and the leaders will understand every word (v. 19).

A man planted a vineyard. Every Jew in that court would have heard the echo. Isaiah’s song of the vineyard tells of a beloved friend who planted choice vines on a very fertile hill, and ends: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:1–7). So the parable needs no key: the vineyard is Israel, planted by God and given everything it needed to bear fruit.

Let it out to tenants. The tenants are Israel’s leaders, and the arrangement was ordinary: absentee landlords commonly let estates for a share of the crop. But the tenants did not plant the vineyard. Everything they work with was made by somebody else and handed to them on terms. Only Luke adds “for a long while”: the long centuries of God’s patience with his people.

Some of the fruit. The owner’s share, as agreed. The servant is a prophet, sent to call Israel back to fruitfulness. And sending him away empty-handed is not a dispute about rent: nobody pleads a bad season. The tenants are simply refusing to pay. It pictures Israel’s long history of rejecting the prophets (Nehemiah 9:26).

The storyteller in the story. As the parable opens, nobody in the court knows where it is going, but the man telling it does. He is the beloved son who will be sent last, standing in the vineyard as he speaks, days before the tenants throw him out. He is about to describe his own coming as the owner’s final appeal and his own death as the tenants’ final answer, with the men who will carry it out listening. No prophet ever told his own story like that. Only the Son could.

In everyday life. God looks for fruit from what he has given you, and fruit is not squeezed out by effort: it grows from the Spirit he gives to those joined to his Son (Galatians 5:22). Pick one gift, time, money, an ability, a relationship, and offer its fruit to him deliberately this week, as a thank-offering to the owner who gave it.

What is the fruit God looks for? The fruit Isaiah’s vineyard should have borne was justice and righteousness (Isaiah 5:7): faith toward God, and lives of love, truth and mercy toward others. It is the fruit John the Baptist demanded (3:8), and the fruit of the Spirit Paul describes (Galatians 5:22–23). It is not a percentage of income or a level of church activity, though both may be part of it. God wants himself acknowledged as owner, and the life he has given returned to him in love and obedience.
verseByVerse.note: The vineyard is Isaiah’s picture of Israel. Absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers.

verseByVerse.quote: And he sent another servant. But they also beat and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty-handed. And he sent yet a third. This one also they wounded and cast out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The owner sends servant after servant, and each is treated worse than the last: the story of God’s long patience and Israel’s long refusal of his prophets.

Another servant, and yet a third. The second is beaten and treated shamefully, publicly humiliated, which in that culture was the worse injury; the third is wounded and thrown out. The tenants grow bolder because nothing has happened to them. In Luke’s telling no servant is killed until the son, which makes the son’s death the climax.

The sending. A landlord with any sense would have gone to law after the first assault. This one keeps sending. The story is showing the patience of God: he keeps sending because what he wants is not damages but his tenants back.

The ownership is the problem. The tenants do not argue or renegotiate; they simply will not have anyone come from him. The messenger is attacked before the message is heard, because what they will not accept is that the vineyard belongs to someone else.

The history in three sentences. Scripture sums it up: the LORD kept sending his messengers out of compassion for his people, and they kept mocking them and scoffing at his prophets (2 Chronicles 36:15–16). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD, on this same site (2 Chronicles 24:20–22). The men listening were hearing their own history read back to them.

How often would I. The patience in this parable has a face. A little earlier on the road Jesus had cried, “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (13:34). Father and Son share one heart toward the rebellious vineyard, and the patience that kept sending prophets now stands in the temple court in person, telling the tenants their own story one last time.

Why is God so patient? Because patience belongs to his very name: “merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love” (Exodus 34:6). He is “not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). His long sending is not weakness. Every servant sent was another invitation, and left the tenants more without excuse. If God has been patient with you, through years of half-hearted faith or outright rebellion, it is because he has been sending, again and again, to bring you home.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’ But when the tenants saw him, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
When every servant has been refused, the owner sends the one he cannot replace, his beloved son, and the tenants resolve to kill him because he is the heir. Here Jesus answers the question of his authority after all.

What shall I do? Only Luke records the owner’s question. It is not helplessness but the heart of God, having tried every ordinary course, pondering how to reach his rebellious people.

I will send my beloved son. “My beloved son” (ton huion mou ton agapēton) is what the voice from heaven said at the Jordan, “You are my beloved Son” (3:22), and close to the voice from the cloud on the mountain, “This is my Son, my Chosen One” (9:35). He is not another servant; he is the beloved Son. And the logic is a father’s rather than a landlord’s: he has run out of servants, and he will send the one person he cannot replace.

Perhaps they will respect him. Did God not know what would happen? He knew. Luke records that the Son was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23), and Jesus has told his disciples three times how this would end. The “perhaps” is the language of a genuine appeal, spoken from the owner’s side of the story, not a report of divine ignorance. It means the tenants can never claim that the offer was not real or that any envoy was held back: the last was the owner’s own son, and their rejection is without excuse. God knew what they would do and sent the Son anyway. That is not a father caught out but a love that kept knocking at a door it knew would not open, so that nobody could ever say the door was not knocked upon.

Let us kill him. They recognise him, and kill him for that very reason: remove the heir and the property is ours. It is what the serpent offered in a garden: “you will be like God” (Genesis 3:5).

The heir who made heirs of rebels. The Father asked, “What shall I do?” and the answer emptied heaven of its dearest treasure. He sent the Son he loved into the hands of those who would kill him, so that the death they meant as a theft of the inheritance became the way the inheritance was given away. The heir they killed has made heirs of rebels (Romans 8:17).

The tenants’ dream: a world without an owner. The tenants’ reasoning is the founding hope of much modern thought: remove the one with the prior claim, and the vineyard is ours. Jean-Paul Sartre argued that if there is no God, there is no given human nature and no one to answer to; we must invent ourselves, and man is “condemned to be free”. But a self that owns itself outright must also make, justify and hold itself together, with no one to receive it and no one to forgive it. The inheritance turns out to be a weight. Religion can make the same move more politely, paying God exactly what is owed so that he has no further claim on the rest. Both are ways of keeping the vineyard. But what the tenants tried to seize by killing the heir is what the heir came to give. We become free not by getting rid of the owner but by being adopted by him, brought in by the Son the tenants threw out, not as tenants on terms but as children of the house (Galatians 4:7).

In everyday life. Where are you saying, in small ways, “Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours”? It is the impulse to enjoy God’s gifts, family, career, health, comfort, while keeping the Giver at the edge. Name one gift you treat as your own, and give thanks to the owner for it today.

Did the leaders know Jesus was the Son of God? Not in the full sense, or they would not have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8; Acts 3:17). But they knew enough. They saw his works, heard his claims and understood this parable (v. 19); their opposition was not ignorance but refusal. People do not reject Christ because they cannot see who he is, but because they see enough to know he would claim them. That is the root Scripture names; it does not make every honest doubter a liar, and Jesus was patient with real doubt, as he was with Thomas (John 20:27).

verseByVerse.quote: And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.' When they heard this, they said, 'Surely not!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tenants kill the son, so the owner will destroy them and give his vineyard to others: judgment on Israel’s leaders, and God’s people gathered from every nation.

Threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. Mark puts the killing first; Luke keeps the order of what was about to happen, for Jesus was crucified outside the city wall: “Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). He is telling it in the temple, days before it happens, down to the place.

What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? He asks the crowd for the verdict. In Matthew’s telling the hearers supply the answer and condemn themselves out of their own mouths; here Jesus gives it, and the effect is the same.

Destroy those tenants. Judgment on the leaders, and it landed within a generation, in AD 70 (19:41–44).

To others. The tenancy is transferred: to the apostles whom Christ appoints over his people, and through them to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46). The vineyard is not destroyed. It is now gathered from every nation, Jew and Gentile together in Christ (Ephesians 2:11–22), and that would have been the most offensive part of the story. The vineyard given to others is the story Luke goes on to tell in Acts.

Surely not! Only Luke records it: literally “may it not be!”, the phrase Paul uses again and again in Romans. The crowd has understood, and the thought is unbearable. Within days a crowd in this city will call for the death of the son and get it.

Has God finished with the Jewish people? No, and this parable has been misused to say so. Paul, writing after the resurrection, asks exactly this: “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (Romans 11:1). The tenants in the parable are the leaders, and the men Jesus is looking at are named in v. 19. Many Jews believed: the apostles, the first church of thousands in Jerusalem, Paul himself. Christians differ on what Romans 11 expects for the Jewish people in the future. Some look for a great turning of Israel to Christ before his return; others understand “all Israel” as the whole number of the elect from Jews and Gentiles. All agree that there is one vineyard and one way into it, through faith in Jesus the Messiah, and that Christians should long and pray for Jewish people to come to him.

verseByVerse.quote: But he looked directly at them and said, 'What then is this that is written: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scripture itself foretold that Israel’s builders would reject God’s chosen stone, and that God would make it the cornerstone. Jesus answers the crowd’s “Surely not!” from Psalm 118.

But he looked directly at them. To fix the eyes on someone: the verb used of Jesus looking at Peter after the rooster crowed (22:61). The parable was told to the people; the look is for the men who came with the question, and it could have broken a heart open.

What then is this that is written? If judgment cannot happen, as the crowd has just cried, what does Scripture mean? He answers from Psalm 118:22, the psalm his disciples had sung on the descent of Olivet, hailing the King (Psalm 118:26; 19:38); now he turns it, four verses earlier, against the authorities.

The stone that the builders rejected. The cornerstone sets the angle and the line for two walls at once, so that everything built after it is squared by it: the most important stone in the building. The picture is of professionals, men whose whole competence is judging stone, examining this one and throwing it on the discard pile as unfit. That was what was happening in that courtyard. The chief priests and scribes were the builders, trained and appointed to recognise what God was doing, and their professional judgment was that this stone would not do.

Has become the cornerstone. Then everything is reversed: an authority above the builders took it up and set it at the corner, and their verdict was simply overruled. This is the LORD’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes, the psalm goes on (Psalm 118:23). It was fulfilled in the resurrection. The early church could not let the verse go: Peter quotes it to the Sanhedrin itself (Acts 4:10–12) and again in his letter (1 Peter 2:4–8), as the text that showed how the resurrection overturned the verdict passed on Jesus on Good Friday.

Why does it matter that the experts rejected him? Because their verdict is not the last word. In every generation scholars, institutions and cultured voices have looked at Jesus and set him aside, and some Christians are shaken by it. This verse expected it: the builders’ rejection of the stone is part of the prophecy, not a refutation of it. God has always overruled the builders. The question is not what the professionals think of Christ, but what God has done with him: he raised him and set him at the corner, and everything is now squared by him.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can be neutral toward this stone: whoever stumbles over it is broken, and whoever it falls on is crushed.

Broken to pieces. The stone now appears in two more pictures, both from the prophets. Isaiah had said the LORD would be a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling, and “many shall stumble on it. They shall fall and be broken” (Isaiah 8:14–15).

It will crush him. Daniel had seen a stone cut out by no human hand grind the statue of the world’s kingdoms to dust and become a mountain that filled the whole earth (Daniel 2:34–35, 44–45). The verb means to winnow, to reduce to dust and blow away.

Broken or crushed. To fall on the stone is to trip over it. That is survivable: broken things can be mended, and Saul of Tarsus fell on this stone on the Damascus road and rose an apostle. But when the stone falls on a person, that is the last judgment, and there is nothing left to mend. This stone can be built on, tripped over or fallen under, and there is no fourth option. And the stone that breaks the proud is the rock that holds the humble for ever.

If I have stumbled over Jesus, is it too late? No. The men listening had already stumbled, and what the sentence holds out, terribly and graciously, is that a stumble is not yet the end. Many who once mocked Christ, or walked away, have been broken by him and then healed by him. Peter preached to the very builders who rejected the stone, and thousands believed (Acts 2:36–41). But a day is coming when the stone is no longer lying in the road. The time to fall on him in repentance is now, before he falls in judgment.

Textual note. Matthew has the same saying (Matthew 21:44), though some manuscripts lack it there.

verseByVerse.quote: The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, for they perceived that he had told this parable against them, but they feared the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders understand the parable perfectly and try to seize the son on the spot; only their fear of the people holds them back.

At that very hour. They have just heard a story in which tenants kill the owner’s son, and been told it is about them, and they try to arrest the son at once. The parable begins to come true while its words are still in the air. And they understood it, which settles something about the parables: they are not a code only insiders can break. The leaders were not puzzled but unwilling.

They feared the people. Luke has now said this three times in two chapters (19:48; 20:6). The fear running the council is not the fear of God, which would have stopped them entirely, but the fear of a riot and of losing position, and it will govern the decision they finally take, to arrange the arrest away from the crowd (22:6). The parable’s warning is answered not with repentance but with a new plan: spies (v. 20).

Not until his hour. They wanted him that very hour, and they could not have him until his hour came. Not one of his enemies can move a finger against him except as the Father allows, and the Father allowed it only when it would save us.

In everyday life. Notice your reaction the next time a sermon or a passage of Scripture lands too close: is it humility, or anger at the preacher? Ask God for a soft heart, and when the word cuts, say yes to it before you say anything else.

Why does God not simply tell people plainly what they are doing? He did. There is no gentler or clearer way to say “you are about to kill me and you will be judged for it” than the story he had just told, and it produced a decision to do it sooner. Clarity alone does not change a heart. Only the Spirit of God, opening blind eyes and giving a new heart, can do that (Ezekiel 36:26; 2 Corinthians 4:6). That is why we pray as well as speak when we share the gospel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–26 — The Question about Tribute to Caesar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Caesar may have his coin, but God claims the person who bears his image. Spies posing as sincere enquirers flatter Jesus and ask whether tribute to Caesar is lawful, a question meant either to lose him the crowd or to hand him to the governor (vv. 20–22). He asks for a denarius, and they produce Caesar’s coin in the temple (vv. 23–24). His answer gives the state its due and God everything (v. 25), and they can only marvel and fall silent (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: “Render” means pay what is owed, and civil authority is real. But the weight falls on the second half: Caesar may have the coin; God claims the whole person, who bears his image (this is treated fully at v. 25).
verseByVerse.examples:
A Christian facing a law he thinks unjust can reason from this: the state has real but limited authority, and the question is whether a particular demand crosses into what belongs to God alone.

They marvelled at his answer and fell silent, and that week they had him killed (see the note on v. 26).

verseByVerse.quote: So they watched him and sent spies, who pretended to be sincere, that they might catch him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. So they asked him, 'Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders send actors posing as sincere enquirers, to draw Jesus into an answer that will either lose him the people or hand him to Rome.

Spies. The direct approach has failed twice, so the tactics change. “Spies” (enkathetous) are men hired and planted, and they pretended to be sincere: actors playing devout enquirers, hypocrites in the word’s first sense, a stage actor.

To the governor. Only Luke states their aim so plainly. They want a political charge that Rome will act on, and Pilate does not care about blasphemy.

We know that you speak rightly. The flattery is a trap in itself. Having praised him as a man who shows no partiality, they have publicly committed him to fearless speech before asking the dangerous question, so he cannot now give a diplomatic answer. And every word of the compliment is true. They describe him accurately as a means of destroying him, which is possible only for people who know well enough who he is and have decided against him anyway. Even their lies could not avoid telling the truth about him.

Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not? The tribute was the poll tax, a denarius a head, paid directly to Rome by every adult in Judea since it became a Roman province in AD 6, and bitterly resented. It had provoked the armed revolt of Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37). Say yes, and he endorses the occupation in front of a Passover crowd of patriots and loses them. Say no, and witnesses stand ready to report to Pilate a man inciting tax refusal. The irony is that they will bring exactly that charge anyway, falsely, accusing him of “forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar” (23:2).

How should a Christian respond to flattery? With gratitude for kindness, and with a guarded heart. Flattery is praise with a purpose: it wants something from you, and it is often the prelude to a request you would otherwise refuse (Proverbs 29:5). Jesus was not moved by it at all, because he did not live for human approval (John 5:41). The more you need to be thought well of, the easier you are to manipulate. So when someone praises you before asking something hard, pause, pray, and answer the request on its merits, not on the warmth of the introduction.
verseByVerse.note: The poll tax was paid directly to Rome and bitterly resented. “Yes” would anger the people; “no” would be treason before the governor.

parallels.desc: forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar

verseByVerse.quote: But he perceived their craftiness, and said to them, 'Show me a denarius. Whose likeness and inscription does it have?' They said, 'Caesar's.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sees through the trap and asks for a coin, and his questioners, by producing Caesar’s money in the temple, give away their own case.

Their craftiness. The same word Paul ties to the serpent in Eden (2 Corinthians 11:3). The one who knows what is in man (John 2:25) sees through the actors at once. And the same eyes that read the hearts of his enemies read ours, and he still came to save.

Show me a denarius. He does not answer. He asks for a coin, and somebody produces one immediately, in the temple. It is his accusers, not he, who carry Caesar’s money.

Whose likeness and inscription does it have? The denarius was a silver coin bearing the head of the emperor Tiberius, with an inscription around it calling him “Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus”, and the title “high priest” on the reverse.
