It was a portrait, which strict Jews regarded as a graven image forbidden by the second commandment, and it carried a claim to divinity in writing. The men who had come to catch him on a point of faithfulness to God had it in their purses in the temple courts.

Caesar’s. The only possible answer, and it gives away their whole case. They live in Caesar’s economy and use his money, and whoever uses a currency, and benefits from the roads, order and trade it pays for, has accepted the authority that mints it.

The method. The trap has been broken without a word of teaching, and they have been made to say the awkward thing themselves. Christians in hostile conversations often hunt for wording so careful that it cannot be used against them. Jesus asks for an object and asks what is written on it. Nothing has been conceded and nobody has been insulted.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage. The coin bore the emperor’s head (probably Tiberius) and his titles.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, 'Then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay the state what it is owed, for its claim is real, but give God what bears his image, which is yourself, entire. Caesar may have his coin; God claims the person.

Render to Caesar. “Render” (apodote) means pay back, hand over what is due: the language of a debt settled rather than a gift made. If the coin carries Caesar’s face, giving it to him is not a betrayal of God but returning what is his. Civil authority is legitimate, and Jesus does not tell them to stop paying. Paul develops it: “Let every person be subject to the governing authorities”, and “Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed” (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17).

To God the things that are God’s. The weight falls on this second half. Jesus has made ownership a matter of image, which leaves a second question hanging: what bears the image of God? Every listener knew the answer from the first page of Scripture: “God created man in his own image” (Genesis 1:27). The coin is stamped with Caesar and belongs to Caesar. The man holding it is stamped with God.

A far larger answer. So the answer is far larger than the tax question deserved. Caesar has a genuine claim, limited to things with his face on them. God’s claim is on the whole person, because the image is not stamped on part of a man. Give Caesar his coin; give God yourself, with no part kept back as private property: not your body, your money, your ambitions or your thoughts, for “you are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). And Caesar’s claims are bounded by God’s: he is owed taxes, not worship. When he asks for what belongs to God, worship, conscience, the final allegiance of a life, he is asking for property that is not his, and the answer is the apostles’: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). The verse also exposes two idols of the heart: some make Caesar their saviour, hoping the right ruler or party will put the world right; others make his coin their security. Jesus gives each its proper place, and neither is God.

The Image who rendered everything. Only one man has ever given God all that is God’s. He is himself “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), and within days he would hand over the last thing a man has: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit” (23:46). The coin went to Caesar; the Son gave himself to God, entire, and by that offering he redeems those who have kept back from God what was always his.

The Maker did not throw the coin away. When sin defaced God’s image in us, he came to recover it himself, and he is renewing his people after the image of their Creator (Colossians 3:10). Caesar’s coins wore thin within a generation; every one of God’s people is his twice over, because he made them and because he bought them.

In everyday life. Pay your taxes honestly: no cash-in-hand work kept off the books, no invented expenses. That is rendering to Caesar. Then begin the morning by offering yourself to God, “by the mercies of God” (Romans 12:1), and end it by asking where you kept something back. You will always find something; but the Son rendered himself to God entire in your place, his obedience is counted as yours, and your halting offering is accepted for his sake.

What if my government uses my taxes for things I believe are wrong? Pay them anyway, as a rule. The tax Jesus told them to pay funded a pagan empire that crucified people, kept armies of occupation and supported idol temples, and Paul wrote Romans 13 under Nero. The responsibility for misuse lies with those who spend the money, not with the citizen who obeys God by paying what is owed. Use every lawful means to work for justice: vote, write, speak, protest peacefully. The line is crossed only when the state commands you yourself to do what God forbids, or forbids what God commands. Then obey God, and accept the consequences without violence.

Where Christians differ: how do the two claims relate? Some have read this verse as dividing life into two equal and separate realms, a sacred one where God rules and a secular one where the state rules, each sovereign in its own sphere and neither answerable to the other. Others read it as placing Caesar’s realm inside God’s: the state has real authority, but only as a servant of God, accountable to him and limited by his law. This commentary’s view: Jesus does not make God and Caesar equal partners. All authority is under God; the governing authorities exist because God has instituted them (Romans 13:1), and even Pilate had no authority except what was given from above (John 19:11). Christians should be good citizens, paying taxes, honouring rulers and praying for them (1 Timothy 2:1–2), but their final loyalty is to God alone.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were not able in the presence of the people to catch him in what he said, but marveling at his answer they became silent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The trap fails in front of the very witnesses it needed, and the questioners can only marvel and fall silent, admiring without believing.

In the presence of the people. They needed witnesses to a seditious answer, and instead they have witnesses to a devastating one.

Marveling at his answer. Marvelling is the surprising word. These men had rehearsed the flattery and framed a question with no safe answer, and when the answer came, something in them responded to it. When Jesus was twelve he sat in this same temple among the teachers, and “all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers” (2:47). Now the teachers of Israel are amazed again, against their will. The wisdom has not changed; only their hearts have.

They became silent. Not persuaded: silenced. Admiring the truth is not the same as being moved by it. Herod was glad to see Jesus and questioned him at length (23:8–9); Agrippa asked Paul whether in so short a time he would persuade him to be a Christian (Acts 26:28). The silence is not repentance. It is the end of one line of attack, and the Sadducees come next.

Why did the best answer not convert them? Because the problem was never the quality of the answers. Set this beside v. 7. Twice now this delegation has been reduced to saying nothing, once by choosing not to answer and once by having nothing left to say. Jesus gave the best answer anyone ever gave to a hostile question, in public, and the men who heard it admired it, went quiet, and had him killed that week. Answers matter, and Christians should give them well (1 Peter 3:15). But only God can change a heart that does not want to be changed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–47 — Sadducees on Resurrection, the Son of David, and Scribal Warning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The dead will be raised, because God is the God of the living, and the Messiah is more than David’s son: he is David’s Lord. The Sadducees try to make the resurrection ridiculous with a riddle about seven brothers (vv. 27–33). Jesus shows that the age to come is not this age prolonged (vv. 34–36) and proves the resurrection from Moses (vv. 37–38), until no one dares question him further (vv. 39–40). Then he asks his own question from Psalm 110 (vv. 41–44), and warns the people against scribes who love to be seen and prey on widows (vv. 45–47).
verseByVerse.theology:
Marriage does not continue because death does not continue (see the note on vv. 34–36).

At the bush God says “I am the God of Abraham”, centuries after Abraham’s burial, and the argument rests on God’s faithfulness (this is treated fully at vv. 37–38).

In Psalm 110 David calls his descendant “my Lord” (see the note on vv. 43–44), and Luke has answered the riddle since his first chapter (see the note on vv. 41–42).
verseByVerse.examples:
The widow who has buried a husband of forty years may read “neither marry nor are given in marriage” and fear she will lose him. Jesus says the institution ends, not the people or the love (see the note on vv. 34–36).

The chapter ends with the strong preying on the weak. The scribes’ long prayers are the instrument of their theft from widows (see the note on v. 47), and Luke turns at once to a widow giving all she had (21:1–4).

verseByVerse.quote: There came to him some Sadducees, those who deny that there is a resurrection, and they asked him a question, saying, 'Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies, having a wife but no children, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, take a true law of Moses and set out to make the resurrection look absurd with it.

Some Sadducees. The third delegation of the day. The Sadducees were the priestly, aristocratic party who controlled the temple and managed the relationship with Rome: fewer than the Pharisees and far more powerful. They seem to have treated the five books of Moses as fully authoritative and the rest of Scripture as secondary.

Deny that there is a resurrection. The Sadducees “say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit” (Acts 23:8). So rather than answer from Daniel 12, which teaches the resurrection plainly, Jesus will meet them in Moses.

Moses wrote for us. Deuteronomy 25:5–10 provides that if a married man dies childless, his brother should marry the widow, and the first son would carry the dead man’s name and inherit his portion, so that no family line was blotted out and the land stayed with the family. A related custom lies behind the book of Ruth, and through it comes the line of David and of Christ. It is a good and compassionate law, and their citation is accurate. But they push a true text to an extreme its author never envisaged, to make a doctrine they dislike look ridiculous: a technique available to anybody with a Bible and a grievance.

Is belief in the resurrection not just wishful thinking? The Sadducees thought so, and they were the educated sceptics of their day. But the first Christians were not people inclined to believe it. When the women reported the empty tomb, the apostles thought their words an idle tale and did not believe them (24:11). What changed their minds was not a hope but an event: a tomb that was empty, and a Lord who was seen, heard and touched, by Peter, by the Twelve and by more than five hundred at once (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Paul passes that list on as something he had himself received, a summary most scholars date to within a few years of the events, not a legend grown up long afterwards. Christian hope does not rest on what we would like to be true. It rests on what happened outside Jerusalem on the third day.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection. Levirate marriage (a man marrying his brother’s childless widow) kept the dead man’s name alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died without children. And the second and the third took her, and likewise all seven left no children and died. Afterward the woman also died. In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sadducees’ riddle tries to show that the resurrection would make nonsense of Moses’ law, but it rests on an assumption they have never examined.

Seven brothers. The case is invented: probably a stock argument used to ridicule the Pharisees’ belief in the resurrection, with seven chosen to make the situation as absurd as possible.

In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? The last clause, “For the seven had her as wife”, drives the point home. The argument underneath: if the resurrection and Moses’ law were both true, the age to come would hold an insoluble tangle; therefore the resurrection cannot be true, and Moses could not have believed in it.

The hidden assumption. The argument rests on one assumption the Sadducees have never noticed they are making: that the age to come is this age carried on, the same arrangements, only permanent. Jesus is not going to tell them which brother gets her. He is going to show that the assumption is false, and the puzzle will fall with it.

What the story does to the woman. Nobody in the story has a name, but the brothers are at least counted, first, second, third; she is not even that, and she is given no words. She exists in the riddle purely as contested property, the thing seven men had a claim on, and the question at the end is not what became of her but whose wife she will be. They have taken a law given to protect a widow and used it to build a puzzle in which the widow is an object.

Seven graves and an empty tomb. The riddle is made of seven funerals and then an eighth, offered as the last word on human life. But they put it to the one man in history who would not stay in a grave. Within the week Jesus would die and rise, so that by dying he might break the power of the one who held the power of death (Hebrews 2:14–15). The chain of graves in their story was about to be broken from the inside.

In everyday life. When an argument against the faith seems unanswerable, look for what it takes for granted: that God is like us, that the future must be like the present, that what we cannot imagine cannot be. And never let a debate about doctrine make you careless of the people it concerns. The woman was a person, not a puzzle.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, 'The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage, but those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The resurrection is not this life prolonged but a new kind of life: death is over, and so marriage, which belongs to this age, is no longer needed.

The sons of this age. Jesus draws the distinction the Sadducees had not made: this age and the age to come. Marriage is good, given by God in Eden, and it belongs to the first.

Considered worthy. Only Luke has this fuller form. It is a verdict God gives, through grace, not a merit earned (2 Thessalonians 1:5). Jesus is speaking of the resurrection to life of God’s people. Elsewhere he says that all the dead will rise, “those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:29). No one is worthy in himself; the worthiness is Christ’s, credited to those who trust him.

They cannot die anymore. Only Luke gives this reason. Where people die, people must be born, and the institution that provides for that is marriage. Remove death and that purpose is no longer needed, as scaffolding is no longer needed once the building stands. The Sadducees’ whole puzzle falls apart.

Equal to angels. Like angels in being immortal, not in being disembodied. And the comparison is pointed: the Sadducees denied that angels existed at all (see the note on vv. 27–28), so in one phrase Jesus answers the denial they had not voiced along with the one they had. The resurrection is of the body, and Luke’s last chapter has the risen Christ eating broiled fish to prove it (24:39–43).

Sons of the resurrection. Believers are God’s children already, by adoption, welcomed into his family through faith in Christ (Galatians 3:26; 4:4–7), and we “wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:23). The resurrection will make it visible: “when he appears we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2). The family likeness, now hidden and half-formed, will be complete in body and soul. If you are in Christ, you are a son or daughter of the resurrection. Death has no future for you.

Marriage was a signpost. Paul says the one-flesh union of husband and wife is a profound mystery, and it speaks of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). Every good marriage has been a signpost, and nobody keeps reading the signpost after arriving at the city. What waits at the end of this age is a wedding, the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:6–9). Marriage does not carry over into that day, not because it was worthless but because it was the picture, and that day brings the reality.

In everyday life. If you are married, love your spouse today as a signpost to Christ: serve, forgive and speak kindly, because your marriage is preaching a sermon about him and his church.

What it does not mean. All of this is true, and none of it is what the widow in the third pew is asking. She has buried a husband she loved for forty years, and she reads “neither marry nor are given in marriage” and hears the one thing she was most afraid of: that she will not have him again. The verse does not say that. Jesus says the institution ends: the marrying, the giving in marriage, the arrangement by which this age replaces its dead. He does not say the people end, and he does not say the love ends. Married love is not lost or forgotten; it is taken up into something greater. You will not know your husband less there. You will know him better than you ever managed here, without the tiredness and the half-attention that got between you every day of the forty years.

What about those who never married, or whose marriages were unhappy? This verse is good news for them too. The single believer is not missing out on the final reality, but heading for the same wedding as everyone else, the marriage of Christ and his church, and will lack nothing there. Jesus himself never married. And for those whose marriages were marked by pain, or by a spouse who did not believe, the age to come will not prolong what was broken. Every relationship will be healed in its proper place, and every believer will be satisfied in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed, in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus proves the resurrection from Moses himself: long after Abraham, Isaac and Jacob died, God still calls himself their God, and he is not the God of the dead.

Even Moses showed. Having dismantled the riddle, he proves the doctrine on their own ground: Moses, at the burning bush (Exodus 3).

Not God of the dead. The argument turns on a relationship. God does not say he was the God of Abraham. He says, “I am the God of your father” (Exodus 3:6), centuries after Abraham was buried at Machpelah. To be somebody’s God is the language of a covenant, a solemn binding promise: it means to have bound yourself to a person, to be his shield and his very great reward, to have promised him a future (Genesis 15:1; 17:7). So if God is still Abraham’s God, either the covenant is with a handful of dust, which is no covenant at all, or Abraham is alive. If God is their God, they live to him, and he will keep his promises to them, body and soul.

The ground of hope is in God. The argument rests not on the immortality of the soul, which Scripture teaches elsewhere (Matthew 10:28), nor on any toughness in the human spirit, but on the character of God. He does not bind himself to a man and then let death end it. The ground of resurrection hope is not something in us. It is something in him.

All live to him. Only Luke adds this, and it carries great comfort: those who have died in the Lord are alive to God now (23:43; Philippians 1:23). Nobody who belonged to him has ever been lost track of, and the graves of the patriarchs did not interrupt a single conversation. He called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob over their graves, and he calls himself the God of his people over theirs. The God who spoke from the bush that burned and was not consumed keeps his own through the fire of death, and will raise them on the last day.

The God of Abraham raised his servant Jesus. Within weeks Peter stood in this same temple, in Solomon’s Portico, and used the very words of the bush: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers”, he said, had glorified his servant Jesus, whom they had killed and God had raised from the dead (Acts 3:13–15). The argument Jesus made to the Sadducees from Moses was answered in his own body. The covenant God who will not be the God of dead men did not leave his Son among the dead. On Easter morning the angels asked the women why they were seeking the living among the dead (24:5), and the firstfruits of the resurrection Jesus defended in the temple was Jesus himself.

Are the dead asleep until the resurrection? Not in the sense of being unconscious. Scripture uses sleep as a gentle picture of the believer’s death, because the body rests and will wake (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). But the person is not extinguished or unaware. Jesus told the dying thief that today he would be with him in paradise (23:43); Paul said that to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). So the believer who dies goes at once, consciously, into the presence of the Lord, and waits there with joy for the resurrection of the body at Christ’s return (the Westminster Confession 32.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 31.1). There is no purgatory in between. Roman Catholic teaching holds that many believers are first purified there; but Scripture speaks of the believer going straight to be with Christ, because “by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). All live to him.
verseByVerse.note: “The passage about the bush” is how a passage was located before chapter and verse numbers existed.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of the scribes answered, 'Teacher, you have spoken well.' For they no longer dared to ask him any question.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even scribes commend his answer, and after three failed delegations no one dares question him again.

You have spoken well. Only Luke places it here (compare Mark 12:28, 32). These are scribes, many of them Pharisees, who believed in the resurrection and have just watched a rival party demolished on it. The approval is genuine as far as it goes. It is not “you are the Christ”, not even “we will follow you”, but the approval of men who agreed with the conclusion. They came into this day’s debate to destroy him, and on this one point he was on their side.

They no longer dared. The verdict covers all three delegations. The chief priests ended by pleading ignorance; the spies became silent; the Sadducees are not recorded as replying at all. After the third, nobody would risk a fourth.

Nobody defeated him in argument. What is left is the arrest, at night, with a bribe, away from the crowd. He went to the cross not because the case against him was strong, nor because he lost the argument, but because he chose to save those who lost it.

Applause is not faith. A person can be delighted by a preacher who demolishes a position he already disliked, and walk out having received nothing at all. The test of whether someone is listening to Christ is not whether he applauds when Christ attacks somebody else. The scribes are back within two chapters, seeking how to put him to death (22:2).

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, 'How can they say that the Christ is David's son? For David himself says in the Book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Jesus asks the decisive question himself: if the Christ is David’s son, how can David call him Lord? Three delegations have questioned him and failed; his one question is about who he is.

How can they say that the Christ is David’s son? He is not denying it. That the Messiah would descend from David was not a rabbinic guess but a promise: God would raise up David’s offspring and establish the throne of his kingdom for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16), and “there shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse” (Isaiah 11:1). A blind beggar had been shouting “Son of David” at him outside Jericho (18:38). So the question is not whether the Christ is David’s son, but whether that is the whole of it.

David himself says. The quotation is Psalm 110:1, in Jesus’ day widely taken to be David’s and about the Messiah, and the argument depends on both. Many modern scholars doubt that David wrote it; but the heading names him, Jesus’ hearers did not dispute it, and Jesus builds on it with full confidence. It became the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New (Acts 2:34–35; Hebrews 1:13).

The Lord said to my Lord. The first word is the covenant name of God (in the Hebrew Yahweh), printed LORD in small capitals; the second is a word for a master (adoni, “my lord”). God speaks to David’s Lord.

Sit at my right hand. An invitation to share the throne of God, the place from which he rules, given to someone distinct from the speaker. Every scribe in the courtyard could recite the words, but none had asked who this Lord could be. The one who stood in the temple asking is the Lord David worshipped a thousand years before he was born.

Gabriel had already answered it. Luke’s reader has had the answer since the first chapter. Gabriel told Mary that her son would be given the throne of his father David, and in the same breath that he would be called the Son of the Most High, conceived by the Holy Spirit and so called holy, the Son of God (1:32–35). He is David’s son by human birth, born into David’s house (1:27). He is David’s Lord because he is the eternal Son of God. That is how David could call his own descendant Lord: the child of Mary was the Lord whom David worshipped, come in David’s flesh.

In everyday life. Is your view of Jesus too small? You can believe true things about him, a good teacher, a helper in trouble, and still believe too little. Read Psalm 110 this week and let it change how you pray: not timidly, as to a distant friend, but boldly, as to the reigning King.

verseByVerse.quote: until I make your enemies your footstool.’ David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
David calls his descendant Lord, enthroned until every enemy lies beneath his feet, so the Christ must be far more than David’s son.

Your footstool. The image comes from the ancient world’s pictures of conquest: Joshua had the commanders of Israel put their feet on the necks of five kings (Joshua 10:24). Christ reigns now, and “must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:25–26). “Until” does not mean his reign then ends; “of his kingdom there will be no end” (1:33).

David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son? The question rests on a social fact nobody in that courtyard needed explained: honour ran upward. A son honoured his father, a descendant his ancestor, and a father did not call his son lord. David was the greatest king Israel ever had, and every Jew traced honour toward him. So a psalm in which David calls his own descendant “my Lord” is upside down. It cannot happen unless the descendant is more than a descendant, greater than David himself.

The answer. Jesus does not supply it here (see the note on vv. 41–42). Paul states it in two halves: “descended from David according to the flesh”, and “declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:3–4). Jesus is pointing to himself.

David’s son and David’s Lord. Jesus is both, “the root and the descendant of David” (Revelation 22:16): before David, he made him; after David, he was born of his line. Every grave of every believer is on the list of things he will put under his feet, and the King who has already risen will see to every one.

A true expectation that is too small. The scribes had a Messiah who was David’s son and nothing more. Their expectation was true and too small, and a man with an expectation like that will reject the reality when it arrives, because it does not fit.

Why does it matter that Jesus is both God and man? Because only such a Saviour could save us: as man he could take our place and die our death; as God his obedience and death have infinite worth, and he conquers death.
verseByVerse.note: A conquered king’s neck could be used as a footstool: a picture of total victory.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the hearing of all the people he said to his disciples, 'Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus warns everyone against religious teachers whose godliness is a performance for an audience. He speaks to his disciples in the hearing of all the people, so that both hear it.

Beware of the scribes. The scribes were the Bible teachers, whom ordinary people assumed were the most reliable guides available. He tells the crowd to be careful of them, a warning against their example, as at the Pharisee’s table (11:43). Four marks follow, all about being seen.

Long robes. The dress of learning and rank, and they walk around in it: not wearing one to a function but parading about in it.

Love greetings. The respectful titles due to a teacher, paid in the open square. Not receiving greetings, which they could not help, but loving them.

The best seats. In the synagogue, the bench at the front, facing the congregation; at feasts, the couches nearest the host, which Jesus had watched guests scrambling for at a Pharisee’s dinner (14:7).

The appetite to be seen. Not one of these is a sin in itself. What is diagnosed, four times over, is an appetite for being looked at while being religious. Any position in which a person is watched being godly carries that temptation, and it is hard to notice in oneself, because it feels like enjoying one’s work.

The Teacher who took the lowest place. He had said that “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (14:11), and within days he would take the lowest place there is, “numbered with the transgressors” (22:37), and God would raise him to the highest. Only once in the Gospel is Jesus dressed in a splendid robe, and it is put on him in mockery (23:11). Every scribe who loved the best seat stood before the only one who deserved it, and he wore his robe as a joke and went on to the cross without complaint.

In everyday life. Watch your heart for the love of recognition, especially if you serve in church: the small pleasure when your name is mentioned from the front, and the small sting when it is not. Do one piece of service this week that no one will know about.

Is it wrong for church leaders to have titles or be honoured? Not in itself. Scripture tells churches to respect and honour those who labour among them, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13; 1 Timothy 5:17). The sin is in loving the honour. Leaders should test themselves: would I be content to serve unseen? Do I resent it when I am not thanked? And churches should guard their leaders, not feeding vanity with flattery, but praying for them and holding them to the example of Christ, who “came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45).
verseByVerse.note: Long robes marked out men of learning and rank.

verseByVerse.quote: who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Worst of all, these teachers use their reputation for piety to strip the most defenceless of what they have, and their condemnation will be the heavier for it.

Who devour widows’ houses. Long robes and good seats are vanity; this is preying on the weak, very likely without breaking any law: the abuse of religious standing to extract money from people who trusted the standing (see Uncertain wording below).

The most vulnerable. Widows had no earning power, little legal protection and nobody to complain to, and God’s law had singled them out for that reason: “You shall not mistreat any widow or fatherless child. If you do mistreat them … my wrath will burn” (Exodus 22:22–24). These are the men entrusted with teaching that law.

For a pretense make long prayers. The long prayers are not a separate failing; they are the means of the theft. A reputation for piety gets a man access to a widow’s confidence and her accounts.

The greater condemnation. The principle has run through this Gospel since chapter twelve: “Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required” (12:48). The sentence is heavier because the position was higher, the knowledge greater and the trust betrayed deeper, and because they used religion to cover their sin. “Not many of you should become teachers,” James warns, “for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness” (James 3:1). There are degrees of punishment as there are degrees of reward, and Scripture reserves its severest language for those who use the things of God to get things from people.

He took the widows’ side. God is the defender of widows and the father of the fatherless (Psalm 68:5), and his Son stood in the temple courts and took their side against the most respected men in the nation. He sees every hidden injustice, and he will right it. And he is the true High Priest, who does not devour the houses of the poor but gave his own life for them, and whose prayers for his people are never a pretence (Hebrews 7:25).

The link. Luke sets the next scene immediately: a poor widow at the treasury, putting in everything she had (21:1–4). The chapter that began with the leaders questioning Christ’s authority ends with Christ exposing theirs.

In everyday life. Is there any place where your reputation as a Christian gives you an advantage over someone weaker: an elderly relative’s finances, an employee who trusts you? Handle it as before God. And look out for the widows of your church: visit, help, make sure no one is exploiting them.

What if this has happened in my church? Then it must be named and dealt with, not hidden. When a leader has used his position to exploit the vulnerable, whether financially, emotionally or sexually, the church’s duty is to protect the victims, tell the truth, involve the civil authorities where the law has been broken, and remove the offender from leadership (1 Timothy 5:19–21). Protecting the institution’s reputation at the victims’ expense is to repeat the scribes’ sin. And if you have been harmed by someone who used God’s name to do it, know that Christ is not on their side. He saw the widows, and he warned the whole temple about the men who devoured them.

Does hypocrisy in the church not prove that Christianity is false? No. It shows that Jesus was right. Nobody has ever condemned religious hypocrisy more severely than he did, here in the temple, in front of the very men who practised it. The gospel never claimed that religious people are good. It claims that all of us, scribes and sinners together, need a Saviour, and that this Saviour takes the side of those whom the powerful have used. So the answer to a hypocrite in the pulpit is not to walk away from Christ, but to come closer to the one who saw through the scribes and still went to the cross for sinners.

Uncertain wording. Jesus does not say how the scribes “devour widows’ houses”, and several practices of the day would fit. Scribes were not supposed to charge for teaching the law, and so depended on the hospitality and gifts of the devout, among whom widows were notably generous. A scribe might be appointed to manage a widow’s estate and take a fee from it, or manage it dishonestly; he might accept board and lodging from a woman who could not afford it, or press her into giving that ruined her. Which practice Jesus had in mind is not known. The meaning is clear enough: using a reputation for godliness to drain the property of the defenceless.

parallels.desc: you shall not mistreat any widow

20.text: <sup>1</sup> One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, the chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up <sup>2</sup> and said to him, “Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.” <sup>3</sup> He answered them, “I also will ask you a question. Now tell me, <sup>4</sup> was the baptism of John from heaven or from man?” <sup>5</sup> And they discussed it with one another, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’ <sup>6</sup> But if we say, ‘From man,’ all the people will stone us to death, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.” <sup>7</sup> So they answered that they did not know where it came from. <sup>8</sup> And Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.” <sup>9</sup> And he began to tell the people this parable: “A man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants and went into another country for a long while. <sup>10</sup> When the time came, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>11</sup> And he sent another servant. But they also beat and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>12</sup> And he sent yet a third. This one also they wounded and cast out. <sup>13</sup> Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’ <sup>14</sup> But when the tenants saw him, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.’ <sup>15</sup> And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? <sup>16</sup> He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” When they heard this, they said, “Surely not!” <sup>17</sup> But he looked directly at them and said, “What then is this that is written: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’? <sup>18</sup> Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.” <sup>19</sup> The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, for they perceived that he had told this parable against them, but they feared the people. <sup>20</sup> So they watched him and sent spies, who pretended to be sincere, that they might catch him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. <sup>21</sup> So they asked him, “Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God. <sup>22</sup> Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?” <sup>23</sup> But he perceived their craftiness, and said to them, <sup>24</sup> “Show me a denarius. Whose likeness and inscription does it have?” They said, “Caesar's.” <sup>25</sup> He said to them, “Then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.” <sup>26</sup> And they were not able in the presence of the people to catch him in what he said, but marveling at his answer they became silent. <sup>27</sup> There came to him some Sadducees, those who deny that there is a resurrection, <sup>28</sup> and they asked him a question, saying, “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies, having a wife but no children, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. <sup>29</sup> Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died without children. <sup>30</sup> And the second <sup>31</sup> and the third took her, and likewise all seven left no children and died. <sup>32</sup> Afterward the woman also died. <sup>33</sup> In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife.” <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said to them, “The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage, <sup>35</sup> but those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, <sup>36</sup> for they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection. <sup>37</sup> But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed, in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. <sup>38</sup> Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him.” <sup>39</sup> Then some of the scribes answered, “Teacher, you have spoken well.” <sup>40</sup> For they no longer dared to ask him any question. <sup>41</sup> But he said to them, “How can they say that the Christ is David's son? <sup>42</sup> For David himself says in the Book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, <sup>43</sup> until I make your enemies your footstool.’ <sup>44</sup> David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son?” <sup>45</sup> And in the hearing of all the people he said to his disciples, <sup>46</sup> “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, <sup>47</sup> who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.”

keyVerse.quote: Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’
keyVerse.note: This verse answers the question that opens the chapter, by what authority Jesus acts: he is not another servant but the beloved Son, the title spoken from heaven at his baptism. It also shows the heart of the Father, who after centuries of refused messengers sends the one he cannot replace, knowing what the tenants will do. Everything else in the chapter, the rejected stone, the God of the living, David’s Lord, unfolds who this Son is.

20.reflection:
The leaders asked Jesus for his credentials but would not say what they already knew about John (vv. 1–8). Where are you tempted to ask for more evidence, or to say you are still thinking about it, when the real issue is that you do not want to change?

In the parable the owner keeps sending servants, and last of all his beloved son (vv. 9–15). What does this show you about God’s patience with you? How should it shape the way we pray for people who have resisted him for years?

Jesus says to give Caesar what bears Caesar’s image and God what bears God’s (v. 25). What would it look like this week to give God yourself, wholly? Where does being a good citizen end and giving the state what belongs only to God begin?

The Sadducees assumed that the age to come would be this age prolonged (vv. 27–38). How does Jesus’ answer change the way you think about your own death, about believers you have lost, and about marriage and singleness now?

21.title: The Widow's Offering and the Olivet Discourse
21.overview:
Where we are. Luke 21 is Jesus’ last public teaching, given in the temple courts in the week before the cross. His questioners have been silenced (chapter 20); next comes the plot to kill him (22:1–6).

The message. Do not trust what looks permanent; trust Christ and his word, and keep faith until he comes. The temple’s splendour will fall, while a widow’s two coins are treasured. Wars and persecution will come, but not one of Jesus’ words will fail, not a hair of his people’s heads will perish, and the darkest events of history are leaves announcing the kingdom of God. So his people are to refuse every false christ and every date, endure without panic, and stay awake in prayer until they stand before the Son of Man.

Why it was said. The disciples admired the temple and wanted to know when it would fall (vv. 5–7). They would soon face arrest, betrayal by their own families and the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. Luke’s first readers lived in the long wait afterwards (see the introduction), tempted either to be shaken by every crisis or to grow drowsy.

How the chapter makes its case. A widow who gives all she has (vv. 1–4) is set beside an admired temple (v. 5). Jesus foretells its fall but gives no date (vv. 6–7), warns against false messiahs and panic (vv. 8–11), and promises words and final safety to his persecuted witnesses (vv. 12–19). Luke speaks more plainly than the other Gospels of the siege of Jerusalem, and he alone sets “the times of the Gentiles” between that judgment and the final, visible return of the Son of Man in glory (vv. 20–28). The fig tree shows that the signs announce the kingdom, and his words outlast heaven and earth (vv. 29–33). It ends with a call to watch and pray (vv. 34–36), and Luke closes with Jesus’ quiet daily rhythm (vv. 37–38).

Where it leads. The widow who gives her whole life points to the One who in days will give his. He will stand before Pilate and Herod, as he says his witnesses will; he will bear the wrath he grieves over; and in Gethsemane he will keep watch alone while his friends sleep. And the man teaching quietly in a doomed temple is Daniel’s Son of Man, who will come in a cloud with power and great glory.

For us. Every Christian lives in the times of the Gentiles, between the fall of the temple and the return of Christ. Refuse the date-setters and the panic. Give from trust, bear witness when it costs, endure one day at a time, and lift your head: your redemption is drawing near.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God measures a gift by what it costs and the trust behind it, not by its size. Straight after the warning about scribes who devour widows’ houses (20:47), Jesus watches the rich putting in their gifts (v. 1), and then a poor widow putting in two of the smallest coins minted (v. 2). His verdict is that she has given more than all of them, because they gave from what they would not miss and she gave all she had to live on (vv. 3–4). Whether his words are praise or lament is weighed at the end of the note on vv. 3–4.
verseByVerse.theology:
God values giving on a different ledger from ours (see the notes on v. 1 and vv. 3–4).

The scene is also a small portrait of the cross, days before it (see the note on vv. 3–4). Complete self-giving is not a heroic exception in the kingdom of God. It is what the King himself is like.
verseByVerse.examples:
A church celebrates the total of a giving campaign. The pastor privately knows the costliest gift came from a widow on a fixed income. He has to decide whether the celebration names the total or the sacrifice, and this passage tells him which one heaven has already recorded.

And for anyone whose giving is small, see the note on v. 2: the Lord noticed her, and said so.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus watches how people give, and what he weighs is the cost of a gift, not its size. The rich give much and are not rebuked, but the Lord of the temple is measuring something other than the sum.

The link. Straight after the warning about scribes who devour widows’ houses (20:47), Jesus sees a widow. Luke puts the two scenes side by side on purpose: the men who loved the best seats are condemned; the woman nobody noticed is praised.

He looked up. Jesus lifts his eyes to watch what people put in. Someone at the treasury is interested not in the total but in how people give. He still is.

The offering box. Mark tells us he was sitting opposite it (Mark 12:41). It was probably one of the collection chests in the Court of the Women, which ordinary Israelites could enter. According to the Mishnah, the collection of Jewish legal tradition written down more than a century later, thirteen chests stood there, shaped like trumpets. It is often said that a coin dropped in rang on its way down. If so, the rich are walking past, and it is ringing.

The Lord who came to his temple. Malachi had promised that the Lord whom Israel sought would suddenly come to his temple as a refiner of silver, purifying the priests until they brought offerings in righteousness (Malachi 3:1–3), and Luke has already told us who the messenger sent before him was (7:27). So the man watching the offering chests is not a visitor with opinions about stewardship. He is the Lord of the house, come to his own temple as the refiner, testing what is brought into it. The rich are weighed and the widow is weighed, and his verdict, in the next breath, will overturn every reckoning the court has made.

Nothing is said against the rich. Their gifts were real, and the temple ran on them. His reckoning is not a rebuke of their giving but a revaluation of it, and that is the more searching thing. Hypocrisy is easy to guard against, because you know when you are performing. It is much harder to discover that a gift made in good faith was, on the ledger that finally matters, worth very little, because it cost you nothing.
verseByVerse.note: The offering box was probably one of the collection chests in the Court of the Women.

verseByVerse.quote: and he saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus notices a destitute widow and her two tiny coins, a gift no one else would have counted. Nothing done for him is unwitnessed, and nothing witnessed by him is small.

He saw. The second verb of sight in two verses. In the loudest week of the religious year, with the wealth of Jerusalem filing past, the eye of the Son of God rested on a woman nobody was looking at, holding a sum nobody would have counted. Days from the cross, he was not too preoccupied to notice her, and he was not too exalted.

A poor widow. “Poor” means needy, of very little means (penichran). In that economy “widow” described destitution: no wage, little legal standing, nothing beyond gleaning and charity. The law commanded Israel to care for her (Deuteronomy 14:29), and Jesus had just said what the religious establishment did with women like her: it devoured their houses (20:47). She is the wronged party in the very institution she is about to fund.

Two small copper coins. Each was a lepton, the smallest coin in circulation; two of them came to perhaps a sixty-fourth of a day’s wage. In a trumpet-mouthed chest they would have made almost no sound at all. She could have kept one. She gave both.

The widow at Zarephath. At Nazareth Jesus had preached on her: of all the widows in Israel in Elijah’s time, the prophet was sent to one in Zarephath (4:25–26). She gave him the last of her flour and oil before feeding herself, and the jar did not run dry (1 Kings 17:12–16). God has a long habit of putting the last of somebody’s food into the story and then not letting the story end there. From Nazareth, where that sermon nearly had him thrown from a cliff (4:29), to the treasury, his mission has always moved towards the overlooked.

Does God really notice small things? Yes, and this verse is the proof. The very hairs of your head are numbered (12:7), and a cup of cold water given in his name will not lose its reward (Matthew 10:42). So the small, hidden faithfulness of an ordinary life is not wasted: the prayer no one hears, the care of an elderly parent, the coins given from a pension. Because he spoke about her, this woman is known wherever the Gospels are read, while the names of that morning’s wealthy donors are gone without trace.

In everyday life. If you have little to give, money, time or strength, give it anyway and do not be ashamed. And look around your church for the people who give quietly out of very little, whom no one thanks. Thank them, help them, and make sure no one is taking advantage of them.
verseByVerse.note: Her two coins were the smallest in circulation, a tiny fraction of a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, 'Truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
By heaven’s arithmetic the widow has given more than all the rich together, because God measures a gift by its cost and the trust behind it, not by its size. They gave what they would not miss; she gave all she had to live on.

Out of their abundance. Their overflow, what they would not miss. The money we would never miss is the money we never had to trust God for.

All she had to live on. The Greek says literally “her whole life”. She trusted God for her next meal. And she pictures what Jesus is about to do in a few days: she who gives everything at the treasury points to him who will give everything on Golgotha.

Christ alone gave out of both. The rich gave out of their abundance and the widow out of her poverty. Christ alone gave out of both: rich as the Son of God, and made poor for our sake, he gave not a portion of his wealth but his very self. Her two coins outweighed the silver of Jerusalem; his one offering outweighs the sins of a multitude no one can number.

Does Jesus mean that every believer should give away everything? No. He commends her trust and her gift; he does not command everyone to give away all they live on. Paul says a gift is acceptable according to what a person has (2 Corinthians 8:12), and a believer must provide for his own household (1 Timothy 5:8). No church may press the poor to give beyond their means; Jesus has just condemned those who devour widows’ houses (20:47). What he does ask of everyone is what she showed: a heart that trusts God more than money, and a gift that costs something.

What does the widow teach me about how much to give? The New Testament sets no fixed percentage but gives clear principles. Set something aside regularly, in keeping with your income (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give generously, “not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:6–7). Give first, not from what is left over. Many Christians find the Old Testament tithe, a tenth, a helpful starting point, and many in comfortable circumstances give more. The widow’s question is not “what is the least I must give?” but “what does it cost me to trust God here?” Start where you are, and let your giving grow as your trust grows.

Where Christians differ: praise or lament? Only a few verses earlier Jesus condemned the scribes who devour widows’ houses (20:47); a few verses later he says the temple whose treasury she is filling will be torn down to the last stone (21:6). So some readers conclude that Jesus is not praising her at all but lamenting her, mourning a religious system that has taught a penniless widow to give away her last means of living. It is an honest reading, and the sequence that suggests it is not accidental. This commentary’s view: as in Mark’s account (Mark 12:43–44), the context of corruption is real, but Jesus’ words are clearly praise of her faith and devotion: “this poor widow has put in more than all of them” is commendation. He is not endorsing the temple or saying her coins repaired anything; within a generation the whole apparatus would be ash. He is telling us what God saw at that treasury: not the sums, but a heart holding nothing back. The worth of her gift lay not in the soundness of the institution that received it but in the trust of the one who gave it, and God received it though the building was under sentence. That is a mercy for everyone who has given and served inside a church that was flawed or failing or would not outlast them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–19 — The Temple, the Signs, and the Cost of Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not rest on the stones or chase the dates: trust Christ and bear witness, for your life is safe with him. Someone admires the temple, and Jesus replies that not one stone will be left on another, as in AD 70 it was (vv. 5–6). Asked when, he gives no date, only instructions for the meantime: do not follow those who claim to be the Christ or announce that the time is at hand, do not be terrified by wars, and do not read disasters as the signal of the end (vv. 7–11). Before any of that his disciples will be brought before kings and governors, and it will be their opportunity to bear witness, with a mouth and wisdom promised (vv. 12–15). The cost is named plainly, betrayal by family, death for some, hatred for his name’s sake, yet not a hair of their heads will perish (vv. 16–19).
verseByVerse.theology:
Verse 16 and verse 18 do not contradict each other: enemies can kill a believer, but they cannot destroy the person himself (this is treated fully at vv. 18–19).

The disciple is not promised safety; he is promised what he needs: words when words are needed, and a security no execution can touch. On endurance, see vv. 18–19; and the promises are for suffering “for my name’s sake”, not for every unpopularity (see the note on vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.examples: For those whose faith has cost them a family, it was foreseen and foretold, and a promise is attached to it (see the note on vv. 16–17).

verseByVerse.quote: And while some were speaking of the temple, how it was adorned with noble stones and offerings, he said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples admire the temple’s splendour, and the stage is set for Jesus to show that what looks most permanent is not what lasts.

The Olivet Discourse. Luke’s version of Jesus’ teaching about the future (Mark 13; Matthew 24) is spoken in the temple (vv. 5, 37), and answers two questions: when will the temple be destroyed, and what will happen at the end?

Noble stones. They were not being foolish. The temple rebuilt by Herod the Great was one of the wonders of the ancient world. Some foundation stones still in place are over forty feet (some 12 metres) long, and Josephus says that when the morning sun struck the gold-plated front a man had to look away, and that from a distance it looked like a mountain covered with snow.

And offerings. Gifts dedicated to God and put on display, among them a golden vine over the entrance, added to cluster by cluster by worshippers. Completed only in the early sixties, within a few years it was gone.

The temple of the LORD. Jeremiah had named the instinct six hundred years earlier: “Do not trust in these deceptive words: ‘This is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD’” (Jeremiah 7:4). The people were not chanting a lie. They were resting on a building instead of on the One who had asked for it, which is much harder to see in yourself. The thing admired here was genuinely magnificent, genuinely God-ordained and genuinely doomed, and nothing in the stonework told them which of the three was about to matter.

The glory of this latter house. When this second temple was first rebuilt, the old men who remembered Solomon’s wept (Ezra 3:12), and God answered through Haggai that the latter glory of this house would be greater than the former (Haggai 2:9). Herod’s gold never made that true. What made it true was a child forty days old carried up its steps and taken into an old man’s arms as God’s salvation (2:22–32), a boy of twelve calling it his Father’s house (2:49), and now a man teaching in its courts day after day. Those admiring the stones are praising the frame while the picture stands beside them.

The true Vine under the golden one. The golden vine over the door was a fitting emblem, for Israel was the vine God brought out of Egypt (Psalm 80:8). The true Vine (John 15:1) walked beneath it that week, unadorned, and in a few days he would be cut down. Yet from him, and not from the gold, grows the fruit God sought in every age, fruit that no Roman torch can reach.

Is it wrong to love a beautiful church building? No. Beauty is God’s gift, and the tabernacle and temple were made beautiful at his command (Exodus 28:2; 1 Chronicles 22:5). The danger is trusting in it, or in any institution: assuming that because the building, the denomination or the tradition is old and impressive, God must be pleased with what happens inside it. The church is not the building but the people of God gathered around Christ, and that church will survive any building’s fall.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great had rebuilt the temple on a vast scale, with gleaming white stone and gifts displayed by donors.

verseByVerse.quote: 'As for these things that you see, the days will come when there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus foretells that the temple will be utterly destroyed, and with it Israel’s whole way of coming to God through priest and sacrifice.

The days will come. A phrase the prophets used to announce judgment. He points at the most permanent things in their world and says they will end.

Not one stone upon another. This was the one place on earth where sacrifice could lawfully be offered and where God had put his name. To say it would fall was to say that the old way of coming to God was ending. Jeremiah was nearly killed for saying less (Jeremiah 26:8–11), and a saying about the temple would be brought against Jesus at his trial (Mark 14:58).

The fulfilment. About forty years later, in AD 70, the city fell and the temple burned. The great platform survived, including the Western Wall, but that wall belongs to the platform, not the sanctuary. Of the sanctuary itself, exactly what Jesus said is what is there: nothing. The temple fell, and its Lord stands.

The perishable and the imperishable. He will say the counterpart in v. 33: what we can see will perish and the spoken word of Christ will not, the exact reverse of what the world assumes (Isaiah 40:8).

Why did God allow his own temple to be destroyed? Because its work was done. The temple was a shadow; Christ is the substance. He is the true temple, where God dwells with man (John 2:19–21), and his death is the one sacrifice to which all the temple’s sacrifices pointed (Hebrews 9:11–12; 10:11–14). When the veil was torn at his death (23:45), the old way was finished. The fall of the temple in AD 70 was also a judgment on the generation that rejected the Messiah (19:41–44), and after it no one could imagine that animal sacrifices were still the way to God. There is one way now, and it is open to every nation: Jesus himself.

Was this prophecy written after the event? Some scholars argue that Luke must have written after AD 70 and shaped the saying to fit. Acts, Luke’s second volume, ends with Paul alive in Rome and says nothing about the fall of Jerusalem, the death of Paul or the death of James, events a Christian historian writing later would hardly have left out (see the introduction). And the prediction is not detailed in the way invented prophecy tends to be; it does not even mention the fire. The date of Luke is still debated and cannot be fixed beyond dispute. But the saying does not rest on Luke alone: it stands in Mark, and the charge at his trial shows it was remembered, so many scholars of every outlook accept that Jesus did speak of the temple’s fall. For those who believe he rose, the deeper answer is simpler. Jesus is the Son of God, and the God who declares the end from the beginning (Isaiah 46:10) is able to tell his servants what will happen.
verseByVerse.note: The Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, 'Teacher, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when these things are about to take place?' And he said, 'See that you are not led astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and, ‘The time is at hand!’ Do not go after them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked when the temple will fall, Jesus gives no date; his first concern is that his people are not deceived.

When will these things be? Two questions, both about timing and, in Luke, both about the temple’s destruction: when, and how will we know it is close? It is what any of us would have asked.

What will be the sign? Look at what he does not do. He does not give a date, here or anywhere in Luke, and offers no formula for calculating one. What he gives instead is instructions for living in the meantime, and the very first is a warning about people who will answer the question he has just declined to answer.

See that you are not led astray. The Greek verb gives English its word “planet”, a wandering star. To be led astray is to drift off course while still believing you are travelling in a straight line.

In my name. Claiming to be the Messiah. Acts and Josephus both record would-be deliverers in the decades that followed (Acts 5:36–37; 21:38), and every century since has had them.

The time is at hand. Only Luke adds this. The first claim is about a person; this one is about a clock. Many who would never make the first claim make the second every decade, and Jesus puts them in the same warning.

Do not go after them. The history of the church is littered with the wreckage of announced dates, and the wreckage is always made of people: farms sold, savings given away, and then the morning after, when the sun came up as usual.

The name worth stealing. Counterfeiters copy only what is valuable. That false christs would arise for centuries, all borrowing his title, is itself a testimony to the One they imitate. Every impostor must claim what Jesus simply is (22:70). He is the fixed star by which every wandering light is judged, the same yesterday and today and for ever (Hebrews 13:8), and the test of every voice is whether, like John the Baptist, it is glad to decrease so that he may increase (John 3:30).

How can an ordinary Christian tell whether a teacher is leading people astray? Watch where the teaching takes the people who follow it. Teaching from God sends a person back to ordinary obedience: his work, his family, his prayers, his neighbour, his local church, and above all to Christ himself. Teaching that leads astray gathers a following around a teacher, doing something exceptional at his direction, on a timetable he supplies. Test the spirits (1 John 4:1). The mark of the false is that it makes you dependent on a man who claims to know something Christ declined to tell you (Acts 1:7).

verseByVerse.quote: And when you hear of wars and tumults, do not be terrified, for these things must first take place, but the end will not be at once.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When news of war and upheaval comes, Christ’s people are not to be terrified, because these things lie within God’s plan and do not mean the end has arrived.

When you hear. Not “when you suffer”. Jesus is speaking about the effect on the soul of news from elsewhere. He knew, twenty centuries before the phone on the bedside table, that a person can be crushed by events that are not happening to him.

Do not be terrified. Not ordinary fear, but being startled out of your senses, the mind scattering. He is not forbidding grief or concern; the man who reads of a famine and feels nothing has a worse problem than anxiety. He is forbidding the state in which fear has taken over the controls.

These things must first take place. “Must” is Luke’s word for the settled purpose of God (dei), the very word Jesus used of his own suffering: “The Son of Man must suffer many things” (9:22). He puts the same word under the wars: they are inside the plan, not outside it. God does not do evil or approve of it, and those who start wars are guilty for them (James 4:1–2). Yet he governs even the wicked acts of men for his own good purposes (Genesis 50:20).

But the end will not be at once. What crushes a person watching the world convulse is the conclusion drawn from it: that history is unravelling. Jesus flatly denies the inference. Wars are the weather of a long age, and he says so in advance so that nobody has to work it out during the storm.

The worst “must”. The cross shows what that word means in God’s mouth. The worst thing men ever did was also a “must”, and it became the salvation of the world (24:26). The One who says the wars must come is the One who set his face to go to Jerusalem because he must, and the One who holds the plan bore its worst himself for those who live through it. The world’s foundations are upheld by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3), by hands that were about to be nailed to a cross.

What should I do when the news frightens me? Not look away, but refuse the false interpretation. When the headline arrives, the question is not “is this the end?” He has told you it is not. The smaller and more answerable question is: “what does love require of me today, in this street, with this news in my head?” Pray for the people in it, as specifically as you can. Give if you can. Then do your work and go to bed. And limit what you take in: no one is helped by a mind fed with disaster every hour. “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear though the earth give way” (Psalm 46:1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, 'Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be great earthquakes, and in various places famines and pestilences. And there will be terrors and great signs from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
War, earthquake, famine, plague and fearful signs will mark the whole age before Christ returns, and they are not clues to a date.

Nation against nation. Four categories cover everything that can go wrong on a planet: war, which men cause; earthquake, which nobody causes; famine and plague, which are often partly man-made and partly not; and then the sky.

Famines and pestilences. Only Luke includes “pestilences”. There was a severe famine under Claudius, which Luke records (Acts 11:28), and major earthquakes in the sixties.

Signs from heaven. Only Luke has this. Josephus records portents before the fall of Jerusalem: a star like a sword over the city, armies in the sky, the temple’s eastern gate opening by itself at night.

Not signs of the end. “The end will not be at once” (v. 9). These are “the beginning of the birth pains” (Mark 13:8), the ordinary content of the long age between his ascension and his return, and they have marked every generation since. The plague years of the fourteenth century convinced many that the end had come. A man who thinks he is watching the last act does not plant trees, so Jesus takes the false interpretation away as a kindness.

The Lord of everything on the list. The man who speaks of earthquakes and terrors rebuked the wind and the raging waves until there was a calm (8:24). The one who speaks of famine fed five thousand in a desolate place with five loaves (9:12–17). The one who speaks of plagues laid his hands on the sick of every kind and healed them (4:40). Every disaster he names is a territory he has already entered as its master. He foretells them not as a spectator but as the Lord who will one day end each of them for good. The groaning of creation is real, but it is labour, not death throes, and the first of the new creation has already been born: “the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1:18).

Why does God allow earthquakes, famines and plagues? Scripture does not give a full answer, but it gives enough to trust him. These things are the fruit of a world under the curse of sin (Genesis 3:17–19; Romans 8:20–22), not usually the punishment of particular sufferers for particular sins (13:1–5). They are warnings that this world is not our home and that judgment is coming, calling all people to repentance. And God is not absent from them: his Son entered this groaning world, suffered in it, and will make all things new (Revelation 21:4–5).

In various places. The suffering falls in some places, not everywhere at once, and that is why the church has always been able to answer it. When the famine is in one place, the harvest is in another, as the believers in Antioch found when they heard of the famine in Judea (Acts 11:29–30). Believers whom the trouble has spared are free to send help to those it has struck.

verseByVerse.quote: But before all this they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues and prisons, and you will be brought before kings and governors for my name's sake. This will be your opportunity to bear witness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before any of these upheavals, Jesus’ followers will be arrested and tried because they belong to him, and every trial will be their opportunity to bear witness.

But before all this. Luke stresses the order: persecution of the disciples comes first, before the wars and signs. The disciple’s experience of the last age begins not with a sign in the sky but with a hand on his arm.

Synagogues and prisons. Luke alone went on to write the sequel, and every item on this list happens in Acts: Peter and John arrested (Acts 4:3), the apostles beaten (Acts 5:40), Stephen stoned (Acts 7), James killed with the sword (Acts 12:2), believers delivered to synagogues and prisons (Acts 9:2; 16:23).

Kings and governors. Paul stood before Felix, Festus and King Agrippa (Acts 24–26). And the cause is named: not for being difficult, or political, or strange, but “for my name’s sake”, because they belong to Jesus.

Your opportunity. The Greek says “it will turn out for you as testimony”, and testimony is martyrion, a relative of the word that gives us “martyr”, though here it still means simply the evidence a witness gives. So God does not merely bring good out of an arrest afterwards. The arrest is the appointment. The courtroom becomes a pulpit: kings and governors think they are trying his servants, and they are being preached to. It is hard to see how else a tentmaker from Tarsus, held in chains, could have got a hearing before a Roman governor and a king, and the Lord arranged it.

Paul saw it so. Writing from prison, he said that what had happened to him had “really served to advance the gospel” (Philippians 1:12–14).

Before a governor and a king. The Master would go first. Within days Jesus himself would be brought before a governor, Pontius Pilate, and, as Luke alone records, a king, Herod Antipas (23:1–12), and there he “made the good confession” (1 Timothy 6:13). Every disciple who has since stood before a magistrate for his name has stood where the Son of God stood.

What if I never face a courtroom? The principle does not require handcuffs. It requires only that following Christ has cost you something in front of other people: the awkward silence when you said where you were on Sunday, the promotion that went elsewhere, the family meal that went quiet when you would not laugh at the joke. Those moments feel like loss, and they are counted as testimony. A watching colleague learns more from what your faith costs you than from anything you could have said when it was free. And remember the believers in many countries today for whom this is no metaphor: they are arrested, beaten and imprisoned for his name, exactly as he said.

verseByVerse.quote: Settle it therefore in your minds not to meditate beforehand how to answer, for I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ witnesses need not rehearse their defence in anxiety, because he himself will give them the words and the wisdom to speak.

Settle it. Make the decision now, in advance, and then stop carrying the worry.

Not to meditate beforehand how to answer. The verb was used of rehearsing a speech, as a defendant would rehearse his defence. Jesus is not talking about study, which Luke’s own heroes do constantly, but about the anxious drafting of testimony before a hearing.

A mouth and wisdom. In 12:12 it is the Holy Spirit who will teach them what to say; here it is Jesus himself, for the risen Christ gives his Spirit, and the Spirit speaks Christ’s words. “Wisdom” is what to say. “A mouth” is the ability to say it, the part many of us lack: we know the truth and cannot get it past our teeth when it matters. He who made man’s mouth (Exodus 4:11–12) has promised to fill it. He has never yet sent a witness into a room and failed to arrive himself.

None able to withstand. Luke shows the promise kept: of Stephen, “they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking” (Acts 6:10).

Does this verse forbid preparing sermons or Bible studies? No, and Paul settles it by example. He reasoned in the synagogue from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths (Acts 17:2), quoted Greek poets in Athens, and asked Timothy to bring “the books, and above all the parchments” (2 Timothy 4:13); and standing before Agrippa he plainly received something he had not written. Preparation and this promise are not rivals. One is the ordinary work; the other is the extraordinary supply at the moment when the ordinary work has been taken away. Prepare diligently when you can. When you cannot, trust him.

Does this mean Christians will always win the argument? Not in the sense that their opponents will be persuaded or that they will be acquitted. Stephen’s hearers could not withstand his wisdom, and they stoned him. The promise is that the truth spoken by Christ’s witnesses will not be refuted, that their testimony will stand, and that God will be glorified in it. Your task is to be faithful; his is to give the words and to use them as he wills.

In everyday life. The anxiety this verse addresses is rarely about courtrooms. It is the dread of the question at work or at the kitchen table, or lying awake composing what you should have said. The command is not “try harder” but “settle it”. Pray before the conversation, say what you know simply, and leave the rest with him.

parallels.desc: they could not withstand the wisdom of Stephen

verseByVerse.quote: You will be delivered up even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you they will put to death. You will be hated by all for my name's sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Following Jesus may cost a disciple the loyalty of his own family and, for some, life itself, and the hatred will come because of his name.

Even by parents. The list moves outward from the innermost circle. “Delivered up” means handed over into the power of someone who intends harm: not an argument at a family gathering but a father telling the authorities where his son is (Micah 7:6; 12:52–53).

Some of you. Not all, and he does not say which, though he knows. James would be the first apostle martyred (Acts 12:2); John, as the early church remembered it, would die old.

Hated by all. Hatred that seems universal makes a person suspect the fault is his. But the reason is stated twice in six verses (vv. 12, 17): “for my name’s sake”.
