For anyone whose deepest need is to be liked, this sentence is meant to loosen that need’s grip. The Father’s verdict on his Son, “You are my beloved Son” (3:22), rests on everyone who is in him, and no crowd can take it back.

Delivered up, as he was. The verb is the one Luke keeps for Jesus’ own passion (9:44), and within days Judas, who had shared his table, would deliver him up with a kiss (22:4–6, 48). Jesus is not describing a road he will watch his disciples walk. He is describing the road he is already on. And the Son who was handed over by a friend has become the Friend who hands over no one. He answers the empty chair at the table with a household: his mother and his brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it (8:21).

Not every unpopularity. A Christian can be disliked for being rude, superior or tactless, and has not been promised anything here. Ask whether people would still dislike your behaviour if you were not a Christian. If they would, the remedy is repentance.

What if my family has turned against me for following Christ? Two things in Luke are true for you. First, Jesus said this would happen. The silence at the other end of the phone is not evidence that God has abandoned your family or that you made a mistake. It was foreseen and foretold, by someone whose own brothers did not at first believe in him (John 7:5). Second, he attached a promise to it: “there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life” (18:29–30). The family is not replaced but enlarged, in the church now, so let the church be family to you. Keep loving and praying for your relatives, honour them where you can without denying Christ, and leave the door open. Many have come later.

verseByVerse.quote: But not a hair of your head will perish. By your endurance you will gain your lives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though some of them will be killed, Jesus’ people are completely safe in him, and by enduring they will gain true life.

Not a hair. The sharpest apparent contradiction in the chapter: two verses earlier he said “some of you they will put to death” (v. 16). The two are measured on different scales, and the second is the true measure. They may lose their lives, but they will not perish.

The idiom. “Not a hair of your head” is a Hebrew way of speaking of complete preservation (1 Samuel 14:45; Acts 27:34). Jesus has used it once already, in a passage about being dragged before the authorities: “even the hairs of your head are all numbered” (12:7).

The person is safe. Stephen was stoned to death, and not a hair of his head perished. Luke wrote both sentences.

By your endurance. Endurance means to remain under the load (hypomonē), like a beam still bearing the weight in the morning (8:15). And the verb is “gain”, not “keep”. The life they lose for him is given back, and it is greater than the one they lost.

Why both sentences can be true. The man who spoke them was about to be put to death, and on the third day he showed these same disciples his hands and his feet (24:39). Death did to Jesus everything it can do, and it could not keep him, and his people are joined to him. “Not a hair of your head will perish” is, in the end, a promise of resurrection.

Does my salvation depend on my endurance? Endurance is the evidence and fruit of God’s keeping, not the ground of salvation. “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6), and no one will snatch Christ’s sheep out of his hand (John 10:28). This is the perseverance of the saints: God keeps his people, and they keep going. The call to endure is real, and God uses it as one of the means by which he keeps his people: you must endure; and if you are his, you will, because he will hold you.

What if I do not think I have it in me to last? That is the quieter fear this verse raises in most Christians, not the fear of martyrdom but this: “I do not think I can keep going. Not thirty more years. Not through what is coming.” You are not asked to last thirty years at once. Endurance is not a store of strength held in reserve; it is remaining under, today. Nobody is given the grace for a decade in advance. The saints who endured to the end did it the way anyone does: the next morning, and then the one after that, on mercies that are new every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23) and grace that is sufficient for the day (2 Corinthians 12:9).

In everyday life. If you are facing a long trial, an illness, a hard marriage, a grief that will not lift, do not try to carry next year. Ask for today’s grace from the Spirit who raised Jesus and lives in you (Romans 8:11), do today’s faithful thing, and lie down tonight trusting the One who numbers your hairs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–28 — The Fall of the City and the Coming of the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fall of Jerusalem is God’s judgment and a foretaste; the coming of the Son of Man is the end, and for his people it is redemption. When armies surround Jerusalem, Jesus’ people are to flee the city, not shelter in it (vv. 20–21). Its fall will be God’s judgment, and he grieves as he announces it (vv. 22–23); the city will be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled (v. 24). Then the scene widens from a city to the world: signs in the heavens, nations in perplexity, people fainting with dread (vv. 25–26), and the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory (Daniel 7:13). His people are to straighten up and raise their heads, because their redemption is drawing near (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology:
Serious readers differ on how the fall of Jerusalem (verses 20 to 24) relates to the coming of the Son of Man (verses 25 to 28): see the box “Where Christians differ: is this the Second Coming, or the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70?” at the end of the note on vv. 27–28. On the objection that Jesus predicted a return that did not come, see the note on vv. 32–33.

“They will see” anchors the Christian hope in something public: he will be seen returning.
verseByVerse.examples: Verses 25 and 26 describe a suffering common in comfortable countries: not disaster but dread (see the note on vv. 25–26). Jesus names it, and then tells his own people to lift their heads.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near. Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let those who are inside the city depart, and let not those who are out in the country enter it,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When armies surround Jerusalem, its destruction is near, and Jesus’ followers are to flee the city rather than take refuge in it.

Jerusalem surrounded by armies. Where Mark speaks of “the abomination of desolation”, with “let the reader understand” (Mark 13:14), Luke, writing for Gentile readers, probably gives the plain meaning. It was fulfilled when the Romans surrounded Jerusalem, first under Cestius Gallus in AD 66, then under Titus in AD 70.

Its desolation. The destruction and abandonment of the city, as Daniel had foreseen (Daniel 9:26–27).

Flee to the mountains. Three commands follow, startlingly ordinary: get out of Judea, get out of the city, do not go back in. Under any normal siege the countryside empties into the walled city. Jesus tells them to do the opposite, and history shows why: many who fled into the city were trapped, and famine and fighting between factions killed multitudes before the Romans broke through.

The church heard him. The church historian Eusebius records that the Christians of Jerusalem, warned by a prophetic word, left before the war reached its height and settled at Pella, east of the Jordan, perhaps when Cestius Gallus withdrew in AD 66. The tradition has been questioned, but it fits what plainly happened: the church was not destroyed when Jerusalem was.

He went in so that they could go out. He tells his disciples to get out of Jerusalem in the week he himself has entered it with his face set (9:51). He enters the doomed city so that his people can leave it. Outside its walls he would bear a wrath far deeper than any siege, and the command to flee comes from the One who, a few nights later, would refuse to flee himself.

Is fleeing not simply running away? Should the disciples not have stayed and prayed for the city, and died with it if necessary? Jesus says no, and it is good to have a Lord who will say so. There is a time to stand and a time to go, and the difference is not measured by how brave it feels. Paul was let down the Damascus wall in a basket (Acts 9:25) and was not ashamed to tell of it (2 Corinthians 11:32–33). What decides the answer is not courage but calling: flight from danger is cowardice only when it is flight from a post you were given, and nobody was given the post of dying inside those walls. So for Christians facing persecution today, it is not wrong to flee if God opens a way, and it is not wrong to stay if he calls you to.
verseByVerse.note: Luke speaks plainly of Jerusalem surrounded by armies, as the Romans did in AD 66–70; Matthew and Mark speak of “the abomination of desolation.”

verseByVerse.quote: for these are days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written. Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fall of Jerusalem will be God’s just judgment, fulfilling what he had warned, and Jesus grieves over it even as he announces it.

Days of vengeance. This is judgment: God’s judgment on Jerusalem for rejecting her Messiah (19:43–44). In his covenant God had bound himself to Israel with promises for faithfulness and plain warnings of siege and exile for rebellion (Deuteronomy 28:15, 49–52). Vengeance here is not a grudge but the holy God keeping his word, as a just judge keeps the law.

To fulfill all that is written. The prophets had warned of siege and famine on unfaithful Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 28:49–57; Daniel 9:26; Micah 3:12). God does what he has said.

Alas. Bolted to the judgment is grief. The word is often heard as a threat; here it is the sound a man makes over something unbearable, aimed at the least guilty people in the city: a woman eight months pregnant, a mother with a baby at the breast, on the day the siege begins.

Great distress upon the earth. “Upon the earth” may mean upon the land of Israel. Josephus describes horrors of famine and slaughter that are hard to read.

Judgment and tears together. The judgment is deserved and it is agonising, and the one who says so had wept over this city a few days before (19:41–42). He does not judge half-heartedly, and he does not judge coldly. “I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord GOD; so turn, and live” (Ezekiel 18:32).

The sentence finished. The phrase “days of vengeance” reaches back to Isaiah 61:2, the year of the LORD’s favour and the day of vengeance of our God, the passage Jesus read at Nazareth. There he stopped in the middle of the sentence, announcing the favour and leaving the vengeance unread (4:18–19). Seventeen chapters later he finishes the sentence. He announced the day of vengeance and went to bear it. Yet the year of favour is still being proclaimed to every nation, and the patience that kept the scroll closed at Nazareth has kept the door open for us.

Does God enjoy judging people? No. The answer is standing in the temple court with tears not yet dry, describing a siege a generation off, and grieving in advance for infants not yet born. His judgment is real and just, because sin is real and he is holy. But he takes no pleasure in it. And within the week the wrath he is describing will fall in its fullness on him, so that everyone in that city and every sinner in the world who turns to him might not have to bear it. There is no vengeance in Scripture that God has not first been willing to bear himself for those who trust him (Isaiah 53:5; Romans 5:9).

In everyday life. If you have grown casual about sin, let this passage sober you. If you are afraid of God’s wrath, look at who is speaking, and run to him, not away from him.

parallels.desc: the days of punishment have come

verseByVerse.quote: They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s people will be killed or scattered and the city ruled by Gentiles, but only until the time God has set, “the times of the Gentiles”, is complete.

Led captive. Josephus says over a million died in the siege, probably an exaggeration, and that ninety-seven thousand were taken captive, many sold as slaves or made to die in the arenas.

Trampled underfoot. After the second Jewish revolt (AD 132–135), the Romans rebuilt Jerusalem as a pagan city and banned Jews from it. Empire after empire has held it since.

Until the times of the Gentiles. Only Luke has this clause. Every reading agrees on the word “until”: Gentile rule over Jerusalem is real, but God permits it and has set an end to it. And the times of the Gentiles are also the time when the gospel goes to the Gentiles, as Paul says: “a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in” (Romans 11:25).

A light for the Gentiles. Over the infant Jesus in this temple Simeon had sung of “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (2:32), and the risen Christ will send his apostles to all nations (24:47). So the times of the Gentiles are not empty time between two catastrophes. They are the age in which the light Simeon held in his arms goes out to every people.

A horizon behind the trampling. Jesus sets a limit to the trampling, and the word “until” is God’s. Scripture never describes any oppression in this world, including any you are suffering now, as lasting for ever.

Is the modern state of Israel the fulfilment of prophecy? What this verse will not bear is a calendar. It gives a boundary without a date, deliberately, and every attempt to turn it into arithmetic has expired. The New Testament’s focus is not on territory but on the gospel: the promises to Abraham are fulfilled in Christ, the true offspring (Galatians 3:16, 29), and Jews and Gentiles alike are saved only by faith in him. Christians should pray for the peace of Jerusalem and for all its people, Jewish and Arab, and long for them to know the Messiah. They should not treat the news from the Middle East as a timetable for Christ’s return.

Where Christians differ: the times of the Gentiles. Many Reformed interpreters take the phrase to mean the whole age between the fall of Jerusalem and the return of Christ. Dispensationalists (who see Israel and the church as distinct in God’s plan and expect a future national role for Israel), including teachers many readers have been helped by, understand it as a defined period of Gentile political domination of Jerusalem, and many have seen the founding of the modern state of Israel (1948) and the capture of Jerusalem (1967) as the end of the times of the Gentiles and a sign of the imminent end. Their instinct is sound in this respect: they are trying to let the word “until” mean something, and to take seriously that God has not finished with the people to whom he made the promises. This commentary’s view: Jesus gives no such timetable, and warns against date-setting (vv. 8–9). The times of the Gentiles is the age of Gentile mission and Gentile dominance between the fall of Jerusalem and Christ’s return. This fits Luke’s own flow, where Acts carries the gospel out to the nations, and Romans 11:25 measures the term by the ingathering of the Gentiles, not by who governs a city. Christians differ on whether Paul expects a future large-scale turning of the Jewish people to Christ or means by “all Israel” the whole elect people of God (Romans 11:25–27); on either reading, Israel’s salvation is a work of grace through the gospel, not a political event to be calculated.

parallels.desc: the nations have come into your inheritance
until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in

verseByVerse.quote: 'And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth distress of nations in perplexity because of the roaring of the sea and the waves, people fainting with fear and with foreboding of what is coming on the world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the Son of Man comes, the whole created order will be shaken, and a world without hope will faint with dread at what is coming.

Signs in sun and moon. The discourse now moves from a city to the world and to his return. Every image comes from the prophets, who used it for great acts of God’s judgment: stars withholding their light at the fall of Babylon (Isaiah 13:10), the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood (Joel 2:30–31; Acts 2:20).

Literal or picture? In the Bible’s own usage this is the language of God arriving in judgment and of an old order ending, used both of historical catastrophes and of the last day. Whether the sun will literally go dark is not something this passage settles, and a reader should not be told it does. What it plainly announces is that creation itself will feel the coming of its Maker, and that it will be terrifying to see.

Distress of nations. “Perplexity” is literally no way through (aporia), the state of a person who has run out of options. The sea, in Scripture, is a picture of chaos (Psalm 46:3; Revelation 13:1).

Fainting with fear. Strength simply leaving, with foreboding: fear not of what is happening but of what is coming. That is a common suffering in a prosperous country: the scan that has not come back, the redundancy not yet announced. Jesus does not scold this. He knows what dread does to a person.

The powers of the heavens. Once more, “I will shake the heavens and the earth” (Haggai 2:6): the shaking removes what is made, so that what cannot be shaken may remain (Hebrews 12:26–27). He who made the sun and moon and stars will shake them at his coming, and they will obey him as they obeyed him at the beginning.

The sun’s light failed. On the day Jesus died, darkness lay over the whole land from noon until three, and Luke alone says it: “the sun’s light failed” (23:44–45). The heavens that will be shaken at his return went dark at his death, because their Maker was bearing the sin of his people. That is why a believer can read this verse without terror. The judgment these signs announce has already fallen once, at noon on Golgotha, on the Son of God in the place of all who trust him.

Why are the safest people in history so anxious? Those of us in prosperous countries are, by most measures, safer than any generation before us: longer lives, fewer famines, medicine our grandparents would have called miraculous. Yet anxiety has become one of the signature troubles of the age; W. H. Auden could already call a long poem of 1947 The Age of Anxiety. Part of the reason is in this verse: “foreboding of what is coming”. When this life is all there is, everything is at stake in it. Every symptom, every market fall, every turn in the headlines threatens the only future we have, and we must manage it all ourselves. Comfort does not cure that; it only gives us more to lose. Religion run as a bargain does not cure it either, because a person who must keep God pleased is always one failure away from dread. Jesus does not promise his people that nothing frightening will happen. He tells them what happens next. While the world faints, they lift their heads, because what is coming towards them is not the end of everything but their Redeemer (v. 28), who has already gone through the worst for them.

Should these verses frighten a Christian? They should sober us, but not terrify us. They are meant to warn the unbelieving and wake the sleepy. For those who belong to Christ the same events are the prelude to joy. You do not need to fear the day of the Lord if you are hidden in the Lord of the day. If you are not, these verses are his kind warning to come to him now.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. Now when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end Jesus will return visibly, in the glory that belongs to God, and for his people that day means not terror but final release.

The Son of Man coming. Daniel saw one like a son of man brought on the clouds before the Ancient of Days and handed a kingdom that would never be destroyed (Daniel 7:13–14). He came first in weakness, laid in a manger; he will come again “with power and great glory”.

In a cloud. Luke alone has a single cloud, where Matthew and Mark have clouds, and Luke alone wrote the two scenes that explain it: the voice from the cloud on the mountain (9:34–35), and the cloud that took him out of their sight, with the promise that he would come in the same way (Acts 1:9–11). The cloud is the robe of God’s presence (Exodus 40:34–35). To come in a cloud is to come as only God comes.

They will see. The Christian hope can never be reduced to an inner experience. He was seen when he was born, killed and taken up, and every eye will see him coming back (Revelation 1:7). The gospel is not finally a set of ideas but a report about a Man, and the report ends with him visible.

There is no secret coming. Like every other New Testament description of the return, this passage speaks of one coming, public and seen by all, when the gathering of his people, the resurrection and the judgment come together (1 Thessalonians 4:16; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). On a secret removal of the church beforehand, see v. 36.

Straighten up. Two physical commands. “Straighten up” is the word Luke used of the woman bent double for eighteen years (13:11–13). “Raise your heads”: lift the chin, which nobody under threat ever does. While the world is fainting, the Christian is told to do the opposite of the natural thing with his own body.

Your redemption. “Redemption” means release (apolytrōsis), the word for freeing captives by paying a price. Here it means full and final deliverance, including the resurrection of the body (Romans 8:23). The events that terrify everyone else are, for the believer, the sound of the door opening. The world sees the end of everything. The church sees him.

Hold the picture. Daniel’s figure, given every people and nation into his hands, is the same figure standing in a temple courtyard, days from being flogged, describing what is coming to men who will run away from him before the week is out. The dominion was always going to be handed to a crucified man. He paid the price of our release with his own blood, and he is coming to claim what he bought, body and soul, not to destroy his own but to take them home. The hands that once straightened a woman bent double will one day straighten a whole bowed creation.

How should I think about Christ’s return day to day? As the believer’s great hope, not a subject of dread or calculation: history is going somewhere, every injustice will be put right, the dead in Christ will rise, our bodies will be redeemed, and we will see him face to face. Paul calls it the blessed hope (Titus 2:13). It should make you watchful in holiness, steady in suffering and generous with this world’s goods, because they are not your final treasure, and it should put the prayer of the early church in your mouth: “Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

In everyday life. Practise the posture. When the news is bad, or your body is failing, or the church seems weak, lift your head and say: “my redemption is drawing near.” Let it change one thing today: the fear you will not feed, the grudge you will let go, the thing you will give away.

Where Christians differ: is this the Second Coming, or the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70? Some interpreters read this coming as Christ’s vindication, made visible when the temple fell, pointing out that in Daniel 7 the son of man travels to the Ancient of Days to receive his kingdom rather than down to the earth. This commentary’s view: in Luke the far horizon is in view here. Luke has already set the times of the Gentiles between the fall of the city and these signs (v. 24), and what he describes reaches far beyond AD 70: signs in sun, moon and stars, anguish among the nations of the whole earth, and the redemption of God’s people drawing near (v. 28). The fall of Jerusalem (vv. 20–24) was a real judgment and a foretaste. This is the final, visible return of Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–38 — The Fig Tree, the Weight on the Heart, and the Daily Rhythm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The signs announce not a dying world but the coming kingdom, so live awake and prayerful, trusting words that cannot fail. The parable of the fig tree is deliberately ordinary: trees come into leaf, and everybody knows summer is near (vv. 29–31). This generation would see what the disciples had asked about, though the day of his return is not given, and under it all stands the promise that heaven and earth will pass away but his words will not (vv. 32–33). What threatens readiness is a heart weighed down by indulgence or the cares of this life, and the remedy is to stay awake and pray (vv. 34–36). Luke ends with Jesus himself living that way, teaching by day and lodging on the Mount of Olives by night (vv. 37–38).
verseByVerse.theology:
Watchfulness is not scanning the news for prophetic fulfilment but the steady attention of people who live each day knowing that Christ is coming.

“To stand before the Son of Man” is courtroom language. “If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?” (Psalm 130:3). The strength to stand is asked for (see the note on v. 36). Jude gives the ground: “to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy” (Jude 24).
verseByVerse.examples:
None of this is a call to care less about family or work (see the note on vv. 34–35). It is a diagnosis: what leaves a Christian unready for glory is more often a crowded diary than a scandal.

Verses 37 and 38 give a pattern for anyone overwhelmed by what is coming (see the note on vv. 37–38).

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable: 'Look at the fig tree, and all the trees. As soon as they come out in leaf, you see for yourselves and know that the summer is already near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As new leaves tell everyone that summer is near, the events Jesus has described tell his people that the kingdom of God is near; they can be read, but they give no date.

Look at the fig tree, and all the trees. The last phrase is Luke’s alone. The fig tree is sometimes read as a coded symbol for the nation of Israel, and systems of date-calculation have been built on that; the prophets do use figs of Israel (Hosea 9:10). But “and all the trees” makes it plain that the fig tree is not a code for one nation. Trees come into leaf before summer, and everybody knows it.

In leaf. Signs are readable. You do not consult an expert to know that summer is coming; you look at a branch from your own doorstep. Yet the fig tree gives no date. It tells you the direction of travel and the nearness of the thing, which is enough to keep us watching and not enough to let us calculate.

The kingdom of God is near. Not “the end is near”, not the judgment, but the kingdom. Everything in this discourse has been dark: armies, betrayal, famine, a city under sentence. And all of it announces the reign of God arriving in its fullness. The signs are not the symptoms of a world dying. They are leaves on the branch. Winter is not the last season. It has never once been the last season.

The kingdom is the King. In Luke the kingdom of God is never just an idea. It came near when he came near. Within days he would tell the Twelve that he assigns them a kingdom, as his Father assigned one to him (22:29), and a dying thief would ask, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (23:42). So the summer the leaves announce is, in the end, not a period of history but the King himself, seen face to face. When Christians read the branches, they are watching for him, and every leaf says the same thing: the One who came once in humility is on his way back in glory.

If the kingdom is already here, how can it be near? Both are true. The kingdom came in Jesus: the King was among them, healing and forgiving, and he reigns now from heaven (17:21; Acts 2:33–36). But it has not yet come in its fullness, when every enemy is defeated, the dead are raised and the creation renewed. Christians live between the two: the kingdom has come, and the kingdom is coming.

In everyday life. When you read of the world convulsing, is your emotion dread or expectancy? The difference is whether you believe the thing on the far side of the shaking is a ruin or a King. When bad news comes this week, pray, help where you can, and say quietly, “the kingdom is near.”

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that the disciples asked about would happen within their own generation, and the words of Jesus are more lasting than the universe itself.

This generation. Taken naturally, “this generation” means Jesus’ contemporaries, and “all” means the events leading to and including the fall of Jerusalem, which came within a single lifetime. Sceptics press the point: if “all” includes the return (v. 27), that generation passed away and he did not come. It is the standard charge that Jesus was a mistaken prophet, honestly felt, and it deserves an answer.

Luke’s answer is eight verses earlier. Where Matthew and Mark keep the fall of Jerusalem and the end of the age closely woven together, Luke names the gap: “Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled” (v. 24), an interval of unknown length written into the discourse by Jesus himself. The “all” that must take place is what the disciples asked about in v. 7: the stones thrown down, the siege, the captivity. Every one of them happened within forty years.

The opposite error. Because v. 24 sets a limit on Gentile dominion and v. 32 ties the fulfilment to a generation, people have combined the two to calculate a date, and every such date has passed quietly. When the apostles asked the risen Christ, he declined: “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority” (Acts 1:7). A man who has worked out the date does not need to stay awake. That is why we are not given it.

My words will not pass away. Jesus sets his own sayings against the whole visible universe and says the universe will give way first. Israel’s prophets claimed that permanence only for the word of the LORD: the grass withers and the flower fades, but the word of our God stands for ever (Isaiah 40:8). Jesus claims it for what he himself says, with no “thus says the LORD” in front of it. Earlier he had said that whoever hears his words and does them builds on rock (6:47–48), and after Easter he would point the disciples back to the words he had spoken while he was still with them (24:44). A claim like that is either the gravest presumption or the voice of the LORD himself. The temple stones, lying where he said they would lie, are one witness to which it was; the empty tomb is the greater one. He who spoke the universe into being spoke these words in the temple, and not one of them will fall to the ground.

How can I trust words spoken two thousand years ago? Because they have been tested and have never failed, and because of who spoke them. Within a generation the temple fell as he said. He said he would rise on the third day, and he did. He said the gospel would go to the nations, and you are reading this. And the Spirit who inspired the Scriptures still bears witness to them in the hearts of those who read (John 16:13; 2 Timothy 3:16). They are older than the world and will outlast it. Build on them.

Where Christians differ: what does “this generation” mean? Some take it to mean the Jewish race, which will last until the end. Others take it to mean the generation alive when the final signs appear. Some critics claim that Jesus was simply mistaken. This commentary’s view: the best reading (compare Mark 13:30) is that Jesus’ contemporaries would see the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, the event the disciples had asked about (v. 7), and they did. Elsewhere in Luke “this generation” means the people of Jesus’ own day (7:31; 11:29–32). The day of his final coming itself remains unknown, as Mark records Jesus saying (Mark 13:32). Jesus was not mistaken.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What most threatens readiness for Christ’s return is not panic but a heart weighed down by indulgence or the ordinary worries of life.

Watch yourselves. After the cosmos, the kitchen. Jesus names the things that will actually cost his disciples their readiness, and not one of them is on the news. Only Luke has this application. His first readers were probably living decades after these words were spoken and still waiting, and for a church that has waited long the danger is seldom panic. It is drowsiness.

Weighed down. Made heavy, dull, like eyes too heavy to stay open, as the disciples were heavy with sleep on the mountain (9:32). A heart with too much on it does not become wicked. It becomes slow.

Dissipation and drunkenness. Dissipation is the heaviness in the head the morning after (kraipalē, an old medical word); drunkenness is the night before. Both ask a bottle or a night out for the rest and joy that only God can give, and both leave the heart heavier than before.

Cares of this life. Then the anxieties about ordinary things (8:14): bills, rotas, the boiler, the form that has to go back by Friday. Being taken up with these is not a sin in the ordinary sense, which makes it the most dangerous item on the list. A man can be sober, faithful to his wife, honest in business, in church every Sunday, and be so occupied with things that will not exist in a hundred years that the return of Jesus Christ is no part of how he thinks about Thursday.

Like a trap. A snare works not because the animal is stupid, but because it is head-down in a perfectly reasonable activity when the cord closes. And that day will come upon all (Isaiah 24:17): the only question is whether it finds them ready. The Lord who is coming is not a trap for his people but their deliverer.

The night the warning was tested. Within days, in the garden, Jesus found the disciples “sleeping for sorrow” (22:45): not drunk, simply weighed down by grief. And there, under a weight no one else has ever carried, he stayed awake and prayed: “not my will, but yours, be done” (22:42). He watched when his friends could not. His perfect obedience is counted to all who trust him, though their own watch has failed (Romans 5:19), and he lives to intercede for those whose eyes keep closing (Hebrews 7:25).

Does this mean I should care less about my family and work? No. The remedy Jesus gives at once is not detachment but prayer. He does not tell you to stop paying the bills or caring for your children. He tells you not to let them weigh down your heart. The difference is whether your ordinary duties are done before the face of the coming King, or whether they have crowded him out. Cast your cares on him (1 Peter 5:7), do your work as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23), and let the thought of his coming lighten the load rather than add to it.

In everyday life. If the cares of this week have crowded out every thought of his coming, do not answer that with more guilt. Put one minute of looking for his coming into each day this week.

parallels.desc: like a thief in the night

verseByVerse.quote: But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s people are to live awake and praying at all times, asking for strength to come through what is coming and to stand before him unashamed when he comes.

Stay awake at all times. The whole discourse funnels into two verbs: stay awake, and pray. No preparations to make, no date to mark. “At all times” rules out becoming intensely watchful when the news is bad and forgetting when it is good. Wakefulness that responds to headlines is not wakefulness. It is nerves.

Strength to escape. Prayer is the means of watchfulness (22:40, 46). The escape must be asked for; it is not automatic. And it comes with strength, a word for enduring something, not for being absent from it. It is escape from the judgment, and from being swept away by deception and fear.

To stand. Legal language: what a man does when the case is called. To stand before him at his coming means to be unashamed and accepted (1 John 2:28). “If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?” (Psalm 130:3).

He stood where we could not. Within days the Son of Man would himself stand bound before the council, Pilate and Herod. Pilate found no guilt in him, said so three times, and handed him over anyway (23:4, 14–15, 22–25). The Judge has already stood in the dock in our place, and the sentence we deserved was carried out on him.

Will I be able to stand? That is the fear this verse leaves in many sincere hearts: “have I watched enough, prayed enough, endured enough?” Read the verse again and see where the strength comes from. It is not mustered; it is asked for, and the one being asked is the one before whom we shall stand. He is not an examiner waiting to see whether we managed it. He is the one supplying the answer to his own examination. No one has ever stood before the Son of Man on his own record. The psalm that asks who could stand answers at once: “But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared” (Psalm 130:4). The standing is his doing.

What does staying awake look like in practice? Not sleeplessness or constant anxiety, but a life awake to God: regular prayer, morning and evening; reading Scripture; gathering with his people; confessing sin quickly rather than letting it settle; living each day as if it could be the day, and planning as if he might not come for a hundred years. Ask often: “if he came today, would he find me doing what he left me to do?” Watchfulness is simply faithfulness that remembers he is coming.

Where Christians differ: does strength to escape mean a rapture before the tribulation? Many Christians have been taught to hear in this phrase the promise of a removal: that the church will be taken out of the world, secretly, before the worst arrives, the final period of great distress often called the tribulation. Others read the escape as being kept safely through rather than being spared. Those who hold the first view are not careless readers; they are trying to give full weight to the word “escape”. This commentary’s view: the more likely reading is that it means being kept faithful through what is coming, so as to stand before the Son of Man at the end, not being removed beforehand. Jesus has just said his followers will be persecuted and some put to death (vv. 12–16), and promised that by their endurance they will gain their lives (v. 19). The escape is paired with standing before the Son of Man, which is plainly the final scene, and the New Testament knows only one, public return of Christ (v. 27). There is no secret rapture. Whatever a reader concludes, the verse gives him something to do, and what it gives him is prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: And every day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and lodged on the mount called Olivet. And early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing all that was coming, Jesus spent his last days in calm, faithful routine, teaching by day and lodging on the Mount of Olives by night.

Every day in the temple. Luke ends the greatest prophetic discourse in his Gospel with a daily routine. This man has announced the destruction of the temple he stands in, the death of friends beside him and his own return in glory. He knows that within days he will be crucified, and who will betray and deny him. And what he does with the days that remain is: teach in the morning, sleep on a hillside, and get up and do it again.

Olivet. The Mount of Olives. Pilgrims crowded Jerusalem at Passover, and many camped outside. Jesus may have stayed at Bethany (Mark 11:11), or in the open, at the place where he often went to pray (22:39), which is where Judas would find him. He had said it himself: “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (9:58). In the last week of his life it was still true. And the mountain he slept on was the one from which he had wept over the city (19:41), where he would pray in agony and be arrested, and from which he would ascend (Acts 1:12).

Early in the morning. There is no frenzy in him, no last campaign. He teaches, available to whoever comes. Jesus’ public ministry in Luke ends here as the temple section began, with Jesus teaching daily and the people eager to hear him (19:47–48). Next the leaders and Judas plot (22:1–6), and everything Jesus has said about watching, praying and standing before the Son of Man he is about to live out himself.

The rhythm of a man who knows the future. Work in the day; withdraw at night to pray; be found in the morning where the people who need you can find you. That is what perfect knowledge of a terrible future looked like when it was lived out by an actual man, and it looked like peace: the peace of someone who knows exactly what is coming and is not afraid, because the Father who holds the whole of it is his Father and has never once been late. There is no tremor in him anywhere.

How can I have peace when the future is uncertain? Your future is less known to you than Jesus’ was to him, but it is just as fully known to your Father. Peace does not come from knowing what will happen. It comes from knowing who holds what will happen, and from doing today what he has given you to do. Jesus’ last week shows that faithfulness and peace go together: he did not escape the cross by worrying about it, and he did not lose his peace by facing it. Bring each day to the Father, as he did on the Mount of Olives, and you will find that the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guards your heart (Philippians 4:7).

In everyday life. The crowds got up before dawn to hear him; you can hear him at your kitchen table. Set aside the first part of the morning, before the phone and the news, to read a passage of the Gospels and pray.
verseByVerse.note: Olivet is the Mount of Olives. Pilgrims crowded Jerusalem at Passover, and many camped outside it.

parallels.desc: as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives

21.text: <sup>1</sup> Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box, <sup>2</sup> and he saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins. <sup>3</sup> And he said, “Truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. <sup>4</sup> For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on.” <sup>5</sup> And while some were speaking of the temple, how it was adorned with noble stones and offerings, he said, <sup>6</sup> “As for these things that you see, the days will come when there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.” <sup>7</sup> And they asked him, “Teacher, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when these things are about to take place?” <sup>8</sup> And he said, “See that you are not led astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and, ‘The time is at hand!’ Do not go after them. <sup>9</sup> And when you hear of wars and tumults, do not be terrified, for these things must first take place, but the end will not be at once.” <sup>10</sup> Then he said to them, “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. <sup>11</sup> There will be great earthquakes, and in various places famines and pestilences. And there will be terrors and great signs from heaven. <sup>12</sup> But before all this they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues and prisons, and you will be brought before kings and governors for my name's sake. <sup>13</sup> This will be your opportunity to bear witness. <sup>14</sup> Settle it therefore in your minds not to meditate beforehand how to answer, <sup>15</sup> for I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict. <sup>16</sup> You will be delivered up even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you they will put to death. <sup>17</sup> You will be hated by all for my name's sake. <sup>18</sup> But not a hair of your head will perish. <sup>19</sup> By your endurance you will gain your lives. <sup>20</sup> “But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near. <sup>21</sup> Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let those who are inside the city depart, and let not those who are out in the country enter it, <sup>22</sup> for these are days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written. <sup>23</sup> Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people. <sup>24</sup> They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. <sup>25</sup> “And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth distress of nations in perplexity because of the roaring of the sea and the waves, <sup>26</sup> people fainting with fear and with foreboding of what is coming on the world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken. <sup>27</sup> And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. <sup>28</sup> Now when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.” <sup>29</sup> And he told them a parable: “Look at the fig tree, and all the trees. <sup>30</sup> As soon as they come out in leaf, you see for yourselves and know that the summer is already near. <sup>31</sup> So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near. <sup>32</sup> Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. <sup>33</sup> Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. <sup>34</sup> “But watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. <sup>35</sup> For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth. <sup>36</sup> But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.” <sup>37</sup> And every day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and lodged on the mount called Olivet. <sup>38</sup> And early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him.

keyVerse.quote: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
keyVerse.note: The disciples admired stones that would be thrown down within a generation; here Jesus names what will outlast even the heavens. Every promise in the chapter, from not a hair perishing to redemption drawing near, rests on this verse. Israel’s prophets claimed such permanence only for the word of the LORD, and Jesus claims it for his own words.

21.reflection:
Jesus measured the widow’s gift not by its size but by what it cost her and the trust behind it (vv. 1–4). What would change in how you give your money, time or strength if you measured it his way?

Asked for a date, Jesus warned instead against deception and panic (vv. 7–11). Where do you see people today led astray by predictions, or crushed by the news, and how do his words steady you?

Jesus promises his witnesses words when they need them, and says that not a hair of their heads will perish even though some will be put to death (vv. 12–19). Where has following Christ cost you something in front of others, and how do these promises help you endure?

Jesus warns that hearts are more often weighed down by the cares of this life than by scandal (v. 34). What crowds out the thought of his return in your week, and what would staying awake and praying look like for you (v. 36)?

22.title: The Last Supper, Gethsemane, and the Arrest
22.overview:
Where we are. The long road to Jerusalem (9:51) has arrived. After a week of teaching in the temple, chapter 22 tells the last night before the cross and opens the passion story that runs to the empty tomb.

The message. Jesus is not being swept to his death; he is going to it, as the Passover Lamb and the suffering Servant, to give his body and pour out his blood for people who will fail him that very night. Everyone around him acts from fear, greed, pride or weakness; he alone acts with full knowledge and free love, praying for his friends and claiming before his judges the throne at God’s right hand.

Why it was said. Luke writes so that Theophilus may have certainty (1:4; see the introduction). A Messiah betrayed by his disciple, denied by his leading apostle and condemned by Israel’s rulers looked like defeat. Luke shows every step foretold, chosen and governed by God, and the disciples’ failures not cancelling their place in his kingdom.

How the chapter makes its case. The plot is laid and Judas sells his Lord, while Jesus arranges the Passover down to a man with a water jar (vv. 1–13). At the table (Luke has two cups, vv. 17, 20) he fills the bread and cup with himself: his body given for them, the new covenant in his blood (vv. 14–23). Luke alone sets the quarrel about rank straight after the Supper, the disciples’ ambition beside Jesus serving them with his body and blood; he answers it with the servant’s place, a kingdom, and a prayer for Peter (vv. 24–38). In the garden he yields to his Father’s will, meets the betrayer’s kiss with a question and heals an enemy’s ear (vv. 39–53). Peter denies him and weeps at the Lord’s look, and at daybreak Jesus tells the council that the Son of Man will be seated at God’s right hand (vv. 54–71).

Where it leads. The cup he prays about in the garden is the cup of God’s wrath, which he would drink in the place of sinners (see the note on vv. 41–42), so that the cup his people hold is the new covenant of forgiveness. The prisoner condemned for claiming God’s throne is about to take it.

For us. Come to his table as those he longed to eat with, though you are no stronger than these men. Take the servant’s place, because he took it first. Pray before the hour comes, not only in it. And when you fail, remember the Lord’s look, and turn back: he has prayed for you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Conspiracy, Preparation, and the Last Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While his enemies plot in secret, Jesus goes to his death as the true Passover Lamb, in command of every detail and giving himself away to his friends. The leaders look for a quiet way to kill him, Satan enters Judas, and Judas freely makes his bargain (vv. 1–6). Meanwhile Jesus arranges the meal himself, down to a man carrying a water jar (vv. 7–13). At the table he says how he has longed for this Passover, and fills its bread and cup with himself: his body given for them, and the new covenant in his blood that Jeremiah had promised (vv. 14–20). Only then is the betrayer named, his hand on the same table, fulfilling God’s purpose and guilty all the same (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Supper looks three ways. It remembers, as Passover did, bringing a past deliverance into the present (Exodus 12:14). It proclaims the Lord’s death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26). And it looks forward to the feast of the kingdom, so every communion table is an unfinished meal.

On the four main views of what happens at the table, see the box “Where Christians differ: the Supper” at the end of the note on v. 19. On “for you”, see the note on v. 19.

Verses 21 and 22 set God’s determined plan and Judas’s guilt side by side without reconciling them (see the note on vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.examples:
Some believers fear they could be handed over like Judas. The fear is itself the answer (see the note on v. 3).

Others stay away from the table because they feel they are not good enough to come (see the note on v. 20).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread drew near, which is called the Passover. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to put him to death, for they feared the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the feast of the Passover lamb drew near, Israel’s leaders were looking for a quiet way to kill Jesus. They thought they were managing a political problem; God was bringing his Lamb to the feast on time.

Unleavened Bread and Passover. Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that began with the Passover meal (Exodus 12:15–20), and Luke explains for Gentile readers that the two were spoken of as one. Passover was the feast of the lamb. Every family that could afford one brought a year-old male without blemish to the temple, and on the fourteenth of the month, in the afternoon, it was killed; Josephus reckoned the lambs slaughtered at a single Passover in the hundreds of thousands. The whole ritual kept one night alive in the nation’s memory: the night in Egypt when the blood went on the doorposts and the destroyer passed over the houses that had it (Exodus 12).

Seeking how to put him to death, for they feared the people. The plot had been building for days (19:47; 20:19). They feared not God but the people. They needed a quiet arrest, away from the crowds who hung on his words (21:38), at a festival when the city’s population multiplied several times over and Rome was watching. The men entrusted with the worship of Israel are conspiring against the salvation of Israel, and what decides their plans is the risk of a riot.

Behind them a purpose is running to time. Fifteen centuries of Passovers were rehearsals for one afternoon. Every lamb that died in Egypt and in the temple courts pointed to God’s Son, and this is the week the chief priests choose to kill him, “Christ, our Passover lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Seven weeks later Peter would set two truths side by side in this same city: Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”, and they killed him “by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). The scheming was theirs, freely chosen and fully culpable; and it was the means by which the Lamb was brought to the feast in the very week the lambs died. The priests were thinking about crowds. God was keeping an appointment.

What we fear, we serve. When human approval becomes an idol, even religious men can stand in God’s house planning to kill his Son, because they fear the crowd more than God. Whatever we fear most, we end up serving (Proverbs 29:25).

Does God cause people to do evil, then? No. God never puts wickedness into a heart or approves it (James 1:13). The leaders hated Jesus because they wanted to, and they will answer for it. But God never improvises around human sin. He governs it, restrains it, sets its limits and turns it to his own good ends, as he did with Joseph’s brothers (Genesis 50:20). That is why the cross can be at once the worst crime ever committed and the best thing that ever happened. Hold both: the evil is real and blameworthy, and it is never out of God’s hand.
verseByVerse.note: Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that began with Passover; the two names were used together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Satan entered into Judas called Iscariot, who was of the number of the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devil now took hold of Judas, one of Jesus’ own chosen Twelve, as his instrument against Jesus. Luke names a spiritual event, yet every step that follows is Judas’s own.

Satan entered into Judas. After the temptation in the wilderness the devil departed from Jesus “until an opportune time” (4:13). Now is that time, and he works through a man at Jesus’ side (John 13:2, 27). Luke offers no theory of disappointed political hopes: the enemy of God entered a man who had walked beside Jesus for some three years.

Of the number of the twelve. Not a hanger-on: Judas was one of the Twelve, chosen after a night of prayer (6:12–16), sent out with authority to preach and heal (9:1–2). Nearness to Jesus is not the same as belonging to him. A person can sit in church every week, know the Bible well and even serve, and never have trusted Christ. Belonging is being known by him, given a new heart and joined to him by faith (Matthew 7:22–23; John 10:27).

The stronger man. Jesus had already told the parable of this night. The strong man’s goods are safe until one stronger than he overcomes him and divides his spoil (11:21–22). The devil has chosen as his weapon the very death by which the stronger man will strip him. Satan enters Judas to destroy Jesus; Jesus lets Judas hand him over, so that “through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death” (Hebrews 2:14).

What it does not mean. Not that Judas was not responsible. Satan entered him, and then he went away and conferred: he walked to the meeting, opened the negotiation, named his terms and took the money. Every verb belongs to Judas, and Jesus pronounces a woe on him (v. 22), which would be monstrous if the man were a puppet. Satan does not manufacture desires; he finds them, feeds them and hands a man the opportunity. What entered Judas found a door already unlocked (John 12:6), and Judas had been turning the key quietly for a long time: a coin here, a resentment there, a growing private conviction that he understood things better than his master.

Could Satan enter me like that? Not if you belong to Christ. A believer is indwelt by the Holy Spirit (Romans 8:9), and “he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4). Satan can tempt, accuse and sift a Christian hard, as he will Peter, but he cannot take possession of one whom Christ has bought. Judas was never one of Christ’s sheep (John 6:64, 70; 17:12). Yet the warning stands: do not give the devil a foothold (Ephesians 4:27). Unconfessed sin, nursed resentment and secret greed are exactly the open doors he looks for.

I am afraid I might be a Judas. Some believers fear that the sin they cannot shake is the beginning of a betrayal. The fear itself is the answer. Judas is never once recorded as afraid of what he was becoming. He was calm; he negotiated; he ate the supper; he came to the garden with a kiss ready. A conscience that recoils in horror at betraying Christ is not being handed over. It is being held. And the man in this chapter who did deny his Lord, three times, was being prayed for while he did it (v. 32). Judas went out to a meeting. Peter went out and wept. The difference between them was not the size of the sin (2 Corinthians 7:10).

verseByVerse.quote: He went away and conferred with the chief priests and officers how he might betray him to them. And they were glad, and agreed to give him money. So he consented and sought an opportunity to betray him to them in the absence of a crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas sold Jesus to his enemies as calmly as a business deal, and they were glad to buy. Both sides wanted the thing done in the dark, away from the crowds.

Conferred. He went, conferred, agreed a figure, consented and began looking for an opportunity. No struggle is recorded; it reads like the minutes of a meeting, which is more frightening than any scene of tormented decision. The officers were the captains of the temple police, who would make the arrest (v. 52).

To betray him. To betray is to hand over (paradidōmi), the word Jesus had used in his predictions (9:44; 18:32), and the word Paul uses of the Father who “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). Judas hands him over for money; the Father hands him over for love; the Son gives himself up (Galatians 2:20). Three handings-over in one act, and only one of them was wicked.

Money. Matthew gives the figure: thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15). It is the compensation set in the law of Moses for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32), and the sum weighed out to the rejected shepherd in Zechariah’s strange prophecy, the lordly price at which God himself was priced by them (Zechariah 11:12–13). That is the value the guardians of his own house placed on the Son of God: the going rate for a dead slave.

In the absence of a crowd. Both parties want darkness: the priests because their power cannot survive daylight, and Judas because betrayal cannot be done before witnesses (John 3:20).

Heaven is glad over a ransom. The leaders of Israel were glad, relieved at a problem solved; heaven is glad over a ransom. The one they bought cheaply by lamplight had resolved to buy them at a price no treasury could hold: “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). God settled that price before the foundation of the world, and paid it in full, in the Son they sold.

In everyday life. Is any part of what you are doing arranged so that it happens where you will not be seen? Whatever needs the absence of a crowd usually needs it for a reason. Bring it into the light today, where the blood of Jesus cleanses it (1 John 1:7), with God first and then, if it is needed, with one trusted person.

How could anyone sell Jesus for money? Very easily, and by degrees. Judas kept the common purse and used to help himself to it (John 12:6). He had spent months letting money matter more than the Master, and when the offer came the decision was mostly made. That is why Paul calls the love of money “a root of all kinds of evils” (1 Timothy 6:10). Most of us will never be offered silver for Christ. But every week we are offered small trades: a dishonest claim, a hidden purchase, worship quietly traded for overtime we do not need. Each one teaches the heart what it values.
verseByVerse.note: The officers were the captains of the temple police. Matthew says the price was thirty pieces of silver.

verseByVerse.quote: Then came the day of Unleavened Bread, on which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed. So Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, 'Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the day the Passover lambs had to die, Jesus sent two of his closest friends to prepare the meal he meant to share with them. The law required the lamb on that day, and the purpose of God required the Lamb.

Had to be sacrificed. The lambs were killed at the temple, by the thousands, on the afternoon of 14 Nisan, before the meal that evening. “Had to be” is edei, “it must”, the word Luke uses all through his Gospel for the fixed purposes of God: the Son of Man must suffer (9:22; 24:26).

Peter and John. Only Luke names them, the two who will stand together at the centre of Acts (Acts 3; 4; 8). Their partnership begins here, running an errand.

Prepare the Passover. Securing the room, buying the lamb, taking it to the temple court to be killed, roasting it whole, buying the bitter herbs, setting out the bread and wine: Peter and John spent the afternoon before the Lord’s Supper buying groceries. If your tasks seem too small to matter, do the errands of your day as service to him, not as time stolen from serving him.

That we may eat it. He includes himself, and he is looking forward to it (v. 15). Christ, the Lamb without blemish, foreknown before the foundation of the world (1 Peter 1:19–20), walked towards the altar on his own feet, saying, “that we may eat it”: with us.

Was this a Passover meal? Luke, with Matthew and Mark, says so plainly. John seems at first to put the Passover a day later (John 18:28; 19:14). The more likely explanation is that John’s “Passover” there means the meals of the festival week, and “Preparation” means the Friday before the Sabbath of Passover week. Scholars still debate the calendar, and believers hold both accounts true while the details are weighed. The Last Supper was a Passover meal, and Jesus is the true Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Should Christians keep the Passover today? Christians are free to learn from a Passover meal, which can explain the Lord’s Supper wonderfully, but are not bound to keep it. The Passover was “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:17; Hebrews 10:1). The Lamb has been slain once for all, and Jesus gave his church a new meal to keep until he comes. To treat the old feast as necessary would be to go back to the shadow when the light has risen.
verseByVerse.note: The lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon before the Passover meal.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, 'Where will you have us prepare it?' He said to them, 'Behold, when you have entered the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house that he enters
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gave his disciples a sign by which to find the room, because he, not his enemies, was arranging this night.

Where will you have us prepare it? A reasonable, slightly anxious question: Jerusalem at Passover was overwhelmed, and rooms went early and to the connected.

A man carrying a jar of water. Carrying water was usually women’s work, so a man with a jar on his shoulder would stand out at once in a crowd of thousands.

Follow him. A secret arrangement, probably so that Judas would not know the place in advance: not to save Jesus’ life, which he had resolved to give, but to keep the supper safe until he had placed it in his friends’ hands.

He is not being taken. He is going. Everything from here to the tomb will look like a man carried along by other people’s decisions, and Luke opens the sequence with a man who knows what a stranger will be carrying that afternoon. Of his life he had said, “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18).

Had Jesus arranged this beforehand, or did he know it prophetically? Luke does not say, and both are possible. The parallel is the colt (19:29–34): two disciples sent, a sign, a password, everything found as told. Either way, Luke’s point stands: nothing about this night is merely happening to Jesus.

Does Jesus guide me in the details like this? He governs every detail of your life by his providence, down to the hairs of your head (12:7), and guides his people through his Word, wise counsel and the ordinary sense he gives. He does not promise coded signs about which street to take, and we should not demand them or treat every coincidence as a message. Pray about the details, read the Scriptures, ask advice, decide with a clear conscience, and trust that the one who knew about a water jar is not absent from your house move or your job interview.
verseByVerse.note: Carrying water was usually women’s work, so a man with a jar would stand out.

verseByVerse.quote: and tell the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you, Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ And he will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare it there.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A householder who asked no questions lent Jesus a large room, made ready for the meal he would share with the friends he still calls “my disciples”.

The Teacher says to you. A phrase, not an explanation: the arrangement was understood. The householder is never named, and the room he lent has been remembered for two thousand years.

The guest room. The same word as the inn at Bethlehem (katalyma), where “there was no place for them” (2:7). At his birth there was no room; at his death a room is ready, and he fills it with a gift the world has fed on ever since.

A large upper room furnished. “Furnished” means laid out: carpets down, the low couches arranged around the table (see Meals and Reclining at Table). It may have been the same upper room where the disciples gathered after the ascension (Acts 1:13), and possibly the house of Mark’s mother (Acts 12:12), though we cannot be sure.

My disciples. On the eve of the night when every one of them will fail him, one betraying, one denying, the rest scattering, he calls them “my disciples”. He knows exactly what they will do, and they are still his. “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John 13:1).

We lent him a room for one night. The Lord of heaven and earth borrowed a room, and in it he gave away everything. He took a guest’s place in a borrowed house so that we strangers might have a son’s place in his Father’s house, where he has gone to prepare rooms that will never be lent and never taken back (John 14:2). We lent him an upper room for one night. He gives us a home for ever.

What if my home or my gifts seem too ordinary to matter? Then you are in the householder’s position, one of the quiet heroes of the Gospels. Hospitality is no minor virtue in the New Testament; it is required of elders and commended to all (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9). A kitchen table where a struggling believer is fed, a spare room for a missionary, a lift to church: these are rooms lent to Christ. Do not wait until you have something impressive. Offer what you have, and let him decide what it is for.
verseByVerse.note: Larger houses had an upper room reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything was just as Jesus had said, and his word proved true in small things is a pledge for his word in great ones. The wording repeats the finding of the colt (19:32).

Just as he had told them. Within hours the same two men will hear things almost impossible to receive: that one of them will betray him, that Peter will deny him before dawn, that he himself will be numbered with criminals. If he could be trusted about a man with a water jar, he could be trusted about his death and resurrection. The water jar and the empty tomb come from the same mouth.

And they prepared the Passover. He told them where; they did the work. Foreknowledge in this Gospel never replaces obedience; it directs it. They roasted a lamb, not knowing that they were laying a table for the end of the world’s long night.

The last easy verification. Much of what follows has to be believed in the dark. That is the ordinary shape of a Christian life: a stretch where the promises can be checked, then a season where all you have is that the same voice was accurate before. That does not make the silence pleasant. It makes it survivable, because the silence of a proven friend is not the silence of a stranger.

Does this mean everything I want will turn out as I hope? No. What comes true is what Jesus has said, not what we have wished: a room, and also betrayal, denial and his own death. His promises to every believer are many and certain: forgiveness, his presence, the Spirit, the resurrection of the body, a place in his kingdom. He has not promised you the job, the healing or the outcome you are praying for, though you may and should ask. Trust him for what he has said, and leave what he has not said in his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the hour came, he reclined at table, and the apostles with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the appointed hour came, Jesus lay down to eat with his apostles, Judas among them, at ease like a free man at the feast of freedom.

And when the hour came. The appointed time for the meal, after sunset. But this is the Gospel in which Jesus has walked with his face set (9:51), and the chapter in which he will tell the arresting party, “this is your hour, and the power of darkness” (v. 53). Luke says quietly what John says outright (John 13:1). The hour came, and he sat down to dinner.

He reclined at table. Not on chairs, as in the paintings, but lying on low couches around a low table, propped on the left elbow, which is why the beloved disciple could lean back against Jesus (John 13:23; see Meals and Reclining at Table). Free men reclined; slaves stood and served. The first Passover was eaten standing, ready to leave Egypt (Exodus 12:11), but by Jesus’ time reclining had become the custom, to celebrate freedom: you eat this meal at ease, because you are no longer slaves.

And the apostles with him. All twelve. Luke has told us what Judas has done (v. 3), and places him here without comment, reclining with the rest.

Composure that is real. He lies down among his friends as a free man at a feast of deliverance, with the man who has sold him at the same table. This is composure when it is real: not the absence of dread, for the garden will show the dread, but the refusal to let dread eat the hours that are still good. “You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies” (Psalm 23:5): the shepherd-king of that psalm reclines in an upper room with his enemies already moving in the dark, and he spreads the table anyway.

Does it matter whether we sit, stand or kneel at the Lord’s Supper? Scripture prescribes no posture: some churches sit at a table, as guests at a family meal; some come forward; some kneel. What matters is the posture of the heart: humble, because we are sinners, and at rest, because we are free. A believer may come as these men came, as guests the Master has invited, not as slaves earning a place.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover was eaten after sunset, reclining.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus had longed to share this Passover with his friends before he suffered, and he looks past the suffering to the day it will be fulfilled in God’s kingdom.

I have earnestly desired. Literally with desire I have desired (epithumia epethumēsa), a Hebrew way of doubling a word to intensify it: the language of aching for something (Genesis 31:30). Only Luke records it.

To eat this Passover with you. And the object of the longing is an evening with eleven ordinary men and one traitor, in a borrowed room, eating roast lamb. Of everything available to the Son of God in his last hours, he had set his heart on a table with men who before morning will argue about rank, fall asleep on him, deny him and run. He has not misjudged them. The Son, who had the Father’s company from all eternity and the praise of angels, longed to eat lamb with fishermen. That is the heart of our God: he wants us.

Before I suffer. Then, immediately, the shadow: he dates the meal by his suffering (pathein, the root behind the church’s old name for these events, the Passion).

Until it is fulfilled. Having named the suffering, he looks straight past it. The Passover pointed forward, and its meaning would be filled full first in his death, the true Passover sacrifice, and finally in the banquet of the kingdom (13:29; 14:15), the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9; Isaiah 25:6–8). The meal looks back to Egypt, forward to the cross, and beyond the cross to the feast.

Why would Jesus long to be with people like me? Because his love was never based on our quality, so our failures do not cancel it. He longed for that table knowing every denial to come. He does not tolerate your company while hoping for better; he has set his heart on you, which is what it means to be chosen in him before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). When you come to the Lord’s Supper feeling unworthy, remember that the first table was laid for men about to fail him, and he had ached to share it with them.

Will there really be a feast in the kingdom? Yes, and more solid than we imagine, not less. When Christ returns, the dead are raised bodily and God makes all things new, and Scripture pictures that renewed creation with a table, food and wine, faces and fellowship (Isaiah 25:6; Matthew 8:11). We must not make it thin and ghostly: those who rise will have real bodies, as Jesus did when he ate fish after his resurrection (24:42–43). Whatever the feast is, it is not less than the best meal you ever ate with the people you love, and he will be at the head of the table.

parallels.desc: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verseByVerse.quote: And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he said, 'Take this, and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus shares a cup with his friends and then vows not to drink wine again until the kingdom of God comes, for a death stands between this table and that feast.

He took a cup. Luke has a cup before the bread and another after it (v. 20). By the time the Mishnah (the early written collection of Jewish tradition) was compiled, the Passover was built around four cups of wine, and something like that order was probably already followed: a cup at the opening, one after the telling of the Exodus story, the cup of blessing after the meal, and a cup of praise with the psalms. This cup belongs to the earlier part of the evening; the cup in v. 20, after supper, is probably the cup of blessing (1 Corinthians 10:16). He took a cup at a meal that already carried centuries of meaning, and filled it with himself.

And when he had given thanks. A Jewish host blessed God as King of the universe, who creates the fruit of the vine. On the night of his betrayal his first recorded word over the cup is thanksgiving.

Divide it among yourselves. He gave it to be shared. The Supper is corporate at its root: a family meal, not a private devotion.

Until the kingdom of God comes. He is fasting: the vow of a man with unfinished business. He will not sit down to the feast until his people can sit down with him, and there is a death between here and there. The cup he pushes away at this table is the measure of the cup he accepts in the garden. He declines the wine of the feast in order to drink the cup of wrath, so that when the kingdom comes there will be somebody there to drink with.

In everyday life. When you next share the cup at church, look around at the people sharing it with you: your family at his table, with whom you will drink it new in the kingdom. If there is someone there you are estranged from, go and be reconciled first (Matthew 5:23–24).
