But did he not drink sour wine on the cross? He was offered it, and received it just before he died (23:36; John 19:29–30). That was not the festive fruit of the vine at the table of the kingdom but the cheap sour wine of soldiers, moistening a dying man’s lips so that he could cry out that it was finished. The vow stands: he has not yet drunk the cup of celebration with his people. He is waiting for the whole family to be gathered home.

Wine or grape juice at communion? Faithful churches differ. Jesus used wine, and many churches use it for that reason. Others use unfermented grape juice to protect those who struggle with alcohol, noting that Jesus calls it simply “the fruit of the vine”. Both seek to honour him, and neither should despise the other. What matters is what the cup means: his blood poured out, and the feast to come.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover meal included several cups of wine; Luke mentions a cup before the bread and another after supper.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, 'This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gives the Passover bread a new meaning: it is his own body, given in his people’s place, and his church is to eat it in remembrance of him until he comes.

He took bread. The four actions are those of the feeding of the five thousand (9:16) and of Emmaus (24:30): took, blessed, broke, gave. The hand that fed the crowds will be recognised breaking bread on the evening of the resurrection.

This is my body. At this point in the Passover the host probably held up the unleavened bread and spoke of it as the bread of affliction the fathers ate in Egypt (Deuteronomy 16:3). Jesus says something else: this bread now speaks of his own body, about to be given in death. He broke it before anyone broke him. He gave it before anyone took him. Nothing about that night was extracted from him.

Given for you. Only Luke and Paul record these words (1 Corinthians 11:24). The preposition is hyper: on behalf of, and in a sacrifice like this one, in the place of. Not merely for your benefit, but in your stead: the plainest words he ever used about his death, spoken the night before.

Do this in remembrance of me. As Israel remembered the exodus at Passover, the church remembers Christ’s death at his Supper. The word is anamnēsis, and remembering of this kind is not a private effort of memory but a public act that brings the past into the present: each generation ate the Passover as though it had itself come out of Egypt. So the Supper proclaims his death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26). It also renews the covenant: God sets his promise before his people again, your sins are forgiven for my Son’s sake, and they answer by taking the bread in faith, as a couple renew their vows, not to make the marriage but because it is made.

Remembered at plain tables. He asked to be remembered by a meal, not a monument. The Lord of glory, hours from being forsaken, chose bread, the commonest thing on the table, and put into it the most uncommon promise: “given for you”. Kings are remembered in marble; he is remembered at plain tables in cathedrals, prison cells and village halls. And the One who asked to be remembered never forgets his own. He feeds them with himself by his Spirit, and he will remember them on the day he comes.

What does it mean to feed on Christ by faith? You do not admire bread; you take it into yourself, and it becomes your strength. As the mouth takes the bread and cup, the believer’s heart takes hold of Christ himself, crucified and risen. The Holy Spirit makes that real: he lifts our hearts to Christ where he is, and Christ strengthens our faith, assures us of forgiveness and binds us to him and to one another. Not magic, nor merely thinking hard, but communion with a living Saviour, through means he has appointed.

What if I feel nothing when I take communion? Then you have still received what was given. The Supper rests not on the strength of your feelings but on the faithfulness of Christ, who promised himself in it. Some Sundays the heart is warm, some numb with tiredness or grief; come anyway, trusting his word: “given for you”. A child fed by his father is nourished whether or not he notices the taste. If the numbness persists for months, speak to your pastor; it may be weariness, sorrow or sin that needs care, but it is never a reason to stay away from the means of grace.

How often should we take the Lord’s Supper? Scripture does not fix it. The early church seems to have broken bread often, perhaps each Lord’s Day (Acts 2:42; 20:7); many churches celebrate weekly, as Calvin wished, others less often to guard against routine. What Scripture requires is that it be kept regularly, with self-examination and faith, until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26).

Where Christians differ: the Supper. Four words have divided the church for five hundred years. Roman Catholics hold transubstantiation: at the priest’s word the substance of the bread becomes the actual body of Christ, though everything observable remains bread, and the Mass is offered as a sacrifice. Lutherans reject that but hold that Christ’s body is genuinely present in, with and under the bread. Those who follow Zwingli hold that the bread signifies the body and the Supper is a memorial and a pledge. Calvin and the Reformed churches hold a real spiritual presence: the bread remains bread, yet Christ is truly given, so that by his Spirit the believer really feeds on him, not with the teeth but by faith. This commentary’s view: Calvin’s view is best. “This is my body” is a sacramental sign, a visible sign of a promised reality, spoken while his body was at the table, unbroken, in front of them, which settles what kind of sentence it is: he spoke as he always spoke, “I am the door”, “I am the vine”. Yet the Supper is more than a memory. The cup of blessing is a participation in the blood of Christ, and the bread a participation in his body (1 Corinthians 10:16): believers truly feed on Christ by faith through the Spirit, who joins us to the risen Lord in heaven. Nor is it a sacrifice offered again. Luke’s word is remembrance, not repetition: Christ was offered once for all (Hebrews 9:25–28; 10:10–14), and the Supper receives that offering rather than renewing it. The Westminster Confession, which the 1689 London Baptist Confession follows here, puts it carefully: worthy receivers, inwardly by faith, really and indeed, yet not carnally, receive and feed upon Christ crucified (Westminster 29.7; 1689 30.7).

verseByVerse.quote: And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying, 'This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cup after supper is the new covenant God promised through Jeremiah, sealed in Jesus’ own blood poured out for his people. At its heart is forgiveness: God will remember their sin no more.

After they had eaten. Probably the third Passover cup, the cup of blessing (1 Corinthians 10:16), drunk after the main meal.

Poured out for you. For Jewish men, blood in connection with a cup was close to unthinkable: the law forbade drinking blood because the life is in the blood and God had given it for atonement on the altar (Leviticus 17:11–14). He is not inviting them to drink blood; he is telling them what the cup means: atonement. “Poured out” is altar language, the blood of a sacrifice poured out at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7). Atonement means that sin is covered and the sinner brought back to God because a life has been given in his place: the holy God does not shrug at sin, but neither does he leave the sinner to bear it.

The new covenant in my blood. Jeremiah, six centuries earlier, in the ruin of everything, heard God promise a new covenant, not like the one their fathers broke. It would differ in three ways: the law written on the heart rather than on stone; every member knowing God personally, from the least to the greatest; and the ground of it all forgiveness, “for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more” (Jeremiah 31:31–34). The law on the heart means God’s will is no longer only a rule pressing in from outside but a desire within: you begin to want what he commands, because he has given you a new heart and put his Spirit within you (Ezekiel 36:26–27). That promise had stood unfulfilled through the return from exile and the rebuilt temple. Now a man at a supper table lifts a cup and says: here it is, and it is in my blood.

Covenants are sealed with blood. Abraham’s covenant was cut between divided animals (Genesis 15), and Sinai’s sealed with Moses throwing blood on the people and saying, “Behold the blood of the covenant” (Exodus 24:8). What is new is whose blood seals it. Sinai’s covenant, sealed with the blood of animals, was broken within weeks; the new covenant, sealed with Jesus’ own blood, rests not on our faithfulness but on his (Hebrews 8:6–13; 9:15–22).

Who may come to the Lord’s Table? Those who belong to Christ: baptised believers who trust him and are willing to turn from sin, each examining himself and then eating (1 Corinthians 11:28). It is not a reward for the good but food for sinners who need Christ; yet it is not for unbelievers, nor for those under the church’s discipline for unrepentant sin. Baptist churches, holding that in the New Testament baptism follows faith as the disciple’s first public confession, ask that those who come should first have been baptised as believers; many gladly welcome to the table believers from paedobaptist churches (those that baptise the infants of believers) who love the same Lord, recognising them as brothers and sisters in Christ.

I am struggling with a sin, so should I stay away? Not if you are fighting it. The cup does not commemorate your fitness. It commemorates the death that made you fit, and it is offered by the one who poured it out for a table that included a traitor, a denier and ten men who would run. Examine yourself, confess the sin, and come as a sinner holding on to Christ. The one who should hold back is the person who has decided to keep a sin and stop fighting it; for him the Supper is a call to repent first, today, and then to come.

Does God really forget my sin? He chooses not to remember it against you. God knows all things, but in the new covenant he binds himself never again to bring your forgiven sins up as a charge or treat you as they deserve (Hebrews 10:17–18). They were remembered once, fully, at the cross, and laid on Christ. When your conscience digs them up again, answer with the cup: this was poured out for me, and God has promised to remember my sin no more.

Textual note. Some ESV readers will see a note that a few manuscripts omit the end of v. 19 and v. 20. The longer text has overwhelming support, and the same words are found independently in Paul (1 Corinthians 11:23–25) and in Matthew and Mark. No doctrine rests on Luke’s wording alone.

verseByVerse.quote: But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The betrayer shares Jesus’ table; his act fulfils what God has determined, and yet the guilt is wholly his own. Jesus asserts both in one breath and does not try to reconcile them.

On the table. Matthew and Mark have the announcement of the betrayal before the bread and the cup; Luke puts it after, and the effect is stark. Sharing a dish was a pledge of friendship and loyalty. Psalm 41 had already given words to the wound: the trusted friend who ate the psalmist’s bread and lifted his heel against him (Psalm 41:9). In the Son of David that psalm reaches its fullest meaning, and John records Jesus applying it to this very night (John 13:18).

As it has been determined. Marked out, fixed, appointed by God (hōrismenon; Acts 2:23; 4:28). The cross is not a catastrophe that overtook the plan; it is the plan. “Goes” is the language of a man on a journey, walking a road he has chosen.

Woe to that man. “Woe” is grief as well as doom: the cry of a friend over a man walking to ruin. And the woe that should have fallen on every one of us who has betrayed him fell, for all who believe, on Jesus himself, the Son of Man who goes to the cross.

A word for the wronged. The badly wronged live between two temptations: to conclude that the wrong was outside God’s reach, which makes the world random and God small; or that because God had a purpose in it, the one who did it was not really guilty, a false comfort that leaves the victim unable even to name what happened. This verse refuses both. God’s purpose stood, and the man who did it is answerable. You may say that what was done to you was wicked, and that God was not absent from it, without having to make those two sentences into one. Where the wrong was abuse or a crime, it must be named, reported and stopped; trusting God’s purpose never means covering it up.

If it was determined, how can Judas be blamed? Because he did exactly what he wanted to do. Nobody forced him, and God put no wicked desire into his heart (see the note on vv. 1–2). Scripture never fully explains how God’s purpose and man’s guilt are both true, but it insists on both, and so must we. If God were not sovereign, the cross would be an accident; if Judas were not responsible, there would be no sin for the cross to deal with. A man is judged for what he intends, and Judas intended betrayal (Genesis 50:20).

Could Judas have repented? Yes. Jesus warned him at this table, washed his feet, and in the garden asked him a question that held the door open (v. 48). Judas did not repent because he would not; nothing in God’s decree stopped a man who wanted to come back. Scripture calls him “the son of destruction” (John 17:12), and his end shows a remorse that never turned to God. No one who truly comes to Christ is ever turned away (John 6:37).

Did Judas receive the bread and cup? Luke’s order makes it look as if he did. But Matthew and Mark put the warning before the Supper, and John has Judas leave after the morsel (John 13:30). Luke often arranges events by subject, and the more likely reading is that Judas left before the cup was shared. Either way, he sat at the table with Jesus and betrayed him.

parallels.desc: according to the definite plan of God

verseByVerse.quote: And they began to question one another, which of them it could be who was going to do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus announced a traitor, none of the disciples could tell who it was, and each began to ask about himself.

Which of them. Eleven men, some three years in his company, and not one of them can identify the betrayer. Matthew adds that each asked, “Is it I, Lord?” (Matthew 26:22). Serious spiritual defection does not announce itself in advance; it is generally invisible until it is complete, sometimes even to the person concerned.

The eleven looked inward first. If the Lord says one of us is capable of it, I had better start with myself. It was a sound instinct, the opposite of our reflex to suspect everyone except ourselves. So Paul tells the Corinthians to examine themselves before eating (1 Corinthians 11:28), not each other.

The one who knew. Only one man at that table knew the answer, and he did not give it. Jesus had read hearts all through this Gospel (5:22; 6:8), and he knew Judas’s, yet he did not expose him to the table; he shielded the traitor and left the door of repentance open to the last moment. And the Lord who sees every heart at that table knows yours, better than you do, and he did not send the trembling eleven away.

How do I examine myself without becoming morbid? Look for sin in order to bring it to Christ, not to find a reason to despair. Ask simple questions: Am I trusting Christ, or something I have done? Is there a sin I have stopped fighting? Is there someone I refuse to forgive? Then take what you find straight to the cross and confess it, and stop digging; the purpose of looking at yourself is to look away to him. The eleven asked, “Is it I, Lord?”, and then they stayed at the table. Self-examination that ends in fleeing from Christ has gone wrong; self-examination that ends at his feet has done its work.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–38 — Greatness, Sifting, and the Turning Season
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Christ’s kingdom greatness is service, and the disciples’ future rests not on their strength but on their Lord’s prayer. Minutes after the Supper they quarrel about rank, and Jesus sets the world’s pattern of power beside his own: he is among them as the one who serves (vv. 24–27). Then he gives them what their ambition was reaching for, a kingdom, his table and thrones (vv. 28–30). He tells Simon that Satan has asked to sift them all, but that he has prayed for him, and appoints him to strengthen his brothers once he has turned again; Peter protests, and is told the hour of his denial (vv. 31–34). Last, he warns that the season of welcome is over, in a saying about swords that the disciples take too literally (vv. 35–38).
verseByVerse.theology:
Verse 32 shows in one sentence why true believers keep believing to the end (the perseverance of the saints): it rests on Christ’s prayer (this is treated fully at vv. 31–32).

The teaching on greatness in verses 25 to 27 shows what authority looks like when God himself becomes man (see the note on vv. 26–27).

Verses 35 to 38 must be read together, and the sword saying is weighed at vv. 37–38.
verseByVerse.examples:
Anyone who leads anything can ask when they last did something for their people that carried no credit and that nobody would notice. That is the youngest man’s work, and Jesus took it.

Verses 33 and 34 are for anyone who has made God a promise and broken it (see the note on vv. 33–34).

verseByVerse.quote: A dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest. And he said to them, 'The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and those in authority over them are called benefactors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Minutes after the Supper the disciples quarrel about which of them is greatest, and Jesus begins by naming the world’s idea of greatness: power over others, dressed up as generosity.

A dispute. The bread has been broken, the cup passed, the betrayal announced, and an argument breaks out about rank. Only Luke places it here. It was probably about seating, who would lie nearest to Jesus, and the word is philoneikia, literally a love of winning: not a disagreement they fell into but an appetite they indulged.

Regarded as the greatest. The old argument. They had had it before (9:46), and been answered with a child set in front of them. A church can still hold a moving communion service and a quarrel in the car park afterwards about who was asked to serve at it. Jesus does not shame them; he describes a world they know.

Kings of the Gentiles. They play the lord. The world’s model of greatness is power over others, and it has never needed to be taught.

Called benefactors. “Benefactor” (euergetēs) was a formal honorific, voted by cities, inscribed on stone and coins, and claimed by rulers who meant everyone to remember what they had done; Ptolemy III of Egypt took it as his official title. Worldly power rules by force and arranges to be thanked for it. The test is not whether a person does good, but whether the good is arranged so that it is seen, credited and remembered.

He went about doing good. The verb from this word appears only once in the New Testament, of Jesus, who “went about doing good”, literally benefacting (Acts 10:38). The one true Benefactor never took the title. He took a towel, and then a cross. The kings of the Gentiles had their goodness carved in stone so that it would come back to them. His came back to him as thorns and nails.

Is ambition wrong? Not in itself. Jesus does not tell them to stop wanting greatness; in the next breath he tells them how to have it, and then gives them a kingdom (vv. 26–29). Paul calls it a noble thing to aspire to oversight in the church (1 Timothy 3:1). What is wrong is ambition for yourself: to be seen, ranked and thanked. The test is simple: would I still want this work if nobody ever knew I did it, and someone else got the credit? Godly ambition wants Christ to be great and the church served, and is content to be the youngest at the table while that happens.
verseByVerse.note: “Benefactor” was an official title that rulers loved to claim.

verseByVerse.quote: But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. For who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Christ’s kingdom greatness is turned upside down: the leader is to serve, because Jesus himself is among them as the one who serves.

But not so with you. Five words that set the church apart from the world’s rules of rank. He does not abolish leadership; he redefines it. What is forbidden is not office but what office is used for.

As the youngest, as one who serves. In that world the youngest at a gathering did the menial jobs: he fetched, he could be interrupted at any time, and everybody’s needs came before his plans. Leadership in the kingdom is service (Mark 10:43–45): the leader carries the most weight for others, rather than being carried.

Who is the greater? Jesus asks a question with an obvious answer and gives it himself, so that nobody escapes into cleverness: in every society the served outrank the servers.

I am among you as the one who serves. That same evening, John tells us, he took a towel and washed their feet (John 13:4–15), including the feet of the man who had already agreed to betray him. Here the passage stops being about management and becomes about God. The one speaking is the eternal Son, by whom all things were made, holding a basin, and within a day the One who poured the water will pour out his life. Luke does not record here the ransom saying (Mark 10:45); he shows it, the night before the ransom was paid.

The King waits at his own table. Once he told a parable no one else would have dared to tell, of a master who comes home in the night, finds his servants awake, dresses himself for service, has them recline at table, and comes and serves them (12:37). At this table the Master was already doing it, and he has never stopped. He serves his people now from the throne, and on the last day the Lord of glory will still be the one who serves.

What it means to serve. Jesus means neither a church rota nor being a doormat whose needs never count. The disciples wanted not simply a seat but to be “regarded as the greatest” (v. 24). Underneath the quarrel is a hunger to be noticed and counted, and while that hunger rules us even our kindness is a bid for credit; we cannot serve freely while we are still auditioning. Timothy Keller often pointed out, in The Freedom of Self-Forgetfulness, that gospel humility is not thinking more of yourself or less of yourself, but thinking of yourself less. Only grace makes that possible. The Son of God gave his life for men arguing about seats, and we are no better than they. You have already been regarded by the only One whose regard finally counts, so you can stop keeping score and “through love serve one another” (Galatians 5:13). This week, when someone interrupts your plans, treat the interruption as the table you have been given to wait at.

Does servant leadership mean leaders have no real authority? No. Elders are to be obeyed (Hebrews 13:17), parents hold real authority from God, and Jesus himself is Lord while he serves. The point is the direction authority flows: for the good of those under it, never the comfort of the one holding it. A servant leader still decides, teaches and corrects, as a man carrying others who will give account to God for them.

What does this mean in a marriage and a home? The same pattern is the key to Christian headship. Scripture calls a husband the head of his wife, and in the same breath tells him to love her “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:23–25). Headship is not a right to be served but a call to lead in self-giving love: the first step in prayer, apology and sacrifice; protecting, providing and putting her good before his own. Christians differ on how far headship reaches, and many egalitarian believers read these verses as mutual submission (Ephesians 5:21); this commentary holds that headship is real, and every faithful reading agrees that it never licenses control. A man who uses headship to control, belittle or frighten his wife has turned it upside down into the Gentile model. Abuse is never tolerated in Christ’s church; a wife in danger should seek safety and help at once, and the church must stand with her.

verseByVerse.quote: 'You are those who have stayed with me in my trials, and I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having corrected their ambition, Jesus satisfies it: he honours their faithfulness and leaves them a kingdom, as his Father has given one to him. They have been wanting the right thing in the wrong shape.

You are those who have stayed with me. Within hours they will fall asleep on him and scatter, and one will deny him three times. Yet on the evening before all of it Jesus says: you stayed. And they had stayed, through the hostility, the plots, the crowds falling away when the teaching got hard (John 6:66), the long homeless walk to Jerusalem. The failure coming is real, and it does not cancel what preceded it. He does not judge them by their worst night. He sees the whole, and he counts the staying.

I assign to you a kingdom. To assign (diatithemai) is to appoint or arrange, a word used for making a covenant or a will, the verb behind the noun “covenant” (diathēkē). A man about to die is settling his affairs, and what he has to leave is a kingdom (Hebrews 9:16–17). “As my Father assigned to me”: the Father has given the kingdom to the Son (Daniel 7:14), and the Son gives it to his disciples (12:32). They argued about greatness, and the Son, on the night of his betrayal, wrote his failing friends into the will.

A scramble by heirs. They were fighting over a portion of something already being left to all of them in full. That is nearly always what the hunger for status in the church comes to: heirs scrambling for a slice of what is already theirs, “heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17).

Does Jesus really count my faithfulness when I keep failing? He does, because he sees what is really there. Your falls do not erase your faithfulness, any more than one night erased these men’s years with him. The failures matter, and Jesus names them; but your perseverance is itself his work in you, and he will not despise what he has made (Philippians 1:6). He remembers the cup of cold water given in his name (Matthew 10:42). If you are still following him after many stumbles, he calls that staying.

parallels.desc: he himself has suffered when tempted
if we endure, we will also reign

verseByVerse.quote: that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom Jesus leaves his friends is a place at his own table and a share in his rule over the renewed people of God.

At my table. The meal is not over; it is adjourned (v. 18). The same table, the same host, the same men, and this time nobody is arguing about seats and nobody leaves in the dark.

Thrones. The Twelve stand for the renewed people of God. Judging carries the sense it has in the book of Judges, to govern and put right, more than merely to pass sentence (Matthew 19:28). And all believers will share in some way in his reign: “do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” (1 Corinthians 6:2).

Thrones from the one crowned with thorns. The men handed this promise were not a shortlist of impressive people. They were provincial men who had spent the last few minutes squabbling about precedence and would spend the next few hours failing. The one about to be crowned with thorns (Mark 15:17) was handing out thrones, and every one he gives was bought with his blood.

Heaven is a table. Heaven is usually left vague, and should not be. It is not a choir practice that never ends. It is, in his own image, a table: food, drink, faces, conversation, and the person you most want to be near presiding over it. Everyone who has sat at a long meal with people they love and felt the evening going too fast has been given a small, accurate sample of it.

Will I really rule with Christ? Yes, in the way he appoints. Those who endure will reign with him (2 Timothy 2:12), and the redeemed “shall reign on the earth” (Revelation 5:10). We do not know the details, but the work you do faithfully now, in small things, is training for responsibility in the new creation: service without sin, weariness or rivalry, under a King we love.

Where Christians differ: what are these thrones? Premillennial Christians, who expect Christ to reign on earth for a thousand years after his return, see here a future earthly reign over a restored Israel. This commentary’s view: Matthew places it in “the new world” (Matthew 19:28), the renewed creation. The apostles share in Christ’s rule over his people, the true Israel of all who believe, a rule that begins now through their word, the apostolic foundation on which the church is built (Ephesians 2:20), and will be complete in the new creation. Whatever God still has in store for ethnic Israel, which Christians present differently from Romans 11, the promise here is of the apostles’ share in Christ’s reign.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Satan has asked to shake all the disciples to pieces, but Jesus has prayed for Peter that his faith will not fail, and he already appoints the man about to fall to strengthen the others once he has returned. Their thrones (v. 30) will come not by their own strength but because he prays for them.

Simon, Simon. The doubled name is how Scripture speaks when something enormous is about to be said to one person: Abraham, Abraham; Moses, Moses; Martha, Martha (10:41); Saul, Saul. It is tender and urgent. Not Peter, the rock, but Simon, the name he was born with: he is addressed as the man he still is, as he is about to fail.

Satan demanded to have you. The word means to demand that a person be handed over, as in Job, where the accuser asks for a man, is granted a limit, and cannot exceed it by a hair (Job 1:6–12; 2:1–6). Satan has no free access to God’s people. He has to ask. And this “you” is plural in the Greek, as the ESV notes: he demanded to have all of you. Satan asked for the whole barn.

Sift you like wheat. Sifting is violent. After threshing, the grain was shaken hard in a sieve to separate it from chaff, dirt and stones (Amos 9:9; see Threshing Floor and Winnowing). Satan’s aim was not to shake the chaff out of Peter but to show that Peter was chaff, to shake them until their faith fell apart.

But I have prayed for you. Here the “you” is singular: for Peter, who was about to fall most heavily. Satan asked for them all; Jesus names one man.

That your faith may not fail. Consider what he did not pray. Not that Peter would be spared the sifting; it comes. Not that Peter would not fall; he falls within hours, three times. He prayed for the one thing underneath all of it: that the man would go down and not stay down. Peter fell, but did not fall away. Judas fell away. To fall is to sin badly, even grievously, and then be brought back to Christ in repentance; to fall away is to turn from Christ for good, which shows that the faith was never real (1 John 2:19). The difference is not that Peter was stronger. Jesus prayed for Peter. This is the ground of the perseverance of the saints, the truth that everyone God has truly saved will go on believing to the end because God keeps them: not the strength of our faith but the prayer of our Saviour (John 17:11–15).

And when you have turned again. Repented, returned. The word is “when”, not “if”. Jesus knows Peter will fall, and knows he will come back: the restoration is settled before the fall has happened.

Strengthen your brothers. The man about to be the worst failure in the room is appointed to hold up everyone else, because a man who has been carried back knows the way. Restored, he strengthened others (John 21:15–17), and years later he wrote to suffering churches about the devil who prowls like a roaring lion, and about the God of all grace who “will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you” (1 Peter 5:8–10). He had been sifted, and he knew.

Satan does not hold the fork. John the Baptist had said that the winnowing fork is in Christ’s hand, and that he will gather the wheat into his barn (3:17). Satan may shake a disciple, but he does not hold the fork. The One who does had already counted Simon wheat, and prayed over him. The accuser asks; the Son decides; and what the Son has gathered no sifting will scatter.

How do I strengthen a brother? Peter’s commission passes in some measure to every restored sinner, and is mostly made of ordinary things. Go towards the one who is shaken: a message, a visit, a meal; the struggling rarely ask, so do not wait to be asked. Tell what was done for you: not advice from above but a story from alongside, the comfort Paul describes, given “with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God” (2 Corinthians 1:4). Give them Christ, not only sympathy: put a promise in their hands, such as this one, that he prays for his people. Restore gently: “restore him in a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6:1), remembering how near you came yourself. Your own failures, forgiven, are what fit you to help.

Why does God allow Satan to sift his people at all? Because God means it for good where Satan means harm. Satan wanted to prove Peter chaff; God used the same night to burn away Peter’s self-confidence and make him a humble shepherd. Trials prove faith genuine, more precious than gold refined by fire (1 Peter 1:6–7), and God sets their limits (1 Corinthians 10:13). The sifting is not painless, but it is never pointless, and never outside the reach of Christ’s prayers.

Does Jesus pray for me personally? Yes. The one who prayed for Peter on earth now intercedes for his people at God’s right hand (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25), and his prayer reaches those who believe through the apostles’ word (John 17:20). He knows his sheep by name (John 10:3). When you are being shaken and cannot pray well yourself, the Son is praying for you, and the Father always hears him (John 11:42).

Does “strengthen your brothers” make Peter the head of the church? No. Roman Catholic teaching has seen Peter’s primacy here, and Peter’s leadership among the apostles is plain in Acts. But the commission is personal and pastoral: Peter, restored after his fall, would strengthen the others, as he did in Acts and in his letters. Nothing in it speaks of an office passed to successors, and Paul later rebuked Peter to his face (Galatians 2:11–14).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the first “you” is plural (Satan asked for all of them), while in verse 32 it is singular: Jesus prayed for Peter. Sifting shook wheat in a sieve to separate it.

parallels.desc: Satan asks leave to test Job
shake Israel as one shakes with a sieve

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, 'Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.' Jesus said, 'I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter sincerely promises to go with Jesus to prison and death, and Jesus tells him exactly when and how often he will deny him that very night.

Ready to go with you. Peter means it entirely. Before the night is out he will strike with a sword in front of an armed crowd (John 18:10) and follow into the high priest’s courtyard when the others have gone. What he lacks is accurate knowledge of himself. He heard a warning and answered with a list of his qualities. That is the quiet idol of self-reliance, the belief that my love for God is what will hold me, often strongest in the most devoted people. One day he would go to prison and, by early tradition, to death in Rome (Acts 12:3–5; John 21:18–19), held up by the Lord who had gone before him. But not yet.

I tell you, Peter. The only time in this Gospel Jesus calls him Peter: the rock is about to crumble, and the name he was given is spoken over the moment he will least resemble it. And the reply is exact. Jesus does not say Peter is weak in general; he gives the number and the deadline: this day, three times, before dawn.

Why tell him in advance? Not to prevent the denial, nor to humiliate him, but for the sake of “when you have turned again”. Had Peter denied Christ without warning, he might have concluded that Jesus had misjudged him, that his discipleship had been a mistake, that there was nothing to go back to. Judas seems to have reached a conclusion of that kind, and it destroyed him. Because he was told in advance, the denial could only ever mean one thing: he knew, and he prayed for me anyway, and he told me I would come back.

“Believe in yourself.” It may be the creed our culture repeats most often, from classroom walls to the end of nearly every film, and Peter here is its model believer: he trusts his own love, sincerely, and within hours a servant girl’s glance has undone him. The trouble with self-belief is not that it is too confident but that it rests on the one thing least able to bear the weight. It has to be kept up, so it cannot afford to hear warnings, and when it fails it has nowhere to fall but into self-contempt; crushing self-doubt is the same creed turned inside out, still making everything depend on me. Jesus offers Peter something else entirely: not “believe in yourself” but “I have prayed for you” (v. 32). Peter came through not because his faith in himself held, but because the Son of God prayed him through the fall. That is a confidence that can survive the truth about you, because it never rested on you in the first place.

In everyday life. Think of a promise you made God and did not keep: the habit you were going to give up, the resolve that lasted eleven days. Bring that broken promise to Christ today: he kept perfectly what you have broken, and his obedience, not your record, is counted as yours (Romans 5:19; Philippians 3:9). Then replace it with a humbler prayer: keep me.

Should I stop making promises to God? No, but make them leaning on him. Scripture is full of people pledging themselves to God; Peter’s mistake was not his devotion but his self-reliance and his refusal to hear the warning. So make your promises as prayers: Lord, I want to be faithful in this; keep me, for I cannot keep myself. And when you break one, do not conclude that the whole thing was a sham. Confess it, get up and go on. A broken resolution is a reason to trust Christ more, not to stop following him.

Did the rooster crow once or twice? Mark says the rooster would crow twice (Mark 14:30). Luke gives the general warning, before cock-crow; Mark, whose Gospel early tradition links with Peter’s preaching, gives the precise form. One account is fuller than the other; they do not contradict.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'When I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything?' They said, 'Nothing.' He said to them, 'But now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack. And let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The season of welcome is over: their Master is about to be treated as a criminal, so his messengers must expect hostility and provide for themselves. The sword saying is a vivid warning that belongs to the passion story, not a manual on self-defence.

No moneybag. He makes them answer out loud about the missions on which he sent them out unprovisioned (9:3; 10:4), into a countryside that received them.

Did you lack anything? Their answer is one word: “Nothing.” God had provided through people’s hospitality. Answer it yourself: not has life been easy? but the narrower, testable question, has God ever actually let you go without what you needed? Most Christians, made to say it aloud, arrive at the disciples’ word, and are surprised by it. And if your honest answer is harder, if you have known real want, Scripture does not ask you to pretend: Paul knew hunger and need (Philippians 4:12), and the promise is not that we never lack bread but that he never leaves us (Hebrews 13:5).

But now. The change is not in God’s care but in the world’s welcome. The men at this table will go out to the arrests and courtrooms he described (21:12), and will need to provide for themselves. Everything turns on the sentence that follows: he will be numbered with the transgressors (v. 37).

The Lord who sent them. It was his name that opened the doors (10:17), and the reason the season is changing is himself. The world that welcomed his messengers is about to reject their Master, and the hostility they will meet is the hostility he meets first, tonight. Disciples share their Lord’s welcome, and they share his rejection (John 15:20).

Sell his cloak. One of the hardest sentences in the Gospels. A cloak was a man’s coat by day and his blanket by night (Exodus 22:26–27); to sell it for a sword is to say that the danger ahead is now greater than the cold. His own response shows plainly that it is not a licence to fight (see the note on vv. 37–38).

Does this verse teach that Christians may carry weapons or use force in self-defence? It is not about that question, and should not be made to settle it; Jesus is speaking figuratively of the danger ahead. Christians differ on personal self-defence, and Scripture elsewhere gives the governing authority the sword to punish evil (Romans 13:4). What this passage settles is that the gospel and the kingdom of Christ are never to be advanced or defended by the sword (John 18:36).
verseByVerse.note: The sword saying is a vivid warning of the hostility ahead, not a call to armed resistance, as verses 38 and 51 show.

verseByVerse.quote: For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about me has its fulfillment.' And they said, 'Look, Lord, here are two swords.' And he said to them, 'It is enough.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes to his arrest as the suffering Servant of Isaiah 53, counted among criminals; when the disciples produce two swords, he ends the conversation, because they have misunderstood him.

This Scripture must be fulfilled in me. “Must” is the divine necessity again (dei), the fixed purpose of God written in advance and now arriving.

Numbered with the transgressors. He quotes Isaiah 53:12, the last line of the Servant Song (Isaiah’s poem of the LORD’s suffering Servant), about the servant who “poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors”. It is the only direct quotation of Isaiah 53 by Jesus in the Gospels: he finds his own name there (“has its fulfillment” is literally “has its end”), and goes out to the garden to make it true (23:32–33). That is also why the swords must go: a man being arrested as a criminal cannot be defended by force without becoming one.

Two swords. They take him literally: two short swords or large knives, perhaps used for the Passover lamb. He was telling them the friendly season was over; they heard “sword” and reached for iron.

It is enough. Not that two swords are enough to fight, which would be absurd against an armed detachment, and Jesus knows it. Rather, “enough of this”, the weary words of a teacher closing a conversation that has gone wrong (Deuteronomy 3:26). When the iron did come out in the garden, he stopped it with a word and mended the only casualty of the night with a touch (vv. 50–51).

He made the most of the company. He was numbered with the transgressors, and he made the most of the company. Hanging between two of them, he heard one ask to be remembered, and answered with paradise (23:42–43). He stooped low enough to be counted among the lawless, and stayed close enough to them to save.

What does “numbered with the transgressors” mean for me? He was counted where you belonged so that you could be counted where he belonged. On the cross he was listed among the lawless, and God treated him as the sin-bearer: God made the sinless one to be sin for us, so that in him we might become his righteousness (2 Corinthians 5:21). That exchange is the whole gospel. When your conscience reminds you that you belong in the column of transgressors, answer that Christ has already stood in it, and you have been moved, by grace, to his.

Buy a sword, then put it away, so which is it? The church has misread this both ways: some took v. 36 as a licence for crusades and holy wars; others took v. 51 as a ban on any force whatever, in any hands, for any cause. The passage will carry neither load. Two swords for twelve men about to be surrounded is no armoury, and Jesus says, “It is enough.” The single sword-stroke of the whole passion was struck by a disciple, against Christ’s will, and Jesus reversed it. That is Luke’s last word on swords in the kingdom.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the garden Jesus chooses to drink the cup of God’s wrath, and he goes to his arrest in command, still praying and still healing. He tells the disciples to pray that the coming trial will not make them fall (vv. 39–40). Kneeling, he asks the Father to remove the cup, and yields: “not my will, but yours, be done”; an angel strengthens him, and his sweat falls like drops of blood (vv. 41–44, verses some manuscripts omit). He wakes his grieving friends gently (vv. 45–46). Then Judas comes with a kiss and is met with his name and a question; a disciple’s sword-stroke is stopped and the wound healed; and Jesus tells the leaders, “this is your hour, and the power of darkness” (vv. 47–53).
verseByVerse.theology:
In Gethsemane a true human will, which did not want the cup, freely bent itself to the Father’s will (this is treated fully at vv. 41–42).

On the last healing before the cross, see vv. 49–51; on the hour of darkness, see vv. 52–53.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 39 is for anyone who has tried to pray in an emergency and found nothing there (see the note on vv. 39–40).

Verse 42 answers a woman facing a diagnosis who wonders whether her honest “if you are willing” is weak faith: the Son of God prayed it. Verses 45 and 46 are for the believer whose grief has made prayer feel impossible: the Lord wakes his sleeping friends gently.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came out and went, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed him. And when he came to the place, he said to them, 'Pray that you may not enter into temptation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes to his usual place of prayer, where his betrayer knows to find him, and tells his disciples to pray that the coming trial will not make them fall. He goes to the cross not as a victim swept along but as a Son who has prayed his way to it.

As was his custom. The pattern of the week (21:37), with two consequences. First, Judas knew where to find him (John 18:2). On the one night when his habits could get him killed, Jesus goes to the one place his betrayer would look. He did not hide.

A path already trodden. Second, the worst night of his life did not send him somewhere new: when the crisis came he did not have to invent a practice, only keep one. What carries a person through a night like that is a path already trodden, made in the ordinary weeks when prayer feels unnecessary.

When he came to the place. Gethsemane (Mark 14:32), an olive grove on the slope of the Mount of Olives; the name means oil press. Luke simply calls it “the place”, as if every reader knew where the Lord prayed.

Pray that you may not enter into temptation. About to enter the deepest agony any human being has known, he asks them to pray not for him but for themselves, in words lifted from the prayer he taught them: “lead us not into temptation” (11:4). “Temptation”, peirasmos, is the trial that is coming, testing as well as enticement, which could make them fall. These men still trust their own strength. The danger closing in was real and armed, and the only defence he issued was prayer, at the beginning of the scene and again at the end (v. 46). The Shepherd thought of his sheep while the wolves were climbing the hill, and he still does.

How do I pray against temptation? Pray before the trial arrives, not only in the middle of it. Know your hour. Most of us fall in the same few places: late at night, tired, slighted, alone with a screen. Name yours to God. Pray ahead of it: in the morning for the evening, in the car park before the hard meeting. Do not walk towards it. A prayer to be kept from temptation that then follows it at a distance into the courtyard, as Peter did that night (vv. 54–55), is not yet meant; often the answer is a door you must shut yourself (2 Timothy 2:22). Do not pray alone. His command is plural: tell one trusted friend where you are weak and ask them to pray with you. And go to the one who stood: “we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). He prayed and did not fall; his obedience is counted to you and his help promised, so “draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16) before the hour comes.

How do I build a habit of prayer like this? Start small, regular and fixed: a time and a place, as Jesus had the Mount of Olives, whether a chair, a walk or the first ten minutes after the children leave. Use the Lord’s Prayer as a frame, the Psalms as words when you have none, and a short list of people to pray for. Expect dry days, and pray with others too, in your church’s prayer meeting: a path others walk with you is easier to keep.

Does God lead us into temptation? God tempts no one to sin (James 1:13), but he does bring his people into testing. The prayer asks to be kept from falling when the test comes, and God promises that “he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

verseByVerse.quote: And he withdrew from them about a stone's throw, and knelt down and prayed, saying, 'Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Facing the cup of God’s wrath, Jesus asks his Father to take it away if there is any other way, and then yields his will entirely to the Father’s. He truly did not want the cup, and that is what makes his yielding obedience.

About a stone’s throw. Near enough to be seen and heard, far enough to be alone. Luke, who drew on eyewitnesses (1:2), measures the distance.

And knelt down. Jews customarily prayed standing; kneeling was for extremity, a sign of intensity and submission. In Mark he falls on the ground (Mark 14:35).

Father. Whatever else is said, it begins there, and the address never wavers. Even in agony, the intimate name.

Remove this cup. Everything depends on identifying the cup. In the prophets it is a fixed image, and not of pain in general. It is the cup of the wrath of God: the cup of foaming wine the wicked of the earth must drain to its dregs (Psalm 75:8); “this cup of the wine of wrath” for the nations (Jeremiah 25:15); the cup of staggering (Isaiah 51:17). This wrath has nothing of a man losing control about it: it is the steady, holy resistance of perfect goodness to evil. So what makes him shake is not the nails. Jewish martyrs went to terrible deaths with calm defiance; if Jesus were merely facing execution he would be less brave than his own martyrs. What is in front of him is the undiluted judgment of God against sin, to be drunk in the place of sinners by the only man who never deserved a drop of it.

If you are willing. He does not presume, and the asking is real: if there is another way, let there be another way. There was not, and the silence that followed is the measure of what the cross was for. If the Father would not spare his own Son a single mouthful, there was no other way for you to be saved.

Not my will, but yours. The heart of the prayer: total submission, freely given. Where Adam chose his own will in a garden, Christ says “yours” in a garden. And this obedience is our salvation: “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19; Hebrews 10:7–10).

The other cup, with no mercy mixed in. A few hours earlier he had handed his friends a cup and called it the new covenant in his blood, poured out for them. Now, on his knees in the dark, he is shown the other cup, with no mercy mixed in it, and he takes it. He drank the cup of wrath to the dregs so that the cup his people hold is the cup of salvation (Psalm 116:13).

Is it weak faith to add “your will be done”? No. The Son of God prayed so, on the worst night in history. Telling God plainly what you want and then leaving it with him is not a failure of faith; it is the highest thing faith does. Pray boldly for healing, for a marriage, for a child: ask, and say what you long for. Then add what Jesus added, not as a hedge but as trust in a Father who knows better than you, and who did not spare his own Son.

Is it not cruel for a Father to pour out wrath on his Son? Cruelty would mean punishing an unwilling third party, and the Son is nothing of the kind. The Father and the Son are one God, and the Son laid down his life of his own will: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18). The cross is not God punishing someone else to spare himself trouble. It is God himself, in the person of the Son, bearing the cost of his own justice for those he loves: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

Did Jesus have two wills? Yes. He is one person, the eternal Son, with two natures, divine and human, each with its own will. As God he shares the one will of the Father and the Spirit; as man he has a true human will, which recoiled from the cup as any holy human will must, and which he freely bent to the Father’s purpose. The church confessed this against those who said Christ had only one will (Constantinople, 681), because a Saviour without a human will could not offer human obedience in our place. Gethsemane is where you see it: a real man choosing, at the cost of everything, to obey.
verseByVerse.note: A stone’s throw is a short distance. The “cup” pictures God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father did not take the cup away, but he sent an angel to strengthen his Son to drink it.

An angel from heaven. The angel does not come to rescue Jesus from the cross; it comes so that he can get to it. That is often how God answers his people’s prayers too: not by removing the trial but by strengthening them in it (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).

Strengthening him. In his humanity he needed strength, and the one who made the angel is ministered to by it. He was made “like his brothers in every respect” (Hebrews 2:17), including the need for help from heaven in the hour of weakness, and so “he is able to help those who are being tempted” (Hebrews 2:18).

Do angels help believers today? Yes, though usually unseen. Angels are “ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14), and “the angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him” (Psalm 34:7). But Scripture never tells us to pray to angels, seek them, or build our comfort on stories of them. The angel in the garden pointed Jesus to the cup, not away from it. Our strength comes from God, by his Spirit and his Word, and whether he uses angels to give it is his business.

How should these verses be read, since some manuscripts lack them? Read them, and rest nothing on them that rests nowhere else (see the textual note below). Nothing in them is unique to them. The agony in the garden is in Matthew and Mark without these verses; angels attending Jesus after a great trial are already in the record (Matthew 4:11); and a Christ who prays in anguish is the settled teaching of the New Testament: “In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7). They are true in any case to what we know of Gethsemane.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit verses 43 and 44. The evidence really is divided. The verses are missing from some early and important manuscripts and present in many others, and they were known to second-century writers such as Justin Martyr and Irenaeus. Some copies mark them with a sign showing the scribe knew there was a question. Careful scholars weigh two explanations: either Luke wrote them and some scribes cut them, or they preserve a true early memory later written in. The first has real force. Some early readers were embarrassed by a Jesus who sweated, shook and needed an angel, and a scribe who removed these lines would have thought he was defending Christ’s dignity; he would have been removing the proof of his humanity. Many scholars think they are original, and many do not; most modern Bibles keep them, with a note.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit verses 43 and 44.

verseByVerse.quote: And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ anguish was so great that his body gave way under it, yet the worse it grew, the harder he prayed.

And being in agony. Agōnia, related to agōn, the contest of the arena: the strain of a mind in fierce conflict. This is not despair. It is a battle of the will, at the limit of what a body can bear.

He prayed more earnestly. Under that pressure the human instinct is to stop praying; he went the other way. He has been further into dread than anyone reading this will ever go, he went in freely, and he did not come out until he had drunk the whole cup.

Like great drops of blood. The detail only the physician records. Whatever exactly Luke means (see below), the point is not clinical: it went that far.

Falling down to the ground. In a garden, on the ground. Adam was cursed to eat bread by the sweat of his face till he returned to the ground (Genesis 3:17–19). Here the sweat of the last Adam, as Paul calls Christ (1 Corinthians 15:45), falls on the ground of a garden, and the curse of Adam’s sin is borne by the one who came to undo it.

Is anxiety or deep distress a sign of weak faith? Not in itself. Some teaching treats visible distress as evidence of weak faith, as if fear were failure. This verse ends that argument. The sinless Son of God, in perfect communion with his Father, doing exactly the Father’s will, was in such distress that his body gave way. Anxiety can become sin when it turns to unbelief or grumbling, and we are told to cast our anxieties on God (Philippians 4:6; 1 Peter 5:7). But fear and anguish carried to the Father in prayer are not failure; they are exactly what Jesus did. And if anxiety has become a constant illness, talking to your pastor and seeking out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up, is wisdom, not lack of faith.

Uncertain wording. “Like great drops of blood” can be read two ways. Luke may mean that the sweat fell in thick, heavy drops, the way blood falls from a wound; or he may describe a rare documented condition, hematidrosis, in which extreme distress mixes blood with sweat. His word “like” (hōsei) fits a comparison more naturally, but does not rule out the second. Either way the sweat shows the extremity of his anguish.
verseByVerse.note: Luke, a doctor, describes the extreme anguish; “like great drops of blood” may be a comparison or describe a rare medical condition.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he rose from prayer, he came to the disciples and found them sleeping for sorrow, and he said to them, 'Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus finds his disciples asleep, worn out by grief, and instead of rebuking them he gently wakes them to pray.

Sleeping for sorrow. Matthew and Mark record that the disciples slept; only Luke tells us why: from grief. That is a physician’s observation and a kindness. They had spent an evening being told that one of them was a traitor and their leader was going to die, and grief of that weight does not keep you awake. It shuts you down. Luke is gentle with the disciples, mentioning one return where Mark has three.

Why are you sleeping? No long rebuke, no discussion of their failure. Mark records a sharper word to Peter (Mark 14:37); Luke gives us a gentle question.

Rise and pray. The same command as v. 40. Not “feel better”, nor “stop grieving”, but the smallest possible next action. Within hours Peter will fall at a fire.

Awake while they slept. Bereavement, depression, a marriage coming apart, months of caring for someone, and a believer finds that the thing he most needs to do is the thing he can no longer make himself do; then, on top of the sorrow, comes the accusation that a real Christian would be praying. Look at who is standing over these men. He knows exactly why they are asleep, he has just been through something immeasurably worse, and he wakes them gently, without a word about what they have forfeited. Our Lord was awake in agony while they slept in sorrow, and he is awake still.

What if I cannot pray at all right now? Then pray the smallest prayer you can, and lean on others and on the Spirit. A groan, a single line, the Lord’s Prayer said slowly, a psalm read aloud: God hears all of it. “The Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). Ask a friend or your pastor to pray for you and with you. Rest and sleep are not sins; Elijah was fed and allowed to sleep before he was spoken to (1 Kings 19:5–8). And remember that Christ is praying for you while you cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, there came a crowd, and the man called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. He drew near to Jesus to kiss him, but Jesus said to him, 'Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas arrives at the head of the arresting party and marks Jesus with a kiss, and Jesus meets him with his name and a question that still holds the door open.

While he was still speaking. He was mid-sentence, telling them to pray, and the torches were already coming up the hill. Since v. 3 the chapter has been moving towards this: at night, in a garden, guided by an insider, as foretold at the table (v. 21).

Judas was leading them. Luke says “one of the twelve” again, as though it still cannot be believed. The one who had followed Jesus now leads his enemies.

To kiss him. A kiss was the common greeting of a disciple to his teacher, an act of honour and affection. He could have pointed. He chose the one movement that means “I am yours” and used it as a marker for the temple police. That is what sin does when it is full-grown: it takes what is good and makes it a tool. Worship offered to be seen, truth told to wound, a Bible verse used to win an argument, affection used as a lever.

Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? Only Luke records these words, the last recorded word of Jesus to Judas. It is not a curse. It is a question, and it is his name, the name Luke listed on the mountain when Jesus chose the Twelve (6:13–16). It exposes the obscenity, betrayal with a sign of love, and still he calls himself the Son of Man, the one who will come in glory (Daniel 7:13). It is a last door held open, a last appeal to Judas’s conscience: he puts into words what Judas is doing, at the moment of doing it, and the question hangs there waiting for an answer. This is how the Lord deals with a man walking into ruin: not by ambush, but by naming it to his face while there is still a second in which to stop. And when the question went unanswered, he went on to the cross and died for sinners exactly like the one who kissed him (Romans 5:6).

Why did Jesus choose Judas if he knew? Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray him (John 6:64, 70), and chose him so that the Scripture would be fulfilled (John 13:18; Psalm 41:9). That choice did not make Judas a traitor. It gave him every privilege, some three years of Jesus’ company, teaching and love, and he turned them all down: Christ’s love was offered even to the one who sold him.

Was Judas ever truly a believer who lost his salvation? No. Of those the Father gave him, Jesus lost none except “the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled” (John 17:12), and early on he had said that one of the Twelve was a devil (John 6:70). He shared the outward life of a disciple but never belonged to Christ (1 John 2:19). The true believer may fall terribly, as Peter did, but Christ’s sheep never perish (John 10:28).
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: And when those who were around him saw what would follow, they said, 'Lord, shall we strike with the sword?' And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. But Jesus said, 'No more of this!' And he touched his ear and healed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a disciple strikes with the sword, Jesus stops the violence and heals his wounded enemy: the last healing before the cross.

Lord, shall we strike with the sword? They ask the question and do not wait for the answer, which is the whole trouble with them in one line. They had two swords (v. 38) and had misunderstood. Before the reply comes, a sword is out and a man is bleeding.

His right ear. John names them both: Peter with the sword, and the servant Malchus (John 18:10). Peter was a fisherman, not a swordsman, and an ear rather than a head suggests a wild stroke the man ducked: in the circumstances, suicidal.

No more of this! The last command he gives before he is bound (on the wording, see below). He stops not an enemy but a friend, and not cowardice but reckless, loving courage, because the kingdom does not come that way. He would say it under interrogation the next morning: “If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting” (John 18:36). The one thing he would not permit in his own defence was the thing his followers have most often reached for since.

He touched his ear. Only Luke, the doctor, records it. Minutes from being bound, with torches in his face, he stops his arrest to repair the injury done to one of the men who came to take him. Malchus went to work that night to arrest a man and came home whole. The last miracle of healing before the cross was performed on a member of the arresting party, by the prisoner, without being asked. He does not merely refuse to hit back; he heals. We too were his enemies, and he reconciled us to God by his death (Romans 5:10).

Was Peter wrong to defend Jesus? His love was right and his method wrong: he reached for the world’s weapon to protect Jesus from the cross Jesus had come to embrace. Christians make the same mistake whenever they try to defend Christ with anger, force, manipulation or political power. We stand up for Jesus by speaking the truth in love, suffering wrong patiently, and doing good to those who oppose us (1 Peter 2:23; 3:15–16).

Does Jesus still heal like this? Christ still heals, often in answer to prayer, and we should pray for the sick with confidence (James 5:14–15). But the instant miracles of his earthly ministry and of the apostles were signs confirming the new revelation of the gospel (Hebrews 2:3–4), and this commentary holds, with many Reformed Christians, that such sign gifts, the miraculous healings, tongues and prophecies that marked the apostles, ceased with the apostolic age, because the New Testament calls them the signs of an apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12). Brothers and sisters who believe otherwise, many of whom pray for the sick with great faith and love, are to be loved and listened to. Either way, every healing, through medicine or prayer or both, is his gift, and the greatest healing he gives is the forgiveness of enemies.

Uncertain wording. Jesus’ words are very brief in Greek, literally allow until this. They may mean “No more of this!”, stopping the disciples (as the ESV takes it), or Let them go this far, allowing the arrest to go ahead. Either way, Jesus halts the violence and gives himself up.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke, the doctor, records that Jesus healed the ear. John names the servant Malchus and the swordsman Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus said to the chief priests and officers of the temple and elders, who had come out against him, 'Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus exposes the leaders’ cowardice in coming for him by night as if he were a bandit, and names the moment: their hour, and the power of darkness, permitted by God, and only an hour.

The chief priests. He speaks to the chief priests and officials, not to the muscle: the leadership itself had come out at night to see it done.

As against a robber, with swords and clubs? A robber here (lēstēs) is not a pickpocket but a bandit or insurgent, a man with a weapon and a hillside. They have come out equipped for an armed rebel. Within hours Luke will show a real insurrectionist, Barabbas, set free while the man they treated as one is condemned in his place (23:18–25).

Day after day in the temple. He was there every day, in the open, in their own building. They chose the olive grove, at night, with a paid informant and a crowd carrying clubs, and the choice shows who believed his own case would survive daylight.

Your hour, and the power of darkness. Only Luke records these words. He concedes the hour: it is genuinely theirs, the time God has permitted them to act. He concedes the power: exousia, real authority, the authority of Satan (Acts 26:18). What he withholds is any suggestion that it is more than an hour (4:13). It gets an hour, and it is God who has given it; and the Lord of the hours has already appointed the dawn.

In everyday life. When darkness seems to be winning, in the news, in your family, in your own heart, remember that it looks permanent from inside. It looked permanent to the eleven men running down that hillside, and by Sunday morning it was over. Say it today about the darkest thing you face: this is an hour, and God has set its length.

What is the power of darkness today? The same enemy, still working through human hearts and systems: lies, cruelty, false religion, persecution, and the ordinary pull of the world against God. Christians are not to be naive about it (Ephesians 6:12). But for believers it is a defeated power: God “has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son” (Colossians 1:13). Satan’s hour ended at the empty tomb, and what remains is a beaten enemy’s rage before the end. We resist him with the truth, the gospel, faith and prayer (Ephesians 6:13–18), never with fear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 54–71 — The Denial and the Trial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Outside, the leading apostle fails; inside, the Lord confesses the truth that will condemn him. Peter follows at a distance and sits by his enemies’ fire, and a servant girl’s glance brings the first of three denials that grow worse over an hour, until the rooster crows (vv. 54–60). The Lord turns and looks at him, and Peter goes out and weeps bitterly (vv. 61–62). The guards blindfold and beat Jesus and demand that he prophesy, while his prophecies are being fulfilled around them (vv. 63–65). At daybreak the council asks whether he is the Christ; he claims the seat at God’s right hand and affirms that he is the Son of God, and they need no further testimony (vv. 66–71).
verseByVerse.theology:
Peter and Judas both regretted what they had done, and only one turned with his regret towards the Lord (see the note on vv. 61–62).

Verse 69 joins Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13 in a claim no mere man could make (see the note on v. 69). His enemies understood it as a claim to be the Son of God, and he affirmed it (vv. 70–71).
verseByVerse.examples:
A Christian leader who has failed under pressure may conclude that he has forfeited his calling. Peter is the answer (see the note on vv. 61–62).

Verses 63 to 65 show cruelty with no cause behind it, done only because the prisoner could not hit back (see the note on vv. 63–65).

verseByVerse.quote: Then they seized him and led him away, bringing him into the high priest's house, and Peter was following at a distance. And when they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is led away alone to the high priest’s house, and Peter, following at a distance, sits down by the fire among the men who arrested him.

Into the high priest’s house. John records a first hearing before Annas, the former high priest, and then before Caiaphas (John 18:13, 24). Luke gives us the denial first, then the mocking, then the morning council.

Following at a distance. He was following, which is more than the others managed (Mark 14:50). And he was at a distance: close enough to see, far enough to be nobody, the position of a man who cannot bear to leave and cannot afford to be counted. Many Christians know that distance: the conversation where you did not lie about your faith and did not mention it.

A fire in the courtyard. It was cold (John 18:18), and there is nothing sinful about wanting to be warm. But inside, his Lord is being interrogated, and outside Peter sits shoulder to shoulder with the men who brought him there, faces lit by the same fire.

Peter sat down among them. Peter did not decide to deny Christ. He decided to stay warm. He drifted to the safest available place, sat down with people whose questions he had no intention of answering honestly, and the denial came out of his mouth as the natural consequence of where he was sitting. Nobody plans the third denial. They choose the fire.

Led away alone. The Shepherd has been struck and the sheep are scattered (Mark 14:27; Zechariah 13:7). He enters the high priest’s house without one friend at his side. Even the little that Peter manages, following far behind, he owes to the Lord who had prayed that night that his faith would not fail (v. 32).

Is it wrong to spend time with people who are not Christians? No. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners and was criticised for it (15:1–2), and we are sent into the world, not out of it (John 17:15–18). The danger in Peter’s case was not where he sat but why: he sat there to hide. Be among unbelievers as yourself, a follower of Jesus, friendly, honest and unashamed. The question is not whether you share their fire, but whether you have agreed, without saying so, to keep Christ out of the conversation in order to keep your seat.
verseByVerse.note: John records a first hearing before Annas, the former high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a servant girl, seeing him as he sat in the light and looking closely at him, said, 'This man also was with him.' But he denied it, saying, 'Woman, I do not know him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under the mildest pressure imaginable, a servant girl’s stare, Peter denies that he even knows Jesus.

A servant girl. Luke wants us to see how small the pressure was. The accuser is a young female slave, the person with the least standing of anyone present, whose word carried little legal weight.

In the light. He had put himself where the fire was, and the fire showed his face: he was recognised because he was warm. “Looking closely” is staring intently. That is all: no interrogation, no threat, no soldier.

This man also was with him. As mild as an accusation can be: not that he drew a sword, which was true, merely that he was with him. Yet “with him” is the very essence of discipleship (8:1; Mark 3:14), and that is exactly what he now disowns.

Woman, I do not know him. The first denial, a flat lie, hours after he said he was ready to go to prison and to death (v. 33). He denies not a fact but the person. Some three years of the boat, the storm, the loaves, his own confession, “The Christ of God” (9:20), and the sentence that comes out is that he does not know who the man is.

The gap between intention and action. The force needed to open the gap between what Peter sincerely intended and what he did was one stare from a slave girl. He did not overestimate his love, which was real, but what love can do on its own in a cold yard at night. That is why the instruction was, “Pray that you may not enter into temptation” (v. 40). He slept when told to pray, then sat down at the fire, and then a girl looked at him.

The one he could not unknow. Peter says he does not know him, and the one fact in that courtyard no lie could touch is that Jesus knew Peter. He had called him from his boat (5:10), named him (6:14), prayed for him by name that very night (v. 32) and foretold this very sentence (v. 34). Peter could disown the relationship with his mouth. He could not dissolve it, because it had never rested on Peter’s hold on Jesus but on Jesus’ hold on Peter, and that held through the denial. The disciple denied the Master to save his skin; the Master did not deny the disciple, though it cost his life.

In everyday life. Denials of Christ often happen in small moments, before unimportant people: the joke you laugh at, the weekend you describe vaguely. Before work today, ask the Spirit who filled Peter before the council (Acts 4:8) for courage in exactly those moments, and decide now one simple sentence you could say if asked.

I have denied Christ by silence, so what now? Then you are where Peter was, and the way back is the same. Name it to God honestly, remembering that Christ was not surprised and has prayed for you. Then, where possible, take the next opportunity in the same company to own him plainly. Peter, who denied Jesus before a servant girl, later stood before the very council that condemned him and said, “we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard” (Acts 4:20). Silence can be forgiven, and courage can be given.

verseByVerse.quote: And a little later someone else saw him and said, 'You also are one of them.' But Peter said, 'Man, I am not.' And after an interval of about an hour still another insisted, saying, 'Certainly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean.'
