But Peter said, 'Man, I do not know what you are talking about.' And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter denies Jesus twice more, each time more sweepingly, until the rooster crows exactly as Jesus said it would.

Man, I am not. A little later, a second accuser, and a second denial. Each is worse than the last. The first denied the person: “I do not know him.” The second denies the fellowship: I am not one of them. The third will deny the subject altogether: “I do not know what you are talking about.” Sin does not stay the size it started. The second lie exists to protect the first, the third to protect the second, and each costs less to tell than the one before.

About an hour. Only Luke notes the time. This is not a moment of panic. Peter had an hour to get up, walk out and repent. He stayed.

For he too is a Galilean. The third accuser has evidence: Matthew adds that his accent gave him away (Matthew 26:73). Peter could control what he said, not how it sounded. The very voice denying Christ was proving him a follower with every word.

While he was still speaking, the rooster crowed. Luke does not even let him finish. God sent no earthquake to stop Peter. He used a bird doing at dawn what birds do at dawn, and it was enough, because it had been named in advance (v. 34).

The Lord of the rooster. The Lord who knew where a colt was tied (19:30) and who would be carrying a water jar (22:10) knew the hour a bird would crow. Peter’s lies were running to their own schedule; the rooster was running to Christ’s.

Is denying Christ an unforgivable sin? Not for one who comes back. Peter denied him three times, with oaths (Matthew 26:74), and was forgiven and restored. The sin Scripture calls unforgivable is the settled, knowing rejection of the Spirit’s witness to Christ, calling his work evil (Mark 3:28–30), and such a person does not want to repent. Hebrews warns of those who fall away and never return (Hebrews 6:4–6). But anyone grieving over a denial and longing to come back is plainly not in that condition. The rooster was not the end of Peter’s story. It was the alarm that woke him.

Who accused Peter? The Gospels differ in who spoke: a servant girl, another girl, a man, the bystanders. In a crowded courtyard several people likely spoke at each turn, and each writer records the voices he chose. All four agree on the threefold denial and the rooster. Differences like these are what independent witnesses usually show, and believers hold all four accounts true even where the exact order of voices cannot now be fixed.
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, how he had said to him, 'Before the rooster crows today, you will deny me three times.' And he went out and wept bitterly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord turns and looks at Peter; the look brings his word back to mind, and Peter goes out and weeps the bitter tears of a man who will be restored.

The Lord turned. Only Luke records the look. Perhaps Jesus was being led across the courtyard between hearings. And Luke calls him “the Lord”: even as a prisoner, he is Lord.

What was in that look? The text tells us by what it produced: not despair or self-justification, but memory, and then tears. So it was not a look of anger or contempt; a man looked at with contempt remembers the contempt, not a promise. What Peter remembered was words, surely including the ones just before the prediction: “I have prayed for you”, and “when you have turned again”. So the look said something like: I told you, and I knew, and nothing between us has changed. A look of grief and love, and Peter never forgot it. Bound and about to be beaten, he cannot cross a courtyard and put a hand on his friend’s shoulder. All he has is a turn of the head. It was enough.

Peter remembered. The word of Jesus came back to him. That is how the Lord still restores his people: by bringing his word to mind at the moment it is needed.

He wept bitterly. Peter went out into the night, as Judas had gone out from the supper (John 13:30), but their nights ended differently. Judas, seized with remorse, returned the silver and took his own life (Matthew 27:3–5). Peter wept, and lived. Both regretted; only one turned with his regret towards the Lord he had wronged. That is Paul’s distinction between a grief that leads to repentance and salvation and a grief that ends in death (2 Corinthians 7:10). Judas’s story is a warning against despair; it is not a verdict on everyone who has died by their own hand in illness and anguish, whom we leave, with their grieving families, to the mercy of God. What matters is not how hard a man weeps but which way he faces when he does. Jesus had prayed for him (v. 32), and he would be restored (24:34; John 21:15–19).

Eyes for a failing friend. Seven weeks later the man who had wept in the dark preached Christ to thousands (Acts 2:14–41). The look that broke his heart did not end his ministry; it began it. The eyes that turned towards Peter across a courtyard have never once looked at one of their own who has fallen and looked away.

How do I know if my sorrow over sin is godly sorrow? Look at which way it faces. Worldly sorrow is mainly about me: what I have lost, how I look, what it will cost; it hardens into excuses or sinks into despair. Godly sorrow is about God: I have wronged him, and I go to him. It grieves the sin itself, not only its consequences; it confesses; it hopes in Christ’s mercy; and it turns, slowly but really, from the sin. You need not measure your tears. If your sorrow drives you towards Christ rather than away from him, it is the godly kind.

Does Jesus look at me like that when I fail? Yes. If you belong to him, his look at your failure is the one Peter received: knowing, grieved and full of love, meant to bring his word back to you and lead you to tears that end in restoration. “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1), and his kindness is meant to lead you to repentance (Romans 2:4).
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the men who were holding Jesus in custody were mocking him as they beat him. They also blindfolded him and kept asking him, 'Prophesy! Who is it that struck you?' And they said many other things against him, blaspheming him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The guards make sport of Jesus, blindfolding and beating him and daring him to prophesy, and he bears it in silence, as Isaiah’s Servant would.

Mocking him as they beat him. These are the guards, with hours to fill and a prisoner nobody would ask about, as he had foretold (18:32). It is the commonest kind of cruelty: he was available and unable to retaliate, and it passed the time.

Blindfolded. A cruel game with a rule: blindfold him, hit him, and demand that he name the hand. The mockery aims at the one thing they had heard about him, that he was a prophet. And in the very hours they demand a prophecy, his prophecies are being fulfilled: the kiss, the denials before the rooster (vv. 34, 61), the numbering with the transgressors. They blindfold the only man in the room who can see anything, and then ask him to prove he can see. Isaiah had heard the Servant say it: “I gave my back to those who strike” (Isaiah 50:6).

Blaspheming him. Luke’s word is blasphēmountes. They will condemn him for blasphemy (v. 71), but they are the blasphemers, insulting the Son of God.

Luke records no answer. He could have named every man in that room. He says nothing: “he was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). What is held back is not merely a retort but legions of angels (Matthew 26:53). The power that made the hands striking his face was under perfect control, restrained by nothing but his own settled will to be struck.

That face is still set. In Isaiah the Servant who gave his back to the smiters also set his face like a flint, knowing he would not be put to shame (Isaiah 50:6–7). Jesus had set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51), and here, under a blindfold and a rain of blows, that face is still set. They covered it and struck it, and it did not turn from them.

Why did Jesus not defend himself? Because he had come to suffer, not to win the argument. His silence was chosen obedience: the Lamb led to the slaughter, bearing the punishment our sins deserved. Had he struck back, there would have been no sacrifice and no salvation. Peter, who watched it, later wrote that he answered insult with no insult and suffering with no threat, but handed himself over to the One who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

How should I respond when I am mocked for my faith? With the same trust, though not always the same silence. Jesus did speak when the truth required it (v. 69), and we should be ready to give a reason for our hope, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). But we need not answer every taunt, defend our dignity, or repay insult with insult. Leave your reputation with God. Count it an honour to share a little in his reproach (Acts 5:41), and pray for those who mock you, as he did for those who crucified him (23:34).

verseByVerse.quote: When day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered together, both chief priests and scribes. And they led him away to their council, and they said, 'If you are the Christ, tell us.' But he said to them, 'If I tell you, you will not believe, and if I ask you, you will not answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At dawn the council meets to give its verdict the look of law, and asks Jesus whether he is the Christ, not to learn the truth but to condemn him. The question the whole Gospel has asked, who is this?, is now put by his judges (vv. 67, 70).

When day came. Later Jewish tradition, written down in the Mishnah, held that capital cases should not be tried at night, so at first light the council met formally to confirm a verdict decided days before (v. 2). The most respectable machinery in Israel is being operated correctly in order to kill the Son of God.

The assembly of the elders. The Sanhedrin, Israel’s supreme council, under the high priest.

If you are the Christ, tell us. It sounds like an inquiry and is not one. The council wants not information but a sentence it can take to Pilate. They sat in judgment on the Judge of all the earth, and he let them.

If I tell you, you will not believe. Said without bitterness, and unanswerable: their minds are made up. When Lazarus came out of a tomb, their response was to plan another death (John 11:53). And if he asks, they will not answer, as earlier that week they refused to answer his question about John’s baptism (20:7). Yet he does not stay silent, and what he says next is not a defence but a claim so large that the council will need nothing else.

Religion is never safer than the heart that uses it. Their religion had become the place they hid from God rather than the way they came to him. Procedure, office and the language of God’s law can all be put to work against God.

Was the trial of Jesus illegal? By the later Jewish law code it broke several rules: a night hearing, a hurried verdict, no defence, the judges as accusers. We cannot be sure every rule was in force then, but its verdict was plainly settled before it began. The deeper point is that the court was right about the law and wrong about the man. God allowed injustice to condemn the just so that the unjust could be justified (1 Peter 3:18). To be justified is to receive the Judge’s own acquittal: not a better feeling but a verdict, accepted in his sight because Christ’s righteousness is counted as ours (Romans 4:5).

What if someone I love keeps asking but never believes? Keep answering with patience, but recognise what Jesus saw: some questions are not requests for truth but defences against it. You cannot argue anyone into the kingdom; only God opens hearts (Acts 16:14). So pray for them more than you debate them, live the gospel in front of them, give them the plain claims of Christ as he did here, and leave them with God. One member of that very council, Joseph of Arimathea, had not consented to its decision and came forward for Jesus at the cross (23:50–53), and God changed the heart of a young Pharisee named Saul.
verseByVerse.note: A night hearing had no legal standing; the council met formally at daybreak.

verseByVerse.quote: But from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers his judges with the claim that from now on he, the Son of Man, will sit enthroned at God’s right hand. He gives them far more than they asked.

But from now on. Through his death, resurrection and ascension: said from this room, with his hands tied and a death sentence being drafted.

The Son of Man. The title comes from Daniel’s vision of one like a son of man, brought on the clouds before the Ancient of Days and given an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14). Jesus has used it all through Luke’s Gospel; here, before the highest court in Israel, he speaks it with the whole vision in view.

At the right hand of the power of God. Psalm 110:1, “The LORD says to my Lord: ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool’”, the psalm he had used to silence the scribes that same week (20:41–44). Two Scriptures folded into one sentence make a claim no merely human Messiah could make: that a man will sit down on God’s own throne. The prisoner before them is the judge of all.

Seated, because the work is finished. The right hand is the position of the one who exercises the king’s authority, and to be seated there is to have the business settled. The priests stood daily, offering sacrifices that could never take away sins; Christ, having offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, sat down at God’s right hand (Hebrews 10:11–12). Luke omits the coming on the clouds that Mark records (Mark 14:62) and stresses the present enthronement, which begins at the ascension (Acts 2:33–36; 7:55–56). He is not on his way to the throne in spite of the cross. The road to that seat runs through Golgotha, and he is walking it on purpose.

What is Jesus doing at the right hand now? Reigning and interceding. He rules all things for the good of his church (Ephesians 1:20–22), and “he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25): now, from heaven, as the gospel goes to the nations. And he prays for those who are his (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25). One day he will come again visibly, in glory, to judge the living and the dead and make all things new. Until then the throne is occupied, and nothing in your life is outside his rule.

verseByVerse.quote: So they all said, 'Are you the Son of God, then?' And he said to them, 'You say that I am.' Then they said, 'What further testimony do we need? We have heard it ourselves from his own lips.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council understands Jesus to be claiming that he is the Son of God; he affirms it, and they condemn him on his own true words.

Are you the Son of God, then? “Then” does real work: so it follows that. They have understood v. 69 correctly: a man who takes the seat at God’s right hand claims a relation to God no creature has. That answers a modern idea, that Jesus never claimed to be divine and the church invented it later. His enemies, in front of him, in his own language, drew exactly that conclusion from what he had just said. A sceptic may reply that the church wrote the Gospels. But that Jesus was condemned by his own leaders and handed to Rome is among the best-attested facts about his end, and it is hard to explain unless he made some such claim.

You say that I am. Not evasion but a recognised way of saying yes (Matthew 26:64), and the council took it as one. There may be more in it. The final words are egō eimi, “I am”, which echo God’s own name given to Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:14), and which Jesus had used before in a way that made men pick up stones (John 8:58).

What further testimony do we need? The trial ends without proof of any crime, because there was none. In Luke no witness is called; in Matthew and Mark the false witnesses fail to agree. No act is established. They have their charge: blasphemy.

From his own lips. The only evidence the court ever had was his own confession. Blasphemy is a creature claiming the honour of God, and the charge would be entirely just if the man in the dock were anyone else. They got only one thing wrong: the identity of the defendant. A man who claims this is either guilty of blasphemy or is who he says; the council saw no middle ground, and neither does Luke. The innocent was condemned by the guilty, on his own true testimony, so that the guilty might one day be acquitted on his.

Does “Son of God” mean only that Jesus was a very godly man? No. Israel’s kings could be called God’s sons, and believers are sons by adoption, but that is not what the council heard or what Jesus meant. He claimed to sit at God’s right hand and to be the Son in a unique sense: the eternal Son, one with the Father (John 10:30), sharing the Father’s nature and glory, who became man without ceasing to be God. That is why they called it blasphemy. A merely good man who claimed that would not be good.

Who was responsible for Jesus’ death? A small group of leaders handed him over, and Rome executed him: Jew and Gentile together, as the church confessed (Acts 4:27–28). Behind them all stood God’s plan, and the sins of everyone he came to save. It gives no ground for blaming the Jewish people as a whole, and Peter, preaching to Jerusalem, said they had acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17).

22.text: <sup>1</sup> Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread drew near, which is called the Passover. <sup>2</sup> And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to put him to death, for they feared the people. <sup>3</sup> Then Satan entered into Judas called Iscariot, who was of the number of the twelve. <sup>4</sup> He went away and conferred with the chief priests and officers how he might betray him to them. <sup>5</sup> And they were glad, and agreed to give him money. <sup>6</sup> So he consented and sought an opportunity to betray him to them in the absence of a crowd. <sup>7</sup> Then came the day of Unleavened Bread, on which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed. <sup>8</sup> So Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, “Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it.” <sup>9</sup> They said to him, “Where will you have us prepare it?” <sup>10</sup> He said to them, “Behold, when you have entered the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house that he enters <sup>11</sup> and tell the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you, Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ <sup>12</sup> And he will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare it there.” <sup>13</sup> And they went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover. <sup>14</sup> And when the hour came, he reclined at table, and the apostles with him. <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. <sup>16</sup> For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.” <sup>17</sup> And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he said, “Take this, and divide it among yourselves. <sup>18</sup> For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.” <sup>19</sup> And he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” <sup>20</sup> And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood. <sup>21</sup> But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. <sup>22</sup> For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!” <sup>23</sup> And they began to question one another, which of them it could be who was going to do this. <sup>24</sup> A dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest. <sup>25</sup> And he said to them, “The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and those in authority over them are called benefactors. <sup>26</sup> But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. <sup>27</sup> For who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves. <sup>28</sup> “You are those who have stayed with me in my trials, <sup>29</sup> and I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom, <sup>30</sup> that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. <sup>31</sup> “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, <sup>32</sup> but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.” <sup>33</sup> Peter said to him, “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.” <sup>34</sup> Jesus said, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me.” <sup>35</sup> And he said to them, “When I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything?” They said, “Nothing.” <sup>36</sup> He said to them, “But now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack. And let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one. <sup>37</sup> For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about me has its fulfillment.” <sup>38</sup> And they said, “Look, Lord, here are two swords.” And he said to them, “It is enough.” <sup>39</sup> And he came out and went, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed him. <sup>40</sup> And when he came to the place, he said to them, “Pray that you may not enter into temptation.” <sup>41</sup> And he withdrew from them about a stone's throw, and knelt down and prayed, <sup>42</sup> saying, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” <sup>43</sup> And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. <sup>44</sup> And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground. <sup>45</sup> And when he rose from prayer, he came to the disciples and found them sleeping for sorrow, <sup>46</sup> and he said to them, “Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.” <sup>47</sup> While he was still speaking, there came a crowd, and the man called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. He drew near to Jesus to kiss him, <sup>48</sup> but Jesus said to him, “Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” <sup>49</sup> And when those who were around him saw what would follow, they said, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” <sup>50</sup> And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. <sup>51</sup> But Jesus said, “No more of this!” And he touched his ear and healed him. <sup>52</sup> Then Jesus said to the chief priests and officers of the temple and elders, who had come out against him, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? <sup>53</sup> When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.” <sup>54</sup> Then they seized him and led him away, bringing him into the high priest's house, and Peter was following at a distance. <sup>55</sup> And when they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them. <sup>56</sup> Then a servant girl, seeing him as he sat in the light and looking closely at him, said, “This man also was with him.” <sup>57</sup> But he denied it, saying, “Woman, I do not know him.” <sup>58</sup> And a little later someone else saw him and said, “You also are one of them.” But Peter said, “Man, I am not.” <sup>59</sup> And after an interval of about an hour still another insisted, saying, “Certainly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean.” <sup>60</sup> But Peter said, “Man, I do not know what you are talking about.” And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed. <sup>61</sup> And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, how he had said to him, “Before the rooster crows today, you will deny me three times.” <sup>62</sup> And he went out and wept bitterly. <sup>63</sup> Now the men who were holding Jesus in custody were mocking him as they beat him. <sup>64</sup> They also blindfolded him and kept asking him, “Prophesy! Who is it that struck you?” <sup>65</sup> And they said many other things against him, blaspheming him. <sup>66</sup> When day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered together, both chief priests and scribes. And they led him away to their council, and they said, <sup>67</sup> “If you are the Christ, tell us.” But he said to them, “If I tell you, you will not believe, <sup>68</sup> and if I ask you, you will not answer. <sup>69</sup> But from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” <sup>70</sup> So they all said, “Are you the Son of God, then?” And he said to them, “You say that I am.” <sup>71</sup> Then they said, “What further testimony do we need? We have heard it ourselves from his own lips.”

keyVerse.quote: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter turns on this prayer. The cup is the cup of God’s wrath against sin, and the Son who shrank from it chose to drink it, so that the cup he had handed his friends that evening could be the new covenant in his blood. Where everyone else in the chapter acts from fear, greed or weakness, here is the one free and perfect obedience by which “the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19).

22.reflection:
Jesus longed to eat this Passover with men he knew would fail him that night (vv. 15, 21–34). How does that change the way you come to the Lord’s Supper, especially when you feel unworthy?

Minutes after the Supper the disciples argued about which of them was the greatest (vv. 24–27). Where does the hunger to be noticed and credited show itself in your life or your church, and what would it look like this week to take the place of the one who serves?

Jesus told Peter, “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (v. 32), and Peter still fell. What made the difference between Peter and Judas (vv. 3–6, 61–62), and what comfort does Christ’s prayer give you when you fail?

In the garden Jesus prayed before the hour came and told his disciples to do the same (vv. 40, 46). Where are you most likely to enter into temptation, and how could you pray, and ask others to pray, ahead of it?

23.title: The Trial, the Cross, and the Tomb
23.overview:
Where we are. Luke 23 is the day of the cross, the goal Jesus set his face towards in 9:51, between the council’s verdict (chapter 22) and the empty tomb (chapter 24).

The message. The innocent King dies in the place of the guilty, and by his death opens paradise to them. Luke presses one fact: Jesus is innocent. Pilate says so three times (vv. 4, 14, 22), Herod finds nothing deserving death (v. 15), a dying criminal confesses it (v. 41), and the centurion says it when he has died (v. 47). Yet he is condemned and a murderer walks free: not a miscarriage of justice God failed to prevent, but the exchange at the heart of the gospel, the righteous for the unrighteous.

Why it was said. For Luke’s readers (see the introduction) a crucified founder was a scandal, apparent proof that Jesus was a rebel justly executed, or a failure God had abandoned. Luke answers both. Rome’s own officials found no guilt in him, and everything happened as Scripture said: “he was numbered with the transgressors” (22:37).

How the chapter makes its case. In the trial (vv. 1–25) the verdicts of innocence pile up while cowardice, contempt and a shouting crowd hand him over. On the way to the cross and on it (vv. 26–43) we see his heart: grieving for Jerusalem, praying for his killers, refusing to save himself, promising a thief paradise. His death and burial (vv. 44–56) bring heaven’s answer in darkness and a torn curtain, a death of perfect trust, a Roman’s confession and a witnessed burial. Three sayings from the cross are found only in Luke: the prayer for his killers (v. 34), the promise of paradise today (v. 43), and his last words, a prayer of trust from Psalm 31:5 (v. 46).

Where it leads. The mockers are truer than they know: he saved others, and himself he would not save. The first person the crucified King brings into his kingdom is a criminal who could bring nothing but a confession and a request. Then the chapter ends quietly: the women see the tomb, prepare spices and rest on the Sabbath, not knowing what the third day will bring.

For us. No one is too guilty for this Saviour, and no one too respectable to need him. Each of us stands somewhere in this crowd: with Pilate putting off a decision, Herod wanting a show, or one of the two criminals. Take the second criminal’s place, and pray his prayer: “Jesus, remember me.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Trial before Pilate and Herod
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every judge finds Jesus innocent, and he is condemned anyway while a guilty man goes free in his place. The council, unable to execute, rewrites its charge for a Roman ear: two lies and a truth (vv. 1–2). Pilate finds no guilt (vv. 3–4), and when he hears “Galilee” he passes the case to Herod, who wants only a show, meets silence and sends Jesus back in mockery (vv. 5–12). Pilate declares him innocent again and offers a flogging as a compromise (vv. 13–16), but the crowd demands Barabbas, a rebel and murderer, guilty of the very charge laid against Jesus (vv. 17–19). The shouting prevails (vv. 20–24), and the guilty man walks out as the innocent one is handed over (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology:
The repeated verdicts of innocence are the spine of the chapter, because only an innocent man could die for others (see the note on vv. 3–4). The Barabbas exchange shows substitution in the street before it is accomplished on the hill (see the note on v. 25). “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Verses 23–25 hold two truths together: these men are fully guilty, and behind them stands the purpose of God (this is treated fully at vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.examples:
Pilate’s sin here is not brutality but evasion: he hides behind procedure, and responsibility cannot be passed on to someone else (see the note on vv. 6–7).

Verse 5 alleges no crime, only disturbance (see the note on v. 5).

Herod had killed the prophet who brought him God’s word; now he wanted a trick, and received silence. For the believer who fears that God has gone silent on him, see the note on vv. 8–9.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the whole company of them arose and brought him before Pilate. And they began to accuse him, saying, 'We found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council brings Jesus to the Roman governor and rewrites its charge for a Roman ear: two lies and a truth. They had condemned him for claiming to be the Son of God; before Pilate they accuse him of stirring up revolt, refusing tax and claiming a throne.

The whole company of them. The Sanhedrin, the highest religious body in Israel, marches a bound prisoner across the city to a Gentile, because under Rome it could not carry out a death sentence (John 18:31). And the charge has to change: the council had condemned him for claiming to be the Son of God (22:70–71), and a Roman governor would have thrown that out before lunch.

Misleading our nation. So they make three fresh charges, each designed for a Roman ear. The first means stirring up revolt, the thing a governor most feared at a festival.

Forbidding us to give tribute. A flat lie. They had asked him that exact question in the temple, and he had answered: “render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” (20:25). He had said pay it; they report that he forbade it. False witness usually works this way: not by inventing something, which is easy to disprove, but by twisting something true until it says the opposite.

Christ, a king. They translate Messiah into king, a rival to Caesar. This charge is not false. He is the Christ, and a king, but not the kind Pilate feared, and they trust Pilate to hear the word king and stop listening. So the Son of God is brought before the empire on two lies and a truth, and the truth is the one that will kill him.

The charges that really mattered. The one they slandered stood still and let them, because the list that really mattered was not the one they brought against him but the record of our sins before God, and he had come to have that nailed to the cross (Colossians 2:14).

Is it wrong to defend myself when I am falsely accused? No. Paul defended himself before councils and governors (Acts 24–26), and calmly correcting a lie is often right, especially when others will be harmed by it. Jesus was silent at points in his trial because his hour had come and he had chosen to suffer, not because silence is always godly. Speak the truth plainly and without bitterness, refuse to answer lies with lies, and entrust your name to God, who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). You do not have to win to be vindicated.
verseByVerse.note: The charges are framed for a Roman governor: sedition, tax refusal, and a rival king. The tax charge was false.

verseByVerse.quote: And Pilate asked him, 'Are you the King of the Jews?' And he answered him, 'You have said so.' Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, 'I find no guilt in this man.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus admits that he is a king, and Pilate, the one judge who can have him killed, finds him not guilty. It is the first of the verdicts of innocence Luke wants us to count.

Pilate. Pontius Pilate governed Judea from about AD 26 to 36, known for brutality and contempt for the Jews (13:1). He knew what a rebel looked like; he had very likely crucified some.

Are you the King of the Jews? Pilate goes straight to the only charge that concerns him: are you claiming a throne?

You have said so. Not a denial. John fills in what Luke compresses: “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting” (John 18:33–38). He is a king, but not one who takes or keeps his throne by the sword.

I find no guilt in this man. And Pilate believes him. Luke means you to count the verdicts: Pilate three times (vv. 4, 14, 22), Herod (v. 15), a dying criminal (v. 41), a Roman officer (v. 47). Six declarations of innocence, and the execution proceeds. A pagan governor said it of Jesus; on the last day the holy God will say it of everyone who is in him.

If Jesus was innocent, why did God let him die? Because only an innocent man could die for the guilty. The innocence is not a tragic detail; it is the point. A guilty man dying would only be paying for himself. Christ, who had no sin of his own, bore the penalty of ours in our place, “the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18). God did not merely permit it; he willed it, out of love (Isaiah 53:10; John 3:16). Scripture calls the result justification: the guilty declared righteous, not because they have become innocent but because Christ’s righteousness is counted as theirs (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Uncertain wording. “You have said so” is literally “you say”, the same idiom Jesus used before the council (22:70). It is not a denial, since Pilate does not take it as one, but whether it is a plain yes or a qualified one (“those are your words”) is debated. Since Pilate at once finds no guilt, the qualified yes is likelier: he is a king, but not the kind Pilate fears.
verseByVerse.note: Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were urgent, saying, 'He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to this place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unable to prove a crime, the accusers press the one thing they can say: his teaching has stirred people up from Galilee to Jerusalem. They mean it as a hint of rebellion; without meaning to, they summarise his whole ministry.

From Galilee even to this place. They are insistent, refusing the verdict; at v. 23 the pressing turns into shouting. Judea here means the whole Jewish land (4:44), and from Galilee to Jerusalem is the whole course of his ministry. But Galilee produced rebels, and the revolt of Judas the Galilean was still remembered (Acts 5:37). To tell a Roman governor that a Galilean has been stirring people up all the way to the capital is to say the word rebellion without having to prove it. And the mention of Galilee gives Pilate an idea.

Teaching. The one word in the charge that is not a lie. They cannot point to anything he did, only to the stir his teaching caused. It is the oldest complaint made against Christ and his people: no crime needs naming; it is enough that the message divides people and things were calmer before (Acts 17:6).

How do I know whether the offence is the gospel’s or mine? Sometimes the charge of stirring up trouble is fair. Christians can be needlessly abrasive, and much of the trouble some believers attract has nothing to do with Christ and everything to do with the manner of the man carrying his name. So ask: Am I offensive in tone, timing or pride? Have I spoken the truth with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15)? Am I more eager to win than to love? If the only thing that offended was the truth about Christ, spoken kindly, the offence is the gospel’s, and the complaint is a compliment.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. And when he learned that he belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem at that time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate hears “Galilee” and sends Jesus to Herod, not to do justice but to avoid a decision.

A Galilean. Only Luke records the trial before Herod. He may have learned of it from Joanna, wife of Herod’s steward (8:3), or from Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod (Acts 13:1). The accusers meant Galilee as an aggravating detail; Pilate hears an escape route.

He belonged to Herod’s jurisdiction. Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas, a client ruler under Rome, in Jerusalem for the Passover. The transfer was not a legal necessity: the offence was alleged in Judea too, and Pilate had every authority to try it. He neither releases Jesus, as his verdict required, nor condemns him; he transfers the file. The characteristic sin of this chapter is not brutality but that of a man who knows exactly what is right, does not want to pay for it, and finds a procedure that puts off the decision.

The one who took what was not his. Pilate holds a responsibility that is truly his, and spends the morning trying to put it down. Jesus carries a burden that was never his, the guilt of his people, and will not put it down for a moment. Pilate looks for a door; Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51) and will not take one. Pilate wants the decision to belong to someone else; Jesus had already said in the garden, “not my will, but yours, be done” (22:42). He who will judge the living and the dead let himself be shuffled between judges, so that on the last day those who trust him will not be passed between courts but welcomed home.

Responsibility does not transfer. The man who tried hardest not to be involved is the one the church has named in its creed for centuries: “suffered under Pontius Pilate”. “Whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin” (James 4:17).

Can I avoid making a decision about Jesus? No. You can postpone it, refer it or wait for more information, but not deciding is a decision. Pilate tried every route around the question and was left holding it. A parent’s, a spouse’s or a church’s faith cannot answer for you. If you have been putting it off, ask the question honestly today: read one of the Gospels through, and ask God to show you the truth.
verseByVerse.note: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and was in Jerusalem for Passover. Only Luke records this hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: When Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod wants a show, not the truth, and Jesus gives him nothing, not even a word. The king who silenced John the Baptist now meets the silence of God.

He was very glad. Herod Antipas is delighted at the prospect of entertainment. This is the man who liked listening to John the Baptist (Mark 6:20) and then had him beheaded to save face at a birthday feast. He had wanted to see Jesus ever since 9:9, and got his wish on the last morning of Jesus’ life.

Some sign. There is the whole man in one clause. He does not want repentance; he killed the man who offered it. He wants a display: curiosity, not faith. Jesus has been reduced, in the mind of a king, to an entertainment that has finally been booked.

He made no answer. Herod is perhaps the only questioner in the Gospels to whom Jesus says nothing at all. The silence is not sulking or fear; it is the answer. Herod had silenced the voice of God in John; now God is silent to him, and the mercy of God does not perform on request. “Like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7).

His silence is not his last word. The Word through whom the worlds were made stood before a king and said nothing. He would not perform for the man who had silenced John, yet he walked out of that hall to die for scoffers and killers, and a man brought up with this very Herod would one day be among the prophets and teachers of the church at Antioch (Acts 13:1). His silence to the proud is never his last word to the humble.

Is it wrong to want to see a miracle? Not in itself; God did signs to help people believe (John 20:30–31), and we may ask him to act in power. What is wrong is Herod’s spirit: wanting a show while refusing the message, demanding proof on our terms while ignoring the evidence given. Jesus called it an evil generation that seeks a sign (11:29). If you have his Word, the testimony of the apostles and the empty tomb, you have the greatest sign of all; the right response is not to ask for another but to repent and believe.

Does God ever stop speaking to a man? He does, and Scripture says so (Proverbs 1:24–28; Romans 1:24). But the fear a sensitive believer carries, that this has happened to him, is answered by Herod himself, who was not anxious about it but very glad. A man troubled that God may have gone quiet has, in that trouble, the evidence that he has not; the worry itself is the Spirit still at work. Come to Christ now; he has never turned away anyone who comes (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him. And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Then, arraying him in splendid clothing, he sent him back to Pilate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod, disappointed, treats Jesus as a joke, and the royal robe he throws on him says, without meaning to, that he is a king. Contempt, not a verdict, is Herod’s answer to Christ.

Vehemently accusing him. The chief priests have followed him across the city. There is nothing to answer, so volume has to do what evidence cannot.

Treated him with contempt. Herod does not condemn Jesus; he finds him ridiculous, which is worse than a verdict. The Greek is exouthenēsas, to count as nothing: not hatred, which at least treats a person as someone who matters, but the judgment of a bored man who has decided the whole thing is beneath him. “He was despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3).

Arraying him in splendid clothing. A bright, shining royal robe thrown over a prisoner as a joke, because he had been accused of claiming a throne. This is the first of the mockeries (vv. 35–39), and in every one they mock him by treating him as what he really is: a king. Herod found no grounds to condemn him either (v. 15), and Jesus was led back across Jerusalem, it seems still in the robe.

In everyday life. When you treat something holy as small, a sermon as a performance to be rated, prayer as a box to tick, the Lord’s Supper as a routine, that is Herod’s contempt in miniature. Confess it, and come back to the one who was counted as nothing first, for you.

How should I feel when Jesus is mocked today? Grieved, but not surprised and not afraid. Christ has been mocked from the first, always by people who think they are cleverer than he is. Do not answer with mockery, and do not imagine that his honour depends on you. Pray for the mockers; some, like many in Jerusalem, may yet beat their breasts and believe. And every taunt aimed at him says, without meaning to, who he truly is.

parallels.desc: a similar mockery by Pilate’s soldiers

verseByVerse.quote: And Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before this they had been at enmity with each other.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two rulers who could not stand each other become friends over their contempt for Jesus, as Psalm 2 said the rulers would gather against the Lord’s Anointed. Their plotting cannot stop his reign; it becomes the road to it.

Friends that very day. We are not told the cause of the quarrel; perhaps Pilate’s massacre of Galileans (13:1). Luke cares how it was healed: Pilate sent the prisoner over as a courtesy, Herod sent him back with a joke attached, and united by contempt for Jesus the two men found they could work together. Two people who agree on nothing will warm to each other instantly over a third party they both find absurd; office politics runs on it. A friendship that needs a common enemy is a poor peace.

The fulfilment. A few weeks later the believers in Jerusalem would quote Psalm 2 in prayer, naming both men: “the kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed” (Psalm 2:1–2; Acts 4:25–28). Here is the gathering, reconciled over the body of the Son of God. But the psalm goes on: “As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill” (Psalm 2:6). The gathering of rulers was the very road by which the Anointed went to his throne, and within three days the one they had sent back and forth would be raised, declared the Son of God in power (Romans 1:4).

The true peace made that day. Two rulers found a friendship in despising him, but the true peace made that day was not theirs. By the blood of that same cross God reconciled to himself all things, making peace (Colossians 1:20). Herod and Pilate were joined against the Son; sinners are joined to the Son, and in him to one another, Jew and Gentile, ruler and thief.

Does this mean rulers and governments are always against God? No. Governing authorities are appointed by God for our good, and we are to pray for them and honour them (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Timothy 2:1–2). Psalm 2 describes what rulers do when they set themselves against Christ, and it ends by calling them to kiss the Son and be wise. Even when the powerful unite against him, they plot in vain: the one enthroned in the heavens laughs (Psalm 2:4), and their plans end up serving his.

parallels.desc: the kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD’s Anointed

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate then called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people, and said to them, 'You brought me this man as one who was misleading the people. And after examining him before you, behold, I did not find this man guilty of any of your charges against him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate formally declares Jesus innocent a second time, and shows by how he does it that he cares more for his record than for the man.

After examining him before you. Pilate convenes a formal assembly, draws the people into the decision, and puts his finding on the record with unusual care. “Before you”: no one can afterwards claim the governor rushed it. This is a man building a defensible file, because he already suspects he will need one.

I did not find this man guilty. The second declaration of innocence (v. 4), and the tragedy of Pilate in one motion: scrupulous about the record, careless about the man. Nothing prevented him from letting an innocent man walk out except the calculation of what it would cost him. Underneath it was a god Pilate served more faithfully than justice: his own position. Whatever we cannot bear to lose is what we will, sooner or later, sacrifice someone else to keep. The Son stood before a judge who was protecting himself, and made no effort to protect himself.

What is the fear of man, and how do I fight it? It is letting other people’s approval or anger decide what you do, even when you know what is right. It “lays a snare”, says Proverbs, “but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (Proverbs 29:25). Pilate feared the crowd and Caesar (John 19:12). Our fears are usually smaller: the colleague’s raised eyebrow, the family’s disapproval, the online pile-on. The cure is not bravado but a bigger fear: the fear of God, who sees and judges and also loves. Ask in the moment, “Whose verdict on me matters most?” Then act as if God alone were watching.

parallels.desc: I find no guilt in him

verseByVerse.quote: Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, nothing deserving death has been done by him. I will therefore punish and release him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate admits that Jesus has done nothing deserving death, then offers to flog him anyway, trading an innocent man’s back for peace with the crowd.

Neither did Herod. Two rulers, two verdicts of innocence, like the two witnesses the law required (Deuteronomy 19:15). “Nothing deserving death has been done by him” is the plainest verdict spoken by anyone that day, and the nearest the trial comes to justice.

I will therefore punish and release him. “Therefore”: because Jesus is innocent, Pilate will have him flogged. The verb is paideusas, to discipline, a word used of correcting a child, chillingly mild for what was probably a beating lighter than the full scourging, though Roman flogging was no formality. He is bargaining, and what he has put on the table is somebody else’s back.

How decent men do monstrous things. Almost never by one decision to do evil, but by a series of small compromises, each presented as the reasonable middle course. And this one fails for a reason worth naming. If the man can be flogged though innocent, the argument against crucifying him though innocent is only a matter of degree, and the crowd pressed for the rest.

The chastisement that brought us peace. Pilate’s word shares its root with the Greek Old Testament’s word in Isaiah 53:5: “upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace”. Pilate meant a beating to buy off a crowd, an innocent man punished to keep a guilty city quiet. God meant something infinitely greater by the same innocent suffering: the Servant bearing the punishment due to others, so that those who deserved it might have peace with God. Pilate’s compromise was wicked; the Servant’s substitution was righteous, and it was the only exchange that day that worked.

What should I do when I am pressured to compromise at work or in my family? See the compromise for what it is: not a middle way between two goods but a smaller wrong offered to avoid a cost. Decide what is right before the pressure peaks, and say it calmly and early, as Pilate should have done. Find out what you can actually be made to do; often the threat is larger than the reality. Seek counsel from a wise Christian, and be willing to lose a promotion, a friendship or a peaceful Christmas rather than your integrity. The Lord who stood before Pilate knows what that pressure costs.

In everyday life. Look for one place where you are offering half of something to avoid giving all of it: half the truth to a customer, half an apology to your wife, half obedience to God. None of us has ever given the whole perfectly; the man Pilate flogged did, and his whole obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). So give the whole, not to buy God’s favour but because in Christ you already have it.
verseByVerse.note: To “punish” here means a flogging.

verseByVerse.quote: But they all cried out together, 'Away with this man, and release to us Barabbas'— a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city and for murder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd chooses Barabbas, a man guilty of the very crime Jesus was falsely charged with, and the innocent one goes to the cross prepared for the guilty. Barabbas, of all men, could say literally: “Jesus died for me.”

Away with this man. Literally, “take this one”, the cry later raised against Paul in this city (Acts 21:36). “Release to us Barabbas” appeals to the Passover amnesty (Mark 15:6). Insurrection, his crime, is exactly what Jesus had been falsely accused of in v. 2.

Am I really like Barabbas? Yes, and that is the best news you will ever hear. You may never have led a revolt or killed anyone, but every one of us has rebelled against God, our rightful King (Isaiah 53:6; Romans 3:23), and hatred in the heart is murder in his eyes (Matthew 5:21–22; 1 John 3:15). We stood under a just sentence; Christ was condemned in our place, and we were let go. But Barabbas was released without being changed, while all who trust Christ are not only set free but made new and declared righteous. Seeing yourself in Barabbas is not humiliation for its own sake; it is the door to gratitude.

Textual note. In a modern Bible the text jumps from verse 16 to verse 18, with verse 17 printed only as a note: “Now he was obliged to release one man to them at the festival.” Nothing has been removed from Scripture. Verse numbers are not inspired; they were added in the sixteenth century. Since then far older copies have been found, centuries closer to the apostles, and in the oldest of them this sentence is not there. It appears in later copies and looks very much like a helpful explanation of the Passover custom, written in the margin by a scribe and then copied into the text. So the translators keep the number, print the words in the note, and tell the reader what the evidence is. This shows not damage to the text but the care with which it has been kept, and nothing in the account depends on it; the custom is attested independently by the other Gospels.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 17: “Now he was obliged to release one man to them at the festival.” Barabbas means “son of the father.”

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate addressed them once more, desiring to release Jesus, but they kept shouting, 'Crucify, crucify him!' A third time he said to them, 'Why? What evil has he done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death. I will therefore punish and release him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate asks the one question that matters, and no one answers it, because there is no answer; the crowd simply shouts louder.

Crucify, crucify him! No charge, no reasoning, two words repeated. A crowd in this state cannot be answered, because it is no longer making a case. Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, kept for slaves and rebels.

A third time. As Peter had denied him three times, so Pilate declares him innocent three times (vv. 4, 14, 22). “Why? What evil has he done?” is the right question, the only question, and nobody answers it, in Luke or in Matthew and Mark. So what has defeated the governor of Judea? Not evidence, which does not exist. Not law, which is entirely on the other side. Not force, since the soldiers are his to command. Noise. He is beaten by volume, he knows it, and he gives way anyway.

The question nobody has answered. The question still stands, and neither earth nor hell has ever answered it. “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22). Hearing his own people roar for his death, he called down no fire. He heard them shout “crucify”, and he went, because the evil that was not his had been laid on him, and he had come to carry it away.

How do I stand against a crowd? Few will face a mob, but almost everyone faces its smaller relatives: a room where one view is pressed loudly and confidently, with a force that has nothing to do with whether it is true. Decide what you believe before you enter the room. Speak early and simply, before the noise builds. Find one other person who agrees, and stand with them. “You shall not fall in with the many to do evil” (Exodus 23:2). Pilate saw what was right three times; the question is whether you can still say it when it is expensive, and that courage is the Holy Spirit’s gift to those who ask, not a matter of nerve (Acts 4:29–31).

verseByVerse.quote: But they were urgent, demanding with loud cries that he should be crucified. And their voices prevailed. So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voices win, and Pilate grants their demand: a judicial murder decided by noise, yet carried out inside the settled purpose of God. The men are fully guilty, and the Father is giving up his Son for us.

Their voices prevailed. Not the evidence, not the law, not the verdict given three times: the voices. “Prevailed” means had the mastery, and the mastery belongs to a crowd. Then Pilate pronounced sentence (epekrinen), in phrasing almost administrative, and the flatness is the point: a judicial murder recorded like a request approved. He chose his position over justice (John 19:12).

Two things held together. These men are entirely guilty (Acts 2:23), and behind the crowd, behind Judas’s price and Pilate’s cowardice, stands the settled purpose of God, who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32; Acts 4:27–28). God’s purpose forced no one: every man in that courtyard did exactly what he wanted to do (see 22:22). And Paul’s verb in Romans 8:32, “gave him up”, is the verb Luke uses of Pilate in the next verse: paradidōmi, to hand over. Pilate handed him over to a mob; the Father handed him over for us. The same word, and the difference is everything: one was a surrender to pressure, the other love with nothing forced about it at all.

In everyday life. If someone has handed you over, abandoned you to a situation they had the power to stop and would not pay the cost of stopping, take comfort here. That is exactly what happened to him, and he knows it from the inside. Bring it to him today, and tell him plainly what was done.

Was Pilate less guilty than the leaders who handed Jesus over? Less, but still guilty. Jesus told Pilate that “he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin” (John 19:11): the men who knew the Scriptures and saw the signs sinned against greater light. But Pilate had the power and knowledge to stop it and did not. Scripture never lets anyone off because someone else was worse. Each will give an account for what he knew and did (12:47–48), and the creed still names Pilate.

verseByVerse.quote: He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, for whom they asked, but he delivered Jesus over to their will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The murderer walks free and the innocent man is handed over: substitution acted out in the street before it is accomplished on the hill.

He released the man. Luke repeats who Barabbas was in the same sentence as the release, so that no reader misses who walked out alive. They chose a murderer, as Peter would tell them in the temple: “you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and you killed the Author of life” (Acts 3:14–15).

He delivered Jesus over to their will. “Delivered over” is the word of the passion predictions (9:44; 18:32). Not to justice, but to their will, the most complete abandonment a court can perform. And behind it, the Father’s will (Romans 8:32).

He is not pardoned. A condemned prisoner hears a crowd outside, a door is unlocked, and he walks out into the daylight past a beam being carried the other way. Nobody has said he is innocent, and nothing about him has changed; he goes free because another man is going to die in his place. Barabbas walked free because Jesus took his place; sinners walk free because Jesus took their sin, and with it their sentence.

Can one person really pay for another’s wrong? To many thoughtful people substitution sounds immoral. Immanuel Kant argued that guilt is not like a money debt a friend can settle for you; it is the most personal liability there is, and only the guilty can bear it. That would be decisive if the cross were a stranger punished in place of strangers, but the New Testament never describes it so. Christ dies as one who has joined himself to his people, and he is no third party to the offence: he is the very God against whom it was committed, come in the flesh to bear it himself. Martin Luther, in The Freedom of a Christian, compared faith to a marriage: when the bridegroom takes the bride, her debts become his and his riches become hers, because the two are now one. Barabbas walked free without ever knowing the man who went to the cross in his place. The gospel offers more: not only a substitute, but a Saviour you are joined to by faith, so that what he did counts as yours because you are his.

Does this passage blame the Jewish people as a whole? No. Luke names the actors: a handful of leaders, a crowd stirred up by them, Pilate and his soldiers. Jesus himself, his apostles and the first thousands of believers were Jews. The charge of collective or inherited guilt, used for centuries to justify hatred of Jews, has no ground here, and Christians must repent of it wherever it appears.

Did Barabbas ever believe? We are not told; any tradition about his later life is guesswork. Perhaps that is deliberate: his story stops at the prison door so that every reader can step into it. The question is not what Barabbas did with his freedom but what you will do with yours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–43 — The Way of the Cross and the Crucifixion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The King goes to the cross bearing what is not his, and on it he saves others while refusing to save himself. Simon of Cyrene carries the cross behind him, in the very posture of discipleship (v. 26). Jesus tells the mourning women to weep for themselves, because of the judgment coming on Jerusalem (vv. 27–31). Crucified between criminals, numbered with the transgressors (vv. 32–33), he prays for his killers while they gamble for his clothes (v. 34). Rulers, soldiers and a criminal all mock with the same words, “save yourself”, and Pilate’s notice names the only charge ever proved: he is the King of the Jews (vv. 35–39). The other criminal turns, confesses and asks to be remembered, and is promised paradise today (vv. 40–43).
verseByVerse.theology:
The prayer Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do pleads a real but partial ignorance, and Luke shows it answered in Acts (this is treated fully at v. 34).

The mockery of v. 35 states the atonement exactly, without understanding it (see the note on v. 35).

The dying criminal could not be baptised, make restitution or show any fruit, and the answer exceeded his request (see the notes on vv. 41–42 and v. 43).
verseByVerse.examples:
Most crosses in a Christian life are not chosen, and Simon did not volunteer either (see the note on v. 26).

Verses 27–28 correct a devotion that consists mostly of feeling sorry for Jesus (see the note on vv. 27–28).

Verses 39–40 answer the assumption that suffering makes people better (see the note on vv. 39–40).

And v. 43 is for anyone who thinks it is too late (see the note on v. 43).

verseByVerse.quote: And as they led him away, they seized one Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it behind Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A stranger is forced to carry the cross behind Jesus, because the Son of God had become weak enough to need the help.

As they led him away. A condemned man carried the crossbeam himself, and Jesus set out doing so (John 19:17). The likeliest reason a stranger had to take it over is that, after a night of beatings and the flogging (John 19:1), Jesus could carry it no further.

Simon of Cyrene. A man arriving with plans for the day, from Cyrene in North Africa, which had a large Jewish community. A Roman soldier could compel any provincial to carry a load, and Simon was not asked.

Behind Jesus. Only Luke says it. That is the posture Jesus had described for discipleship: “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me” (9:23; 14:27). Now a man does it literally, and against his will.

Simon’s family. Mark names Simon’s sons, Alexander and Rufus (Mark 15:21), as if his readers knew them, and Paul greets a Rufus in Rome, chosen in the Lord (Romans 16:13). It may be the same family. If so, the man pressed into service that morning did not stay a bystander.

Weak enough to need help. The one who upholds the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3) apparently could not carry a beam of wood up a hill. That is the measure of how truly he became man. He went to the cross in real flesh, as weak as ours, so that he would be a high priest able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), and no sufferer who has run out of strength would ever think him far away. And the one who walked ahead of Simon was carrying a weight no one else could lift: the sin of the world.

Most crosses are not chosen. People speak of taking up a cross as though it were a decision, and sometimes it is. But the illness was not chosen, nor the child’s diagnosis. The redundancy, the parent who needs care for a decade, the marriage that became a long endurance: none of it was volunteered for. It was laid on. Simon may have resented every step. And apart from Jesus himself, he is the only man who ever carried the cross of Christ.

What does it mean for me to carry my cross? It means following Jesus wherever he leads, accepting the cost of belonging to him, and saying no to self when self and Christ conflict (9:23–24): giving up a sinful relationship, telling the truth at a price. And it means carrying the suffering you did not choose not with resentment but behind Jesus, trusting him with it. Your cross is never his cross. He alone carried our sins; we carry only what comes from following him, and he walks ahead.
verseByVerse.note: Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community.

verseByVerse.quote: And there followed him a great multitude of the people and of women who were mourning and lamenting for him. But turning to them Jesus said, 'Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On his way to die, Jesus turns from his own suffering to grieve for others: the women should weep not for him but for themselves and their children.

Mourning and lamenting for him. Not all the multitude were hostile. Only Luke records this formal, audible grief, as at a funeral. There is no hint that Jesus thinks it insincere, and he does not rebuke it.

Do not weep for me. Even on the way to the cross he thinks of others. He wept at the grave of a friend (John 11:35) and over a city that rejected him (19:41), and now, bleeding, he grieves for its daughters. His suffering is worth weeping over, but pity is not what he needs from anyone. Some devotion consists mostly of feeling sorry for Jesus, and produces sympathy and no repentance.

Weep for yourselves and for your children. For the judgment coming on Jerusalem (19:41–44; 21:20–24): their children would see the siege and destruction of AD 70. These are the last of Jesus’ words over the city in Luke (13:34–35; 19:41–44), and between the trial and the cross Luke has placed not a word of self-pity but a warning and a grief. Grief that fastens on someone else’s situation can be a way of not looking at your own; it is easier to weep over a tragedy on the news than to face the state of one’s own household.

Is it wrong to be moved by the sufferings of Christ? No; it would be strange to read of the cross and feel nothing, and the church has always sung of his wounds with tears. The question is where the feeling leads. If it ends in a pleasant sadness, it has missed the point. If it leads you to see the seriousness of sin, repent of your own, and trust and love him, it is what the cross is meant to produce. Do not weep for him as a victim. Weep over the sin that put him there, and then rejoice that he chose to go.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, the days are coming when they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed!’ Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus foretells a judgment on Jerusalem so terrible that childlessness will seem a mercy and people will beg the hills to bury them. He speaks it not with satisfaction but with grief.

Blessed are the barren. In that world childlessness was the standard image of grief and shame (1:25). Jesus says a day is coming when women will be congratulated on it. That is a measurement of horror: in the siege of the year 70 the worst thing that could happen to a woman would look like an escape, because she would not have to watch her children die.

Fall on us. A quotation from Hosea 10:8, spoken over the northern kingdom on the eve of its destruction: the cry of people who would rather be crushed than face what is coming. John heard it again at the end of all things, from those hiding from the wrath of the Lamb (Revelation 6:16). Being buried under a mountain is not what they are fleeing; it is the alternative they prefer.

Walking towards a hill to bear it. A day is coming when men will find the presence of God unbearable, and the terror of it is not that he is cruel but that he is holy and they are not. And the one who spoke of that day was walking towards a hill to bear it. The wrath of the Lamb is real; so is the blood of the Lamb, and whoever hides in him will never need to hide from him.

If you have longed for children. If you have longed for children and not had them, or have lost a child, hear this gently: Jesus is not calling childlessness a blessing, and he is not making light of your grief. He is measuring a horror, and the Lord who said it wept over the very mothers he was speaking of.

Is Jesus speaking about AD 70 or about the final judgment? Both, as prophecy often works. The nearer fulfilment came within forty years, when Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem (21:20–24). But Revelation’s use of the same cry shows that the fall of Jerusalem foreshadowed the last day, when all who have refused Christ will face the holy God. The first came exactly as he said, a sober warning that the second will too.

parallels.desc: they shall say to the mountains, “Cover us”

verseByVerse.quote: For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
If this is done to the innocent, far worse awaits the guilty. Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater: if fire takes green wood, what will it do to dry?

When the wood is green. It has the sound of a proverb, and it probably was one. Green wood is living wood, full of sap; it resists a fire and has to be forced to burn. Dry wood is dead, and goes up at a spark. The rabbis argued in this form constantly: if this is what happens in the unlikely case, what will happen in the likely one?

The fire fell on the living wood. If judgment falls like this on the green wood, the one man who never deserved a stroke of it, what will it be when it falls on the dry? If judgment begins at the household of God, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel (1 Peter 4:17–18)? What is happening on that hill is the wrath of God against sin, absorbed by a substitute, and even so it produced three hours of darkness and, as Matthew and Mark record, a cry of forsakenness that has never stopped echoing (Mark 15:34). That wrath is not rage; it is the holiness of God meeting sin, as light meets darkness. Its name is propitiation (Romans 3:25): the wrath falls, but it falls on the sacrifice, and so it is turned away from those for whom he dies. The fire that should have consumed us consumed the living wood, and for all who are in him there is no fire left.

Is God’s judgment not out of all proportion? Look at what God was prepared to do to his own Son rather than overlook sin. Nobody who has understood Calvary can think he takes it lightly. Sin is no small thing, because it is committed against an infinitely holy God, and the punishment of those who refuse his mercy is conscious and eternal (Matthew 25:46). The cross is the fullest evidence of how serious judgment is, and, in the same act, the reason a sinner need never face it.

Uncertain wording. Jesus does not say who “they” are or what the green and dry wood stand for, so the saying is read two ways. If Rome does this to a man who is entirely innocent, what will it do when the city is full of real rebels? (Jerusalem burned within a generation.) Or: if God’s judgment falls like this on the innocent Son, what will it be for the guilty? After the warning of vv. 28–30 both are probably meant: the fire coming on Jerusalem, and behind it the judgment of God that Jesus is about to bear.
verseByVerse.note: A proverb: if this is done to the innocent (green wood), what will happen to the guilty (dry wood, ready to burn)?

parallels.desc: every green tree and every dry tree

verseByVerse.quote: Two others, who were criminals, were led away to be put to death with him. And when they came to the place that is called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on his right and one on his left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is crucified between two criminals, numbered with the transgressors, in the place of the guiltiest.

Two others, who were criminals. Isaiah 53:12, which Jesus had quoted at the table only hours before, “he was numbered with the transgressors” (22:37), is carried out by a squad of Roman soldiers.

The place that is called The Skull. Luke gives the meaning of the Aramaic Golgotha; the Latin is Calvary. Why it had that name is not known: perhaps from the shape of the rock, perhaps because executions were carried out there. It lay outside the city wall (Hebrews 13:12) but near the city (John 19:20), probably beside a road, since the Romans crucified people where passers-by would see them (Mark 15:29).

There they crucified him. One word: his readers knew exactly what crucifixion was. Cicero called it the most cruel and disgusting penalty, and said the very word should be kept far from the ears of Roman citizens. Its purpose was public degradation over hours, and Luke’s restraint is a kind of reverence.

One on his right and one on his left. Exactly the arrangement James and John had once asked for: “Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory” (Mark 10:37). When the places either side of him were finally filled, it was by convicted criminals. He is placed in the middle, the place one would give a ringleader. Yet what hung there was the Lord of glory, put in the worst place on the hill by men who did not know what they were doing, and it was the right place, because he had come to stand exactly where the guiltiest stands.

In the flow. Around the crucifixion Luke sets three sayings found only in his Gospel: a prayer for his killers (v. 34), a promise to a thief (v. 43) and a prayer of trust as he dies (v. 46). Between them come the mockers, three times telling him to save himself (vv. 35, 37, 39). The shape carries the meaning: the one who will not save himself spends his dying hours saving others.

Why did Jesus have to die by crucifixion? Because crucifixion was a death under curse. The law said that a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23), and Paul explains that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). It was also the most shameful death the world knew, and he despised the shame (Hebrews 12:2), taking the lowest place so that none of his people would be beneath his reach. And it was public: lifted up, as he said, to draw all people to himself (John 12:32).
verseByVerse.note: Luke uses the Greek name, “The Skull”; the Aramaic is Golgotha.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said, 'Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.' And they cast lots to divide his garments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ first word from the cross is a prayer that his Father would forgive the men who are killing him. While they gamble for his clothes, he pleads their ignorance before God.

Father, forgive them. A prayer for the men holding the hammer. “Father”: nothing they are doing has changed how he addresses God. “Forgive them”: the soldiers, the leaders, the crowd. He practises what he taught: love your enemies, pray for those who abuse you (6:27–28). It is the prayer of a high priest pleading for others, begun before he is dead, for people who have not asked and are not sorry. Stephen would pray the same as he died (Acts 7:60); he had learned it from his Lord.

For they know not what they do. The ignorance is real and partial. They knew they were killing a man; they did not know they were killing the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8), the Author of life (Acts 3:15, 17). Ignorance does not remove guilt; if it did, no forgiveness would be needed. But it is a ground on which to plead, and Peter pleaded it in the same city (Acts 3:17). And the prayer was answered. At Pentecost thousands in that city, very likely including some who had shouted for his death, repented and were forgiven (Acts 2:36–41), and a centurion at the foot of the cross praised God (v. 47).

They cast lots to divide his garments. A condemned man’s clothes were the perk of the execution squad, and it is Psalm 22:18 happening word for word: “they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots”.

The gospel in the mouth of the dying Lamb. The gamblers were the very men he was praying for. Nailed to a piece of wood by men dividing his clothes before he was dead, the Son of God spent his first words asking his Father to let them off. “Father, forgive them”: those three words are the gospel in the mouth of the dying Lamb, and every forgiven believer since has been an answer to them.
