Must I forgive someone who has not said sorry? You must let go of revenge and bitterness, and wish them good, even before they repent, as Jesus did here. “Never avenge yourselves” (Romans 12:19). But full reconciliation, the restoring of trust and relationship, needs repentance on their side (17:3–4), and forgiveness does not mean pretending nothing happened or putting yourself back in harm’s way. Where there has been abuse or crime, forgiveness and reporting it go together; you can forgive from the heart and still let the authorities do their God-given work. Start where he started: bring them to the Father in prayer, and ask him to forgive them.

Were they forgiven even if they did not repent? No. God answered the prayer by bringing many of them to repentance and faith, and forgiveness is always received through turning to Christ (Acts 2:38; 3:19); there was no blanket pardon for those who went on rejecting him. But the prayer shows that no one who had a part in his death, and no one today who has despised him, is beyond the reach of his mercy if they come.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the prayer. It is missing from some important early copies but present in many others, very early and widely attested, and it fits Luke perfectly; no evangelist is more preoccupied with forgiveness. Some have suggested that a later scribe, looking back on the destruction of Jerusalem, thought the prayer had gone unanswered, or that the Jews should not be forgiven, and left it out. If so, he stopped reading too soon, because Luke wrote a second volume telling what became of it. Most scholars accept it as an authentic saying of Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the prayer “Father, forgive them.”

verseByVerse.quote: And the people stood by, watching, but the rulers scoffed at him, saying, 'He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rulers sneer that a saviour who cannot save himself is no saviour, while the people stand silently watching. Their taunt is far truer than they know.

The people stood by, watching. No mockery is attributed to them. They are silent, and they will go home beating their breasts (v. 48).

The rulers scoffed at him. They turned up their noses, sneered (exemyktērizon). “All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads” (Psalm 22:7).

He saved others; let him save himself. “He saved others”: they concede his miracles in the middle of a taunt. The soldiers and one of the criminals will repeat the sneer. It is the settled assumption of the whole hill: real power rescues itself.

The Christ of God, his Chosen One. They use Peter’s confession (9:20) and the Father’s word at the transfiguration, “my Chosen One” (9:35), in mockery; “chosen” is Isaiah’s word for the Servant (Isaiah 42:1). They are quoting the Father’s own delight in his Son back at him as an insult, and their words are true.

Exactly wrong, and exactly right. The logic is exactly wrong. He could not both save himself and save others. Not because the power was lacking, for he had told Peter that legions were available for the asking (Matthew 26:53), but because the two things could not both be done: to come down would leave the work undone and every person he came for still under sentence. So the mockery states the gospel with perfect accuracy and no understanding whatever. Atonement means sinners and God made one again, at one, by sin being dealt with, and this is how it was done: Jesus stayed under the penalty our sins deserved, so that it would never fall on us (Isaiah 53:5). Behold the Chosen One, in whom the Father delights, choosing not to come down.

Could Jesus really have come down from the cross? Yes. Nothing held the eternal Son there but his own will and his love for the Father and for us: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18). It was not the nails that kept him on the cross. It was the will to save.

verseByVerse.quote: The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine and saying, 'If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers join the mockery, toasting the “King” with cheap wine and repeating the devil’s old temptation: prove who you are by saving yourself. He meets it on the cross as he met it in the wilderness.

The soldiers also mocked him. Jews and Gentiles together. The rulers mocked him with religious arguments; the soldiers are an execution detail passing the time.

Offering him sour wine. The cheap wine soldiers drank, offered as a toast to the king. And this too was written: “for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink” (Psalm 69:21). He will drink the fruit of the vine again with his people in the kingdom (22:18), and they will not be mocking then.

If you are the King of the Jews. The phrase was said to him before, in the wilderness: “If you are the Son of God” (4:3, 9), and the devil departed until an opportune time (4:13). This is that time. Three times on the cross he is told to save himself (vv. 35, 37, 39), as he was tempted three times in the wilderness: prove it by using your power on your own behalf. The answer is the same: he will not use his power for himself. In the wilderness he answered with Scripture; on the cross he answers with silence.

If God loved me, would this be happening? A Christian hears it in a hospital corridor, in a marriage gone cold, in the fourth month of looking for work: if you really were what you claim to be, you would not be in this position; if God loved you, this would not be happening. Answer it from the cross. The beloved Son, in whom the Father delighted, was in the worst position any man has ever been in, not because God did not love him but because God was doing the greatest good through it. Suffering is never proof that you are not loved. For the Christian it is always held inside the love that gave the Son (Romans 8:32, 35–39).
verseByVerse.note: Sour wine was the cheap wine soldiers drank.

verseByVerse.quote: There was also an inscription over him, 'This is the King of the Jews.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The only charge Rome ever posted against Jesus is the truth: he is the King of the Jews. Pilate meant it as a sneer; God made it a proclamation to the world.

An inscription over him. A legal document: the board carrying the charge, posted as Roman custom required so that everyone who passed knew what he was dying for.

This is the King of the Jews. Pilate wrote it as a sneer at the men who had forced his hand, and refused to change it: “What I have written I have written” (John 19:21–22). It was written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek (John 19:20), so that every kind of person in the festival city could read it. Without meaning to, Pilate proclaimed to the world who Jesus is: he reigns from the cross.

In what sense is Jesus a king now? In the fullest sense. He is not only King of the Jews but King of kings and Lord of lords (Revelation 19:16), raised and seated at God’s right hand, with all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). He rules now over all things for the sake of his church, gathers his people from every nation through the gospel, and will return visibly to judge and make all things new. His kingdom does not advance by armies or elections, but no throne on earth is outside his rule. To be a Christian is to be his willing subject.

Why do the Gospels give different wordings? Matthew has “This is Jesus, the King of the Jews”; Mark, “The King of the Jews”; John, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews”. This is what happens when four witnesses report a sign written in three languages: each gives the substance, and the substance is identical in every one. It is the ordinary variation of honest testimony; accounts that agreed word for word would be more suspicious, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the criminals who were hanged railed at him, saying, 'Are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us!' But the other rebuked him, saying, 'Do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two dying criminals hang equally near Jesus and go opposite ways: one mocks him, and the other begins to fear God.

One of the criminals railed at him. “Railed” is eblasphēmei: he blasphemed. Matthew and Mark report both men reviling him at first (Matthew 27:44), so the difference emerged during those hours, perhaps as the second heard him pray for his enemies.

Save yourself and us! The first man repeats the rulers’ sneer and adds a request entirely about his circumstances: get me down. He wants rescue from the cross, not from sin. That is a real and common form of religion, sincere in hospital wards and financial crises: it wants God to change the situation, and has no interest in God himself.

Do you not fear God? The second man’s first recorded words are not about Jesus or himself, but about God. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10), and here is a dying criminal, with no religious education anyone knows of, arriving at the one thought that no amount of pain had produced in the man on the other side.

Under the same sentence of condemnation. He is not lecturing from above; he includes himself. We are all dying; how can you mock? The rebuke rests on this: we are both getting what we deserve, which is a thing almost nobody says about himself.

Set for the fall and rising of many. Old Simeon took the baby in his arms and said that this child was appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel (2:34). Here is that word in its starkest form: one Saviour, a cross on either side, and nothing separating the two criminals except what each made of Jesus. Even while he is dying, every human destiny turns on him.

Suffering does not make people better. People assume that a man facing death will naturally turn to God. These two, in identical pain, hearing identical words, were nailed up on the same morning for the same kind of crime. Suffering did not soften one of them. Only grace did that.

What does it mean to fear God? Not cringing terror before a tyrant, but reverence and awe before the holy God who is our Judge, joined, for those who know his mercy, with love and trust. It means taking him seriously: he sees, sin matters to him, and we will stand before him. Such fear draws people to him, because with him there is forgiveness, that he may be feared (Psalm 130:4). The thief feared God, and that fear sent him to Christ, which is always where true fear of God leads.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew and Mark report both men reviling him at first.

verseByVerse.quote: And we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong.' And he said, 'Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The dying criminal confesses that he deserves his sentence, declares Jesus innocent, and asks the crucified man to remember him when he comes as King. It is repentance and faith with everything stripped away.

And we indeed justly. In two sentences this man states the gospel as exactly as many Christians could, confessing his guilt without excuse and saying the sentence is right. Repentance is not feeling sorry at being caught; it is agreeing with God about your sin and turning from it to him. This man could not undo a single deed, but he could stop defending himself, and he did. That is true repentance, and it speaks as David did: you are justified in your words and blameless in your judgment (Psalm 51:4).

This man has done nothing wrong. One more witness to Jesus’ innocence, from a man with nothing to gain by saying it: the only declaration in the chapter made by someone who was himself dying.

Jesus, remember me. Astonishing faith. He is looking not at a miracle-worker surrounded by crowds, but at a man nailed to a beam a few feet away, bleeding, mocked by everyone present, visibly dying, with a Roman notice over his head calling him a king as a joke. He calls him by his name, Jesus, which means the Lord saves, and asks to be included in a kingdom for which there was not one visible sign on that hill. At that hour even the disciples seem to have given up hope (24:21).

Faith with everything stripped off it. He has no Bible, no baptism, no church, no time, and no capacity to do a single good work; he cannot even come down and be useful. He brings nothing but an honest verdict on himself and a conviction about who the man beside him is. And the request is modest: remember me, do not let me be forgotten when you come into what is yours, as Joseph once asked the cupbearer to remember him (Genesis 40:14).

In everyday life. Measure your own prayers against this one. Many Christians pray apologetically, working out whether they have the standing to ask. This man had none, and asked anyway. Pray the thief’s prayer today, in his words, when you are most aware of your failure: “Jesus, remember me.”

Is a deathbed conversion real? It can be, and this man is the proof; but there is one such thief, so that none need despair, and only one, so that none should presume.

Do I need to be baptised to be saved? Baptism is commanded by Christ for every believer (Matthew 28:19), and a Christian who refuses it is disobeying his Lord. But baptism is not what saves; Christ saves, through faith. As far as we know, the thief was never baptised, and on the cross he could not be, yet he was in paradise that day. Baptism signs and confesses a salvation already received, which is why this commentary, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession (29.2), holds that it is for those who have believed, while honouring paedobaptist brothers and sisters (those who baptise the infants of believers, as a sign of God’s promise to families) who see it differently. So if you have come to faith, be baptised, gladly and soon; but never think that the water does what only the blood can do.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, 'Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus promises the dying criminal not only to remember him but to have him at his side in paradise that very day. Every part of the answer gives more than he asked.

Today. Not after an interval of waiting: before the sun goes down on the worst day of his life. “Today” is Luke’s great word of present salvation: “unto you is born this day” (2:11); “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled” (4:21); “Today salvation has come to this house” (19:9). There is no purgatory in that sentence and no room for one: the same day, straight through, from a Roman cross to paradise.

You will be with me. That is the heart of heaven: being with Jesus. Paradise is not described, and it does not need to be (Philippians 1:23). Whatever else heaven contains, its heart is a person, and the man who has him has everything in it.

In paradise. A Persian word for a walled garden, used in the Greek Old Testament of Eden (Genesis 2:8) and in the New Testament of the place of the blessed dead with God (2 Corinthians 12:4; Revelation 2:7): Eden restored. The last promise Jesus makes before he dies is that the garden is open again, and he makes it to a criminal.

The garden opened with a word. The first Adam was driven out of paradise, and cherubim with a flaming sword guarded the way back (Genesis 3:24). The last Adam, dying on a tree, opened it with a word, and walked a thief in. The curse that closed the garden fell on him as he hung on a tree (Galatians 3:13), so that the way in could stand open to the guilty; and for everyone who trusts him, the day of death is simply today, with him.

In everyday life. Read this verse to anyone who thinks it is too late: a man raised near the church but never committed, dying in a hospice, wanting to know whether there is time. The answer is unqualified. There was no baptism, no probation, no changed life to show; there was a confession, a recognition and a request, and Jesus took him home that afternoon.

Is it fair that a criminal should be in paradise on the day he died? Not if heaven is a reward for good lives, but it never was. If it were, none of us would be there (Romans 3:23). The thief is in paradise on exactly the same ground as the apostle Paul: Christ’s death in his place, received by faith. The objection usually comes from the elder brother in us, who has kept the rules and quietly expects credit (15:28–30). Grace offends the religious as much as it surprises the irreligious, and both need it equally. The real wonder is not that the thief got in, but that anyone does.

Where was Jesus between his death and resurrection? His body lay in the tomb, and his soul went to the Father (v. 46), which is why he could promise the thief today.

Are my loved ones who died in Christ aware and happy now? Yes. They are with the Lord, conscious, at rest and blessed (Revelation 14:13). When Scripture calls death sleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14), it speaks of the body resting until it is raised and of death’s gentleness for the believer, not of the soul’s unconsciousness. We are not told what they know of us, and we must not try to contact them (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). But we can grieve with hope: they are with Christ, which is far better.

If they are already in paradise, why do we still need the resurrection? Because God made us body and soul, and he will not leave half of us in the grave. Their state now is blessed but not yet complete; Paul longs not to be unclothed but further clothed (2 Corinthians 5:4). At Christ’s return the dead in Christ will be raised with glorious bodies like his (1 Thessalonians 4:16; Philippians 3:21), and the paradise the thief entered that day will become a whole new creation. The thief’s body probably went into a criminal’s grave; it will come out as Christ’s did.

Where Christians differ: purgatory and soul sleep. Roman Catholic teaching holds that most of the saved must pass through purgatory after death, to be purified before they enter heaven. Others teach soul sleep: that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. Some have tried to move the comma, reading I say to you today, you will be with me, so that today describes when Jesus spoke rather than when the man would arrive. The Greek carries no punctuation, so the question is fair. But truly I say to you is a fixed formula on Jesus’ lips, used scores of times in the Gospels, and not once does it take a trailing today; and it would be pointless to say, since the man could hardly suppose he was being answered on some other day. This commentary’s view: today goes naturally with you will be with me, as Luke uses the word elsewhere. The thief, a criminal with no time for penance, went straight to paradise with Christ. There is no purgatory: Christ’s sacrifice is sufficient, for by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14), and the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). And there is no soul sleep: believers who die are with the Lord at once, consciously, which is why Paul could call it far better (Philippians 1:21–23), and why the souls under the altar speak (Revelation 6:9–10). The Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession put it carefully: the souls of men neither die nor sleep, and the souls of the righteous, being then made perfect in holiness, are received into the highest heavens, where they behold the face of God, waiting for the full redemption of their bodies (Westminster 32.1; 1689 31.1).
verseByVerse.note: “Paradise” is a Persian word for a walled garden, used for the dwelling of God’s people after death.

parallels.desc: the tree of life in the paradise of God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 44–56 — The Death of Jesus and the Burial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus’ death bears God’s judgment and opens the way to God, and it is witnessed, confessed and sealed in a known tomb. Darkness falls at noon, the language of judgment, and the temple curtain is torn (vv. 44–45). Jesus dies with a loud prayer of trust from Psalm 31:5, adding the word “Father” (v. 46). The centurion praises God and declares him innocent, the crowds go home beating their breasts, and his friends and the women watch from a distance (vv. 47–49). Joseph of Arimathea, a councillor who had not consented, lays him in a new rock tomb (vv. 50–53) as the Sabbath begins (v. 54). The women see where and how he was laid, prepare spices, and rest according to the commandment (vv. 55–56).
verseByVerse.theology:
The darkness speaks of judgment, not merely grief (see the note on vv. 44–45).

The torn curtain means the way into God’s presence is open (vv. 44–45). Now we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus (Hebrews 10:19–20).

Luke does not record the cry “my God, my God, why have you forsaken me” (Mark 15:34), but he has not softened the death (see the note on v. 46).

The burial is not an appendix: it proves Jesus was dead and fixes the place where he would be found alive (see the notes on vv. 52–53 and vv. 55–56). Isaiah had written it: and with a rich man in his death (Isaiah 53:9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Mark’s centurion speaks of the Son of God; Luke’s says “innocent” (see the note on vv. 47–48).

Verse 49 is for anyone whose service to Christ goes unrecorded (see the note on v. 49).

Verse 54 leaves a silent Saturday, and much of the Christian life is lived in such gaps (see the note on v. 54).

And vv. 55–56 show faithfulness with no feeling left in it (see the note on vv. 55–56). Anyone holding on like that should remember how their Saturday ended.

verseByVerse.quote: It was now about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour, while the sun's light failed. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Darkness at midday and the tearing of the temple curtain show what Jesus’ death means: God’s judgment falling on sin, and the way into his presence thrown open.

About the sixth hour. The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about three in the afternoon. This is not evening coming on early; it is darkness at the brightest part of the day, for three hours. Luke says only that the sun’s light failed, and leaves the mechanism alone: it was a supernatural darkness.

Darkness over the whole land. The Old Testament supplies the meaning. Amos, prophesying judgment: “I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight” (Amos 8:9). And Egypt had a darkness that could be felt for three days (Exodus 10:21–22), the plague immediately before the Passover lamb. The sign is not merely grief but judgment: God is dealing with sin. Only this time the blow does not fall on a nation. It falls on one man, the Son, in the middle of the day, in the dark.

The curtain of the temple was torn in two. The second sign happens across the city, where nobody at Golgotha could see it. The curtain separated the Most Holy Place, the place of God’s presence, from the rest of the temple. Behind it nobody went but one man, one day a year, with blood, and not without trembling (Leviticus 16; Hebrews 9:7). The whole architecture of Israel’s worship said that the way in was closed; for fifteen centuries the message of that room was “not yet, and not you”. Matthew and Mark note that it tore from top to bottom (Mark 15:38). A tear from the top down is not vandalism; it reads as a verdict passed from above, and a sign that the temple system was ending.

In the flow. Up to this point every voice in the chapter has been human. Now heaven answers without a word. Mark places the tearing after the death; Luke groups the two signs just before it (v. 46), so that the reader hears Jesus’ last words knowing what the death means. At his arrest Jesus had said, “this is your hour, and the power of darkness” (22:53); God has turned that hour into the hour when the way to himself was opened.

The new and living way. In one afternoon, while the sky was dark and a man was dying outside the walls, God tore the curtain from the top and left it hanging open, and it has never been mended. The way into God’s presence is open through the death of Christ: “we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:19–20).

Can I really come to God directly, without a priest? Yes, through Christ, and only through him. “There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5), and he is our great high priest. You do not need a human priest to confess to, a saint to plead for you, or a holy building to stand in. You may pray to the Father, in Jesus’ name, anywhere, at any hour, about anything. Pastors are given to teach and care for you, and fellow believers to pray with you, but none of them stands between you and God. The way in is open, and it is open because of blood.

Uncertain wording. “The whole land” could equally be “the whole earth”; Luke does not say how far the darkness reached. The verb behind “the sun’s light failed” is the one from which we get eclipse, but a natural eclipse is impossible: Passover falls at full moon, and no total eclipse lasts more than a few minutes. So it is best taken simply as “failed”. Many manuscripts, followed by older English versions, read “the sun was darkened”. Either way, at noon the light failed by the hand of God.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m. The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus, calling out with a loud voice, said, 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!' And having said this he breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus dies not in a fading gasp but with a loud cry of perfect trust, giving his spirit into his Father’s hands.

Calling out with a loud voice. That was not how crucified men usually died. Death on a cross came slowly, by exhaustion and failing strength, and the end was commonly a fading, not a shout. He chose the moment of his death (John 10:18).

Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! The words quote Psalm 31:5, “Into your hand I commit my spirit”. Later Jewish tradition used that verse as an evening prayer, said before sleep: Jesus dies with a bedtime prayer. And he adds one word. The psalm says, “into your hand”; he says, “Father”. The relationship is unbroken. “Commit” is paratithemai, to deposit, to place something valuable into safe keeping: not resignation but a deliberate entrusting. Stephen, dying, would say almost the same words, addressed to Jesus (Acts 7:59), because the first Christians took this sentence as the pattern for how to die.

He breathed his last. He died. Truly. Not a swoon, not an appearance of death, but the separation of his soul from his body. The Son of God died.

Where is the cry of dereliction? A reader who knows Matthew and Mark will miss the cry, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34). Has Luke softened the death? No. He does not hide the horror: the sweat like drops of blood in the garden and the angel sent to strengthen him are his alone (though those two verses, 22:43–44, are missing from some early manuscripts). Having shown the anguish there, he chooses for the last moment the other true thing about this death, and both are needed. The cry of dereliction (of being forsaken) tells you what the cross cost; this word tells you how it ended, in perfect trust, the work finished. After the darkness, after whatever passed in those three hours that no writer describes, the last sentence out of his mouth is the one a child says to a father he is sure of.

How can I die well? By learning to say this prayer before you need it. Jesus did not invent new words at the end; he used a psalm he had known all his life. Fill your memory now with Scripture and with prayers of trust: Psalm 23, Psalm 31, Romans 8, John 14. Settle your trust in Christ while you are well. Put your affairs in order, forgive those you need to forgive, and tell those you love that you belong to him. And when the time comes, slowly or suddenly, you may commit your spirit to the Father with confidence, because Jesus has gone ahead of you and is waiting to receive you (Acts 7:59).

How do I commit myself to him now? Peter took this word into ordinary life: “let those who suffer according to God’s will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good” (1 Peter 4:19). It is the same verb, and it is not only for deathbeds. To commit something to God is to deposit it with him and stop clutching it, like handing a bag over at a counter and walking away without it. At night, name what you are carrying, the diagnosis, the child, the job, and say, “Father, into your hands”; then sleep. When you are wronged, hand your cause to the one who judges justly, as Jesus did (1 Peter 2:23), and let the grievance go. When you cannot control an outcome, pray from the same psalm: “My times are in your hand” (Psalm 31:15). Then do the next good thing. You can trust those hands because of what they did with this deposit: the Father received the spirit of his Son on Friday and gave him back his life on Sunday.
verseByVerse.note: Later Jewish tradition used Psalm 31:5 as an evening prayer.

parallels.desc: into your hand I commit my spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the centurion saw what had taken place, he praised God, saying, 'Certainly this man was innocent!' And all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle, when they saw what had taken place, returned home beating their breasts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officer in charge of the execution praises God and declares Jesus innocent, and the crowds who came to watch go home in grief. It is the last and weightiest of the verdicts Luke has been counting.

The centurion. The first voice after the death belongs to the officer in charge of killing him. A centurion commanded about eighty soldiers, and executions were routine duty for the garrison. He is the last man on that hill who could be moved by sentiment.

He praised God. It is how Luke’s Gospel greets every mighty work of God (2:20; 5:25; 7:16; 18:43), and even here, at a death, a Roman soldier does it.

Certainly this man was innocent! The word (dikaios) means righteous, or innocent, depending on the setting. In Mark he says, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” (Mark 15:39); a man watching an execution probably said more than one sentence, and each writer has kept the one that serves his account. Luke’s choice is the key to his passion narrative. This verdict follows Pilate’s three, Herod’s and the dying criminal’s, and it comes from a Gentile commanding the execution squad. Luke is building a case for a Roman reader, who will read in Acts of Christians before magistrates while the charges keep collapsing: their founder was pronounced innocent by every competent authority, and executed anyway. That is not a smaller confession than Mark’s but the same verdict from the other side: Mark tells you who he was, and Luke tells you what Rome could not find in him. The righteous one has died for the unrighteous (1 Peter 3:18).

Returned home beating their breasts. They came for a spectacle and go home in remorse. The gesture has appeared once before in this Gospel. A tax collector, standing far off, who would not even lift his eyes to heaven, beat his breast and said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!”, and went home justified, declared right with God (18:13–14). Here is the beginning of repentance, and it would bear fruit at Pentecost, when the people were cut to the heart (Acts 2:37). Such is the power of the dying Christ: before he has risen, before the Spirit has come, his death is already turning hearts.

What did the centurion actually understand? Probably not everything. He saw how Jesus died: the prayer for his killers, the promise to the thief, the darkness, the loud cry of trust, and he knew this was no criminal. Whether he believed in Jesus as Lord we are not told. But he praised God, and spoke truer words than the council. God often begins there, with an honest recognition that Jesus is not who the world says he is. Pray for that beginning in those you love, and do not despise it when you see it.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded a century, nominally a hundred soldiers but in practice about eighty. Beating the breast was a sign of grief or remorse.

verseByVerse.quote: And all his acquaintances and the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance watching these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ friends and the women from Galilee watch him die from a distance, and the women become the witnesses of his death, his burial and his empty tomb.

All his acquaintances. His friends, perhaps including some of the disciples; Luke does not put a single apostle at the foot of the cross by name. “At a distance” is the phrase he used of Peter in the high priest’s courtyard (22:54), and here it covers everyone who loved him. They stayed until it was over, at a distance, which is probably where soldiers kept the friends of a condemned man, and where grief itself often stands. “My friends and companions stand aloof from my plague, and my nearest kin stand far off” (Psalm 38:11).

The women who had followed him from Galilee. Luke has named them: Mary called Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Herod’s household manager, Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means (8:2–3). They had travelled with him and paid for the ministry, and they are still there, watching the end of everything they had given themselves to.

Watching these things. Eyewitnesses. They see him die, see where and how he is buried (v. 55), and come back with the spices. The unbroken chain of witness from the cross to the empty tomb is held, in this Gospel, by women, whose testimony in that world often carried little weight in a court. God chose them anyway. The Lord who noticed a widow’s two coins noticed these women, and wrote their faithfulness into the Gospel. He is not ashamed of those the world overlooks; he gives them the best news first.

Alone in the middle of a crowd. “At a distance” echoes the Greek Old Testament wording of the psalms in which a righteous man suffers (Psalm 88:8), and the echo is probably deliberate: the righteous sufferer is dying, and his friends cannot come near. The one who touched lepers, took children in his arms and let a sinful woman wash his feet dies with no one who loves him within reach. He bore the distance as well as the wounds. And because he was left alone, none of his people will ever be: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

In everyday life. Faithfulness sometimes means simply staying, watching, not running away. If you are sitting beside someone in a long illness or a grief you cannot fix, your presence is not nothing; it is the ministry of the women at the cross. Stay. And thank someone this week whose quiet service has held your church together.

What does this say about women in the church? It honours them highly. In the Gospels women were the most faithful followers at the cross, the witnesses of the burial and the first to hear of the resurrection. They supported Christ’s ministry, served him, and were sent to tell the apostles. This commentary holds, with the complementarian reading of the New Testament (men and women equal in worth, given different and complementary callings), that the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church are given to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), and that this is a pattern of order, not of worth. Paul grounds it in creation rather than in the customs of his day (1 Timothy 2:13), which is why we hold to it. Many faithful Christians read these passages differently and welcome women as pastors, and we honour their love for Scripture while we differ. Women and men are equally made in God’s image and equally heirs of grace (Galatians 3:28; 1 Peter 3:7), and every church should value, use and thank its faithful women as Luke does.

parallels.desc: my friends stand aloof from my plague

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. He was a member of the council, a good and righteous man, who had not consented to their decision and action; and he was looking for the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A good man from the very council that condemned Jesus, who had not agreed to its verdict, now steps forward to bury him.

A man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. Luke introduces Joseph as a witness whose credentials matter. Arimathea was a town of Judea, perhaps Ramathaim, Samuel’s birthplace.

A member of the council, a good and righteous man. The Sanhedrin, the very body that had condemned Jesus a few hours earlier: the man about to take the body down belonged to the court that condemned him. Yet Luke calls him good and righteous, as he described Zechariah and Elizabeth (1:6) and Simeon (2:25) at the start of the Gospel.

Who had not consented. Only Luke records that Joseph agreed neither to the council’s decision nor to its action. Perhaps he was absent from the night hearing, or voted against it. But the passage does not hide the honest question: where was the dissent when it might have mattered? John says Joseph was a disciple, but secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38). By the time he acts, the man he might have defended is dead. He is neither hero nor coward, but something more recognisable: a believer who was afraid, whose silence had a real cost, and who then did the bravest thing still available at the moment he had left.

Looking for the kingdom of God. Waiting for it, as Simeon waited for the consolation of Israel and Anna for the redemption of Jerusalem (2:25, 38). The Gospel begins and ends with faithful people waiting.

Waiting for a kingdom that had just come. Joseph thought his waiting had ended in failure; it had ended in the very thing he waited for. The kingdom of God was not defeated on Friday; it was won, by a King who reigned from a tree and conquered by dying. Joseph went to Pilate believing he was burying the hope of Israel. He was laying in the tomb the King who would walk out of it.

Late love, and none of it wasted. A frightened disciple who had kept silent in the council found his courage only when it seemed too late, and the Lord he had failed to defend wasted none of it. His late, trembling love put the tomb, and its emptiness, on the record for ever. “A bruised reed he will not break” (Isaiah 42:3).

Am I a secret disciple? Many believers are at times: you love Christ, but at work, with certain friends or family, nobody would know. Joseph’s story is both warning and hope. A warning, because silence when it matters has a cost, and Jesus says that whoever is ashamed of him, he will be ashamed of (9:26). A hope, because Christ did not reject Joseph, and gave him a magnificent act of courage at the end. If you have been hiding, the way forward is not despair but a step into the open: one clear, kind word that shows whose you are.
verseByVerse.note: Arimathea was a town of Judea. The council is the Sanhedrin.

verseByVerse.quote: This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then he took it down and wrapped it in a linen shroud and laid him in a tomb cut in stone, where no one had ever yet been laid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph risks his name to ask Pilate for the body, and lays Jesus in a new rock tomb: a real burial, in a known place, before witnesses.

Asked for the body of Jesus. Crucified bodies were not usually surrendered, though in Judea the Romans sometimes allowed burial out of respect for Jewish law (Deuteronomy 21:23). To ask the governor for the body of a man executed for treason was to risk being identified, on the record, with the treason. Mark says Joseph took courage and went (Mark 15:43), hours after his own council had procured the execution. Whatever he had been keeping quiet, he is not keeping it quiet now.

Wrapped it in a linen shroud. Somebody had to draw the nails and take the weight of the body as it came free, and Joseph, a wealthy councillor (Matthew 27:57), did it or saw it done. John adds that Nicodemus came too, with a great weight of spices (John 19:39).

A tomb cut in stone. Every detail from here serves as evidence. Not a shallow grave that could be disturbed, but a chamber hewn out of rock, the kind wealthy families had, with one entrance, sealed with a large stone. And Isaiah had put it in writing seven centuries before, in the passage that numbered him with the transgressors: “and with a rich man in his death” (Isaiah 53:9).

Where no one had ever yet been laid. A new tomb (John 19:41), so that on Sunday there could be no confusion about whose body was missing. Like the colt on which no one had ever yet sat (19:30), it was set apart for him. Its location was known to a named member of the council and to the women watching from a few yards away, and so was checkable by anyone in Jerusalem who cared to walk out and look. They laid the Author of life in a borrowed grave, in a hurry, before sundown, and the stone was rolled across a room that would be famous for being empty.

Did Jesus really die, or did he only faint? He really died. Roman executioners were experts in death, and the centurion confirmed it to Pilate (Mark 15:44–45). John saw a soldier pierce his side, and blood and water came out (John 19:34). His friends handled his body, wrapped it and laid it in a tomb, and his enemies sealed and guarded it (Matthew 27:62–66). A half-dead man, flogged and crucified, could not have rolled away the stone, overpowered guards, and then persuaded his disciples that he was the conqueror of death. The burial is in the creed and in Paul’s summary of the gospel (1 Corinthians 15:3–4) precisely because it is the proof that he was dead.
verseByVerse.note: Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone.

verseByVerse.quote: It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sabbath is about to begin, so the burial is done in haste and left unfinished, and the Lord of the Sabbath rests in the grave.

It was the day of Preparation. This explains the haste of everything around it. The day of Preparation was Friday, when everything for the Sabbath had to be done, because from sunset nothing could be: food cooked, lamps lit, work finished.

And the Sabbath was beginning. The Sabbath began at sundown. So they are working against a clock, with no time for the full anointing, and the women note where the tomb is because they can see the burial is unfinished. Then the sun goes down, and nothing more is done for a day and a half.

The Sabbath rest. On the seventh day God rested from the work of creation (Genesis 2:2). The Sabbath came on, as it did every week, and the Lord of the Sabbath (6:5) lay still and kept it, his work finished (John 19:30). On the first day of the week, the new creation would begin.

The silent Saturday. Between the last verse of this chapter and the first of the next lies a whole day in which nothing is said. God had become man, and was dead, and was in a grave, and it was the Sabbath, and nobody knew anything. A great deal of Christian life is lived in that gap: the flat interval when the worst has already happened and nothing is moving, prayers seem to land nowhere, and the only thing available is to keep the ordinary rules of an ordinary day, getting up, praying, going to church, while your heart is in pieces. Nothing in this chapter suggests that the gap is a sign of abandonment. The most decisive work in the history of the world had just been finished, and from the outside, on the Saturday, it looked exactly like defeat.

How is Friday to Sunday three days? In Jewish reckoning any part of a day counted as a day (compare Esther 4:16 with 5:1), so “three days and three nights” (Matthew 12:40) and “on the third day” mean the same span. All four Gospels say Jesus died on the day of Preparation, the day before the Sabbath (Mark 15:42), and theories of a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion have arisen largely to fit a literal count of hours.

Uncertain wording. “Was beginning” is literally “was dawning”, an odd word for an evening. It may simply be the ordinary language of a new day beginning, or refer to the lamps lit for the Sabbath, or to the first evening star. Whatever the picture, the meaning is clear: sunset on Friday was near.
verseByVerse.note: The day of Preparation was Friday; the Sabbath began at sundown.

verseByVerse.quote: The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid. Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women see exactly where and how Jesus was laid, prepare spices to anoint his body, and rest on the Sabbath in obedience, expecting no resurrection.

Saw the tomb and how his body was laid. The last three verbs of the chapter: they saw, they prepared, they rested. They watched the laying out, and on Sunday they would not go to the wrong tomb.

Prepared spices and ointments. To anoint the body properly after the Sabbath. Mark says they bought spices once the Sabbath was over (Mark 16:1); perhaps they made a start on Friday. They are preparing to anoint a corpse. Everything they are doing is the work you do when hope is finished, and they do it beautifully, at speed, with care, for a man who cannot thank them.

The word they had forgotten. The spices measure how completely they had missed what he said. He had told them plainly that the Son of Man must be killed, and on the third day be raised (9:22; 18:31–33). Their grief and love were real, but their plans had no room for his promise. And the promise did not depend on their remembering it: while they ground spices, the word of the Son of God was on its way to fulfilment.

On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment. Faithful Jews keeping the law even in grief (Exodus 20:8–10): obedience with nothing left to fuel it. Every instinct says go, and the commandment says rest, so they rest, with the jars ready by the door. Faithfulness sometimes has no feeling in it at all; it is done simply because God is God.

In the flow. The chapter that began with the council marching Jesus to Pilate ends with a handful of women resting at home, who will be first at the empty tomb with these very spices (24:1). So the burial is not an epilogue but the first half of the resurrection account: a dead man laid in a known tomb before witnesses is what makes an empty one mean something.

Spices he never needed. They rested on the Sabbath with the spices ready, and every one of those jars was wasted, because before they could use them he was up and out, and angels were asking why they sought the living among the dead. Their love brought ointment for a corpse; his love brought them a living Lord. So God lets his people’s faithful grief be overtaken by his joy, and his answer to the tomb is the third day.

Does this mean Christians must keep the Sabbath? These women lived under the old covenant, and Christ had not yet risen, so their example does not settle the question. Christians hold different views. Many Reformed and Baptist Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Sabbath command continues, moved by Christ’s resurrection to the first day of the week as the Lord’s Day, to be kept holy for worship, rest and mercy (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8). Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10), while the church gladly gathers on the first day, the day of resurrection, without Sabbath rules. This commentary’s view: the second view fits the New Testament best; the first day is set apart gladly, out of joy and wisdom, not as the fourth commandment transferred to Sunday. Both seek to honour the Lord of the Sabbath, and believers should not judge one another over it (Romans 14:5–6). The Westminster and 1689 view is held by many godly brothers and deserves respect. All agree that the day of rising is a gift, and that weekly rest and worship are wise and good.

23.text: <sup>1</sup> Then the whole company of them arose and brought him before Pilate. <sup>2</sup> And they began to accuse him, saying, “We found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.” <sup>3</sup> And Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” And he answered him, “You have said so.” <sup>4</sup> Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, “I find no guilt in this man.” <sup>5</sup> But they were urgent, saying, “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to this place.” <sup>6</sup> When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. <sup>7</sup> And when he learned that he belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem at that time. <sup>8</sup> When Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. <sup>9</sup> So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer. <sup>10</sup> The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him. <sup>11</sup> And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Then, arraying him in splendid clothing, he sent him back to Pilate. <sup>12</sup> And Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before this they had been at enmity with each other. <sup>13</sup> Pilate then called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people, <sup>14</sup> and said to them, “You brought me this man as one who was misleading the people. And after examining him before you, behold, I did not find this man guilty of any of your charges against him. <sup>15</sup> Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, nothing deserving death has been done by him. <sup>16</sup> I will therefore punish and release him.” <sup>18</sup> But they all cried out together, “Away with this man, and release to us Barabbas”— <sup>19</sup> a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city and for murder. <sup>20</sup> Pilate addressed them once more, desiring to release Jesus, <sup>21</sup> but they kept shouting, “Crucify, crucify him!” <sup>22</sup> A third time he said to them, “Why? What evil has he done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death. I will therefore punish and release him.” <sup>23</sup> But they were urgent, demanding with loud cries that he should be crucified. And their voices prevailed. <sup>24</sup> So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted. <sup>25</sup> He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, for whom they asked, but he delivered Jesus over to their will. <sup>26</sup> And as they led him away, they seized one Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it behind Jesus. <sup>27</sup> And there followed him a great multitude of the people and of women who were mourning and lamenting for him. <sup>28</sup> But turning to them Jesus said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. <sup>29</sup> For behold, the days are coming when they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed!’ <sup>30</sup> Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’ <sup>31</sup> For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?” <sup>32</sup> Two others, who were criminals, were led away to be put to death with him. <sup>33</sup> And when they came to the place that is called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on his right and one on his left. <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.” And they cast lots to divide his garments. <sup>35</sup> And the people stood by, watching, but the rulers scoffed at him, saying, “He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One!” <sup>36</sup> The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine <sup>37</sup> and saying, “If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!” <sup>38</sup> There was also an inscription over him, “This is the King of the Jews.” <sup>39</sup> One of the criminals who were hanged railed at him, saying, “Are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us!” <sup>40</sup> But the other rebuked him, saying, “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation? <sup>41</sup> And we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong.” <sup>42</sup> And he said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” <sup>43</sup> And he said to him, “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.” <sup>44</sup> It was now about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour, <sup>45</sup> while the sun's light failed. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two. <sup>46</sup> Then Jesus, calling out with a loud voice, said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” And having said this he breathed his last. <sup>47</sup> Now when the centurion saw what had taken place, he praised God, saying, “Certainly this man was innocent!” <sup>48</sup> And all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle, when they saw what had taken place, returned home beating their breasts. <sup>49</sup> And all his acquaintances and the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance watching these things. <sup>50</sup> Now there was a man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. He was a member of the council, a good and righteous man, <sup>51</sup> who had not consented to their decision and action; and he was looking for the kingdom of God. <sup>52</sup> This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. <sup>53</sup> Then he took it down and wrapped it in a linen shroud and laid him in a tomb cut in stone, where no one had ever yet been laid. <sup>54</sup> It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning. <sup>55</sup> The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid. <sup>56</sup> Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.

keyVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter meets here: the innocent King, mocked for not saving himself, spends his dying breath saving a guilty man who asked only to be remembered. Each part of the answer gives more than was asked: today, with me, in paradise. It is the gospel in one sentence, salvation by grace alone through faith alone, for those who bring nothing but their need.

23.reflection:
Luke records six declarations that Jesus was innocent (vv. 4, 14, 15, 22, 41, 47), yet he was condemned and Barabbas set free. Why does it matter for the gospel that Jesus was innocent, and what does it mean to you that he took the place of the guilty?

Pilate tried to pass the decision to someone else, Herod wanted a show, and the crowd simply shouted (vv. 6–25). Which of these responses to Jesus do you recognise in yourself or in the people around you? Where are you tempted to let the loudest voice win?

Three times Jesus is told to save himself, and he stays (vv. 35–39). How does his refusal deepen your understanding of his love, and how might it change the way you read your own suffering?

The criminal brought nothing but a confession and a request (vv. 40–43), and the women kept faith in grief with no hope left (vv. 49–56). What do these two pictures teach you about coming to Christ, and about staying faithful in dark seasons?

24.title: Resurrection, Recognition, and Commission
24.overview:
Where we are. The last chapter of Luke’s Gospel. Jesus has died and been buried (23:46–56). Chapter 24 tells the first Easter Sunday as though it were one day, running on to the ascension, which Acts places forty days later (Acts 1:3).

The message. The crucified Jesus is alive in his body, and the cross that seemed to disprove him was exactly what the Scriptures said must happen. The whole Old Testament is about him, he is known as he opens it, and the forgiveness he won is now to be offered in his name to every nation.

Why it was said. Luke wrote so that Theophilus might have certainty (1:4; see the introduction). Gentile readers could hear the resurrection as a ghost story or a pious myth, so Luke gives checkable witness: named women, sceptical apostles, a body that could be touched and that ate fish, and a risen Lord who grounded it all in the book God had already written.

How the chapter makes its case. Three scenes, each moving from confusion to recognition and back to what Jesus said and the Scriptures wrote. At the tomb (vv. 1–12) the women find the body gone and are told to remember his words; the apostles call their report nonsense. On the Emmaus road (vv. 13–35) two downcast disciples have every fact and no hope, until the stranger opens Moses and the Prophets and is known in the breaking of the bread. In Jerusalem (vv. 36–53) he gives peace to the men who fled, shows his hands and feet, opens their minds to the Scriptures, and sends them as witnesses to all nations once they are clothed with power from on high; then he blesses them and is carried up into heaven.

Where it leads. The Gospel began in the temple with a priest who could not speak the blessing (1:22). It ends with the great high priest lifting scarred hands over his people and going up still blessing them, and with his people in the temple blessing God. Every promise of the opening chapters has been kept.

For us. Our faith rests on what happened and on what God has said, not on feelings. When a hope has died, take it back to the Scriptures and ask the risen Christ to open them. Then tell what you know of him, in his strength, beginning with the people nearest you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tomb is empty because Jesus has been raised, just as he said, and faith begins by remembering his word. The women come with spices for a corpse and find the stone rolled away and the body gone (vv. 1–3). Two angels ask why they seek the living among the dead and send them back to Jesus’ own prediction (vv. 4–7). The women remember, believe and tell the eleven (vv. 8–9), who dismiss it as an idle tale (vv. 10–11), and Peter runs to the tomb and goes home marvelling, which Luke is careful not to call believing (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology:
The resurrection is a bodily event, and Luke records the physical detail, the stone, the body, the cloths, because the claim is not that a spirit survived but that the one who died was raised (on why it matters, see the note on vv. 6–7).

That women are the first witnesses, named, and dismissed by the apostles, is a strong sign that the account is not invented (see the note on vv. 10–11).

And the angels’ word remember is the key to the chapter. The failure to understand the resurrection was a failure to believe the word already given (see the note on vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.examples:
The women’s walk to the tomb was obedience with no expectation attached: they were going to finish a burial. Much faithful service has that shape, and it was those carrying the spices who reached the empty tomb first.

Verses 6–8 are practical (see the note on vv. 6–7). In a frightening season, go back to what God has actually said, not to what you feel.

Verse 11 is for anyone who has told the truth about Christ and been treated as a fool (see the note on vv. 10–11). And v. 12 describes a real stage on the road (see the note on v. 12).

verseByVerse.quote: But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they went to the tomb, taking the spices they had prepared. And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, but when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At dawn on the first Easter Sunday the women came to anoint a corpse, and found the stone rolled away and the body gone. The first fact of the Christian faith arrives as an absence, discovered by people who had come expecting a dead man.

On the first day of the week, at early dawn. Sunday (see the week). Chapter 23 ended with spices standing ready while the Sabbath was kept (23:56); this one opens with them being carried out of the door as soon as the law allowed and there was light to see the path. That is what love does when it has been made to sit still for thirty-six hours.

The spices they had prepared. To anoint a dead body (see burial customs). Every step was taken expecting a corpse, which tells heavily against the theory that wishful people talked themselves into the resurrection. Their only practical worry, Mark tells us, was who would roll away the stone (Mark 16:3).

The stone rolled away. Luke does not describe the rolling: no earthquake, no angel heaving at it, none of the drama a storyteller would supply (Matthew says an angel did it, Matthew 28:2). He reports what they found: it was open, and someone else had done it. And it was not moved to let him out; the Lord who would vanish from a table at Emmaus that evening (v. 31) needed no doorway. It seems to have been moved to let the witnesses in.

The body of the Lord Jesus. Not a vision or a voice, but an empty shelf in a rock chamber. And Luke chooses this moment for the full title, “the Lord Jesus”, the only time this Gospel uses it, written over the place where the corpse should have been: the crucified one is the Lord.

In everyday life. Think where you, like the women, are making careful arrangements around something you have already decided is dead: a prayer you have stopped praying, a person you have given up on. God may already have acted.

Could the body simply have been stolen? By whom? His enemies would have produced it the moment the apostles began preaching in the same city, and never did. His friends were hiding and disbelieving, and men do not die, as several of them did, for a story they know they made up. Grave robbers take the valuables and leave the body; here the linen was left and the body gone (v. 12). And a stolen body could not explain the appearances: to the women, to Peter, to two on a road, to the eleven, to more than five hundred at once (1 Corinthians 15:6). The simplest explanation of the empty tomb is the one the angels gave.

Why do Christians gather on Sunday? Because this is the day he rose. The first Christians, most of them Jews who had kept the seventh-day Sabbath all their lives, began meeting on the first day of the week (Acts 20:7), and John calls it the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10). Christians differ on whether it is the Christian Sabbath, carrying over the fourth commandment. This commentary holds that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and that the Lord’s Day is his gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest rather than kept as a law of rules, with no one binding another’s conscience (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17), while honouring those who hold the Westminster and 1689 view. All agree that every Sunday is a small Easter, a weekly announcement that the tomb is empty.

Textual note. A few manuscripts lack “of the Lord Jesus” in v. 3, but the earliest have it.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. And as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them, 'Why do you seek the living among the dead?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s messengers met the women in their bewilderment and corrected the one thing they had wrong: they were looking for a living Lord in a place for the dead.

Perplexed. At a loss, with no way through, a word close to the one Luke used of the nations in perplexity (21:25). The messengers came while they were in that state; resurrection was not their first thought.

Two men in dazzling apparel. Angels (“a vision of angels”, v. 23), called men because that is what they looked like. Two: the number of witnesses the law required (Deuteronomy 19:15), like the two at the transfiguration (9:30) and the ascension (Acts 1:10).

Frightened. Again and again in this Gospel an angel’s coming has begun with a frightened human being: Zechariah at the altar, Mary in Nazareth, shepherds on a hillside. Here the women go face down on the floor of the tomb.

Why do you seek the living among the dead? A gentle rebuke, and a claim no sentence had yet made. Not that he is alive again, which would put him back where he was, but “the living”: a permanent condition. He has not returned to life like Lazarus, to die again; he has passed into a life that death has no further business with. “I died, and behold I am alive forevermore” (Revelation 1:18); “Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again” (Romans 6:9).

Where might I be looking for Jesus among the dead? Many people honour Jesus as a teacher, an example, a great moral figure of the past, and every one of those categories is a tomb: you can hold him in the highest regard and still look for him among the honoured dead. Christians can do it too, treating him as a memory, a doctrine or a tradition rather than a living Lord to speak to today. Seek him where he is: risen, reigning, present by his Spirit, speaking in his Word.

Do the Gospels disagree about the angels? Matthew has one angel, Mark a young man, Luke and John two; the women named and the times differ a little too. Each Gospel is a selective, independent report, and to mention one angel, the spokesman, is not to deny there were two; the women also seem to have come in more than one group. All agree on the empty tomb, the women first, and the message that he had risen. Accounts that agreed word for word would look rehearsed; these look like witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men and be crucified and on the third day rise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angels announce that God has raised Jesus, and send the women back to his own words: he had told them this would happen.

He is not here, but has risen. Literally “has been raised” (ēgerthē), by God: the resurrection is the Father’s verdict on the Son. The council had condemned Jesus as a blasphemer and Rome had executed him as a rebel; by raising him, God reversed both verdicts in front of the world and declared him to be his Son in power (Acts 2:23–24; Romans 1:4). The tomb was not broken out of; it was opened from the throne.

Remember how he told you. The messengers do not explain the greatest news ever delivered; they tell the women to remember. Jesus had said it three times, plainly: the Son of Man must suffer, be killed, and on the third day be raised (9:22); “Let these words sink into your ears” (9:44); and on the road to Jerusalem, with the mockery and spitting named in advance (18:31–33). The women had heard.

The Son of Man must. It had to happen, because God had planned it (dei). He went into the hands of sinful men and came out of the hands of death, exactly as he said.

Faith fails for lack of memory. What the women are handed in the worst confusion of their lives is a promise made in Galilee months earlier. Faith rarely fails because God has said too little; it fails because we forget what he has said. That is why his book is full of commands to remember, and why he gives bread and wine and says, “Do this in remembrance of me.” In a frightening season, go back to what God has actually said, not to what you feel.

Why does it matter that Jesus was raised bodily, and not just that his spirit lives on? Because everything depends on it. “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” (1 Corinthians 15:17). The resurrection is the Father’s public declaration that the sacrifice was accepted and the debt paid: he “was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25), that is, for the Father’s acquittal of guilty sinners, resting on Christ’s death in their place and received by faith. And it is the firstfruits of our own resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:20), like the first sheaf of the harvest brought to God as the promise that the whole field would follow (Leviticus 23:10). A spirit living on would prove none of this. An empty tomb proves all of it.

Textual note. A few manuscripts lack the words “He is not here, but has risen”, as the ESV notes; the earliest copies have them, and Mark gives the same message (Mark 16:6).

verseByVerse.quote: And they remembered his words, and returning from the tomb they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women remembered Jesus’ words, believed, and went straight to tell the eleven.

They remembered his words. The first act of Easter faith recorded by anyone. They have not seen him: only an empty tomb, a message from two strangers, and a sentence from Galilee suddenly coming back with everything in it they had missed. They believe a promise before any appearance at all.

They told the eleven. The eleven had slept in the garden, Peter had denied him, and none of them had come to the tomb; the women had every human reason to nurse a grievance, and none of it appears. So the risen Lord let the news of his victory go first to the men who had run away, carried by those who had stayed. The first proclamation of the Christian era was made to a room of disillusioned men who did not want to hear it, and every proclamation since has had roughly the same shape.

Faithful in the background. Luke has tracked these women across three chapters without once putting them in the foreground. They funded the ministry (8:3), watched the crucifixion (23:49), marked the tomb (23:55), and came at dawn. They were the first to be told, and the first to tell.

May every Christian share the good news, women included? Yes, gladly. These women were sent with the message, and in Acts the whole church went about speaking the word (Acts 8:4), Priscilla with Aquila explaining the way of God to Apollos (Acts 18:26). The New Testament reserves the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), but that silences no one from telling a neighbour, a child or a colleague that Jesus is risen. Christians who read those passages differently are our brothers and sisters, and on this verse we stand together: the risen Lord sent women first.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it was Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles, but these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke names the women who first carried the news, and records that the apostles dismissed it as nonsense.

Mary Magdalene and Joanna. Named, checkable witnesses, some probably still living when Luke wrote. Mary Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out (8:2); Joanna, the wife of Herod’s household manager (8:3), named only by Luke; Mary the mother of James.

An idle tale. The word (lēros), found nowhere else in the New Testament, could be used by Greek medical writers of the babbling of a delirious patient. The apostles did not merely doubt the report; they dismissed it as the raving of women unhinged by grief. They were not gullible.

They did not believe them. A woman’s testimony carried little weight in court at the time, and a pagan critic would later sneer that the whole religion rested on the word of a hysterical woman. A forger would have put the discovery in the hands of a respected man. Luke puts it in the hands of women whose report the apostles themselves rejected, and he names them.

Unbelief met by the Lord himself. That same evening the Lord would stand among the scornful apostles, show them his hands and feet and eat in front of them (vv. 36–43). He sent no rebuke by the women; he came himself, wounds and all, and that has been his way with doubting disciples ever since. What they called nonsense on Sunday morning they were ready to die for in the years that followed.

Told the truth and treated as a fool. The women were right, they were disbelieved, and the disbelief did not alter the fact by one degree. If a friend calls the resurrection a fairy tale, do not be rattled: the first people to say so were the apostles. Offer to read Luke 24 and 1 Corinthians 15 together.

Is it wrong to have doubts? Doubt is not the same as unbelief. The apostles began here as sceptics, and Jesus dealt with them patiently and with evidence (vv. 38–43). Do not hide honest questions or feed them, but bring them into the light: read the evidence, talk to a mature believer, pray as the father did, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). Scripture warns not against the struggling doubter but against the settled refusal to believe what God has made plain. “Have mercy on those who doubt” (Jude 22), including yourself.
verseByVerse.note: A woman’s testimony carried little weight in court at the time; no one inventing the story would have made women the first witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter rose and ran to the tomb; stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths by themselves; and he went home marveling at what had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter, who had denied Jesus, ran to the tomb, saw the empty grave-clothes, and went home amazed but not yet believing.

Peter rose and ran. In Luke’s telling Peter is the one who runs (John adds another disciple, John 20:3–10). His last recorded act was to weep bitterly in a courtyard after denying his Lord three times, and his restoration is still to come (v. 34). Shame’s instinct is to withdraw, and if the report were true, he would have to face the man he had disowned. He ran anyway, and he could, because Jesus had prayed that his faith would not fail (22:32). Real sorrow for sin moves towards Christ, not away from him; that is the whole difference between Peter and Judas, visible here in a pair of running feet.

The linen cloths by themselves. Stooping to look in through the low entrance, he saw the wrappings lying there without a body. No robber unwraps a corpse in the dark and carries it out naked, leaving the valuable linen behind.

Marveling. Not yet believing fully. Luke is precise, and the honesty is a mercy: Peter looked at the strongest physical evidence anyone had yet seen and walked home wondering.

He went looking for Simon. Grace had reached the denier before he knew it: the Intercessor who had prayed for him was alive, and later that day would appear to him (v. 34). Blessed be the risen Lord, who left the linen lying in the tomb and went looking for Simon.

What if I am still at the marvelling stage? Then you are in a real place on the road, not a disqualified one. The old explanations no longer fit, and settled faith has not yet arrived. Do what Peter did next: stay near the other disciples, keep listening to the word, and wait for Christ to show himself. Ask God plainly to make him real to you. Marvelling is not believing, but nobody who ran to the tomb was left outside it for long.

Textual note. Some manuscripts omit this verse, as the ESV notes, but it is well attested in the earliest and best copies, and John tells the same story at greater length (John 20:3–10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The risen Christ goes after his discouraged disciples and makes himself known to them through the Scriptures and at the table. Two walk away from Jerusalem with every fact and no hope; Jesus joins them unrecognised and lets them tell him their story, down to its “we had hoped” (vv. 13–24). He shows them from Moses and all the Prophets that the Christ had to suffer and so enter his glory (vv. 25–27). At their table the guest becomes the host, and as he breaks the bread their eyes are opened (vv. 28–32). They hurry back that night to find the eleven already saying that the Lord has appeared to Simon (vv. 33–35).
verseByVerse.theology:
Was it not necessary turns their difficulty upside down. The suffering was not a detour from God’s plan but the way into the glory (see the note on vv. 25–26).

Verse 27 is how the church has read its Bible ever since (see the note on v. 27).

And the afternoon’s order, Scripture opened and then bread broken, became the pattern of Christian worship (see the note on vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 16 describes a common condition of the Christian life (see the note on vv. 15–16).

Verse 21 is for anyone living inside a we had hoped (see the note on v. 21).

And v. 32 answers the Christian for whom the Bible feels dead with a prayer: “open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). On burning hearts that still walk the wrong way, see the note on v. 32.

verseByVerse.quote: That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That same Sunday two disappointed disciples walked away from Jerusalem, going over everything that had happened.

That very day. Only Luke tells this story in full (the longer ending of Mark gives it a sentence, Mark 16:12–13). The two belong to the wider company, not the apostles. One is named Cleopas (v. 18); the other never is. Some suggest it was his wife, since they share a home: a reasonable guess and no more.

About seven miles from Jerusalem. About sixty stadia, as the ESV notes (see stadion), around two hours on foot. They are probably going home, because it is over, to pick life up again.

Talking with each other. Grief on a long walk turns the events round and round, looking for a shape that does not hurt so much, and gets nowhere.

The Shepherd goes after them. Luke’s whole Gospel has travelled towards Jerusalem since Jesus set his face to go there (9:51). Everything has been accomplished there, and these two are walking away from it. The risen Lord does not wait for them to come back. The Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to go after the one that is lost (15:4) goes after two, on foot. “The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (19:10), and the resurrection has not changed his ways.

In everyday life. If you are walking away from something, a church, a hope, a calling, because it seems over, talk it through with another Christian before you settle into the village.

Why did the risen Jesus not appear to everyone? God made him appear, Peter later said, “not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10:41). It was not a show to compel belief from the hostile, who would not be convinced even if someone rose from the dead (16:31). He gave his church reliable eyewitnesses, so that we who have not seen may believe through their word (John 17:20; 20:29).

Uncertain wording. Where Emmaus was is not known. Several villages have been proposed, at different distances from Jerusalem, and none is certain. Legends gather round famous places, not villages nobody can now find.
