verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is about sixty stadia; the location of Emmaus is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were talking and discussing together, Jesus himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Jesus joined the two on the road, but God kept them from recognising him.

Jesus himself drew near. Not a messenger, and the verb is entirely undramatic: he came alongside, as any traveller does who catches up with people going the same way, and let them talk.

Their eyes were kept. The wording points to God: he kept them from recognising him until the right moment (v. 31). Not a failure of observation, not a disguise, but deliberate, temporary, and lifted later by the same hand. Mary Magdalene also did not recognise him at first (John 20:14).

He withheld himself to give them more of himself. Had he made himself known at the roadside, there would have been joy and no Bible study: the fact without the meaning. Instead he keeps his face hidden long enough to walk them through Moses and the Prophets, so that they learn to know him first through the Scriptures. The Lord of glory, hours out of the grave, matched his pace to two people who had given up on him, and walked with them for two hours while they explained his death to his face. “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it” (Genesis 28:16).

Is Jesus with me when I cannot sense him? Yes. This is a common condition of the Christian life. He has promised, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20), by his Spirit who dwells in every believer. These two later said their hearts had been burning the whole way; at the time they would have told you they were walking home from a funeral with a stranger. Your feelings are not the measure of his presence; his promise is.

parallels.desc: the disciples did not know that it was Jesus

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'What is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk?' And they stood still, looking sad. Then one of them, named Cleopas, answered him, 'Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asked the two what they were discussing, and listened patiently while they told him the news about himself. He draws out their grief before he answers it.

What is this conversation? He asks a question he does not need answered, as he has throughout this Gospel: “Where is your faith?” “Who was it that touched me?” “What do you want me to do for you?” He is opening a door for them to walk through in their own words.

Looking sad. The question stops them dead in the road. When a stranger asks, the whole weight comes back. “Sad” (skythrōpoi) is the look of someone who has stopped expecting anything.

One of them, named Cleopas. He may be the Clopas of John 19:25, whose wife Mary stood at the cross; if so, perhaps she was the other disciple. An early tradition says Clopas was Joseph’s brother, which would make him Jesus’ uncle by law, but we cannot be sure.

Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know? The irony is complete. The crowd saw an execution, the council a problem solved, the soldiers a shift completed. One man knew what had actually taken place on that hill, and he was standing in the road being asked whether he had heard the news.

He does not correct him. He does not say, “I was there.” He asks another question and lets Cleopas go on, listening to a mistaken account of his own death without interrupting, because the man needs to say it more than he needs to be corrected, and everything he gets wrong will be answered a few minutes later. How gentle Christ is with our confusion: never too great to listen to the small, wrong, sad story of a disciple.

Is it all right to tell God that I am sad and disappointed? Yes. He asked these two to tell him, and he listened. Around a third of the psalms are laments, honest prayers of grief, confusion and complaint (Psalm 13; 42; 88). Honesty with God is not unbelief; it is faith speaking to the only one who can help. Lament turns to sin only when it accuses God of wrong or turns away from him. Tell him the whole thing, in your own words, as Cleopas did. Then let him answer you from his Word.
verseByVerse.note: Cleopas may be the Clopas of John 19:25.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'What things?' And they said to him, 'Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, a man who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two give an accurate account of Jesus as a mighty prophet put to death by their own leaders, and it is not enough.

A prophet mighty in deed and word. Two words from him, and they tell the story: a small creed, all of it true. “Jesus of Nazareth”: the right man. “A prophet”: Moses had said one would come (Deuteronomy 18:15). “Mighty in deed and word before God and all the people”: his ministry was public, and God attested it (Acts 2:22). But they do not call him the Christ, still less the Son of God.

Our chief priests and rulers. Accurate to the last detail. They do not blame Rome; they say our leaders did this (see chief priests), and use Luke’s word for Pilate’s act, “delivered him up” (23:25). So the sum of their creed is a dead prophet and a walk home. They are about to be told that they had the rest of it in the Scriptures all along.

What is the difference between knowing about Jesus and knowing him? Many people are not hostile to Christianity in the least. Jesus was a remarkable man, his teaching profound, his death unjust, and the world would be better if people lived as he said. All true, and it will save nobody, because it describes a corpse. Knowing Christ means trusting him as the living Saviour who died for your sins and rose again, and the Lord to whom you belong. “This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). Ask yourself: do I speak about him, or to him? Do I admire him, or depend on him?

parallels.desc: a man attested to you by God

verseByVerse.quote: But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two confess that their hope that Jesus would redeem Israel has died, though it is the very third day he had spoken of. They gave up hope on the day it was being fulfilled beyond anything they had asked.

But we had hoped. Few tenses are sadder. Not “we hope”, which is alive; not “we never hoped”, which is safe. “We had hoped” is the tense of a thing once real and now over, and everyone who has prayed for something and watched it not happen knows its weight.

To redeem Israel. Not a small or foolish hope. To redeem (lytrousthai) is to ransom, to buy out of slavery, Zechariah’s word when he sang that God had “visited and redeemed his people” (1:68). They understood it mainly as liberation from Rome. They were right to want God to act, and wrong about the shape and the timing, which is nearly always where hope goes wrong. The redemption they wanted for Israel was walking beside them, and it was a redemption for the world.

It is now the third day. He had told them again and again that the Son of Man would rise on the third day (9:22), and here they recite the timetable as the reason their hope is finished. Unbelief does not ignore evidence; it counts it as a reason for despair.

What Christian hope is. In ordinary English, hope is a wish with a shrug attached: I hope it stays dry, I hope the scan is clear. A hope like that leans on how things turn out, and dies when they turn out badly. The Bible’s word is stronger: the confident expectation of what God has promised but not yet given, as sure as the one who promised. Timothy Keller argued in Hope in Times of Fear that what we expect about the future governs how we live now, and that the resurrection gives a hope no circumstance can overturn. It rests not on a good outcome but on a living person: God “has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3). It is living because he is, and a hope fastened to a man who was crucified and is now alive has already come through the worst that can happen to it.

What do I do when my hopes are dashed? First, tell God, as they told the stranger: “we had hoped.” Then ask whether what you hoped for was God’s promise or your own picture of how he should keep it. These two had the right God and the wrong expectation. A quiet idol can hide there: we want God mainly as the means to something else, a healed marriage, a career, a nation put right, and when it does not come we decide he has failed us, when he was offering us himself. God does not always give what we hoped for; he always keeps what he has promised, often in a far larger way (Ephesians 3:20), working all things, not every disappointment in itself, together for good (Romans 8:28). Go back to his actual words, as Jesus took these two back to Moses and the Prophets. And add what these two did not yet know: “The Lord has risen indeed” (v. 34).

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, some women of our company amazed us. They were at the tomb early in the morning, and when they did not find his body, they came back saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. Some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two report every piece of evidence for the resurrection, and are still walking away from it.

Some women of our company amazed us. Read what they have, and then where they are going: the gap between the two is the point.

A vision of angels. In their retelling the sight survives and the message, that he was alive, is held at arm’s length. A report filed as a vision requires nothing of anybody.

Just as the women had said. Peter went, and, John tells us, another disciple with him (v. 12; John 20:3–10). So they have three strands pointing one way: the empty tomb reported by named witnesses, the announcement of angels, and independent corroboration. And they are walking to Emmaus.

But him they did not see. Honest, and the sticking point: they have decided in advance that only a sighting will count, and the promise from Galilee has not entered the conversation. So he does not say, “Look at me.” He spends two hours in the Old Testament, because their problem was never a shortage of evidence.

Is evidence enough to bring someone to faith? Evidence matters, and God has given a great deal of it; the apostles appealed to it constantly (Acts 2:32; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Christianity is not a leap in the dark. But evidence alone does not change the heart. So give people the evidence, gladly and honestly, give them the Word, and pray, because only God can open eyes (2 Corinthians 4:6).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus rebukes the two for believing only the glorious half of the prophets, and shows them that the Christ had to suffer before entering his glory. The cross they thought disproved him was the very thing the Scriptures said would mark him out.

O foolish ones. Not stupid, but failing to put together what they already have (anoētoi), the word Paul uses of the Galatians (Galatians 3:1).

Slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken. Slow of heart, not of mind: slow to be persuaded of something already half known. And slow to believe “all” that the prophets said. They believed the glorious parts: a throne, a kingdom, an everlasting dominion. The suffering was on the same pages and had been left unread: the servant despised and rejected, led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53); the man of Psalm 22 with hands and feet pierced; the shepherd struck (Zechariah 13:7). It was all there, and nobody had wanted it.

Was it not necessary. The same divine “must” as in v. 7, gathering up every time Jesus foretold his suffering (9:22; 17:25; 22:37). The cross was not a defeat that ruined God’s plan; it was the plan. They think the crucifixion is the reason he cannot be the Christ. He tells them it is the reason they should have known he was.

And enter into his glory. Suffering first, then glory (1 Peter 1:11): the pattern of the whole Bible. Glory is not a consolation after the suffering but a destination reached through it. “Enter” is a word of going in by a door, and the door was a cross. He entered his glory through it, and he holds it open for all who follow him.

Is my suffering a detour from God’s plan? This verse does not remove the pain, but if suffering was necessary for the Christ on the way to glory, it is not evidence of a mistake in anyone else’s case either: “we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him” (Romans 8:17). Your hard road is not God having lost the thread. It may be the very door to the glory he has prepared.

Why was it necessary? Could God not simply forgive? God is love, and he is also just. He cannot treat sin as though it did not matter without ceasing to be the holy God. The cross is how he can “be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26): the punishment our sins deserved was laid on Christ, our substitute, so that God’s justice was satisfied and his mercy set free. Not that God was reluctant to forgive, but that he would not forgive at the cost of his justice, and so he paid the cost himself, in his Son.

parallels.desc: it was necessary for the Christ to suffer

verseByVerse.quote: And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus led the two through the whole Old Testament, showing them what it said about himself. This is the key to the Bible: one book, with one subject.

Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets. The whole Old Testament. There is no transcript, but the New Testament writers pass the lesson on. Beginning with Moses, he probably took passages like these: the offspring of the woman who would crush the serpent’s head and be struck in the doing of it (Genesis 3:15); the promise that in Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3); a ram caught in a thicket, dying in the place of a son (Genesis 22); a lamb’s blood on the doorposts so that death would pass over the house (Exodus 12); a scapegoat carrying the sins of the people into the wilderness (Leviticus 16); a bronze serpent lifted on a pole, so that anyone dying of the bite could look and live (Numbers 21). And from the Prophets: a servant pierced for our transgressions, on whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53); a son of man coming with the clouds to receive a kingdom (Daniel 7); a new covenant, with sins remembered no more (Jeremiah 31); and the psalms of suffering and vindication (Psalms 22; 16; 110).

He interpreted to them … the things concerning himself. The verb (diermēneusen) is also used for translating a foreign language. They had heard the Scriptures read every Sabbath of their lives; what they had never had was the key. And the claim is enormous. The Old Testament is not religious literature with some predictions in it. It is one book with one subject, and the subject was walking down a road to Emmaus explaining himself (John 5:39, 46).

His own face on every page. The Author of the book had come to read it aloud. Every altar, lamb and promise in Israel had pointed down the centuries at one person, and that afternoon he showed two travellers his own face on every page. The Scriptures were never a puzzle with Christ as one of the pieces; they were his portrait, drawn in advance by the love of the Father.

Where should I start, if the Old Testament feels like a closed book? Where Jesus started, with the big story and a few signposts: Genesis 1 to 3, 12 and 22; Exodus 12 and 20; Leviticus 16; Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12; Psalms 2, 22 and 110; Jeremiah 31:31–34. Ask three questions as you read: What does this show me about God? What does it show me about our need? How does it point forward to Christ? Read the New Testament passages that quote the Old, especially Hebrews. (On how, and how not, to find Christ in the Old Testament, see the note on v. 44.)
verseByVerse.note: “Moses and all the Prophets” means the whole Old Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: So they drew near to the village to which they were going. He acted as if he were going farther, but they urged him strongly, saying, 'Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent.' So he went in to stay with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus made as if to walk on, and the two pressed him to stay the night with them.

He acted as if he were going farther. Some readers find this uncomfortable, as though it were a pretence. It is not. He is a traveller who has reached the point where his companions turn off, and the courteous thing, the only thing that leaves them free, is to keep walking unless he is asked.

They urged him strongly. Hospitality to travellers at nightfall was a duty, and the roads were not safe after dark. But something in those two hours had also made them unwilling to let this man walk away, and they would tell each other later what it was: their hearts had been burning (v. 32).

Stay with us. They think they are doing a kindness to a man with nowhere to sleep. The sentence has been the prayer of Christians ever since, for the reason they first said it: the day is far spent. It is in the old hymn: “Abide with me, fast falls the eventide.”

He went in. He went as far as the door and would not go in until he was wanted, and the moment he was asked he came in and sat down.

In everyday life. Tonight, as the day ends, pray their prayer in your own home: “Lord, stay with us.” And look for a way to open your home this month to someone who would otherwise be alone at evening.

If Jesus waits to be invited, does salvation depend on my asking? Our asking is real, and he answers it: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in” (Revelation 3:20). But notice who began this afternoon. He drew near to them first, unasked, and it was his words that set their hearts burning so that they wanted him to stay. That is how grace always works. God’s call is effectual, meaning it brings about what it calls for: he opens the heart, and the heart, opened, gladly invites him in (Acts 16:14; John 6:44). So ask him in, without waiting to feel sure you are chosen; that you want to is the sign of his work.
verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to travellers at nightfall was a duty.

verseByVerse.quote: When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the table Jesus took the bread, blessed and broke it, and God opened their eyes to know him; then he vanished.

At table with them. It is their house (see meals and reclining at table), yet at their table the guest becomes the host, as he does wherever his people make room for him. The four actions, taking, blessing, breaking, giving, Luke has recorded twice before: on a hillside with five thousand (9:16), and in an upper room three nights earlier (22:19). These two may well have seen those hands break bread before; now the hands were marked.

Their eyes were opened. Opened by God, the same hand that had kept them closed (v. 16). Perhaps they knew the way he broke bread, or saw the wounds in his hands. Recognition, from first to last, is a gift and not an achievement.

He vanished. The instant they see him, he is gone. It can seem cruel, and it is the opposite. Once they knew him, they did not need to see him; he would be known through the Scriptures and the breaking of bread. And they do not sit down and grieve his going. They get up and run.

Word and table. The order of the afternoon, the Scriptures opened and then the bread broken, became the pattern of Christian worship. The meal at Emmaus was an ordinary meal, not the Lord’s Supper, yet the church’s instinct is right: the Word preached and the Supper given belong together, as the Reformers insisted.

Why do I not seem to recognise Christ in worship? Sometimes because, like these two, we come with eyes held by grief or tiredness or distraction; sometimes because we come expecting a performance, not a meeting. Recognition is his gift, so ask for it before you go: “Lord, open my eyes to see you in your Word and at your table.” Listen to the preaching as Christ speaking through his servant. He was present with these two long before they saw him. A dull Sunday is not an absent Lord.

parallels.desc: he took bread and broke it

verseByVerse.quote: They said to each other, 'Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Looking back, the two realised that their hearts had been set alight while Jesus opened the Scriptures to them.

Did not our hearts burn within us? They say it afterwards. Only when they knew who he was did they understand what had been happening to them for two hours, and that is often the shape of it: a Christian looks back on a hard year and sees that God was at work in him unnoticed. Jeremiah knew the feeling: “a burning fire shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9). In Scripture the heart is the whole inner person, thinking, willing, loving; this is not a mood but something catching light.

On the road, in the Scriptures. “While he talked to us on the road”: the person. “While he opened to us the Scriptures”: the book. Neither alone did it. A stranger’s company would not have set a heart burning, and the Scriptures had been read to them every Sabbath without producing this. It was Christ, in the Scriptures, opening them. He still walks beside his people in his Word, and his voice still sets cold hearts alight.

What do I do when the Bible feels dead? The answer here is not to try harder or find a better method. The burning came from a person, so the remedy is a prayer rather than a technique, that the one the book is about would open it: “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). Pray before you read. Read whole passages, look for Christ in them, and keep reading on the dull days; the fire is his to give. And the reverse error is real: they had burning hearts and were still walking the wrong way. Feeling is not the test of where you stand with God.

parallels.desc: a burning fire shut up in my bones

verseByVerse.quote: And they rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem. And they found the eleven and those who were with them gathered together, saying, 'The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!' Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two hurried back to Jerusalem that night, and found the disciples already saying that the Lord had risen and appeared to Simon.

That same hour. The meal is abandoned. It is dark, they have already walked seven miles, and the day that was “far spent” for him is far spent for them. They go anyway, back over the road they had walked in despair, because there are people in Jerusalem who need to hear this tonight.

Risen indeed. Before they can say a word, the news is shouted at them. “Indeed” (ontōs) means really, truly, and the sentence has become the ancient Easter greeting. And “Simon”: not Peter the rock, but the old name, the one Jesus used when he warned him (22:31). Somewhere in that Sunday the risen Christ met privately with the man who had denied him three times.

The meeting no one described. Neither Luke nor anyone else describes it, though Paul confirms it and names Peter first among the witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:5). Whatever passed between them stayed between them. The church heard that the Lord had appeared to Simon. It never heard what was said.

The breaking of the bread. Luke’s summary of the Emmaus story is the shape of the whole afternoon: the road, and the bread. The phrase would become Luke’s term for the church’s fellowship meal and the Lord’s Supper (Acts 2:42, 46; 20:7).

Does God make public everything I have confessed to him? No. Some sins must be confessed to people we have wronged, and some public sins need public repentance, but much of our dealing with Christ is private, as Peter’s was. What God has covered, he has covered (Psalm 32:1). And what he says to you in that private meeting, his forgiveness, his restoration, your new commission, is as real as if it were announced from the housetops.
verseByVerse.note: Simon is Peter.

parallels.desc: he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–53 — Jerusalem, the Commission, and the Ascension
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The risen Lord, in the same wounded body, turns his failed disciples into his witnesses and goes up to reign, still blessing them. He gives them peace and proves he is no ghost: hands and feet to see, a piece of fish eaten in front of them (vv. 36–43). He opens their minds to see that the Scriptures foretold his suffering and rising, and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins must be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (vv. 44–48). They are to wait for the Father’s promise (v. 49). At Bethany he lifts his hands, blesses them and is carried up into heaven, and they return with great joy, blessing God in the temple (vv. 50–53).
verseByVerse.theology:
Verses 39–43 rule out a resurrection that is only the survival of a soul, a vision, or a cause living on; on Paul’s “spiritual body”, see the note on vv. 38–40. And the wounds remain: the Lamb stands in the midst of the throne as though it had been slain (Revelation 5:6).

Verse 45 shows that understanding Scripture is finally God’s gift (see the note on v. 45).

The ascension is not the end of the story but the beginning of his reign at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Hebrews 1:3), as he had told the council (22:69; see the note on vv. 50–51). And the disciples’ worship of him is the first worship of Jesus in this Gospel (see the note on vv. 52–53).
verseByVerse.examples:
Disbelieved for joy is a common form of unbelief among genuine Christians: believers who know the gospel is true and cannot quite accept that they are forgiven. Jesus did not rebuke it (see the note on vv. 41–43).

Verse 48 shows what any Christian is asked for: to say truthfully what he knows of Christ (see the note on v. 48).

Verse 49 is for anyone in a season of enforced waiting (see the note on v. 49).

verseByVerse.quote: As they were talking about these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them, 'Peace to you!' But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus suddenly stood among the disciples and greeted them with peace, and they were terrified, thinking he was a ghost.

Jesus himself stood among them. He arrives mid-sentence, into a room where he is being discussed, and with the doors locked (John 20:19). No entrance is described: one moment he is not there, the next he is.

Peace to you! The ordinary greeting, shalom, and the first word of the risen Christ to the gathered church. The last time most of these men saw him, he was being arrested while they ran. If ever there was a moment for a reckoning, this was it, and he says, “Peace to you!” Peace with God, made “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20), was bought on Friday; on Sunday evening the one who bought it stands in the room and says the word. The angels announced peace on earth at his birth (2:14); the risen Lord delivers it in person.

They thought they saw a spirit. They have just been shouting that the Lord is risen, and when he appears they conclude they are looking at a ghost: not a flattering detail, which is why it is worth trusting. The ancient world had a settled category for the appearance of the dead, and it was ghosts, not resurrection. They were expecting a haunting, and they were terrified.

In everyday life. If you are carrying guilt over a failure you have already confessed, hear the first word of the risen Christ to his failed disciples, “Peace to you!”, and receive it today. Then carry it to one person you are at odds with.

What does it mean to have peace with God? It means the war is over. We were God’s enemies, under his just wrath (Romans 5:10; Ephesians 2:3), and through Christ’s death that hostility is ended for everyone who trusts him: “since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). It is not first a feeling but a settled relationship that does not rise and fall with your mood, and from it flows the peace of God that guards the heart in anxious times (Philippians 4:6–7).

Textual note. Some manuscripts lack this greeting, as the ESV notes, but the earliest copies have it, and John records the same words (John 20:19).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.' And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered their doubts with his wounded hands and feet: the risen Lord is the crucified one, in a real body of flesh and bones.

See my hands and my feet. He asks about their doubt and answers it with evidence, a remarkable thing for the risen Son of God to bother doing. Hands and feet, because that is where the nails went. He is proving not only that a body is present but whose: the risen Lord is the crucified one.

Touch me, and see … flesh and bones. Not a vision, but a body that can be handled; John would write of what “we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands” (1 John 1:1). That closes off a whole family of misunderstandings. The resurrection is not the survival of a soul, a vision granted to grieving friends, or a cause living on. It is a body, transformed but real (1 Corinthians 15:42–44).

Scarred in glory. The resurrection body is glorious, imperishable, and scarred. He did not leave the marks in the tomb; he carries them still: the Lamb standing in the midst of the throne, “as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6). His hands, still marked, hold the world.

In everyday life. If your body is failing, in pain or limited, read 1 Corinthians 15:42–44 and say it of your own body: “raised in power”.

But does Paul not call it a spiritual body? He does (1 Corinthians 15:44), and that can sound like the opposite of flesh and bones. It is not. Paul is describing not what the body is made of but what rules and animates it, as when he calls a person spiritual without meaning that he has no body (1 Corinthians 2:15). A spiritual body is one wholly governed by the Spirit of God: imperishable, glorious, powerful. It is not a ghost. Paul’s whole argument is that ours will be like Christ’s, and Luke goes on to show him eating fish.

Could the disciples simply have seen what they wanted to see? Hallucinations are private experiences of one mind; they are not shared by a roomful of people at once, and they do not eat fish. Nor were these men primed for it: they had called the women’s report nonsense that morning (v. 11). A vision, however vivid, does not empty a tomb in a city full of enemies who wanted the body produced. The appearances came to the unwilling as well as the willing, and changed frightened men into witnesses who would die rather than deny what they had touched.

What kind of body will I have in the resurrection? A real body, continuous with this one, but transformed: sown perishable, raised imperishable; sown in dishonour, raised in glory; sown in weakness, raised in power (1 Corinthians 15:42–43). No more sickness, ageing, disability or death; recognisably you, as Jesus was recognisably himself, yet changed. The Christian hope is not the escape of the soul from the body but the redemption of the body (Romans 8:23), in a renewed earth, and the ground of it is standing in a room in Jerusalem holding out his hands.

Where Christians differ: a spiritual or bodily resurrection? Some modern theologians speak of the resurrection as spiritual only: a vision, or the disciples’ renewed faith, or Jesus living on in their memory and mission. This commentary’s view: Luke goes out of his way to insist on bodily resurrection: flesh and bones, wounds, touch, eating. The empty tomb, and Jesus’ own words, rule out a merely spiritual resurrection. As he rose bodily, so will his people: he “will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body” (Philippians 3:21).

parallels.desc: which we have looked upon and touched

verseByVerse.quote: And while they still disbelieved for joy and were marveling, he said to them, 'Have you anything here to eat?' They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate before them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the disciples still could not believe for sheer joy, Jesus ate a piece of fish in front of them.

Disbelieved for joy. Only a very honest writer would have set that phrase down. The fright has passed. What holds them back now is not scepticism but the fear of accepting something too good to be true, in case it turns out not to be so.

Have you anything here to eat? An ordinary, disarming sentence. The Son of God, three days out of a grave, with the life of the world to come in his body, asks whether there is anything in the house.

A piece of broiled fish. He did not need it. He ate because they needed to watch him do it. A ghost cannot chew, and Peter would later preach that they “ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10:41). Their joy was too big to be trusted, so he made the moment small enough to be believed. How tender he is with weak faith: he will stoop to the smallest kindness to help his people believe the greatest news.

I believe the gospel, but I cannot feel forgiven: what should I do? Many believers can recite the doctrine of justification and cannot quite take it for themselves. Jesus did not rebuke that in his disciples, or demand that they feel more; he gave them something solid to look at. Look away from your feelings to the facts: Christ died for sinners; he rose; he has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37); God declares the one who trusts in Jesus righteous (Romans 3:26). Come to the Lord’s Supper, where he puts bread and wine into your hands. Let a trusted Christian remind you of the promises. Feelings often follow facts slowly. Keep looking at him until joy lets itself believe.

parallels.desc: who ate and drank with him

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, 'These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells the disciples that everything written about him in the whole Old Testament had to be fulfilled, as he had told them before. The risen Lord’s first lesson to the gathered church is a lesson in reading the Bible.

While I was still with you. He is with them at that moment, so he is marking off the years of walking Galilee together as ended, and speaking from the other side of them. And as on the road, he sends them back to the book (9:22, 44; 18:31–33).

Everything written about me. Not a few verses, but everything. A man in a room in Jerusalem says that the whole Bible is about him: the garden and the flood, the altar on Moriah and the blood on the doorposts, the throne of David, the laments and the love songs, the exile and the return. He says it of the book God wrote, and it is true.

The Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms. The Hebrew Bible named by its own sections: the whole Bible they possessed, with nothing left out (on the wording, see below).

Must be fulfilled. The same “must” that has governed this Gospel, from the boy who must be in his Father’s house (2:49) to the Son of Man who must suffer. “Scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35). Not that he happened to satisfy some prophecies: the whole of it is about him, and it had to come out this way.

Is every Old Testament passage about Christ? Genealogies, sacrifices, a tabernacle measured in cubits, kings who mostly failed: the Old Testament is not a different religion stuck on the front of yours, but the same God working towards the same person, and its promises, patterns and law find their goal in him. But each passage has its own meaning in its own setting, and that must be read first. Finding Christ is not hunting for hidden symbols in every detail; it is tracing how each part of the story moves towards him, shows our need of him, or is fulfilled in him. Try it this week with Exodus 12, Isaiah 53 or Psalm 22.

Uncertain wording. “The Psalms” may mean only the book of Psalms, singled out because it speaks of the Messiah so often (Psalms 2; 16; 22; 110), or it may stand, by its largest book, for the whole third division of the Hebrew Bible, the Writings. We cannot be sure. The likely meaning is the second: set beside “the Law of Moses and the Prophets”, the phrase names the whole Old Testament.
verseByVerse.note: The Law, the Prophets and the Psalms (the Writings) are the three divisions of the Hebrew Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus opened the disciples’ minds to understand the Scriptures: understanding God’s Word is, in the end, his gift.

Then he opened their minds. He unlocked (diēnoixen): the verb’s third appearance in this chapter, after their eyes at the table (v. 31) and the Scriptures on the road (v. 32). What was hidden from them before (9:45; 18:34) is now revealed.

To understand the Scriptures. These men had the text from childhood; two of them had just spent an afternoon with the risen Christ expounding it. Understanding Scripture is not finally a matter of intelligence, education or access, but of a closed mind opened by God. “The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him” (1 Corinthians 2:14). Luke shows it again in Acts, when the Lord opened Lydia’s heart to pay attention to what was said (Acts 16:14).

Humbling and freeing. Humbling, because if you understand the gospel, someone opened your mind, and you did not do it. Freeing, because if the opening is his work, then the right response to a Bible that will not open is to ask him.

Can an unbeliever understand the Bible? He can understand its words, history and arguments, sometimes very well; many scholars who do not believe have explained the text accurately. What he cannot do without the Spirit is receive it as true, see the glory of Christ in it, and believe it savingly. So we share the Scriptures with unbelievers and pray for them at the same time. The Word is the means; the Spirit is the one who opens.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to them, 'Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sums up what the Scriptures had written about the Christ: he would suffer, and on the third day rise from the dead.

Thus it is written. He might have argued from what had just happened, and it would have been unanswerable: the wounds, the fish, the empty tomb. He argues instead from Scripture, which tells you what he intends the church to stand on when the eyewitnesses are gone.

That the Christ should suffer. The half nobody had wanted. Christ means the anointed King, and a suffering King was not what Israel was watching for. It was in the book all the same: in Isaiah’s servant (Isaiah 53), in the psalms of the righteous sufferer (Psalm 22), in the one whom they have pierced (Zechariah 12:10) and the shepherd struck (13:7).

And on the third day rise. Where is that written? No verse says it in so many words. The apostles pointed to particular texts: Peter at Pentecost quotes Psalm 16:10, that God would not let his Holy One see corruption, and argues that David’s tomb is still here, so David was speaking of another (Acts 2:25–31); Isaiah’s servant, after being cut off, prolongs his days (Isaiah 53:10–12); Hosea speaks of being raised up on the third day (Hosea 6:2), and Jonah supplied the pattern (Matthew 12:40). But the deeper answer is the shape of the whole. A story that runs from a garden lost to a people redeemed by blood, from exile to return, from a valley of dry bones to an army standing up, does not end in a tomb.

In everyday life. Learn to say the gospel in one sentence from Scripture: Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, he was buried, and he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

parallels.desc: on the third day he will raise us up

verseByVerse.quote: and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Scriptures also foretold the church’s mission: forgiveness of sins, received through repentance, is to be offered in Jesus’ name to every nation, starting with the city that killed him.

Repentance for the forgiveness of sins. The sentence still depends on “thus it is written” (v. 46): the church’s mission stands in the Scriptures on the same footing as the suffering and the rising. This is the message, and much else gets preached in its place: moral improvement, respectability, a technique for a better life. Repentance is a turning of the whole person from sin to God; forgiveness is the gift won by Christ’s death, the thing a guilty person actually needs and cannot obtain for himself (1:77; 3:3).

Should be proclaimed in his name. Isaiah had written it: “I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). And it goes in his name: on his authority, by his power, through faith in him (Acts 2:38), not in the name of the church or on the strength of anyone’s sincerity. “There is salvation in no one else” (Acts 4:12).

To all nations. The scope is the world, the climax of Luke’s great theme. “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (3:6). Simeon held a baby and called him “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (2:32), and Luke traced Jesus’ line back not only to Abraham but to Adam (3:38).

Beginning from Jerusalem. The city that had just done it: where the crowd shouted “Crucify”, where the council condemned him, where the cross went up outside the wall. The first offer of forgiveness goes to the people who killed him, in the city where they did it: the gospel goes first to the guilty, and the guiltiest first. If that seems unfair, it is the only kind of gospel that could include us; a forgiveness that reached only the respectable would never reach anyone, because no one is. About three thousand were forgiven there in a day (Acts 2:41), and Acts follows this exact plan: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and the end of the earth (Acts 1:8).

In everyday life. Choose one practical thing this month: learn about one unreached people and pray for them by name; give regularly to a missionary; welcome an international student; or speak of Christ to the person in your own Jerusalem, the one nearest you, who seems least likely to listen.

What does repentance actually look like? A turning round: away from sin and towards God, grieving over the sin and hoping in his mercy, as the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession describe it (Westminster 15.2; 1689 15.3). It sees sin as an offence to God, not merely a harm to you; it lays hold of mercy in Christ, for grief with no hope of pardon only drives a sinner further away; and it turns, in the Spirit’s strength, to new obedience. In practice that means naming the specific sin to God, putting right what can be put right, removing what feeds it, and starting again the next time you fall, knowing that your standing rests on Christ’s perfect obedience counted as yours, not on the quality of your repentance (Romans 5:19). It is not only the first step of the Christian life but the shape of the whole of it.

Must people hear of Christ to be saved? Yes. Salvation is through conscious faith in Christ, for “there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12), and “how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard?” (Romans 10:14). The Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession hold that elect infants who die in infancy, and others unable to understand the outward call, are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when, where and how he pleases (Westminster 10.3; 1689 10.3), in ways we are not told. Parents who have lost a little one may rest in the kindness of the Lord who said the kingdom belongs to such as these (18:16). But for all who can hear, the gospel must be preached. Missions are not an optional extra for keen Christians; they are the reason the church is still here.

Isn’t mission just another kind of empire? For many people “to all nations” calls up gunboats and colonial governors, and missionaries as the polite face of conquest. Some were complicit, and the church should say so plainly. But the Gambian-born historian Lamin Sanneh, who taught at Yale, argued that Christianity spread above all by translation: unlike faiths that keep their scriptures in one sacred language, it put the Bible into the mother tongues of the peoples it reached, and so often preserved and renewed their languages and cultures rather than erasing them. Today most Christians live in Africa, Asia and Latin America. The message began not in Rome or Europe but in Jerusalem. No culture owns the gospel, because every culture needs it, and every culture is both honoured and judged by it. Its goal is not one empire but a multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language, gathered round the Lamb (Revelation 7:9).

verseByVerse.quote: You are witnesses of these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples are Christ’s witnesses: their task is to tell truthfully what they have seen. And he entrusts it to men who had all just failed him.

You are witnesses. A witness is not an advocate or a theorist. He was present and can say what he saw; he may not embellish or speculate. The word is martyres, from which English gets martyr, because several of the men in that room died for their testimony. The apostles’ testimony is the foundation of the church (Acts 1:22; Ephesians 2:20), and we believe through their word (John 17:20).

Of these things. Christianity is not first a philosophy or a set of values. It is a report: that a particular man, under a named Roman governor, was executed and buried, and three days later was alive, and here are the people who saw it. Paul staked everything on it: “more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive” (1 Corinthians 15:6). That is a man saying: go and ask them.

Look at who is commissioned. The men who fell asleep in the garden, denied him in a courtyard, dismissed the women’s report as nonsense, and minutes ago thought they were seeing a ghost. They will be asked not to be impressive, only truthful. He entrusted the report of his own resurrection to eleven men who had all failed him within the previous seventy-two hours, and he has never taken it back. The testimony has passed from hand to hand ever since, and it has reached you.

I did not see the risen Christ, so am I a witness? Not in the apostles’ sense: they were eyewitnesses, and their testimony, written in the New Testament, is a foundation that cannot be repeated or added to. But every Christian is a witness to what Christ has done for him, and to the truth of the apostles’ report. You do not need answers to every question. You are asked to say what you know of Christ, accurately, and let it be weighed (1 Peter 3:15). The man born blind could not answer the theologians, but he could say: “One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see” (John 9:25).

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus promises to send the Holy Spirit, the promise of the Father, and tells the disciples to wait in Jerusalem until they are clothed with power from on high.

The promise of my Father. The Holy Spirit, poured out at Pentecost (Acts 1:4–5; 2:1–4, 33), and promised long before: “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh” (Joel 2:28); “I will put my Spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:27). And Jesus himself sends the Spirit (John 15:26; 16:7). Only God can send the Spirit of God: another claim to divine authority, made almost in passing.

Stay in the city. They had the greatest news in the world and were forbidden, for the moment, to take it anywhere. Stillness can be disobedience or obedience, and both feel like wasting time. These men were not idle; they devoted themselves to prayer (Acts 1:14). But they went nowhere, on orders, until the power came.

Clothed with power. Clothed is the verb for putting on a garment, and the power (dynamis) is the Spirit’s (Acts 1:8). It comes from outside and is put on; it is not a capacity discovered within. The Father promised, the Son sends, the Spirit clothes: the whole Trinity at work in the weakest witness. Zeal without the Spirit was exactly what Peter had shown in the garden with a sword (22:50).

What the Spirit’s power looks like. Not necessarily something spectacular, or a feeling that sweeps you along. In Acts it looks like frightened men who had hidden behind locked doors speaking of Jesus in public: “they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness” (Acts 4:31). It looks like “love, joy, peace, patience” (Galatians 5:22) growing in ordinary people, and like strength in weakness, not instead of it: “my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). It is Christ’s own: the Spirit who came upon him at his baptism (3:22; 4:1, 14), now poured out by him from the throne (Acts 2:33). You do not need to feel powerful to have it. You will usually notice it afterwards: you spoke when you would have kept silent, forgave when you could not, kept going when you had nothing left.

In everyday life. Before your next act of service, the class, the visit, the conversation about Christ, ask plainly for the Spirit’s power. And if you are in a season of enforced waiting, of illness or delay or a closed door, use it as they did: pray, stay close to God’s people, and be ready.

Should Christians today wait for the Spirit as the disciples did? No. They waited for one unrepeatable event, Pentecost, which marked the new age. Now every believer receives the Spirit when he believes (Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13; Acts 2:38–39). Some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians teach a later baptism in the Spirit, to be sought after conversion, often with speaking in tongues. This commentary holds that the sign gifts, such as tongues and healings, ceased with the apostles, because they served to confirm the apostles’ message while the New Testament was being given (Hebrews 2:3–4). It does not believe Scripture teaches a second baptism for all believers, and holds that view charitably towards brothers and sisters who see it otherwise and often shame us by their zeal. We are not waiting for the Spirit to come; we are asking him to fill us (Ephesians 5:18), and depending on his power in everything.

Stay in the city, or go to Galilee? Sceptics press a difficulty. Here Jesus says, “stay in the city”; but in Matthew and Mark he is going ahead of them to Galilee, and Matthew’s great commission is given on a mountain there. The objection only bites if all this happened on one evening, and it did not: Luke’s own second volume says Jesus appeared over forty days (Acts 1:3). Restore that span and the accounts fall into order: Jerusalem on Easter Day and the week after; then Galilee, where Matthew’s mountain and John’s breakfast on the shore belong; then Jerusalem again. Luke compresses the forty days, and “stay in the city” was given, and repeated, at the end of them (Acts 1:4).
verseByVerse.note: The promise of the Father is the Holy Spirit, poured out at Pentecost.

parallels.desc: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh

verseByVerse.quote: And he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus led the disciples out to Bethany, lifted his hands and blessed them like a priest, and while he was blessing them was carried up into heaven.

As far as Bethany. On the slope of the Mount of Olives, about two miles from Jerusalem: the village of Martha and Mary and Lazarus, where he had wept at a grave and called a dead man out of it (John 11). Acts 1:9–12 gives a fuller account, and shows that this came forty days after Easter (Acts 1:3), time Luke does not mark here.

Lifting up his hands he blessed them. The posture of the priest. Aaron “lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them” (Leviticus 9:22), and the priests were given the words: “The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you” (Numbers 6:24–25). Luke opened his Gospel with Zechariah coming out of the sanctuary unable to speak the blessing (1:22); he closes it with a priest whose hands are raised and whose blessing is not silent. Jesus is the great high priest, and the hands lifted over his people had holes in them.

While he blessed them, he parted from them. He did not finish and then go. He went in the middle of the blessing, as though it never stopped, and he is doing it still: “he always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25), his finished sacrifice speaking for them, so that no accusation against them can stand (Romans 8:34).

Carried up into heaven. Not vanished, as at Emmaus, but taken up: not an exit from the story but an enthronement, all things put under his feet (Ephesians 1:20–22). The man the world crucified now governs the world, as he had told the council (22:69), and this same Jesus will come again in the same way (Acts 1:11). Every earthly priest lowered his hands at last and died; this one was lifted up with his hands still raised. He has gone into heaven as a forerunner on our behalf (Hebrews 6:20), a man in our flesh at the Father’s right hand, and the benediction he began on the Mount of Olives will not end until he comes again.

Why did Jesus have to leave? He said it was for our good: “if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you” (John 16:7). Ascended, he reigns, intercedes and is present by his Spirit with every believer at once.

Where is Jesus’ body now? In heaven. The ascended Christ is truly human still, his glorified body at the Father’s right hand until he returns (Acts 3:21). That is why Reformed Christians do not believe his body is physically in the bread at the Lord’s Supper. He is present to his people by his Spirit, really and spiritually, lifting our hearts to him where he is. And one day the heavens will open and we will see him, in the same body, with the same marked hands.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit “and was carried up into heaven”. Some older editions left out several short phrases in this chapter, because a small group of manuscripts lacks them. Then a very early papyrus copy of Luke, published in the twentieth century, was found to contain them, and opinion moved back; that is why the ESV prints them. Mark the direction of that story: the evidence did not erode the text as it accumulated. It confirmed it.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany lay on the Mount of Olives. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit “and was carried up into heaven.”

parallels.desc: Aaron lifted up his hands and blessed them

verseByVerse.quote: And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple blessing God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples worshipped Jesus and went back to Jerusalem full of joy, blessing God continually in the temple.

They worshiped him. They fell down before him (proskynēsantes); a few manuscripts lack these words, as the ESV notes, but the earliest copies have them. It is the first time in Luke that anyone worships Jesus. These Jewish men had said every day of their lives, “The LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4), and Jesus himself had said, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve” (4:8). Yet they worship, with no one correcting them, a man they had watched eat fish. This is no doctrine developed over centuries by a church drifting from its roots: it is men who worshipped one God only, on their faces outside Jerusalem, and Paul’s letters, most likely written earlier still, already speak of every knee bowing to Jesus (Philippians 2:10–11).

With great joy. The strangest phrase, because he had just left; it should have been a bereavement. But the “good news of great joy” announced at his birth (2:10) is now theirs, because they finally understood where he had gone: not another loss but the coronation of the man they loved, alive, reigning, coming back, and about to send his Spirit. Grief looks at an empty sky. They looked at a throne.

Continually in the temple blessing God. The Gospel began in that temple, with an old priest who came out mute and could not give the blessing (1:9–22; see Zechariah and Elizabeth). It ends there, with ordinary people who cannot stop blessing God. The horn of salvation, the sunrise from on high (1:68–79), the light for revelation to the Gentiles: every promise made at the start has been kept. Luke’s first volume ends in worship and joy, waiting for the Spirit; his second tells what the risen Lord went on to do through his Spirit and his church (Acts 1:1), and the story continues in every congregation that gathers on the first day of the week to bless God.

In practice. Their response to his going is the pattern for ours. They worshipped him: so speak to Jesus in prayer as the Lord on the throne, not only about him. They went back with joy: so when he seems absent, look where they looked, and “seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians 3:1). They were continually together blessing God: so do not let gathering with his people become optional.

How can Christians worship Jesus if only God is to be worshipped? Because Jesus is God. Christians do not worship a man alongside God, but the one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Son is the eternal Word who was with God and was God (John 1:1), who took our flesh without ceasing to be divine. So when the disciples fell down before him, they were not breaking the first commandment but keeping it. The Father wills “that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father” (John 5:23).

Joy that has never been contained. The Gospel that began with an angel announcing good news of great joy for all the people ends with that joy spilling out of a temple, and it has never been contained since. The one they worshipped on the hillside is alive for evermore, seated on the throne of the universe in our flesh, and he will come again. To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honour and glory and might for ever and ever (Revelation 5:13). Amen.

24.text: <sup>1</sup> But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they went to the tomb, taking the spices they had prepared. <sup>2</sup> And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, <sup>3</sup> but when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. <sup>4</sup> While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. <sup>5</sup> And as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them, “Why do you seek the living among the dead? <sup>6</sup> He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, <sup>7</sup> that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men and be crucified and on the third day rise.” <sup>8</sup> And they remembered his words, <sup>9</sup> and returning from the tomb they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest. <sup>10</sup> Now it was Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles, <sup>11</sup> but these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them. <sup>12</sup> But Peter rose and ran to the tomb; stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths by themselves; and he went home marveling at what had happened. <sup>13</sup> That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, <sup>14</sup> and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened. <sup>15</sup> While they were talking and discussing together, Jesus himself drew near and went with them. <sup>16</sup> But their eyes were kept from recognizing him. <sup>17</sup> And he said to them, “What is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk?” And they stood still, looking sad. <sup>18</sup> Then one of them, named Cleopas, answered him, “Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days?” <sup>19</sup> And he said to them, “What things?” And they said to him, “Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, a man who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, <sup>20</sup> and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him. <sup>21</sup> But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened. <sup>22</sup> Moreover, some women of our company amazed us. They were at the tomb early in the morning, <sup>23</sup> and when they did not find his body, they came back saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. <sup>24</sup> Some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.” <sup>25</sup> And he said to them, “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! <sup>26</sup> Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” <sup>27</sup> And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. <sup>28</sup> So they drew near to the village to which they were going. He acted as if he were going farther, <sup>29</sup> but they urged him strongly, saying, “Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent.” So he went in to stay with them. <sup>30</sup> When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. <sup>31</sup> And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight. <sup>32</sup> They said to each other, “Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?” <sup>33</sup> And they rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem. And they found the eleven and those who were with them gathered together, <sup>34</sup> saying, “The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!” <sup>35</sup> Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread. <sup>36</sup> As they were talking about these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them, “Peace to you!” <sup>37</sup> But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit. <sup>38</sup> And he said to them, “Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? <sup>39</sup> See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” <sup>40</sup> And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet. <sup>41</sup> And while they still disbelieved for joy and were marveling, he said to them, “Have you anything here to eat?” <sup>42</sup> They gave him a piece of broiled fish, <sup>43</sup> and he took it and ate before them. <sup>44</sup> Then he said to them, “These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.” <sup>45</sup> Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, <sup>46</sup> and said to them, “Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, <sup>47</sup> and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. <sup>48</sup> You are witnesses of these things. <sup>49</sup> And behold, I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.” <sup>50</sup> And he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. <sup>51</sup> While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven. <sup>52</sup> And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, <sup>53</sup> and were continually in the temple blessing God.

keyVerse.quote: Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.
keyVerse.note: These words gather up the whole chapter. The cross and the empty tomb were not a disaster God repaired but what the Scriptures had said must happen, and the same Scriptures foretold the church’s message of forgiveness for every nation. The gospel we believe and the gospel we carry rest on one word of God, and at the centre of both is the risen Christ.

24.reflection:
The women, the Emmaus pair and the eleven all had Jesus’ own words, and the evidence, yet understood only when they remembered what he had said or he opened the Scriptures to them (vv. 6–8, 25–27, 44–45). Why do we forget what God has said just when we most need it? What helps you remember?

“But we had hoped” (v. 21). Where are you living inside a disappointed hope? How does Jesus’ answer, that the Christ had to suffer and so enter his glory (v. 26), change the way you see it?

Jesus met frightened, doubting disciples with peace, his wounded hands and a piece of fish (vv. 36–43). What does his patience teach you about handling your own doubts, and those of others?

Jesus sent eleven men who had all just failed him to proclaim forgiveness to all nations, beginning with the city that had killed him (vv. 47–48). Who is in your “Jerusalem”, the person least likely to listen, and what would it look like to be a witness to them this month?
